en: The first chapter, on the movement of musical notes (*svaragata*), contains therein the first section, titled "A Compendium of Subjects" (*padārthasaṃgraha*). [It begins:
With a mind following the breath born from the knot of Brahma within the lotus of the heart...
I bow for the sake of joy to that Śaṅkara, whose body is sound (nāda), who delights the wise, who shines by himself as the very source of the Vedas,
and from whom proceed the divisions of musical scales (grāma), the arrangement of notes (varṇa), the ornaments (alaṅkāra), the musical modes (jāti), and their sequence,
while being sung aloud by the entire world.
There exists a noble lineage, a source of well-being, originating from illustrious Kashmir;
born from the sage Vṛṣagaṇa, its fame has washed the very quarters of the horizon.
It is filled with performers of sacrifice, preeminent in their devotion to dharma, who have crossed to the further shore of the ocean of the Vedas.
There lived Bhāskara, a treasury of splendor who resembled the sun; he was adorned by the best of the twice-born Brahmins as if by the Vedas descended to earth.
He undertook the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*) in order to adorn the southern quarter.
He had a son, the illustrious Soḍhala, possessed of great discipline and mature intellect, by whom,
having propitiated King Bhillama— whose power was increased by the office of the *śrīkaraṇa*—
glory that pacifies the sorrow of all the world was attained.

Victory was bestowed upon Jaitra, and great fortune upon Śrī Siṅghaṇa. He alone is the foremost of kings in the circle of the earth, his rows of toe-nails variegated by the rising luster of the sapphire-like crest-jewels of the crowns of rival monarchs as they bow before him.
Victorious is the illustrious Siṅghaṇadeva alone, whose fierce fire of majesty, though pervading the entire universe, consumes only the hearts of his enemies.
Having propitiated that virtuous king, who is fond of merit, the preeminent among the wise—
With a multitude of virtues, he satisfied the brahmins with services beyond measure;
what did he not give? What did he not know? What prosperity did he not possess?
What dharma did he not perform? And by what virtues did he not shine? (7-8)
Therefore, Śārṅgadeva was born from that ocean of milk like the moon;
he who surpasses all others, with his rays flashing through supreme generosity,
having served at the feet of his guru and having gratified all the gods.

This Śārṅgadeva alone has mastered all the sciences, honors every worthy recipient, possesses widespread fame throughout the world, bears a form as noble as that of the God of Love, and is endowed with abundant discernment. 10.
Wandering through various places, Sarasvatī became weary;
yet, ever fond of dwelling together with him, she now finds rest in his abode. He, whose sole delight is in diversion, is a vessel of fortune and cleverness.
Having removed the eternal suffering of Brahmins by the gift of wealth,
and [the suffering] of those seeking knowledge through sciences and those afflicted by disease through elixirs,
he now desires to dispel the threefold afflictions of all people.
For the sake of the eternal Dharma, for fame, and for the attainment of the supreme good,
the one of noble intellect reveals the *Saṅgītaratnākara*.
Sadāśiva, Śivā, Brahmā, Bharata, and the sage Kaśyapa.
Mataṅga, Yāṣṭika, Durgāśakti, Śārdūla, Kohala,
Viśākhila, Dattila, Kambala, Aśvatara,
Vāyu, Viśvāvasu, Rambhā, Arjuna, Nārada, and Tumburu. (15–16)
Āñjaneya, Mātṛgupta, Rāvaṇa, Nandikeśvara, Svāti, Gaṇa, Bindurāja, Kṣetrarāja, and Rāhula;
Rudraṭa, Nānyabhūpāla, and likewise Bhoja, the beloved of the earth. 17.
And Paramārtha, Someśa—the sole sovereign of the world—and the commentators on the Bhāratīya [Śāstra]: Lolḷaṭa, Udbhaṭa, Śaṅkuka, Bhaṭṭa Abhinavagupta, and the supreme Śrīmat Kīrtidhara. (18–19)
Furthermore, having churned the ocean of the opinions of many other ancient masters who were experts in musical performance by means of the churning-stick of unfathomable wisdom,
the illustrious Śārṅgadeva has composed this *Sāroddhāra*.
Song, instrumental music, and likewise dance—these three are called *saṅgīta*. It is of two kinds: *mārga* and *deśī*.
Among these, that which is called *mārga* is said to be that which was sought out by Viriñci and others, and employed by Bharata and his successors.
That which bestows certain prosperity in the presence of Lord Śambhu,
and which, according to the taste of people in various regions, delights their hearts—
such singing, instrumental music, and dancing— is called *deśī*. 23.
Dance is said to follow instrumental music, and instrumental music follows song.
Therefore, because of its preeminence, song is described here first;
the Grandfather (Brahmā) collected this song from the Sāmaveda.

The omniscient Lord, the husband of Pārvatī, is delighted by song; even the infinite Lord of the Gopīs has come under the sway of the sound of the flute. Brahmā is devoted to the chanting of the Sāman, and Sarasvatī is attached to the lute.
What then of others—the yakṣas, gandharvas, gods, dānavas, and humans?
A child who has never known the taste of the objects of the senses, while sitting upon his cradle, attains a height of joy upon drinking the nectar of the *Gītā* while weeping. (27–28)

A forest-dweller, subsisting on grass, a wondrous young deer, and even a beast—when the song of the hunter is sung, they give up their very lives. Who is capable of praising the majesty of that song? (29)
This alone is the singular means for attaining dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.

Therein, in the first chapter concerning the movement of the voice (svaragata), the body, the origin of sound (nāda), the places of articulation (sthāna), and the qualities of sound (śruti) are set forth. 30–31.
From that [arose] the seven pure notes and these twelve modified ones;
the lineages, castes, classes, islands, the sixfold deities, the meters, the applications of the notes, and the musical scales (jātis) born from the intervals (śrutis). 32.
The musical scales (grāmas), the melodic modulations (mūrchanās), and the melodic figures (tānas)—both pure (śuddha) and artificial (kūṭa)—along with their numerical counts;
the systematic array (prastāra), the partial mountain-diagram (khaṇḍameru), and the methods for resolving lost or indicated notes (naṣṭoddiṣṭaprabodhaka);
furthermore, the commonality of notes (svarasādhāraṇa) and the commonality of modes (jātisādhāraṇa). 33–34.
The correct application of the *kākalī* and *antara* [registers] is the characteristic of the phonemes (*varṇa*).
There are sixty-three ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), and from that [arise] thirteen kinds [of characteristics].
Then there are the characteristics of the *jāti*, the *graha*, the *aṃśa*, and so forth, as well as the *kapāla*s and the *kambala*.
And various types of songs—this much is the summary of the subject matter.
(36) Now, in the chapter titled "The Discrimination of Rāgas," we shall explain in due order the grāmarāgas, the uparāgas, the rāgas, the bhāṣās, and the vibhāṣikās. (37)
Then, the intermediate scriptures (*antarabhāṣā*), all the limbs of passion (*rāgāṅga*),
as well as the limbs of discourse (*bhāṣāṅga*), the secondary limbs (*upāṅga*), and the limbs of ritual action (*kriyāṅga*) according to their true nature [will be explained].
Thereafter, in the third chapter, the *Prakīrṇaka*, they will be discussed.
The composer of songs, the musician, the primary musical notes, and likewise the singer;
the female singer, the merits and defects [of singing], and the various distinctions of sound for those two;
the merits and defects of sound, the physical body, and likewise its qualities. (39–40)
The *doṣas*, *gamakas*, *sthāyas*, *ālapti*, and the characteristics of the *vṛnda* follow;
thereafter, in the chapter on compositions (*prabandha*), there are the *dhātus*, *aṅgas*, and *jātis*. The *sūḍa* of compositions is twofold: the pure (*śuddha*) and the shadow-like (*chāyāla*).
The sequences of *ālīs*, the *sūḍas* situated therein which depend upon the *ālīs*, the scattered [elements], and then the *chāyālagas* based on the *sūḍas*,
as well as the merits and defects pertaining to song— all these will be explained by Śārṅgasūri. 42–43.
In the fifth chapter on *tāla*, however, there are the *mārga-tālas* as well as the *kalās*;

the four *pātas* and the four *mārgas*, as well as the eight *mārga-kalās*; the measurement of heavy (*guru*) and light (*laghu*) syllables and so forth; and the distinctions such as being of a single *kalā*.
Likewise, the divisions of the feet, the measures (mātrās), the rules for the time-units (kalās) in the rhythmic cycle (tāla),
the regulation of the fingers, the distinctions such as the pairs (yugma) and so forth, the transitions (parivarta), the tempos (layas), their pauses (yatayas), and the songs (gītakas). 45–46.
The *chandaka* and other songs, as well as the collection of *tāla*-limbs,
the limbs of song, and the regional *tālas* (*deśītāla*) shall be explained in their true nature by Niḥśaṅka Śārṅgadeva, along with the means of verifying those *tālas*.

In the sixth chapter, various kinds of instrumental music will be discussed; in the seventh, dancing and the various *rasas* and *bhāvas* in their proper sequence. Thus ends the first section, titled "A Compendium of Subjects," in the first chapter on musical notes (*svara*).
Now begins the second chapter, on the arising of the *piṇḍa*.
Song consists of sound (*nāda*); instrumental music is praised for its manifestation of sound;
and dance follows both of these. Therefore, this triad is dependent upon sound.
The phoneme is manifested by sound (nāda); from the phoneme comes the word, and from the word, speech.
This worldly discourse proceeds from speech; therefore, the entire universe is dependent upon sound.
Sound is said to be of two kinds: the struck (āhata) and the unstruck (anāhata).
This very [consciousness] shines within the body; therefore, it is called the "body" (piṇḍa).
There exists Brahman—consciousness and bliss, self-luminous, stainless, the Lord, described as the Liṅga, non-dual, unborn, and all-pervasive.

He is changeless, formless, the Lord of all, imperishable, omnipotent, and omniscient; those known as individual souls (jīvas) are His portions, conditioned by beginningless ignorance, like sparks from a fire. 5.
Pervaded by limiting adjuncts such as wood and the like, they are constrained by beginningless karmas consisting of merit and demerit which bestow pleasure and pain;
[they obtain] a body, lifespan, and experience born of karma, each associated with its respective species.
In each birth they undergo, there exists for them another [body];
that subtle *liṅga-śarīra* is considered imperishable until liberation.
The wise know this to consist of the state of the subtle elements, the senses, and the vital breaths.
The Unborn creates this world for the enjoyment of living beings;
he, as the Self and the Supreme Self, then withdraws it for their rest.
Thus, this process of creation and withdrawal is held to be beginningless by way of a continuous flow.
Those living beings are not different from the Self, nor is the world different from the Self;
creating through His power, He is non-different from it, just as gold is non-different from earrings and the like.
Others say that He creates through ignorance (avidyā), just as a rope [creates] a serpent.
First from the Self came space, then wind, then fire;
from fire came water, and from this, earth was born.
These great elements are the body of Virāj Brahmā.
Brahmā created Brahmā (the secondary creator) and, having bestowed the Vedas upon him,
he brought forth the elemental world from the words of the Vedas;
by his command, Brahmā then created the Prajāpatis through his mind alone.
From them, however, the emission of semen is described as the cause of bodies;
it is fourfold due to the distinctions of causes: sweat-born, sprout-born, womb-born, and egg-born.
Bodies such as those of lice arise from sweat, while those such as creepers arise from sprouting. 15–16.
From the womb come humans and the like; from the egg, birds and the like.
Among these, the human body is said to be the most suitable for the practice of *nāda*.
The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), residing in space, has emerged from space into the air.

From the wind comes heat, and from that, mist; from mist, it abides in the cloud. 18. Satiated by the oblation and having its essence consumed by the sun's rays during summer, the sun deposits that water-essence in the cloud; [that is] the rain-cloud (valāhaka). 19.
When it rains with rain, the living soul then enters unperceived into the trees and herbs born upon the earth.
From them food is produced; that food, when consumed by men, becomes semen.
If the semen is discharged into the womb of a woman whose menstrual flow has been purified,
and if it remains pure along with that menstrual flow upon reaching the uterus,
then, impelled by the karma of the living being, it initiates the formation of the embryo.
In the first month, a state of liquidity arises known as *kalala*;
in the second month, however, there is the solid mass (*ghana*), the oval-shaped lump (*peśī*), and the elongated mass (*arbuda*).
These are, respectively, the initial stages of males, females, and neuters.
In the third [week], however, the five sprouts—the hands, feet, and head—are considered to exist;
at that time, the parts of the limbs and minor members would also be subtle and arise simultaneously, with the exception of the beard, teeth, and so forth, which arise after birth. (24–25)
This is considered by the wise to be the primary nature (*prakṛti*), while anything else is regarded as a modification (*vikṛti*).
In the fourth [stage], the manifestation of those dispositions also arises in men, such as heroism and the like, while in women they are timidity and so forth. (26)
It is said that for those who are neuter, the dispositions are mixed. (27) His heart, born of the mother, yearns for sense-objects;
therefore, one should fulfill the mother’s desires for the sake of the embryo’s prosperity. (28)
The wise call that woman who possesses two hearts "one with a craving" (*dauhṛdinī*).
From the non-granting of her cravings, defects such as physical deformity may arise in the fetus.
Furthermore, if the mother fails to obtain the objects of her desire, the son is born afflicted by that very lack.

The fetus will be purposeful and enjoyer of pleasures if the pregnancy longing (dohada) was for seeing a king; it will be graceful if for ornaments, and most righteous if for the hermitage of ascetics.
It will be devoted to the gods if for seeing deities, and cruel if for seeing snakes. (30–31)
If it eats a lizard, the child will be sleepy; if it eats beef, he will be strong;
if it eats buffalo meat, it gives birth to a son with red eyes like a boar's and hairy body.
In the fifth week, the mind becomes awakened and there is nourishment from flesh and blood.
In the sixth month, there occurs the distinct separation of the bones, tendons, nails, hair, and body hair;
in the seventh, strength and complexion increase, as does the fullness of the limbs.
Covering the openings of his ears with his hands, which are separated by his palms, he— (33–34)
Agitated by dwelling within the womb, he remains within the fetal chamber,
remembering the various types of torments experienced in previous lives;
contemplating the means of liberation, he persists with devoted application.
In the eighth week, however, skin and memory arise, as well as vitality (*ojas*), which originates from the heart; it is considered pure, yellowish-red, and the sign of life.
Again, that flickering [vitality] rushes toward the mother and again toward the embryo. (36–37)

Therefore, one born in the eighth month does not live, being deprived of vital energy (ojas); its remaining for a short time is like a body with maimed limbs due to residual impressions (saṃskāra). The proper time for birth occurs in the ninth month and onwards.
Connected to the mother’s rasa-carrying vessel (nāḍī), it is called the "other" (parā); this nāḍī situated at the navel carries the essence of the mother’s food to the fetus.
With palms joined at its forehead, it remains positioned against the mother’s back.
With limbs contracted, he occupies the womb situated on the right side;
if the woman is on the left side, it is considered a female child, and if situated in the middle, a neuter.
Then, by the powerful winds of labor, he is turned head-downward.

The infant, its limbs pained, is drawn out through the opening of the machine (42). Immediately upon birth, its activity is directed toward the mother’s milk; this [instinct] is due to the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of consciousness from a previous birth—such is the eternity of the living being (43).

His bodily constituents (bhāva) are of six kinds: those derived from the mother, those derived from the father, those derived from nutrition (rasa), those derived from the self (ātman), those arising from the mind (sattva), and those arising from suitability (sātmya). [The soft tissues are] blood, fat, marrow, spleen, liver, and rectum.
The heart, the navel, and so forth— such constituent elements are considered to be derived from the mother.
Bearded hair, body hair, head hair, sinews, veins, arteries, nails,
teeth, semen, and other such firm parts are derived from the father.

The nourishment of the body, complexion, growth, sleep, strength, stability, lack of greed, and enthusiasm—these and others are known as born of rasa (nutritive essence). Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, merit and demerit, and mental impression (bhāvanā)— [are born of sattva]. 47-48ab.
Effort, knowledge, and lifespan are considered to be born from the Self (ātman).
The organs of knowledge are said to be hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell; their five respective objects are as follows. 48–49.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are said to be the objects in their respective order;
the organs of action, however, are speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the genitals.
Their functions, in order, are speaking, grasping, walking, excretion, and pleasure.
Their functions are the mind (*manas*) and the intellect (*buddhi*); these two constitute the internal organ (verse 51).
Pleasure and pain are to be known as the objects of the mind's function;
memory, error, conceptualization, and so forth are considered the functions of the intellect (*dhi*), while determination is regarded as the function of the intellect (*buddhi*) (verse 52).
Others have declared that the senses are born of Brahmā and are material (bhautika).

The internal organ, known as *sattva*, is considered to be threefold according to the differentiation of the *guṇas*: *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. From the *sattva* [aspect] arises the *sāttvika* [nature]. 53.1–2.
Faith, purity, devotion to the singular Dharma, and so forth are considered to arise from sāttvika nature; whereas desire, anger, pride, and the like arise from rājasa nature;
and sleep, laziness, negligence, affliction, deceit, and so on arise from tāmasa nature. 54–55.
Clarity of the senses, health, lack of laziness, and so forth, arise from wholesome habits (sātmyaja).
Since the body is composed of the elements (bhūtātmaka), it therefore acquires these qualities [from them]:
the ear receives sound, the faculty of hearing, porosity, distinctness, and the capacity for subtle perception.
From space (ākāśa) come sound and the sense of hearing; from air (vāyu) come touch and the sense of touch.
Lifting up, lowering, contracting, moving forward, and likewise extending—these are the five types of action (karma). Dryness (rūkṣatā) [is the quality of air]. 57–58.
Likewise, one grasps the ten transformations of the vital air— namely prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, samāna, udāna,
as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya—
and thereby attains lightness.
The most principal among them is Prāṇa, situated below the navel-knot (nābhikanda).
It moves through the mouth, the two nostrils, the navel, and the heart-lotus;
it is the cause of the utterance of sounds, exhalation, inhalation, coughing, and so forth.
The *apāna* wind resides in the anus, the penis, the waist, the calves, the abdomen,
the umbilical bulb, the groins, the thighs, and the knees;
its function is proclaimed to be the expulsion of urine, feces, and so forth.
Vyāna resides in the eyes, ears, ankles, waist, and nose;
its functions consist of supporting, releasing, and seizing the prāṇa and apāna.
Samāna, together with the internal fire, pervades the entire body.
Moving through the seventy-two thousand channel-apertures,
properly conveying the essences of what has been eaten and drunk, it nourishes the body.
The udāna wind resides in the feet, the hands, and the joints of the limbs.
His karma is proclaimed as the lifting up of the body, its departure [at death], and so forth.

The five [winds] beginning with Nāga are situated, resting upon the five constituents (dhātus) such as the skin; they correspond respectively to belching and the like, closing the eyes and the like, and hunger and the like. 66–67.
Lassitude and so forth, as well as swelling and the like, are proclaimed to be their functions.
Of fire, however, the eye is the organ; its form is bile (pitta), which brings about digestion, luminosity, impatience, sharpness, heat, vitality, brilliance, and courage.
Likewise, it takes from water intelligence, as well as the sense of taste and flavor;
[it takes] coldness, oiliness, fluidity, perspiration, urine and so forth, and even softness.
From earth, it takes the olfactory organ, odor, stability, fortitude, and weight.
The beard, hair, nails, teeth, bones, and other such hard parts;
likewise, the nature of the elements such as wind and the nature of space and so forth—these constitute the sevenfold *sāttvika* form, which is the body of Brahmā, Indra, and Yama. (71)
Furthermore, there is that which belongs to Varuṇa, Kaubera, the Ṛṣis, and the Gāndharvas;
that which is Rājasa is sixfold, as are those of the Piśācas and Rākṣasas;
and likewise those of the Asuras, Śakunas, Sarpas, and others with the bodies of Pretas.
The tamasic [birth] is of three kinds, consisting of the forms of animals, fish, and trees;
fearing excessive length of the book, we do not describe their characteristics.
They say that the body has six limbs: the head, the two feet, and likewise the two hands.
And now the middle [portion] will be described, as well as all the individual limbs:

there are seven layers of skin and seven *kalās*, covered by sinews, phlegm, and the fetal membrane; these are cooked by the internal fires within the sheaths, situated one after another among the constituent elements (*dhātus*).
The elements are considered to be the boundaries [of the body], like the heartwood of a tree.
The first layer is the sustainer of flesh; within that flesh are the veins (*sirā*) and arteries (*dhamanī*).
The sinews and channels grow therein like the stalks of a lotus in the mud. (77)
Blood, fat, phlegm, feces, bile, and semen are other [impurities].
Skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen are the seven constituent elements (*dhātus*). Among these, it is said that skin and blood are transformed by the digestive fire (*jāṭharavahni*).
From the digested essence of food, blood and the other elements arise;
likewise, the bodily constituents (dhātus) are produced in succession by their respective internal fires once they have been digested.
Thus, from the digested blood, phlegm, undigested matter, bile, and wind [the subsequent tissues are formed].
There are seven receptacles for urine, known as āśayas in their respective order;
the eighth is the uterus (garbhāśaya) in women, located between the gallbladder and the large intestine. The heart is shaped like a lotus and is formed from clear phlegm and blood. 81–82.
The hollow space situated below the face and between the liver and the spleen is the seat of consciousness; when this is enveloped by darkness,
the self closes its eyes and sleeps, yet it also wakes up and expands when that [space] opens.

Sleep is twofold, by way of dreaming and deep sleep. When the external senses dissolve into the heart while the mind remains awake, that is called dreaming. When the mind dissolves into the vital breath (prāṇa), that is the deep sleep of the self.
Because one drinks [experiences] one's own supreme Self, one is considered to "sleep" as the Self; thus it is understood.
The ears, eyes, nostrils, mouth, anus, and genitals—these nine channels in embodied beings carry external impurities outward. (86)
In women, there are three additional [parts]: two in the breasts and one in the womb.
There are sixteen networks (jāla) consisting of bones, ligaments, vessels, and flesh;
and six tufts (kūrca), located in the two hands, the two feet, the neck, and the genitals. 87–88.
On both sides of the spinal column, there are four muscular cords;
there are five sutures (sīvanīs) in the head, and two are considered to be in the tongue and the penis. The number of bone-cavities (asthirāśayas) is held to be either fourteen or eighteen.
The number of bones in the body is three hundred and sixty.
The wise say that these bones are of five types: valves (valaya), cranial plates (kapāla), rings (rucaka), young bones (taruṇa), and shafts (nalaka). 90–91.
Dhanvantari has stated that there are exactly three hundred bones here;
furthermore, there should be two hundred and ten bone-joints (sandhis) here.
There are korakas, pratara, tunnā, sīvanyas, and ulūkhala [joints].
The joints of the bones are declared by the lords of sages to be of eight kinds: *sāmudga*, *maṇḍala*, *śaṅkhāvarta*, and *vāyasatuṇḍaka* (93).
It is held that there are two thousand joints consisting of muscles, ligaments, and vessels (94).

There are nine hundred sinews; sinews are considered to be of four types: those that are spreading, those that are tubular, those that are tendons (kaṇḍarā), and those that are broad. Bound by many ligaments, it becomes capable of bearing a great weight.
Just as a boat upon the water is bound together by a hundred tendons, so too is this body;
the wise say there are five hundred muscles located within the body,
twenty more in women, ten of which are in the breasts.
These ten increase during youth;
among them, two are internal, two are external, and three lead to the path of the womb.
In this third [category], the womb has the shape of a conch-shell navel and possesses three spirals.
In the *āvarta*, there is the bed of the embryo (*garbhaśayyā*) between the receptacle of bile (*pittapakvāśaya*); therein is a fleshy mass (*peśikā*) resembling a fish named *rohitā*.
Three *pracchādikā* [membranes] are considered to enter into the semen and the menstrual blood. 99–100.
There are twenty-nine and a half lakhs of vessels (sirā-dhamanikās),
as well as nine hundred and fifty-six.
Furthermore, there are ten root-vessels (mūla-sirās) located in the heart that carry the vital essence (ojas).
When the sutures have extended like the leaf of a tree, having reached two finger-breadths, a half-finger, a barley-corn, and likewise a half-barley-corn,
they are then severed; their number is seven hundred.
Among those, two located in the tongue are the causes for the cognition of the essence of speech;
two in the nose carry fragrance; and two in the eyes perform the functions of opening and closing.
Two in the ears convey sound; among these, two were declared by the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Twenty-four vessels (dhamanīs) that carry rasa have been described;
by them, like fields by irrigation channels, the body is nourished and grows.
These are established in the navel like the spokes in the hub of a wheel.
Ten extend upwards, ten downwards, and four extend transversely;
those going upwards reach the heart and then branch out separately in three ways.
Each pair releases wind, bile, phlegm, blood, and lymph.
Therein, two perceive sound, form, taste, and smell;
and two perform speaking, crying out, sleeping, waking, and weeping.
Two males produce semen, while in the female, two secrete breast milk.
Those moving downwards are also threefold, residing separately in the stomach and the large intestine.
Among them, the first ten set [the humors] in motion as previously described for wind and the others.
Food that has been eaten is carried by two vessels which flow from the seat of water.
There are two channels each for urine, feces, and semen; these same two discharge the menstrual flow of women.
There are two channels connected to the large intestine that discharge feces, and eight that convey sweat; these are considered to be transverse and manifold. 111–112.
In the pores of their skin there are openings for the release of sweat, and they draw in the essences produced by massages, ointments, and other applications.
They know that there are one hundred and seven vital points (marmas) which are the seats of the life-force (jīva). 113.

The body hairs number three and a half crores; the beard and head hair are three hundred thousand. Including the channels, veins, beard, and head hair, the total number of body hairs is said to be fifty-four crores and sixty-seven and a half lakhs.
Now the measurement of the combination of the bodily constituents (dhātus), such as water and the rest, in lakṣas is being stated:
water is known to be ten añjalis; chyle (rasa) is nine añjalis;
blood is eight; feces (purīṣa) is seven; and phlegm (śleṣman) is six.
Five or four añjalis of bile, three of urine;
two of fat (vasā) and muscle-fat (medas), while one añjali is considered the measure for marrow (majjan).
Half an añjali is the measure for the marrow of the head, as well as for the essence of phlegm (śleṣmasāra) and strength (bala).
Thus is the summary of the individual limbs; however, the detailed account according to reality should be examined by the wise in the *Adhyātmaviveka* composed by me.
(119) Between the anus and the genitals is the four-petalled wheel called the *ādhāra*.
Likewise, there is the supreme innate bliss preceded by the Hero;
and therein, in the powers beginning with Aiśānī, lies the fruit known as the bliss of yoga.
Kuṇḍalinī, the power of Brahman, resides in the lotus of the foundation.
This [channel], which bestows nectar, has been led straight up to the aperture of Brahmā (ābrahmarandhra).
Its own seat is at the base of the *liṅga*, and it possesses a six-petaled wheel (*cakra*).
They say that these fruits are obtained in sequence from the eastern petal onwards.
Humility, cruelty, the destruction of pride, and thereafter fainting;
then comes contempt and lack of trust—this is the domain of the power of desire (kāma-śakti).
At the navel is the ten-petaled wheel known as Maṇipūraka. 123–124.
In this context, deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is thirst; likewise, envy, malice, shame, fear, disgust, delusion, passion (*kaṣāya*), and despondency [are the afflictions].
These occur respectively on the petals starting from the east; and that is the abode of the Sun.
In the heart is the Anāhata-cakra of Śiva, whose form is that of the Praṇava;
they desire it to be the place of worship, endowed with twelve petals. Therein, the destruction of greed becomes manifest, as do discursive thought and remorse.
Hope, illumination, anxiety, exertion, equanimity, then pride, deficiency, discernment, and likewise egoism—
these they declare to be the fruits, in order, of the Self situated on the petals starting from the east.
In the throat is the location of Bhāratī, the Viśuddha [cakra], which has sixteen petals (129).
Therein are the Praṇava, Udgītha, Huṃphaṭ, Vaṣaṭ, Svadhā, Svāhā, Namaḥ, and Amṛta; as well as the seven notes beginning with Ṣaḍja, which are the poison (130).
Thus, there are sixteen fruits within the self located on the petals starting from the east.
The wheel called Lalanā at the uvula has twelve petals:
intoxication, pride, then affection, sorrow, perspiration, and greed.
Discontent, agitation, the wave, faith, contentment, and obstruction—these are the fruits in the petals starting from the east in the wheel of the woman (the *lalanācakra*).
However, in the three-petaled wheel known as the *ājñā* at the center of the eyebrows, the fruits are as follows: 132–133.
The manifestations of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are considered to occur in succession.
Beyond that is the six-petaled wheel of the mind (*manaścakra*), whose fruits are dreaming, the enjoyment of tastes, smelling, and the perception of forms.
Touch and the cognition of sound are located in the petals starting from the east;
beyond that is what is called the sixteen-petaled moon-wheel (somacakra).
Within its sixteen petals, the sixteen digits (kalās) are situated.
Compassion, forgiveness, straightforwardness, fortitude, detachment, steadfastness, and joy;
then laughter, horripilation, tears of meditation, and stability;
followed by profundity, exertion, clarity, magnanimity, and one-pointedness, in succession. (137)
Fruits arise for the living being as it moves toward the petals in the east and other directions.
The thousand-petaled wheel at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) holds nectar;
by means of the streams of its essence, it causes the body to flourish.
When the *jīva* (vital breath) is situated in the eastern petal of the *anāhata* [cakra], as well as in the eighth, eleventh,
and twelfth petals, one attains mastery over song and other such arts.
Through the fourth, sixth, and tenth petals, song and the like are destroyed.
The eight petals beginning with the eighth are indeed based on purity;
they grant perfection in song and so forth, while the sixteenth is their destroyer.
On the tenth and eleventh petals, however, [they reside] in the lalanā and grant accomplishment.
They know the first, the fourth, and the fifth petal to be the cause of destruction.
When the individual soul (jīva) situated in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) is flooded with nectar, it becomes satisfied and accomplishes songs and other such tasks with excellence. 143.
The individual soul (jīva) situated in the remaining petals of these [lotuses], in the other wheels (cakras), and elsewhere, shall never attain perfection in singing and the like.
[It resides] two finger-breadths above the ādhāra and two finger-breadths below the mehana.
The middle of the body is one finger-breadth in width, with the luster of molten gold;
there resides a slender flame of fire. Nine finger-breadths from that wheel, there is the *kanda* (root-tubular organ) of the body, measuring four finger-breadths in both height and length.
The name of this [knot] was proclaimed by the ancients as the "Brahma-knot.
In its center, the navel-cakra stands with twelve spokes;
there this individual soul (jīva) wanders, like a spider situated within a web of threads. 147–148.
Mounted upon the vital breath (prāṇa), the individual soul (jīva) ascends and descends through the *suṣumṇā* to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), just as a puppeteer moves along a rope.
Surrounding the *suṣumṇā*, the channels (nāḍīs) extend from the root-center (*kanda*) up to the aperture of Brahmā.
Having become established as the *kanda*, they extend their body through the branches of the *kanda*.
These are exceedingly numerous, yet among them fourteen are declared to be the principal ones:
Suṣumṇā, Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Kuhū, and Sarasvatī. (150–151)
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, the illustrious Vāruṇī,
Viśvodarā, Śaṅkhinī, then Pūṣā, Payasvinī, and Alambuṣā— among these, the first three are considered the most principal. 152.
Among the three, Suṣumṇā is the most excellent; it belongs to Viṣṇu and leads to the path of liberation.
Situated in the middle of the *kanda*, Iḍā is on its left and Piṅgalā on its right;
the Moon and the Sun move through Iḍā and Piṅgalā respectively. 153–154.
Due to the gradual passage of time, Suṣumṇā is the drier of time;
Sarasvatī and Kuhū reside on the two sides of Suṣumṇā. Gāndhārī and Hastijihvikā are situated behind and in front of Iḍā, respectively.
In sequence, Pūṣā and Yaśasvinī are located at the eastern ends of Piṅgalā and Pṛṣṭha;
Viśvodarā should be in the middle region between Kuhū and Hastijihvā;
and Vāruṇī is considered to be situated in the middle between Kuhū and Yaśasvinī.
The milk-yielding Sarasvatī lies between Pūṣā and Sarasvatī;
Śaṅkhinī dwells between Gāndhārī and Sarasvatī (158); Alambusā is in the middle of the bulb (kanda), and there, Iḍā and Piṅgalā are situated respectively.
Kuhū resides at the end of the left nostril, Rāmā in front of the genitals,
Sarasvatī above the tongue, and Gāndhārī is situated behind it.
Āvā resides from the left eye down to the big toe of the left foot.
Hastijihvā extends everywhere; Vāruṇī is glorious;
Viśvodarā resides in the entire body starting from the right big toe;
Śaṅkhinī reaches to the left ear; and Pūṣā starts from the southern eye. 161.

The *payasvinī* extends widely as far as the right ear; the *alambuṣā* is situated supporting the root of the anus. In such a body as this, which is filled with a collection of impurities, [the *suṣumnā* remains].
The wise accomplish both worldly enjoyment and liberation through skillful means.
In this regard, enjoyment arises from meditation with attributes (*saguṇa-dhyāna*), while liberation arises from that without attributes (*nirguṇa*).
Meditation, which can only be achieved by a one-pointed mind, is not easy for human beings to perform.
Therefore, in this matter, the sages worship the glorious *nāda* and *anāhata*, which are easy means to bliss, according to the path taught by the Guru.
Yet even that does not delight the minds of men, because it is devoid of aesthetic relish (*rasa*).
Therefore, we shall describe the origin of this struck sound as it unfolds through the medium of the *śrutis* and so forth—
[a sound] which, when sung, brings delight to the world and shatters worldly existence (bhava),
and likewise its status as the cause of the *śrutis* and other musical elements. 167.
Thus ends the second section, on the Origin of the Piṇḍas, in the first chapter on Vowels.
Now begins the third section, on the Places of Articulation, Śrutis, Svaras, Jātis, Kulas, Deities, Ṛṣis, Metres, and Rasas:
"The consciousness of all beings has manifested as the soul of the universe."
We worship that Nāda-Brahman, which is blissful and non-dual. (1) By the worship of Nāda, the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are truly worshipped, because they are essentially composed of it. (2)
This self (ātman), desiring to speak, impels the mind;
the mind strikes the fire residing in the body, and that fire impels the vital air (māruta).
Then, situated at the *brahmagranthi*, it proceeds gradually along the upward path.

It manifests sound in the navel, heart, throat, head, and mouth. Abiding in these five locations in sequence, the *nāda* assumes five designations: the extremely subtle (*atisūkṣma*), the subtle (*sūkṣma*), the developed (*puṣṭa*), the undeveloped (*apuṣṭa*), and the artificial (*kṛtrima*).
They know the letter *na* to be the name of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the letter *da* to be fire (*anala*).
Because it is born from the union of the vital breath and fire, it is therefore designated as *nāda*.
In common usage, however, this is threefold; in the heart, it is called *mandra*.

The *kaṇṭha* [note] is in the throat, the *madhya* in the head, and the *tāra* is double that, each succeeding one being twice the previous; its twenty-two divisions are considered the *śrutis* based on their audition. Twenty-two *lāḍyas* are considered to be connected to the upper channel in the heart.
In those [channels] called *tiraścī*, there are likewise as many *śrutis* as there were in the *māruta-hati*;
they arise one after another, each being higher and higher in pitch.
In this same manner, twenty-two *śrutis* are considered to exist in the throat and likewise in the head.
To demonstrate them clearly, we provide an illustration using a pair of lutes (vīṇā-dvandva).
Two lutes should be made identical so that their sound may be equal. Each of these two lutes has twenty-two strings, and among them, each possesses a first string. (10–11)
The sounds should be produced most softly; the second sound should be slightly higher.
There is no interval between two *śruti*s because no other intervening sound is heard.
Those [sounds] which are progressively lower and more intense are considered the *nāda* arising therefrom, which is known as *śruti*. 12.12–13ab.

The notes should be established on two lutes; among them, the *ṣaḍja* with four *śrutis* is to be placed on the fourth string, then the *ṛṣabha* with three *śrutis* on the third [string], and then the *gāndhāra* with two *śrutis* on the fifth [string]. 13–14.
From the eighth [note] to the second, the middle [note] (madhyama) has four śrutis;
from the tenth to the fourth, the fifth (pañcama) has four śrutis.
From the fourteenth to the fourth, the dhaivata then has three śrutis.
On the third [day], there are eighteen [strings]; then, on the twenty-first, there is a Niṣāda of two intervals (dviśruti).
On the second [day], one lute here should be fixed;
the second, however, is a movable lute, and upon it one should tune the strings.

The seven notes are to be brought forth by the wise on its penultimate string from the notes of the *dhruvavīṇā*; thus, on this movable [string], those notes are then reduced by one *śruti*. In the same way, other *sāraṇās* [tuning sequences] may also be performed.
Due to the merging of two *śrutis* within this [third string],

the notes *ga* and *ni* (19) enter the range of the movable *vīṇā*; and on the third *sāraṇā*, the notes *ri* and *dha* (20), having entered the range of the fixed *vīṇā*, enter [the range of the movable one] in succession.
In the *Nigamas*, those of equal measure enter sequentially on the fourth [note] through the fourfold progression of the *sāraṇās* across twenty-two *śrutis*. Thus,
when they have dissolved into the fixed *śrutis*, their exact extent becomes clearly known.
Beyond this, however, no further lowering should be performed, as it destroys the aesthetic sentiment (*rasa*).
From the Vedic scriptures, there are seven notes: *ṣaḍja*, *ṛṣabha*, *gāndhāra*, *madhyama*, *pañcama*, *dhaivata*, and *niṣāda*. 22–23.
Their other designations are considered to be sa, ri, ga, ma, pa, dha, and ni. That which arises immediately after a *śruti*, being smooth and consisting of a resonance (*anuraṇana*),
and which by itself delights the mind of the listener— that is called a *svara*.

[Objection: But surely the *śruti* of the fourth [note] and so forth is thus the cause of the [subsequent] *svara*s; how then can the preceding *śruti*s be the cause for those [third and subsequent notes]? [Reply:
We say that the *śruti* of the fourth, third, and so forth, is [the cause] through the requirement of its predecessor.
Therefore, even the preceding *śrutis* are determined here to be causes [of the *mūrchanās*].

There are five types of *śrutis*: the radiant (*dīptā*), the extended (*āyatā*), the compassionate (*karuṇā*), the soft (*mṛdu*), and the middling (*madhyā*). Their arrangement among the notes (*svaras*) is as follows.

In the case of *ṣaḍja*, [the *bhakti*] is intense (*dīpta*), long (*āyata*), gentle (*mṛdu*), and moderate (*madhya*). Furthermore, in the case of *ṛṣabha*, it is established as compassionate (*karuṇā*), moderate, and gentle. Moreover, in the case of *gāndhāra*, those two—intense and long—are established as gentle and moderate in the case of *madhyama*.
In the fifth [jāti], there is the compassion (karuṇā) known as soft, medium, and extensive;
furthermore, in the seventh, Dhaivata, there is the compassion that is extensive, medium, and intense. We shall now describe the distinctions among these jātis.
Tīvra, Raudrī, Vrajikā, and Agni—thus the fourfold Dīptā is described. Furthermore, Kumudvatī, Āyatā, Krodhā, Prasāriṇī, Sandīpanī, and Rohiṇī are proclaimed as its five varieties. (31–32)

Dayāvatī, Tathālāpinī, and then Madantikā—these three are varieties of *karuṇā* (compassion). Together with *mṛdu* (gentle), there are four varieties of that. Furthermore, *mandā*, *ratikā*, *prīti*, and *kṣiti* constitute the sixfold *madhyā* (middling) type.
Chandovatī, Rañjanī, Mārjanī, Raktikā, Ramyā, and Kṣobhiṇī—now we shall describe the placement of the notes (*svara*) among these.
Chandovatī, Tīvra, Kumudvatī, and Mandā have the *ṣaḍja* note as their basis. (34–35)
Dayāvatī, Rañjanī, and Raktikā reside in Ṛṣabha;
Raudrī, Krodhā, Vajrikā, Prasāriṇī, Prīti, and Mārjanī—these are the *śrutis* that depend on Madhyama. (36)
Kṣiti and Raktā reside in Ṣaḍja; Sandīpanī and Ālāpinī in Pañcama (37); Madantī, Rohiṇī, and Ramyā—these three—in Dhaivata;
and Ugrā and Kṣobhiṇī—these two—in Niṣāda. (38)
These are considered to be of three kinds according to the distinction of their positions known as low (*mandra*), middle (*madhya*), and high (*tāra*).
These very same [notes], in their modified states, are established as twelve.
The *ṣaḍja* [note] is twofold—*cyuta* (fallen) and *acyuta* (unfallen)—and becomes modified by two *śruti*s.
In the case of the common *kākalī* [octave], the *niṣāda* is also observed [to be modified].
When the *ṛṣabha* resorts to the *ṣāḍjī* *śruti* in the common [octave], it then attains four *śrutis*, and thus one [of the notes] becomes modified. 40–41.
In the *sādhāraṇa* state it possesses three *śrutis*, and in the *antara* state it possesses four *śrutis*;
these two varieties of Gāndhāra were proclaimed by Niḥśaṅka.
Madhyama, like Ṣaḍja, is twofold due to its reliance on the *antara* and *sādhāraṇa* states.

In the Madhyama-grāma, the fifth [note] is tri-śruti; furthermore, in the Kaiśika [grāma], having attained one śruti of Madhyama, it is four-śruti—thus it is twofold. In the Madhyama-grāma, Dhaivata becomes four-śruti when modified.
In the Kaiśika and Kākālī [melodic styles], the Niṣāda possesses three or four śrutis;
thus, there are two varieties in the modified state, making twelve [Niṣādas] in total.
Together with those seven pure [Niṣādas], they become nineteen.
The peacock, the cātaka bird, the goat, the curlew, the cuckoo, the frog, and the elephant—these seven utter the notes beginning with ṣaḍja in sequence.
There are four types of notes: the leading (vādī), the concordant (saṃvādī), and the discordant (vivādī).
The *anuvādī* (respondent) and the *vādī* (proponent) are those for whom the *svara* (scale) is frequently employed in practice;
they possess twelve or eight *śrutis* within their respective ranges. These two are mutually concordant (*saṃvādinau*), while the other two are discordant (*vivādinau*). 48.
Or rather, those two [the *śeṣa* and *anuvādin*] may be the *ṛidha*, or the *ṛidha* may also belong to those two [the *vādī* and *saṃvādī*].
(49) In this context, the king is proclaimed as the *vādī* because he is the one who speaks;
however, the minister is designated as the *saṃvādī* because he follows him. (50)
Because he is contrary [to the truth], the disputant is said by the wise to be like an enemy.
The notes Ṣaḍja, Gāndhāra, and Madhyama are born from the lineage of the Gīvaṇis;
Pañcama arises from the paternal lineage; and R̥ṣabha and Dhaivata are born from the lineage of the R̥ṣis. 52

Niṣāda is born from the lineage of Asuras; Brāhmaṇas are associated with Ṣaḍja and Pañcama; Kṣatriyas are known to be associated with Ṛṣabha and Dhaivata; Vaiśyas are considered to be associated with Gāndhāra and Niṣāda; and Śūdras are associated with Antara and Kākali. These are the castes corresponding to the notes in order.
Padmābha, Piñjara, Svarṇavarṇa, Kundaprabha, Asita, Pīta, and Karvura—now I shall describe their birthplaces:
[they reside] on the islands named Jambū, Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śālmali, and Śveta. (54–55)
In these continents, including Puṣkara, these [notes] beginning with Ṣaḍja were born in sequence:
Agni, Brahmā, the Moon, Viṣṇu, and Nārada.
These five sages beheld the notes beginning with Ṣaḍja, while Tumburu was the wealthy one.
Agni, Brahmā, Sarasvatī, Śarva, Śrīśa, and Gaṇeśvara—these are declared to be the deities of the six notes beginning with Ṣaḍja, respectively.
Furthermore, their meters are, in order: Anuṣṭubh, Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, and Bṛhatī.

They say that *paṅkti*, *uṣṇik*, and *jagatī* are the meters for the [sentiments of] *sādhya* and so forth; *sa* and *ri* are for the heroic (*vīra*), the marvelous (*adbhuta*), and the furious (*raudra*); *dha* is for the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) and the fearful (*bhayānaka*);
*kā* and *ya* are for the pathetic (*karuṇa*); and *ma* and *pa* are for the comic (*hāsya*) and the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*). (59)
Thus ends the third section, on the Locus of Sound, the Sthānas, the Śrutis, and the Svaras, in the first chapter on Svaras.
Now begins the fourth section, on the Gramas, Mūrchanās, Kramas, and Tānas.
A Grāma is a collection of notes (svaras), serving as the common substratum for the mūrchanās and other musical elements.
Those two exist there upon the surface of the earth: the first is the Ṣaḍja-grāma, and the second is the Madhyama-grāma; their characteristics are now stated.
The Ṣaḍja-grāma occurs when the fifth [note] is situated in its own fourth śruti.
When this [gāndhāra] is situated at its own penultimate śruti, the Madhyama-grāma is desired;
or else, if gāndhāra resorts to one śruti each of ri and ma— [that is], if it occupies three śrutis in ṣaḍja and four śrutis in madhyama.
But Niṣāda, having resorted to the *sa* note and the *dha* note as its *śruti*, [produced] the *dha* note;
then the sage Nārada described that as the Gāndhāra scale.
This scale prevails in the heavenly world, not on the surface of the earth.
Ṣaḍja is the primary [note] because it is the first, and likewise because of the preeminence of its ministers;
in the scale (grāma), madhyama is the leader because it is not lost.
Because he was born from this lineage, Gandhāra is also a leader in heaven.
In the three villages, in due order, the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are to be sung of during the winter, summer, and rainy seasons respectively,
in the forenoon, at midday, and in the afternoon by those seeking prosperity.
The successive ascent and descent of the seven notes is called a *mūrcchanā*;
there are seven such *mūrcchanās* in each of the two scales (*grāma*).
Among these, in the scale beginning with *ṣaḍja*, the first is *uttaramandrā*, followed by *rajanī* and *uttarāyatā*.
Śuddha-ṣaḍjā, Matsarīkṛt, Aśvakrāntā, and Udgatā [occur] in Ṣaḍja;
in Madhyama there would be Sauvīrī, and after that Hāriṇāśvā; then there would be Kalopanatā, Śuddhamadhyā, Mārgī, and Pauravī. 10–11.
Now, the definition of those [mūrcchanās] is set forth: the first mūrcchanā begins with the ṣaḍja situated in the middle register (madhyasthāna). 12. *Hṛṣyakā*.
The other six *mūrchanās* follow in sequence starting from the lower *niṣāda* and so on;
beginning from the middle *madhyama*, there is the *sauvīrī* *mūrchanā*.
Likewise, the other six [begin] in sequence starting from the notes situated progressively lower than that.
Those who know the tradition hold that *aja*, *janya*, and others are produced by *ni* and the other notes situated in the *ṣaḍja* position;
while *hāriṇāśva* and others are produced by *ga* and the other notes situated in the *madhyama* position.
One should then successively shift the *ṣaḍja* and other notes, as well as the *madhyama* and other notes, upward from there.

These [four] are pure individually, as well as combined with *kākalī*, with intervals (*sāntara*), and endowed with both; thus they are said to be fifty-six. If Niṣāda should resort to two *śrutis* of Ṣaḍja, then...
That [scale] of the middle [grāma] is *kākalī*, while *gāndhāra* is the *antara* note. 17.
Niḥśaṅka has declared that whichever ordinal position the *ṣaḍja* and *madhyama* notes hold respectively in the two *grāmas*, that scale (*mūrcchanā*) occupies that very same ordinal position. 18.
Starting from the first vowel and so forth, each one becomes sevenfold;
among those, having pronounced the final vowels, one should pronounce the preceding ones in sequence.
Those sequences, when added together, constitute a total of three hundred and ninety-two.
Yakṣa, Rakṣas, Nārada, Abjabhavana, Aśvin, and Pāśin—these are the deities of the *mūrchanās* in the Ṣaḍja-grāma in their respective order.
Brahmā, Indra, Vāyu, Gandharva, Siddha, Druhiṇa, and Bhānu [are the deities] in the Mārgī-mūrchanā. 20–21.
These are, in order, the deities of the *mūrchanās* of the middle scale (*madhyamagrāma*).
Sage Nārada has declared other names for them as well: the first is called *Mūrchanottaravarṇā*, and in the *ṣaḍjagrāma*, it is known as *Abhirudgatā*.
Aśvakrāntā, Sauvīrī, Hṛṣyakā, Uttarāyatā, and Rajanī—these are known as the seven *mūrcchanās* of the sages. Āpyāyanī, Viśvakṛtā, Candrā, Hemā, and Kapardinī [are the others]. 23–24.
Maitrī, Cāndramasī, and Pitryā— these are the three *mūrcchanās* in the middle [scale].
Nandā, Viśālā, Sumukhī, Citrā, Citravatī, Sukhā,
and Ālāpā— these are the seven *mūrcchanās* in the Gāndhāra-grāma.

And these, being specifically impelled by him, are to be employed in heaven. There are seven pure *tāna* scales, which may be rendered as *ṣāḍava* (six-note) or *auḍuvita* (five-note), beginning with *ṣaḍja*; they are formed by successively omitting the *sa*, *ri*, and *sa* notes. 26–27.
At that time, there are twenty-eight *tānas* in the middle [scale], with *ṛṣabha* and *gāndhāra* omitted;
when the seven *tānas* occur in succession, there are then twenty-one.
Thus, these two groups together are considered to be forty-nine *ṣaḍavas*.

In the Ṣaḍjagrāma, twenty-one distinct auḍuva tānas are formed by excluding [the notes] from the two *sapa* and the two *ripha*. Those belonging to the Madhyamagrāma, however, are formed by excluding [the notes] from the two *ridha* and the two *dviśruti*. 29–30.
The deficient [melodies] would be fourteen, and those combined [with the full ones] are thirty-five;

all the *ṣāḍava* and *auḍuva* melodies, when added together, would be eighty-four. These include both the incomplete and the complete [melodies], with their notes uttered in regular and inverted order.
The *kūṭatānas* are the *mūrchanās*; we shall state their number:
there are five thousand and forty full *kūṭatānas* for each *mūrchanā*, together with the *kramas*. 32–33.
When the full *kūṭas* situated in the fifty-six *mūrcchanās* are combined,
they are counted as two hundred thousand, eighty-two thousand, two hundred and forty. Now we shall describe the incomplete ones.
Due to the absence of each preceding and following [note], there are six variations for each of the six notes and so forth (35).
Here, even though a single note is without variation, it is mentioned for the sake of establishing the *naṣṭa* and other [types of melodic inquiry].
The sequences (*krama*) are also mentioned as useful among them, despite being neither *akūṭa* nor *tāna* (36).
There are seven hundred and twenty varieties of *ṣāḍava* scales;
one hundred and twenty varieties of *auḍuva* scales are likewise accepted;
and twenty-four four-note (*catuḥsvara*) melodic figures (*kūṭa*) have been declared.
Six [notes] have three accents (*svara*), two have two accents, and one is considered to have a single accent.
(38) These are the designations for the four types of *tāna* beginning with *ekasvara*: namely, the *ārcika*, the *gāthika*, the *sāmika*, and the *svarāntara*. (39)
The four types [of scales], beginning with the pure (*śuddha*), have been described as being joined with the *niṣāda*.
When each of those two is diminished by one, they are considered to be the two-fold root-orders (*mūlakrama*).
The two beginning with *ṣaḍja* and the two beginning with *madhyama* thus become four, each occurring in two ways.
The other four types are ten each;
thus, these forty-eight sequences (krama) multiplied by the previously mentioned seven hundred and twenty result in thirty-four thousand five hundred and sixty. 42.
Thus ends the enumeration of the ṣāḍavas; now I shall state the pentatonic scales (pañcasvara).
Those beginning with Ga, those beginning with Dha, and those beginning with Niṣāda constitute four varieties each for the ṣaḍjas and auḍuvitas.
There are eight others of two kinds; thus, these forty modes follow in sequence.
When one hundred and twenty is multiplied by those [twenty], the total number for the five vowels is eight hundred and forty-four (4,844).
Regarding the four-vowel combinations, there are two beginning with *ny-* which are fourfold, and twelve others.
The two types of *krama* multiplied by thirty-two and twenty-four respectively result in seven hundred and sixty-eight; this is the measure of the four vowels.
However, among the three-vowel combinations, the first two are non-distinct (*abheda*), while the others are twelve.

The twenty-six [notes] are twofold; when multiplied by six in sequence, they become one hundred and fifty-six. Furthermore, among those with two vowels, there are eight types beginning with *rigadha* and *nya*, which are pure, while the others are sequential [impure]. 47–48.
These twenty-two, when doubled, become forty-four;
however, because they are not distinct, the primary ones remain only fourteen.
(49) For the *śuddhamadhyā* scale beginning with *ṣaḍja*, the fifth note is the differentiator, excluding it [from the calculation].
In the pair of sequences with four notes (catuḥsvara), forty-eight tānas are said;

in those with three notes (trisvara), these are twelve; in those with two notes (dvisvara), there are two; and in those with one note (ekasvara), there is one. Thus, there are sixty-three [tānas] by means of the auttara-mandrakas.
Furthermore, the sequences of the nyāsādi-mārgas are considered to be redundant.
Of those four pentatonic scales (pañcasvara), there are four hundred and eighty-four [melodic forms]; of the four tetradic scales (cātusvarī), there are ninety-six.

There are twelve [notes] in the pair of triple-syllable [combinations], and four in the pair of double-syllable [combinations]. There is one in the single-syllable [combination]; thus, these totals amount to five hundred.
When combined with the ninety-three [notes] occurring in the nights, they remain undivided. (53–54)
From the *dhaivata*-based *pauravī*, there are four [melodies] with six notes (*ṣaṭsvara*) in sequence;
their *tānas* are considered to be one hundred twenty-eight.
The number for the four previously mentioned *auḍuva* [melodies] and those with four notes (*catuḥsvara*) is as follows: [56].
The three-syllable [melodies], the two-syllable [melodies], and the single-syllable [melody] are of the number previously stated;
when combined with twenty-five, this total becomes one hundred and thirty-four. This is equal in form to the *tānas* by means of the *tānas* that extend upward.
Thus, there are four thousand and eighty-one [verses] of *tānas*,
including repetitions, both complete and incomplete, along with their sequences; if these were subtracted, this would be the measure of the *kūṭatānas*.
Three hundred thousand, seventeen thousand, five hundred and thirty-nine; this is declared here as the means for knowledge.
One should write the digits in sequence from one to seven, each placed successively above the other.
In those [notes], starting from the first in each successive group,
the number of notes beginning with the first note shall be determined sequentially for each *mūrcchanā*.
Having placed the sequence, each preceding note is to be set below the following one.
If that [first] is above, then those preceding it are in front; those following it are behind according to the sequence of the root-order; such is the *prastāra*.
There are seven rows below the boxes numbered from one to seven.
In those [rows], one should write the number one in the first cell of the first row, and zeros in the subsequent ones;
one should place pebbles (*loṣṭaka*) in those very cells, equal in number to the vowels of the *vedya-tāna*.
In the rows situated above and below, there is the conjunction of the numbers at the end of the preceding row.
Below the "void" (śūnya), one should write a single [unit], and below that, one's own squares;
this is considered the Khaṇḍameru, which should be placed multiplied by the number of squares.
As for the vowels, starting from the last of the root sequence, whichever vowel occurs at a certain position... 65–66.
One should place a pebble in the bottom of the very last cell indicated by the problem number.
The movement of the pebble from the end occurs by subtracting the quotient; this sequence is established.
By summing the numbers occupied by the pebbles, the measure of the problem number is obtained.
If the lost number is to be found by means of marks combined with the original single unit (the first digit), one should place a pebble at the root;
that which is measured by the position of the pebble shall be the position of the lost tāna-svara. Then, in whichever step [that position falls], [the result is obtained].
From the bottom upwards, there is a clod; the vowel would be of that many [units].
From the vowel preceding the last vowel of the sequence, the process of taking and discarding is as before.
By mixing the final numbers from the rows above and below, measured by the *tāna* vowels—
The number of these various *ekasvara* melodies arises in sequence [as follows]: 71.
Now, we shall here declare the names of the pure *tānas*:
Agniṣṭoma, Atya-gniṣṭoma, Vājapeya, and Ṣoḍaśī. 72.
Puṇḍarīka, Aśvamedha, and thereafter Rājasūya—
these shall be the seven names, in order, for those [sacrifices] devoid of the Ṣaḍja note: Sviṣṭakṛt, Bahusauvarṇa, Gosava, and Mahāvrata.
The Viśvajit and the Brahmayajña are the seventh, the Prājāpatya;
these are, in order, the names of the eight *tāna* scales devoid [of the sixth note].
Following that are the Aśvakrānta, the Rathakrānta, and the Viṣṇukrānta.
Sūryakrānta, Gajakrānta, Valabhin, Nāgapakṣaka—
these are considered the seven names for the five great sacrifices (mahāyajñas) in their respective order.
Then there are the Cāturmāsya, the one called Saṃsthā, the Śastra, and the Uktha as the fourth.
The Sautrāmaṇī, likewise the Citrā, and the seventh named Udbhid—
these are, in order, the designations for the Niṣādahīna ṣāḍavas.
Then there are the Sāvitrī, the Ardhasāvitrī, and that known as the Sarvatobhadra.
The Ādityānām-ayana, the one named Gavām-ayana,
the Sarpāṇām-ayana as the sixth, and the Kauṇapāyana as the seventh—
these they considered to be the names of the six *tāna* scales that are devoid of the *ṣaḍja* note. 79
The Agnicit, the Dvādaśāha, the Upāṃśu, the Soma-abhidha,
the Aśvapratigraha, the Varhis, and then that known as the Abhyudaya— these they consider to be the names for those [sacrifices] devoid of the Ṛṣabha.
The *sarvasvadakṣiṇa*, the *dīkṣā*, the one called *soma*, the one named *samit*,
the *svāhākāra*, the *tanūnapāt*, and then the *godohana*—
these are declared to be the names in sequence for those [stomas] excluding the *gāndhāra*. (81–82)
Iḍā, Puruṣamedha, Śyena, Vajra, Iṣu,
Aṅgiras, and Kaṅka— these are the names of the [seven] Saptahas in order. Then follow Jyotiṣṭoma, Darśa, the one called Nāndī, and Paurṇamāsaka.

The Aśvapratigraha, Rātri, and Saubhara are recorded as the seventh; these are, in order, the names of those [melodies] devoid of Niṣāda and Gāndhāra. Furthermore, they bring about good fortune, rain, peace, and nourishment respectively. 84–85.
Vainateya, Uccāṭana, and that known as Vaśīkaraṇa—these are the names of the *tānas* devoid of the fifth and Ṛṣabha notes. [86] Trailokyamohana, Vīra, and Kandarpabalaśātana. [87]
Śaṅkhacūḍa, Gajacchāya, Raudra, and Viṣṇuvikrama— these are,
in order, the names of those who are devoid of the Ṛidha [notes].
Bhairava, Kāmadākhya, Avabhṛtha, and Aṣṭakapālaka.
Sviṣṭakṛt and Vaṣaṭkāra are considered the [first] six, and the giver of liberation (Mokṣada) is regarded as the seventh.
These are accepted as the designations for those [melodies] that are devoid of Niṣāda and Gāndhāra.
Whatever sacrifice one performs, the fruit of that [sacrifice] is desired for that [melody]. 89–90.

In the Gāndharva tradition, the *mūrchanās* and *tānas*, as enjoined by the sacred scriptures, lead to spiritual welfare; through mastery of the vocal registers (*sthāna*) in singing, the *kūṭas* (melodic patterns) are also put to use.
The *sādhāraṇa* (common tone) is of two kinds, distinguished by its relation to the scale (*svara*) and the genus (*jāti*).
In that regard, the *svarasādhāraṇa* is proclaimed to be fourfold,
due to its distinction by means of *kākalī*, *antara*, *ṣaḍja*, and *madhyama*.
For the *sādhāraṇa* of *ṣaḍja* and *niṣāda* consists indeed of *kākalī*.
Because it is common to both, they know that to be the "common" (sādhāraṇa); likewise, even for the internal [notes], that which is common to both is considered "common.
Having uttered the *ṣaḍja*, the two notes *kākalī* and *dhaivata* are to be employed in succession.
Having thus uttered the madhyama, one should employ the antararṣabha and the ṣaḍjakākalinī; or, having uttered the ṣaḍja, one should return again to the ṣaḍja,
and likewise to whichever of those following it, as well as to the madhyama and the antarasvara.

Having applied [the notes], the middle one should be grasped, or else another following it; in all cases, there is a slight application, and the intermediate tone is the *kākalī*. If *niṣāda* should take recourse to the first *śruti* of *ṣaḍja*, [it becomes *kākalī*].
Then, Ṛṣabha is said to be the final [note], which is the Ṣaḍja-sādhāraṇa;
likewise, the Sādhāraṇa of Madhyama is considered to consist of Ga and Pa alone.
The Sādhāraṇa of Madhyama certainly belongs to the Madhyama-grāma.
Those two [jātis], Kaiśika and Sādhāraṇa, are so called because of their subtlety, like the tip of a hair;
they are described by the wise as being common to both scales (*grāma*).
That which occurs among jātis arising from a single scale and belonging to a single part [of that scale]—
The noble ones have declared that *gāna* (singing) is common to all [styles], being shared by those *jātis*.
Some, however, describe the *rāgas* themselves as being common to the *jātis*.
The act of singing is called *varṇa*, and it is defined as being of four kinds.
The stationary (*sthāyin*), the ascending (*ārohin*), the descending (*avarohin*), and the moving (*saṃcārī*): such is the definition.

That vocalization which consists of the repeated application of a single note after pausing again and again is to be known as the stationary (*sthāyin*) tone; the other two have names that correspond to their literal meanings.
From the blending of these, the *sañcārī* (transitory) sentiment is proclaimed;
they declare a specific arrangement of words to be an *alaṅkāra* (ornament). Its varieties are many; among them, I shall describe those pertaining to the *sthāyin* (permanent sentiment).
Those [notes] which have a single vowel at their beginning and end are called *sthāyivarṇa*.
Then there are those known as *prasannādi*, *prasannānta*, and *prasannādyanta*;
after that comes *prasannamadhya*, and the fifth is *kramarecita*.
Prastāra and Prasāda—these seven reside in the Sthāyin;
in this context, the first note of the Mūrcchanā is called Mandra. That same note doubled is Tāra, or else each preceding one may be so designated.
The low tone (*mandra*) is followed by the high tone (*tāra*), which is clear and soft as well.
The high tone (*tāra*) may be radiant (*dīpta*), while the low tone (*mandra*) has a dot above it;
the high tone (*tāra*) has an upward stroke above it. In written notation, the protracted (*pluta*) vowel is indicated by a triple articulation.
When the two *mandra* notes are followed by the *tāra*, it is called *prasannādi*;
*saṃ saṃ s*. When this is reversed, it is *prasannānta*.
Saṃ saṃ | 2 When [the vowel] is between two clear [consonants], it is 9; when [the consonant] is flared, there should be a clear [vowel] at the beginning and end.
When the two *tāra* notes are again situated between them,
scholars know the ornament named *prasannamadhyam* in the *mandra* register. 10
If there is a *mūrcchanā* and so forth at the beginning and end, and the second note is internal,
that is one *kalā*; likewise if the third and fourth notes are in the middle.
If the second, fifth, and first [notes] are internal, it is the supreme *kalā*;
thus, by means of these three *kalās*, the ornament known as *kramarecita* is described:
saṃ risaṃ saṃ gamasaṃ saṃ padhanisaṃ. 5.
If the *prastāra* has its end illuminated at every step, it is called *saṃgama*; for example:
*saṃri-saṃga-masaṃ-padha-ni*. When there is a reversal of high (*tāra*) and low (*mandra*) pitches, they call that *prasāda*. 13.
*Srisaṃ*, *sgamasaṃ*, and *spadhanisaṃ* [are the names of ornaments].

There should be broad *niṣkaṣas* (neck-ornaments), and the *bindu* (dot) is the supreme *abhyuccaya* (elevation). Likewise, there are the *hasita* (laughing), *preṅkhita* (swaying), *ākṣipta* (thrown), *sandhi* (joint), and *pracchādana* (covering). 14.
Similarly, those consisting of three syllables carried by the *udgīta* are called *veṇi*;
these are proclaimed as the twelve *alaṅkāras* (ornaments) based on the ascending (*ārohi*) notes.
Where there is a sequential ascent of the notes and so forth, beginning with the *mūrcchanā*, it occurs [in this manner].
Having paused repeatedly with long vowels, it is called *vistīrṇa* (expanded):
*sā rī gā mā pā dhā nī*.
With short vowels, repeated twice each without interruption, it is *niṣkarṣa* (extracted).
Sasa riri gaga mama papa dhadha nini.
(17) They know this sequence of bodily colors to be uttered three or four times for each syllable:
Sasasa ririri gagaga mamama dhadhadha ninini.

When one ascends by degrees while performing [the sequence], then it is considered the *ari* bindu;

The *saga* (the consonant cluster) and the *pani* (the vowel following it), along with the subsequent *kalās* beginning with the third vowel, are each preceded by their respective preceding [consonants]. Where there is a *kalā* consisting of three vowels, that is the "concealment of the junction" (*sandhipracchādana*). 23.
When the first [note] of each [tetrachord] is repeated three times in two kalās consisting of three notes each, it is called *udgīta*. *sariga gamapa padhani* (is an example).
sasasariga mamamapadha | 9 This is considered to be the *udgrāha* (refrain) in the middle [register], being of the same form [as the *dhruva*].

When the final [note] is repeated three times, they describe this as *trivarṇa*:
sa-ri-ga-ga-ga ma-pa-dha-dha-dha. When three [notes] are each repeated three times, it is called *pṛthagveṇi*. 11, 25.
Sasa-sa, ri-ri-ri, ga-ga-ga, ma-ma-ma, pa-pa-pa, dha-dha-dha;
these twelve [notes] in descending order constitute the *avarohiṇī* (descending scale).
Beyond this, there shall be the *mandrādi*, the *mandramadhyā*, and the *mandrāntā*. 26.
Prastāra, Prasāda, Vyāvṛtta, Skhalita, Parivarta, Ākṣepa, Bindu, Udvāhita, Ūrmi, Sama,
Preṅkha, Niṣkūjita, Śyena, Krama, Udghaṭṭita, and Rañjita. (27)
Then there are *saṃnivṛttapravṛtta*, *veṇu*, and *lalitasvara* (28); *huṅkāra*, *hrādamāna*, and then *avalokita*.
These twenty-five are the transitory (*sañcārin*) ornaments (29).
The first [scale] consists of three notes; the others are formed by omitting one note at a time from the low (*mandra*) register.
If the scale consists of three notes starting from the low register, then it becomes as follows: sa-ga-ri, ri-ma-ga, ga-pa-ma, ma-dha-pa, pa-ni-dha. (30)
If those *kalās* consist of the low (*mandra*), middle (*madhya*), and high (*anta*) registers respectively, then the other two [types] follow. An example of the low-middle type is:
*gasari*, *mariga*, *pagama*, *dhamapa*, *nipadha*. 2.
The *mandrānta* [jāti] is as follows:
ri-ga-sa-ga-ma-pa-dha-ni-pa.
Having omitted two intervening notes, a pair of notes is begun again from that same starting point. 31.
One should ascend such a pair; by this, the *prastāra* is described:
*sa ga ri ma ga pa ma dha pa ni*.
Each preceding vowel is placed above and below each subsequent one. (32)
At that time, Śrī Karaṇeśvara spoke to Prasāda:
"Sarisari gamagama magama padhapadha dhanidha.
Therein, the first four-syllable *kalā* [is formed] from the third [syllable] of the second [group]. (33)

Having reached the fourth [note], one should proceed to the first; thus, by the omission of each one in turn, that state where only four notes remain is known as *vyāvṛtta* by the wise. (34) *Sagarimasarimaparima pamadhadhamadhapanim*
If, having applied a *kalā* (time-unit) to the first note (*mandra*) and so forth, one descends while repeating [the notes] and accompanied by ascending notes, then that is called *skhalita*.
Sagarima, marigasa, rimagapa, pagamari, gapamadh, dhamapaga.

Madhapaṇini-padhama: If, having omitted the second note, the first *kalā* consists of three notes, and the subsequent *kalās* starting from that omitted note are likewise [three-note], then it is *parivartaka*. 36.
If there are three notes (*trisvara*) in the *sagama*, *rimapa*, and *gapadha* scales, then by discarding each preceding one and transferring it upward,
there is an "implication" (*ākṣepa*).
*sa-ri-ga*, *ri-ga-ma*, *ga-ma-pa*, *ma-pa-dha*, *pa-dha-ni*.
Now, as for the *bindu*: where it makes the following vowel protracted (*pluta*), like fire, having touched the lower consonant with its own [contact], all the *kalās* [are manifested]. 37.
