*sarigari rigamaga gamapama mapadhapa padhani* || 11 || Having made the fourth note from the beginning of the *mūrcchanā* (and so forth) a *pluta* (protracted), and having returned to the first, there are other [melodic patterns] here where each subsequent one is formed by the reduction of one *kala* (time-unit) at a time. || 39 ||
May he be a wave, *sama-sam-ripas*.
Form, smell, smell, jewel, jewel.
That [scale] is even (sama) where there are four notes in each kalā; others are likewise characterized by equal ascent and descent with a single-step reduction:
sarigamamagarisa, rigamapapamagari, gamapadhadhapamaga.

The *mapadhaninidhapama* (13) [is formed] by the movement of the *kalās* through the successive reduction of one at a time from each pair of notes; where other [varieties] are similar, that would be the *preṅkha*.
*Sa-ri-sa ri-ga-ri ga-ma-ma ma-pa-pama pa-dha-dhapa dha-ni-nidha* || 14 || Furthermore,
the *niṣkūjita* [is formed] by singing a quarter-measure (*kalā*) of *prasāda*, and then the third [quarter-measure] of that same *kalā*. || 42 ||
Having gone from the first *gāna*, there arise:
*sarisaga-sa*, *rigarima-ri*, *gamagapa-ga*, *mapamadha-ma*, and *vadhapani-pa*. This is the Śyena [tāla], characterized by pairs of consonants in correspondence. 43. 15.
In sequence, by means of *sa*, *ri*, *ga*, *ma*, and so forth, there would be *sa*, *pa*, *ri*, *dha*, *ga*, *ni*, *ma*, and *sa*;
the *kalās* consist of two, three, and four notes respectively.
The first three [notes] beginning with the first vowel (A), and likewise those beginning with the second [vowel] (Ā) and so forth—where this occurs, it is called *krama*. For example:
sa-ri-sa-ri-ga, sa-ri-ga-ma, ri-ga-ri-ga-ma, ri-ga-ma-pa, ga-ma-ga-ma-pa, ga-ma-pa-dha.
Mapa-mapa-dha-ma-padhani. 17.
That, however, is called udghaṭṭita, wherein, having sung two notes, one proceeds from the fifth [note] to the other four notes. 45.
One should descend through the *kalās*, singing the subsequent ones by omitting each one in turn:
*sa-ri-pa-ma-ga-ri*, *ri-ga-dha-pa-ma-ga*, *ga-ma-ni-dha-pa-ma*.
If these are stated twice with the final note as the low (*mandra*) pitch, then those *kalās* begin from the low pitch. (18, 46)
rañjitaḥ sagarisagarisa rimagarimagari gapamagapamaga madhapamadhapama panidhapanidhapa || 13 ||
Now, this may be the *saṃnivṛttapravṛttaka* [rhythm],
wherein, having sung the first and the fifth [notes], one descends from the fourth through nine [steps];
where that *kalā* proceeds in sequence, and others likewise by a reduction of one at a time.
*Sapamagari*, *ridhapamaga*, and *ganidhapama*. 20.
Where the first [note] occurs twice, and the second, fourth, and third [notes] occur once each, with the other notes occurring once and decreasing by one [syllable] each, this is considered *Veṇu*.
*sasarimagaririgapama gagamadhapa mamapanidha* || 21 || Having sung the first two [notes] and the fourth of each [tetrachord], where those [notes] descend, that is *kalā*;
and where there are others such as these, it is *lalitasvara*. || 49 ||

*sarimarisa rigapagari gamadhamaga mapanipama* || 22 || Wherein the first *kalā* consists of two notes and so forth, proceeding through ascending and descending sequences with notes increased by one at each step, that is called *huṅkāra*. || 50 ||
*sarisa sarigarisa sarigamagarisa sarigamapamagarisa sarigamapadhapamagarisa sarigamapadhanidhapamagarisa* (23).
These are known as the *kalās* beginning with the low (*mandra*) register, ending in clarity (*prasannānta*), and characterized by joy (*hrādamāna*). (51)
Sagarisa, rimagari, gapamaga, madhapama, panidhapa 24. When one abandons its own second [note] during both ascent and descent, that four-note scale (catusvara samālā) would then be Avalokita. 52.
*sagamamarisa rimapapagari gapadhadhamaga madhaninapama* (25).
Thus have the *sañcārya* ornaments been demonstrated by way of ascent (*āroha*).
The foremost of the Śrīkaraṇas has declared these very same [ornaments] by way of descent (*avaroha*). (53)
Other seven ornaments have also been demonstrated by those who know song:
tāramandraprasanna, mandratāraprasannaka, āvartaka, sampradāna, vidhūta, and upalolaka. 54.
And now, their characteristic is described as being "exhilarated" (ullāsita).
Their secondary [notes] and so forth are formed by the successive omission of one [note] at a time, starting from the first;
if one ascends up to the eighth note and then returns to the first, [that is the definition]. 55–56.
When this [scale] is clear with high and low notes, it is then called an ornament (alaṅkāra).
[The sequence] saṃ-ri-ga-ma-pa-dha-ni-saṃ [is formed] by leaping from the low (mandra) to the eighth [note] and descending through the heptatonic scale. 57
The supreme follower of Maheśvara spoke of that which is called "soft," "high-pitched," and "clear":
That which begins with *sa* once in the *kalā* and is repeated is called *āvartaka*.
*sasariri-sasarisa ririgaga-ririgari gagamama-gagamaga mamapapa-mamapama papadhadha-papadhapa dhadhani-dhadhadhani-dha* (3 times).

When this very [scale] is sung after omitting the last two notes of each quarter-tone (kalā), the wise know that as the *sampradāna* ornament. sasari risa ririga gariga gamama magaga mapapa pamama padhadha papapa.
If the *dha-dha-ni-dha-dha* [pattern] occurs twice, separated by one [note], even when omitted from the previous [formula],
and is likewise applied twice, then it is the *vidhūta*, as approved by the wise.

Sagasaga, rimarima, gapagapa, madhamadha, panipani (5). If the first two [groups] are each used twice, and the third and second [groups] are likewise used twice, it is called *upalola* by those who know [the meters]. (61)

*sarisa ri ga ri ga ri | ri ga ri ga ma ga ma ga | ga ma ga ma pa ma pa ma | ma pa ma pa dha pa dha pa | dha pa dha ni dha ni dha* (6). Having sung the first and the third [phrases] twice, and the first and the third again (62).
They say that when one sings once in the *yatkalā* measure, it is called *ullāsita*:
*sasagasaga ririmarima gagapagapa mamadhamadha papanipani*.
Thus, sixty-three well-known ornaments have been described by me. 63.
However, because they are infinite, they have not been proclaimed in their entirety in this treatise.
"The acquisition of passion, the knowledge of musical notes (*svara*), and the variety of the limbs of the letters"—
these, they say, are the purposes in the exposition of figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*).
Thus ends the sixth section, on the ornaments of syllables (*varṇālaṅkāra*), in the first chapter, "Concerning the Notes" (*svaragata*).
Now begins the seventh section, on the musical scales (*jāti*):
there are seven pure scales (*śuddhajātayaḥ*), which are named after the notes beginning with *ṣaḍja*.
The Ṣaḍjyārṣabhī, Gāndhārī, Madhyamā, Pañcamī,
Dhaivatī, and Naiṣādī— thus the characteristics of the pure (śuddha) scales are described;
in these, the note that serves as their name is the nyāsa, the apanyāsa, an aṃśa, and likewise the grāha.

Those [notes] which are devoid of the *tāra-nyāsa* (high-register placement) are considered to be "full" (*pūrṇa*) and designated as "pure" (*śuddha*). Those that are devoid of this [pure] characteristic and lack the *nyāsa* are called "altered" (*vikṛta*). Through the omission of one or another among the fullness, the *graha*, the *aṃśa*, and the *apanyāsa*, [the notes become altered].

There are four varieties when two [of the six] are abandoned; six are recognized when three are abandoned; four when four are abandoned; and one when all four are abandoned. These fifteen varieties of the *ṣaḍja* [scale] have been determined by the wise. 4–5.
Among those, eight are deficient in completeness (*pūrṇatā*), while seven are devoid of the others.
Those deficient in completeness are of two kinds, being further divided into six according to the *auḍuva* scale.
Therefore, there are eight [jātis] in addition to those beginning with Ārṣabhī, which arise from the *auḍuva* genus.
Thus, twenty-three varieties are said to arise from each of the six [melas];
however, eleven are recorded as being born from the combination of the modified (vikṛta) melas.
These are Ṣaḍjakaiśikī, Ṣaḍjodīcyavā, and Ṣaḍjamadhyamā.
Gāndhārodīcyavā, Raktagāndhārī, Kaiśikī,
Madhyamodīcyavā, Kārmāravī, Gāndhārapañcamī, as well as Āndhrī and Nandayantī— now I shall state their causes.
From the combination of Ṣāḍjī and Gāndhārī, Ṣaḍjakaiśikī is born (10).
From Ṣāḍjī and Madhyamā, however, Ṣaḍjamadhyamā is born;
and from Gāndhārī and Pañcamī, Gāndhārapañcamī is born (11).
From Gāndhārī and Ārṣabhikā, however, Jātirāndhrī is born;
likewise, Ṣāḍjī, Gāndhārikā, and Dhāivatī— when these are combined—
they produce the Ṣaḍjodīcyavatī jātī, and furthermore, the Kārmāravī.
The Naiṣādī, Pañcamī, and Ārṣabhikā together produce [the first]; the Nandayantī, however, is produced by the Gāndhārī, Pañcamī, and Ārṣabhikā together;
these others are produced by the Gāndhārī, Dhaivatī, Ṣaḍjī, and Madhyamā together. 13–14.
They should perform Gāndhārodīcyavā and Madhyamodīcyavā;
furthermore, they perform these same two together with Pañcamī, excluding Ṣaḍjī.
They should perform Raktagāndhārī and Naiṣādī, but not Dhaivatī.
Excluding the Ārṣabhī and Dhaivatī, Kaiśikī arises from the remaining five.
There are four *ṣaḍjaśabdinī* [jātis], as well as Naiṣādī, Dhaivatī, and Ārṣabhī; these seven are the *jātis* of the Ṣaḍjagrāma. 16–17.

The remaining [jātis] belong to the Madhyama-grāma; because they are always complete, they are now described: Kārmāravī, Gāndhārapañcamī, Ṣaḍjakaiśikī, and Madhyamodīcyavā—these are proclaimed as being eternally complete.

The sage Kāśyapa has declared that these four—Ṣaḍjī, Nandayantī, Āndhrī, and Gāndhārodīcyavā—are complete (*sampūrṇa*) as well as hexatonic (*ṣāḍava*). The remaining ten are considered to be both complete and pentatonic (*auḍuvita*). 19–20.
The *svarasādhāraṇa* has been proclaimed by the sages, such as Bharata and others, in the five *jātis* known as Pañcamī, Madhyamā, and Ṣaḍjamadhyamā.
This occurs when the *aṃśas* are all equal (*samapā*), according to their respective rules.
Kambalāścata and others have stated that this [definition] applies to scales (*nigā*) with few notes;
their opinion also extends to *rāga-bhāṣās* and the like that possess only two notes.
However, that [definition] would not apply to the *ṣaḍja-madhyamā* scale, where both *ni* and *ga* are the *aṃśas*. 22–23.
In that case as well, these are indeed modified [jātis], based on their own respective primary notes (*svarasādhāraṇa*):
Ekāṃśā, Nandayantī, and Madhyamodīcyavā; likewise, Gāndhārapañcamī—these three have two *aṃśas* (notes), while Dhaivatī has two.

Gāndhārodīcyavā or Pañcamī—these are declared [to be three-partite]. Naiṣādī, Ārṣabhikā, Ṣaḍjakaiśikī, and Tryaṃśikā are considered [three-partite as well]. Āndhrī, Kārmāravī, Ṣaḍjodīcyavā, and [the others] are four-partite.
Raktagāndhārī has five *aṃśas*, as do Gāndhārī, Madhyamā, and Ṣāḍjī—these four; Kaiśikī alone has six *aṃśas*. Ṣaḍjamadhyamā is proclaimed by the learned masters to have seven *aṃśas*.
Thus, there are sixty-three divisions within these eighteen *jātis*:
the *graha*, *aṃśa*, *tāra*, and *mandra* notes, as well as the *nyāsa* and *apanyāsa*, and likewise the *saṃnyāsa* and *vinyāsa*; from these, there is then multiplicity and scarcity.

These thirteen, along with the *antara-mārga*, are said to be the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) in the various *jātis*; thus they are called "sixth" (*ṣāḍava*) and "seventh" (*auḍuvita*) in certain cases.
Among these, the note established as the *gīta* (the melody) is called the *graha*.
In this context, when either "partial" (aṃśa) or "grasping" (graha) is mentioned, both are to be understood.
That which manifests passion in song, that which consists of the concordant (saṃvādī) and the following (anuvādī),
and because they are abundant in the *vidārī*, from them arises the distinction between the high (*tāra*) and low (*mandra*) registers.
That other *svara* which corresponds to and follows the principal [note],
having attained the status of a *nyāsa*, *apanyāsa*, *vinyāsa*, *saṃnyāsa*,
and *graha*, shall become a frequent part of the performance (*prayoga*) according to its suitability. (33)
Abundance in the applications is the characteristic of pervasiveness (vyāpaka) for the [lower] quarter (aṃśa).

In the middle group of seven notes, there would be a quarter; therefore, from that which is situated in the high register (tāra), one should ascend four notes—this is the supreme limit of the high register. 34–35.
But downward movement may occur at will; even if omitted, it is counted as occurring on the *tāra* (high) register.
In the *Nandayantī*, an ascent from the *aṃśa* note situated in the middle register (*madhyasthāna*) to the *aṃśa* note in the lower register (*mandrasthāna*) is proclaimed.
(36) From the *aṃśa* situated in the middle register, one should proceed to the *aṃśa* in the lower register.
Alternatively, the nyāsa may be on the *āmandra* [note], or even on the *ri* situated below it; this is the limit of the *mandra-gati*, and below that, there is freedom of movement (*kāmacāritā*).
In song, the *nyāsa* brings about completion, and it is of twenty-one kinds.

For the seven [grāmarāgas] beginning with Ṣāḍjī, the final note (nyāsa) should be the note that gives the name [to the rāga]. However, in the case of Ṣaḍjamadhyamā, two notes are considered to give the name; [namely, ṣaḍja and madhyama]. In Udīcyavā, the three [notes] ending in ma [are the nyāsas], while in Kaiśikī, they end in ni, pa, and ga.

The *kārmāravī* ends on the fifth note (*pañcama*), while the other five [melodies] are known to end on the *gāndhāra*. That which concludes a *vidārī* (a melodic extension) is considered the *apanyāsa* (intermediate note). This applies to the *kārmāravī*, the *naiṣādī*, as well as the *āndhrī* and the *madhyamā*.
Those notes which are the *aṃśas* in the two *ārṣabhya* scales are proclaimed as the *apanyāsas*.
In the triad of *udīcyavā* scales, *ṣaḍja* and *dhaivata* are the *apanyāsas*.
In *raktagāndhārī*, *madhyama* is the *apanyāsa*; in *gāndhārī*, *ṣaḍja* and *pañcama* are the *apanyāsas*.
In the Ṣaḍjakaiśikī scale, *sa*, *ni*, and *pa* are prescribed; in the Pañcamī, *ni*, *ri*, and *pa* are remembered.
In the Gāndhārapañcamī, *ri* and *pa* [are used]; in the Ṣaḍjī, *ga* and *pa*;
in the Dhaivatī, *ri*, *ma*, and *dha* are declared; and in the Nandayantī, *ma* and *pa* are considered [to be used].
Others have stated that six notes are to be avoided in Kaiśikī, while some say all seven;
however, they declare Ṣaḍjamadhyamā to possess the application (apanyāsa) of all seven notes.
In this regard, those which are both *aṃśas* and *apanyāsas* are nineteen in number.
Those [notes] are thirty-seven, and when joined with fifty-six,
they are known as fifty-seven in the Kaiśikī mode within the seven-pakṣa system.
The *aṃśa* and *vivādī* notes bring about the conclusion of the first *vidārī* of the song.
The placement [of the fingers] is indeed like the division of the *oṃ*; however, that which remains at the edge of the word-form consisting of the *vidārī* portion is called *vinyāsa*.
Furthermore, due to non-transgression and likewise through practice, its multiplicity is considered to be of two kinds. 48.
And that [defect] resides in the aspect of the synonym, even for both the proponent and the opponent. (49) Scarcity is said to be of two kinds: from lack of practice and from skipping.
Lack of practice is generally maintained to occur in the case of parts that are to be omitted or not developed. (50)
The touch [of the breath] during leaping (laṅghana) is slight; generally, that [touch] is beyond the range of perception.

Experts in song maintain that this occurs even in the case of the "partless" (anaṃśa), when there is a state of slightness occurring intermittently in the midst [of the breath], having abandoned the locations such as the nyāsa. 51.
That combination of notes, such as the *aṃśa* and others, which produces various effects among the musical tones (*svaras*),
may— when performed through lack of practice or solely by means of occasional leaps—
become an "internal path" (*antaramārga*) primarily within the modified (*vikṛta*) *jātis*.
Those notes which proceed toward the *ṣaḍava* (the hexatonic scale) are considered *ṣaḍavas*;
because the six-note song (*ṣaṭsvara*) arises from among them, it is called *ṣāḍava*. Since the stars (*uḍavas*) go forth or move within this, the sky is called *uḍuva* by the wise.
That fifth [note] exists among the [seven] elements, and its arising is numbered as five (55).
That which possesses these [five notes] is called *auḍuvī*; those notes themselves are considered *auḍuva*.
When they have arisen within a song, that is termed *auḍuvita* (56).
Through association with that [note], they know this to be the *auḍuva* scale with five notes (*pañcasvara*).
In the states where the hexatonic (*ṣāḍava*) and pentatonic (*auḍuva*) scales are produced, the [notes] become progressively rarer;
however, in the state of completeness (*sampūrṇatva*), there is a reversal in the case of the fifth note (*pañcamī*).
In this context, an injunction (*vidhi*) consists of a statement regarding that which has not been previously established, whether it be something small or great (58).
An exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) occurs when both [alternatives] are applicable, and one is restricted for the sake of emphasizing a particular quality.
Now, the definition of each of these types is stated (59).
In Ṣāḍjī, there are five notes as its constituent tones (aṃśas), excluding Niṣāda and Ṛṣabha.
By the omission of Niṣāda, it becomes Ṣāḍava; in its full form, the Kakalī [note] occurs occasionally.
Here, there is a frequent conjunction of Sa and Ga, as well as Sa and Dha, and the note Ga is very common.
In the Gāndhārī scale, there is no elision of *ni*; the *mūrcchanā* begins with *dhaivata*.
The *tāla* is of three kinds, and here the *pañcapāṇi* has one *kalā* and so forth. Furthermore, the *mārgas* are respectively Citra, Vṛtti, and Dakṣiṇa; the *gītis* are likewise [three]. 61–62.
Māgadhī, Saṃbhāvitā, and Pṛthulā— these are prescribed in sequence for the *naiṣkrāmikadhruvā* in the first performance (*prekṣaṇa*). Here,
the application consists of twelve *kalās*, and each *kalā* contains eight short syllables (*laghu*).
In this Ṣāḍjī, Ṣaḍja is the nyāsa; Gāndhāra and Pañcama are the apanyāsas;
Varāṭī is observed [in it]; its prastāra is that of Ṣāḍjī.

I bow to that fire which consumes the body of Kāma, which is superior to the lotus-eye on Śiva’s forehead, which arises from the playful dalliance with the Daughter of the Mountain, and which is smeared with the fragrant paste of the *tilaka* mark.
In the Ārṣabhī scale, there are three notes: Niṣāda, Ṛṣabha, and Dhaivata.
There is a conjunction with the two [notes] having two śrutis, and there is an omission of Pañcama by the remaining [notes].
It is called Ṣāḍava through the omission of Ṣaḍja, and Auduva through the omission of Pañcama.
The *mūrcchanā* is Pañcamādi, and the *tāla* is considered to be Caccatpuṭa;
there are eight *kalās* here, and the application is as before. In this [rāga], Ṛṣabha is the *nyāsa* on the scale of Ārṣabhī; the *aṃśas* themselves are the *apanyāsas*; and the *deśī* is Madhukaya.
These two are seen. Its *prastāra* is:
ārṣabhī rī gā sā riga mā rima gā riri 1.
O you whose mind is characterized by the virtues of tranquility and insight!

Obeisance to that which is immeasurable, superior to the eyes of Muni, infinite, immortal, ageless, inexhaustible, and invincible.
I bow to Bhava, the immeasurable one, whose pure abode is like a mirror made of divine jewels.

In the Gāndhārī [jāti], five notes are to be excluded, with the exception of Ṛṣabha and Dhaivata; furthermore, the *saṃgati* (conjunction) occurs between the *nyāsa* (final note) and the *aṃśa* (tonic).
For the others, there is a transition to Ṛṣabha by way of the three [notes] beginning with Ṣaḍja.
Through the omission of Ṛṣabha and the omission of Dhaivata, the scales become *ṣāḍava* (six-note) and *auḍuvita* (five-note) respectively.
The fifth [note] is an enemy of the *ṣāḍava* (six-note scale); *ni*, *sa*, *ma*, and *pa* are the *aṃśas*. Two [notes] are enemies of the *auḍuvita* (five-note scale). Sixteen *kalās* are proclaimed;
the *mūrcchanā* begins with *dhaivata*; the *tāla* is considered to be *caccatpuṭa*.
Its application (*viniyoga*) occurs in the *dhruvā* chant during the third act.
In this *gāndhārī*, *gāndhāra* is the final note (*nyāsa*). *Ṣaḍja* and *pañcama* are the introductory notes (*apanyāsa*).
*Gāndhāra*, *pañcama*, *deśī*, and *velāvalī* are observed [in its structure]. Its *prastāra* is as follows:
Gāndhārī 3:

In this context, the *tāla* (tempo) not explicitly mentioned shall be of three kinds, beginning with one beat (*ekakala*). Furthermore, the *mārgas* (styles) are, in order: *citra*, *vṛtti*, and *dakṣiṇa*. The *gītis* (melodic modes), moreover, are said to be, in sequence: *māgadhī*, *saṃbhāvitā*, and *pṛthulā*.
The number of *kalās* we have mentioned is established for the Southern Path (*dakṣiṇapatha*).
It should be known as double in the *Vārttika* style, and fourfold in the *Citra* style.
One should understand that in all musical genres (*jāti*), the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) resides within the *aṃśa-svara*. 111–112.
Those who know [the truth] perceive portions of passion born from the produced [effects] within the classes of the producers;
these were correctly explained previously by means of the words spoken by Brahmā when Śaṅkara was praised.
Even these castes purify the slayer of a Brahmin from sin.

Just as the Ṛg-verses, Yajus-formulas, and Sāman-chants are produced and not otherwise [than according to their rules], so too are the *jātis* (melodic classes) originating from the Sāmans, which are commensurate with the Veda. Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Definition of *Jāti*," in the first book, the *Svarādhyāya*. 7.114–115.
Now begins the eighth chapter on Gīti.
I shall now describe the *kapālas* arising from the pure (*śuddha*) *jātis*;
the *rāgas* are considered to be contained within those *kapālas* of the parent *jātis*.
In this [rāga], Ṣaḍja is the *graha*, *aṃśa*, and *apanyāsa*; Ga is the *nyāsa*; Ga and Ni are very frequent;
Ri, Pa, and Dha are rare; Ri is the *laṅghya* (to be leaped over); twelve *kalās* are prescribed.
That in which these characteristics exist is called Pāḍjī-kapāla by those learned in song.
Where Ṛṣabha is the *aṃśa*, Ga is the *nyāsa*, Ma is the *anta*, and there is a scarcity of Ga, Ni, Pa, and Dha, that is *aty-alpa*; it is the *kapāla* type, characterized by the arrival of Ṛṣabha.
Where Madhyama is the *aṃśa*, Ga is the *graha* and *nyāsa*, and Dhaivata is abundant, [that is *madhya-alpa*]. 3–4.

Where *ṛṣabha* (*ri*) and *pañcama* (*pa*) are omitted due to the scarcity of *ṣaḍja* (*sa*), *gāndhāra* (*ga*), and *madhyama* (*ma*), it becomes the *auḍuvita* scale; that is the *gāndhārī-kapāla*, constructed with eight *kalās*.
Where *madhyama* (*ma*) is the *aṃśa* (tonic) and *ṛṣabha* (*ri*), *niṣāda* (*ni*), *gāndhāra* (*ga*), and *pañcama* (*pa*) are very scarce, it consists of nine *kalās*.
It is the consensus of those free from doubt that its middle *kāpāla* should be thus;
they know the *kāpāla* born of the *pañcamī* *jāti* to consist of eight *kalās*, containing the *ṛṣabha* portion along with the *graha*, and having *ni*, *dha*, *ṣa*, *ḍja*, and *ga* as minor notes.
With very little *ṛṣabha* and *gāndhāra*, with *panyāsa* and abundant *madhyama*;
like the *kapāla* of *ṣāḍjī*, that [tune] is the complete (*sakala*) form of *haivata*.
It has *ṣaḍja* as its *graha*, *aṃśa*, and *nyāsa*, and it consists mostly of *ṛṣabha* and *gāndhāra* with very little *ṛṣabha*.
The eighth kapāla should be *nidhanamaiṣādī*;

thus, by singing these seven kapālas with the words proclaimed by Brahmā and with the musical notes (*svaras*) in praise of the Beloved of Pārvatī, one shall become a partaker of auspiciousness. (9–10)

Where the *graha* (leading note) is *ga* (gāndhāra), the *aṃśa* (tonic) is *pa* (pañcama), the fifth note (*ri*, ṛṣabha) is frequent, and *ni* (niṣāda) is the *nyāsa* (concluding note), while *ma* (madhyama) and *ga* (gāndhāra) are rare— that is considered *Kambala*.
It is born from the *Pañcamī-jāti* according to the predominance or scarcity [of its constituent notes].
Many varieties of these musical notes were described by the ancients; pleased by Kambala’s singing, the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva) granted a boon to Kambala in the past,
and for that reason, Śiva is delighted by them even today.
We shall now describe, in sequence, the series of words proclaimed by Brahmā for the skull-bowls:
"Jhaṇṭuṃ jhaṇṭuṃ" [1] and "the bearer of the khaṭvāṅga staff" [2].
With fangs formidable [3], with a tongue like lightning [4], hau hau hau hau hau hau hau hau [5].
Possessing many forms and faces, with a wealth of terrible roars: 6 hau hau hau hau hau hau hau hau 7.
ŪM ŪM HRĀM RAUM HAUM HAUM HAUM HAUM (8) adorned with human skulls (9).
Hūṃ hūṃ, kaha kaha, hūṃ hūṃ;
I bow to the god Bhairava, who has made his face terrible.
Thus are the six syllables of Ṣāḍjīkapāla:
1. *jhaṇṭuṃ jhaṇṭuṃ*, bearer of the skull-topped staff; 2. *daṃṣṭrākarālam*, having terrifying fangs.
With a tongue like lightning; 3 hau hau hau hau hau hau hau hau 4;
with excellent fragrant flowers. 5.

1 *calattaraṅga*, and 2 *bhaṅgura*.
It was well-served by gods and asuras with many golden-yellow rays of light.
"O Jāhnavī, do not sprinkle me with drops," thus [ends] the third section on the skull of Gāndhārī.
Holding a trident and a skull-cup (1), the destroyer of the three cities with his hand (2), and wearing the crescent moon (3).
The three-eyed one with the trident, 4 always accompanied by Umā, 5 that bestower of boons. 6
Hau hau hau hau hau hau hau hau 7;
hau hau hau hau hau hau hau hau 8; [I] praise Mahādeva 9.
Thus are the words for the middle skull:
"Victory, O three-eyed one" (1),
"O burner of the body of Madana" (2).
O you who have the gait of a noble bull, 3;
O you whose vehicle is the three cities, 4; O you to whom all the worlds bow, 5.
O you whose face is like a white lotus,
be the remover of my fear;
be my refuge from cyclic existence.
Thus are the words for the fifth skull:
1. Agnijvālā (Flame of Fire), 2. Śikhāvalī (Possessing a Crest).
O you who feed on flesh and blood! O all-devouring one! O fleshless one!
"O Leather-skull, 7;
homage be to you, 8"— these are the six steps of the *dhaivatī-kapāla*.
1. A leather garment dripping with blood;
2. Matted hair entwined by terrifying serpents; 3.
The sound of...
I bow to that Śiva, Hara, the unconquered, whose face is distorted by laughter— Caṇḍa... [3] ...4.
His snout is invincible;
he wears a crown adorned with skulls;
he is the destroyer of the pride of desire.
"Salutation to that Hara, the Supreme Śiva"—
thus are the seven skull-words of the Naiṣādīka.
Thus are the seven skull-words.
Vocal performance adorned with phonemes and other ornaments, and accompanied by metrical feet, is called *gīti*; and that is said by the wise to be of four kinds:
the first is to be known as *Māgadhī*, and the second as *Ardhamāgadhī*.
We observe these characteristics of the [verses] beginning with *saṃbhāvitā* and *pṛthulā*:
having sung the first quarter-verse (*kalā*) in a slow tempo (*vilambita-laya*),
one should sing the second quarter-verse in a medium tempo (*madhya-laya*), joined with the interval between those two quarters.
"And those [wise ones] declared that the Māgadhī [meter] consists of three repetitions of the foot, with the third foot occurring at a quick (druta) tempo.
For example: The wise have declared the *māgadhī* to consist of three repetitions of the foot, with the third foot occurring at a quick tempo.
For example: [Example follows]
Do not go, do not place [it],
O Devas.
Vaṃ.
Dhani dhani sani dhā de vaṃ ru draṃ riga riga maga risa.
When one utters "devaṃ rudraṃ vaṃ de" in the first two quarters and twice in the last quarter,
they call that the Ardhamāgadhī [Prakrit]. 18.
For example:
mā rī gā sā de 0.
Vaṃ 0 sā sā dhā nī vaṃ rudraṃ 0
Pā dhā pā mā draṃ vaṃ de 0; [this is] followed by twice-repeated quarters.
For example: mā mā mā mā de 0.
Vaṃ 0 dhā sā dhā nī devaṃ rudraṃ.
The *saṃbhāvitā* is considered to have its feet abbreviated (*saṃkṣiptapadā*), with many heavy syllables (*bhūriguru*), in the *pā*, *ni*, *dha*, *mā*, *mā*, *ru*, *draṃ*, and *vaṃ* [meters]. 19.
For example:
dhā mā mā ri ga bha 0.
O Goddess,
you who are the source of all prosperity,
grant us that very [blessing].
Vaṃ 0 nī dhā sā nī ru 0
draṃ 0 dhā nī mā mā vaṃ 0
That [meter] which consists of many short syllables and words, and is extensive, is esteemed by the wise;
for example—
Mā gā rī gā su ra na ta sā dhani dhā dhā.
Ha Ra Pa Da Dhā Sā Dhā Nī Yu Ga Laṃ.
When there is *pā*, *nidha*, *pa*, *mā*, *mā*,
*pra*, *ṇa*, *ma*, *ta*, *ya*, *dvā*, or when it follows the syllables *yathākṣara* in a pair of heavy syllables (*gurū*) at the beginning [of a quarter], [it is called *vānavāsikā*]. 20.
When each individual path, such as the *citramārga*, is employed and consists of a group of syllables (*cagaṇa*),
joined with eight *mātrās* on the right side by means of the *dhruvaka* and other measures, then that song is designated as *Māgadhī*.

When the third [syllable] of the even [pāda] is light and joined with half a *chagaṇa* (22), it is further conjoined with the first two and the last two *mātrās*. Then, having made the *pluta* [syllable] joined with a *sārdhagaṇa*, it is employed (23).

With the eight [mātrās] beginning with *dhruvaka* and the two final ones repeated, that is the *Ārdhamāgadhī*; those two likewise exist in other *tālas*. In the *Vārtika* path, when there are two beats (*dvikala*), it is considered to have many long syllables (*bhūriguru*).
In a four-beat measure (*catuṣkala*), the *pṛthulā* is considered to have many short syllables (*bhūrilaghu*) in the right [hand].
(25) Thus ends the eighth section on singing (*gīti*) in the first chapter on the movement of notes (*svaragata*).

Thus concludes the first chapter on the movement of notes in the *Saṃgītaratnākara*, composed by Śrī Śārṅgadeva—known as Niḥśaṅka—who is the son of Śrī Soḍhaladeva, the chief minister (*śrīkaraṇādhipati*), and who takes delight in faultless learning (*anavadyavidyāvinoda*).
Now begins the second chapter, "The Discrimination of Passion" (Rāgaviveka). Then, with a text composed of concise and lucid lines, he fearlessly composes this entire "Discrimination of Passion. 1.
There are five types of *grāmarāgas*, based upon the five *gītis*.
The five *gītis*—beginning with the *śuddhā*—are the *bhinnā*, the *gauḍī*, the *vesarā*, and the *sādhāraṇī*; among these, the *śuddhā* consists of straight and graceful notes.
Distinguished by subtle modulations of tone, curved melodies, and sweet *gamakas*, possessing firm *gamakas* in the three registers and charming *rohāṭī* notes,
the Gauḍī style is considered by the wise to maintain its integrity across all three registers.
With deep, trembling, and very rapid sounds produced by the opening [of the throat],
through the conjunction of the syllables *ha* and *u*, the heart is established when the chin is pressed against it;
likewise, with forceful sounds, there is an intense attachment even to the group of four letters.
The *vegasvarā* is called *rāgagīti*, and the *vesarā* is so called by the wise (6). That which resorts to the characteristics found in the four types of *gīti* is considered *sādhāraṇī*.
Through their association with the *śuddhā* and other *gītis*, the *rāgas* are considered *śuddha* and so forth (7).
Born from the Ṣaḍja scale are Ṣaḍjakaiśika, Madhyamā, and Śuddhasādhārita; the Ṣaḍja scale, however, consists of [the notes] up to Madhyama.
Pañcama belongs to the Madhyama scale, as do the Ṣāḍava and Śuddhakaiśika scales.

The seven pure [melodies] are thus divided; there are five [others]: Kaiśikamadhyama, Bhinnaṣaḍja, and in the [jāti] called Ṣaḍjamadhyamā, Tānamadhyama, Kaiśika, and Bhinnapañcama—these are Gauḍakaiśikamadhyama. 9–10.
Gauḍapañcamaka in Ṣaḍja, and Gauḍakaiśika in Madhyama—
these are the three Gauḍa rāgas in Ṣaḍja; while in Madhyama, there are Ṭakka, Vesara, Ṣāḍava, Sauvīrī, Voṭṭa, and Mālavakaiśika.
Mālava with Pañcama at the end, then Dvigrāma, Aṣṭavaktra, and Kaiśika;
Hindola—these eight are the hybrid (vesara) scales. Following those, seven are the common (sādhāraṇa) scales:
among them, Rūpasādhāraṇa occurs in Ṣaḍja, as do Śaka and Bhammāṇapañcama. 12–13.
In the middle [scale], there are Nāṭa, Gāndhāra, Pañcama, Ṣāḍja, and Kaiśika;
Kakubha belongs to two scales. These are considered to be the thirty grāmarāgas. There are eight uparāgas: Tilaka, Śaka, Ādiṣṭaka, Saindhava, [and others].
Kokilā-pañcama, Revagupta-pañcama-ṣāḍava,
Bhāvanā-pañcama, Nāga-gāndhāra, Nāga-pañcama, Śrīrāga-naṭṭa, Vaṅgāla, and Bhāsa-madhyama-ṣāḍava. 15.
Raktahaṃsa, Kolhahāsa, Prasava, Bhairavadhvani,
Megharāga, Somarāga, Kāmoda, Abhrapañcama, those known as Kandarpa and Deśa, Kakubhānta, and Kaiśika. (16–17)
And Naṭṭanārāyaṇa—thus twenty *rāgas* have been declared:
Sauvīra, Kakubha, Aṣṭaka, Pañcama, Bhinnapañcama, Ṭakkakaiśika, Hindola, Boṭṭamālava, and Kaiśika. (18)
Gāndhārapañcama, bhinnaṣaḍja, vesaraṣāḍava,
mālava, pañcamānta, and the tāna pañcamaṣāḍava—
these fifteen, proclaimed by Yāṣṭika, are the progenitors of the bhāṣās. 19–20.
In Sauvīra there are four languages: Sauvīrī, Vegamadhyamā, Sādhāritā, and Gāndhārī; in Kakubha there is Bhinnapañcamī; and likewise Kāmbojī, Madhyamagrāmā, Ragantī, and Madhurī. 21.
The six *vibhāṣā* meters beginning with *Śakamīśrā* increase the enjoyment:
*Ābhīrikā*, *Madhukarī*, as well as *Ekāntarabhāṣikā*, *Śālavāhanikā*, *Aṭakkā*, *Travaṇā*, and *Travaṇodbhavā*. 22–23.
Vairañjī, Madhyamagrāma, Dehā, Mālavavesarī, Chevāṭī, Saindhavī, Kolāhalā, and Pañcamalakṣitā;
Saurāṣṭrī, Pañcamī, Vegarañjī, and Gāndhārapañcamī. 24.
Mālavī, tānavalitā, lalitā, ravicandrikā (25), tānā, vāherikā, dohyā, and vesarī— these are the twenty-one *bhāṣās*. Then there are devāravardhanī, āndhrī, and gurjarī (26).
In the fifth [chapter], there are four vibhāṣās known as bhāvanī;
furthermore, there are kaiśikī, trāvaṇī, tānodbhavā, ābhīrī, gurjarī, saindhavī, dākṣiṇātyā, āndhrī, and māṅgalī—these ten are bhāvanīs. 27.
Thus, there are two, Bhāṣā and Vibhāṣā; then Bhammāṇī and Andhālikā (28).
In the fifth [tāna], when divided, there are four: Bhāṣā adorned with Dhaivata, Śuddhā, Bhinnā, and Vārāṭī; then Viśālā and Kauśalī (29).
Vibhāṣā, Mālavābhinavalitā, and Ṭakvakaiśikī—these are two *bhāṣās*; Drāviḍī is one *vibhāṣā*; and Preṅkhaka consists of nine *bhāṣās*. There are also Vesarī, Cūtamañjarī, and Ṣaḍjamadhyamā. 30.
Madhurī, Bhinnapaurālī, Gauḍī, and Mālavavesarī; 31.
Chevāṭī and Piñjarī are one [set], while in Boṭṭa there is the Māṅgalī dialect;
Bāṅgālī, Māṅgalī, Harṣapurī, and Mālavavesarī. 32.
Khañjinī, Gurjarī, Gauḍī, Paurālī, Ardhaveśarī,
Śuddhamālava-rūpā, Saindhavī, and Ābhīrī— these thirteen dialects (bhāṣās) are to be known by the learned as belonging to the Mālavakaiśika rāga. 33.
But there are two *vibhāṣās*: Kāmbojī and likewise Devāravardhanī (34).
In the *gāndhāra-pañcama* scale, there are the *bhāṣās* Gāndhārī, Bhinna-ṣaḍjakā, Gāndhāravallī, Kacchellī, Svaravallī, and Niṣādinī (35).
Travaṇā, Madhyamā, Śuddhā, Dākṣiṇātyā, Pulindikā,
Tumburā, Ṣaḍjabhāṣā, Kālindī, Lalitā,
Śrīkaṇṭhikā, Bāṅgālī, Gāndhārī, and Saindhavī— these are they. 36.
Seventeen *bhāṣās* are to be known, along with four *vibhāṣikās*:
Paurālī, Mālavā, Kālindī, and Devāravardhanī; furthermore, there are two *bhāṣās* belonging to the Vaiśeṣika-ṣāḍava, namely Bāhyā and Bāhyaṣāḍavā. (37–38)
In the Pārvaśīśrīkaṇṭha there is Vibhāṣā; then, in the Mālavapañcama, there are three languages: Vedavatī, Bhāvinī, and Vibhāvinī (39).
In the Tāna and Tānodbhava, there are the languages of Bhāṣāpañcama and Ṣāḍava.
Some know the *potā* as the *bhāṣāṃśaka*, while others know it as *revagupta*.
The *vibhāṣā*, the *pallavī*, the *bhāsavalitā*, the *kiraṇāvalī*, and the *śaṅkādyāvalitā*—these three are the *antarabhāṣikā*s. 40–41.
These four unmentioned janakas are recorded as belonging to the *bṛhadveśyā*;
thus, ninety-six *bhāṣās* and twenty *vibhāṣās* are recorded.
There are four *antarabhāṣās*, according to the opinion of Śārṅgadeva.

Speech is said by Mataṅga to be of four kinds: the primary (mukhyā), that called "vocal" (svarākhyā), that called "regional" (deśākhyā), and that born of "coloration" (uparāgajā). The primary is that which does not depend on anything else;
that called "vocal" is known by the names of the notes (svara); and that born of the region is known by the names of the regions, respectively. 43–44.

Furthermore, those arising from the influence of other [melodic types] were described by Yāṣṭika as being of three kinds: the *mālavavesarī* is pure, the *īragantī*, and that which originates from mixed regions, known simply by the name *chāyā*. 45.

The primary [rāgas] are six; the remaining ones, however, are well-known and possess clear characteristics. Some, though distinct in their defining traits, share identical names. Thus ends the first section, titled "The Differentiation of Grāmarāgas, Uparāgas, Rāgabhaṣās, Vibhāṣās, and Antarabhāṣās," in the second chapter, "The Differentiation of Rāgas. 46.1.

Now, the son of Soḍhala undertakes the determination of the primary moods (rāga), the secondary moods (rāgāṅga), the linguistic styles (bhāṣā), the primary movements (kriyāṅga), and the secondary movements (upāṅga), relying on the opinion of certain authorities:
"Because it causes delight, the state of being a mood (rāgatā) is attributed not only to the primary moods but also to the secondary moods and the rest."
The fourfold group beginning with Rāgāṅga is declared to be of the *deśī* (regional) variety.
While the well-known *grāmarāgas* and others are sometimes also called *deśī*, an enumeration of those previously established [in the former sense] is now undertaken. 2–3.
They spoke of Śaṃkarābharaṇa, Ghaṇṭārava, Āhaṃsa, Dīpaka, Rīti, Pūrṇāṭikā, Lāṭī,
and Pallavī as the eight limbs of melody (rāga): Gāmbhīrī, Vauhāṭī, Khaśikā, and Utpalī.
Gollī, Nādāntarī, Nīlotpalī, Chāyātaraṅgiṇī, Gāndhāragatikā, and Rañjā—these they consider to be the eleven *bhāṣāṅgas*. Then there are Bhāvakrī, Svabhāvakrī, and Śivakriya. 5–6.

The wise have declared that there are twelve limbs of action (*kriyāṅga*), namely: *marukrī*, *trinetrakrī*, *kumudakrī*, *anukriya*, *ojaskrī*, *indakriya*, *nāgakṛti*, *dhanyakṛti*, as well as *vipāyakrī*. 7.
The three secondary limbs (*upāṅga*) are Pūrṇāṭa, Devāla, and Guruñjikā. (8) These thirty-four *rāgas* are proclaimed as those well-known from former times.
Now, the enumeration of those currently well-known is set forth. (9)
Madhyamādi, Mālavaśrī, Troṭī, Vaṅgāla, Bhairava,
Varāṭī, Gurjarī, Gauḍa, Kolāhala, Vasantaka,
Dhānyāsī, Deśi, and Deśākhyā— these are the thirteen subsidiary rāgas (rāgāṅgas). 10.
They declared nine regional dialects (*bhāṣā-aṅgas*): Ḍauṃbakī, Āsāvarī, Velāvalī, Prathamamañjarī, Āḍikā, Modikā, Nāgadhvani, Śuddhavarāṭikā, Naṭṭā, Karṇāṭa, and Baṅgāla. 11–12.
The three limbs of action (kriyāṅga) are the Rāmakṛti, the Gauḍakṛti, and the Devakrī; next, the twenty-seven subsidiary limbs (upāṅga) are stated as follows:
the Kauntalī, the Drāviḍī, the Saindhavī, and the Sthānavarāṭikā.
There is also *htasvaravarāṭī* and *pratāpavarāṭikā*.
Thus, there are six *varāṭīs*. As for the *chāyās*, they are *turuṣkā* and so forth;
while the *toḍikas* are *mahārāṣṭrī*, *saurāṣṭrī*, *dakṣiṇā*, and *drāviḍī*. 14–15.
The four *gurjarī*s have been mentioned; [the others are] the *bhuñchikā*, the *stambhatīrthikā*,
the two *velāvalī*s with the prefixes *chāyā* and *pratāpa*, the *bhairavī*,
the *kāmodā*, the *siṅghalī*, the *chāyānaṭṭā*, and likewise the *rāmakṛti*.
Vallātikā, Mahlārī, Mahlāra, and then Gauḍaka;
Karṇāṭa, Deśabāla, Tauruṣka, and Drāviḍa—these are now well-known as the fifty-two charming [melodic types]. 17–18.
The venerable Śārṅgadeva, the foremost of musical authorities, states that there are two hundred and sixty-four rāgas in total when all are combined.
Among these, we shall first describe the characteristics of some of the grāmarāgas.
Regarding the remaining causes such as the regional melodies (deśīrāga) and so forth, [the details] are found here and there.
Born from the Ṣaḍjamadhyamā [jāti], it has the raised Ṣaḍja (tāra-ṣaḍja) as its *graha*, *aṃśa*, and *nyāsa*; it is complete (*pūrṇa*), with the *mūrcchanā* beginning with Ṣaḍja. (20–21)

Adorned with the *avarohi*, *prasanna*, and *anta* ornaments, having the Sun as its presiding deity, it is to be sung in the heroic (*vīra*) and furious (*raudra*) sentiments during the first watch of the day;
it is employed by the wise in the *garbha-sandhi* (the juncture of development) as a *śuddha-sādhārita*. 22–23.

That in which the manifestation of the portions of the *grahas*, of the low (*mandra*) and high (*tāra*) registers, as well as of the final note (*nyāsa*), the secondary final note (*apanyāsa*), their scarcity or abundance, and also of the hexatonic (*ṣāḍava*) and pentatonic (*auḍuva*) scales is observed, is called *rāgālāpa*. 24.
The *rūpaka* should be similar to that, distinguished by its separate unfolding (25).

The *ākṣiptikā*, adorned with the three paths (*mārga*) and performed to the *cañcatpuṭa* and other *tālas*, is described by the wise as being composed of musical notes (*svara*) and words (*pada*) (26).
The two [melodic patterns] existing in the *karaṇa* are not mentioned here because they fall within the scope of the *prabandha*;
therefore, according to the opinion of Mataṅga and others, we state that the *rūpaka* occurs only in the *bhāṣā* and other [varieties].

The Gauḍakaiśikamadhyama [rāga] is created from Ṣaḍjamadhyamā; it has Ṣaḍja as its *graha* (opening note) and *aṃśa* (concluding note), with *panyāsa* (repeated note) on Ṣaḍja; it is complete (*pūrṇa*) and endowed with the *kākali* ornament.
It possesses ascending melodic figures (*varṇa*) in the *prasannamadhyā* scale and follows the *mūrcchanā* beginning with Ṣaḍja. (39)

Thus ends the *ākṣiptikā*. Thus ends the *gāndhārapañcama* [rāga]. From that [rāga] is born the *sphuritagāndhāra*, known as a *deśī* [rāga], which omits *ṛṣabha*, has *gāndhāra* as its *graha*, *aṃśa*, and *nyāsa*, and is characterized by a low-pitched *mandra* and equal intervals (*samasvara*). (106)

Thus ends the description of the region (deśa). Thus end the components of the rāga. Travaṇā is a variant of Ṣaḍja; it abounds in Dha, Ni, Sa, and Bha; it is embellished by Dha, Ni, and Sa; its tonic (aṃśa), leading note (graha), and final note (nyāsa) are Dha; and it is devoid of Ri and Pa.
The *vijaya* [jāti] is considered to have two *gama*s (octaves), with *mandra* (*dha* and *ni*) as its primary notes; it consists of 108 beats.
Its formula is: *dhā dhā dhā mānī sā nī sāsa nī sā sāsa nī dhā dha sāsa sani sā sani dhā nī nī dhā nī sā sā sa ni sa ni ni dha dhā dhā māṃ gā gaṃ sāṃ sa sa ni dha dhā*.
māṃ gāṃ māṃ māṃ nī dhāmāṃ magāga sā sa sani dhānī dhānī nidha nidha gāgamāṃ sasanī nīnidhānīnidhāni dhāni sani | dhādhadhamādhādhā— this is the *ālāpa* (introductory melodic phrase).

Thus, the Bhāṣā Ragantī is derived from that [Rāga]; it ends on Dha, possesses the Gāndhāra as its final note (gatārā), has Madhyama in the lower register (mandra), with Ma as both the primary (graha) and secondary (aṃśa) notes;
it contains very little Ṣaḍja, is devoid of Pañcama, and is employed in the sentiment of pathos (karuṇa). 113.
Thus ends the Āsāvarī.

The *vibhāṣā* is on the *kakubha* scale; it increases enjoyment, moves with high and low notes, has *dhaivata* as its *aṃśa*, *graha*, and *nyāsa*, with *gāndhāra* as its *apanyāsa*, and is devoid of *ṛṣabha*.
It is employed for intense detachment (*vairāgya*) through the frequent use of *dhaivata*, *gāndhāra*, *pañcama*, and *ṛṣabha*. 114.

Dhā-dhā-dhādha gāmā-pā papa mama pāpā-pama mā gā mānī dhā-sanī gā-sanī | Dhā pāmā-pāmā-nī-dhā pāmā dhāya-pa madha pama-madhā dhā-dha-gā-pāmā-gā mā-pā-pā-papa-gā mapa-ga-manī dhā-sanī gā-sanī dhā-pamā gāmā-nī-dhā-dhā | Dha-pa-madha-pa-ma-dhā-dhā— thus the recitation.

Ga-ma-dha-pā-ma-gā ma-ga-ma-ma-dha dha-ni ni-ni ṣaḍja sa-dha-dha dha-ni pa-pa-pa-ga-gā ma-dhā pā ma-dhā-pā ma-dha-ni dhā-dhā-nī sā-dha-dha-ni dha-ma-pa-pa ma-ma-dha-gā-gā | ma-ga-ma-ma-dha-ni ni-ni ṣaḍja sa-dha-dha-nī ni-ni dha-ma-pa-pa-pa-ga-gā-ma-dhā pā-ma-dhā-pa-ma dha-ni-dhā— thus is the *rūpaka*.

Thus, Bhogavardhanī, born from that [raga], is Velāvalī; it is tāra-dhā with gamandra, possesses equal svaras, has dha at the beginning and end of its *aṃśa*, features a trembling ṣaḍja, and is dear to Hari in the sentiment of separation (*vipralambha*). 115.

Thus, the Velāvalī rāga, with the nyāsa on the fifth part (pañcamāṃśa), containing the dhā and rī notes, intense in ga and low in ga, should be sung by experts during festivities; this is the first Mañjarī. 116.
Thus ends the first mañjarī.
The Bhāṣā known as Dhanyāśā has the Vāṅgālī rāga; it is formed from the *bhinna-ṣaḍja* scale, with *ga* as the *panyāsa*, long *ri*, and *dha-ma* in the *uddīpana*. 117.

Lord Śārṅgin ordained that the *dhapa* [scale] should be applied to the *vīra-rasa*.
Thus ends the sound of *nāda*;
the *sauvīra* [tune], produced with the *ṣaḍja-madhyamā* [grāma], is accompanied by the *kākalī* [interval]. 120–121.
Gālpa has Ṣaḍja as its *graha*, *nyāsa*, and *aṃśa*; it possesses the *mūrchanā* beginning with Ṣaḍja;
and through the *vārṣabha* and *prasanna-ādi* [tānas], it is dear to Śiva for use at the commencement of entry by self-restrained ascetics and householders in the *śānta* rasa. 122.
It should be performed in the final watch of the night, in the heroic, the fierce, and the marvelous sentiments.
Sāṃ sapā padhānī dhāpā padhā sā sapāpa dhā sā sapāpadhā dha gāri mā gā ri sani sa pā dhā sani sāṃ | māṃ māṃ magārī ri mā ma pā pa dha ni dhā pāpadhā.

Sāṃ sa pā padhā dhagā ri mā gā rī sanidhā dhapā sā sanī sāṃ sāṃ | Mama sama ṣaḍja sasaṃ sāṃ ga saṃ ga ga rī ga sā saṃ saṃ sa dha dha ni ni dha sa ni dha ni dhā dha pa | Papa padhadha dha sa ni sāṃ sāṃ saṃ saṃ saṃ sama ṣaḍja sasaṃ sasaṃ ||

ga sa sa ma ri ri ga sa sa ga dha dha ni dha dha ga saṃ saṃ saṃ dha ni dha sa ni dha ni dha dha pañcama pā pā pa ri pā pani dha dha sa sā sa sā dha ma ri ri dha ma ri ri dha ma sa pa | dha dha ni ga dha dha sa sa dha dha ni dha sa ni dha ni dha dha pā | pā pā pā gāndhāra gā.

Ga ga ma ri sa ga sa ni dha sa sa | Pa pa dha dha sa ni sa | Sa saṃ sa pa pa pa ni ni ni ṣaḍja sa sa sa ri ri ri ri pa ri pā dha dha sa ni sā | Sa dha ma ri ri dha ma mā ri ri ga sa sa ga dha dha ni dha dha ga sa sa sa dha ni dha sa ni dha ni dha dha pa dha dha ri ni |
Dhadhadha garimagarisani dhasanidha nidha papandhari nidhasadha garimagarimagarimagarisani dhasamāpapadhadha sanisā— this is the *ālāpa*.
Ṣaḍja sapañcamanīdhā dhā dhā nī pañcamanīdhā dhā dhanī ṣaḍja.

Sasārī ri ri papani dhādhā dhadhasa dhani dha pā | Papa ni dha paṃ paṃ niṃ riṃ riṃ ga ri mari sāsā mama ri ga sā sa sasa sa ri ga sā sasani dha pañcama dhā ni ṣaḍja sa sa | Mama sa sasa sa masa sāṃ sasari ga gasaṃ ga sāṃ ga ||

Saṃ gāṃ sa ga sa ni dhi ni dhā dha dha ni pā | pa gāṃ dha gāṃ dha gāṃ ga ga sa mā rī ṣaḍja sa ni dhā pā pā pā dhā pā dha ni ni ṣaḍja sa māṃ māṃ ga gā rī ṛṣabha ri ri ma ma dha ma ma | mā sāṃ sa pañcama dhā sā dha ni ni pā ni dha pā rī pa pa pa pa dha dha saṃ saṃ saṃ dhaṃ dhaṃ dha dha ma ma ma.
ri ri ri ri ga ri ga sa sā dha ni dha sā dha ni dha ri pa pa pa pa | pa dha dha dha ni ni pañca ma pa ma dha dha dha ni ṣaḍja sa sāṃ— thus is the *karaṇa*. This is the *sauvīra* [jāti].
Sāṃ sāṃ sāṃ sāṃ sāṃ sāṃ sāṃ sāṃ taruṇa-taru-śikhara nī nī dhā dhā pā pā pā mā.

*lā gatiḥ* 0—this is the *ākṣiptikā*. Thus ends the *sauvīra*.
The *sauvīrī* is the root language derived from that, characterized by an abundance of middle [syllables].
In this [raga], there is a melodic agreement (saṃvāda) beginning with Ṣaḍja and ending with it, as well as between Sadha and Ridha. 124.
Sā gā sā sā nī dhā sā sā mā dhānī dhā pā pādhā mā dhā samadhāni dhānirigā rimāmā gārīsā sā mādhānīdhāsāsā.

Thus is the sauvīrī. The varāṭikā born from that is the same as the caṭukī; it consists of the portions of the *sanyāsa* and is employed in the *śānta* [raga] with a high tonic (*tāra*) and soft (*sāndha*) [intervals]. 125.
Thus ends the *śuddhavarāṭī*.
In *hindola*, the *piñjarī* dialect consists of the notes Ga, Ma, Pa, Ni, Sa, and Dha, excluding Ri;
it is: gā-gā-ri-sā-dhā-ri-sā-sā-ri-gāṃ-māṃ-mā-mā-ri-ri-sā-dhā-sā-pā-pā-gā-pā-dhā-sā-ri.
gā-pā-mā-gā-rī-sā-sā-ni-sā-dhā-rī-sā-sā-rī-gā-sā-rī-gā-gā-mā-mā-gā-rī-sā-rī-ri-ga-ri-rī-sa-ri-māṃ | pāṃ-dhā-pā-sā-ri-gā-mā-ri-rī-sā | Thus ends Piñjarī.
The Naṭṭā [jāti] born from that [Gāndhāra-grāma] has equal tones (samasvarā), with *tāra* (high) *gāndhāra*, *pañcama*,
*saṃnyāsa*, *aṃśa*, and *graha* notes on *ṣaḍja*, and *mandra* (low) *niṣāda* and *tāra* *dhaivata*.
127 Thus ends the description of Naṭṭā.
The Lord of the Śrī-Karaṇa states that in the *śṛṅgāra* [rasa], the *aṅga* consists of the Karṇāṭa and Vaṅgāla [styles], excluding the *vegarañjī*, and ending with the *gāṃśa*.
(128) Thus ends the Karṇāṭa-Vaṅgāla.
Thus are the components of the *bhāṣā*:
it extends up to the fifth note; it has *ṣaḍja* as its final (*nyāsa*), introductory (*aṃśa*), and tonic (*graha*) notes; it is characterized by a high-low (*tāramandra*) range;
and it abounds in *riṣabha* and *ṣaḍja*. This is considered the *rāmakṛti* by the wise. 129

Thus ends the *Rāmakṛti*. Those who know it declare that the *Gauḍakṛti* has *ṣaḍja* as its *aṃśa*, *graha*, and *nyāsa*; it abounds in *ma* and *pa*, omits *ri* and *dha*, and has *pa* as its low (*mandra*) note. (130)

Thus, the Gauḍa-kṛti is slow in tempo, has a medium range, omits the *ri* note, consists of even tones, and possesses the *nyāsa*, *aṃśa*, *dhā*, *graha*, and *samāpatti* notes; it is used in the heroic (*vīra*) sentiment. 131.
Thus, the *devakṛti* [is established]; these are the primary limbs (*aṅga*) of the *kriyā*,
while the six *sanyāsa-aṃśagrahas* are the secondary limbs (*upāṅga*) of the *varāṭī*.
In that [context], the Kauntalī is accompanied by the mandra [note] and is characterized by a pervasive tremor (kampadhārita);
thus ends the description of the Kauntalī-varāṭī.
The Drāviḍī is characterized by the bhūri-nimandra [note] and the throbbing ṛṣabha [note].
Thus, the Drāviḍī,
Varāṭī, Saindhavī, Bhūrigāndhārā, and Sadhakampitā have been described by Śārṅgadeva as being in the low and middle registers for the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra). 133
Thus ends the *maṇḍitā* in the Saindhava style, with slow tempos and the *varāṭikā* for the *apasthāna*.
Thus ends the *apasthānavarāṭikā*.
Itasvarā is that which is soft (dhamandra) and trembling, while Hatapañcamā is said to be Hatasvaravarāṭī; Pratāpavarāṭī is soft (dhamandra), trembling, and possesses the *pa* and *sa* notes. 135.
Thus, the *pratāpavarāṭī* and the *varāṭyupāṅgas*;
while the *toḍī* itself when abandoned by its *ripha* is celebrated as *chāyātoḍī*.
Thus, the *Chāyā-toḍī* is like a *Toḍī* struck by a *Gālpā*; it is exceedingly similar to the *Turuṣkī*. (136) Thus ends the *Turuṣka-toḍī*.
Thus, these two are the *upāṅgas* of *Toḍī*, abandoned by the fifth note (*pañcama*), with *mandra* *niṣāda* struck during the festival;
they should be sung ending on *ṛṣabha*. Now, however, is *Mahārāṣṭrī-Gurjarī*. (137)
Thus, the Mahārāṣṭrī and Gurjarī [traditions]— or rather, the Gurjarī itself— may become Saurāṣṭrī due to regional variation;
thus, it is the Saurāṣṭrī-Gurjarī.
The *dakṣiṇagurjarī* has a trembling middle [register] and the other [registers] are struck;
thus ends the *dakṣiṇagurjarī*.
When the low (*mandra*) and high (*tāra*) notes of *ri* are vibrated (*sphurita*) in joy, it is the *drāviḍagurjarī*. 138–139.
Thus, the Drāviḍa-gurjarī; and the Gurjarī-upāṅgas are those which do not abandon the āndolita-sapā, and are endowed with the dhanyāsa, aṃśa, and graha [notes].
"In the case of *vipralambha*, it should be *bhuñchī*; so said the son of Soḍhala. Thus ends *bhuñchī*, which is modulated by the middle *niṣāda* and has abandoned the fifth note (*pañcama*).
Ending with the *khaṃbhāita* bite, it is employed in the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).
Thus ends the *khaṃbhāiti*.
The *chāyāvelāvalī* has a trembling, low-pitched tone like that of the *velāvalī*. 141–142.
Thus, that very *Chāyāvelāvalī* (Series of Shadows), preceded by *Pratāpa* (Heat/Valor) and struck [by the sun], becomes free from enemies. 143.
Thus ends the *Pratāpavelāvalī*.

Thus, there are four subsidiary sections (*upāṅgas*) of the *Velāvalī*: the *Dhaṃśanyāsagrahā*, which is adorned with the high (*tāra*), low (*manda*), and *gāndhāra* notes; and the *Bhairavī*, which is the subsidiary section of *Bhairava* and possesses all the musical notes (*svara*) in equal measure. 144.

Thus has Bhairavī been described as a subsidiary form (upāṅga) of Kāmodā; it is called Siṃhalī by the wise, endowed with the characteristics of Kāmodā, possessing a low-pitched *mandra* tone, and featuring a trembling *dhaivata*. 145

Thus is the Siṃhalī; the Kāmodā is a shadow-dance (chāyā-naṭṭā), while the Naṭṭā is adorned with the mandra-pañcama, possesses the maṭṭa-auxiliary (upāṅga), and is trembled by niṣāda and gāndhāra. 146

Thus, the *cchāyānaṭṭā*, *kolāhalā*, *ṭakkabhāṣā*, and *sagrahāṃśā* [melodies] are excluded; they are accompanied by *dhaivatamandra*, abound in *madhyama*, and are endowed with *gamakas* in the *kalahe* [rāga]. 147.

Sā-sā-sā-sā, mā-sā-sā-sa, sa-rī-gā-mā-mā-ga-rī, sa-rī-rī-dha, mā-rī-ga-rī, dha-ma-ma-gā-mā-rī-dhā, sā-dhā-sā-gā, rī-mā-dha-gā, ma-rī-ga-sā, sā-sā-sā-sa, ni-ga-sā-rī, mā-gā-mā-mā, rī-ga-rī-dha, ma-dha-ma-mā-rī-dhā, sā-gā-sā-dhā, sā-mā-rī-mā-dhā, gā-sā— thus the *ālāpa*.

*Ri ga sa dha sa ri ma dha ma ga ma gā ma ga rī sa ni dha sā ri ga rī gā mā dha dha sa sa saṃ sa ga rī ma ma dha ma ga ri sa ni dha sā ri gā mā dha ma rī ga ma sā dha ni dha sa ri gā mā ma ga ma dha ma gā rī sa ni dha sā ri gā sa rī gā sā mā gā rī mā rī gā sā sā— thus is the *rūpaka*.
Thus ends Kolāhalā.
From that [Kakubh] arises Rāmakṛti; in the heroic (vīra) sentiment, it consists of twenty-one mātrās and is devoid of the śānta [rasa].
Furthermore, although it is a *bhāṣāṅga* (a limb of the style), it is here considered an *upāṅga* (subsidiary limb) due to its extreme proximity.
This has been determined by Śārṅgadeva; let it be inferred by the wise in other cases as well (148).
Thus ends the *rāmakṛti* in the Hindola-bhāṣā, the Chevāṭī rhythm, with *ma* as the introductory note (*nyāsa*) and an abundance of *dha* and *bha*.
In the *ṛṣabha-hīna-aṃśa-graha-nyāsa-ṣaḍja* [rāga], which possesses *ṣaḍja*, *ga*, *ma*, and *mandra*,
it should be sung with *gamakas* during the *saga-tāra-utsava* (joyful high-pitched *sa-ga*) and the *hāsya* (comic) sentiment.
*Sāsā sā-sa-ga-ma pa-pā pa-pa-ma ga-pa-ma-gā-pā-dhā-gā dhā-nī pa-pa-ga-ma nī-dhā-pā-pā*...
*Magapagā gasāsāsā sagamapapāpā pamagāpamagā dhānīpāpamagapamagapamagāgasā sapānīsā sāsāgāsā magāmapa panisāsā— this is the *ālāpa*.
Sama gama gapā pāma pamapama gāgā gāgasasāsagamani nisa nisasasagasa mama.*
*nini sani sāsasagasagamapapasanisāgāsā dhāni pānī nīpā magā gapamama gāmasāṃsāṃ gāṃmāṃ pānī māsā gāsa nī sāsā*— this is the *rūpaka*, and this is the *cchevāṭī*.

The Vallātā is its subsidiary (upāṅga); it is devoid of Ṛṣabha, possesses a deep Dhaivata as its final note (nyāsa), and has both the tonic (aṃśa) and the opening note (graha) as Dhaivata; it is to be sung in the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), as declared by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow (Viṣṇu).
Thus ends the Vallātā.
Born from the middle and fifth notes, joined with *kākali* and *antara*, having the fifth as its *aṃśa*, *graha*, and *nyāsa*, and possessing the *mādhyamasaptaka-pañcama* scale;
endowed with the *hṛṣyakā* *mūrcchanā*, it should be sung, having Kāma and others as its presiding deities. (151)

And *Cārusaṃcārivarṇa*, characterized by graceful movement, is employed during the first watch of a summer day at the juncture (*saṃdhi*) of the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and comic (*hāsya*) rasas, specifically in the *Avamarśa* (the crisis) juncture. The sequence is:
*pā-dhā-māṃ-dhā-nī-dhā-pā-pā; pa-dha-nī-ri-ma-pa-dhā-mā; dha-ni-dha-pā-pā-riṃ-gāṃ-sāṃ-sāṃ*.
māṃ pamā gāṃ rī rīṃ | rī māṃ pa dha mā pa ni dha pā pā | sāṃ gāṃ nī dha pā pa ni rī māṃ pā dha mā dha ni dha pā pā— this is the *ālāpa*.
pā pa dha pa dha ma dha dha ni dha pā pā | pā pā dha ni ri ga pa pā mā dha ni dha pā pā pa pa dha ni.
*rīrī gaṃgaṃ saṃsaṃ gaga rīṃrīṃ rīṃrīṃ mama papa dhama dhadha nidha pā*—this is the *karaṇa*. It is *śuddhapañcama*.

"Save me, save me! O Nīṃ, protect, protect! O Bhava, be my refuge! Thus ends the *ākṣiptikā*. This concludes the *śuddhapañcama* [melodical mode].
Its language should be South Indian (Dākṣiṇātyā), with G, R, and D as the primary notes (nyāsa), and Dha as the secondary note (dhaivata).
In this rāga, R is the introductory note (panyāsa), while T, N, M, P, and Dha are the concluding notes (tāra).
Its application is for the recollection of a beloved.

Pāpā dhāsā nirīrīrī garimari gapagaga nīsānīmā nīdhā pāpā pādhā sanī rīrīrīrī garī sagārīsanī rīrīrī nīnī gapanīdha nīnī sānī sanī māgarīrī rīrī marī sanī nīdha nidhā pānī nidhāpāpamadhā pāsā pādhāsanī.
*rīrī rīrīrīrī garīgaga pāpānīdhā pāpāpā*— this is the *ālāpa*.
*papadhadhasanī rīrī garī sanī dhanī nīpa padha dhasa nīrī rīga nīsa nīrī rīga nīsa nidhā nīnī pāpā*— this is the *rūpaka*.

Thus ends the Dākṣiṇātyā style of speech. Its variant, known as Āndhālikā, is considered to have its *graha* and *nyāsa* on the fifth note (*pañcama*), with few syllables and a great abundance of musical notes. 154
With *tāra* (high) *ṣaḍja* and *mandra* (low) *ṣaḍja*, with *dha* as the *nyāsa*, and devoid of *ga*,
this [rāga] is proclaimed by the Lord Śārṅgin to be sung in the *viyuktabandhana* (separated-binding) mode:
*pā pā mā mā sa rī, mā pā, dhā pā, dhā pa, dha dha, pa dha, dha pa pa sā, mā sā, sā rī, rī mā, pā dhā*.

*Padha māsa nidhā pāpadhapadhapapamā māsā sārī pādhā pādhā papa dhadha padha dhadha dhama pāpā masā rīmā sārī māsārī mā sārī māsārīmādhāpa dhadhapadhā padha dhapa mamamāma sārīmāpā dhāpa dhapā dhāsā nīdhā pāpa dhapa papāpā*— this is the *ālāpa*.
*rīrī sārīrī sarīrīsarī rīsa rīpa rīsa rīsa dhadha pādhadhapa dhadhadhadha pamamā | mamā pamadhā | padhāmāmapapamādhasadhasadhapamadhā*— this is the *rūpaka*. This is the *āndhālī* dialect.

Mahārī is its subsidiary (upāṅga); it is devoid of the *mandra* [register], possesses the *pañcama* as its *aṃśa*, *graha*, and *nyāsa*, and is considered to be struck (*tāḍita*) in the *śṛṅgāra* rasa.
Thus ends Mahārī.
Geya is Karṇāṭagauḍa, which has Ṣaḍja as its nyāsa, graha, and aṃśa; that same [Karṇāṭagauḍa], when modulated (āndolita) on Ṣaḍja and devoid of Ṛṣabha and Pañcama, is Deśavāla. 158.
Thus, the Deśavāla [rāga],
which abounds in gāndhāra, is struck in the low register (mandra), is devoid of riṣabha,
and has niṣāda as its aṃśa, graha, and nyāsa, is called the Gauḍa-turuṣka. 159
Thus, this Drāviḍagauḍa is to be sung with the Turuṣkagauḍa and the Gāndhāratiripa, featuring a shimmering Ṣaḍja and Pañcama, and having the seventh note as its grāha, aṃśa, and nyāsa. 160
Thus, there are the Drāviḍa and Gauḍa [styles], the Gauḍa-aṅgas and upāṅgas,
and together with the Janaka, fifty-two [in total].
Now, the definition of the musical mode (rāga) Śrīrāga, which is well-known for its passionate expression: it originates from the Ṣaḍja scale, possesses a diminished pañcama,
has the nyāsa, aṃśa, and graha notes on Ṣaḍja, a low gāndhāra, and a high madhyama.
The foremost of the illustrious *karaṇas* teaches that in the *vīra-rāga*, the final note (*śeṣasvara*) is the same [as the tonic].
Thus ends the *śrī-rāga*.
In the *ṣaḍja-grāma*, it is devoid of the low register (*mandra*) and is formed by the *ṣaḍjamadhyamā* scale.
The Baṅgāla has all its notes equal to the Ṣaḍja [scale], with the nyāsa, aṃśa, and graha on the Ṣaḍja. (162) Thus ends the Baṅgāla.
The Kaiśikī-born [rāga] has the nyāsa, aṃśaka, and graha on the Madhyama and Ṣaḍja.
The fifth note (*pañcama*) situated between *tāra* [and *mandra*] shall be the *samasvara* (equal tone) in Baṅgāla;
thus ends the second Baṅgāla.
It should have *ṛṣabha* as its *aṃśa*, end with *pañcama*, and have *dhaivata* as its *apanyāsa*.
It possesses the heroic, the fierce, and the marvelous sentiments; its *pālya* is *madhyama-ṣāḍava*.
Thus ends *madhyama-ṣāḍava*. It should be endowed with *dhaivata* as its *aṃśa*, *graha*, and *nyāsa*, and it should consist of equal notes (*samasvara*).
This Śuddhabhairava has *tāra* (high) *ṣaḍja* and *mandra* (low) *gāndhāra*, and is characterized by *ṣaḍja*.
Thus ends Śuddhabhairava;
it arises from *dhaivatika* in the *ṣaḍja* scale, and its primary note is equal to *ṣaḍja*.
Megharāga is devoid of *mandra* (low pitch), with *dhaivata* as its *graha*, *aṃśa*, and *nyāsa*.
Thus ends Megharāga.
[Next is] Ṣāḍjī-born, which arises from Ṣaḍja; it has Ṣaḍja as its *graha*, *aṃśa*, and *anta*, and is predominant in *niṣāda*.
Somarāga is remembered as being in the heroic (vīra) sentiment; its *madhyama* [note] is situated between the sharp (*tāra*) and the middle (*madhya*).
Thus ends Somarāga.
Its *graha* (tonic) is sharp-ṣaḍja; it arises from Ṣaḍjamadhyamikā in the scale of ṣaḍja.
With *gata* and *aramandra*, it is *kāmoda*, having *dha* as its *aṃśa*, ending on *sa*, and possessing equal intervals (168).
Thus ends *kāmoda* in the *ṣaḍja* scale, which arises from *ṣāḍjī* and is endowed with *ṣaḍja* as its *graha*, *aṃśa*, and *nyāsa*.
Samasvara is another [type of] Kāmoda; Mandragāndhārasundara is [another].
Thus ends the second Kāmoda.
[The next is] that which has Gāndhāra as its *aṃśa*, *graha*, and *nyāsa*, and arises from Madhyamāndhrī.
The *rāga* Āmrapañcama, devoid of the *mandra* [register], has been described by Śārṅgadeva as having the comic (*hāsya*) and the marvelous (*adbhuta*) sentiments as its basis.
Thus ends Āmrapañcama. (170)

Thus are the ten well-known rāgas. Kaiśikī would be the bhāṣā of the pure pañcama; it is abundant in ma, with pa as the nyāsa, aṃśa, and graha; it has sa as the nyāsa, and possesses ga, ma, and ta at the beginning. 171.
Some have stated that the *bhāṣā-aṅga* should be employed in the expression of envy (*īrṣyā*).
In a festival, there should be equal tones, *aritārā*, *sāma*, and *mandrā*. [The melodic pattern is:
*pā-pā-pā*, *samadhā*, *sānī*, *sā-sā-sā-dhā*, *mā-sa-sama*, *dhā-sa-nī-sarī*, *gā-sā-sā*, *sa-dha-ma*.
*māmāsasa dhasamanī nīdhā māmagamā pāpa samadhāsā mā dhāsā | pādhāsāmādhā-samādhāsani sani rīsanī gasā | sadhamāgā gasa sāsa dhamāsasa dhasamanī nīdhāmāma gāmā pāpā*— thus the *ālāpa*.

*pāmā-mā-dhasa-ni dhasa-ni dhasa-ni-dhā mā-dha-gā-ga-sa sa-ni-dha pā-pā-ri-ga-sa-ri-ga mā ri-ga-sa-dha-ni-dhā mā-ni-dha-sa-sā-sa ma-mā ni-dhā sa-pā dha-ma-ri-ga ri-mā-dha-ma-dha-ni-dha-ni dha-ni dha madhyama ma-ni-dhā sā-sa ma-mā ni-dha sa pā-pā— thus is the *rūpaka*.

Thus, from the Kaiśikī [jāti] itself, the Saurāṣṭrī language has *pa* as its final note (*graha*) and *aṃśa*, is devoid of *ri*, possesses *ga* and *dha*, is characterized by high notes (*tāra*), lacks low notes (*mandra*), and consists mostly of equal intervals. 173.

Appointed among all states of being by the sages, it is endowed with the means of understanding (174). It is the destroyer of sin, the non-sinful, the one who possesses no wealth, the one who abides in the teaching, the one who bestows peace, the singer, the singer, the supporter, the supporter, the one who holds, the one who holds, the one who gives, the one who gives, the sinful,

the one who destroys sin, the protector, the one who supports the protectors, the one who is not a mother, the one who is the mother, the one who possesses wealth, the one who is the mother of wealth, the one who is the wealth of the mother, the peaceful one, the peaceful one, the singer, the singer, the song.

*Sā sā sa ni gā ni dhā dhā dha dha sā dha ma pa pā pa pā dhā pā dhā pā mā mā | ma dha ni ma dha ni | māṃ dhani sā sā pa mā ni ni dha pa ma dhā pa ma dha pā pā— this is the *ālāpa*. Pā pa ma sa ni sā sa ni ga ga sa sa ni ga ga ni ni ga ma ga ni dhā dhā dha dha ma dha.*

Sasa | pādhā pādhā pāmā māmā mamadhama dhadhanī sā sani gaga sāsa | nidhadhasa nidhamapā pamadhadha pamadhasa pamadhadha dhaga manī dhadha pā | pamanī nī nīdhā pama dhadha pama dhadha pā— this is the *rūpaka*.

Thus is the Saurāṣṭrī. The Saurāṣṭrī ends with the *saṃśagraha* (the *sānuprāsa*); it is characterized by many *ṭakkara*-agamas, many *tārās*, and is slow (*mandra*) and devoid of *paha*. It occurs in the Karuṇa rasa. 175.

Sā sā sānī dhanī nīdha nīnī māṃ nī dhanī dhānī dhānī dhanī nī māṃ nīdhā nīsā sādha nīdhamadha nīdhanīdha mādhanīdha maṃ gāgāga maṃgāṃ sagā sanī dhanī nīdha nī nī dhanī nī nī māṃ nīdhā nīsā sā— this is the *ālāpa*.

Sa ni dha ni ni ni māṃ ni dha ni sā sā dha ni ni māṃ ni dha ni sā dha sa sa dha rī rī rī dha ma ma | dha ma ma madhyama ma gāndhāra ga ṣaḍja sa sā gā sā gā dha ni ni ni dha ni ma dha sā ni sā gā ni dha dha sā sā— thus is the *rūpaka*.

Thus ends the second Saurāṣṭrī; it is like the Ṭakka dialect, charming with soft and forceful notes, having Ṣaḍja as its *aṃśa*, *graha*, and *nyāsa*, with Ṣaḍja as the lowest note (*mandra*), and devoid of R̥ṣabha and Pañcama.
In the festival of heroes, the wise have declared the *tāragāndhāradhaivata* [rāga] to consist of the following sequence:
sā-sā sā-sa ma-ma dha-dhā dha-dha ma-dhā mā-ma gā-ga ma-sā sa-ga ma-sa-ga ma dha-dhā dhā-dhā dha-ma-dha-nī nī-dhā-mā-ma gā-ga-māṃ sāṃ sa-dha-nī-nī dha-nī nī-dha nī-gā-ga-sa sā-gā-sa-nī.

*Dhanī sā-sā sā-sa-ma-ma-sā ma-sa-gama dha-dhā dhādha ma-dhā-nī-nī dhā-mā-ma-gā ga-ma-sā-sa dhā-nī nī-dha nī-nī-dha-dha nī-gā-ga-sā | sā-gāṃ sa-nī dhā-nī sā-sā— this is the *ālāpa* (introductory melodic phrase).
Sa-ma-ma-dha dha-dhā-maṃ-dha dha-mā-mā gāṃ-dhā-ra ga-sā-sā-ga ma-dha-dha-nī nī-dhā-mā | dhā-mā— * [The text continues with the melodic progression.]*
*madha gāgāgasa sāsasasa gagasaga masagama dhādhādhanī dhadhanīma mapadhamā gasasa-masa gasāsāsasanīdhadhanī dhanīgāgāgasāṃ ga dhānīṃ sāsā— thus is the *rūpaka*;
thus is the *lalitā*.
Even when the *ṣaḍja* is divided, the *lalitā* [jāti] has *dhaivata* as its *graha*, *aṃśa*, and *nyāsa*.
It is endowed with the *ṛṣabha*, *gāndhāra*, and *madhyama* notes played in a graceful manner at both high and low pitches, and it possesses *dhaivata* in the lower register.
This is to be employed for expressions of grace and affection, according to the consensus of the sage Mataṅga. (177–178)

Dhā-dhā-dhā-dha sa-nī, dhā-dhā-dha-dha nī-rī, gā-sa-nī-sā, nī-dhā-dhā-dha sa-nī, rī-gā-mā; Ga-rī, mā-gā, rī-rī-rī-rī-rī, ga-ma-pa-dhā-dha-pa nīṃ-dhā, pā-mā, gā-rī, mā-gā-rī; Rī-ga-rī-ga, ma-ga-ma-rī, gā-mā-gā-rī, dha-nī, rī-gā-sa-nī; Dhā-dhā-dha-ma, dhā-dhā-dha-dha, nī-rī, rī-dhā, nī-rī.
Dhānī rīgā sanī sanī dhādhādhadha sariga magari māmā rīrīrīrīrī magapadhā padhanīdhāpāmā gārī māgā rīrī gamagamaṃ rīgāmāgā rīdhānīrīmā sanī sanī dhādhā— this is the *ālāpa*.

Dhaivata sa-ga-ni-sa ri-ga ri-ma sa-ni dha-ni dha-ma-mā-dha dha-ma-ni-ni dha-dha-dha-dha rī-rī-rī-rī ga-ma | maṃ-maṃ gā-rī dhā-pā-ma-ga-rī-mā-gā-rī sa-nī dha-dha-nī ga-gā | sa-nī sa-nī dhā-nī-māṃ-dhā sa-nī-nī-dhā-dhā— thus is the *rūpaka*.
Thus ends the second *lalitā*.

Therein, the *saindhavī* [tāna] is fourfold; it is in the *ṭakkabhāṣā*, devoid of the *ripa* [note], dense with *saṃnyāsa*, *aṃśa*, and *graha*, and characterized by *gamakas* that glide over the notes.
This [melody], characterized by the *Ṣaḍjamandra* scale with the *arā* notes omitted, should be sung in all sentiments (rasas).
Sā Sā Sā Sā | Māṃ Sā Māṃ Sā | Maṃ Sa Gā Mā Gā Sā Sā Gāṃ Sā Māṃ Sā Sa Ma Ma Gā Mā Ga Ma Ma Sa Nī Ga Sa Sā Sa Nī Māṃ Sa Nī Gāṃ Nī Dhāṃ Dhāṃ | Dha Mā Dhāṃ Dhā Dhaṃ Mā Nī Nī Nī || 179 ||
*Dhā mā dhā dhā dhā dha ma nī nī nīṃ dha nī dha nī sā sā*— this is the *ālāpa*.
*Ma madhyama ma ṣaḍja sa sā ga āsa sā | nī nī nī nī sa dha nī sa nī dhā dhā dha mā dha ma ma nī dhā dhā dha ma ma nī nī nī nī nī nī sa nī sa nī ga ga sā sā ma ma ga ma ma dha ga*

*gagasama nīnīdhadha mamadhama dhanīnīnī madhanīnī nīdhanīsagamadhadha gadha maga sanī sanī sasanīdha nīnīnīsanīdhamama dhadha nīnī samagaga nīnīnīma nīdhamamadhadhanīnīgagasā sā*— thus is the *rūpaka*.

Thus, there is also a Saindhavī in the fifth [jāti], characterized by the *graha*, *aṃśa*, and *nyāsa* on the fifth note (pa), joined with the *apanyāsa* on the fourth (ri), and beautiful with the notes sa, ga, and ma. 180.
The *nītarai* [tune] is employed as before, beginning with *ribahustārapā*. 181.
*pāpāpā sa padha sarī rī rī rī rī pamadhapama dhapāpāsa padhasarī rīrīrīsa-rīgārī | mārī pādhā sārī gāsā rīrīrīrī gāpāṃ rīṃ rī gāsasarī rīmādhā* ||

*Pamadha-pamadha pāpā-sapadhama padhama-padha mapadha-sanīrīrī marīsarī rīpamadha pamadha-pāpā | sapadhasarī | rīrīrīsa rīrīrīsa rīgārīmādhāpādhāsārī gāsārīrīdharīrī gāṃ pāṃ rīrī māsasarī rīsā dhāpamadhāpamadhāpāpā— thus the *ālāpa*.

*padhasadhasarī gasarigarīsarī | garīsādha madhaṃ dhaṃpa pasarīrī rīrīpārī papapārī rimamāmāṃmāsasārī sarīrīrī rīsasadha dhapapapadhadhasaga paṃdhaṃ sarī sarīgama dhadhapādhā pamadhadha pamadhadhapāpā— thus is the *rūpaka*.
Thus ends the second *saindhavī*.
In the *mālava-kaishika* [jāti], there is also a *saindhavī* characterized by soft *pañcama*, with *mandra* [notes], devoid of *ni* and *ga*, and having *ṣaḍja* as its *nyāsa*, *graha*, and *aṃśa*.
This [rāga], proclaimed by the son of Śrī Soḍhala, is to be employed in all musical modes (sarvabhāva):
Sā-sā-sā-sā sa-ma-rī-mā pā-pā-pa dha-pa-dhā-pā mā rī-rī mā rī-rī sāṃ sāṃ sa-ma-rī-mā pā-pā pa-pa dha-pā-mā | pa-pa dha-pā mā pā-pā pa-pa-dhā sā pa-pa dhā-sā dhā-rī || 182 ||

*rīmapādhāpama rīrī marīrīsarīsārīsasāsārī māsārīmāmārī māpāpāpapadhāpā-dhāpadhāpāmārīrīmārīmāsā | samarīmā pāpā papa dhāpāpāmā dhāpāmāpā papa padhā sāṃ papadhā pamārīṃ rīṃ mapādhāpamarīmārī rīsāsā— thus the *ālāpa*.

sama rīrī mamariri papa ripa papādhāpa marīrī samamamari papa papa dhadha ṣaḍja saṃ pādhāpāmārīmarīmarīsarīsādhadhasadha ṣaḍja sasa mama riri papa riri sa risa ri sāsa dhasa sasaṃ maṃ riri mama riri pādhāpama ririsarisāmariririsā—
Thus ends the *rūpaka*.
Thus is the third *saindhavī*; in the *bhinna-ṣaḍja* [jāti], it has *dhaivata* as its *nyāsa*, *aṃśa*, and *graha*.
In the *uddīpana* [sentiment], one should employ the *dhamandrā* [scale] devoid of the note *ri*:
dha dha dha dha ga ma dha ni, ni ni dha ni, sa ni sa ni sa dha, ni dha ni ni, dha dha ma ma ga ma, sa ni dha dha, pa ma dha dha dha ga sa dha ga ma ga dha ma dha ni ni, ni ni ni, dha ni sa dha ni ni.
The vocalization is: *madhāsānīdhādhamadhādhā*.
*Dhādha gamadhanī nīnī sanī dhanī nīnīnīdha ṣaḍja saṃ sanīnī sanī dhadha gamadhagamadha nīnī manī dhanī nīdha nīdha gāṃ sagamā nīsanī dhanīdhagamadhagama*.
*dhanīnīmanīdhanīnīdha dhāsā dhamanī sanī dhanīdha gamadhagamadhanī nīmanīdhanī-nīdhanīdhādhā*— this is the *rūpaka*. This is the fourth *saindhavī*.
The Hindola-bhāṣā is of the Gauḍī type; it has Ṣaḍja as its final (nyāsa), tonic (graha), and dominant (aṃśa) notes.
It is rich in gamakas arising from Pañcama, is devoid of Dhaivata, and should be employed by the wise with Ṣaḍja as the lowest note during affectionate conversation. (184)

Sāṃ māṃ sāṃ sa magāmāpāpāmāpāmāpā māgāmasāṃsāṃ sasa sagāmāpāpāgamagā magāpagāmapāpā | māgagasāsanīsāgāmāmagāsanīsāmāsa sagāsāsā sasa gāmā sāgāmāpa magā sāpā pāpā māmā gāga sāsā samagā | māpā māpā pā ||

*Pamagā | pa mā gama paga-pamā gama-pagā pamā-pagā pāsā-sāsaga-sāmā-gāsa-nisāṃ sāṃ— thus the melodic phrase (*ālāpa*). Ṣaḍja: sa ga ma ga pa ma ma ga ga sāṃ; Ṣaḍja: sa sa gā mā mā mā pā pa ma gā pa ma.*
*pagā gagasāpānī sanīsa magama gamapama pama gama mama ganisāṃ gagasagasanisāma-gāgasāsā— thus is the *rūpaka*. Thus ends the Gauḍī style.*

The Gauḍī rāga, which has Ṣaḍja as its *anya* (secondary note) and is characterized by the placement of the *aṃśa* (tonic) on the *graha* (principal note), is described by Mataṅga as being used in the Mālavakaiśika.

It possesses a high (*tāra*) and low (*mandra*) Ṣaḍja and abounds in Niṣāda; it should be employed in the sentiments of longing (*raṇaraṇaka*) and heroism (*vīra*), though it is used differently by others. 185–186.

Sāṃ sāṃ sāni dhāsāṃ pamā gāmānī nīdhanī dhadhamapamamagama magā gasāsagārī sāgāmagamanīnī dhama pama pāpa mama magarīmaṃ sāṃ sanī nīrīpā | sanīrīsa nīsāsā | magamanī gā mā nīgā mānī | nīdhasāpā māgāmanī nīdhadhanī.
*Dhā pa mā ga mā gā mā pā ma garī rī ma pa ga mā nī dha nī sa pā ma ga mā pā pā sāṃ ma ga rī rī sā sa nī rī rī pā sa nī rī sa nī rī sa nī sā sā— this is the *ālāpa*.
Sāṃ nī dha sa sa pā pā ma ma ga dha ni dha ni dha ni dha ma pa ma ga ma ma sā ma ga rī rī sāṃ sa nī.*
*rīrī pāṃsanī rīrī pāṃ sanī rīrīsā gamapā gānīdha pamamapamamagamagarī sani-sāsani sāsani riri sāsā*— this is the *rūpaka*.
This is the second *gauḍī*.

In the *yāṣṭika* [tāla], the *trāvaṇī* speech-pattern of the fifth [note] consists of the *graha*, *aṃśa*, and *sānta* [notes]; it is considered to have two *śrutis* due to the frequent conjunction of *sa*, *ri*, *ma*, and *pa*. 187.
*Sāsāsāpā pāpādhādhānīnī sānidhānidhā sārī sāsānīdhanīdha sārī*.
*gārī māsanī pāpādhānīsā sanīmadha dhasanīmadhamadhasanidhāmāgāmā sānīsa-sāsasaṃ sanisāṃsāṃ nigāsa nidhāmā māmāṃ sari sāsā sādhānidhāpāpā*.
Thus ends the *trāvaṇī*.
This is the *bhāṣāṅga*: "The other *dhagrahas* are abandoned by *ni*;
it is without *tārā*, and in a prayer, it is filled with deep *dhagas* and has a broad middle.
(188) Thus ends the *bhāṣāṅga*.
The *bhāṣā* is Harṣapurī; it is in the *ṣaḍjamandra* scale and the *mālavakaiśika* *jāti*.
Its *nyāsa*, *aṃśa*, and *graha* notes are *ṣa* (ṣaḍja), while *ma* (madhyama) is absent from the high register (*tāra*). It is used in the sentiment of joy (*harṣa*).
Sā sā sā sa ni sa ni sa ri sa ni sā sā | ma ga mā pā pā pā | sa ma pā pā pa ma mā ma || 189 ||

Gā-ga-rī | Rī-sāṃ-sa-ni-pāṃ-sa-ni-ma-ma-gā-rī-nī-nī-pā-sa-nī-sāṃ-sāṃ-sa-ri-rī-pāṃ-sa-ni-rī-sa-ni-rī-sa-ni-sā-sā | Sa-ni-sāṃ-rī-ni-sā-nī-nī-ni-sā-rī | Sa-ni-sāṃ-sāṃ | Ma-gā-mā-pā-pā | Sa-ma-pā-pa-ma-gā-ga-ma-mā-rī-rī-sā-ma-nī-pāṃ-sa-nī-sā-sā-gā-ga-rī-nī.

*nīpāsanīsāṃsāṃ | sanirīrī pāṃsanirī sanirī sanīsāṃ sāṃ*— this is the *ālāpa*. *sānī rīsā nī nīgarī sā | nirīrīga rīmarīga nīrīgarī nīsa madhyama ma gāndhāra gārī gagarīsārīgarīpāgarī sanī rīga rīnīsāsā*— thus [the *jāti-tāna*].
The *rūpaka* is thus [defined] in Harṣapura.
The fifth [note] may be a *vibhāṣā*, characterized by *bhammāṇī* and possessing a deep *ṣaḍja*.
In the *Utsava* [rāga], it begins with *pa*, *ā*, *nta*, *aṃśa*, and so on, with *sa*, *ma*, *ni*, *pa*, *i*, *ta*, *ra*, and *tyakta-ri*.
*pā-pā pā-ma-gā-mā pā-pā |* *mā-mā nī-dhā mā-ma-ga-mā pā-pā |* *pa-gā ga-mā sa-nī-dha-pā pā-pa-ma-nī nī-dha-nī-sāṃ sāṃ ga-ma-mā-pā pā-pa-ma-pa-ma-nī-sa-nī-dhā-pā-pā-pa-ma-pa-ma-nī-sa-ni-dhāṃ pā |*
"Pāpā pama ninidhāgāṃ māṃ pamani nidhāpasadhāpamadhapamadhāpāpā"— this is the vocalization (*ālāpa*).
Pāṃ pañcama paṃga gama pāmama gaga mama gaga mamani dhadhamagā ṣāpā | papagama-samasanidhasanidhapāpamaninini dhani nisamama gapamapamani sāni manidha pāpā pama ||
*Ni pāni nidhanī sasa pa ma ma mā dhāṃ dha ma dha pa ma dha dha sa ma dha dha pa pā— thus is the *rūpaka*.
This *ṭakkakaiśika* arises from *bhammāṇī*, *dhaivatī*, and *madhyamā*.
With Dhaivata as its *aṃśa*, *graha*, and *nyāsa*, adorned with *kākali* and *antara*,
possessing an ascending scale (*sārohi*), beginning with *prasanna*, and endowed with *uttarāyata*, it is employed in a forceful dance performed by a chamberlain during a festive gathering. 191–192.

Drāviḍī has Gāndhāra as its *aṃśa* and *graha*, and Dhaivata as its final note; it is a variant (*vibhāṣikā*) of that [Mālava].
In that [scale], the two intervals of Śruti for Ṣaḍja and Dhaivata should be conjoined. 195
Gā-sā-gā-mā dhā-dhā pā-mā dhā-dhā gā-sa ni-dhāṃ-dhā-sa gā-sa-ni dhā-pa-ni-mā-gā ma-ni-dhā.
Thus ends the Drāviḍī dialect.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Analysis of Rāgas," in the *Saṃgītaratnākara* composed by Śrī Śārṅgadeva—known as Niḥśaṅka, the son of the illustrious Soḍhaladeva, the sovereign of the illustrious Karaṇa department, and a delight in faultless learning.
Now begins the third chapter, titled "Miscellaneous Matters."
Now, Śārṅgadeva, the best among the learned, speaks of the miscellaneous [section], which is an unconfused elixir for the ears and which relies upon the regional (*deśī*) and path (*mārga*) styles:
(1) that which is sung is called *vāṅmātu* (the mother of speech), and it is designated as *dhātu* (the root).
He who composes both speech and song is a *vāggeyakāraka*. [The qualifications for this are:
knowledge of the science of grammar (*śabdānuśāsana*), proficiency in terminology (*abhidhāna*), mastery of the various types of meter (*chandas*), and skill in poetic ornaments (*alaṃkāra*). (2–3)
Mastery in discerning aesthetic sentiments and emotional states, proficiency in regional customs, knowledge of all languages, skill in the arts and sciences,
expertise in the three types of musical instruments, and possession of a charming physique.
Knowledge of the arts of laya and tāla, discernment among the various modulations of voice (kāku), the possession of abundant awakening of creative intuition (pratibhā), auspiciousness of song,
proficiency in regional melodies (deśī-rāgas), and eloquence of speech [are required] for success in the assembly.

The abandonment of passion and hatred, freshness, knowledge of what is appropriate, persistence in speech that is not stale, the creation of new themes, thorough understanding of the minds of others, and eloquence in compositions. (7)

The composition of rapid songs, skill in the use of varied meters, proficiency in the *gamakas* (modulations) of the three registers, expertise in various *ālaptis* (improvisations), and attentive concentration—
one who possesses these qualities is an excellent composer of lyrics.
One who composes excessively is superior; one who is slow in composing is middling;
one who is unskilled in composing both elements and measures is also middling in his compositions (10).
Even one who fashions beautiful measures is inferior if he is a maker of slow elements.
The composer of the *vastuka* is called the superior poet (*varakavi*), while the composer of the *varṇaka* is called the mediocre (*madhyama*).
Furthermore, the composer of the *kuṭṭikā* is proclaimed as the composer of the *mātrkā* in another classification. Thus ends the definition of the *vāggeyakāra*.
"He who knows both the *mārga* and the regional (*deśī*) [styles] is called a *gāndharva*";
thus, one who knows only the *mārga*, such as the notes (*svara*) and so forth, is designated as a *gāndharva*. 12.
Thus ends the section on vowels and so forth.
One who is pleasing, possesses a healthy body, is skilled in the release of the *grahas*, and is an expert in *rāga*, *rāgāṅga*, *bhāṣāṅga*, *kriyāṅga*, and *upāṅga*. 13.

Expert in the singing of musical compositions (*prabandha*), knowing the true principles of various improvisations (*alāpti*), his movement is effortless and graceful in all *sthāna*, *ucca*, and *gamaka*;
he possesses a controlled voice, knows the rhythmic timing (*tāla*), is attentive, and has overcome fatigue. (14)
He is skilled in perceiving pure shadows, understands all the nuances of vocal modulation, possesses boundless stability and movement, is free from all defects,
is intent on action, possesses the power of concentration (*jakvalaya*), is well-composed, and is endowed with meditative retention (*dhāraṇā*).
