The Hari who is radiant, swift, the maker of days, and preeminent in devotion is praised by those skilled in song as the foremost of singers belonging to the excellent tradition (susampradāya).
One who is devoid of only a few qualities but free from defects is considered "middling" (madhyama). 17.

The Mahāmāheśvara said: "The singer is of five types: the faulty, the inferior, the one who follows the rules of training, the imitator, the one who relishes the aesthetic flavor (*rasika*), the one who delights the audience (*rañjaka*), and the one who possesses emotional expression (*bhāvuka*). Thus they have declared the singer to be fivefold. (18–19)
One who is skilled in teaching without deficiency is considered by the wise to be a "maker of instruction" (śikṣākāra);
one who imitates another's style is called an "imitator" (anukāra).
One who is permeated by aesthetic flavor (rasa) is a "connoisseur" (rasika), and such a person is a "delighter," one who delights the listeners.
One who brings excellence to the song is celebrated as a *bhāvuka*.
There are three types: the soloist (*ekalla*), the pair (*yamala*), and the group singer (*vṛndagāyana*).
He who sings alone is indeed the soloist (*ekallagāyana*). 21–22.
He was accompanied by a twin brother, along with a host of singers;
there were female singers endowed with beauty and youth, regarded as equal to male singers, whose voices were preeminent in sweetness and who were clever and dear to the wise. (23)
Biting, rubbing, hissing, terrified, suspicious, and trembling;
Karālī, Vikala, Kākī, Vitālaka, Karabha, Udvaha, Jhombaka, Tumbakī, Vakrī, Prasārī, and Vinimīlaka. 24.
Lacking passion, having a discordant tone, indistinct, missing the proper register, and lacking stability;
mixed, inattentive, nasalized, and another [type]; these twenty-five singers are considered censurable. 25–26.
One who bites his teeth while singing is said to be "bitten" (saṃdaṣṭa);

one who utters a discordant sound is "rubbed" (udghṛṣṭa); and one who repeatedly makes hissing sounds is "hissing" (sūtkārī). One who is afraid, filled with terror, and sings with haste is considered "apprehensive" (śaṅkita).
One should know that *kampita* arises from trembling, due to the natural state of the limbs and the sound; *karālī* is described by the wise as one whose mouth is opened wide like a gaping maw;
while *vikala* is he who sings notes with deficient or excessive *śruti*s. (28–29)
One who has a harsh cry like a crow, a female crow, or a tāla bird, whose rhythmic timing is lost,
and who holds his neck upright, is called a *karabha* by the wise.
One who makes a face like a goat while singing poorly is known as an *udvaḍa*.
One with veins showing on the forehead and neck is a *jhombaka* singer;
a *tumbakī* singer is one whose cheeks are distended like a gourd while singing.
A *vakrī* singer is one who sings with a crooked neck, as described by the learned. 31–32.
It is called *prasārī* by those who know it because of the stretching of the limbs while singing;
*nimīlaka* is considered to be one who sings with eyes closed; and *virasa* is tasteless, being an off-key song due to the avoidance of appropriate notes. 33.

That which has a faltering sound and indistinct phonemes is called "indistinct" (avyakta). That which is unable to reach the three places of articulation is said to be "displaced from its place" (sthānabhraṣṭa), because the places of articulation are not properly established.
The *Miśraka* (Mixed) is known as that which blends the *Śuddha*, *Cchāyālaga*, and *Rāga* [melodies];
and the *Miśraka* of other *rāgas* arises from extensive blending.
The *Anavadhānaka* (Inattentive) is that which is devoid of careful attention toward the *sthāyi* (fixed) notes and so forth. 36.
The *geya* [style] is sung through the nose; it is sung with nasalization (*sānunāsika*). (37) Thus end the defects of singing. Sound may be of four types: *khāhula* and that called *nāraṭa*.
The *bombaka* and the *miśraka*—their characteristics are now described.

(38) That which arises from *kapha*, is thick (*khāhula*), unctuous, sweet, and endowed with delicacy is the *āḍilla*; this very same [type] becomes a *prauḍha* when it possesses the *mandra* and *madhya* registers. (39)

A sound arising from bile (*pitta*) is dense, deep, and resonant in three places; it is called *nārāṭa* or *bombaka*. A sound arising from wind (*vāta*), as declared by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow (Viṣṇu), is harsh, very loud, and gross, yet it is devoid of internal substance. 40.
Because of this mixture, it is called the "mixed" (miśraka) or "combined" (sāṃnipātika) type. [Objection:
The *bomba* has the qualities of being light and dry, while the *khāhula* is endowed with unctuousness;
how can there be a mixture of these two, which possess such contradictory qualities? 42
To this it is replied: "The abandonment of harshness, which is its opposite, while allowing for the mixture of non-contradictory qualities such as sweetness and robustness, is what is intended.
By this [principle], [the coexistence of] the qualities of density and lack of substance, and of the *nārāca* and *bomba* [rhetorical figures], is explained.
The objection regarding the possession of contradictory qualities and its resolution have been set forth.
(44) There are four varieties of the mixed [type]: Nārāṭa and Khāhula joined together;
Nārāṭa and Bombaka; and Bombaka and Khāhula—these three are combined. (45)
One who is deficient in both lack of essence and roughness, yet possesses a mixture of the three qualities, is called "the most excellent" (uttamottama), like Śaṅkara among the gods.
Furthermore, one mixed with *nārāṭa* and *khāhula* is "excellent" (*uttama*), while *khāhula* alone is likewise [excellent]. 46.

The *madhyama* (middle) sound is that which is joined with the *bomba*; the *bomba* sound joined with the *nārāṭa* is declared by the illustrious Soḍhala’s son to be the lowest (*adhama*) among sounds.
Any sound endowed with both lack of essence (*niḥsāratā*) and harshness (*tārūkṣatā*) is considered the lowest of all. 47–48.
There are many varieties [of voice] due to the various mixtures of those qualities:
one may be sweet, smooth, and thick; another smooth and soft;
another thick; and yet another sweet, gentle, and possessing the three registers. 49.
Another is soft, deep in three places, smooth, soft, and dense (50).
Another has three places that are sweet, soft, and dense; yet another has three places that are sweet, smooth, and soft (51).
Another [type] possesses sweetness, smoothness, depth, density, and resonance across the three registers;
another is smooth, soft, deep, dense, and resonant across the three registers;
and yet another is smooth, sweet, soft, thick, and resonant. 52.62–63.1a.
"Beautiful in three places" and "profound"—these ten varieties have been proclaimed.
Then, from the *khāhula* mixed with *nārāca*, there arise *khāhula* and *bomba*;
one is smooth, tender, and insubstantial, while the other is sweet and soft. (53–54)

One is rough, another is soft, smooth, and hollow with a higher [pitch], another is tender, smooth, and hollow, another is thick, and another is smooth and tender; the sixth variety is described as rough, hollow, and stout. Thus, the six types are proclaimed.
In the *nārāca* [tune], there are bomb-like bursts; it is dense, occupying three places, and harsh.
One [variety] is dense, deep, and harsh; another is hidden and thick;
another is sapless and harsh; and another is hidden, dense, very high, and thick. (56–57)

Another [type] is thick, deep, sluggish, and harsh in three locations; another is sluggish, sapless, harsh, and gross in three locations—these six are the varieties born from the combination of two [humors]. Now, these are the [varieties] arising from the combination of all three (sāṃnipātika).
Another [sound] is smooth, originating from three places, essence-less, soft, sweet, and dense (59).
Another is deep, higher-pitched, and harsh;
yet another is smooth and tender, dense and resonant, full-bodied, and very high-pitched, and smooth and tender (60).

Another [type of *madhura*] is described as being thick and very high, with its three places (*tristhāna*) submerged and devoid of essence (*niḥsāra*). Yet another *madhura* is thick but dry, with its three places submerged and very high; however, another is sweet, glossy, and soft.

One [type of sound] is dense, deep, and resonant in three places, while another is exceedingly high-pitched; 62 Another is sweet, soft, deep, resonant, and rough in three places; yet another is hollow and very high-pitched, while a further type is tender, sweet, and dense. 63
Combined with the qualities of being sluggish, located in three places, rough, very high, and thick—
these eight are the varieties of the "threefold mixed" [type]; indeed, all those born of mixture,
totaling thirty, have been proclaimed by Niḥśaṅka for the enlightenment of the simple-minded.
There is no end to other subtle distinctions arising from the intermixture of qualities; we have not mentioned them here for fear of excessive prolixity.
(65) Thus ends the definition of the varieties of words.
The wise describe [the voice] as polished, sweet, playful, bringing happiness to the three places,
abundant, tender, firm, audible, compassionate, dense,
smooth, delicate, endowed with passion, and radiant. 66.
By these qualities, sound is said to be of fifteen varieties:
that which soothes the ear, that which is polished, that which is not discordant in the three registers (sthāna), the sweet, the high-pitched, the mature, and the sweetly enchanting. (67–68)
Neither too thick nor too thin, glossy, dense, and dark— this [musti-bandha] should be used for men up to the neck, but for women at all times.
It is uniform in its three positions through qualities such as luster and coloration.
That which has three locations and is pleasant to the mind brings happiness;
it was spoken by the beloved of Śrī Śaṅkara as being endowed with abundant thickness, soft, and truly worthy of its name, like the song of the cuckoo. 70–71.
The *gāḍha* (firm) is considered powerful; the *śrāvaka* (hearer) is so called because of hearing from afar;

the *karuṇa* (compassionate) is that which illuminates the essence of compassion within the listener's mind. (72) The *ghana* (dense/solid), however, is fit for hearing from afar and is endowed with internal solidity.
A voice that is not harsh, audible from afar, and smooth is considered by the wise to be *snigdha* (unctuous).
That which is *ślakṣṇa* (smooth), like a continuous stream of oil and without interruption, is approved by the learned;
it is called *raktimān* (red/affectionate) because it generates affection. 73–74.
Because its source is a pure throat, that sound which is perceived by the wise as "this is radiant" is called "possessing luster. Thus end the qualities of sound. 75.
Thus end the qualities of sound.
Rūkṣa, sphuṭita, niḥsāra, kākolī, keṭika,
eṇaja, kṛśa, and bhagna— these are said to be the eight varieties of defective sound (duṣṭa-dhvani).
Rūkṣa is devoid of smoothness (snigdhatva), and sphuṭita is so named because its meaning is self-evident [as it is broken or cracked].
That which is as pithless as the core of a castor-oil plant stem is proclaimed "niḥsāra" (pithless).
That which is known as "kākolika," harsh with the cawing of a flock of crows, devoid of attainment in the three stages, and lacking in qualities, is called "keṭi. 77–78.

A sound that is difficult to open [the lips for], slow, and high-pitched is called *keṇi*; one that is excessively subtle, thin, broken, harsh, like the bray of a camel, or flavorless—these are the defects of sound (*śabdadoṣa*). (79) Thus end the defects of sound.

That capacity of sound to manifest passion even when there is no practice is called "corporeal" (*śārīra*), because it arises together with the body. [This is known] through its qualities of resonance, reverberation, sweetness, passion, depth, and softness. (80)

That which is endowed with qualities such as density, smoothness, and an abundance of luster is called "excellent *śārīra*" by those skilled in the definitions of characteristics and the objects characterized.
It is devoid of resonance, dry, and lacks redness. (81–82)
One should recognize a bad body by such poor defects as worthlessness, discordance, being like a crow, displacement from its proper place, emaciation, and hardness.
(83) [But this is remedied] through the gift of knowledge, austerity, or devotion to the Lord of Pārvatī.
A beautiful body is obtained through abundant fortune and power.
(84) Thus ends the description of bodily characteristics.
A tremor of the voice is a *gamaka* that brings pleasure to the hearts of listeners.
Its varieties are: *tiripa*, *sphurita*, *kampita*, as well as *līna*, *āndolita*, *valita*, *tribhinna*, *kurula*, *āhata*, *ullāsita*, *plāvita*, *gumphita*, and *mudrita*. (85)

The *nāmita* and *miśrita* are proclaimed as fifteen [varieties]. (86) The *tiripa* is proclaimed as being beautiful through its imitation of the shaking caused by the sound of a very light hand-drum (*ḍamaru*), with a speed equal to one-fourth of a quick tempo (*druta*). (87)
When [the movement] occurs with a speed equal to one-third of a *druta*, it is considered *sphurita*;
when it vibrates with a speed equal to half a *druta*, they know that *gamaka* as *kampita*.
On the other hand, *līna* is [a movement] oscillated with the speed of a *druta* and a light (*laghu*) speed.
Due to the force of a speed characterized by various types of curvature, it becomes *vali*.
When divided into three parts at three places, with a dense sound that does not rest, it is *kurula*; indeed, *vali* itself is knotted, while *kaṇṭhya* is soft. 89–90.
Having struck the foremost note and then ceased, it is considered "struck" (āhata);
however, that which proceeds through successively higher notes is called "exhilarated" (ullāsita).
But when one proceeds through the notes in sequence with a floating measure, it is a "tremor" (kampana).
It should be composed with a deep *huṃkāra* that reaches the heart (92).

That which arises from the sealing of the mouth is considered "sealed" (*mudrita*) because it conveys meaning; it is called "bent" (*nāmita*) by those who know sound because of the lowering of the vowels (93).
From the combination of these, there would be many mixed varieties;
however, an exposition of those will be provided in the section on the permanent emotions (*sthāyibhāva*).
(94) Thus ends the definition of *gamaka*.
The *sthāya* or the *vāga*, which is a constituent part of *rāga*, is called the *gamaka*;

the characteristics (*lakṣma*) of those *vāgas* have already been stated, and now the characteristics of the *sthāyas* are being described. (95) Furthermore, I shall state the characteristics of certain *vāgas* as well, in connection with this context. (96)

And those [qualities]—namely, being surpassed by the tone, being impelled, and being sharp—are said to be the characteristics of sound, the *ḍhala* drum, beauty, a vehicle, musical instruments, machines, and shadows; they are defined as being distinct and unmixed. 97

Thus, the ten well-known permanent states (*sthāyins*) have been defined with unmixed characteristics: devotion (*bhajana*), installation (*sthāpanā*), attainment (*gati*), resonance (*nāda*), melody (*dhvani*), beauty (*chavi*), attachment (*rakta*), support (*dhṛta*), sound (*śabda*), and the two—sustenance (*bhṛta*) and attention (*avadhāna*). (98)
The *apasthāna* consists of *nikuti*, the two types of *karuṇā*, *gātra*, *upaśama*, and that which is endowed with *kāṇḍa*, *araṇa*, and *nirjava*.
[These are] the *gāḍha*, the *lalitagāḍha*, the *lalita*, the *lulita*, and the *sama*. 99.

Softness (*komala*), expansion (*prasṛta*), smoothness (*snigdha*), purity (*cokṣa*), suitability (*ucita*), and the appropriate place (*sudeśika*), as well as the required resonance (*ghoṣa*) of the voice—
these are established by convention as the designations for the various qualities of the *sthāyas*. (100–101)
Thus, the thirty-three well-known *sthāya* variations created by the groups are: *vahākṣara*, *āḍambara*, *ullāsita*, *taraṅgita*, *pralambita*, *avaskhalita*, *trāṭita*, and *saṃpraviṣṭaka*. 102.

It may be *utpraviṣṭa* (entered upward), *niḥsaraṇa* (emerging), *bhrāmita* (whirled), *dīrghakampita* (long-shaken), *pratigrāhya* (grasped), or *ullāsita* (raised); it may also be *alamba-vilambika* (hanging down and suspended), *troṭita-pratīṣṭa* (snapped and established), *prasṛta* (extended), *ākuñcita* (contracted), or *sthira* (steady). 103.
The *sthāyuka*, the *kṣipta*, and the two *sūkṣma* and *anta*— these have unmixed characteristics.

Thus, these twenty [states] of a word abiding in its natural form (*prakṛtistha*), as well as those undergoing the process of phonetic modification (*kalā-kramaṇa*), have unmixed characteristics and are thus easily established.

In the movement of the event, of pleasure, and of the life-force (jīva-svara), the resonance of the Veda became slackened; the protracted note (pluta) was loosened, and the manifestation of the desired secondary notes within the melodies was bound by soft sounds. 105.
The *chāndasa* [style] has the appearance of being easy; the *saṃhita* is light and compact;
the *vakra* is radiant and clear; the *prasanna* is bright and soft; the *guru* is heavy;
the *hrasva* is loose; the *gāḍha* is firm; the *dīrgha* is long; and after that, the *asādhāraṇa*. 106.
The common, the supportless, and that called "difficult-to-perform" (107),

as well as the mixed— these too are intermingled with qualities and differentiated as before (108). Thus, there are thirty-three varieties distinguished by their qualities, which are only slightly established.
Thus, ninety-six *sthāyas* have been proclaimed by Śārṅgadeva.
(109) The *sthāyas* that receive the designation "mukta" (released) are proclaimed as those of sound; the movement of the *ḍhāla* is like that of a pearl, consisting of a rolling motion. (110)
These [movements] of yours would be the bending of a *dhāla* (shield), which is exceedingly delicate; that which is joined with it is proclaimed as *lavanyā*, the grace of the dancer.
Furthermore, that which may be a trembling while ascending or descending [the stage]—

That [vocal expression] is either expressive (*vadanī*) or mobile (*saṃcāriṇī*), as well as steady-trembling (*sthirakampana*). It is considered to be of two kinds according to the distinction between song (*gīta*) and improvisation (*ālapti*);
furthermore, the steady type is of two kinds—abundant in tempo (*vega*) and otherwise—and is said to be of three types.
The *vahanī*— which resides in the heart, the throat, and the head, and originates from the heart—
is further divided into two types based on the distinction between *khutta* and *utphulla*.
Because the vowels seem to enter within it, that [first type] is considered *khutta*.

In that [gati] where the vowels are uttered with a slight opening as if they were emerging upward, it is called *sotphulla*. The *vali* which has been described in the *gamakas* also possesses such varieties.
Those *sthāyas* in which these [vowel qualities] are carried are designated as *vahanyāḥ*.
Those musical sounds which are immersed in passion (*rāga*) are "born from musical sounds" (*vādyaśabdaja*).
Those which are seen primarily in mechanical instruments (*yantra*) are "born from instruments" (*yantraja*).
Melodic form (*chāyā*), modulation (*kāku*), and the sixfold structure (*ṣaḍjakārā*) arise from other melodic modes (*svararāga*) and non-melodic modes (*anyarāga*). 117

Now, the characteristics of place (*deśa*), field (*kṣetra*), and instrument (*yantra*) shall be stated. (118) That which arises from the deficiency or excess of the *śruti*, and which relies upon another *svara* within a *rāga*, is considered to be the *svarakākura* of that other *svara*. (119)
That which is the innate shadow of passion, they know as *rāgakāku*; but that which is a modulation of passion based on another passion within a state of passion is *rāgāntarāśrayā*.
That which arises from the nature of a particular region within a state of passion is *deśakāku*. 120.

The body is said to be the "field" (kṣetra), and by its very nature, it possesses a field-tone (kṣetrakāku) consisting of various kinds of modulation in passion. The tone produced by the mechanisms of instruments such as the lute and the flute is considered by the wise to be the "instrumental tone" (yantrakāku). 121–122.

Those who, while another note is being produced, take refuge in another note, are considered "shadows" (chāyā) by those expert in the science of music. One who leaps over many notes at intervals is called a "leaper" (svaralaṅghita).
Impelled by the impelling notes situated horizontally, above, and below,
and filling the ear with its resonance at the highest pitch (*tāra*), that which is sharp is called *tīkṣṇa*.
(124) Thus, the ten unmixed *sthāyas* [are described].

The cultivation [of the path] through effort is considered the intensification of passion; those possessed of that [passion] would be [the category of] "cultivators," while those who possess the [capacity for] stabilization are considered "stabilizers.
These are the ones whose activity consists in stabilizing again and again at every step. (125)
The gait of song is playful, like that of an elephant in rut (126).
The postures of gait associated with that [playfulness] are those in which the sound is smooth, rich in sweetness, and abundant; these are proclaimed as the characteristics of sound (127).
Those *sthāyas* which consist of very long applications are considered to belong to *dhvani*;

those *sthāyas* which are joined with soft brilliance are described as belonging to *chavi*. Furthermore, the wise have declared that *sthāyas* belong to *rasa* (passion) by virtue of the excellence of that passion. 128.

The names of the *dhṛta* (sustained) and *bhṛta* (supported) [notes] are appropriate to their meanings because they sustain the sound. A *rāga-aṃśa* (limb of a melody) is a constituent part of another *rāga*, and it is of seven kinds:
the causal part (*kāraṇāṃśa*), the effect part (*kāryāṃśa*), and the part belonging to its own kind (*sajātīyāṃśa*). 129–130.
The similar portion, the dissimilar portion, another which is the middle portion,
and the portion of portions— this is the portion that arises from a cause within the passion (rāga) when an effect is to be produced.
Indeed, this is the causal portion (kāraṇāṃśa), like the portion of clamor in the act of Rāma.
Just as in the case of Bhairava, there is a portion of the effect within the cause and a portion of the cause within the effect;
likewise, those such as the Karṇāṭas who have resorted to a common caste, such as the Gauḍas, are of the same genus, and that which is a portion of one exists in the other. (132–133)

That [raga] would be a *sajātīya-aṃśaka* (of the same class) if it were a partial constituent of two similar *rāgas*, just as the pure (*śuddha*) *naṭṭā* and *avarī* are mutually similar parts. However, when two [rāgas] are devoid of similarity, that part is an *atyanta-visadṛśāṃśaka* (an extremely dissimilar part). 134.
Just as in the mutual relationship between the Velāvalī and Gūrjarī scales,
their middle notes (madhyastha-rāga) are devoid of both similarity and dissimilarity;
likewise, the middle note serves as the *aṃśa* for those two [scales] known as Naṭṭādeśā and the other.
Because it involves the movement from one part (*aṃśa*) to another part, it is called "part-of-a-part" (*aṃśāṃśa*).
Those *sthāyas* in which a part is perceived are proclaimed as belonging to that part (verse 137).
Those which are to be grasped by the mind alone through that very [mental] activity are born of focused attention (*avadhāna*).

That place where sound is abundant without effort is the *svasthāna* (natural position); that from which it arises with effort is the *apasthāna* (secondary position). Those *sthāyas* (fixed notes) which arise from the *apasthāna* belong to the *apasthāna*. 138–139.

From the stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*) of wonder and compassion, which possess names corresponding to their meanings, various derivative states (*vyabhicāribhāva*) arise, assuming diverse modulations;
they are born of manifoldness and, producing an exceedingly intense resonance, they are intent upon limb after limb of the body. (140)
Those upon whom tranquility is practiced become [the objects] of that tranquility.
(141) The practice of the arrow-shaft (*kāṇḍāraṇā*) is well known; from that state, [the mind] arises as straight, supple, and red, gradually brought to extreme subtlety. (142)

Among the first [categories] of tone, those *sthāyas* are said to be endowed with speed (*nirjava*); that which is firm (*gāḍha*) and free from laxity is the same when endowed with softness (*mṛdutā*). The *lalita-gāḍha*, however, is graceful (*lalita*) and full of charm (*vilāsavat*).

That which is swayed by softness is called *lulita*; when it is even (*sama*), it is again [so termed]. That which is deficient in both speed and slowness is considered *yathārtha*, while *komala* is regarded as such.
*Prasṛta* is possessed of extension; *snigdha* is devoid of roughness. 144–145.
He is described as radiant (*ujjvala*), pure (*uccha*), and appropriate (*ucita*) because he is true to his purpose; he is a good guide for the wise, beloved, and desired.
(146) He is one who is sought after to fulfill the preceding [requirements] through each successive stage.
That deep, resonant, smooth, sweet, and great sound which occurs in the *vala* (throat) and the *vahani* (chest) is called *ghoṣa*; those [notes] endowed with it are considered *ghoṣaja*.
Those [notes] of the voice which possess a deep and sweet resonance in the *mandra* (low register) are [also so classified]. 147–148.
Thus, there are thirty-three mixed types.

Those in which the vowels seem to flow and vibrate are "vahasya"; those in which the flourish of syllables (*akṣarāḍambara*) is predominant are "mukhya," and they are associated with that [latter category]. (149)
That [melodic movement] is considered *taraṅgita* (wavy) where the notes, impelled with force, rise upward and cause the waves of the Gaṅgā to surge;
it is like water swaying within a jar that is half-filled. 150.
In song, such a stationary note is called *pralambita* by those who know [the art].
That which falters rapidly during a descent from the low register (*mandra*) is called *avaskhalita*; however, when it occurs at some point within a note, it is called *trāṭita*. (151–152)

Having remained for a long time like fire, it returns after touching the ascending note; in the descending scale it is "deep-toned" (ghanasvara), and likewise, when it has entered [the ascent], it is "penetrated" (saṃpraviṣṭa).
It would be "ascending-penetrated" (ārohiṇyutpraviṣṭa); the other three [terms] are literal in their meaning.
He who is received [as a guest] becomes uplifted once he has been received (154).
Beautiful as a play-ball that is repeatedly tossed up and falls down, he who was previously swift becomes slow at the end; such is the "slowly hanging" (*alambavilambaka*) [gait]. (155)

It may be *troṭitapratiṣa* where, after first striking one [note] between the high (*tāra*) and low (*mandra*) registers, there is the reception of the other; it is a sustained (*sthāya*) note that is extended and then contracted, having a sound that is first expanded and then drawn back. 156.

The stability of a fixed color (varṇa) and its vibration is called *sthira*. Having paused at each individual note, or having paused after two notes, or even after three notes, that which is thus composed is considered *sthāyuka*.
"Upright," "stretched out," "thrown," and "attaining smallness at the end of the subtle body"—
thus twenty distinct sounds manifest, excluding [terms such as] *dhṛti* and *bhṛti*.

Those [states] in which sounds are rendered subtle are proclaimed as belonging to *kalā*; they are considered by you to belong to the word (*śabda*) in its natural state, residing in its own essence (159).
Those which are intensely perceivable by the vital breath (*prāṇa*) belong to the stage of *ākramaṇa* (160).
Those *sthāyas* which are fashioned by the artisan like a potter for an event should be pleasant;
they are known as the *ālirjakka* of happiness. (161) The *sthāyas* associated with that *ālirjakka* are considered the *jīvasvara*, a portion of the *ālirjakka*.
Those *sthāyas* which are sung primarily with that [quality] belong to the *jīvasvara*. Those *sthāyas* whose resonance resembles the sound of the Vedas are considered to belong to the *vedadhvani*.
Just as the internal essence of density is considered to be truly relaxed (*śithila*). 162–163.
The *avaghaṭa* is said to be difficult to perform, while the *pluta* is extremely slow;
that which is desired for the sake of fulfilling a melody (*rāga*) is celebrated as *rāgeṣṭa*.
That [melody] would be a semblance of a wrong note (*apasvara*), appearing like a wrong note.
When the pause is fixed and the sweet sound is abundant, that [type of composition] is called *chāndasa*, which is pleasing to the clever;
though difficult to achieve, it appears easy and is thus termed "the difficult that resembles the easy. (165–166)
That which arises from the sound of a bell is *vāyāta*; *tāra* is high-pitched while *mandra* is deep; that which is joined together is *saṃhita*;
that which is devoid of heaviness is *laghu*. That which exists in the *dhruvaka* and the *ābhoga* is [so called];
that which is between is *antara*; that which is crooked is *vakra*; and that which is according to its meaning is *yathārtha*, while that which is easy to perform is *sukara*.
The *tāra* is radiant and clear; the *sukara* has a soft sound. (168) The *prasanna* is said to be mild; the *guru* is true to its name.
The two following [the *laghu*], being short and slight, are likewise true to their names. (169)
That which is easy to produce or possesses a beautiful tone by virtue of its vocal or physical qualities, yet belongs to only one person and not to all, is called "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa).
However, that which is similar for everyone is known as "common" (sādhāraṇa). 170.

He who does not desire firewood and the like for the sake of his own sustenance is called "unsupported" (nirādhāra); he is like one performing what is easy while appearing to perform what is difficult, and is thus described as the "semblance of difficulty" (duṣkarābhāsa). Because of its mixture [with other types], it is considered the "mixed" (miśraka) type.
Thus, there are thirty-three mixed characteristics; because they are infinite, it is not possible to describe all the variations of the mixed type.
These are stated merely for the purpose of indicating the general direction, and among them, only a few are mentioned. 173
Whatever state is predominant in a particular [movement] is designated by that name;
however, when there is equality [of states], it is simply called "mixed. This is now explained in detail:
*tiripa*, *āndolita*, *līna*, *kampita*, and *kampitāhata*.
Tiripasphurita, līnasphurita, sphuritāhata; 175 līnakampita, līna, and tribhinnakurulāhata; plāvitollāsitavali, valihumphita, and mudrita. 176
The Supreme is [experienced as] distinct, merged, vibrating, overflowing, and oscillating;

it resides in the two channels (vahnyoḥ), the two abodes (ālayoḥ), the two moving streams (dhālavahanyoḥ), the two sounds (śabdau), the two abodes of sound (śabda-ālayoḥ), the two channels of movement (vahanī-yantrayoḥ), the two shadow-instruments (chāyā-yantrayoḥ), and the two sound-instruments (śabda-yantrayoḥ). 178–179.

The subsequent sound arising from the vehicle, the shadow, the machine, and the musical instrument is "tīkṣṇaprerita" (impelled by the sharp); it is impelled by the sharp and transcends the musical scales.
The subsequent sound arising from the *ḍhāla* shield and the sound arising from the machine and the musical instrument is likewise produced.
Another [sound] arises from the shadow of the *ḍhola* drum, the sound of mechanical instruments, and vocal sounds;
another is characterized by being struck (*jhallambita*), stumbling (*avaskhalita*), rattling (*strāṭita*), and exultant (*ullāsita*);
and there is that which has entered (*saṃpraviṣṭa*), has entered forth (*utpraviṣṭa*), and is rippled with entry (*saṃpraviṣṭataraṅgita*). 181–182.
One [type of dancer] would have his hands received, raised up, held out, and let hang;
another would have them withdrawn, thrust forward, entered, and drawn back;
and yet another would have them long shaken, slightly bent at the ends, whirled around, and then held steady.
The [hand] extended from the palm, the clenched fist, the steady [hand],
the whirled, the thrown, the subtle, the one with the curved fingers,
and the raised— these thirty-six [types of hands], as well as others, are to be understood by this same method. 184–185.
Thus ends the definition of *sthāyavāga*.
*Ālapti* is considered to be the vocalizing of a *rāga*, its manifestation;
it is said to be of two kinds, distinguished by the *rāga* and the *rūpaka*. 186
That which occurs without regard for the musical form (rūpaka) is known as *rāgālapti*;
those learned in song know that it consists of four types of *svasthāna*.
That rāga in which one settles upon a particular note is called *sthāyī*. 187.
Then the fourth [note] shall be at the interval of two and a half *mātrās* on the preceding vowel;
this shifting is "mouth-shifting" (*mukhacāla*), and that is the first placement in its own position.
Having shifted it by two and a half *mātrās* on the vowel, that is the second placement. (188–189)
The eighth note from the tonic (sthāyisvara) is proclaimed to be double [the interval].

The notes situated between the one-and-a-half-fold and the double intervals are the "half-situated" (ardhasthita) notes. Having shifted the two half-situated notes, the third placement (nyāsana) is performed. 190.
Having moved through the doubled [scale] and then from the *sthāyi* [note], the fourth [note] is reached;
by means of these four *svasthāna* positions, the *rāgālapti* is considered by the wise.
Then, with increasingly subtle *sthāyas*, clear and possessing many melodic variations (*bhaṅgi*).
"The establishment of the rāga occurs primarily through the pervasion of the life-breath (jīva) and the vowels.
Thus concludes the exposition on rāga (rāgālapti).
It is performed with a rāga situated in a *rūpaka* and with a *tāla*.
Furthermore, that which is called the conventional designation of a *rūpaka* is of two kinds:
one is the *pratigrahaṇikā*, and the other is termed the *bhañjanī*.
If, having established the fixed measure, a constituent part of a *rūpaka* is designated... 193.
"That which is accepted is called *pratigrahaṇikā* by the wise" (194).
Thus, *pratigrahaṇikā* and *bhañjanī* should be known as two types, because of the breaking of the form of the deposit (*sthāya-rūpaka*).

When a *sthāya* (a sustained melodic phrase) established in a particular form is performed in various ways according to that measure (*māna*), it should be known as *sthāyabhañjanī*. If the entire *rūpaka* is [performed] with those same words and that same measure, [it is likewise]. 195.

If she should sing in various ways and different manners, breaking the structural form [of the melody], yet endowed with phonetic ornaments (*varṇālaṃkāra*) and embellished by *gamakas* and *sthāyis*,
it is called *ālapti* by those who know it— charming with its manifold aesthetic modulations. (196–197)
Such is the definition of *ālapti*.
A collection of singers and instrumentalists is called a *vṛnda*;
it is of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior. (198)

There are four principal singers, twice as many (eight) who sing in unison, twelve female singers are prescribed, and a quartet of flute players; where there are also four drummers, that ensemble is considered supreme. (199)

The medium [orchestra] should consist of half that number; in the smallest [orchestra], there should be one principal singer (*mukhyagāyana*), three singers (*gāyana*), four female singers (*gāyanikā*), two pairs of lute-players (*vāṃśika*), and two pairs of mṛdaṅga drummers (*mārdalika*). 200–201.

In the highest class of singers, there should be two principal female singers, ten female singers who sing in unison, and likewise two flute-players; there should be a pair of lute-players. In the middle class, there is one principal female singer.
There may be one lead singer (*samagāyinī*) and likewise four instrumentalists (*vāṃśikā*);
a group smaller than this would be inferior, while a larger one may be as desired.
A superior group that exceeds [the standard] is called a *kolāhala*. 203–204.
Adherence to the primary [leader], meeting together, following the rhythm and grace, mutual maintenance when interrupted, the capacity to pervade the three places,
and similarity of sound— these are declared to be the six qualities of the *vṛnda*. 205
The sage Bharata, however, has declared the *kutapa* to be a specific type of ensemble (*vṛnda-viśeṣa*). This [ensemble] is threefold for both *tatam* (stringed) and *āvanaddham* (percussive) drama.
Among these, the *kutapa* of the *tatam* [category] is to be understood as the singer together with his retinue.
The vīṇā, ghoṣavatī, citrā, vipañcī, parivādinī, vallakī, kuṅnikā, jyeṣṭhā, nakuloṣṭhī, kiṃnarī,
jayā, kūrmī, pinākī, hastikā, and śatatantrikā. 208.

The Audumbarī, the Ṣaṭkarṇa, the Pauṇa, the Rāvaṇahastaka, the Sāraṅgī, the Ālapanī, and so forth—these are the players of stringed instruments (tata-vādya). Then there are the flute-players (vāṃśika), the reed-players (pāvika), the drummers (pāvakāhala), and the conch-blowers (śaṅkhavādaka). 209–210.
Next are the *muhurī*, the *śṛṅga*, and other instruments, as well as the excellent *tāladhara*s;
then, among the covered drums (*avanaddha*), the principal is the *mārdaṅgika* (drummer), followed by the *paṇava*,
*dardura*, *ḍhakkā*, *maṇḍiḍakkā*, and *ḍakkulī*.
The *paṭaha*, *karaṭā*, *ḍhakkā*, *ḍhavasa*, and likewise the *ghaḍasa*;
the *huḍukkā*, *ḍamaru*, *ruñjā*, *kuḍukkā*, and likewise the *kuḍuvā*;
the *niḥsvāna*, the *trivalī*, the *bherī*, the *tambakī*, and likewise the *bombaḍī*. 212–213.

The *paṭṭavādya* (cymbals), the *paṭaha* (drum), the *kamra*, the *uḍāva*, the *jāva*, the *jasa*, the *selluka*, the *jayaghaṇṭā* (victory bell), the *kāṃsyatāla* (bronze cymbal), the *ghaṇṭā* (bell), and the *kirikiṭṭaka*;
such is the collection of various instrumentalists for these and other musical instruments. 214.
[He was attended] by those from Varāṭa, Lāṭa, Karṇāṭa, Gauḍa, Gurjara, and Kauṅkaṇa;
by those from Mahārāṣṭra, Andhra, Hammīra, Caula, Malaya, and Mālava; and by those from Aṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, and other regions—all of whom were experts in various dramatic gestures (abhinaya).

The theatrical performance was carried out by actors of superior, inferior, and middling rank, who were experts in the application of *aṅgahāra* movements, skilled in the *lāsya* and *tāṇḍava* dances, proficient in various *sthānaka* postures, and well-trained in difficult maneuvers. (217)
"The collection of these *kutapas* is called a *vṛnda*. (218) Thus ends the definition of the *vṛnda*.

This concludes the third chapter, the *Prakīrṇaka-adhyāya*, in the *Saṃgītaratnākara* composed by Niḥśaṅka Śārṅgadeva, the son of the illustrious Soḍhala-deva, the lord of the royal court and one who delights in faultless learning.
Now begins the fourth chapter on composition:
A pleasing arrangement of notes is called *gīta* (song); its two divisions are declared to be *gāndharva* and *gāna*. 1.
The wise have declared that which is employed by the Gandharvas as an eternal tradition is the cause of ultimate welfare; that is Gāndharva.
Furthermore, that which is composed by a master of song and endowed with the proper characteristics [is also Gāndharva].
That singing which is proclaimed among the regional melodies (*deśī-rāga*) and so forth is for the delight of people.
Among those, *gāndharva* was described previously; now singing (*gāna*) is being discussed.
That is declared by the wise to be of two kinds: composed (*nibaddha*) and uncomposed (*anibaddha*).
That which is composed of elements (dhātu) and bound by limbs (aṅga) is called "bound" (nibaddha);
because it lacks such binding, "unbound" (anibaddha) is said to be conversational discourse (ālapti).
That [unbound discourse] was previously explained by us; now, however, the "bound" is being described.
For one bound by the three designations (*saṃjñā*), the composition is the *vastu-rūpaka*. The constituent part of the composition is the *dhātu*, which is described as being fourfold:
among these, the first is the *udgrāha*, followed by the *melāpaka* and the *dhruva*.
And the *ābhoga*; we shall now describe their characteristics in order:
the first part is the *udgrāha*, followed by what is known as the *melāpaka*;
then comes the *dhruva* because of its fixed nature, and finally the *ābhoga* is considered the last part.
Born within the interval of Dhruvābhoga is another element called Antarā; it is seen only in the Rūpakas situated within the Sālagasūḍa.
Just as wind, bile, and phlegm are the elements (dhātus) because they sustain the body.
Thus, these are the elements (*dhātu*) of the continuum, so called because they sustain the body (10).
Among them, the gathering (*melāpaka*) and the enjoyment (*ābhoga*) do not exist anywhere [independently];
that [continuum] is threefold: consisting of two elements, three elements, and four elements (11).

The composition (*prabandha*) has six constituent parts (*aṅga*): tone (*svara*), title (*viruda*), word (*pada*), *tenaka*, *plāṭa*, and rhythm (*tāla*). These belong to the "Person of the Composition" (*prabandhapuruṣa*), whose limbs manifest auspicious meanings. 12. Just as [the body] has limbs, these are its limbs.
In that regard, the feet are considered the "pada" (the ground), the eyes are the "netra" (the guides), and the hands are the "pāṭa-biruda" (the rhythmic strokes and titles).
Because the effect arises from the hands, they are metaphorically designated as the cause.
The feet are regarded as the "tāla" (tempo) and the "svara" (melodic tone), because they are the cause for the progression of the composition.
The notes beginning with *ṣaḍja* are the [musical] scales (*svaras*), and their designators are *sa*, *ri*, *ga*, and so forth.
When these are joined with the manifestation of the notes, they are designated by the term "note" (*svara*).
A *biruda* is a name based on a quality; other than that, it is a word that denotes [the person]. (15–16)
The word "iti" is a thief [of meaning], yet it reveals the sense of auspiciousness;
the designation "Oṃ tat sat" arises from such statements as "That thou art.
"Tat" refers to Brahman; therefore, by means of that Brahman, whose nature is auspiciousness—
The reading "lakṣitas tena tena" refers to the collection of instrumental syllables; *tāla* will be explained in detail in the section on *tāla*.
Furthermore, [the *mūrchanās*] are Medinī, Ānandinī, Dīpanī, and likewise Bhāvanī.
There are five types of compositions known as *tārāvalī*.

According to the opinion of some, these are called *śruti*, *nīti*, *senā*, *kavitā*, and *campū*, being classified by their constituent parts (*aṅga*) which range from two up to six, beginning with the note *ṣaḍja*. 19–20.

Composition (prabandha) is considered to be of two kinds: the non-structured (aniryukta) and the structured (niryukta). The former arises from the lack of fixed rules regarding meter, rhythm, and so forth; the latter arises from such fixed rules. Furthermore, compositions are of three types: those based on the *sūḍa* and those based on the *ālī*.

Since these are scattered [throughout the text], the characteristics of the *sūḍas* are stated first. (22) The *sūḍa* is said to consist of eight: *elā*, *karaṇḍa*, *iṅkī*, *vartanī*, *jhombaḍa*, *lambha*, *rāsa*, and *ekatālī*. (23)
Varṇa, Varṇasvara, Gadya, Kaivāḍa, Aṅkacāriṇī,
Kanda, Turagalīlā, Gajalīlā, Dvayadyapi (24),
Cakravāla, Krauñcapada, Svarārtha, and Dhvanikuṭṭinī.
The Āryā, Gāthā, Dvipathaka, Kalahaṃsa, Toṭaka (25), Ghaṭa, Vṛtta, Mātṛkā, as well as Rāgakadambaka,
Pañcatāleśvara, and Tālārṇava— among these, a certain [meter] [is employed]. 26.

If this Ālikrama were to occur in the midst of the Sūḍakrama, then, due to the connection between the Sūḍa and Āli sequences, they are proclaimed to be thirty-two. Other than those, there are the *viprakīrṇas* (scattered ones); I shall mention some of those that are well-known.
Śrīraṅga and Śrīvilāsa; beyond these is Pañcabhaṅgi (28).
Then there are Pañcānana, Umātilaka, Tripadī, Catuṣpadī, Ṣaṭpadī, Vastu, Vijaya, and likewise Tripatha (29).

The four-faced, the lion-play, the swan-play, then the staff, the jhumbaḍa, the ball, the triple-bend, and the sport of Hara; the beautiful-to-behold, the marked by vowels, the increaser of prosperity, and the increaser of joy.
Vadana, Cañcarī, Caryā, Paddhaḍī, and likewise Rāhaḍī;
31 Vīraśrī, Maṅgalācāra, Dhavala, and likewise Maṅgala;
Ovī, Lolī, Ḍhollarī, and Dantī—these are the thirty-six. 32
The two feet consist of two segments with alliteration by means of a single phoneme;
following that is the *prayoga*, and then the three-word section called *pallava*.
Among those, two are slow (*vilambita*) and the third is at a fast tempo (*drutamāna*). (33)
Thus, the first three feet of the *geya* should have the same *dhātu* as the *udgrāha*;
however, in the third foot alone, it should be accompanied by words of awakening (*saṃbodhaka*).
The final application (*prayoga*) must be performed; there is no placement of *pallava* words. 34.
Someśvara and others call this application "melāpa.
It is marked by the name of the deity to be praised, consists of three middle-paced lines followed by a *dhruva*,
and therein, at the beginning, there are two lines in a single *dhātu*.

The third [section] should be of a different musical mode (bhinnadhātu); immediately after that comes the *ābhoga*, which is sung by the composer (*vāggeyakāra*) and adorned with his own name. Having sung it again at the *dhruva* section, there should be a release (*tyāga*), while the *graha* (the concluding phrase) should be irregular (*viṣama*). 37.
This general definition of these [rāgas] was proclaimed by the former teachers.
Among the tālas—maṇṭha, dvitīya-kaṅkāla, and pratitāla—a certain tāla is used here;
it consists of a description of renunciation, good fortune, heroism, and fortitude.
There are many varieties of cardamom (*elā*); some among them, as taught in the systems of Mataṅga and others, are described here for the sake of etymological understanding.
(40) Viṣṇu is the presiding deity in the syllable *a*, and the flower-armed god [Kāmadeva] is the deity in the syllable *i*.

"Lakṣmī" is the deity for the letter *la* among the letters; it is like Kāma and Manmatha, charming, victorious, intoxicated, and transformative. Māndhātṛ and Sumati are the deities for "Śobhī," while Gītaka is praised as "Suśobhī. 41–42.
Vicitrā, Vāsavā, Mṛdu, Sucitrā—these sixteen names belong respectively to the sixteen Elā plants:
Padmālayā, Pattriṇī, Rañjanī, Sumukhī, and Śacī. (43)
Vareṇyā, Vāyuvegā, Vedinī, Mohinī, Jayā,
Gaurī, Brāhmī, Mātaṅgī, Caṇḍikā, and Vijayā—
these sixteen deities reside respectively in the sacred sites of Cāmuṇḍā and Elā. 44–45.
Even, sweet, dense, lovely, radiant, composed, 46 non-vulgar, delicate, clear, and powerful— these ten vital breaths (*prāṇas*) should be present in the ten words beginning with "Māndhātṛ. 47

Even (samāna) is that which has little sound, is sweet, and is not born of a [specific] beginning; it is joined with a slight modulation (mūrcchanā). Dense (sāndra), however, is that which consists of compact syllables.
That which has little sound, a high pitch, and is lovely is considered "lovely-sounding" (kānta). 48.
The *dīpta* [style] is characterized by a brilliant resonance; the *sthāyistha* is composed and steady.

The *agrāmya* is described as consisting of the repetition of syllables and sounds, while the *sukumāra* is so called because of the softness of its phonemes, sounds, and melodic sequences (*mūrcchanā*). 49–50.
Through the clarity of the words, positions, vowels, and so forth, one becomes serene;

endowed with these and all other qualities—being full of vitality and possessing vigor—the *elā* [melodic ornament] grants the listener and the performer the attainment of dharma, kāma, and artha. 51.
These [syllables] are of four kinds, distinguished by *gaṇa*, measure (*mātrā*), vowel (*varṇa*), and place (*deśa*).

(52) A *gaṇa* is a group; it is twofold due to the distinction between vowels and measures. A syllable (*varṇa*) is twofold as heavy (*guru*) or light (*laghu*). A syllable joined with an *anusvāra* is heavy. (53)
A syllable ending in a consonant followed by a visarga, a long vowel, or one followed by a conjunct consonant is heavy;
however, at the end of a word, it may optionally be light. A syllable consisting of two morae is called *vakra* (crooked), while one of one mora is *laghu* (light).

In writing, a syllable is *ṛju* (straight) when it occurs before the letters *bh*, *re*, *ṣka*, and *ṣpa*; furthermore, that syllable is optionally light when followed by the conjunction of *ra* and *ha*.
In Prākṛta, *e*, *oiṃ*, *hiṃ*, or *vā* at the end of a word are considered light (laghu).

In Apabhraṃśa, even in the middle of a word, *huṃ*, *he*, *e*, *o*, and *iṃ* are likewise [light]. In that [Apabhraṃśa], a syllabic foot (*varṇagaṇa*) consists of three syllables and is of eight kinds.
The *ma* syllable is heavy at the beginning (*pūrvala*), the *ra* is heavy in the middle (*madhyala*), and the *ga* is heavy at the end (*antaga*).
The *ta* is heavy at the end (*antala*), the *ja* is heavy in the middle (*madhyaga*), and *na* consists of three light syllables (*trilaghu*) starting with *ga*.
(57) Thus, their deities are Earth, Water, Fire, Wind, and Space. (58)
The Sun, the Moon, and the abodes of the gods (the planets) shall, in sequence, produce for you these results:
prosperity, growth, death, displacement from one's position, poverty, disease, honor, longevity, and renown through poetry, song, and the like. 59.
The Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, the Sun, and Rāhu are, in order, the presiding deities of the consonant groups *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, *śa*, and *na*.
Their respective fruits are longevity, fame, misfortune, and ill-repute. (60–61)

Prosperity, good fortune, fame, infirmity, death, and emptiness—these are said by the wise to be the results of the application [of syllables] in verses, songs, and so forth, when addressed to one worthy of praise. (62) A *mātrā* is a unit of measure; a short vowel is a *kalā*, and a consonant (*la*) is likewise. Their *gaṇas* are *cha*, *pa*, and *ca*, and so on.
There are six, five, four, three, and two syllabic instants (*mātrā*) respectively.
For example: ' ' is the *cchagaṇa*; ' ' is the *pagaṇa*; ' ' is the *cagaṇa*; ' is the *tagaṇa*; and ' is the *dagaṇa*. These are the five *mātrā*-groups.
The four varieties of the *atyuktā* meter are considered to belong to the *rati* class; however, among those whose first foot begins with *la*, there is an additional short syllable at the beginning.
Thus, the eight varieties belonging to the *madhyā* meter are known as the *kāma* class.
Likewise, there are sixteen varieties of the *bāṇa* group within the *pratiṣṭhā* meter;
these are the groups of morae (*mātrā-gaṇas*).
Among them, that which is produced by groups of syllables (*varṇa-gaṇas*) is proclaimed as *gaṇailā*.
That [practice] is of three kinds: pure, mixed, and likewise modified.
(66) The pure is of four types: Nādāvatī, Haṃsāvatī, Nandāvatī, and Bhadrāvatī; now their characteristics are described.
The rule for the *gaṇas* and so forth of these [meters] rests upon two divisions of feet. Nādāvatī consists of five *bhagas* ending with *ṭa*, *kka*, and *maṇṭha*.
She is the Brahmin woman exhaled by the Ṛgveda and has resorted to the Kaiśikī style.
The Pāñcālī style, which increases the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), brings delight to the Bhāratī style.
Thus, Nādāvatī is described by the wise as consisting of five *ragaṇas* ending with *sa*; Haṃsāvatī is likewise declared.
In the second tāla, within the Hindola rāga, there is the Kṣattriyā [mudrā], born from the Yajurveda (69).
Resorting to the Lohita-ārabhaṭī vṛtti and the Lāṭī rīti, it is employed for the propitiation of Caṇḍikā in the raudra rasa (70).
Thus, Haṃsāvatī consists of five *tagaṇas* ending in *ja*; Nandāvatī is considered to consist of *elās*.
It should be sung in the *pratitāla* measure and in the *mālavakaiśika* rāga. 71.
Born from the Sāmaveda, yellow in complexion, belonging to the Vaiśya caste and born of the Sātvata mode of life,
the Gauḍīya style— relying on the heroic sentiment— is for the pleasure of Indrāṇī. (72) Thus ends Nandāvatī.

Bhadrāvatī, arising from the Atharvaveda, is situated in the Kakubha meter; it employs five types of drums ending with the mṛdaṅga, the kaṅkāla rhythm, the Vaidarbha style, and the Bhāratī vṛtti, and is filled with the sentiment of disgust (bībhatsa). 73.
These were proclaimed by Śārṅgadeva for the pleasure of the goddess Vārāhī.
Thus, in Bhadrāvatī, these [melodies] are considered to be of many kinds due to various mixtures; they are regarded as being manifoldly mixed.
But those [varieties] are not well-known in the objects of illustration; therefore, they have not been elaborated upon here.
The first three may be pure or modified through the alteration of their constituent groups (*gaṇa*):
namely, the Vāsavī, the Saṃgatā, the Tretā, and the one called Caturā or Bāṇā. (75–76)
Due to having one, two, three, four, or five modifications, they are of five kinds;
each of these Vāsavī types is fivefold and delightful to the mind. These are called Unnata, Śānti, and Nāgarī by the wise. (77)
From the first of the *gaṇas* up to the fifth, there are:
Ramaṇīyā, Viṣamā, Samā, Lakṣmī, Kaumudī, Kāmotsavā, Nandinī, Gaurī, and after that, Saumyā. (78–79)
Thus, the *ratideha* is said by the wise to be tenfold when combined [with its constituents].
Of the first [element], there are four modifications when joined with the second and the others; of the second, three when joined with the third and the others.
The characteristic of these [melodies] is, respectively: two for the third [melody] by means of modification;
two for each of the even [melodies] beginning with the fourth; and one for the fourth and fifth.
Thus, the *tretā* is said to be of ten kinds: Maṅgalā, Ratimaṅgalā, [and so forth].
Kalikā, Tanumadhyā, Vīraśrī, Jayamaṅgalā,
Vijayā, Ratnamālā, Gurumadhyā, and Ratiprabhā— here, the inclusion of the first [mudrā] and the others is intended by means of their initial syllables. 83–84.

From the permutations of *pra*, *dvi*, *tri*, *ca*, and *pa*, these [names] arise in sequence: *pradvitrīṇām*, *pradvicānām*, *pradvipānām*, *pracatriṇām*, *pratripānām*, *pracapānām*, *dvitricānām*, *dvipatriṇām*, *cadvipānām*, and *catripānām*. (85)
By omitting one group at a time from the first four, there would be four variations due to modification;
therein, the first is fivefold: Utsavapriyā, Mahānandā, Malaharī, Jayā, and Kusumāvatī. 86.

From the first [syllable], by means of five modifications, there arises the *bāṇā* [mudrā], which is dear to Pārvatī. (87) Each of those thirty-one [forms] resides within the *nādāvatī* and other [mudrās]. Including these, there are ninety-three divisions; furthermore, these others number fifteen. (88)
The *sāvitrī*, the *pāvanī*, and the *vātasāvitrī* are considered to be threefold; they are formed by the successive combination of the group of *savitṛ* and the group of *pavana*.
Furthermore, when combined with the first two varieties, the *vāsavī* is considered to be twofold in the second [category]. 89.
These divisions of Nādāvatī and Haṃsāvatī are also threefold:
Vyomajā, Vāruṇī, and Vyomavāruṇī, joined with their respective presiding deities; likewise, Vāsavī is twofold. (90–91)
The fire-born [Vaiśvānarī] is in Nandāvatī; Vāruṇī and Vahnivāruṇī are there as well.
Joined by their respective groups, the [form] of Vāsava is threefold and likewise twofold.
Thus, these modified divisions are considered to be one hundred and eight.
According to the tradition of Pārvatī, that Mātrailā should be known as fourfold by means of the groups of mothers (mātrāgaṇas):
Ratilekhā, Kāmalekhā, Bāṇalekhā, and another. 94.
If there are eleven *kalās* (syllables) in the first quarter, twelve in the second, and ten *mātrās* in the third, then it is *Candralekhā*.
*Ratirekhā* is formed by the groups of syllables of *Rati*, while *Kāmalekhā* is formed by those of *Manmatha*. 95.
By doubling the *kalās*, there would be [the *mātrā*]; by tripling them, the *mātrā* arises.
The *bāṇalekhā* consists of five groups [of syllables], while the *candralekhā* consists of mixed groups. Now I shall describe four others that possess four times the *kalās*. 96–97.
First is Indumatī, then Jyotiṣmatī, followed by Nabhasvatī and Vasumatī;
among these, the wise say that Indumatī consists of five *cha*s (six-syllable feet), while Jyotiṣmatī consists of five *pa*s (eight-syllable feet) along with the *saca* group [of syllables]. 98.
If these same three gaṇas are repeated, it would be *nabhasvatī* (99). That [meter] is *vasumatī*, in which there are three *da-pa-cā*s followed by *cha-tau* (100),
according to the *Nandimatā*.
The *mātrās* such as *nādāvatī* and others are formed by the initial [syllables] arising from the breaking of their own *gaṇas*.
There are five *gaṇas*, with a three-mora unit at the end;
there are seven *gaṇas*, with a light syllable (*laghu*) at the end; and there are eight *gaṇas*, with a three-mora unit at the end. (101)
"Those [lines] are *lakṣmāṇī*," Savyasācin said to them in succession.
When there is an increase of one, two, three, four, or five morae (*mātrā*) in the feet, then Dhanañjaya called that *vicitramātrailā*. (102–103)
Nandinī, Citriṇī, Citrā, and Vicitrā—by these names, Ratilekhā and the others are declared, respectively, according to their various classes.
In this [Vaitālīya], the feet of the first two *elās* (syllables) are inverted in the odd [feet]. 104–105.
Thus, there are twenty *mātrailā* meters; those not restricted by the number of syllables in a *gaṇa* or *mātrā* are *varṇailā*,
which range from six syllables up to twenty-nine syllables per quarter-verse (*pāda*).
Thus, by increasing one by one, twenty-four *elās* have been described.
The first is joined with *madhukarī*; then comes *susvarā*, followed by *karaṇī*.
The fourth is called *surasā*, while the fifth is *prabhañjanī*.
The sixth is said to be Madanavatī, then Śaśinī and Prabhāvatī; 108 Mālatī and the one called Lalitā are considered next, followed by Bhogavatī;
then there is the one named Kusumavatī, and another shall be Kāntimatī. 109
Then there were those known as Kumudinī, Kalikā, Kamalā, Vimalā, Nalinī, Kālindī, Vipulā,
Vidyullatā, Viśālā, Saralā, and Taralā. (110)
Regarding this, others have declared that there are twelve *varṇamātrailās* of the final type;
in the *maṇṭha*, *dvitīyakaṅkāla*, and *pratitāla* tempos, some specific tempo (*tāla*) should be employed for them, but there is no fixed rule regarding the *rāga* or other such factors.
Ramaṇī, Candrikā, Lakṣmī, Padminī, Rañjinī, Mālatī, and Mohinī—these seven have been proclaimed by Mataṅga;
they are distinguished merely by the placement of the pause (yati), and thus have not been shown by us. 113

Thus, according to the scholars, five types of *elā* have been described based on the languages of Karṇāṭa, Lāṭa, Gauḍa, Āndhra, and Draviḍa— known as the regional *elās*— and categorized by the *maṇṭha* and other *tālas*. 114.

Others know the *karṇāṭī* meters as those beginning with *nādāvatī*, which are adorned with alliteration (*anuprāsa*) occurring at the beginning, middle, and end of the *karṇāṭailā* and other such [syllabic] feet;
their sixfold nature will be explained by the qualifiers to follow. (115)
The birth of Śambhu, the lord of the Gaṇas, from the command of Brahmā as before;
the first two quarters [of the verse] contain the *ādyanuprāsa* (alliteration at the beginning), while there are two instances of *madana* (internal alliteration) up to the end of the *rati*;
and the third quarter contains the *ādimadhyaprāsa* (alliteration at both the beginning and the middle) for each of those two. 116–117.

If she possesses four breasts, reaches the height of her thighs, and has beautiful lines, then she is of the first type; one born with a right-facing face has Sāvitrī as her deity and Hari as her lord. Gaṇādhipa [states that] each pair of feet corresponds to the "four desires."
The third foot consists of a *prāsa* situated at the beginning and middle, followed by three *prāsas*.
This is declared to be *Kāmalekhā*, which possesses eight *kāmās*; she is also called *Haṃsāvatī*.
She is born from the western face, and Brahmā is her *gaṇādhipa*. 119–120.

The deity is Gāyatrī; its three feet have alliteration at the beginning, middle, and end respectively; it is four times the number of Smaras (sixteen syllables) long; it is Nandāvatī; it is Svaralekhikā. 121.
Its birth is from Uttara; its presiding deity is Gaṇeśa; and it has six Manmathas (sixteen syllables).

That [meter] in which there are eight *bāṇa* (five-mora) feet at the end of each third [syllable], and whose three feet have *prāsa* (three-mora) groups at the beginning, middle, and end, is *Bhadrāvatī*, also known as *Bhadralekhā*; it is approved by the Karṇāṭas. 122–123.
There are five *kāmas* and one *rati*; thus there are six *kāmas* in the three feet respectively.
If all these possess the required *chandas* (syllables), they are considered complete.
Due to a deficiency or excess in the number of syllables in the *gaṇas* and so forth, these are considered mere semblances (*elābhāsā*) of the meter. 124–125.

If, for the sake of completing the feet, one, two, or three [syllables] have been placed at the end, and there is another foot measured by a third foot, that is the *śikhāpada*; however, the *melāpaka* and so forth are located in the third foot. 126.
Thus, the Lāṭī style is characterized by the use of the Karṇāṭa and Elā regions, while the Gauḍī style is considered to consist of a single rasa, being devoid of *gamakas* and *prāsas*. 127.

The *Drāviḍī* [elā] is characterized by feet that are intense with various applications of passion (*rāga*), portions (*aṃśa*), rasa, and emotion (*bhāva*), and it possesses an excellence of abundant emotions and rasas; it is devoid of the *prāsa* ornament.
(128) Thus ends the *elā* known by its regional name.
When the fourth foot is composed with those respective characteristics among them, then all these are called *chandovatī* by the ancients.
(129) Two feet are devoid of *prāsa*, while the third is joined with *prāsa*.
In those [meters], there should be two *dhruva* sections and four distinct *yatis*;
that in which there is an *ilāvat* section followed by *varṇa* syllables is defined as *vastvelā*.
It is stated that there are three hundred and fifty-six such *elās*.
But because of its infinity, the beloved of Hara cannot enumerate them in their entirety. (131) Thus ends the definition of *ilā*;
therein, the eightfold instrumental method begins with the musical notes (*svara*) and is preceded by rhythmic recitation (*pāṭa*).
The characteristics of these— the *bandha*, the *padādya*, the *tenādya*, the *birudādima*, the *citrādya*, and the *miśrakaraṇa*— are now described.
(132) In that [type] where the *udgrāha* and *dhruva* are composed of dense syllables (*sāndrasvara*), and furthermore [the *antara*] consists of words (*pada*).
In that [performance], there should be *ābhoga* (the concluding section), and furthermore, the grasping (*graha*) by the singer and the leader;
there should be placement (*nyāsa*) on the desired note, the *rāsa* rhythm, a fast tempo (*druta-laya*),
and the instrumental accompaniment (*karaṇa*) preceded by the notes— likewise, other elements should also be clearly manifest.
However, we shall now describe the differentiating factors regarding their placement of vowels (svara).
The execution of the recitation (pāṭakaraṇa) certainly occurs through both vowels and manual gestures (hastapāṭa);
it is proclaimed to be of two kinds based on the distinction between sequential order and its reversal. 134–135.
That which is composed of musical notes (*svara*) and the rhythmic strokes of the *muraja* drum is considered *tadbandha-karaṇa*.
That *karaṇa* which is bound by both musical notes and words (*pada*) is *padādi*. That *karaṇa* which is bound by musical notes and *viruda* (panegyrics) is *virudādi*. 136.

That which is composed with notes (*svara*) and *tenaka* syllables is considered *tattenakaraṇa*. That which is bound by notes together with *kara-pāṭa* syllables and the syllables of the drum (*muraja*) is designated as *citrakaraṇa* by the beloved of Hara (Śiva). 137–138.
There may be a mixed composition (miśrakaraṇa) bound by musical notes (svaras), recitations (pāṭas), and tenakas.

These three—namely, the auspicious beginning (maṅgalārambha), the increase of joy (ānandavardhana), and the wave preceded by fame (kīrtipūrvikā laharī)—are each further divided according to the distinctions of singing (gānabheda). 139–140.
If, after singing the *udgrāha* twice and the *dhruva* and *ābhoga* once each, the *dhruva* and *udgrāha* are then sung once more, that is the *maṅgalārambhaka*.
In this case, the *udgrāha* and *dhruva* are as before, followed by the latter half of the *dhruva*.
The *ābhoga*, *dhruva*, and *udgrāha* [occur] once in the *ānandavardhana*.
If the second half of the *udgrāha* is situated in the position of the *dhruva*’s half, while the other [half] is as before, then it is proclaimed as the *kīrtilaharī*. 142–143.
Thus there are twenty-seven *karaṇas*;
this is the sequence of *karaṇas*. Having sung the first half of the *udgrāha* twice, one then sings the second half once.
The *melāpaka* may consist of the *prayoga* or it may not; both of these should be performed without *tāla*, or in the *ḍheṅkikā-tāla*, or in the *kaṅkāla-tāla* at a slow tempo (*vilambita*).
In another tempo (*laya*), the *dhruva* and *ābhoga* sections should be performed with a different *tāla*; however, in this case, the *dhruva* remains [with its original tempo]. 144–145.
In that [form], there are three sections; two sections are sung with equal tempo (samadhātu), while the third is high (ucca).
This [third] is performed twice as an ābhoga, and then once more. Having sung it again, the final placement (nyāsa) occurs in the *dhruva*; that [melodic form] is considered a *ḍheṅkikā*.
The *ḍheṅkikā* is of four kinds: the *muktāvallī*, the *vṛttabandhinī*, the *yugminī*, and the *vṛttamālā*. Now, their definitions follow:
[the first] is the absence of meters; [the second] is a single meter; [the third] consists of two meters in succession; and [the fourth] consists of a series of meters. 147–148.

The second and subsequent [types] are of three kinds: *varṇikā*, *gaṇikā*, and likewise *mātrikā*; these consist of meters based on syllables (*varṇa*), meters based on morae (*gaṇa*), and meters based on measures (*mātrā*).
Furthermore, all ten [of these] are again threefold, including those with equal ornaments (*samālaṃkaraṇā*).
The *viṣama* (uneven) ornament, the *citra* (pictorial) ornament, the *lakṣaṇas* (characteristics),
the enumeration of the *sama* (even) ornaments, and the *miśrita* (mixed) uneven [ornaments] follow in sequence; thus there are thirty sections marked with the numeral thirty.
Thus ends the section on the ḍheṅkī;
like the *vartanī* of one who does not employ the primary notes (*svaras*), what is the characteristic here?
It should be known that the *tāla* is other than *rāsaka*, and the *laya* is slow (*vilambita*). 152.
If it is composed with *dvārudgrāha*, *dhruvābhoga*, and *sakṛnmokṣa* in the *dhruva*,
*kaṅkāla*, *pratitāla*, *kuḍukka*, and *drutamaṇṭhaka* meters,
then it should be known as a *vivartanī*, which is indeed a *vartanī*. 153.
"Thus is the path, thus is the path"— this is the definition of the *vartanī*,
wherein the first half and the second half are each preceded by an *udgrāha*, and then [the whole] is performed once. 154.
The *melāpaka* consists of the *prayoga* and so forth; all [parts] should be repeated twice, then the *dhruva* [is repeated].
Having sung the *ābhoga* only once, the final cadence (*nyāsa*) is placed upon the *dhruva*; that is the *jhombaḍa*.
(155) The *niḥsāruka*, the *kuḍukka*, the *tripuṭa*, and the *pratimaṇṭhaka* [are also types of *jāti-tāla*].
The second [type] consists of *gāru*, *gīrāsa*, *tilagna*, and *ḍatālikā* (156). These ten—namely *ekatālī* and so forth—are the fixed *tālas* in the *jhombaḍa*;
some also desire *maṇṭha*, but it is not observed in the authoritative treatises (*lakṣya*). (157)
Jhombaḍa is considered to be of two kinds: *tāraja* (born of the high register) and *atāraja* (not born of the high register).
*Tāra* refers to the placement of the vocal resonance; that which is joined with this is considered *tāraja*.
It is fourfold, according to its placement within the *udgrāha* and other sections of the musical structure.

All this [sound] is considered to be of two kinds: devoid of dust (rajas) and not devoid of dust. Furthermore, it would be twofold as consisting of three elements (tridhātu) and four elements (caturdhātu).
These are clearly [further divided into] those that convey much and those that convey little. 159–160.

The *prāyogika*, the one called *krama*, then the *kramavilāsaka*, the *citra*, and the *vicitralīla*— these five are distinct [types], produced sequentially by groups of four up to eight [syllables]. (161)
Likewise, Mātṛka and Śrīpati, as well as Soma, are not elaborated upon by us here because they do not apply to the objects of perception (*lakṣya*) when in conjunction with *Rucira*.
Due to their specific application, these [melodies] have thirteen distinct varieties. (162–163)
Through metaphors, similes, and puns, Brahmā is [the presiding deity] for the heroic (*vīra*) and erotic (*vilāsa*) sentiments;

Viṣṇu, as the Lord of the Discus (*cakreśvara*), is [the deity] for the heroic and the loathsome (*bībhatsa*); Caṇḍikeśvara is [the deity] for the loathsome; Narasiṃha is for the marvelous (*adbhuta*) sentiment; and Bhairava is for the fearful (*bhayānaka*). (164)

The *haṃsa* is [the best] for the comic (*hāsya*) and erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) sentiments; the *siṃha* for the heroic (*vīra*) and the fearful (*bhayānaka*); the *sāraṅga* for the sentiment of separation (*vipralambha*); and the *śekhara* for the pathetic (*karuṇa*).
The *puṣpasāra* is proclaimed as the best for the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) sentiment.

In the *raudra* (fierce) sentiment it is *pracaṇḍa*, while in the *śānta* (peaceful) sentiment it is declared by the wise to be *nandīśa*. These are of three kinds— born from prose, born from verse, and born from both prose and verse—
and they are reckoned as *jhombaḍas*, numbering [in total] fifty-one.
Thus are the *jhombaḍas*; such is the definition of the *jhombaḍa*:
the *udgrāha* (introductory section) is either twice [repeated], once, a single segment, or divided into two parts.
Where there are two *dhruvas* or an *ābhoga*, and liberation (*mukti*) occurs at the *dhruva*, that is the *lambhaka*.
In this *jhombaḍa*, there is also a section above the *dhruva* resembling the *udgrāha*;
therefore, others have stated that the *dhruva*, *ābhoga*, and *dhruva* should be sung thereafter. 169–170.
If the *udgrāha* is devoid of *tāla*, it is called *ālāpalambhaka*;
that is *pralambha* when the *udgrāha* in the *dhruva* section belongs to a different rhythmic element (*dhātu*).
Where there is a division within the *lambha*, that is termed *bhāgalambha*.
Where a *dhruvaka* is sung three, four, or five times, accompanied by distinct *udgrāha*s, it is called a *lambhapada*.
When there is a variation in the *dhruva*, it is an *anulambha*; when there is a double variation, it is an *upalambhaka*. (172–173)
These three are also effortless; that is called *vilambha*.
In it, there are many *udgrāhas* which are permanently devoid of effort (*ābhoga*).
These are considered to be composed with the *tālas* found in the *sālagasūḍa*. 174
Thus, there are eight types of *lambhaka*; this is the definition of *lambha*. That which possesses the characteristics found in *jhombaḍa*, yet is devoid of the *gamaka* positions, [is *lambha*].
This *rāsaka* is performed; it is sung with the *rāsa* rhythm (*tāla*) by means of *gaṇas*, *varṇas*, and *mātrās*. Some have declared it to be of three kinds.
It may be the *rāsavalaya*, the *haṃsatilaka*, or the *ratiraṅgaka*. (175)

The fourth among them is the Madanāvatāra; those born from chagaṇa and other materials are described as twenty-five, beginning with six syllables per foot and extending up to thirty syllables per foot, starting from eight mātrās per foot. 176–177.
It is said that [the duration] extends up to sixty *mātrās*, yet there are fifty-three *mātrās* [in some versions];
because these lack established usage in actual practice (*lakṣya*), we disregard them.
(178) Thus ends the definition of the *rāsaka*.
Thus is the definition of *rāsa*:
where there is a double *udgrāha*, a *dhruva* also repeated twice, and then an *ābhoga* and *dhruvaka* likewise repeated twice, followed by the *nyāsa*, that is called *ekatālikā*. 179.
In this [form], some have declared the *udgrāha* by means of mere recitation (180).
Thus ends the section on *ekatālī*. This concludes the sequence of *sūḍas*;
thus ends the definition of *ekatālī*.
Thus concludes the sequence of the pure *sūḍa*.
The *varṇa* [melodic form] is characterized by birudas, *varṇa*-tālas, and the Karṇāṭa language; its threefold nature is declared by the wise according to the three types of tāla. 181.
Thus is the phoneme;
thus is the sequence of phonemes; by means of vowels, recitations, and words, there is a composition according to the desired order.
That which has its placement (*nyāsa*) by means of the *tenaka* [syllables] is called *varṇasvara*.
This [type of *varṇasvara*] is fourfold, due to the different placements at the beginning of the vowels and so forth. Thus ends the section on *varṇasvara*.
Prose (gadya) is defined as a collection of words devoid of meter;
it consists of six types: ṣoḍhā, utkālikā, cūrṇa, lalita, vṛttagandhi, and khaṇḍa, as well as citra; and their origin is from the Sāmaveda. 184.

In the Heroic sentiment (*vīra*), the *Gauḍīyā* style—characterized by a longing to sing, red in color, presided over by Rudra as its deity, and beautiful—is to be sung while employing the *Ārabhaṭī* mode.
In the Quietistic sentiment (*śānta*), the yellow *Cūrṇa* powder is to be used, which is to be sung with Brahmā as its presiding deity. 185.
It is endowed with the Vaidarbha style, employs the Sātvatī mode of action, is bright, has Love as its presiding deity, is colored by the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa),
is graceful, employs the Kaiśikī mode of action, and follows the Pāñcālī style.

The *vṛttagandhi* [section] is for the *śānta* rasa; it is yellow in color, has the Sage as its deity, belongs to the *pāñcālī* style within the *bhāratī* mode, is composed of a mixture of prose and verse, is dedicated to Gaṇeśa as its deity, and is based on the *sātvatī* dramatic style. 188.
This white [poem], which brings forth laughter, has been commenced; it arises from the nuances of the Vaidarbha style (189).

It is variegated with the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), characterized by the Vaiṣṇava meter, born from the diverse *Kaśika* rhythmic patterns, and composed in the Vaidarbha manner with its manifold and wonderful varieties of style (190).
Others say there are two further types, *veṇī* and *miśra*.
*Veṇī* is composed of all [the meters], while *miśra* consists of *cūrṇaka* verses interspersed with those having the character of *vṛtta*.
These are further classified as *drutā*, *vilambitā*, *madhyā*, and *drutamadhyā*. (101)
The *gati* (pace) may be fast-slow (*drutavilambā*), and the sixth is medium-slow (*madhyavilambitā*);

thus six *gatis* of prose have been declared by the ancient masters. The first three [of these] correspond respectively to a predominance of light syllables, a small number of light syllables, and an even distribution [of heavy and light syllables]. (192)

When applied separately, and likewise with mixed *laga*s, there are three further [varieties]. (193) With each [variety] having six types of movement (*gati*), thirty-six varieties arise from prose (*gadya*).
(194) It begins with the *praṇava* and is endowed with all the *mata-tālas* and *gamakas*.

Where the musical compositions (*prabandha*) are sung with the sounds of cymbals (*tāla*) and the notes (*svara*) of various syllables interspersed here and there; where the pair of words, marked by the composition and accompanied by *tāla*, is then sung separately twice; and where the performance (*prayoga*) is also rendered at a slow tempo (*vilambita*). 195–196.

The name of the singer and the name of the description, each with a *tāla* beat, are sung at a slow tempo (*vilambita*), and then again at a non-slow tempo; when the finale (*nyāsa*) is performed with a slow *tāla*, that is desired as *gadya*. 197.
Thus is the prose;
thus is the prose composition. In the *kaivāḍa* style, there should be the *dhruva* and *udgrāha* sections through recitations, and the *nyāsana* (concluding placement) occurs upon the *graha*. 198.
That [kaivāḍa] is considered to be of two kinds: by means of readings that are meaningful and those that are devoid of meaning.
It is further twofold: pure and mixed, according to whether the readings are pure or mixed.
(199) Thus ends the section on kaivāḍa.

Bound by birudas associated with the heroic and the fierce, moving through the *aṅkas*, possessing an extent endowed with the names of the characters to be described, it is sung in the desired *tāla*.
Then there is the *vāsavī* *kalikā*, and after that, the *vīravatī* *vṛtta*. 200.
That [Vedottarā] is considered to be of six types, including the Jātimatī;
its tālas are one, two, three, four, and five, while the virudas (epithets) are eight, sixteen, and likewise thirty-two, in successive order. 201–202.

In the first five [classes], the rule is one hundred and fifty-four; however, in the *jātimatī* [class], there is no restriction regarding the support of the *tāla* and *viruda*. (203) Thus ends the *Aṅkacāriṇī*.
In the Āryā-gīti in the heroic (vīra) rasa, when performed with the *karṇāṭa* and other *pāṭas* and *virudas*, it is devoid of *tāla* and consists of *pāṭa-muktakas*; this is the *kanda*.
[The four types are] Pavana, Ravisamjña, Dhanada, and Havyavāhana. 204.
Suranātha, Samudra, Varuṇa, Śaśin, and Śailaka (205);
then those named Madhu and Mādhava, followed by Madanadhvaja; Jayanta, Madhupa, and then Śuka, Sārasa, and Ke kin (206).
Hari, Karabha, Hastī, Kādamba, Kūrmaka, Naya,
Vinaya, Vikrama, Utsāha, Dharma, Artha, and Kāma—
these twenty-nine are declared by the ancients to be the varieties of the *kanda*. (207)
From thirty *gurūs* down to two *gurūs*, by means of each successive reduction, [there are twenty-one varieties].
Thus is the *kanda*.
With the *tāla* called *hayalīla*, the *hayalīlā* is of two kinds.
