It is both prose-born (*gadyajā*) and verse-born (*padyajā*); as for the verse-born, it is of four kinds. (209) If the first half or the second half of the *āryā* is joined with a *tāla*, there would then be three [types]; however, the fourth is that which has [the *tāla*] in the first *dala*.
It is considered composed with musical notes (*svaras*), words (*padas*), epithets (*birudas*), and rhythmic beats (*tālas*).
Some wise scholars, however, know it by the meter *hayalīlā*.
Thus end the nine *turagalīlās*.
Thus ends the definition of Hayalīlā; when set to the Gajalīla tāla, it is called Gajalīlā. Any other characteristic that lacks the [specific] meter is considered to belong to the Hayalīlā category.
Thus ends the definition of *gajalīlā*.
The *dvipadī* is of four kinds—pure (*śuddhā*), fragmentary (*khaṇḍā*), based on morae (*mātrādi*), and complete (*saṃpūrṇā*)—and it is sung to the *tāla* known as *karuṇa*. 213.

In each quarter, there are six gaṇas, with a short syllable (ga) at the end; the sixth and second gaṇas consist of two short syllables (ja), and the rest are four mātrās each. With such quarters, the *śuddhā dvipadikā* is defined.
Others say that the vowels (*svaras*) occur at the end of the half-line; it is called *khaṇḍā* when it consists of a single *śuddhā* half-line. 214.
The *mātrā-dvipadikā* is considered to consist of six long syllables (*guru*) and two short syllables (*laghu*), known as the pure and complete form when it ends with an additional long syllable.
The *pluta-dvipadī* is of four kinds: *Mānavī*, *Candrikā*, and *Dhṛti*.
If there is a *mānavī* [meter] with a *chagaṇa* at the beginning and two *tavayas*, it is called *tāritā*.
If there is a *nagaṇa* at the end and two *laghus*, it is considered *candrikā*.
With three *chagaṇas* (each consisting of four *mātrās*), it is called *dhṛti*.
"Tārā consists of four *chagaṇas* with a heavy syllable (*guru*) at the end" (217).
Thus, in the *dvipadī*,
if the final group of syllables within each preceding sequence of syllables [is as described], [it is a *tārā*].
When it consists of a succession of verses beginning with the *saṃgha* and so forth, it is then called *cakravāla*;
that is described by the wise as being of two kinds, distinguished as prose (*gadya*) and verse (*padya*).
(218) Thus ends the *cakravāla*.
It is sung with words and notes, using the *krauñcapada* rhythm and the *pratitāla* tempo; it is a placement of notes (*svaranyāsa*) performed in that same meter or as a detached verse (*muktaka*).
Thus ends the *krauñcapada*.
Thus ends the definition of the *krauñcapada* (the crane-step).

Where the intended meaning is expressed by means of the musical notes (*svara*) and syllables (*akṣara*) alone, that is the *svarārtha* (meaning conveyed by notes), which is of two kinds: pure (*śuddha*) and mixed (*miśra*), according as those [notes and syllables] are used either purely or in combination. 220
The placement of the *graha* (seizers) for this [mantra] is further performed sevenfold by means of the vowels starting from one;
the combinations of two vowels and so forth are differentiated many times through both direct and reverse order. Thus ends the section on the vowels.

Thus is the definition of the notes and their meanings: in this [rūpaka], the *dhruva* and *udgrāha* sections have distinct *tālas*, excluding the *maṇṭha* and *kaṅkāla*; and there is no *yati* or *melāpaka* in its equal *mātrās*. 222.
It should be sung with two *tāla*s, like a *ḍheṅkī*, as a "striker of sound" (*dhvanikuṭṭinī*).
Thus [ends] the *dhvanikuṭṭinī*:
having placed the vowels at the end of the half-verse or at the end of the quarter-verse, one places the first half [of the melody].
A song sung twice in the Āryā meter, with the interval between sections (dalāntara) sung once, wherein the name of the singer appears in the *ābhoga*, is the *Āryā-grahamuktikā*.
[The meters] are Lakṣmī, Vṛddhi, and Buddhi; likewise Līlā, Lajjā, and Kṣamā. 224.
Dīrghā, Gaurī, Rājī, Jyotsnā, Chāyā, and Kāntikā;
then Mahī, Mati, Kīrti, and thereafter Manoramā should be known, along with Rohiṇī, Viśālā, Vasudhā, and Śivā. (225–226)
The Hariṇī, the Cakrā, the Sārasī, the Kurarī,
the Haṃsī, and the Vadhū are declared to be the twenty-six Āryās in sequence.
The first [variety] consists of all heavy syllables from the sixth [position] onwards, while the others consist of other gaṇas.

By the successive breaking of one or more heavy syllables (gurus), these characteristics [of the *udīcyavṛtti*] are to be known according to the definitions of prosody (*chanda-lakṣaṇa*); the remaining numerous varieties are to be understood from the same source.
Thus ends the *Āryā*.
The *gāthā* should be sung in the *prākṛta* language; it may consist of five quarters or three quarters. Other wise scholars have declared that it may also consist of six quarters.
Thus ends the section on the *gāthā*.

By means of *chandas* (meter) there is the *dvipatha*; the *dvipatha* may consist of free melodic phrases (*svaramuktika*) or be devoid of rhythmic time-measures (*tāla*), or it may possess them—it should be known as being of four kinds:
one consisting of *svaras*, another of *prayogas*, and the other two consisting of both. 231.
In Prakrit, this is known as *doha*; its nine varieties are as follows:
the *sārasa*, the *bhramara*, the *haṃsa*, the *kurara*, the *candralekhaka*, the *kuñjara*, the *tilaka*, the *haṃsakrīḍa*, and the *mayūraka*. (232–233)
In the *sārasa* meter, there are thirteen morae in an odd pāda and twelve in an even one;
in the *bhramara*, there are fourteen morae in an odd pāda and twelve in an even one.
In the *haṃsa* meter, there are fifteen morae in an odd pāda and thirteen in an even one. (234)

In the Kurara [yoga], there are thirteen digits (*kalā*) in the odd [tithi] and fourteen in the even; 235. In the Candralekhā [yoga], there are fifteen digits in the odd and twelve in the even; in the Kuñjara [yoga], there are thirteen digits in the odd and fifteen in the even. 236.

In the *tilaka* meter, there are fifteen syllables in the even feet and fourteen in the odd feet; in the *haṃsakrīḍa*, there are sixteen syllables in both the even and odd feet. If at the end of their two halves there are five or more short syllables, it is called *śikhā*.
The wise call that *śikhādvipatha*, which also includes the *mayūra*;
in these meters, there may be a placement of the feet even by way of transposition (238).
There occur varieties based on the single or double occurrence of the feet.
These *dvipathas*, which have many variations, are to be recognized by the wise among various metrical targets (239).
Thus ends the *dvipatha* meter of *Chandasa-kalahaṃsa*, characterized by feet ending in vowels.
The *kalahaṃsa* is to be sung with a placement (*nyāsa*) on the note *niṣāda* (svarāṅga) and according to the *jhampa* and other time-measures (*tāla*).

The *kalahaṃsa* is considered to be of two kinds: that born of syllables (*varṇaja*) and that consisting of measures (*mātrika*). If it consists of prose (*gadyātman*), then, having taken the musical phrases (*svarāṅga*), there follows the arrangement of words (*padaniveśana*).
Thus ends the *Kalahamsa* [section].
As for the *Toṭaka* meter, it is defined by the rule that the *svarita* accent is placed at the end of each foot;
but surely, since the *Toṭaka* will be mentioned again later in the discussion of meters (*vṛtta*), its definition here is redundant. (142)
It is true; however, in the opinion of those for whom the *vṛtta* (meter) is defined by its metrical *vṛtta* (foot-pattern), there is no tautology here in the case of the *toṭaka*.
Thus ends the *toṭaka*.
By those [syllables], half [is used] for the *dvipadī* and half for the *ghaṭa*; by that [same measure], the *muktikā* [is formed].
(244) Thus, the *ghaṭa* is sung in any meter (*chandas*) with any desired rhythm (*tāla*).
One should place vowels at the end of its metrical foot (vṛtta) or at the conclusion of the verse;
others say it is "devoid of vowels," while still others maintain that the meter (vṛtta) resides in the prosody (chandas).
One must discern the various meters within the arrangement of prosody, for there are many divisions of prosodic meters. 245–246.
Thus, if the words preceded by each individual letter of the *mātṛkā* are sung in sequence according to their occurrence, that *mātṛkā* is considered to be threefold. (247)
It is of three kinds: divine, human, and both divine and human.
Among these, the divine is sung in the Sanskrit language with the rhythms of the *mārga* style;
the human is composed in the Prakrit language with the rhythms of the *deśī* style.
From the blending of both, the Mātṛkā is said to be divine and human (249).
It is twofold—unbound and bound—and consists of prose and verse;
for it is composed entirely of mantras and bestows all accomplishments.
She, beloved by the hosts of gods, is to be constantly and invariably sung by those who are self-restrained.
Thus, the Mātṛkā consists of two types: the Nandyāvarta and the Svastika, which together form the cluster of melodies (rāgakadambaka).

The Nandyāvarta consists of four *vṛttas* and four *tālas*, and is adorned with a row of melodies (*rāga*). It may consist of two measures of *tāla*, or its conclusion (*nyāsa*) may be with the *udgrāha*; others have declared it to be in prose (*gadya*). 251–252.
According to some, [the first] is one *tāla*, while the *svastika* is double that;
the *abjapatra*, *abjagarbha*, *bhramara*, and *āmreḍita* are considered by some to be each double the size of the preceding one. (253)
Thus ends the *rāgakadambaka* section.

The *ālāpa* should be performed with the *prāgatāla*, consisting of five distinct phrases each repeated twice; thereafter, the notes (*svaras*) and the syllabic ornaments (*pāṭas*) are played with that same *caccatpluta* rhythm. 254.

An *antara* should be performed with *pāṭas* arising from the *dvicaccatpluta* measure; then, a five-word phrase (*padapañcaka*) should be made with the *cācatpuṭa* measure. Likewise, the notes (*svaras*) and *pāṭas* should be performed with that [same] measure, and an *antara* with its double measure.
Thereafter, with *huḍukkāpāṭas* and *ṣaṭpitāputrakas*, there are five separate sections; by that same [measure] doubled, there is a section of vowels (*svarapāṭaka*).
Beyond that *vimāna*, there should be an interval of *śaṅkhapāṭas*, and after that, six [sections]. 256–257.
Each [instrument] should have two types of *pada*s, from the *saṃpakva* up to the *iṣṭaka-tāla*; then likewise the vowels (*svara*) and the *pāṭa*s, with an interval according to that measure (258).
Then, in the *udghaṭṭa*, there are six *pada*s produced by the *kāṃsyatāla*.
As before, there are likewise the vowels (*svaras*) and the beats (*pāṭas*) produced by the muraja drum (259).

The *antara* section is as previously described, followed by the *ābhoga*, which is not slow. Then follow the name of the composition, the measure, the name of the leader, and finally the auspicious benediction.
The placement [of the syllables] in the *Vākyamālāpaka* constitutes the *Pañcatāleśvara*;
it is twofold, namely the *Vīrāvatāra* and the *Śṛṅgāratilaka*.
By means of these two, all the deities are pleased through the heroic (*vīra*) and erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) sentiments. (260–261)
Thus [are] the *Pañcatāleśvara* and other such compositions in the *Āli* meter; that ocean of rhythms (*tālārṇava*), consisting of many *tālas*, is twofold: in prose and in verse. 262
Thus ends the Ocean of Tālas.
These are the characteristics of the *Ālikrama* composition: it should consist of four *tālas* and *rāgas*, and at the end, it should be joined with a *pada*. 263.
Thus ends Śrīraṅga, which concludes with a vowel; Śrīvilāsa consists of five tālas and rāgas.
(264) Thus ends Śrīvilāsa.

The *pañcabhaṅgipañcānana* consists of five sections (*bhaṅgī*) with five recitations (*pāṭa*), ending with two [sections] and two [recitations], as well as two melodies (*rāga*) and two tempos (*tāla*).
Thus are the *pañcabhaṅgī* and *pañcānana*.
Furthermore, the Umātilaka consists of three tālas and rāgas at the end of the *biruda*; these are the *sarvāṅgika* [melodies].
Thus ends the Umātilaka. (266)
The first two quarters consist of two groups of two syllables each, the third quarter consists of four groups, and the fourth quarter consists of three groups;
thus, there are these eleven groups in the quarters.
In the *rateḥ* meter, the sixth and tenth groups are [specific], while the remaining groups are those of the god of love (*mānmatha*).
Having sung the first two quarters and then a small portion of the third,
if that entire third quarter is then sung and the fourth is sung [subsequently], then it would be a *tripadī* in the Karṇāṭaka language, devoid of rhythmic beat (*tāla*). (268–269)

Thus, in a four-line verse (*catuṣpadī*), there should be sixteen morae (*mātrā*) in each even line consisting of three feet (*tripadī*), while in the odd lines there are fifteen; furthermore, in such a verse, the two halves of the *yamaka* (rhyme) must be distinct.
"Joined with *svara*, *tena*, and *ka*, and joined with *tena* and *kanyāsa*" (270)—
thus is the four-line [verse];
the sixth and third [feet] consist of three *gaṇas*, while the others consist of two *gaṇas* each.
The fourth foot consists of four *caraṇa* gaṇas, while the sixth and third feet consist of two *bāṇa* gaṇas at their ends;
this is the *ṣaṭpadī*.
That [verse] in which the remaining [feet] consist of *manmatha* gaṇas is considered a *ṣaṭpadī*.

In the Karṇāṭa language, the *nādamuktikā* is devoid of rhythmic time-measures (*tāla*). Thus, the varieties of the six-footed meter (*ṣaṭpadī*) are to be known; furthermore, there are many varieties of the three-footed meter (*tripadī*) and others according to the characteristics of prosody (*chandas-lakṣaṇa*). 272–273.
There are fifteen morae in the first foot, and likewise in the third and fifth;
in the fourth and second [feet], there are twelve [morae], ending with a vowel.
The first half-verse ends with a *tena* (the word "thereby"), and following that is the *dohaka*.
"Wherever there is a deposit (nyāsa) upon that [specific] one, the wise know that to be the *vastu*.
Thus, in this *vastu*, by means of those notes (*svara*), articulations (*pāṭa*), words (*pada*), and the *vijaya-tāla*:
It is sung by the Vijaya-thieves; that Nyāsa is considered Vijaya (276).
Thus ends Vijaya;
it consists of three quarters, with recitations, titles, and notes in the Tripathaka meter (277).
Thus, the *tripathaka* is to be sung through its notes, recitations, words, and syllables, along with the *sthāyī* and other elements in sequence;
it has four quarters, and the final cadence (*nyāsa*) occurs on the fourth syllable during the *graha*. 278.
Thus, that which is composed by the four-faced one with vowels, *pāṭas*, birudas, and *tenakas*, performed with the *siṃhalīla* rhythm (*tāla*), is called *siṃhalīla*. 279.
Thus, in the *siṃhalīla* [tāla], the two feet are in the *padapāṭaja* [rhythm] within the *svanāma* [tāla]; this is the *haṃsalīla*. 280.
Thus ends the *haṃsalīla*.
The *daṇḍaka* is considered to be composed of feet consisting of vowels according to the *daṇḍaka* meter;
its numerous varieties have been described in the treatises on prosody (*chandolakṣma*).
Thus ends the section on *daṇḍaka*.
The *jhampaṭa* is to be sung in the *jhampaṭa* meter with the *krīḍā* rhythm. Thus ends the *jhampaṭa*.
The *kanduka* is celebrated through verses, syllabic sounds (*pāṭas*), and epithets (*birudas*). 282–283.
Thus the *kanduka* has been described with its vowels, *pāṭas*, and words, characterized by the *tribhaṅgī*; and it is of five kinds:
one is performed with the *tribhaṅgī tāla* and another with the *vṛtta* meter, while the others are likewise characterized by the *tribhaṅgī*. 284.

Whether accompanied by three rhythmic cycles (*tāla*) and three musical modes (*rāga*), or endowed with three meters (*vṛtta*), or consisting of praises to the three deities, it is characterized by a doubling of the rhythm;
thus is the *tribhaṅgi*. 285.
By means of words, titles, and verses, [they call him] Haravilāsaka (the Play of Śiva) 286;
thus ends the Haravilāsa.
By means of words, titles, and verses, they designate Sudarśana 287.
Thus, according to Sudarśana, the three parts beginning with the *udgrāha* are formed respectively by words, vowels, and birudas;
there should be one, two, and three *tālas*, and the placement [of the syllables] upon the vowel-mark is done by means of the vowels. (288)

Thus, the *svarāṅka* (notation of notes) is that which increases the beauty [of the composition] through birudas, pāṭas, words, and notes; it consists of the placement of two measures of rhythm (*tāla*) and tempo (*māna*), as proclaimed by Niḥśaṅka. 289
Thus, by his titles he was Śrīvardhana, and by his birudas he was Harṣavardhana; by his musical scales he was Svarapāṭaka.
Thus [ends the account of] Harṣavardhana.
Two *chapa*s constitute a *vadana*; the interval between them is joined with *svarapāṭa*.
Likewise, an *upavadana* is said to be formed by being covered with *chagaṇas*. Similarly, a *vastuvadana* is made from two *chayas*, *adda*, *cha*, and *chai*. (291)

Thus is the threefold *vadana*; the *rāga* is Hindolaka, the *tāla* is Caccarī, and it consists of many feet (*aṅghri*), in which there are sixteen *mātrās*, with two [feet] each joined by a pause (*prāsa*). (292)

This *caccarī* is to be sung during the spring festival using Prakrit verses; others say it is in the *caccarī* meter, or even in the *krīḍā* rhythm (*tāla*), or in the *ghuttā* meter and so forth—the distinctions of its meters are declared in the *Chandolakṣmī*. (293)

Thus, meters such as *caccarī* and *paddhaḍī*, adorned with alliteration at the end of the quarters, constitute the spiritual practice (*caryā*) which, beginning from the second *tāla*, pertains to the domain of the inner self. 294.

That [dhruva] is of two kinds: full, by virtue of fulfilling the meter, and incomplete, by virtue of not fulfilling it; furthermore, it is of two types—the even-dhruva and the uneven-dhruva—and that is sung either by repeating all the quarters or by [repeating] the dhruva alone. 295

Thus, this *paddhaḍī*— composed in the *paddhaḍī* meter with rhymes at the ends of even-footed lines, adorned with honorific titles (*biruda*) ending in the recitation of musical notes (*svarapāṭa*)— is considered a *caryā*. 296.
Thus, where there is a *paddhaḍī* consisting of praise for battle through the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) and composed of many feet (*caraṇa*), it is here proclaimed as a *rāhaḍī*. 297.
Thus, composed of the words and titles of Rāhaḍī, she is celebrated as Vīraśrī; thus ends [the section on] Vīraśrī. 298.
Thus ends Vīraśrī.
That auspicious performance (*maṅgalācāra*) composed in prose, verse, or a mixture of both, belonging to the Kaiśikī style, which possesses an exodus (*niḥsāra*) and is endowed with musical notes—
this is the auspicious performance (verse 299).
The *dhavala* meter is of three kinds: *kīrti*, *vijaya*, and *vikrama*;
these are formed respectively by four, six, and eight feet.
If there is a *ḍa* in the odd [feet], and either *ta* or *da* is added in the even [feet], it is [the *dhavala*]. (300)

Then it would be white with fame in victory; however, in the first and fourth [pādas], there is *koda* (the syllables *ka*, *o*, *da*), and in the sixth and second, the remaining two are *cha* or *pa*.
In the first [pāda], there should be three *da*s, and in the third, there are three *dā*s.

That which has four *dās* at the end of the fourth and second [padas], as well as in the fifth and seventh, and in the sixth and eighth, is considered *vikrama*. It should be sung with auspicious blessings (*āśīs*) and accompanied by words such as "dhavala. (302–303)
Or, according to popular custom, the *dhavala* may be sung at will; thus ends the *dhavala*. In the *kaiśikī* or the *boṭṭa-rāga*, the *maṅgala* [is performed] with auspicious words.
It should be sung in a slow tempo (*vilambita-laya*) or in an auspicious meter (*maṅgala-chandas*);
thus, the *Maṅgala* is sung in three sections (*khaṇḍa*), joined with alliteration (*prāsa*), in the local dialect (*deśabhāṣā*). 305.
If that [same] *ovī* occurs at the end of that [verse], it is called *ovīpada* by those who know it (306).
There may be variations among the three quarters (*caraṇa*) due to repetition one or more times,
and due to alliteration (*prāsa*) occurring at the beginning, middle, or end of each quarter (307).
To be sung in many meters, pleasing to the people,
adorned with three sections featuring alliteration and Prakrit words, and ending with the *lolīpada*, the *lolī* should be sung by the learned. (308)
Thus, when there is a *lolī* *dohaḍa* at the conclusion with the words "prollasaḍhḍhollarī," it is called by the name *ḍhollarī*, adorned with the Lāṭa dialect. 309
Thus, if the *ḍhollarī* is primarily characterized by alliteration (*anuprāsa*), consists of three sections, and is concluded with the word *dantī*, it is then called *dantī*. (110)
Thus, in the case of *dantī*, there is the conceptualization of unmentioned objects of experience through words; however, the four beginning with *ov* are devoid of such experiential engagement. 311
Thus, the thirty-six miscellaneous compositions are described;
*sūḍa* is said to be of two kinds: pure (*śuddha*) and shadow-like (*chāyālaga*). That which begins with *elā* is called pure, while that which begins with *dhruvā* is considered shadow-like. (312)

Just as in the world, whatever is accepted by the teachers regarding the *chāyālaga*, *melāpa*, and so forth, even though it is pure because of its similarity to the pure, [it is classified] from the *jāti* up to the various *bhāṣās*, as contained within the section on the pure. 313.
The pure *sūḍa* has been described there previously; now the *sālagasūḍa* is being discussed.
First is the *dhruva*, then the *maṇṭha*, *pratimaṇṭha*, and *nisāruka*; after that, the *aḍḍatāla*, then the *rāsa*, and finally the *ekatālī*—this is how it is considered. 314–315.
There should be one *dhātu* consisting of two *khaṇḍas*; after that where there is an *udgrāha*, the subsequent *khaṇṇḍa* should be somewhat higher, and this triad is repeated twice (316).
Then the *ābhoga* consists of two *khaṇḍas*, of which the first *khaṇḍa* [is as follows].
It consists of one *dhātu* and two *khaṇḍas*, with the latter *khaṇḍa* being higher;
it is marked by the name of the person being praised, and in some cases, there is a single high *khaṇḍa*.
The placement (*nyāsa*) occurs in the first *khaṇḍa* of the *udgrāha*, together with the *dhruva*. (317–318)
From the eleven-syllable *khaṇḍa*, there shall be sixteen *dhruvas* by increasing one syllable at a time, up to twenty-six syllables; these are Jayanta, Śekhara, Utsāha, Madhura, and Nirmala. (319)
Kuntala, Kāmala, Āra, Nandana, Candraśekhara, Kāmada, Vijaya, Kandarpa, Jayamaṅgala,
Tilaka, and Lalita— these are their names in successive order. (320–321)

In the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) rasa, the *jayanta* is sung by the wise using the *āditāla* meter; it is considered to increase the lifespan and prosperity of the protagonist, the audience, and the singers.
In the *vīra* (heroic) rasa, the *śekhara* occurs in the *niḥsāru* meter and bestows wealth and good fortune. (322)
In the comic sentiment (hāsya), the *pratimaṇṭha* rāga produces enthusiasm and increases one's lineage; it should be sung sweetly for the attainment of fortune.
In the pathetic sentiment (karuṇa), it is sung with the "horse-play" (*hayalīlā*) rhythm;
in the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), the *nirmala* [rāga], sung with the *krīḍātāla* rhythm, spreads forth a brilliant luster.
In the *adbhuta* (wonderful) sentiment, Kuntala grants desired boons when accompanied by the *laghuśekhara* rhythm;
in *vipralambha* (erotic separation), Kāmala is the giver of success (*siddhi*) through the *jhampa* rhythm.
And in the *vīra* (heroic) sentiment, Āra bestows an abundance of joy through the *niḥsāra* rhythm. 325.
Nandana is for the heroic and erotic sentiments; Ekatālī bestows the desired Siddhis.
(326) In the heroic, comic, and erotic sentiments, Candraśekhara is sung with Pratimaṇṭha, granting the cherished fruits to both listeners and singers. (327)
In the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) rasa, the *kāmoda* [tāla] grants desired desires;
in the *hāsya* (comic), the *vijaya* [tāla] with a second beat (*dvitīyatāla*) is for the longevity of the leader.
It is sung in the *hāsya*, *śṛṅgāra*, and *karuṇa* (pathetic) rasas with the *āditāla*.
Kaṃdarpa bestows enjoyment upon men and is approved by Śrī Sadāśiva (329).
Jayamaṅgala is used for the erotic and heroic sentiments with the *krīḍātāla* rhythm; it grants victory and enthusiasm to men. Dhruvaka is known as the *tilaka*. (330)
In the heroic (vīra) and erotic (śṛṅgāra) sentiments, the *ekatālī* is sung;
in the erotic sentiment, the *lalita* is sung with the *pratimaṇṭha* for the attainment of all success.
There should be a restriction of syllables for every section (*khaṇḍa*), as well as for the two halves. 331.
"The best of sages declared: 'He who, with a discerning intellect, sings the hymns beginning with Jayanta as they have been described, shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices'—
thus ends the definition of the Dhruva."
That section called the *udgrāha* consists of two [lines] with a single pause; then follows the section called the *dhruva*, which is likewise repeated twice.
After singing that, one returns to the *dhruva* and then the *ābhoga* is sung once. This is the optional *antara*. 333.
The placement [of the tāla] is declared to be on the *dhruva* (refrain); that is *maṇṭha*, derived from the *maṇṭha* rhythm.
Jayapriya, Maṅgala, Sundara, Vallabha, Kalāpa, and Kamala—these six varieties are considered to belong to the *maṇṭha*. 334–335.
The *maṇṭha* rhythm is of six kinds; by it, the *rūpaka* is divided.
In the heroic (*vīra*) sentiment, the *jayapriya* is to be sung with the *maṇṭha* consisting of a *jagaṇa*.
In the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) sentiment, the *maṅgala* is [sung] with the *bha*, and the *sundara* with the *sa* for that same sentiment. (336)

The *vallabha* [rhythm] is sung by experts in the *hāsya* (comic) rasa with a *karuṇa* (long) *kalāpa* and a *nagaṇa* ending in a pause (337). The *kamala* [rhythm] in the *adbhuta* (wonderful) rasa is sung with two *druta* (short) syllables at the end of the pause, followed by a *laghu* (short) syllable (338).
Thus is the definition of the *maṇṭha*;
the definitions of the *pratimaṇṭha* and others, as well as their *udgrāha* (refrains) and so forth, are considered to be like those of the *maṇṭha*.
However, their specific distinctions will be explained individually. 339

And therein, by means of the *pratimaṇṭha* rhythm, the *pratimaṇṭhaka* is fourfold: namely, *amara*, *tāra*, *vicāra*, and also *kunda*. Among these, *amara* consists of one heavy syllable (*guru*) and is prescribed for the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*). 340
Thus says Amaruka:

from two *druta* [mātrās] ending in a pause, followed by a pair of *laghu* [mātrās], this *pratimaṇṭha* called *tārā* arises; it is appropriate for the two sentiments of heroism (*vīra*) and wrath (*raudra*). (341)
Thus, with the *tāra* [syllable] followed by three short syllables ending in a pause, there is *vicāra* in the *karuṇa* [rasa];
thus is *vicāra*.
The *kunda* occurs in the *adbhuta* [rasa] with three *la*s in the middle of the pause;
thus is the *kunda*.
Those who know the characteristics also proclaim four [varieties] in the *śṛṅgāra* [rasa]. 342–343.
Thus ends the definition of the fourfold *pratimaṇṭha*.
The *niḥsāruka* is said by the experts to be composed with the *niḥsārutāla*;
its varieties are Vaikuṇṭha, Ānanda, Kāntāra, Samara, and Vāñchita. (344)
Thus it is declared by the sage Śārṅgin to be sixfold, including Viśāla.
Vaikuṇṭha occurs in Maṅgala from two *druta*s followed by two *laghu*s; Ānanda produces joy through two *druta*s at the end of the pause. (345)
Thus, Vaikuṇṭha and Ānanda are [the first two];
that which occurs in separation (vipralambha) through the *laghu* and *guru* [meters] is called *kāntāra*.
Thus ends *kāntāra*.

"A battle within the domain of heroes [occurs] from two short syllables ending in a pause" (346)— thus is "battle" [defined]. From three short syllables, or from a pair of *druta* [syllables], the "desired" [meter] bestows what is desired.
Thus, when desired in *saṃbhoga*, it is called *viśāla* after two *laddhutas* followed by a short syllable; thus ends *viśāla*.
Thus, the sixfold *niḥsāruka* is proclaimed; by means of the *aḍḍatāla* rhythm, the *aḍḍatāla* is described, as well as the *niśaṅka*, *śaṅkaśīla*, *cāra*, and *makarandaka*. 348.
And it is called *vijaya*; thus it has been declared as sixfold by Soḍhala’s son.
From two heavy syllables followed by a pair of light syllables, *niḥśaṅka* occurs in the *vismaya* meter. (349) Thus ends *niḥśaṅka*.

A *śaṅkha* occurs when there is a light syllable followed by two *druta*s in the *śṛṅgāra* and *vīra* rasas; in the *śānta* rasa, a *śīla* occurs when there is a light syllable at the end of a pause, following a pair of *druta*s. (350)
Thus, according to Śīla,
when there is a rapid movement of the feet from one pair [of limbs] to another, it is the *cāra* (movement) in the heroic (*vīra*) and marvelous (*adbhuta*) rasas;
such is the *cāra*.
In the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), there should be *makaranda*; after two short syllables (*druta*) followed by a long syllable (*guru*), it is thus called *makaranda*.
In the heroic sentiment (*vīra-rasa*), that which is known as *vijaya* occurs with two short syllables followed by a short syllable (*laghu*). 351–352.
Thus, Vijaya;
such is the sixfold Aḍḍatāla.
Rāsaka is described as being fourfold by means of the Rāsa tāla.
Vinoda, Varada, Nanda, and Kambuja— among these,
Vinoda occurs in the *kautuka* [rāga] from the *dhruvapada* at the end of the *ālāpa*. (353) Thus ends Vinoda.

"From the middle of the *dhruva* [section] during the praise of the deity, [the singer should perform] the *varada* [melody]. (354) Thus, the first section (*khaṇḍa*) of the *varada* is composed of the *ālāpa* of the two-part *udgrāha*.
"That Nanda, who is sung as the giver of prosperity, belongs to this *rāsaka*.
(355) Thus, Nanda [is used] from the introductory dialogue (*ālāpa*) up to the fixed refrain (*dhruvapada*); in the *karuṇa* [rasa], it would be *kambuja*.
Thus, in all these *rāsakas*, the *kambuja* [meter] is employed for the two-part introductory sections (*udgrāha*). (356) Thus ends the definition of the fourfold *rāsaka*.
There is the Ekatālī with its tāla; that [Ekatālī] is threefold:
Ramā, Candrikā, and likewise Vipulā. Now, the definition [is as follows]: the *udgrāha* consists of a single pause, while the *antara* is composed of syllables. 357.
In that [melody], this Ramā shall serve for the glory of both the singer and the listener (358).
Thus, the *udgrāha* is Ramā; it consists of two *dalas*, and its internal section (*antara*) is composed of an *ālāpa*.
The *candrikā* meter consists of dense and swift feet, possesses a dense internal rhyme (*anuprāsa*), and is like a sandy bank of moonlight; it bestows abundant good fortune.
(359) Thus ends the *candrikā*.

The *udgrāha* preceded by *ālāpa* bestows abundant joy; *ālāpa* is considered to be the improvisation (*gama*) devoid of fixed syllables, and that very thing has been designated by Śārṅgadeva with the term "application" (*prayoga*). 360
Thus [ends] the *vipulā*;
thus [ends] the definition of the three types of *ekatālī*;
thus [ends] the definition of the *sālagasūḍa*.
A new *rūpaka* (musical composition) is excellent when it is endowed with qualities, free from defects, and fresh.
O Rāma, a *rūpaka* is truly new through its novelty of *rāga*, *dhātu*, *mātrā*, as well as *tāla*, *laya*, and *auḍuva*, and it is fresh through various novel *sthāyas*. 361–362.

The ninefold nature of the *mātṛkā* arises from the distinctions among the elements (*dhātu*), the portions of passion (*rāga-aṃśa*), and the specific recipients of instruction; it is also distinguished by the varieties of aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and ornaments (*alaṃkāra*).
The ninefold nature of the *tālas* is considered to arise from the specific distinctions of tempo (*laya*) and rhythmic measure (*graha*). (363)
A new *laya* (tempo) arises through a resting point other than the rest at the *tāla*.
(364) Through new meters, groups (*gaṇas*), *grahas*, *nyāsas*, and the constituent parts of a musical composition (*prabandha*), the arrangement known by the synonym *auḍuva* attains novelty. (365)
Rūpaka is known to be of three kinds: *parivṛtta*, *paṭāntara*, and *bhañjanī-saṃśrita*, as proclaimed by Śārṅgadeva (366).
Furthermore, *khalloṭṭāra* and *anusāra* are considered the lowest among the *rūpakas*.
A *rūpaka* is that which was previously established by its own original position; or, that which is composed with a different *rāga* or *tāla* is called a *parivṛttaka*.
In a *rūpaka*, whatever position was formerly composed for a particular *sthāyī* [melodic phrase], [that remains]. 367–368.
That [melodic form] remains in its own place, while that which is other than it undergoes a transformation of the stable [elements];
clearly, this transformed [form] arises from a change in *rāga*, *tāla*, and meter, yet it should be composed within that very same *rasa*, *rāga*, and *tāla*. 369.
Due to the diversity of the mother-stations (mātṛsthāya), another cloth (paṭa) arises, noble in its qualities.
(370) A certain *rūpaka* song is sung by someone in a musical mode (*dhātu*) other than their own; because it belongs to that other mode, it is considered to be dependent on a *bhañjanī*. (371)
If the *asthāyas* belonging to the original form (*prāgrūpaka*) are composed with a different meter (*mātrā*) while situated in a different position, then it is indeed an *uttāra*;
in that case, it remains within the same *rāga* and *tāla*, though its *dhātu* is somewhat distinct. 372.
"Following [the sequence] without a break, yet devoid of excellence in quality"—
this is the definition of the five varieties of *rūpaka*.
It is manifest (*vyakta*), complete (*pūrṇa*), lucid (*prasanna*), delicate (*sukumāra*), and adorned (*alaṃkṛta*).

Even, well-tuned, smooth, drawn-out, and likewise sweet—these ten are the qualities of song. Therein, it is clearly expressed through distinct notes, by means of roots and suffixes, and through meters, melodies, words, and tones. (374–375)
That which is complete, whose limbs convey the full meaning, which is lucid, whose sense is manifest,
delicate, born of the throat, arising from the three places, adorned,
and situated in the equalization of syllables and *laya*, is called "even" (*sama*). 376.
Deeply impassioned, it possesses a unity of sound like that of a lute, a bamboo flute, or the throat;
when smoothness is present in low, high, fast, or medium [tempo] and so forth, it is called "smooth" (*ślakṣṇa*).
Because of its high articulation, it is termed "drawn-out" (*vikṛṣṭa*) by Bharata and others.
Sweet, full of the beauty of excellence, and captivating to the hearts of people—
these are the qualities of song (gīta).
That which is condemned by the world, by the scriptures, and which contradicts the sacred texts or the proper time is defective.
Tautology, deviation from the musical scale, loss of sequence, meaninglessness, vulgarity, and ambiguity—thus, the tenfold defects of song.
These are the faults of singing. 379. Thus end the defects of song.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, on Musical Compositions (*prabandha*), in the *Saṃgītaratnākara* composed by Śrī Śārṅgadeva—known as Niḥśaṅka, the son of the illustrious Soḍhaladeva, the lord of the royal court, and a delight in faultless learning.
Now begins the fifth chapter, on Time-measures (*tāla*): wherein, in that treasury of arts, the tempo (*laya*) occurs through various paths and the rhythmic pauses (*yati*).
I bow to that auspicious Dakṣiṇa, who is manifold, consisting of various modes of existence, and eternal.
Now, as for *tāla*: it is derived from the verbal root *tal* in the sense of "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*), with the suffix *ghañ*.

Song, instrumental music, and likewise dance are established upon *tāla*. Time is measured by actions consisting of short and other durations; *tāla* provides the measurement for song and the rest, and it is recorded by the wise as being of two kinds.
Because it pertains to one who has reached the state of the teacher of the path, the first action therein is twofold:
soundless and accompanied by sound; the soundless one is called *kalā*.
There may be inhalation (*āvāpa*), exhalation (*niṣkrāma*), distraction (*vikṣepa*), and entry (*praveśaka*).
The "silent" (niḥśabda) is said to be fourfold, and the "with sound" (saśabdā) is also fourfold;
these are declared to be *dhruva*, *śampā*, *tāla*, and *saṃnipāta*. These should be known as *pāta* and *kalā*; we shall now state their defining characteristics.
In that context, *āvāpa* (deposition) consists of the contraction of the fingers of the upturned hand;
*niṣkrāma* (emergence) would be the extension of the fingers of the downward-turned palm;
and *kṣepa* (projection) is the throwing out of the right side with the palm upturned and the fingers extended.
The spreading [of the fingers] is for the lower surface; the entry is the contraction of the fingers. The falling of the hand is the *dhruva*; it is preceded by the sound of a snap (*śoṭikā*).
The *śampā* belongs to the right hand, while the *tāla* belongs to the left hand.
The conjunction of both [the breaths] occurs; their measure is according to the path (mārga).
There are four paths there: Dhruva, Citra, Vārtika, and Dakṣiṇa. Among them, in the Dhruva, there is a mātrikā-kalā.
In the remaining [mudrās], there are two, four, and eight measures (mātrās) respectively; these are the kalās.
Dhruvakā, Sarpiṇī, Kṛṣṇā, Padminī, Visarjitā, the one called Vikṣiptā, Patākā, and Patitā as the eighth shall be the measures.
The *dhruvā* breath should be known as having sound; the *sarpiṇī* moves to the left; the *padminī* is black and moves to the right; and the *adhogatā* goes downward.
The *visarjitā* has gone outside; the *vikṣiptā* consists of contraction.
The *patākā* (banner) is so called because it moves upward; it should be employed in the *dhruvapāta* (fixed fall), but never in the *āvāpa* (insertion) or similar sections.
The *dhruvakā* (fixed) occurs in the *citra* (variegated) style, while both of these first two occur in the *vārtika* (explanatory) style.

The last two [mātrās] should be employed, and eight [mātrās] in succession on the right. Here, a mātrā is said to be measured by the duration of the pronunciation of five short syllables; by this measure, the arrangement of light (laghu) and heavy (guru) syllables and so forth is established here.
The *tāla* is considered to be of two kinds: square (*caturasra*) and triangular (*tryasra*);
their respective names are *caccatpuṭa* and *ācapuṭa*. Furthermore, it is of three types: according to syllables (*yathākṣara*), two-mora (*dvikala*), and four-mora (*catuṣkala*). 17.
"In each case, those [syllables] are understood according to their names and [their] morae (*mātrā*);
in this *caccatpuṭa*, the last [syllable] is known to be protracted (*pluta*), while the others are single-mora.
Thus ends the *yathākṣara-caccatpuṭa*. Thus ends the *yathākṣara-cācapuṭa*.
In this [system], the *guru* (heavy syllable) consists of two *kalās*. In the first [type], there are eight [syllables] with two *kalās* each; in the other, there are six *kalās*.
Thus, the *caccatpuṭa* consists of two *kalās* (represented as: ʼ ʼ ʼ ʼ), and the *cācapuṭa* consists of two *kalās* (represented as:
ʼ ʼ ʼ). When these two are doubled, they consist of four *kalās*.
"''' ''' ''' '''" is the *caccatpuṭa* in four beats; "''' ''' '''" is the *cācapuṭa* in four beats.
In the two-beat [mātrā], it is considered to be in two beats. 20.
A quarter-part (*pādabhāga*) consists of four *kalās*;
thus, in the four-*kala* measure, a *mātrā* is formed by those four quarter-parts in the *mandrakā* and other [tempo]s.
That six-*pitāputraka* triple-triangle division is likewise threefold.
Regarding the *yathākṣara* [tāla], there is a distinction here: a *pluta* (protracted) mora occurs at the beginning and the end.
"E! | '' | E!"—this is the *yathākṣara* *ṣaṭpitāputraka*, which consists of twelve *kalās* when measured by two *kalanās*.
"'' '' '' '' '' "—thus is the six-pitāputraka in two *kalās*.
In four *kalās*, however, it is doubled:
"'' '''' '''' '''' '''' "—thus is the six-pitāputraka in four *kalās*.
"Uttara has five hands; its two supreme designations are Udghaṭṭa and Tryasrabheda; it is according to the syllables in the *prastāra*. (23) Thus ends the *yathākṣarodghaṭṭa*.
The *saṃpakeṣṭāka* variety is also a division of the *ṣaṭpitāputraka*;
it should be performed syllable by syllable (*yathākṣara*), just as the final syllable is protracted (*pluta*).
"E! E!"—this is the *saṃpakeṣṭāka* performed syllable by syllable.
These two should reside in their own source (svayoni), being of two *kalās* and four *kalās* respectively:

Māna is intended by an action accompanied by rest at the proper time. (47) Rest immediately following an action is considered *laya*, and it is held to be of three kinds:

From that, the medium and slow tempos should be known as being double and double [the duration] respectively.

Due to the different paths [of recitation], tempo (laya) is manifold through its states of being long, quick, or medium; however, that [tempo] which applies to syllables, words, or sentences is not employed here. 48–49.
The rule for the application of tempo (*laya*) is designated as "the ascetic" (*yati*);

When there is unity of tempo at the beginning, middle, and end, it is threefold as "even. (50)

In the beginning, middle, and end of the three tempos (laya), they are respectively considered to be slow, medium, and fast (ciramadhya-druta-laya) when following the flow; another is characterized by slow and medium tempos, while yet another possesses medium and fast tempos. 51–52.
The *gopucchā* [tāla] may consist of fast, medium, and slow tempos;

In the *tāla*, the beat (*graha*) is considered to be of three kinds: even, past, and future. (53)

But when the hands are level and the palms are level at the same time as the singing and so forth, that is [the *samapāṇi*]. The *layas* (tempo-modifications) in the *samādhi* [mārga] are, in order, medium (*madhya*), fast (*druta*), and slow (*vilambita*).

(61) That which is endowed with all its constituent parts is *niryukta*; furthermore, *padaniryukta* is that which is composed of verses of praise (*stutipada*), while having abandoned the introductory (*upohana*) and the secondary introduction (*pratyupohana*). (62)
In that context, the *madraka* is of three kinds when not restricted to mere *vastus*:

The wise maintain that there are three types: *sāmudga*, *ardhasāmudga*, and *vivṛtta*.
A composition is considered *sāmudga* when there is equality of words, syllables, and so forth between the two halves of the *vidārī*.
It is considered *ardhasāmudga* when there is equality only between the portions of the two *vidārīs*.
It is of three kinds: belonging to the first [section], the last, or both;

The *vivṛtta* (turning back) should be the *vidārī*, and that *gītakhaṇḍa* is of two kinds: the *mahatī* (great) and the *avāntarā* (intermediate).
The *mahatī* concerns an extensive subject matter and concludes at the end of a word or syllable; the *avāntarā*, however, pertains to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). 74.

In the case of a six-topic [text], having written the main branch (*śākhā*) and the title (*śīrṣaka*), one should write the sub-branches (*pratiśākhā*) with three topics—which is half of that—and write the *tālikā* and the title as before. Likewise, in the case of a seven-topic [text], having written the main branch consisting of seven topics, the *tālikā*, and the title, one should write the sub-branches with three and a half topics—which is half of that—and then write the *tālikā* and the title as before.
Thus, in the *aparāntaka* [tāla], there is one beat (*ekakala*).
In the *dvikala* *aparāntaka*, the musical substance (*vastu*) consists of twelve beats; it should be performed like the *ekakala* [version], but a specific distinction is now stated. (99)

The *upohana* may consist of one *kalā* or two *kalās*, while the *pratyupohana* consists of a single *kalā*; here, in the fourth section of the song, there should be a tempo (*laya*) half that of the preceding words and melody. 100. In the song, the tempo of those words and melodies shall be half the tempo [of the previous part].

Some maintain that this [section], which concludes the meaning and is joined with a formal placement (*nyāsa*), should be sung during the first six *kalās* of the fifth *vastu*, using the northern path (*uttaramārga*) according to the syllables and the southern path (*dakṣiṇamārga*) according to the rhythm (*vṛtti*). 101–102.

(108) In that [first variety], the *ekakala*, there are two heavy syllables (*guru*) followed by two light syllables (*laghu*), and a heavy syllable at the end; thus it consists of one *mātrā*, and it is called *mātrāsamāptika*. (109)
In the two-measure [tāla], a mātrā consists of eight kalās; however, in the four-measure [tāla], the mātrā is double that.

In the first half [of the measure], the various [sections] known as the *mukha* (introduction) should be performed; in the latter half, the *pratimukha* (counter-introduction), joined with various meters (*vṛtta*), should be performed. 110.
A fissure (vidārikā) is described as being of two types: circular, measuring three, four, five, or six fingers in width, and deep-seated or spreading.
The first type has an upward-sloping color, while the second spreads with a downward-sloping color. 111.
In some cases, among the *nyāsa*, *apanyāsa*, *saṃnyāsa*, and *vinyāsa* [of the musical scales],

the placement (*nyāsa*) may occur in a portion that is either concordant (*saṃvādin*) or repetitive (*anuvādin*). The conclusion is reached with the immediately following notes or with those separated by one interval.
Viśākhila declared that there should be *vidārīs* here;
elsewhere, having commenced with a section containing equal presentation and correspondence, there may be a fourfold ascent or descent. (113–114)
It should be suspended in the air above the *mātrā* at four *kalās*;
or else, by the application of *kalās*, from that which is situated above the *mātrā* and empty, this [emerges] from the duration of the four *kalās* as one, three, and so forth. 115.
This [performance] ranges from one limb up to six limbs, and even up to twelve limbs; it is of various kinds. Its first limb may consist of a single [verse], and thereafter [the others follow].

Then, the withdrawal (*antāharaṇa*) is taught as occurring in five beats according to the syllables. This is called *saṃharaṇa*, which brings the song to its conclusion.

Alternatively, there are three kinds of *vividha* based on the distinction between even (*yuṅ*) and odd (*ayug*) [syllables]: among them, the first is an even *anta*, while Dantila says that the third is a triangle (*tryasra*). It is also described as "established" (*sthita*), "proceeding" (*pravṛtta*), and "the great producer" (*mahājanika*). 121.
The characteristics of these three components are explained separately:
[122] that which is situated in the *yugma* (the pair) by means of a pair of two *kalās* is considered to belong to the *sthāyī* (the stable beat).
By that same [pair], it should proceed; the *udghaṭṭa* occurs in those three *kalās*. [123]
One should join the four *kalās* in the first part and the *padas* in the latter part;
its first portion may be of various kinds, but thereafter it consists of a single [unit].
Through the repetition of the *padas* situated in the first half, they know this as *yuṅmahājanika*.
Whether or not there is a fixed rule for the limbs of the song, it should be joined with the *sthita-tāla*.

At the end of the triangle (tryasra), it should be established with the *tryasra-tāla* in a two-beat (*dvikala*) measure; in that context, it is proclaimed to proceed according to the *yathākṣara* and *uttara* patterns.
By means of the three-cornered [meter], the *mahājanika* is considered to be like the *mahājanika*;

It may also be of one kind or various kinds in cases where the status of the unmentioned feet is established, and so forth. (126–127)

When there are various types of feet, or when they are all identical, or when they exist in pairs, such that one of the odd-numbered feet is different, it is considered *pravṛttasthita*. The final [measure] may consist of two *mahājanika* units, and the one following it consists of one unit. When it consists of two units, then it is at the end and is devoid of the *mahājanika*;

In the *ullopyaka* of one *kala*, there are one hundred and one *kalās*; in the two-*kala* version, there are one hundred and two; and in the four-*kala* version, there are one hundred and four *kalās*, respectively. The *kalās* that have reached their measure become the *āśavis*, which are the *ānivis*. In the aerial space (*vaihāyasa*), however, there are hundreds upon hundreds of *viniśānis*;

A *prakarī* should consist of four *vastus*, or else it may have three and a half *vastus*.

Here, the wise have declared that the *saṃharaṇa* is the *kaniṣṭhāsārita*.

The second *mātrā* at the end of the *tāla* is considered the *prakari* of the *vasta*;
in the fourth [measure] there is the twelfth *tāla*, and in the fifth, it is the eighth.

Of the sixteen *kalās* that have been mentioned, the last two in the Madraka [meter] are considered to be the final *mātrās* of the sixth [syllable], the second, and the penultimate; in the remaining positions, O Brahmins, one should place them in the divisions of the quarters until the end. 142.

The *oveṇaka* consists of twelve parts and seven parts, both superior and inferior; it includes the *pāda*, the *pratipāda*, the *māṣaghāta*, the *upavartana*, the *saṃdhi*, the *caturasra*, and then the *vajra* and the *saṃpiṣṭaka*. 145.

Just as the four-line *vastu* was previously described in the *aparāntaka*, so too is each quarter-verse (*pāda*) thereafter [constructed] with different words.

Therefore, the vajra is said to be like a pair in its application, resembling a joint;

Regarding the sevenfold and twelvefold divisions, some have declared that the fourth and fifth [divisions] among the syllabic divisions should be omitted here;

Alternatively, after the *caccatpuṭa* in the *dvikala* tempo, there should be [the *veṇī*] according to the syllables (154).
The *caccatpuṭa* may be in the *vikala* tempo, or the *veṇī* may be according to the syllables;
however, the *praveṇī* is considered by the sages to be in the *pañcapāṇi* [tempo] in the *dvikala*.
Some maintain that after the *praveṇī*, there should be an *upavartana* (155). This is performed with a *tāla* of one and a half *mātrās* (*pādottarārdha*) or with a *dvikala* *uttara*;
thereafter follows the *upapāta*, and then the *antāharaṇa* without the *anta*. Alternatively, it may be without [the *upapāta*].
In your view, that [ullōpyaka] exists as two-fold; elsewhere, however, it is three-fold within the seven-limbed [song].

Here, the ullōpyaka and other such forms should be understood as ending with the *lakṣma* (the final syllable), following the removal [of the previous one], or else, according to another opinion, they are to be applied in the *veṇī* (the interwoven pattern). 156.

Some authorities say that when it has entered the *praveṇī* (the furrow), it is called *avagāḍha* (deeply penetrated); others have declared it to be *pādopapāta-saṃpiṣṭa* (crushed by the falling of the foot). The wise have described these as various types;
the *vajra* (thunderbolt) is of one kind, while the *ekaka* (single) occurs during the *upavartana* (turning). 157–158.
In the square [measure], there may be various [variations], or perhaps one, or even another single [variation];
freed from the application of *kalās*, it should be applied by the hand of the singer, and those who know the science of song should employ the various [forms] within the eight *kalās*. 159
In the *māṣaghāta* [rhythm], the three [beats] beginning with the second are [placed] in sequence;
in the *saṃpiṣṭaka*, there are three *niśampās*, three *tālas*, and two hundred [beats] together, totaling one hundred and sixty (*160*);
it is considered to have seven limbs (*saptāṅga*) when joined with the repetition of the melodic phrases (*gītipada*).
In the *oveṇaka* with twelve limbs, there is a uniform melody (*tulyagīti*) with distinct words (*pṛthakpada*). Its musical expansion (*prastāra*) is as follows:
*āni vipra āni vipra āni viśa āni vitā*.

"Ātā viśa āni viśa" is a quarter-verse (*pāda*). In this very manner, there is a "quarter-verse for each quarter" (*pratipāda*). Or, the latter half of a quarter-verse may constitute a *pratipāda*, as in the case of the *gīti* which has separate words.
"Those [are] the Viśas, the Viśas, the Ātas, the Viśas"—
thus is the *pratipad*.

Whether by repetition of the verse, repetition of the words, or repetition of both; or by repeating twice or thrice, or even without repetition—

In a triple repetition, it becomes *madhyamā*, sung at will and conjoined with the limbs of song. O Brahmins, regarding the divisions of the quarters (*pādabhāga*), the specific distinction is now being stated.

Two paths are taught for songs, known as *śaṅkha* and *chatraka*. The *śaṅkha* path is the contraction of the limbs, while the *chatraka* is the expansion of the limbs.

Thus are the seven *gītakas*. At the end of the *gītakas*, the *chandaka* is to be sung; its body is of two kinds: either square or triangular, and it is square.

As before, the *mukha* (face) should be in the *chanda* meter, and each *prativaktra* (counter-face) should consist of one quarter-verse (*pāda*).

Thus is the three-part body (*tryasra-śarīra*). Its *mukha* (introduction) is like the introduction of another *gītaka*. The *pratimukha* (counter-introduction) is like the *mukha* or like a *pāda*. At the end is the *śīrṣaka*, which is similar to any [standard] *śīrṣaka*. The others are like the *mukha* and *pratimukha*. This is the *cchandaka*. The *āsārita* is of four kinds: the *kaniṣṭha*, the *layāntara*, the *madhyama*, and the *jyeṣṭha*; we shall now declare their characteristics. 178

The northern [line] should be known as having two units (kalās); among those, the first three are units.

Of these, there should be five, six, seven, and eight *kalās* respectively; one should designate three *vastus* and three *upohanās*. Among them, the *mukha* is the *upohana*, and the *saṃnipāta* is the *samāpti*. 182.
The *yugmatāla* occurs in the *pratimukha* [sandhi], while in the *kaniṣṭha* [version] there is a change in tempo (*layāntara*).
It is proclaimed that there are eight *kalās* in the *madhyama*, and sixteen in the *jyeṣṭha*.
The triangular (*tryasra*) [tāla] and the bodily dissolution (*śarīrasaṃhāra*) are proclaimed in succession for all [versions]. (183–184)

In the practice of finger-movements (*aṅgulikarman*), one should set aside the first *śampā* and take one-quarter parts from the remaining divided limbs; however, when there is no division, they remain as they are.
It is held that for the *upohanās*, there are two heavy syllables (*guru*) at both the beginning and the end.
In the middle [of the *kalās*], there are eight, twelve, sixteen, and twenty *lā*s respectively.
Among these, the *dhruvapāta* occurs at the end of the two *kalās*;
each of these is a single syllable, while the remaining *kalās* consist of four *mātrās* each.

In the *āsārita* meter, all the four-mora syllabic groups (*gaṇas*) are used at the beginning; however, the *kalā* (measure) consists of a conjunction occurring at the end of a half-group (*ardhagaṇa*). Furthermore, this [conjunction] is considered to occur within the middle of a divided limb (*vibhaktāṅga*), either by means of a full group (*gaṇa*) or by a half-group.
Others say that those [melodies] lacking in *aṅgas* and *upohanās* are called *āsārita*.

When uttered two or three times respectively, they are counted as two or three; there should be two repetitions of the *mātrā*, and it is desired that the tempo (*laya*) be half and half again. 189–191.
In all paths according to the syllables, the supreme is found in both the *vṛtti* and *dakṣiṇā*;
in the *dakṣiṇā*, it is reckoned as threefold, while in the *vṛtti* and *citra*, it is the lowest (*kaniṣṭha*).
In the *Khatantra*, there is an interval of dissolution (*layāntara*), whereas others have declared it to be otherwise.
"The *dhruvāsārita* is devoid of repetition (*āvṛtti*) due to its fixed path (*dhruvamārga*). (193) Thus, there are thirteen types of *āsārita*.
Alternatively, the *kaṇḍikāvardhamāna* is also called *āsāritābhāsa*.

The *vardhamānāsārita* and the *vardhamāna* are threefold [in their application]. By means of four *kaṇḍikās*, there is the *kaṇḍikāvardhamānaka*. Furthermore, there are the *viśālā*, the *saṃgatā*, the *sunandā*, and likewise the *sumukhī*. 194–195.
There are four *kaṇḍikās*; their *kalās* are to be known as nine, eight, sixteen, and thirty-two respectively, according to the method of the *caturāsārita-sthava*.
Their respective *upohanās* follow in sequence, beginning with "jhaṃṭum," and the first two syllables are long (*guru*).

At the end of the [first] *vā*, there should be [the syllables] for the faces; however, in the *viśālā* meter, there are fourteen middle [syllables], while in the others, there are four each, which are additional.
Regarding these, the Creator ordained fixed syllables for the sake of prosperity. 197–198.
The Blessed Bharata also said that those [sounds] are manifest, as follows:
"I shall declare those syllables which were formerly sung by Brahmā:
*jhaṃṭuṃ digidigidigidigidigi kucajhalajhaṃṭum*. (199–200)
"In the same way, it should be known for the *bālā* [mudrā]: *tiṃ ti jha la vṛddhi laya antare* is said;
in the middle [the *madhyamā*] it is accompanied by *kuca jha la*, and in the *jyeṣṭhā* it should be joined with *ti ti ku ca*.
(201)" Thus it is said.

In the *viśālā* and *saṃgatā* [melodies], the *tāla* is desired as being like the *madhyamāsārita* and other such established forms; it is known as "even" (*yugma*) and consists of two beats (*dvikala*).
In the *sunandā* and *sumukhī*, that same *tāla* is said to consist of four beats (*catuṣkala*). (202)
At the end of the two [sections], there is a *saṃnipāta* in the *upohana*;
in the first [section] there is a *cācapuṭa* of two *kalās*, and in the *upohana* of the other, there is the *uddhaṭṭa* and so forth in the *sunandā* [tāla], which is even and syllable-perfect. 203.
That same *tāla* with two beats (*dvikala*) should be used for the introductory section (*upohana*) of the *sumukhī*; thus they speak of the *kaṇḍikās*. Others say there are ten *parivartas*:
the first being *viśālā*, the next *saṃgatā*, then *sunandā*, and the first [of the others] is *saṃgatā*.
Sumukhī, Sunandā, and others, along with Saṃgatā and Viśālikā—
here too, the calculation of the groups of kalās is like that of the āsārita;
this is the *prastāra*.
Twenty hundred times a hundred.
Thus Viśākhā spoke at night, her desires completely extinguished.
Thus it is concluded.
"Enter, O inspired one, enter! Enter, O inspired one!
said Sunandā. "Enter, O inspired one, enter! Enter, O inspired one! [she repeated].
O inspired sage, enter; you have entered; enter now.
Thus [ends] Sumukhī. Thus [end] the four kaṇḍikās.
Hundreds upon hundreds.
Thus ends the exhortation of Viśālā.
Night, night, night.
The expansion of the connection.
A hundredth part of a hundredth part of a night.
The departure of Sunandā; night, destruction, and peace.

Thus ends the introductory section (upohana) for the Sumukhī. However, in the case of the *parivartana* [recitation], the arrangement (*prastāra*) of the sections (*kaṇḍikās*) should be understood according to the sequence beginning with "Viśālā" or "Saṃgatā."
Thus ends the increasing section of the Kaṇḍikās.
Just as in the *āsārita*, here too there is a calculation of the *kalās*;
the *prastāra* is:
[the sequence] beginning with *ni*, *śa*, *tā*, *ni*, *śa*, *ta*, *pra*, *ni*, *saṃ*.
Thus ends [the section on] Viśākhā.
Night, the end of night, and the evening.
Thus it is connected.
"Enter, O inspired one, enter; enter, O inspired one!"—thus said Sunandā.
"Enter, O inspired one, enter; enter, O inspired one! [she replied].
O inspired sage, enter into us; you who are already entered, enter further.
Thus [ends] Sumukhī. Thus [end] the four sections (kaṇḍikā).
Hundreds upon hundreds.
Thus concludes the introductory exposition of Viśālā.
Night, night, night.
The augmentation of the connection.
A hundredth part of a hundredth part of a night.

Thus ends the *opohana* of the *sumukhī*. However, in the view of Parivartana, the arrangement (*prastāra*) of the sections (*kaṇḍikā*) should be understood as follows: first *viśālā*, then *saṃgatā*, and so on in sequence;
this is the *kaṇḍikā-vardhamāna*.
Since the origin of the *āsāritas* arises from the *vardhamāna*, [it follows accordingly].
Then, according to the method to be described, it appears as if woven together.
(207) If the *viśālā* consists of nine *kalās* and is divided eighteenfold, then by omitting the final *kalā*, it appears like the *kaniṣṭhā*. (208)
The *prastāra*: śatā śatā saṃtā śatā śatā saṃtā śatā śatā saṃ.

Thus, when the *vardhamāna* has the appearance of the *kaniṣṭhāsāritā*, and if the *viśālā*— which consists of six *kalās* at its opening— is followed by another *layāntarābhāsa*, that *tāla* is the *vardhamānaka*. 209
Its *prastāra* (metrical expansion) is: śatā śatā saṃtā śatā śatā saṃtā śatā śatā saṃ.
At the beginning is the *upohana*, and as before, there is a doubling of the *tāla*, *laya*, and *mārga*.

Thus, when *sunandā* and the others, accompanied by the *upohana*, are joined together with the appearance of the internal dissolution (*laya*), then, in the *madhyamāsārita* tempo, there shall be that appearance. 210.
The *prastāra* (expansion): śanitā niśatā prani saṃ ni pratāśa nitā niśatā pranisaṃ nipratāśa.
The *ni*, *tā*, *ni*, *śa*, *tā*, *pra*, and *ni* are at the beginning; the *upohana* consists of seven beats.
Thus is the appearance of the Madhyamāsārita.
If the Sumukhī Kaṇḍikā follows, and then Sunandā is joined at the beginning with the Jyeṣṭha tāla, then it is the appearance of the Jyeṣṭhāsārita. 211
The *prastāra*:
āniviśa ānivipra ānivipra āniviśa ānivipra āniviśa ānivitā ānivitā.
*Āniviśa ānivipra ānivisaṃ ānivipra āniviśa ānivitā ānivipra ānivisaṃ*.
The introductory *aṣṭakala* (eight-beat) *upohana* is as before. Thus is the *jyeṣṭhāsāritābhāsa*.
Thus, "the fourfold *āsāritābhāsa-vardhamāna*" refers to the fourfold *āsāritābhāsa* that is increasing;
it is intended that the *vardhamāna* (increasing scale) arises from the *āsārita* (transitions).
Whenever they perform those *kaṇḍikās* which have been sung according to the previous sequence with those same *tālas*,
they then call that the "Vardhamānāsārita," consisting of four [parts] as before. (212–213)
Here, the smallest [unit] and the others shine forth as parts of the *tāla*, increasing like a *vardhamāna*;
furthermore, all of them are threefold according to the distinctions of *yakṣa*, *akṣara*, and so on.
(214) Just as there is a triad beginning with *yathākṣara*, there are two in the *vārtika* on the right.
In the *Citra* [meter], however, there is one [syllable]—these six types [of feet] according to the path.
215 Their arrangement (*prastāra*) is as follows: śa, āni, vitā, āni, viśa, ātā, vipra, tāni, visaṃ.
Thus is the *kaniṣṭhāsārita*, which is a semblance of the *vardhamāna*; thus is another variation of the *laya* (tempo), which is a semblance of the *vardhamāna*.
"Come hither, enter, come hither, O inspired one; enter, indeed, increasing in splendor"—this is the *madhyamāsārita* [melodic pattern].
The *ānivisa* and *ānivita* [stomas] have fifty-four variations each; these are the increasing [stomas].
Thus, there are fifty-four varieties of the *vardhamāna* meters.

The first, belonging to the *rovindakaga* class, has one *mātrā* for its opening (*mukha*) and one *pāṇikā*; the subsequent [half] is considered to have eight *aṅgas*, while the other is considered to have sixteen *aṅgas*. (216)
Experts know that the arrangement of *ullopyaka* and *vadaṅga* consists of words of praise separated by syllables;
here, they may be formed by words of praise interspersed with syllables, or alternatively, by words of praise and syllables occurring in succession without interruption. (217)
After the *mukha*, there should be the *pratimukha* with other words similar to those of the *mukha*.
(218) Then, the *śarīra* should consist of four syllables each; thereafter, the *śīrṣa* should be made with one additional syllable by means of the *saṃpiṣṭaka*. (219)
Others do not desire the *śīrṣaka* without the removal of the ends; its expansion (*prastāra*) is:
*ānivipra*, *ānivitā*.
"Thus is the introduction (upohana).
'O Agni, enter! O Agni, enter!
Thus is the introduction; this is the 'united face' (militamukha)."
"Āniviśa, ānivitā, ānivipra, ānivisaṃ, santāśatāśatā"—thus facing forward. Then the body [is formed] with four subsequent syllables according to the phonemes. The *prastāra* is as follows:

"Niśa śaśa tātā śatā śatā tāsaṃ"—this is the *śīrṣaka*. Others, however, say that the *śīrṣaka* consists of the final verse together with the concluding summary; this has been demonstrated in the section on *collyaka*. This is the *pāṇikā*.
One may begin with the *anuṣṭubh* meter and proceed with verses ending in the *jagatī* meter.
They declared that a verse (ṛc) should be sung either with worldly or Vedic melodies.
Forty-eight *kalās* consisting of single syllables are stated here;
the completion of these *kalās* is achieved through mantra-words and also through *stobha* syllables.
Now, those *brahmagītās* are being pointed out here as follows:
"Jhaṃṭuṃ jagatiyavalitakakucajhalatitijhalapaśupatidigidigivādigaoṃgaṇapatititidhā"—thus did Brahmā speak.
The syllable *oṃ* and the letter *ha*, joined with vowels and consonants, whether consisting of three or six beats (*kala*), constitute the *stobha* here as approved by the sages (224). Furthermore,
they have declared that there are seven components of the *sāman*, beginning with the *prastāva*.
"One should arrange the *vidārīs* and the syllables here according to their beauty.
Thus, the sages have declared that the four-syllable *gāthā* is a division (*kalā*) of the *ṛc*.

Therein, one hundred and twenty-eight *kalās* are proclaimed; the completion of the *mātrā-vṛttas* and the *kalās* must also be accomplished by means of *stobha*-syllables. Here, the *varṇa-alaṃkāras* and songs are to be performed individually. 226–227.
"The constituent parts of a *sāman* are numerous, while those of the *vivadha* here are few" (228)—
this is a *gāthā*;
such is the definition of a *gāthā*.
One should understand the manner of the *stobha* as being like the Vedic *sāman*;
likewise, it was sung of old by Brahmā, consisting of the *prastāva*, *udgītha*,
*pratihāra*, *upadrava*, and the *nidhana* is considered the fifth.

Then there are the *hiṃkāra* and the *oṃkāra*, and thus the seven limbs. In that regard, however, the names for the first five are, in order: *udgrāha*, *anudgrāha*, *saṃbodha*, *dhruvaka*, and *ābhoga*. (230–231)
In that context, the *hiṃkāra* and *oṃkāra* are considered to fulfill the [required] portions (*kalā*).
Here, the meters (*chandas*) beginning with *gāyatrī* and ending with *saṃkṛti* are intended;
this is called the "arrangement of Ṛks" (*ṛgvyūḍha*), as stated in the Sāma-veda, and in prose there are ninety-six portions.
In the chanting of the *sāman*, some sing single syllables while others sing half-syllables;
here too, for the mantra-obstructions (*stobha*) and the verses (*ṛc*), there are three measures (*kalā*) and so forth. (233) Thus ends the *sāman*; thus end the sections.
Having bowed to Śrī Kīrtivijayānanda, who is a festival for the eyes of Pārvatī and the crest-jewel of kings, I shall describe the *deśī* rhythmic cycles (*tāla*).
(234) A *deśī* rhythm is considered to be defined by actions measured by short syllables (*laghu*) and so forth. (235)
It is considered that the sound of a bell-metal cymbal (*kāṃsyatāla*) and so forth may be performed according to what is aesthetically pleasing;
a *druta* [beat] consists of half a *mātrā*, while a *pluta* is said to consist of three *mātrās*.
Due to the various arrangements of *druta* and the other tempos, the types of *tāla* are also manifold.
Now we shall proclaim the enumeration of those *tālas*:
first *āditāla*, second, third, fourth, fifth *niḥśaṅkalīla*, *darpaṇa*, and *siṃhavikrama*. (237–238)

Alternatively, because an abundance of *laghu* (short) and other [temporal] units is observed here, the ancients designated these as *khaṇḍatāla*.
They should be understood by their initial syllables, such as *druta* and so forth; furthermore, they possess other designations as well. (254)

The half-mora, as well as space, the consonant, and the bindu, are [described] in the *druta* (quick) tempo. In the *alaghuni* (non-heavy) tempo, the short *mātrika* is pervasive, straight, and likewise two moras; it is curved and long, and is proclaimed to be heavy (*guru*). 255–256.

In a protracted (pluta) vowel, the three parts consist of three morae (trimātra), as well as being radiant (dīpta) and born of Sāman; likewise, in a short (druta) vowel it is Śambhu, in a light (laghu) vowel it is Devī, and in a heavy (guru) vowel it is Śiva joined with Gaurī.
In a protracted vowel, the three deities beginning with Viriñci are remembered by the sages.
In the *druta* (quick) tempo, the syllable at the end of the pause is said to consist of one *mātrā*;
in the *pluta* (protracted) tempo, it is declared by the venerable Śārṅgin to consist of three *mātrās*.

The filling of the numbers for the rows of those divisions born of three-fold conjunction (*triyoga*) and that which arises from four-fold conjunction (*caturyoga*) should be understood in exactly this same way.

For those [combinations] beginning with *saṃnihita*, the reversal of the numerical markers previously mentioned applies (369).

However, regarding the fourfold combination (*caturyoga*), the same reversal of the previously stated numerical markers should be applied to the very figures that constitute the four varieties arising from the threefold combination (*triyoga*) (370).

Those four varieties arising from three *yogas*, with the fifth arising from four *yogas*, are to be known as occurring in the rows, sequentially in the final rows: those situated on the *dala* (petals), those on the *dalapa* (petal-edges), those on the *dagapa* (petal-tip), and those on the *lagapa* (petal-base). 371.
Those born from three yogas and those arising from four yogas are "dalagapā" (372);
this is the Meru of combinations (saṃyogameru). From this, that which is to be known is now stated:
by means of the various numerical figures located in the horizontal rows, all the fast (druta) and other [tempo] varieties are determined.
The measurable [beats] are those situated in the upward row; their absence, however, constitutes emptiness (śūnyatā).
As long as the row extends across [the grid], so long shall there be a rapid *tāla* here.
Starting from the topmost [row], the count is determined by the conjunction of the numerical marks of the rows. 374–375.
Thus is the Meru of combinations; this is the square for the Meru of combinations.
E!
"E! E! E! E!"
Thus is the Meru of combinations;

as for those varieties such as *druta-hīna* and so forth which were explained in the context of Meru, their arrangement (*prastāra*) is like that of all [other] arrangements; however, among them, that which...
The rule regarding the *druta* (short) and other prosodic units must here be observed with great care;
thus ends the *khaṇḍaprastāra*.
This number [of varieties] is derived from the figures in the *meru*-table according to the method previously described.
In that case, one should drop the lost syllable from the remainder;
in the *apāta* (falling) positions—the third, fifth, and penultimate—a short syllable is obtained.
If the subsequent [syllable] were unfulfilled, then both [the preceding and following] together with it [constitute the position].
If both of them have not yet achieved their purpose, this [new] one is obtained by them even without their own [previous] effort;
but when the other has achieved his purpose, the former one who has not achieved his purpose should be accepted.
(379) From the fallen [state], there is the attainment of the Guru; then, together with the previous one, there is the supreme [attainment].
If the fourth mark (aṅka) ceases, or if the fifth also falls, then the heavy syllable (guru) becomes a prolated vowel (pluti); this [prolation] ceases together with the preceding one.
Upon the attainment of the form, this same rule applies again to the remaining [marks] from the marks that cause attainment.
Upon obtaining a heavy [syllable], however, the fifth [syllable] becomes eligible for the *apāta* [measure], and the remainder proceeds to the state of being a residual [element].
(381) But in the absence of a [heavy] mark (*aṅka*), light [syllables] are taken to complete the *tāla*.
(382) Thus ends the section on the *naṣṭa* [method].
Thus ends the section on the destruction of the equal squares in the row below Meru.
However, when a specific problem is posed (*uddiṣṭa*), the third [element] is obtained from the guru, being the one preceding the last;
as before, there is a cessation after four, and likewise the third and fifth. 383
The cessation of the process occurs when the number to be multiplied is exhausted; however, the rule applies again for the six [operations].

If no mark (aṅka) can be obtained for the smaller number, the cessation occurs upon two marks. When the final term is subtracted from the sum of the obtained marks, the remainder provides the understanding of the problem posed. 384.
Thus, what was indicated:
when the indicated [number] is equal to the number of squares in a row below Mount Meru,
the "all-naṣṭa" (naṣṭa of all) naṣṭa occurs in the odd square.
When the quotient is obtained, the "even-square cell loss" (samakoṣṭhanaṣṭa) is then determined by the preceding figures;
thus, the "odd-square cell loss" (viṣamakoṣṭhanaṣṭa) is found below the Meru-line.
When the cell is situated in an even vertical line, it becomes greater than the others.
The second [syllable] below is to be dropped; however, those that have not yet fallen there are swift.

From among those that have fallen, the *la* is to be dropped. Between the dropping and the non-dropping, the small becomes large. (387) Upon the completion of the form, those situated in their own row revert as before. (388)
If there were another [number] below that which has been combined, then there would be a rule again for the cessation;
because if, in whichever upward row that number resides, it is odd, then the rule is as stated for the odd square;
but if it is even, then this [following] is considered the rule.

"In a square situated on an uneven upward row, [the result] arises from an uneven downward [row]" (390)— this is "the destruction of the upper row" (*parapaṅktinaṣṭa*), meaning the destruction of the upper row of the *drutameru*.
From those figures which have fallen away and been lost, by means of which the *pluta* and other [longer measures] are obtained,
the recovery of those figures is desired from their designated positions.
(391) In the upward rows of squares beginning with those deficient in *druta*, whichever is the short (*laghu*) [syllable]...
Therefore, no number whatsoever is obtained from the stated form of the position;
rather, the knowledge of the stated [number] is derived from the remainder of the last digit diminished by the obtained number. (392) Thus ends the "Stated Problem of the Opposite Row."
Thus, as indicated by the upper row of the *laghumeru*,
from the remainder at the end of the lower row of the *naṣṭa* [table], when the preceding [values] are subtracted and there is no further subtraction, it is swift as before. (393)
If a *ga* (long syllable) follows the two preceding *pa* (short syllables) after a *ta* (short syllable), it constitutes a *guru* (heavy) [syllable];
when a *ga* occurs immediately after a *vṛtta-guru-aṅka* (a heavy syllable at the end of a metrical foot), it becomes a *pluti* (protracted).
Thus, the understanding of the "lost" [meter] is achieved; so it was stated by the wise Śārṅgin. 394
Thus is the solution for the "lost" (naṣṭa) problem regarding the row below the small Meru.
However, in the case of a "lost" problem, one should drop the numbers from the subsequent rows in reverse order:
the second, the one below the third, and the fifth. 395.
And when the others have ceased, this procedure applies again to the remaining [syllables]; here, the attainment of the "fast" (druta) and other speeds is desired as if they were entirely lost.
However, once a light syllable has been obtained among the remaining ones, the operation proceeds from beneath the first one.
Thus, the bottommost [element] should proceed according to the rule established for its own row.
However, in the absence of elements in the row supported by the remaining digits, they are considered "light" (laghu).
This is recorded as the rule for determining the position of the lost element within the count of the bottom row.
Thus ends the "lost" (naṣṭa) calculation for the light Meru.
Thus ends the "lost" calculation for the upper row of the light Meru; the "lost" calculation for the lower row of the heavy Meru is like the "lost" calculation for the complete [Meru].
The attainment of the leap (*plutalābha*) is like that of the Guru; thus, what was lost in the row below the Guru-Meru is now described in the subsequent rows. 399
In the third lower position, the third digit is subtracted;
however, in the position below the fifth, the fifth is subtracted like a short syllable when a long syllable is obtained.
Thereafter, the descent proceeds downward, and the acquisition of long and short syllables follows from the remainder as before. (400)
"But like the *laghumeru*, when [a syllable] is lost, it occurs in the subsequent rows";
thus is the *gurumeru-naṣṭa*, meaning the *naṣṭa* [calculation] for the subsequent row of the *gurumeru*.
When all [the syllables] have been lost, it is declared that the Meru has "floated" (pluta).
However, this specific distinction is stated regarding the second and subsequent rows:
when a full [unit] has floated, one should descend below, as in the case of a long syllable (guru) in the Meru.
A *pluta* (longest) [syllable] is obtained by dividing [the total] by the final figures, whether they be short (*laghu*), long (*guru*), or protracted (*pluta*).
Having passed over six figures together with those situated below them,
this same procedure is repeated with the remaining figures located in the lower row.
"But in a *parpaṅkti* that is devoid of a *pluta*, the last [syllable] does not become a *pluta*. (404) Thus ends the *Plutameru-naṣṭa*.
Thus ends the *Plutameru-parpaṅkti-naṣṭa*.
As with all that has been previously indicated, the *uddiṣṭa* (indicated) [varieties] of the three, beginning with *laghumeru*, are as follows: 405.
