Thus ends the section on the *uddiṣṭa* of the three *merus*, beginning with *laghumeru*.

This concludes the fifth chapter, the Chapter on Tālas, in the *Saṃgītaratnākara* composed by Śrī Śārṅgadeva—known as Niḥśaṅka, the son of Śrī Soḍhaladeva, and the illustrious lord of the royal court who delights in faultless learning. 5.
Now begins the sixth chapter on musical instruments.
I meditate upon that Hara, who is a mass of bliss, within the aperture of Brahman, by whose own *māyā* the world is stretched out and covered. 1.
Variegated words proceed, variegated by the functions of the elements; therefore, I bow to that Śiva who follows the flood of the principles of expansion.
And song arises from the four kinds of musical instruments and is colored by them.

And because it is measured (*mīyate*) by us from that [source], the musical instrument (*vādya*) is described today as being of four kinds: *tata* (stringed), *suṣira* (wind), *āvanaddha* (percussion), and *ghana* (idiophonic).
Among these, the first two arise through the medium of the *śrutis* and so forth.
Then, song is delighted by and measured through the *avanaddha* (membranous) instrument.

The *tata* (stringed) instrument is considered a stringed musical instrument, while the *suṣira* (wind) instrument is considered a wind instrument. That which is played with a mouth covered by leather is the *avanaddha* (membranous) instrument.

That which is solid is called *ghana* because it is struck (*abhighāta*) there; that which is stretched is the *tata*, such as the lute (*vīṇā*). That [lute] is of two kinds, according to the distinction between *śruti* and *svara*.
Among these, the venerable Śārṅgadeva previously described the *śrutivīṇā*.
The *svaravīṇā* will be described here; on it as well, the wise, having marked the portions of the pitch-locations (*svaradeśa*), discern the *śruti*s.
Its varieties include the single-stringed (*ekatantrī*) and the three-stringed *nakula*.
The Citrā, the Vīṇā, and the Vipañcī; then there is the Mattakokilā (9), the Ālāpinī, the Kiṃnarī, and another known as the Pinākī;
and the Niḥśaṅkavīṇā and others have been proclaimed by the divine Śārṅgin (10).
The *vaṃśa*, *pāva*, *pāvikā*, *muralī*, and *madhukarī* are [types of flutes];

the *kāhalā* and *tuṇḍukinī* are [types of trumpets]; then there are the *cukkā* and the horn (*śṛṅga*). Beyond these, the conch (*śaṅkha*) and so forth are considered varieties of wind instruments (*suṣira*). 11.
The *paṭaha*, *mardala*, *huḍukkā*, *karaṭā*, and *ghaṭa*;
the *ghaḍasa*, *ḍhavasa*, *ḍhakkā*, *kuḍukkā*, and likewise *kuḍuṣā*;
the *ruñjā*, *ḍamaruka*, *ḍakkā*, *maṇḍiḍakkā*, and *ḍakkulī*. 12–13.
The sellukā, jhallarī, bhāṇa, trivalī, dundubhi,
as well as the bherī, niḥsāṇa, and tumbakya, are the varieties of covered drums (avanaddha).
Then there are the tāla, the kāṃsyatāla, the ghaṇṭā, and the kṣudraghaṇṭikā.
Then the *jayaghaṇṭā*, the *kesrā*, the *śuktipaṭṭa*, and others— these varieties of solid percussion instruments (*ghanavādya*) were described by the son of Soḍhala.
[There are also] the dry (*śuṣka*), that which follows song (*gītānuga*), that which follows dance (*nṛttānuga*), and another which follows both (*dvayānuga*).
The view is that there are four types; among them, that which is without song and dance is called *śuṣka* (dry). That which is without song and dance is called *goṣṭhī* by the wise.
Beyond that, however, the triad [of the remaining forms] possesses names according to their literal meaning.
To dispel the agitation caused by the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, Śambhu, out of curiosity, performed a musical concert along with Nandin, Sātī, Tumburu, and Nārada.
[This music is used] during the coronation of kings, as well as on processions and festivals. 18–19.
In all auspicious occasions such as marriages and initiations, during portents, in times of agitation, in battle, and in heroic or fierce dramas (20),
all musical instruments are played, though some are played only in minor auspicious events.
These [songs] provide rest for those standing on the stage, whether they are singing or dancing;
they inspire the heroic, serve for their auspiciousness, cause the heart to throb with vigor, and uproot sorrow. (21–22)

Furthermore, there are stringed instruments such as the *tata* (lute) and others, which are skillful at concealing deficiencies in singing, dancing, and movement; among these, we shall first speak of the *tata*.
(23) We shall also describe its various methods of playing and the diverse finger-techniques (*karasāraṇā*).
The hollow drum (suṣira-paṭaha), its beats (pāṭas), as well as their compositions; musical instruments produced by those beats, and musical structures (prabandhas) based on instrumental performance;
then the instrument called mardala, and the varieties of the mardalika player.
And that group [of experts] [should know] the merits and defects, as well as the characteristics of their own form,
along with the specific playing techniques for instruments such as the *huḍukka* and other covered drums (*avanaddha*),
as well as the merits and defects of the *ghana* (solid) instruments associated with the instrumentalists.
And here, in the first chapter on musical instruments, the qualities of the two hands are described in sequence:
the length of the thumb's joint is one *aṅgula*; twelve *aṅgulas* make a *vitasti*, and two of those make a *hasta*, which serves as the measure for musical instruments. (27–28)
Free from knots, cracks, or splits, smooth, made of khadira wood,
well-rounded, straight, and with a circumference of one vitasti,
the staff should be three hastas in length and possess a hollow of that same measure in its middle.
With a circumference of one and a half finger-breadths at the top and bottom of its mouth,
it should have three apertures within its interior measuring the size of the little finger,
or else two apertures measuring the size of the index finger, arranged like the three sacred fires.
One should place a single peg at the lower position, made of *kakubha*, *sāra* wood, *khadira*, or another type of timber, measuring one and a half finger-breadths in width,
three finger-breadths in length, and eight finger-breadths in horizontal thickness. (32)
The sides should be more than a finger-breadth [in width], and in the middle, it should have the shape of a raised tortoise; it should be provided with a hollow for holding the leaf-strips,
and in the center of that hollow, it should be joined with an aperture in the shape of a vulva.
Into that aperture, one should insert a needle of the same thickness as the hole,
and attach to it a slip of paper made of mixed metal, two finger-breadths long and four finger-breadths in length, which is raised like the shell of a tortoise in the middle and flat on the outside.
With its middle portion slightly depressed, it should be held inward at the bottom;
furthermore, it should have two staff-like projections joined by a peg eight finger-breadths long, which is circular,
three finger-breadths thick, and has a smooth surface on its upper half.
It was adorned with a middle section of the upper half raised like the back of a tortoise,
joined with a lower part that gradually increased in thickness like a staff,
and it shone with a lower portion that entered the mouth of the staff.
For such a stick, measuring seventeen finger-breadths from top to bottom, one should fashion two apertures resembling eyes on the lower part; then,
having inserted a double string through one aperture, [one should do the same] through the other aperture.

Having cast it between the ends of the strings, it should then be threaded through them; from that double [length], one should pull it out by means of a double [force], and thus one should perform it again.
That which is sixty finger-breadths in circumference, well-baked, and circular— 41.
The mouth of that gourd, twelve finger-breadths in height,
is provided with a navel situated in a circular position, facing downwards, three finger-breadths in length, and having its back joined to the back [of the gourd]. 42–43.

A gourd-shell (*tumbaka*) with a central cavity, or a coconut-shell (*karpara*) with a hole through its middle, should be used; having fixed its two ends within that central cavity by means of the hole in the back, one should then insert the two ends of the strings there. 44.
Having wrapped it around a peg placed inside, one should rotate the peg repeatedly until a firm binding of the *tumbaka* itself is achieved;
thus the *tumbaka* is fastened face-up onto the staff by those who know the technique.
Then, having wound around the staff from the upper part of the gourd a foot-strap made of very strong and smooth thread provided with a double-folded serpent-noose,
one should fasten it firmly and tightly to this serpent-noose with its ends secured. 47.
Having drawn out a smooth string made of sinew and pressed down the leaf-stalk,
one should then wrap it around the *kakubha* joint and bind it firmly.
A bamboo tube, one barley-corn in width, slender, and two finger-breadths in length, should then be inserted.

For the perfection of the sound, the skilled luthier should apply a doubtful leaf— acting as an internal life-vein between the string and the leaf— to ensure the adhesion of the string. (50) A beautiful three-fold cord made from the inner bark of ripe bamboo is auspicious.
The [reed] should have a width equal to the nail of the little finger and a length of twelve finger-breadths (51).
It should be well-rounded and smooth; at three finger-breadths below the bulbous base, one should wrap it around the staff to mark the location for the production of the deep (mandra) tone (52).
That single-stringed lute (*ekatantrikā-vīṇā*) which the wise have declared to be the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) of all lutes was proclaimed by the illustrious wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
its sight and touch bestow both worldly enjoyment and the bliss of liberation. 53.
Purified from the sins of killing a Brahmin and other such crimes, he [perceived] the fallen person as Daṇḍa;
Śambhu as Umā; the lute as Kakudha; the Lord of Kamalā as Indirā; the leaf as Brahmā; the gourd as the navel; and Sarasvatī as the [string]. 54–55.
The cord is Vāsuki, the life-force is the Moon, and the cord is the Sun;
therefore, this lute, consisting of all the gods, is entirely auspicious. (56) Below is the gourd-shaped resonator facing downward, while the strings are positioned above.
Likewise, having placed the end of the staff upon his left shoulder (57),
and having carefully pressed the heel of his right foot against the side of the knee,
he places the wrist-strap of his left hand upon his back (58).

Having said "sāraṇā, sāraṇā," [the player] should wrap the ring finger around the thumb, bend the middle finger so that its side touches it, press down on the tip of the index finger, and place the string near the chest. 59.
And having placed the string there...
To achieve mastery over the *nāda*, one should move the right hand upward and downward;
having abandoned [the distance of] one span (*vitasti*) from the *jīva* and placed it upon the *tantrī*, one should move it.
It should not be moved elsewhere beyond the upper limit of the instrument, nor should it be brought above the region of the chest.
The *kamrikā* and its performance are called *sāraṇā*, and it is of four kinds:
the *utkṣiptā*, the one named *saṃniviṣṭā*, the *ubhayī*, and also the *kampitā*.
When the string (*tantrī*), having leaped up, repeatedly falls [upon the finger], that is the *śliṣṭā* *sāraṇā*.
Then, when raised and settled, it becomes a *saraṇā* as soon as it is touched (63).
By means of these two [movements] in succession, that which is considered the twofold *saraṇā* occurs.
When there is a trembling at the place of the note (*svarasthāna*), it is called *kampitā* or *kamrikā* (64).

Striking (ghāta), falling (pāta), scraping (saṃlekha), then the line (lekha) and the wiping away (avalekhaka), the circle (bhramara), the joined (saṃhita) and the severed (chinna)— the ninth is the nail-shears (nakhakartarī). These are the functions of the right hand, while for the left hand there are two.
These—sphurita, khasita, and so forth—belong to both hands.
Furthermore, ghoṣa, repha, bindu, kartarī, ardhakartarī, the one called niṣkoṭita, skhalita, śukavaktra, and mūrchanā [are also among them]. 66–67.
The *talahasta*, *ardhacandra*, *prasāra*, and another called *kuhara*—
these thirteen, when added together, make twenty-four;
those who know the science of musical instruments consider these to be the names of the *karas*.
"Striking (ghāta) occurs when the middle finger is pressed against the index finger, hitting the string (tantrikā). (69) Thus ends "Striking.
"Falling (pāta) occurs by means of the [index finger] alone."
Thus, there is the morning emaciation,
as well as the internal emaciation;
such is "emaciation" (saṃlekha).
They declare that with the *antarmadhyamā* [finger], one should perform the striking and the marking (*ullekha*).
Thus ends the section on *ullekha*.
With the *madhyamā*, there should be *avalekha*, which is the striking of the strings from the outside.

Others say that with each finger individually there is *saṃlekha* and *avalekhaka*; they further declare that it occurs with all three fingers or with two. They describe those two as the internal and external strikes (*ghāta*), respectively. 71–72.
Thus is *avalekha*; *bhramara* is the rapid striking with four fingers in successive order from within;
thus is *bhramara*.
"By means of the middle and ring fingers, the external stroke is joined here" (73)— thus it is joined;
[the stroke] is outside the string that is pressed against the side of the index finger by the ring finger.
The illustrious son of Soḍhala describes *hanana* as being "cut";
thus, *chinna* (the cut) consists of four rapid nail-strikes in succession, known as *nakha-kartarī*.
Thus, "the nail-shears" and so forth are the nine operations of the right hand; the vibrating strings are shaken, as if the melodic slides (sāraṇās) were clinging to their backs. 75.
Thus it is called *sphurita*. Repeatedly rubbing the strings with a *sāraṇā* is considered *khaśita*; thus it is called *khaśita*.
Thus, there are two operations of the left hand:

[the string] is struck like a pair of scissors with the side of the thumb resting upon it (tantrī-lagnāṅguṣṭha-pārśvā), or where it is struck by the little finger and the *sāraṇā* [finger], that is called *ghoṣa*. 76.
Thus says Ghoṣa:
when a string here is struck internally by the middle finger of the left hand [while held] with the *ayā* of the *dakṣiṇās*, they call that the *repha*. 77.
Thus, when the sound produced by the striking of the external strings with the ring finger is held by the index finger, the *bindu* then arises without hesitation; this is called *repha*. (78)
Thus, when the four fingers successively strike the strings on the outside of both hands rapidly, it is called *kartarī* by the wise; this is the *bindu* [technique]. (79)
Thus, when the right hand forms the *kartarī* and the left hand holds the string,
and one strikes with the *sāraṇā*, they call that the *ardhakartarī*. (80)

Where the *sāraṇā* is released in the *ityardhakartarī*, and the forefinger strikes the string while the hand is called "extracted" (*niṣkoṭita*), those who know the art of playing know this as the *hanit* [technique]. 81.
Thus, when the left string is struck swiftly with the *sāraṇā* stroke that has been drawn out and raised, and the right hand slips as it becomes equal to the *kartarī*, then [this occurs]. 82.
Thus, when the pulling of the strings is faltering, [the position] formed by the tips of the thumb and forefinger is the *śukavaktraka* (parrot-mouth).
Thus ends the *śukavaktra*.
By means of winding and turning on the string, moving rapidly to the right pitch-position, the *kamrāsāraṇā* is considered a *mūrchanā*. Thus ends the section on *mūrchanā*.
The right hand strikes the string with its palm, while the other [hand] touches it with the forefinger;
wherever the palm of the hand is applied, that is the *talahaṣṭa* (palm-hand) position. Thus ends the *talahaṣṭa*.
The "half-moon" (ardhacandra) is defined as the contact made by the thumb and the little finger;
it is formed when the palm has the four fingers joined together and the thumb is bent.
The *prasāraka* (the stretcher) is the touching of the sides of the little finger and the index finger; it is the stretching of the string [of the hand].
Thus, the *prasāraka* of the hand consists of slightly contracting all the fingers along with the thumb.
"The hand with the little finger and thumb touching the string is the *kuhara*.
Thus ends the *kuhara*.
These are the thirteen operations involving both hands.
From the joining of these hands, playing is called *vādya*.
[The meters are] *chanda*, *dhārā*, *kaikuṭī*, *kaṅkāla*, *vastu*, and *druta*;
after that, *gajalīla* and *daṇḍaka* are the upper instruments (*uparivādya*). 88.

Instrumental music and the cries of birds—thus it is proclaimed to be tenfold. (89) Where the hands are moved and vibrated in many ways, and the high pitch (*tāra*) is touched, that shall be the *chanda* which is captivating to the mind. (90)

Thus, when there is a lapse in the meter (*cchandaḥ-skhalita*), a modulation (*mūrchanā*), and the presence of both *kartarī* and *repha*, as well as *ullekha* and *repha*, Harapriya calls that a *dhārā*. 91.

Thus, when there is a *dhārā* [movement], the *śukavaktra*, the *sphuritaka*, and the *ghoṣa*, and these hands are positioned in succession as the *ardhakartarī*, the wise call that the *kaikuṭī*. 92.
Thus, Kaikuṭī,
joined with the throbbing movements known as *mūrchanās* and with these three successive *kartarī* gestures of the hands, is called *Kaṅkāla* by the wise. 93.

Thus, those who know the essence of things recognize that musical instrument as consisting of a skeleton joined with a sharp-pointed blade, and further characterized by a rattling sound and a hollow resonance. 93
Thus, when the *vastu*,
*kartarī*, and *khasita* occur in sequence, where there is a hollow sound (*kuhara*), the hand (*kara*),
and the buzzing of bees (*repha-bhramara-ghoṣa*), the wise call that *druta*. 94.
Thus, where there is a rapid modulation in many ways, trembling hand-movements, the *kartarī* strike, and then the *khasita*, those who know the arts call that the *gajalīla* (elephant-play). 15.
Thus [ends] the *gajalīla*; the *skhalita* and that called *mūrchanā*, joined with the *kartarī* and the *repha*;
the *khasita* and that called *mūrchanā*, joined with the *kartarī* and the *repha*.
Where there is a *khasita*, those who know instrumental music call that a *daṇḍaka*.
Thus ends the *daṇḍaka*:
the hands, moving upwards and downwards in succession, are called the *repha* and the *kartarī*.
When the palm of the hand is turned upward, both [hands] are likewise for the *uparivādyaka* (97).
Thus ends the *uparivādyaka*;
however, when all the hands are played together, that performance is considered the *pakṣiruta* (bird-song).
Thus,
the "song of the birds" and the tenfold instrumental music—
comprising both the manifest (*sakala*) and the unmanifest (*niṣkala*)— are said to constitute the two types of musical performance. 98

Where a thick sound arises from a string attached to a bridge (jīvā), that is called *sakala* (complete) instrumental music; others, however, have declared it otherwise. If the *ādirika* [instrument] is a *patrika*, it is devoid of contact with the index finger (*tarjanī*).
When the *kamrikā* instrument is played, they call that the *sakala* [state].
(100) Having removed the *kalā* from the beautiful [instrument] below the *naiṣāda* region, if one does not allow the touch of the index finger upon the *tantrī*, then it is *niṣkala*. (101)

In this context, the sound (*nāda*) should be subtle; some authorities maintain that *sāraṇā* occurs here. Regarding the application of *sāraṇā*, they have reached the conclusion that it resides in the position of the middle tone (*madhyama-svara*).
Thus spoke Niḥśaṅka for the sake of his disciples' practice concerning the playing [of the instrument].

When the completion of the song occurs according to the sequence of the Śruti and so forth, one should instruct as follows: (103) We shall explain that the positions of the notes and the finger-holes in a flute of eighteen aṅgulas are the same as those held for the vīṇā in its first seven [frets]. (104)
Among the flutes, however, there is a gradual increase in pitch from the lowest to the highest; the first position consists of seven notes, after which there is an interval double that amount.
The third position consists of seven notes, and after that, there is again an interval double that amount.
And one should memorize these locations of the notes for the sake of ease;
through the division of the various notes according to their respective places, there will arise an understanding of the intervals and regions,
and from that, the awakening of the scales (*grāma*), the melodic modulations (*mūrcchanā*), and so forth, becomes easy.

This is called the *piñjaraka*, and the *ghoṣaka* has a single string (107). Such is the definition of the single-stringed lute (*ekatantrī*). With two strings it becomes the *nakula*; the three-stringed one is so named according to its literal meaning (*anvarthā*).
The *vipañcī* is considered to be variegated with seven strings, while the *matā* has nine.

The *koṇa* is to be played with the fingers, and the *vādanīyā* is likewise variegated; thus, others have described the respective arrangement of fingers and plectrums for these two instruments in sequence. (108–109)
In the *citrā* [tuning], there is a span of one finger-breadth; in the *vipañcī*, both [measures] apply; and with twenty-one strings, it is proclaimed as the *mattakokilā*.
This is the primary [tuning] among all vīṇās, characterized by seven notes across three registers.
Because it is fully accomplished, the others are said to be its individual limbs;
as they embellish her through their various instruments, they serve as her coloring agents.
Form is that which has been fashioned and refashioned; beyond that is differentiation.
I shall describe its sixfold instrument—namely *syāt*, *rūpaśeṣa*, *mogha*, and *pratiśuṣka*—along with their definitions and examples.
That which occurs through the breaking of a heavy syllable (*guru*) and so forth employed in the primary *vīṇā* [meter] is [the first]. (112)
Simultaneous playing is the form [of performance] on instruments such as the *vipañcī* and others, as follows: 113.

When two short notes are played on the principal *gurū* string, then it is [the case] on the *vipañcī* and others; however, when there is a long note (*la*) on this [string], there are two short notes on the others. 114.
Thus, this form is "done-in-return" (*kṛtapratikṛtam*); in the subsequent playing of each individual limb,
it is "done-in-return."
Just as there would be a distinction due to the reversal of form and action:
when the pair of *la* sounds is played by experts on the intoxicated cuckoo [lute], it is then heavy; such is the rule for the *vipañcī* and other lutes. 115–116.
Thus is the distinction:
when the principal lute-player performs a *vidārī* (division), the playing of the other [lutes] that remains in that form is called *rūpaśeṣa*. 117

When the principal lute-player thus performs the remaining portion of the form with a slow tempo (vilambita-laya), at that very moment [the accompanist] performs it with an extremely fast tempo (atidruta-laya) through the application of manual dexterity.
If the Vaipañcikīs and others should perform [the rite], they then declare it to be an *ogha*.
Thus ends the section on *ogha*.
When [it occurs] through either the consonant or the vowel that corresponds to the [specific] portion (*aṃśa*), 119.

"Since the playing of both the primary and secondary lutes (*mukhyāmukhya-vīṇā*) may be accomplished with the very same single string, Śārṅgadeva, the best among the learned, then describes that as *pratiśuṣkā*.
Thus ends [the section on] *pratiśuṣkā*.
I shall now describe those elements which nourish the playing of the lute, which possess incomparable passion, and which produce the growth of the unseen;
those notes arising from specific strokes are considered to be the elements (dhātus). 121.
The elements (dhātus) are characterized by expansion and the piercing of subtle forms;
among them, expansion is understood by the wise to be fourfold:
that born of expansion, that born of aggregation, and that born of combination. 122–123.
The "consequent" (*anubandha*) constitutes the fourth variety; thus, that which arises from combination (*saṃghātaja*) is fourfold.

Furthermore, that which arises from conjunction (*samavāyaja*) is eightfold: twice with the upper [vowel] first and the lower [consonant] last, twice with the lower [vowel] first and the upper [consonant] last, with the lower vowel at the beginning and the upper at the end, and with the upper vowel at the beginning and the lower at the end. 124.
Three times the upper first, then three times the lower; then twice the upper preceded by [the lower], ending with the lower;
then twice the lower ending with the upper, followed by one beginning with the upper; then twice the lower, and then twice the upper beginning with the lower. (125–126)
With the middle and upper [parts] twice the lower, and the lower and middle [parts] twice the upper—
thus has the fourteen-fold expansion been declared by the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow (Viṣṇu). Furthermore,
the divisions of the *karaṇa* are known as *ribhita* and *uccaya*.
Likewise, *nīraṭita*, *hrāda*, and *anubandha*—these five;
then *kṣepa*, *pluta*, *atipāta*, and *atikīrṇa* as well as *anubandhaka*:
these are the five varieties of *āviddha*. However, ten [varieties] are considered to exist when a consonant (*vyañjana*) is involved. (128–129)
Puṣpa, kala, tala, bindu, repha, nisvanita, then niṣkoṭita, unmṛṣṭa, and avamṛṣṭanibandhana— thus all thirty-four elements combined are considered [to be the phonemes]. (130)
Because it possesses an extensive variety of sounds, the *dhātu* is called *vistāra*;
by means of the lightness of the stroke (*prahāra-lāghava*), one brings the notes to their conclusion, and thus the *svara* is born from *vistāra*.
Other wise scholars have declared that this is known as *ekavistāra*. (132)
He has also confidently established its status as an ornament (alaṃkāra).
Thus ends the section on "Arising from Expansion" (vistāraja).
Here, the upper and lower [notes] should be understood as the low (*mandra*) and high (*tāra*) pitches, respectively.
For here, the upper and lower striking points are the producers of those two;
the four in the aggregate and the eight produced by combination— these divisions have names that correspond to their actual meaning, so a description of their characteristics is redundant.
Nevertheless, for the sake of awakening the dull-witted, we shall explain them;
because the verbal root is uttered twice here with a low tone, it is "dviruttara" (repeated).
Thus ends the section on "dviruttara."
"By striking twice at the place of *tāra*, the *dhātu* becomes *dviradhara*";
thus it is *dviradhara*.
That which begins with *tāra* and ends with *mandra* becomes that which begins with *adhara* and ends with *uttara*. 137.
Thus, from the lower limit to the upper limit is "from the beginning as low to the end as high"; then, from the high to the low at the beginning is "from the end as high to the beginning as low.
Thus, [it is] "from the end as high to the beginning as low."
"These are considered the four varieties of the *saṃghāta-ja* [breath] arising from two strikes. Thus ends the fourfold division of the *saṃghāta-ja*.
From three strikes with a deep tone (*mandrasvara*), they call it *dhātu*, which is three times higher.
Thus, with the striking of the three expanded vowels (*tristārasvara*), the lower element becomes threefold; thus it is "threefold-lower" (*triradhara*). 139. Thus [it is] "threefold-lower."
"The end of the upper and lower [registers] twice, and the end of the high and low [registers] twice shall occur"—
thus, having struck the position of the high register (tāra) twice at the end of the upper and lower [registers], one should establish the low register (manda) at the very end. 140.

Ah! Then, the element is said to be "ending with the twice-low and the twice-high" (*dviradharottarānta*); thus, the twice-low and twice-high refers to the low (*mandra*) and high (*tāra*) notes beginning with the upper [register]. 141

Thus, there is a *dviradhara* [scale] beginning with the upper notes (*uttara*) once, a *tāra* [scale] twice, then a *mandra* [scale], a *dviruttara* [scale] beginning with the lower notes (*adhara*) twice,
and finally a *dviruttara* [scale] beginning with the lower notes (*adhara*).
In the *madhyottaradviradhara* [scale], the *tāra* (high register) notes are the middle and the two upper [notes], while the *mandra* (low register) notes are situated in the middle. 142.
Thus is the *madhyottaradviradhara*;
in the *adharamadhyadviruttara*, the *tāra* would be at the beginning and the end, while the *mandra* notes are in the lower and middle [registers].

Thus, in the case of a three-stroke combination, there would be these variations arising from the union [of the three]: two low, one middle, and two high. These are the eight variations arising from the union.
The *dhātu* known as *anubandha*, which arises from the blending of distinctions between similar and dissimilar [elements], has been proclaimed by Śārṅgadeva.
(144) Thus ends the section on *anubandha*.
Thus, there are fourteen varieties of the *vistāra* meter.
Now, regarding the operations of *karaṇa* and *āviddha* through beats consisting of light and heavy syllables—wherein *karaṇa* has few heavy syllables—I shall describe its varieties here. 145
The *ribhita* consists of two short syllables followed by a long syllable at the end;
it is an accumulation of four short syllables and one long syllable.
Thus is the *uccaya*;
"the six syllables with a long [guru] at the end are called *nīraṭita*," so it is called *nīraṭita*.
The *hrāda* [meter] consists of eight short syllables ending with a long one (146);
the *anubandha* of the *karaṇa* [meter], however, is like the *anubandha* of the *vistāra* (147).
Thus is the *anubandha* (phonetic marker);
whether it is heavy (*guru*), light (*laghu*), or devoid of weight, I shall explain its varieties; its modification (*āviddha*) occurs through the presence of both light and heavy syllables.
Thus, the *kṣepa* (intermediate pause) is a *pluta* (protracted); it may be light or heavy. 148.
Thus ends the section on the *pluta*.
An *atipāta* consists of two *laghu*s;
thus, an *atipāta* occurs four times when there are *laghu*s.
Where this short [vowel] is excessively scattered, it is called "atikīrṇa" (excessively scattered);
however, the *anubandha* is as before. 149
Thus, regarding the "addendum" (anubandha),
others have stated that here there are four [operations], beginning with addition, which occur respectively by means of two, three, four, and nine light syllables. 150.
Thus, there are five varieties of the *āviddha* stroke; I shall now describe their distinctions based on the mere variation of the fingers.
(151) With both thumbs, a single string is struck at the little finger [position].
"Where the ancients depicted that flower as simultaneous"—
thus, when the flower has a single sound, there are two strings located in different places.
When one strikes with both thumbs at the same time, that is *kala*;
thus, one strikes from the right thumb [the breath] which is pressed by the left thumb. 153. Thus is *kala*.
Whereupon Soḍhala’s son then explained the *tala*:
"The *tala* consists of a single drop (*bindu*) upon one string, which is a stroke that produces a deep resonance. (154)
Thus is the *bindu*;
the *repha*, however, is a single vowel, struck [with the breath] sequentially by all the fingers.
(155) Thus is the *repha*.
"Having made the palm [of the hand], a downward blow is considered *nisvanitam*";
thus is *nisvanitam*.
A blow upward and downward with the left thumb is considered *niṣkoṭitam*. 156.
Thus is "striking" (ghāta) defined; when there is an exceedingly sweet sound, it is called "rubbed" (unmṛṣṭa), as in the phrase "rubbed by the threatening [wind].
Thus is "rubbed" (unmṛṣṭa).
Moving downward with the right little finger and the thumb,
he strikes the three strings at three points, each producing a single note separately;
where this is performed, the one who adorns the sacrificial arena declares it to be the *avamṛṣṭa* stroke.
The definition of a secondary element (*anubandha*) has been stated as being similar to that of the primary elements;

but surely, since this constitutes a distinction within a single characteristic, why is it not counted separately for each? Do not say so, for where a great abundance of those verbal roots (*dhātu*) is observed, [the distinction is not made].
"By means of that specific root, that suffix undergoes differentiation.
(160) Thus ends the section on suffixes. These roots have been declared, which are useful for all grammarians.
And these, which depend on the *vṛtti*, should be employed according to their proper place.

Among them, the *jāti* [melodic type] is considered to be *udāttā* (elevated) in the *vistāra* [extension], *ghanā* (dense) in the *karuṇa* [pathetic] sentiment, *ribhitā* (variegated) in the *āviddha* [pierced] *dhātu*, and *lalitā* (graceful) in the *vyañjana* [consonant]. 161–162.
Thus, there are thirty-four elements (*dhātu*).
Activity (*vṛtti*) is considered to be the conventional usage consisting of the nature of being subordinate or predominant.
There are three activities: the variegated (*citrā*), the southern (*dakṣiṇā*), and [the third]. (163)
When instrumental music is predominant and song is subordinate, it is called *citrā*;
when both function with equal status, it is declared *vṛtti*; and when song is predominant and instrumental music is subordinate, it is considered *dakṣiṇā*. (164)
Others prescribe for the *lambā* meters beginning with *druta*,
respectively, a pause (*yati*) that is even, flowing, and cow-tail-shaped; and likewise,
for the *māgadhī*, the one called *saṃbhāvitā*, and the *pṛthulā* *gīti*, they prescribe pauses in sequence.

These instruments follow in sequence the flood (*ogha*), the reality (*tattva*), the manifold path (*mārga*) known as *vārtika*, and that called *dakṣiṇa*; and here they consider them as the abandonment of the future and the past. 166–167.

Thus, the three modes of performance—tattva, anugata, and mogha—have been described; now the characteristics of that instrumental music (vādya), which follows the *Gītā* and is of three kinds, are being stated. 168
Laya, tāla, virāma, yati, gīti, as well as akṣara,
the division of the groups of syllables (varṇagrāma), and the various types such as the aṃśaka— these,
when manifested in song and integrated with the singing, are called "tattva" (the essential reality). 169.

Thus, some consider the reality [of the Gītā] to be that which follows from its imitation; it is regarded as being like the cessation [of movement] elsewhere, even while remaining in other places. 170.
When the tempo of the song was slow, he played rapidly out of skill;
thus, at the end of the song, the imitator also followed it part by part through his cleverness.
When a player displays a continuous succession of drum-beats performed with uninterrupted strikes of the palms, imitating a collective movement,
that is called *augha* (the flood).
Thus ends the section on *augha*.

This playing of the *dhātu* and other ornaments situated on twenty-one strings should be applied accordingly to lutes (*vīṇā*) with one string and so forth; and that which has been taught for the single-stringed lute should be understood to apply to the *nakula* and other instruments as well. 173.
Those who possess mastery over the flute also desire this [application] for the flute.
(173) Thus, instrumental music follows the song;
now we shall explain the varieties of instrumental music performed in accompaniment to the song, specifically that of the flute. (175)
Next is the procedure for the commencement of the *āśrāvaṇā*, followed by *vaktrapāṇi*;
then the fourth is *saṃkhoṭanā* and the fifth is *parighaṭṭanā*. [Then there are] *mārgāsāritaka* and the three *līlākṛta-āsārita*s. (176)
"Ten" refers to dry musical instruments; now describe their characteristics.
(177) Among the various types of *vistāra* rhythms, the first is applied twice, and the second is also applied twice; then the first type is applied as the second. (178)
Having uttered the form of *līna* twice, one should likewise employ the other pairs, starting from the prior pair and proceeding to the subsequent ones; at that time,
it becomes the *āśrāvaṇa* dry instrumental music— thus says Viśākhila.
In the application of the various extensive *dhātu* divisions, there is a rapid form [of movement].
In the first section (*ādyakhaṇḍa*), when the eleventh and fourteenth syllables, as well as the fifteenth and twenty-fourth, are long (*guru*), [the movement is swift]. (180–181)
There are eighteen other short syllables (laghu) in the second section;
likewise, in the third [section], the third, eighth, and fifteenth are long (ga), while the remaining twelve are short (la). With these three sections, the *dhruvā* is thus formed.
That [Gāndhāra] should be sung by wise men desiring success during the Āśrāvaṇā month.
We shall explain from the perspective of the Sage the rule for its *pāta-kalās*;
some say there are twenty-two *kalās*, while others say there are twenty-eight *kalās*. 183–184.
Others say there are thirty-two; the application of the *tāla* measures therein is as follows:
three *śamyās*, then three *tālas*—this is for the *anāgata-graha*;
then for the *samagraha*, two *śamyās* and likewise two *tālas*.
Then, in the apprehension of the past, those twelve digits (kalās) are [assigned] to Śampāta;
for each subsequent syllable, there are six and four [digits] born in pairs.
Thus, the rule applies to twenty-two and likewise to twenty-eight. 187.
In this case, there are twelve digits (kalās), as in the Dvikalottara;
thereafter, the remaining twelve digits should be like a pair of single digits.
Then, there would be twenty-two of the former and twenty-four digits.

As in the second *pakṣa*, at the end there should be eight [beats] like a pair of two *kalās*. (189) In all three of these *pakṣas*, the *uttaracaccatpuṭa* likewise occurs; now I shall describe the *vidārī* according to the preceding *graha*. (190)
The first [beat] is with three *śampās* and three *tālas*;
the second is with two *śampās*; the third should be with two *tālas*;
the fifth is with a *śampā* and a *tāla*; and the sixth should be with five *pāṇis*.
The seventh [meter] is *caccatpuṭā*; others consider those three [to be the same].
*Vidārikā* consists of two repetitions of the *yathākṣara-yugma*;
the first [foot] should be like that, and the second should likewise be so, with two *kalās* at the end of those two.

Thus there are eighteen *kalās*; thereafter, from the pair [of syllables] according to the letters, there should be the third *vidārī*. Others have described the *vidārīs* differently: the first consists of a pair of two *kalās*, and the second should be likewise.
According to the *Yathākṣara* and *Uttara* systems, the third [set] is formed; others have sung otherwise.
The twelve previously mentioned *kalās*, beginning with *vidārī*, are again [grouped] as *parā*; according to the *Yathākṣara* and *Uttara*, the remaining pairs are derived from the *Yathākṣara*.
Thus spoke the illustrious leader of the sacrifice, the foremost of those who summon the gods (āśrāvaṇa).
These āśrāvaṇas are thus characterized by ascent and descent, and are born from the elements of expansion.
The variations are mixed with *talena*, *ribhita*, and *hvādā* in sequence (197).
Then, having practiced the differentiation of the instruments two or three times until they seem to have dissolved (198),
one should likewise apply them extensively in a single expansion.
One should practice this very same [method] twice for the higher varieties of *karaṇas*.
That in which there is an initial rule (*ārambhavidhi*) shall be as follows; now I shall state its fixed [measure]:
eight *gurus*, twelve *laghus*, and five *gatis*.

The first section shall consist of twenty-five syllables; following that, the second section consists of nineteen syllables: eight short (laghu) syllables, a long (guru) syllable, four long syllables, a group of four short syllables, and a long syllable.
201. Thus, with these nineteen syllables, the second section is formed.
That [meter] in which there are eight *lagaṇas* in its third section, and a *ga* at the end, is fixed (*dhruva*) here;
(202) a pause should be made on the twenty-first *guru* in the first section, and one should rest on the fourteenth syllable, which is a *guru*, in the second section. (203)
The first section may consist of twelve beats (kalās), while the other is six beats;
the third should be four beats. Now, the rhythmic timing (tāla) herein is described: there is one *śampā* for three *tālas*, and two *śampās* for two *tālas*.

There are two *tāla*s and two *saṃnipāta*s; thus, in the first *śakala*, there are twenty-five *kalā*s (205). The *kalā*s of the *yathākṣara*, the *uttara*, and the *caccatpuṭa* occur respectively in the second and third *śakalas* as well (206).
Thus is the procedure for initiation:

one whose faculties are abundant and unimpaired, who possesses a small amount of secondary humors (*vyañjana-dhātu*), and who is deficient in the expansive humor (*vistāra-dhātu*), is proclaimed as *baktrapāṇi*. 207
The *mukha* and *pratimukha* [sections] should each consist of two *tālāṅgas*, and the *pravṛtta* should consist of one *varṇāṅga*; now I shall describe the *dhruvā* here.
(208) There are five long syllables (*guru*), six *la*s, six long syllables, and two short syllables (*laghu*). (209)

Where there are four *gā*s, three *lā*s, and eight *laghu*s, with a *guru* at the end, that is certainly the *vaktrapāṇi* meter. Whatever the final *mātrā* of a poetic subject may be, it remains fixed in the *madraka* when it is deficient.

In this [sandhi], the *tāla* should be performed for those eight *kalās*, with its opening (*mukha*) at the beginning. Then, the *pratimukha* (counter-opening) should be performed by one employing four repetitions;

they say it follows after the northern [section]. That which was previously mentioned as the group of eight *kalās*— [Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding the specific structure of the *kalās*. The translation reflects the available portion.]
Regarding this, Vaktrapāṇi says that the *vidārikā* should be performed three times with the proper measure (*mātrā*),
while pressing the string with the thumbs and the index fingers and playing it.

One should cause the *bindu* to merge with each other; the two vowels that agree with the *vādi* (the primary note) should be employed in many ways according to its qualities, while those that follow it (*anuvādinaḥ*) should be made few by the *vivādin* (the conflicting note). Likewise, one should create various distinctions within the expansion. 213–214.

Having mixed them with other elements, one should practice this twice; then, having applied those [elements] separately twice by themselves, one should apply other elements as if submerged within them—this they call *saṃkhoṭana*. 215
Where there are two heavy syllables (*guru*), eight light syllables (*laghu*), two heavy syllables, a light syllable, and a heavy syllable—
totaling twelve *la*s (light syllables)— and it ends with a *ga* (heavy syllable), that is the *saṃkhoṭanādhruvā*.
In this [meter], the *kalās* of the latter two [feet] should consist of two syllables each.
The number of these piercing (vidārī) types has not been stated here by Bharata and others.
Thus, the varieties of *saṃkhoṭanā* arise from the consonant elements (*vyañjanadhātu*) through the divisions born of the instrumental elements (*karaṇadhātu*). 217–218.
When [the syllables] are variegated, graceful, and smooth due to manual dexterity,
and it consists mostly of ascending [notes], they call that *parighaṭṭanā*.
There should be eight heavy [syllables] and twenty-four light ones.
Where there are two [syllables], sixteen light syllables, and a heavy syllable at the end, that is the *dhruvā* here;
or else, like the *saṃpiṣṭaka*, the *kalās* may be like those of the *saṃpiṣṭaka*.
Previously, the *kalās* in the *saṃpiṣṭaka* were said to be ten or twelve.
In this context, it is generally agreed that there are exactly twelve *saṃpiṣṭaka-kalās*.
Others, however, speak of a combination of twelve and ten; some, having doubled the *dvikala* measure, add the *saṃpakva-iṣṭakatāla*.
In this context, they declare that there is a combination of twelve *kalās* (time-units) and *tālas* (beats).
Some authorities here state that when two syllables and two *kalās* are joined with eight *iṣṭakas*, eighteen *kalās* are combined in total. 223–224.
Thus, through the application of parighaṭṭanā, vistāra, āviddhakaraṇa, bheda, and śmiśra,
the mārgāsāritaka arises from the two known as kalatala.
Others describe the characteristic as the mixing of *ka*, *la*, and *ta*.
225. Four *ga*s, eight *la*s, two *ga*s, then eight *la*s;
226. *ga*, *la*—thus the first section (*khaṇḍa*) would be; likewise, there are two further sections.
In this [composition], that which is known as the *dhruvā* should be based on the *mārgāsārita*.
There is one *khaṇḍa* in the *caccatpuṭa* rhythm and two *śakalas* in the following [rhythm].
The rule for the *tāla* and *kalā* should be performed according to what was stated regarding the *kaniṣṭhāsārita*. 227–228.
Thus, for one who has advanced along the path, there should be the application [of practice] as it was traversed, and likewise for one who has moved around;
so too in the movement between tempos, and in the rules for the measures of instrumental rhythm.
At that time, sweetness and tenderness arise from the performance of the *līlā*.
That which is sung on the path of the *vārtika* in the *jāti-aṃśa* belonging to the *ṣaḍja-grāma* is called *āsārita*; it is described by the wise as *abhisūtāhaya*. 229–230.
When the *jātyaṃśa* is situated in the *madhyamagrāma*, this [scale] is called *parisṛta*; however,
others call the seven-limbed scale beginning with *māṣaghāta* "Aparāntaka," while that which has nine limbs beginning with *pradāna* is called *abhisṛta*.
They say that in the *Tālādhyāya*, the *parisṛta* is to be sought as a variation of tempo (*layāntara*).

Thus, through the combination of the three types of song (*gītaka*), the *līlākṛta* is threefold; its two applications consist of meaningful words (*pada*) and meaningless syllables (*sāryaka*). 233–234.
Some say that the lute performance (vīṇāvādya) is accompanied by the *māna* rhythm and is devoid of *śampā* and the like; however, Viśākhila says it may even be devoid of *māna*.
Regarding the *dhruvā*, others maintain that both types of rhythm (*tāla*) apply, while still others hold that there is no fixed rule. 235–236.
Thus, the three *āsārita*s performed as a play (*līlākṛta*) were previously described in the chapter on *tāla* (rhythm) as being of three kinds:
according to the syllables (*yathākṣara*), counted as two, and counted as three. 237

In this method of constructing the lute, the wise should create a design embellished with varṇālaṃkāras, where each part is repeated; it should be adorned with three types of rhythmic patterns (vṛtti), musical instruments, the principles (tattva) and so forth, as well as by means of the constituent elements (dhātu). 238.
Thus I shall describe the three *āsārita* variations pertaining to the *ālāpinī*, as recognized by those who know the characteristics:
a bamboo flute, nine *muṣṭis* in length and having internal holes. (239)
The staff, measuring two finger-breadths in circumference, free from knots and the like as previously described, smooth, even, and well-rounded, should bear the *kakubha* insignia;
it should likewise be two finger-breadths in width and half a finger-breadth in length.
Half of that [length] is joined with the *piṇḍa* (the bulbous base), facing upward and devoid of leaves;
it has a single staff at its lower part, adorned with a *śaṅku* (peg), four finger-breadths in length, and elevated in the middle of its exterior. 241–242.
Its girth at the base of the bulb is twelve finger-breadths,
its mouth is four finger-breadths wide, and it is provided with a "tooth" and a "navel.
Below the tip, at a distance of three-quarters of a cubit, it is fastened to a pair of fists.
In this [instrument], there should be a string made of sheep's intestines that is fine, smooth, even, and firm (244).
A coconut-shell bowl, a handle, and likewise a cord— where these three are joined together, it is considered an *ālāpinī* (245).
Others say that the staff here should be made of khadira wood and measure ten muṣṭis;
it should have a string made of silk thread or perhaps of cotton thread.
Others have declared that all vīṇā-staffs should be made from red sandalwood.
In some practical applications, a measurement exceeding ten *muṣṭis* is observed.
(247) Having placed the *tumba* against the chest and pressed its base with the left thumb while holding it, the wise practitioner should then [hold] it with the middle finger. (248)

One should play with the right hand, or with the ring finger like a drop-element, or with the "drop-hand" (binduhasta); one should play in the low (*mandra*), middle (*madhya*), and high (*tāra*) registers.
There are three [notes] from the right hand, and four notes by name.
Thus it was said by some teachers, but others have sung otherwise:

"The middle [note] is produced by the released string; from the three fingers beginning with the index finger of the left hand—with the ring finger excluded—the three notes beginning with the fifth [pañcama] arise. (250–251)
Then, with the thumb released, there is the note Ṣaḍja; Ṛṣabha arises from the index finger;
Gāndhāra is produced by the middle finger. Thus, the playing is performed with the right hand through both ascending and descending scales across the two groups of seven notes. 252.
One should discourse upon the manifold melody (rāga) composed with these notes;
and a skilled musician should sing a song structured [upon them] with this lute.
This definition of Ālāpinī was proclaimed by Śrī Niḥśaṅka. 253–254.
Such is the definition of the *ālāpinī* [vocal style].
The *kiṃnarī* is proclaimed to be of two kinds: the small (*laghvī*) and the large (*bṛhatī*). Among these, the characteristics pertaining to the small one are now being set forth. (255)
The bamboo staff should be three vitastis in length, with a measurement exceeding five aṅgulas;
its circumference should be five aṅgulas,
and it should have a hole extending through the interior made from the wood of the *kakubha* or *śāka* trees.
It is two and a half finger-breadths in width and five finger-breadths in length;
in its middle, there should be a copper leaf-plate shaped like a tortoise, raised up, and measuring half a finger-breadth less in both length and width. 257–258.
The *gṛdhravakṣas* (vulture-breasted) bone-pipe, measured by the little finger,
made of iron or bell-metal, or else known by the name *sārikā*,
is joined [to the mouth] with fourteen [fingers] of lac mixed with cloth and ink. 259.
One should place [the first *sārikā*] at the position of the fourteenth vowel on the back of the staff (260).
That which is the *niṣāda* below the second of the seven [notes],
its position shall be the first *sārikā*, one finger-breadth above the other (261).
One should place [the subsequent lines] at intervals slightly greater than the preceding;
up to the eighth line, the interval from the previous one is two finger-breadths, while for the eighth, it is three finger-breadths.
Having thus established them, the remaining six lines should be placed with intervals each greater than the one before.
One should fix the *sārikās* at a distance of four finger-breadths [from the end].
One should place the *tumba* of the staff at the lower joint of the *kakubha*;
however, the second one should be placed below the middle of the third and fourth *sāris*. 263–264.
The subsequent bulb should be slightly larger in width than the preceding one;
having made a hole two finger-breadths below the tip of the staff, one should then insert the movable pin,
which has a hole in its neck [measuring] one finger-breadth from that point.
Having fashioned a base (meḍhaka) one finger-breadth high, resembling the feathered end of an arrow, one should then place a small, steady peg slightly in front of it.
Then, [one should prepare] an iron [rod] that is smooth, circular, even, and firm.

Having firmly tied a string resembling an elephant's hair to a peg, one should bring it over the head of a sarika bird and place it upon a ram; then, with its second end fixed there, one should wind it around a movable peg. 268.
One should rotate that peg until the string becomes firm.

(269) Rotating it in the opposite direction is the cause of loosening the string; however, for the sake of tightening the string when it is too long, one should place the movable peg at the throat [of the instrument]. (270)
Then, one should insert a peg into the hole of another [string] upon a fixed peg;
this is called the *laghvī* *kiṃnarī* by the learned Śārṅgadeva.
In this [instrument], one should count two groups of seven starting from the *sthāyin*.
Between the *sārī* and the *kubha*, one should play the string of the *kiṃnarī-vīṇā* with the right hand using the three fingers beginning with the index finger (272),
while [pressing] the string with the three fingers of the left hand (273).
One should press the string at each respective *sārī* position to clarify the tone;
it should be more than a span (*vitasti*) in length and more than one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) in circumference. A string made of sinew with three gourd resonators may be either small or large.
And in this Ālāpinī, a third gourd should be placed;
furthermore, the characteristic mark located on the *laghvī* should rest upon the *bṛhatī* kinnarī. (275) Thus ends the description of the two types of kinnarīs.

In this context, there are three types of *kiṃnarī* established according to regional tradition; otherwise, they are classified as large (*bṛhatī*), medium (*madhyamā*), and small (*laghvī*). Now, their characteristics will be described: here, one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) consists of six husked barley grains placed side by side.
The *bṛhatī* staff should be fifty finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length;
its circumference should be six finger-breadths. In the case of the *kākubha* staff, the head should be six finger-breadths in both length and width. (277–278)
One should insert a *kākubha* staff measuring four finger-breadths in width and two finger-breadths in height upon the top of the lute's neck; likewise,
the remaining portion of the staff here should be of the same measure as that which remains.

Situated between the end of the neck of the lute and the middle of the head, the section for the strings shall measure three finger-breadths plus one-third. In the middle of the head, one should insert a metal plate (patrikā) raised like a tortoise. 280–281.
This [hole] at the head is proclaimed to be half an aṅgula less on all sides;
situated one and a half aṅgulas below the "head of the lute" (vīṇāśīrṣa),
it is a cavity with a vertical height of two parts and a width of half an aṅgula.
The horizontal length and the other aperture should likewise have openings on both sides.
(283) At the horizontal aperture, a movable peg is fixed;
its ends are joined by an iron rod inserted into the upper aperture. (284)
The wise man should fasten [the string] at the base of the head of the *sārikā* lute on the *kākubha* neck;
two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in front of the hole for the string, there should be a *meḍhaka* (a small knob).
It should be provided with a *kartarī* (a notch), or otherwise, it may have a hole in its neck. 285.
One should insert that *sārikā* into the throat-opening of the *kartarī*;
in that opening, one should fashion a space for the handle measuring one and a half finger-breadths.
In front of the *meḍhaka*, there should be a firm peg (*śaṅku*) at a distance of one and a half finger-breadths.
Its insertion into the lateral opening is said to be like that of a movable pin;
the rotation of the movable pin and so forth should be understood according to the method previously described.
Or else, [the channels] are born from the bones of the vulture’s breast or produced from the bones of its feet.
The tubes (nalikā) are considered to be made of bell-metal or iron;

they should be one and a half finger-breadths (aṅgula) in circumference and fixed upon the back of the handle. The space between them should begin from the middle of the head of the *yaṣṭimeḍhaka*. 289–290.
Now, the measurements for the neck, the head, and the middle [of the body] are being determined:
therein, the first interval is considered to be five finger-breadths plus one barley-corn;
the second interval, however, is four finger-breadths more.
Therefore, while the third and fourth [intervals] are considered by the wise to be less than a barley-corn (yava),
the fifth interval should be known as three finger-breadths (aṅgula) plus one barley-corn;
the sixth is two finger-breadths minus one barley-corn, and then again two finger-breadths plus one barley-corn.

The seventh [space] should be an interval of two and a half finger-breadths; the eighth is considered to be measured at one and a half finger-breadths plus half a barley-corn; the ninth is held to be one and a half finger-breadths;
the tenth is two finger-breadths less a barley-corn; and the eleventh is likewise.
The twelfth [measurement] should be less than one-third of that;
the thirteenth should be one finger-breadth (aṅgula) plus one-third of a finger-breadth, while the fourteenth should be exactly one finger-breadth.
One should place the downward-facing bowl (tumba) below the second interval.
One should arrange another *kakubha* [wood] above and below as the *tumbaka*;
on the wheel, the circumference (*paridhi*) should be thirty-six finger-breadths,
while the lower *tumbaka* should be slightly less than that on the circumference.
One should place those *sārikā* bricks so that they are slightly indistinct;
their firm adhesion should be made with mortar mixed with the powder of *madana* seeds, or appropriately with cloth-ink mixed together. (298–299)
Having made the first note the fourteenth by means of the loose strings (*muktatantrī*), the subsequent notes of the *sārīs* should be produced with intervals of fourteen [frets];
thus there would be two heptads, exceeding the single-pitch notes (*ekatārasvara*). 300.
According to their respective tones, places, and degrees, experts discern its *śruti*;
thereafter, one should bind two or more than that number of *sārīs*, while the wise here observe the intervals between them through the manifestation of the notes (*svaras*). 301–302.
Through the instruction of Śrī Śārṅgadeva, the understanding of this [instrument] is easily accessible to men;
some wise ones here place thirteen sāris upon it.
This [lute], known as the Bṛhatī-kiṃnarī, was proclaimed by Śārṅgadeva. (303)
In the middle [section], the length of the staff is forty-three finger-breadths (304).
There, the circumference is seen to be six finger-breadths less two barley-corns;
the width is three and a half finger-breadths, while the eastern length is the head of the *kākubha* [measure] (305).
One should insert three finger-breadths of the *kakubha* staff into the neck of the lute; that [insertion] remains as much as the remainder, such that when [the remaining portion] is measured,
the parts of the *sārikā* are situated at the end, the top, the middle, and the tip of the staff.
At the end of the staff (daṇḍa), the height of the *sārikā* should be three fingers minus one-third; it should be two fingers less one barley-corn (*yava*).
Half of that [measurement] should be the interval between the *sārikās* at the end of the *meḍhaka*. 307–308.
The first [measurement] is proclaimed by the wise to be four and a half finger-breadths;
the second interval to be measured at three finger-breadths plus one barley-corn;
and the third with three finger-breadths increased by a third part.
The fourth is said to be three finger-breadths; the fifth is the interval of the *sārikā*, considered to be measured by two and a half finger-breadths plus one barley-corn (yava).
The sixth is two finger-breadths minus two barley-corns, and the seventh is likewise.
The eighth [interval] is two fingers and two barley-corns;
the ninth is one finger and two barley-corns;
and the tenth is again two fingers less one barley-corn; furthermore, there are three intervals. (312)

Each of these from the other side measures one and a quarter finger-breadths (sapādāṅgula). This is the specific distinction here; however, the other characteristic belonging to the *bṛhatī* is that the short staff (*laghudaṇḍa*) should be thirty-five finger-breadths in length.
The rim (paridhi), however, shall be five finger-breadths plus one-third;
the head of the kakubha [neck-piece] shall have a width of three finger-breadths.
As before, the kakubha staff is placed upon the neck of the lute.
The remainder should be such that it is like a string at the end of a staff;
from the middle of the head of the *kākubha* [pillar] downwards, it should measure three finger-breadths (*aṅgula*),
and at the end of the staff, the height of the *sārikā* should be one and a half finger-breadths.
Half of that, at the edge of the meḍhaka, is said to be the first *sārikā*-interval, measured at four fingers plus one barleycorn (318).
The second shall be measured at two fingers plus two barleycorns.
The third [interval] is measured by the wise as being two finger-breadths less a barley-corn;
the fourth is two and three-quarter finger-breadths; then the fifth interval is two finger-breadths less half a barley-corn; and the sixth is eight and a half barley-corns.
The seventh, however, is measured by two finger-breadths plus one barley-corn;
the eighth should be one and a half finger-breadths, and the ninth by eight barley-corns.
The tenth and eleventh are each stated to be one and a quarter finger-breadths.
The twelfth and thirteenth [types] measure nine and ten finger-breadths respectively;
furthermore, the characteristic of the small Kiṃnarī is said to be as before.
For the Bṛhatī, the measurement is neither more nor less than thirty finger-breadths.
One should pay attention to the *kiṃnarīs*, because they lack both passion (*rakti*) and sweetness (*mādhurya*);

however, between these two, the determination of the measure (*māna*) may be made as desired. Those who know this [science] are capable of discerning the positions of the notes (*svarasthāna*) even here. 324–325.
In this *kiṃnara-vīṇā*, the illustrious Karaṇeśvara describes the sequence of playing certain *rāgas* for illustrative purposes:
[beginning] with the *sthāyin* (fixed note) of *madhyama* in the low (*mandra*) or middle (*madhya*) register, followed by those notes dependent upon that fixed one.

Having ascended through the five notes beginning with *pa* and ending with *ni*, one should descend through the notes in sequence starting from *ṣaḍja* up to the stationary note (*sthāyin*), just as one would strike the *dhaivata*. Having ascended through the five notes beginning with *pa* and ending with *ni*, one should descend through the notes in sequence.
Just as one would strike the *dhaivata* starting from *ṣaḍja* up to the *sthāyī*,
so too is the first *svasthāna* declared for the *madhyama* group;
likewise, having ascended to a tone that is double [the original], situated at half and two-and-a-half [the distance].

One should abide in the primary *svasthāna*; in the other three [notes], one should abide in the *svasthāna*. However, when that is impossible, one should ascend through the vowels in sequence, from each preceding vowel to the next succeeding one; this is the rule for all *rāgas*.
Thus, when the Kinnarī instrumentalists generally employ the fifth note (pañcama) as the fixed tonic (sthāyin) in the Rāga Madhyamādi in Bengal, that is merely a manifestation of ignorance. 331
For in this treatise, a moderate degree of passion is proclaimed as the ideal;
or rather, these treatises consider that they primarily deal with actual practice (lakṣya). Therefore, whatever in a treatise contradicts actual practice must be interpreted otherwise. 332–333.
The term "middle" (*madhyama*) and so forth should be understood as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the fifth [note] and the others;

or else, because of their similarity in being primary, one must assume a restriction (*niyama*) when grasping the middle note and so on—[the question being] whether this applies when this middle note is grasped. (334–335)
If Gāndhāra were to be the lower [note] while Pañcama is held as the middle,
even with such a transposition of the fourth and other notes, how could there be equality of the rāga?
Here Niḥśaṅka resolves this by stating that the starting point [such as Gāndhāra] is not the determining factor.

However, as for those notes beginning with the fourth (the *turya*) that start from the *sthāyin* [note], which are capable of manifesting the *rāga*, surely they would be useless in the treatises? 337. As for those notes beginning with the fourth (*turya*) that are capable of manifesting the *rāga*, [they would be] indeed useless in the scriptures.
It might follow that there would be a mention of *ṣaḍja* and so forth; this is true, but it is said here:

since the apprehension of *madhyamā* and the others is fixed in the treatise, it is logically consistent that the fourth and subsequent notes become *niṣāda* and the rest in relation to that. 338–339.

Whether it concerns the rules for the placement of planetary portions (*grahāṃśa*) or the application of the meaning of the scriptures, the arrangement of different musical notes (*svarāntara*) contradicts the requirements of the actual performance (*lakṣya*). In every such case, this resolution applies: that in the actual performance, there must be no contradiction with the aesthetic mark (*lakṣma*). 340.
This has been determined among the regional melodies (deśīrāgas) by the learned Śārṅgadeva:

having established Madhyama as the fixed tonic (sthāyin), one ascends five notes starting from Gandhāra—the note immediately below it—down to Niṣāda, and then descends to the end of the scale (gapa). 341–342.
Having established *sthāyin* and *niṣāda*, and having struck *dhaivata* and descended down to the end of *sthāyin*, when this occurs, then the *baṅgāla* arises.
(343) Thus ends the *baṅgāla*.
Having established Dhaivata as the stationary note (sthāyin), and having performed the third and fourth notes, one should descend from there back to the stationary note; then,
having placed the third note below that, one should proceed to the stationary note.
"When [the *sthāyin*] is observed in the target [note], it becomes *bhairava*;
thus, *bhairava* is when the *sthāyin*, having arrived at the note preceding *dhaivata*, [proceeds] to the notes following it. (345)
Having ascended from the fifth [note] to the fourth, and having applied the second [note] twice, the *rāga* is placed upon the *sthāyin*; then *varāṭī* arises.
In the practical application (*lakṣya*), however, the *sthāyin* is seen as the note of Ṛṣabha in the *kiṃnarī*. 346–347.
Thus, in the *varāṭī* [jāti],
having made the middle *ṛṣabha* the stationary note (*sthāyin*), one descends to the two notes below it, and then, starting from the stationary note, ascends three notes and descends again. (348)
If the five notes are assigned to Ṛṣabha, then it is Gurjarī;
in the sphere of practical observation (lakṣya), its *graha* (tonic) is seen to be Gāndhāra alone.
Thus ends Gurjarī. (349)

Having approached the third note before the middle *ṣaḍja* which serves as the *graha*, and having uttered the fourth, one ascends and descends through the three notes beginning with the second; thus, with the *graha* and *nyāsa* on [the same], it becomes *Vasanta*, though in actual practice (*lakṣye*) its *graha* is *ṛṣabha*. 350–351.
Thus Vāsanta,
having made Madhyama-Ṣaḍja the *graha*, having uttered the third and the fourth, having touched the second and the third, and [uttered] the fourth and the fifth; 352.
In this sequence, the descent occurs by leaving the second *sthāyin* and returning to the end of the preceding *sthāyin*; from there, the third,
then the fourth, and then the third again is proclaimed and placed in its respective house (353).
"Then Dhannāsī would be seen; the fifth note (*graha*) should be in the *lakṣya*. Thus, having made Ṛṣabha the stationary note (*sthāyin*) in Dhannāsī, one touches the next [note] after that.
Having lingered, having oscillated the fourth [note], and having touched the two notes below the fourth,
one should exit from those notes; then, having uttered the next two [notes] and arrived at the second [note],
if the final cadence (*nyāsa*) occurs on the *sthāyin*, then it becomes a *deśīrāga*.
"The *gāndhāra* note is seen as the *graha* in the *deśī* [rāga], and it is observed in the *deśīvedīs*.
(356) Thus, in the *deśī*, having made *madhya-gāndhāra* the *sthāyin*, and having descended to the fourth [note] below, [the *mūrcchanā* proceeds].

Therefore, having ascended up to the sixth [note] from that [starting point] and descended through those same notes, if one places the third note below the *graha* upon the *graha* itself, then that is called "region" (*deśa*) in the observed [scale]; its middle *graha* is thus seen. (357–358)

Thus, if one reaches the second note from the middle *ṣaḍja* known as *deśāntara*, and having lingered over the third note below it, touches the *sthāyin* [the central note], [it is called *antarita*]. 359

When the third and fourth notes from below are made to descend again to that third note, and the final cadence (nyāsa) is placed on the tonic (sthāyi-svara), then the *Ḍombakrī* arises; it is called *Bhūpālī* by people, and its tonic is considered to be the middle note (*madhyama*). 360.
Thus, having made Pañcama the tonic note situated in the low register (*mandra*), and ascending together with it through six notes, one should descend to the third [note] among them. 361.
Having lingered and made it tremble, one should approach the fourth note as the *sthāyin*.
If it arises in this sequence, then it is the first *mañjarī*; in practical performances (*lakṣya*), its *sthāyin* is observed to be the deep-toned *gāndhāra*. 362–363.

Thus, having made the note *dhaivata* the stationary point (*sthāyin*) in the first *mañjarī*, when one moves from there downward by oscillating (*āndolita*) and reaches the *gṛha*, it shall be *kāmodā*; in this [rāga], *madhyama* is the *graha*. (364)
Thus, in the Kāmodā [rāga],
having established Ṣaḍja as the tonic (sthāyin), and having reached the note preceding it,
one ascends twice through two notes and then to the third and fourth.

Then, having trembled on the third [note] and lingered while striking the fifth (366), if one descends through the notes ending with the *sthāyin*, excluding *ṛṣabha*—having made *madhyama-ṣaḍja* the *graha* along with the two preceding notes (367)— [This constitutes the *mukha* of the *jāti*. [The *garbha* follows: Having performed the *kampa* on the third note, having struck the fifth, and having trembled on the third, one should descend through the notes ending with the *sthāyin*, excluding *ṛṣabha*. Having made *madhyama-ṣaḍja* the *graha*, together with the two preceding notes, one should perform the *kampa* on the third note, strike the fifth, and tremble on the third. Then, having made *madhyama-ṣaḍja* the *graha*, one should descend through the notes ending with the *sthāyin*, excluding *ṛṣabha*. This is the *garbha*. [The *nirvahaṇa* follows: Having made *madhyama-ṣaḍja* the *graha*, together with the two preceding notes, one should perform the *kampa* on the third note, strike the fifth, and tremble on the third. Then, having made *madhyama-ṣaḍja* the *graha*, one should descend through the notes ending with the *sthāyin*, excluding *ṛṣabha*. This is the *nirvahaṇa*. [The *dhruva* follows: Having made *madhyama-ṣaḍja* the *graha*, together with the two preceding notes, one should perform the *kampa* on the third note, strike the fifth, and tremble on the third. Then, having made *madhyama-ṣaḍja* the *graha*, one should descend through the notes ending with the *sthāyin*, excluding *ṛṣabha*. This is the *dhruva*. [The *samudga* follows: Having made *madhyama-ṣaḍja* the *graha*, together with the two preceding notes, one should perform the *kampa* on the third note, strike the fifth, and tremble on the third. Then, having made *madhyama-ṣaḍja* the *graha*, one should descend through the notes ending with the *sthāyin*, excluding *ṛṣabha*. This is the *samudga*. [The *sannipāta* follows: Having made *madhyama-ṣaḍja* the *graha*, together with the two preceding notes, one should perform the *kampa* on the third note, strike the fifth, and tremble on the third. Then, having made *madhyama-ṣaḍja* the *graha*, one should descend through the notes ending with the *sthāyin*, excluding *ṛṣabha*. This is the *sannipāta*. [The *vikṣepa* follows: Having made *madhyama-ṣaḍja* the *graha*, together with the two preceding notes, one should perform the *kampa* on the third note, strike the fifth, and tremble on the third. Then, having made *madhyama-ṣaḍja* the *graha*, one should descend through the notes ending with the *sthāyin*, excluding *ṛṣabha*. This is the *vikṣepa*. [The *saṃprayoga* follows: Having made *madhyama-ṣaḍja* the *graha*, together with the two preceding notes, one should perform the *kampa* on the third note, strike the fifth, and tremble on the third. Then, having made *madhyama-ṣaḍja* the *graha*, one should descend through the notes ending with the *sthāyin*, excluding *ṛṣabha*. This is the *saṃprayoga*. [The *viśleṣa* follows: Having made *madhyama-ṣ

Having uttered the fourth [note] with a pause, and then touching the third along with the second while holding the breath (*graha*), when the placement (*nyāsa*) occurs, then it becomes the *rāmakṛti* form.
(368) Thus ends the *rāmakṛti*.
Having established the middle [note] as the stable [starting point], having reached the fourth below it,
having ascended three notes lower than the *graha*, and having touched the third note,
one returns by descending as far as the fourth note below the *graha*.
Then, having ascended the third [string], having reached the *karaṇa* and shaken it,
when there is a placement (*nyāsa*) on the *graha*, then it becomes the Gauḍa style;
the fifth [note] is perceived as the stable (*sthāyin*) by those who know the characteristics in the actual performance (*lakṣya*).
Thus ends the composition by Gauḍa:
having made Madhya-Ṣaḍja the *graha* (tonic), descending to the lower note, making that again the *graha*, and shaking the third and fourth notes, [he reaches] the fifth note. 372.
Having played the fourth note from the *graha*, one should likewise play the third as the *sthāyin*;
then, having caused the second to tremble, one should touch the third note.
If the *nyāsa* is then on the *graha*, it becomes *devakṛti*.
"However, the middle placement (nyāsa) for this [jāti] is stated by the venerable Śārṅgin to be on the *lakṣya*.
Thus ends the work of Deva.
Having made *dhaivata* the stationary note (*sthāyin*), one goes to the lower [note] and then returns to the *graha*. 375.
Then, having first approached that subsequent *sthāyin* from that [previous] one, and having ascended the *graha*, one should descend from the fifth [note] after three notes, such as the third;
then, having uttered the six *svara*s of the *graha*, one should thereafter cause the third to vibrate (*kampayet*).
Having touched the fourth, fifth, and fourth-quarter notes, and having uttered the third, second, and [first], when this placement occurs in the *graha*, then it is Bhairavī;
in practical examples, Gāndhāra is seen to be the fixed note (*sthāyin*) of this *rāga*. (377–378)
Thus Bhairavī,
having made the deep *ṣaḍja* the starting note (*graha*), having reached the middle *ṣaḍja*,
and having descended from there, returns to the starting note by way of ascent. 379.
Having arrived at *pa*, delayed there, and touched this [note], one should proceed to *dhaivatam* by descending from the *graha*; if that occurs, it is then called *cchāyānaṭṭā*.
(380) Thus ends *cchāyānaṭṭā*.

Having made the middle *ṣaḍja* the *graha*, and having made the two following it and the fifth [note] the sixth, one descends from these two; and having descended from the third, one descends from the previous third, or from the *graha* itself, or from the previous third. (381–382)
If, after shaking [the instrument] and uttering that [mantra], it is placed upon the [target] planet,
then it is called *rāmakrī* by people, preceded by the term *bahulī*. (383) Thus ends the *bahulī-rāmakrī*.
Having made the *dhaivata* the stationary note (*sthāyin*), one should then linger upon the next;
having touched the second from the *graha*, one should then touch the third preceding the *graha*.
Having lingered slightly, one should ascend to the third from the *graha* and so forth.

Having paused there, or having descended to the space below it, one should touch the three notes beginning with *graha*; then, having uttered the *graha* note, if the *rāga* is applied to that *graha*, then the *mahlāra* occurs. (385)
"In this *rāga*, the fifth [note] is seen as the stable tone (*sthāyin*) within the range of the musical scale.
Thus ends the *mahlāra*;
if the *sthāyin* is five notes lower than *madhyama*, it is called *māvadhī*.

One should not go beyond the third [note] from that; rather, having ascended four *svara*s, touched the *sthāyin*, and made the preceding one slow (*vilambita*), if it is then placed upon *ṣaḍja*, the Gauḍakarṇāṭa [rāga] is produced. (387–388)
In this Gauḍa rāga, however, a fifth *sthāyī* (fixed note) is observed in the *lakṣya* (practical application):
if, after pronouncing the notes starting from *mandra-ṣaḍja*,
one proceeds to the next note, and then having gone to the third and fourth [notes], one reaches the third *sthāyī*.
Having made the fourth [note] of the *sthāyin* [the *graha*], and having descended five notes from that;

then having stated the fourth below the *sthāyin*, then the one below the *sthāyin*, then the *sthāyin* itself, and then the one following it, and finally the fourth of the *sthāyin* after the *graha*.
When the *nyāsa* (concluding note) is placed on *griha*, it then becomes *Gauḍatauruṣka*;
that same [melodic form] is called *Mālavī*. In performance (*lakṣye*), its *sthāyī* (stable/tonic note) is the fifth (*pañcama*). Thus ends *Turuṣkagauḍa*.
Having made the *graha* of the *mālavinī* and having spoken the second [syllable] immediately following it, one should leap;
then, having leaped, one should ascend three [steps] and descend from there. Having shaken the leaped [spot], one should speak the previous [syllable] and proceed to the *graha*. 393.
