At that time, he is known by people as Drāviḍa or Gauḍa, along with the Sālaka [raga].
Those who know the characteristics of musical forms state that the fifth note (pañcama) is the stable tone (sthāyin) for this as well.
Thus ends the Drāviḍa-Gauḍa.
Thus are the *upāṅgas*:
having descended from the *sthāyin* *dhaivata* to the preceding [note], and having stated another *graha* and a *graha*, one should make the third and fourth notes slow (*vilambita*). 396.
Therefore, having touched the two lower [strings], one should let the third vibrate;
if, after touching the string following the *graha*, one touches the two preceding ones and speaks first of the *graha* when it vibrates, then the *rāga* placed therein is called *Lalita*.
"Those who know the characteristics of musical practice declare that in this [raga] the Gāndhāra note alone is the tonic (sthāyin).
Thus have several rāgas been described for the sake of those with limited understanding; such is the Lalita.
In reality, the playing of the notes (rāgas) in all musical instruments is identical;

let the wise investigate this by way of the origin of the notes such as *graha* and so forth—namely, those notes which, residing in their respective positions within the *kiṃnarī*, give rise to [the melody]. 399.

That passion of his is seen even in the bamboo flute and other instruments; (400) such is the description of the Kinnarī. On the Pinākī [bow], the bow is forty-one finger-breadths long for one who is desirous.
The middle width should be two and a quarter finger-breadths (sapādāṅguladvaya) in length;
at the end, one should fashion the lower crest (śikhā) according to the measure of one finger-breadth.
The upper crest of the bow, however, should be exactly one and a quarter finger-breadths (sapādāṅgulamātra). 401–402.
The two *khaṭaka* [elements] should be one finger in length and three-quarters of a finger in thickness;
they are joined at the tips of the *śikhās*, and from there inward toward the ends,
a measurement of one and a half fingers in width is desired.

The wise man should determine the width in the space between the middle and the end; the skillful one should fasten the string at the two tips according to the measurement of the strings. The measurement for the sounding surface should be twenty-one finger-breadths.
In length, the width at the fist is measured here as three finger-breadths;
however, that [width] should be reduced by one-third of a finger-breadth at both ends after setting aside the two upper and lower points of the crest (śikhā).
The measurement for the pair of upper and lower crests is three-quarters of a finger-breadth.
The string of the bow-wielder, made from hair finer than a horse's tail,

was placed upon the ground with its gourd end held down by his feet and facing downward; then, the tip of that string became fixed there, pointing upward and resting against the shoulder of the wielder of the Pināka bow.

Having pressed the base of the gourd held in the left hand with that [string], one should then sound the bow-string held in the right hand; and by means of this string smeared with lac, one should determine the locations of the musical notes. 409.
The wise man [should play] with a single string, according to the gradation of lower and higher notes.
(410) Thus is the description of the Pināka [drum];
the length of the string, excluding the portion at the binding edge, is four cubits. (411)
It is bound at one end to a wooden plank placed above,
and at the other end to another wooden plank placed below; it extends for one and a half cubits (sārdhakara),
and in thickness it is equal to an ālāpinī, excluding two finger-breadths from the tip.
Then, having fastened the string and attached the wooden gourd below it, he placed his left leg—
its forepart pressed against the root of the left thigh and its shape bent— at the ankle of the right leg, the outer side of which was touching the ground. 413–414.

Having stepped upon it with his right foot, as if playing a *pinākī* lute, he produced a resonant sound with the gourd held in his left hand; [he played] a dry piece of leather, provided with a plectrum and a bow.
315. A piece of leather, whether moist or dry, equipped with a plectrum and a bow.
Taking it with the left hand or by its corner, there may be a *sāraṇā*;
where that *niḥśaṅkavīṇā* is employed, as described by Śārṅgadeva, the manifestation of the notes, melodies (*rāga*), and so forth across the three registers occurs through it. 416–417.
Thus ends the definition of the *niḥśaṅka-vīṇā*:

"In whatever way there may be clarity and abundance of passion (*rakta*) in the tone, in that same way should the stringed instrument (*tata*) be prepared, in accordance with worldly convention. (418)
Some stringed instruments have been described as suitable for correct tuning;

the wise man should infer others as well by this same method. (419) He who knows the playing of the lute in its true essence, and who understands the musical intervals (*śruti*) and scales (*jāti*), [is qualified]. (420)
"One who is skilled in the art of beating the *tāla* attains liberation without effort;
therefore, one should practice the *vīṇā*," so said Yājñavalkya and others.
[One should be] a knower of the reality of sound, the *śruti*, the *svara*, the *grāma*, the *jāti*, the *rāga*, and so forth.
Endowed with physical excellence, having mastered the practice of steady posture (āsana),
having conquered the pair of hands through the overcoming of fatigue, free from fear, and having subdued the senses;
possessing bold intelligence, a robust physique, and skill in singing and playing musical instruments.

And "one whose mind is attentive"—these are the qualities described for the lute player (vaiṇika). Thus ends the description of stringed instruments (tatavādya). [The materials for the lute are] bamboo, acacia, ivory, sandalwood, and red sandalwood.
It may be made of iron, bronze, silver, bamboo, or even gold;
it should be circular, straight, smooth, and free from knots, fissures, or scars,
with a width equal to the little finger and possessing a hollow interior.
Its length should be equal to its own height, and it should be uniform in shape on all sides;
leaving two, three, or four finger-breadths from the top of its head, a hole for blowing should be made measuring one finger-breadth in width. 426.
Within the opening of the mouth, there should be one finger-breadth (aṅgula) between the openings;
the other seven openings should be separated by half a finger-breadth each.
These eight are said to resemble the seeds of the jujube tree (badarī).
The bamboo flute should be left with two finger-breadths remaining at all its holes;
among those, they consider seven holes to be for the division of musical notes (svaras), while the eighth is intended for the exit of the wind that causes resonance (nāda). 429.
The wind produced by blowing is filled through the aperture of the mouth;
when played through nine holes situated on the flute, it is called *ekavīra*.
This occurs in the interval between the mouth-aperture of the flute and its highest-pitched hole.
There should be fourteen other bamboo tubes, each increasing by one finger-breadth (aṅgula) from the preceding one;
this increment of one aṅgula begins from the bamboo tube that is eighteen aṅgulas long.
There should also be seven other holes with intervals of half an aṅgula.

Those [holes] are said to be eight in number, resembling the seeds of the jujube fruit. The bamboo tube should remain below all the holes for a length of two finger-breadths; they consider there to be seven holes for the division of the musical notes (*svara*), while the eighth is intended for the exit of the wind that produces the sound (*nāda*).
The wind produced by blowing is filled through the aperture of the mouth;
when played through nine holes situated on the flute, it is called *ekavīra*.
[This occurs] between the mouth-aperture of the flute and its highest (tārā) hole.
By increasing by one finger-breadth (aṅgula) at a time, there should be fourteen other types of bamboo;
this increment of one aṅgula starts from a bamboo of eighteen aṅgulas.
The Umāpati [type] should be two aṅgulas [in height], and the Tripuruṣa [type] should be three aṅgulas.
The Four-faced one should have four [fingers], while the Five-faced one has five.
The Six-faced one is six fingers wide, and the Sage (Muni) is considered to be seven fingers.
The Vasu is declared to be eight fingers, and the Lord Indra is nine fingers.
Mahānanda is ten finger-breadths; Rudra is eleven finger-breadths (435).
Āditya is twelve finger-breadths; Manu’s lineage is fourteen;
Kalānidhi would be sixteen; and Anvartha is eighteen finger-breadths (436).
Because its internal intervals are not clearly defined, a flute seventeen finger-breadths long is not desired,
nor one thirteen finger-breadths long, nor likewise one fifteen finger-breadths long;
another bamboo flute called the *muralī* is recorded by others as being twenty finger-breadths long.
Another flute of twenty-two finger-breadths is also seen among those who know the subject; people learned in flutes call that flute a "repository of sound" (*śrutinidhi*),
yet it is not approved by the discerning because of its excessively deep resonance.
Because they are exceedingly thin, flutes are rare that are less than five finger-breadths [in length];
however, when the seven sound-holes in an eighteen-finger-long flute are closed, the *ṣaḍja* note situated in the low (*mandra*) register arises. (440–441)
In this manner, in the other six tubes, the notes beginning with *ṛṣabha* arise in sequence.
Starting from eight finger-breadths [above the mouth], in the seven tubes below, the seven notes beginning with *ṣaḍja* arise in sequence, situated at their respective middle points. (442–443)
When the *tāra* (high) position is reached, the *ṣaḍja* note arises for the *ekavīra* flute.
(444) In all these flutes, when the last two holes are opened, the second note arises; from that point, the third and subsequent notes follow in sequence.
Seven [sounds] arise from the release of three or more apertures; however,
when the aperture of the *tāra* (high pitch) is released while the other apertures are closed,
the production of the eighth sound has been proclaimed by the former teachers.
When the fingers are fully released, the tone becomes complete;
when a finger trembles there, one *śruti* is diminished.
When half-released, two *śrutis* are diminished, but if it trembles, three *śrutis* are diminished. (447)
Some here describe the arising of the seven notes differently:

having placed both hands upon the flute like the hoods of a serpent with a half-moon [on its head], the note *ṣaḍja* is produced by the left ring finger, and furthermore, by the middle finger. 448–449.
From the left hand, three notes are produced: *ṛṣabha* from the index finger and *gāndhāra* from the [thumb]; from the right hand, four notes are produced:
*madhyama* from the little finger, and the note *pañcama* from the ring finger. (450)
The *dhaivata* [note] occurs with the middle finger, while the *niṣāda* occurs with the index finger (451).
They have sung otherwise regarding the accomplishment of the three positions in this [context],
[arising] from a well-practiced whistle produced within the middle seven [notes] (452).
Notes arise that correspond to the natural tones of the bamboo body;
when the mouth-joint is narrow within the mouth-cavity, people call that method of playing "ṭīpā. 453–454.
Whatever sound is blown through a hole by that [wind], its pitch becomes doubled; however,
due to the proximity or distance from the opening of the hole, the notes become low (*mandra*),
while the intensity of the wind— whether very strong or weak— results in the state of being rapid or slow.
Through filling and not-filling, and through the increase and decrease of sound, those who know this produce the arising of various notes even within a single aperture:
[the notes] kampitā, valitā, muktā, ardhāmuktā, and nipīḍitā. (456)
Thus, the fivefold movement of the flute has been described by Śārṅgadeva.

When the flute is held below [the mouth], the production of phonemes (varṇas) and ornaments (alaṃkāras) through its trembling is considered "trembling" (kampitā); its application in performance is the purpose of this technique. 457–458.
Thus, it becomes *kampitā* (trembling) upon the completion of *saṃcāriṇī*; it is *valitā* (twisted) when there is the movement of the fingers—
thus it is *valitā*.
When released from the opening with the fingers slightly extended, it produces the sound "muktā";
thus it is called *muktā*.
When half-released, it produces the sound "ardhamuktā," and when released halfway, it produces the sound "ghṛta. (459–460)
When one who knows the art fills the flute by covering all the holes on every side with the fingers, leaving only half of them open, then it should be known as *nipīḍitā*. 461
Thus pressed,
Kīrtidhara here accepted another arrangement:
"Bamboo poles measuring six, seven, or eight finger-breadths produce the notes tāra."

The three middle tones (*madhyasvara*) consist of nine, ten, and eleven finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). That which consists of twelve finger-breadths and that which consists of thirteen are the causes of the low tones (*mandrasvara*); furthermore, both of these are made entirely of bamboo.

A flute fourteen finger-breadths long is capable of producing notes in the three registers (*tri-sthāna-svara*) and is fit for harmonizing with vocal ornaments, musical scales (*dhātu*), and other instruments; those who know what is proper and improper recognize that there are exactly nine such types of flutes. 465
Some experts on local traditions (deśīvidaḥ) state that these lineages, beginning with Ekavīra and others, are measured by a different standard; I shall now set forth their opinion:
they say that at the end of the fourteen previous lineages, one finger-breadth (aṅgula) consists of five barley-corns (yava).
In the fourteen-line [verse] and other lineages, this [measure] is five and a half barley-corns (yava).

They declare the staff (daṇḍa) for the Ekavīra [style] to be fourteen finger-breadths (aṅgula); the two ends of the head are one and a half finger-breadths each, and at the mouth of the individual caste-mark (jāti-mukha), it is one finger-breadth. 467–368.
The measurement for the *tārā* (star) and other [elements] consists of nine *yavas* each;
the intervals between them are three *yavas* each at their respective locations.
From the base, the measurement is reduced by one-fifth, measured from the middle of the little finger joint. (469)
The staff (daṇḍa) for the lineage of Ubhāpati is fifteen aṅgulas; however, in its intermediate sections, it is increased by two yavas and three-quarters.
Its measurement is three yavas and one-quarter, while the other [parts] are as before. 470.

In the *tripuruṣa* lineage, the staff (*daṇḍa*) is considered to be seventeen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) plus two barley-corns (*yava*). When there are seven separate intervals, another measurement is one finger-breadth less than a barley-corn; the other characteristics are as previously described.
On the four-faced staff, it is measured by eighteen and a half finger-breadths plus two barley-corns; however, the head and the base are each measured separately.
The characteristic mark is as before, measuring three-quarters of a finger-breadth.

The measurement of the staff (*daṇḍa*) for the five-faced [liṅga] is considered to be twenty-two finger-breadths less by one and a half quarters of a barley-corn (474). The measurement at the head and the end is two and a half finger-breadths each, while the measurement for each of the seven intervening sections is separate (475).
The [first] staff is four *yava*s longer by one and a half *pāda*s; the others are as before.
In the case of the six-faced [staff], the staff is measured from that [base] by twenty-four *aṅgula*s, including two and a half *pāda*s and one *yava*.

In the eight openings beginning with Tārā, the measurement is three and a quarter *yavas* each; in the intervening spaces, the measurement is five *yavas* minus a sixteenth part. The remaining characteristics should be as in the case of the Five-Faced [Mañjuśrī].
Beyond this, in the seven subsequent lineages, the *yava* is seen to exceed its own measure by one in the hollow of the *tāra*, at the opening of the *jāti*;
when combined with a half-*yava*, it becomes twenty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
The measurement of the sage’s staff (*munidaṇḍa*) is as follows: at the eight intervals, each is said to be three *yava*s and one and a half quarters;
separately, at the intermediate spaces, it is five *yava*s and a half, while the rest is as before. 480–481.
In the lineage of Vasu, however, the measurement of the staff (daṇḍa) is twenty-eight finger-breadths (aṅgula);

the "face of the species" (jātimukha) is one finger-breadth plus a barley-corn (yava). The measurement for the intervening sections should be known separately as one finger-breadth plus a barley-corn.
482. The measurement for the intervals is to be understood as one finger-breadth plus a barley-corn.

The remainder is as before; in the lineage of Nāthendra, the measurement of the staff (daṇḍa) is thirty finger-breadths increased by one-quarter of a barley-corn at both the head and the end. The measurement for each of the seven intervening sections is three finger-breadths less one-quarter. 483–484.

The measurement from the base of the pit should be one and a quarter finger-breadths less than the [total] measurement; the middle [measurement] should be equal to the joint of the little finger. The other [measurements] on the staff are to be understood as before, according to the Mahānanda [scale].
By a quarter less than a quarter of a barleycorn, it should be increased;

at the end of those thirty-two finger-breadths, the two [parts] at the head are each three finger-breadths wide; the face of the *jāti* is one and a quarter finger-breadths within the seven intervals.
The measurement of a finger (aṅgula) is increased by one-quarter of a quarter [of its own measure] starting from the base;
the cavity is measured by the middle joint of the little finger minus one-seventh, and the supreme characteristic has been declared by them as previously stated. 488.
The measurement shall be thirty-four and a quarter finger-breadths (aṅgulas), plus half a barley-corn (yava). In the seven intervals of the Rudra-staff,
the individual measurement is one and a half finger-breadths, according to the joint of the middle of the little finger.
The opening is limited; the remainder shall be described as in the previous lineage.
However, there are thirty-seven finger-breadths (aṅgulas) increased by half a barley-corn (yava).
For the Sun, the measure of the staff (daṇḍa) should be one and three-quarter finger-breadths.
In the intermediate periods, there is another separate measurement like that of the lineage of Rudra (492).
During the reign of Manu, it is thirty-nine and one-quarter *aṅgulas*,
plus one *yava* and one-eighth of a *yava* with a quarter-part (493).
The measurement for the *sahita* [type] is said to be three fingers minus one-quarter finger;
at the two ends of the head, in the face of the distinct species (*pṛthagjāti*), the measurement should be one finger.
Furthermore, in the eight perforations (*randhra*), it is increased by one-sixteenth of a quarter-finger.
The three [measures]— the separate, the half, and those within the seven—
are each two finger-breadths less by one-quarter of a barley-corn; the other characteristic of measurement shall be like that of the Solar dynasty.

In the *Kalānidhi*, the staff (*daṇḍa*) at the end of the bamboo (*vaṃśa*) is measured by forty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) plus nine thirty-second parts of a barley-corn (*yava*) and one and a half quarters; the two ends of the head [of the staff] are each three finger-breadths wide.

In the intervals, two finger-breadths (aṅgula) each, joined with equal barley-corns (yava), is declared to be the measurement; this is the view of other authorities, considered by some to be the correct doctrine. [It is formed] by adding one-quarter of an eighth part of a barley-corn. 498–499.
It should be measured at thirty-nine and three-quarter finger-breadths;

the staff (daṇḍa) is eighteen finger-breadths, and the two [other parts] are two and a half finger-breadths each. In the intervals, the measurements for the others should be understood separately from the "Treasury of Kalās" (Kalānidhi).

In this case, the thirteenth lineage is not accepted as being fifteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) long due to the smallness of the difference; rather, it is desired to be seventeen finger-breadths long.
Thus, these lineages are considered to be exactly fifteen [in number], and these [following] are regarded as belonging to them.

Endowed with sweetness and passion, these are the causes for the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (rāga). Whether it be this characteristic declared in the treatises (śāstra) or that which is considered to belong to the regional styles (deśī), both are capable of delighting the minds of those who know the arts. 503

When the blowing-hole is at the mouth, whose expanded form could even its two very long arms reach the sound-holes? Furthermore, the distance between the sound-holes is said to be half a finger-breadth. (504)
By that treatise, the manifestation of some particular *svara* has been declared.
(505) Regarding those seven *svaras*, sa, ri, ga, ma, and so forth, which follow the previously mentioned sequence, that specific sequential arrangement is not seen here at the end. (506)
Any talk of *mūrchanās*, *rāgas*, *bhāṣās*, and so forth, is utterly remote from the works composed by those great-souled ancient masters;
even a critique of them would lead to no fault—what need have we for such talk? (507)
Let that be; however, something is said regarding those who know the regional traditions (deśī):
why is an additional *yava* seen here in the measurement of five *yavas*, and how is it that in bamboos (*vaṃśa*) of seven *aṅgulas* and so forth, there is [an increase] beyond fourteen? 508–509.
If there are seven or eight barley-corns (*yava*) in excess of the previously stated measurement,
then at a measurement of five and a half barley-corns, the defining mark (*lakṣma*) would be unstable.
Furthermore, the three lineages (*vaṃśa*) beginning with the thirteen [finger-breadths], which were previously rejected, [are likewise untenable].
There is not even a trace of reasoning therein by which the wise might be satisfied.
Furthermore, that which was stated regarding the "slight difference" is utterly insubstantial; for among them, a difference equal to the interval between different lineages is observed. 511–512.
Just as from an eleven-holed flute it is sealed with twelve half-tones less [than the full octave],
so too from that [eleven-holed one] it becomes thirteen-holed;
likewise, from a fourteen-holed flute it becomes fifteen-holed, and from a sixteen-holed one.
If it is argued that the seventeenth [chapter] on the bamboo pole (*vaṃśa*) is not well-known by its defining characteristics (*lakṣma*), that is not so;
for according to the method stated therein, the definition can indeed be applied to those as well:
"The bamboo pole, thirteen finger-breadths in length, is declared to be the Universal Form (*viśvamūrti*). (514–515)
The measure of the staff (daṇḍa) for the Viśvamūrti [image] should be forty fingers plus one-quarter of a barley-corn (yava); for the eight hollows beginning with the pupil (tārā),
each of the seven intervals should be three and a half barley-corns.
The measurement for each [face] is two fingers, like the sun;
it is considered to be forty-two fingers plus one-quarter of a finger, increased by one-eighth of a barley-corn (yava) plus one-quarter of that. 517–518.
The staff (daṇḍa) described by the venerable Śārṅgadeva is fifteen finger-breadths (aṅgula) in length for the bamboo pole;
the measurement at the three points— the tip of the head and the two ends— is three finger-breadths each,
while in the intervals between them, it is increased by half a barley-corn (yava).
The supreme measurement of a *yava* is two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) according to the standard of Manu;
it is measured by forty-six finger-breadths less one-quarter, increased by a thirty-second part of a *yava* plus half a quarter [of a *yava*]. (520–521)
In the seventeenth lineage, the *daṇḍa* measures two fingers across the intervals;
its measurement is separately two barley-corns (*yava*), and it is supreme like the moon-treasury (the sun).
Thus, these [measures] possess well-known characteristics and are the causes for the manifestation of the *rāgas* and other elements.
The thirteen and other lineages are refuted in vain by others (523).
Even regarding the measurement of fifteen barley-corns for all eighteen lineages,
the wise master, the foremost of the Śrīkaraṇa, is clearly capable of speaking (524).

Therefore, Śārṅgadeva, who understood the true nature of the definitions and the things to be defined according to local custom, established the nature of the flute differently; he fixed its length at one *aṅgula* based on the principles of mathematical science. 525. He established this as a proven fact through the treatises on calculation.
For an *aṅgula* consisting of five barley grains (*yava*) is not seen in either the scriptures or the world.
An *aṅgula* should consist of six dehusked barley grains placed side-by-side; this is the measure for the depth of the pit at the little finger of the right hand.
It should be neither too thick nor too thin, but rather of medium thickness;
the term "root" (mūla) here refers to the middle joint.
The internal cavity should be uniform throughout; an uneven [cavity] causes a break in the tone.
The staff of the Solitary Hero (Ekavīra) is seen to be fourteen finger-breadths (aṅgula) long;
the measurement for the two ends of its head is two finger-breadths each,
while the measurement for the blowing-holes called the "mouths of the castes" (jātimukha) is one finger-breadth.
Below that, at a distance of one finger-breadth, the *tāra* (central) hole is prescribed;
its measurement is known to be half a finger-breadth plus a sixteenth part.
One should fashion seven holes below that, each separated by the same distance.
Among those eight [cavities], there should be seven upper openings for the sake of the accomplishment of the musical notes (svarasiddhi).

The last one is the wind-opening (vāyurandhra), and there are seven intermediate spaces between them, each measuring half a finger-breadth (ardhāṅgula); however, the central cavity (garbharandhra) is measured differently.

From the base, by a fifth part [of the length], at the joint of the little finger and the middle finger, that is called the *khāni*; in the regional language (*deśī*), it is the aforementioned arising of the vowels (*svarodaya*).
There are thirteen others, beginning with the types born from the hollows of the *tāra* [vowels] and within the openings of the mouth.
By increasing by one finger-breadth (aṅgula) for each successive lineage up to the fourteenth, the measurement of the staff for both types of lords shall be fifteen fingers.
The other characteristics, however, are like those of the Ekavīra; furthermore, in the case of the Tripuruṣa [lineage], [the following applies].
The staff (daṇḍa) is measured at sixteen and a half finger-breadths (aṅgula), including half a yava;
the seven intervals from the bottom tier are each measured at three and a half yavas.
The remaining characteristics are declared to be as in the previous section on the beam (vaṃśa).
The staff for the Four-faced [Brahmā] measures eighteen and a half aṅgulas;

the seven separate intervals between the four parts, including the feet, are measured by four barley-corns each, and the remainder is as previously described. As for the measurement for the Five-faced [Śiva], it is as follows: 538–539.
The staff (daṇḍa) is twenty fingers increased by two barley-corns;

the measurement for each of the seven intervening spaces is five barley-corns. Furthermore, the other characteristics are as before, but the measure of the staff in the six-faced [image] is as follows.
Twenty-two half-yavas of finger-breadths are declared [for the intervals];
the measurement for each of the seven separate intervals is five and a half yavas;
the remainder is as before, and the measure of the staff for the sage (Viśvāmitra) in the Vaṃśa [style] is again as follows. 541–542.

In a span of seven intervals, each measuring twenty-three and a half finger-breadths (aṅgulas), the measurement for each individual interval is one aṅgula; the remainder is to be understood as before.
In the bamboo pole (vaṃśa) of eight [units], the measure of the staff (daṇḍa) is increased by four barley-corns (yavas).
The twenty-five intervals between the fingers are said to be seven *yavas* each; the remainder is held to be as previously stated.
The measure of the *nāyendra-daṇḍa* (the staff of Indra) should be twenty-seven and a quarter [units].

The intervals between the fingers should each be one and a quarter *aṅgulas* from the base; the pit for the little finger is measured by the middle joint minus a sixth part, while the other characteristics are as previously described.
The *māna* [staff] on the *mahānanda* [pitcher] is measured at thirty finger-breadths (547).

There should be seven separate intervals, each measuring one and a half finger-breadths. The subsequent mark is like that of the *nāya* and *indra*; furthermore, the measurement of the staff on the *rudra* [pitcher] is as follows (548).
The measurement for each of the internal spaces is declared to be thirty-three and a quarter finger-breadths (aṅgulas),
while for the eight apertures beginning with the *tārā*, it is two finger-breadths less a quarter.
The measurement from the base of the pit (khāni) shall be half a finger-breadth less than the individual measurement;
the middle [measurement] shall be reduced by one-seventh of the smallest joint (kaniṣṭhāparva).
Other matters previously mentioned apply to the Āditya lineage; now the staff (daṇḍa) is described. 550–551.
The measurement is thirty-five finger-breadths increased by one-eighth;
in the intervals, each is two finger-breadths less by one-eighth. However, for the excavation (khāni), the measurement from the base is reduced by one-eighth.

The previously mentioned [measurement] for the little finger and middle finger, and the other [fingers] like those of Rudra’s lineage, consists of thirty-seven fingers minus sixteen parts, plus a half; thus the staff is measured at thirty-seven and a half fingers,
while in the Viśvamūrti [form], there is an increase of two fingers in the intervals.

In measurement, each joint of the little finger is one-sixteenth more than the middle joint; the hollow [of the fist] is measured by that [length], and the remainder is like that of the Solar lineage (Ādityavaṃśa).
In the Manu [era], the staff, however, is thirty-nine fingers minus a quarter.
The two side-ends of the head [of the pedestal] are each two and a half finger-breadths in measure;
the measurement for each of the intervening spaces is two and a quarter finger-breadths.
All other characteristics are as those of the Viśvamūrti, as proclaimed by the venerable Śārṅgin.
Thus, exactly fourteen lineages have been described by the son of Soḍhala;
beyond these, no further occurrence of such lineages exists.
Indeed, among them, the reaching of the finger-joints [of the penis] is not seen in anyone at all. (558)

Furthermore, because their sound is excessively dull, they are not considered by the knowers of reality [to be the best]. However, the three beginning with Ekavīra are mentioned merely due to the tendency of following others; they do not possess the quality of being preeminent in passion and sweetness.
Therefore, eleven charming flutes beginning with the *caturmukha* are accepted in my own system by the son of Soḍhala;
Śārṅgadeva, however, described the form of the flute differently through another limb [of his treatise].
In this system, one *aṅgula* consists of four and a half dehusked barley grains; beginning from the "Single Hero" (*ekavīra*) according to the previously stated method,
there are twenty-two specific types of bamboo (staffs), among which we shall now describe [the first].
Niḥśaṅka has described this lineage known as Anupamā;
in the Ekavīra style, the *daṇḍa* (staff) should be sixteen finger-breadths long,
with an additional three-quarters of a barley-corn at both its head and base.
The measurement for each [of the eight openings] is proclaimed to be two and a half finger-breadths (sārdhāṅguladvaya).
Furthermore, at the mouth of the birth [opening], it is one and a quarter finger-breadths; in the other eight openings, a measurement of one finger-breadth less a third part is desired.

The intervals between each [section] shall be half a finger-breadth, and from the base, the excavation should measure five hundred and sixty-seven units— measured by the middle joint of the little finger minus one-fifth— and the distance between the openings of the various types of central apertures [should be as specified].
Known by names such as Ekavīra and others throughout all lineages,
the measurement of the staff for the Lord Umāpati is seventeen finger-breadths (aṅgulas), increased by half a barley-corn (yava) and diminished by one-eighth [of a finger-breadth]. (568–569)
A staff for three persons is considered to be one finger-breadth longer than that;
the remaining characteristics of these two types of *vaṃśas* (bamboo poles) should be like those of the *ekavīra*. The measurement should be twenty finger-breadths less by one-quarter of a *yava*.
In the intervals between the four faces of the staff, the measurement is half a finger (ardhāṅgula) increased by one-eighth; the other [measurement] is as before,
measured by two and three-quarter barley-corns (yava) increased by one-sixteenth.
The staff of the five-faced [deity] is proclaimed to be twenty-one finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in length;

the intervals between them are each measured at three-quarters of a finger-breadth less a quarter (pādonatribhiraṅgulaiḥ). There are seven such [intervals], and the further characteristics are as previously described.
The measurement of the staff for the six-faced deity (Ṣaṇmukha) shall be twenty-three and a half finger-breadths plus one barley-corn;
however, the measurement of the head and the end is each three-quarters of a finger-breadth, while the measurement of the seven intervening sections is as follows: 574–575.
The measurement [of the staff] is one *māna* plus a quarter *yava*, while the width is separately one *aṅgula* minus a quarter;

the remainder is as before. In the case of the sage (Vasiṣṭha), the measurement of the staff is equal to the *daṇḍa*. It is considered to be twenty-six *aṅgulas* minus a quarter *yava* and minus a quarter of that quarter.
In the seventh interval, each measurement is declared to be one finger-breadth less by one-quarter of a barley-corn (yava-pāda); the remainder is like that of the six-faced lineage (Ṣaṇmukha-vaṃśa).
In the eighth lineage, it is increased by half a barley-corn along with a thirty-second part.
The measurement of the staff (daṇḍa) may be twenty-seven and a half finger-breadths (aṅgulas), or it may be thirty-two and one-quarter finger-breadths;
however, in the intervals between these, each finger-breadth is increased by a measure exceeding a barley-corn (yava). 579.

The remainder, however, is equal to that of the Lord of Nāthas (Nāthendra) as measured by the staff of the Sage; it is said to be twenty-nine finger-breadths increased by one-eighth of a *yava*, along with an additional quarter, for each of the eight separate apertures. 580–581.
In the case of Tārā and others, the measurement shall be half a finger-breadth increased by a barley-corn;
for the intervals, there is a separate measurement of one-eighth of an aṅgula and so forth.
The remainder is as before; such is the measurement of the staff of Mahānanda.
It is stated that thirty-one fingers minus one-eighth of a *yava* is desired [for the total];
in the intermediate spaces, the measurement for each is said to be one and a quarter fingers; the remainder is as previously mentioned, as declared by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.

Thirty-three finger-breadths plus one-eighth constitute the measurement of the staff (*daṇḍa*) for Rudra. When increased by three-quarters of a finger-breadth, this is declared to be the individual measurement for each of the seven intervals; however, the measurement of the pit (*khāni*) is from its base. (585–586)
The middle joint of the little finger is declared to be reduced by one-sixth;

the remainder is as previously described. Now, for the Āditya [measure], the length of the staff (daṇḍa) is thirty-five finger-breadths (aṅgula) plus one-eighth of a barley-corn (yava); this is the interval.
Each excavation is declared to be one and a half finger-breadths (sārdhāṅgula) in measure;
from the base, it is reduced by a seventh part up to the middle joint of the little finger.
As before, this is the measurement of the staff upon the bamboo pole in the Viśvamūrti [temple]. 588–589.
The head [of the vessel] should be thirty-seven finger-breadths (aṅgulas) plus one-eighth of a finger,
together with a half-quarter (one-sixteenth) more; at the two ends, each is three finger-breadths wide,
and in the intervals between them, each is one and a half finger-breadths minus one-eighth.
The measurement of the *māna* (the hollowed portion) is considered to be less than one-eighth of the *khāna* from its base;
the middle joint of the little finger is desired as the remainder, as previously stated.
The measurement of the handle (*daṇḍa*) is thirty-nine finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), according to the system of Manu. (591–592)
With seven separate intervals, each measuring two finger-breadths less a quarter (one-and-a-half fingers), along with three-quarters of a barley-corn; however,
the *khāni* should be measured by the middle joint of the little finger.
The previously mentioned other [measurement] is equal to forty-one and a half finger-breadths (aṅgulas) plus two and three-quarter yavas;
this constitutes the fifteenth staff (daṇḍa), and thereafter it is increased by three and a half yavas.
Each [of the eight] apertures should be two fingers wide, with a measurement of one-eighth less for the spaces between them; each subsequent [space] should be like the mind (manu).
In the case of the Moon (Kalānidhi), it should consist of forty-three and a quarter fingers.
In the seven intermediate sections, the measurement of the *daṇḍa* increases by two fingers and one-quarter finger each, as before;
the *daṇḍa* of the eighteen-ribbed [structure] consists of forty-eight fingers.
Measured by one and a quarter *yavas* plus an additional quarter for each,
the measurement between the intervals is considered to be two and a half *aṅgulas* minus a sixteenth part; the further dimensions are intended to be as previously described.
In the case of the *daṇḍa*, the measurement for the nineteenth [unit] is fifty fingers plus one-quarter (50¼);
however, in the seven intervening [units], the measurement is two and a half fingers, each increased or decreased by a sixteenth part. (600–601)
As before, the length of the *muralī* staff should be increased by one *yava*;
it should be fifty-two and a half *aṅgulas*. However, the intervening spaces should each be two and three-quarter *aṅgulas*, as previously described.

In the twenty-first [section], the measure of the staff is fifty-five finger-breadths (aṅgulas), increased by one-sixteenth part plus a quarter and joined with a barley-corn; the intervening spaces should each be as previously described. 603–604.
The measurement of the *daṇḍa* is fifty-eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) according to the *Śrutinidhi*,
plus one and a half barley-corns; however, within its intervals, the measurement is considered separately as three finger-breadths less by a quarter of a sixteenth part.
Another characteristic previously mentioned was proclaimed by Śārṅgadeva:
"The aggregate of all flutes (vaṃśas) should be one and a half barley-corns;
those below the Pañcavaktra [flute] are devoid of redness and sweetness. (606-607)
The lineages beginning with Caturmukha and others are not desired by the venerable Śārṅgi-sūri;
rather, among all the regional (deśī) lineages, they are [derived] from the previously printed lineage. The subsequently printed lineage shall be increased by half a tone (svarārdha). 608.
For flutes of small measurement, superiority is considered to lie in every respect [in being longer].
Half a *svara* should be added to the length by means of the right little finger; thus, when that [finger] is pressed down, the [proper length] of the eastern flute is produced. (609–610)
The northern sealed lineage has a rising of breath-sounds identical to the eastern;
when the raised fingers increase, the sealed lineages meet with the ancient ones in their respective order, each succeeding one following from the previous. 611.
"Likewise, in the *Svarodaya*, it has been stated by the venerable Śārṅgin that the fingers are of the same type in both the *Śāstrīya* and *Laukika* systems regarding the respective divisions;
the finger-holes (*randhra*) consist of single notes, whether in proximity or at a distance."
"The beloved of Hara says that all lineages meet [in the same way];
however, that which is a hole devoid of honor, or a pit where such exists, does not meet with other holes of its own kind due to the breaking of its tone. (614)
From the single hero Āvaṃśa, there arose fourteen lineages and so forth;
now Śārṅgadeva, whose intellect has been purified by the grace of Śiva, describes this very arrangement of the nature of these lineages.
This lineage of the *vaṃśa* is called the *śārṅgavidva*;

herein, one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) is considered to consist of six barley-corns (*yava*) for the measurement of the holes and so forth. In the *ekavīra* [tune], the measure of the staff (*daṇḍa*) is twelve and a quarter finger-breadths.

Half a barley-corn more than that [is the measure] at the end of its head, with two separate finger-breadths [for the ears]. The measurement for the mouth-opening is one finger-breadth; for each of the eight hollows beginning with the pupil, it is half a finger-breadth, while the interval between them is seven [finger-breadths].
Regarding that which was stated by the venerable Śārṅgisūri as two separate measurements—

the measurement in finger-breadths (aṅgula) for the *tāra* and for the mouth-opening (*mukharandhra*) within all flutes— it is to be understood through the designations such as *ekavīrā* and so forth. 621.
In the case of Umāpati and Tripuruṣa, the measurement of the staff (daṇḍa) increases by one finger-width for each; however, the supreme characteristic is said to be like that of Ekavīra.
For Caturmukha, the measurement of the staff is increased by a quarter-yava more than the previous.
In its internal sections, however, the measurement is fifteen and a half finger-breadths;
the other [measurement] is separately as before,
being seventeen and three-quarters finger-breadths plus a quarter-yava.
The measurement of the staff (daṇḍa) for the five-faced [Liṅga] should be in finger-breadths;
however, in the intervals, the measurement is increased by one-sixteenth part, and separately, it is three barley-corns less than a quarter [of the whole].
The remaining [details] regarding the staff for the six-faced [Liṅga] are measured as before.
It is stated that there are nineteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in the intervals, excluding one-eighth part and including one and a half barley-corns (yavas);
separately, there is half a finger-breadth added with two quarters of a barley-corn. 627.
O Sage, another previously mentioned characteristic regarding the staff (*daṇḍa*) is that its measurement should consist of twenty-one *aṅgulis*,
increased by two and a half feet and combined with one-eighth of a *yava* plus a quarter.
The measurement of the interval should be one and three-quarter fingers, increased by a thirty-second part; separately, it is one finger less than a quarter.
The remaining characteristics in the eighth [digit] of the lineage should be understood as being as before. 630. Furthermore, in the eighth [digit], the lineage... [is as follows].
The measurement for the twenty-four finger-breadths [of the base] should be increased by one barley-corn less than an eighth part;
the measurement for each of the eight holes is three barley-corns plus a quarter.

In each of the intermediate spaces, the measurement is one finger-breadth minus one-eighth part plus an additional quarter-finger; another mark is as before. Thus, there would be twenty-six finger-breadths together with a quarter-yava.
The measurement for the *nātha* and *indra-daṇḍa* within the seven intermediate spaces is one finger (*aṅgula*) plus an eighth part, as before;
that [measurement] is considered to be twenty-eight and a half [fingers] together with an eighth part of a *yava*. 634–635.
The measurement of the staffs in finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) is as follows: in the intervals up to Mahānanda, they are each one and a quarter *aṅgulas* plus an additional quarter of a *yava*;
beyond that, as before, in the Rudra-staff, they are increased by a *yava*.
The measurement is thirty-one [units], plus three and a half barley-corns (637).
Each of the seven intermediate spaces shall be eight *randhra*s (nine) [units] (638),
and the remaining measurement is desired to be one and a half *aṅgula*s each, as previously stated.
The measurement of the staff (daṇḍa) at the Āditya [point] shall be thirty-four finger-breadths (aṅgula),
increased by one and a quarter barley-corns (yava) plus a thirty-second part;
separately, it is also increased by two thirty-second parts minus one-quarter of a barley-corn.
In the seven intermediate spaces, the measurement is one and three-quarter finger-breadths (pādonamaṅguladvaṃdva),
as before; however, in the Viśvamūrti [mandala], the measurement of the staff (daṇḍa) should be thirty-seven finger-breadths,
increased by two quarter-finger-breadths and one and a half barley-corns (yava).

In each of the intermediate spaces, two finger-breadths are prescribed; each subsequent space is increased by one and a quarter barley-corns. A *daṇḍa* consists of [fingers] combined with one-eighth of a barley-corn plus a quarter.
The [length] of Manu is measured by forty-four finger-breadths (aṅgula).
The two ends of the head are considered separately to be each two and a half finger-breadths,
increased by three and a sixteenth part of a barley-corn (yava).
The foremost of experts on the *karaṇas* has stated that the measurement for the seven intervening spaces is three-quarters of a finger; the remaining characteristics are as previously described.
In all the bamboo sections (*vaṃśas*), there is a hollow measured by the middle joint of the little finger.
"It should be made equal to the root [measure]," so it was stated by Soḍhala’s son. All other [measures] for lineages originating from regional treatises (*deśī-śāstra*) are the same;
here too, the three beginning with *ekavīra* are not accepted, as before. (646–647)
I previously explained the elements, the three modes of operation, the qualities following the principles,
and those instruments such as the flute and the lute upon which I played; as well as the song, the musical intervals, notes, scales, and modulations as they are understood.
All of that should be demonstrated here specifically on the flute (vaṃśa).
These three—the flute, the lute (vīṇā), and the human body—are the causes of musical notes;
among them, the flute is praised for being graceful, sweet, and resonant.
The wise know that the measure of a particular passion lies in the sound produced by the unification of the bamboo flute, the lute, and the human body—
especially for travelers on their journeys and for those who have been conquered by amorous women. 651.
One should employ soft, medium, and slow tempos for those afflicted by grief (652). One should employ the flute in the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiment with a quick and graceful sound,
using a trembling and vibrating resonance based on a fast tempo.
One should employ [these qualities] for anger and pride, as proclaimed by Mataṅga:
glossiness, density, manifestation of redness, abundance of sound, elegance, softness, and likewise the resonance of the tone. (653–654)

The twelve qualities— namely, being situated in three places, the state of a Śrāvaka, sweetness, and attentiveness— are proclaimed by the Sage Śārṅgin (Kṛṣṇa) regarding the *phūtkāra* [breath-exhalation].
Among those, eleven of the qualities of sound have their characteristics as previously described.
656. "Attentiveness in blowing, and the avoidance of deficiency or excess"—these are the twelve qualities of blowing.
[The defects are: the blowing being double, too little, thin, or faltering; these are they.
The Yamala state is described as the fault of "blowing" (phūtkāra), which is countered by "counter-blowing" (pratiphūtkṛti);
thus, because its name is descriptive of its nature, no separate definition is stated. [These states are] Kapila, Tumbakī, Kākī, Saṃdaṣṭa, and Avyavasthita. 657.
Others have further stated that there are five defects arising from hissing sounds (phūtkṛti).

That [sound] which becomes discordant and cracked due to the mouth being afflicted by phlegm is called *kapila*; it is mostly like the sound of a gourd (*tumbudhvāna*) and is thus termed *tumbakī*. 658–659.
That which is deficient in *tāra* (high pitch) and has the voice of a crow is called *kākī*;
that which appears small as if bitten is called *saṃdaṣṭa*;
and that which is either deficient or excessive and harsh is called *avyavasthita*. 660
Those qualities and defects of the throat which were previously mentioned should be applied by the wise, as appropriate, even to the *phūtkāra* (hissing sound).
Thus end the ten defects of the *phūtkāra*.
The practice of finger-stretching, being well-situated, having a beautiful luster, possessing sweetness that manifests that luster, moving with speed in the ascending and descending scales,
skill in singing and instrumental playing, and providing the proper support for singers!
"Concealing those faults, skill in the melodies that indicate the path,
and boldness in the arising of passion during the performance of the *nāda*—
the foremost of the illustrious *karaṇas* speaks of these as the virtues of the flute-player. (663–664)
Such are the qualities of the flute-player; the opposite of these qualities results from excessive false performance,
as well as the failure to reach the desired pitch and the shaking of the head.
"Such are the defects of the flute-player which should be avoided with great effort.
(665) Thus end the defects of the flute-player.
There may be one principal flute-player, and four who follow him.
"By those who know [the art], a group of flute-players is generally called *vāṃśika-vṛnda*.
Thus ends the section on the group of flute-players;
now, for the sake of easy understanding, here is an illustration by way of example alone.
I shall now describe the playing of certain regional (deśī) rāgas belonging to the Vaṃśa [flute] lineage.
When the third stationary (sthāyin) note is made to vibrate slowly, and then the second stationary note is placed upon it; 667.

When the placement (*nyāsa*) in the planet occurs by first making the fourth vowel the second, then the wise declare the first [placement] to be its own place (*svasthāna*), the third after the middle one, and then the fourth and fifth. 668–669.
Then, Śārṅgadeva has described the second *svasthāna*:
having struck the fourth note, then having uttered the next stationary (*sthāyin*) note, and having lingered upon the fifth note which follows the fourth. (670–671)
When the sixth and fifth notes are made [the first two], and the second is placed as the *graha*, then the third becomes the *svasthāna*; so say those who know this.
Then, the second, fourth, fifth, and seventh notes from the *graha* [are used].
Having made the eighth [note] linger, then the second, and after that the next;
having made the second, the seventh, the fifth, and the fourth,
and the second— this is the placement (nyāsa) in the *graha*, and the fourth is desired as its own place (*svasthāna*).
"The capture [of the notes] beginning with the Madhyama-tāna is seen as sealed within the *vaṃśas* (flutes).
Thus, in the Madhyama-tāna,
when the *ṣaḍja* is captured, having struck the *ṣaḍja* and multiplied, the *ṛṣabha* and *madhyama* are struck.

Having oscillated *pa* and having caused it to tremble slightly, and having applied *ma* twice; then, having oscillated *ma* and caused it to tremble slightly, and having produced the light *ṣaḍja*; and having caused *ri* and *ma* to vibrate two or three times, one should sing *ṣaḍja*.
In the *sthāyinī* scale of Mālavaśrī,

one should first establish the primary tonic (*ādyasvasthāna*) according to the rule for the primary tonic; having thus established the five notes, if the descending [scale] is performed slowly, the former [note] is made to reside in its own place (*svasthānaga*).
Then, by oscillating the second *svasthāna* ending in *dh* and striking the seventh,
the descent (*avarohaṇa*) of the second *svasthāna* is performed;
where that third *svasthāna* arises, it is proclaimed as such by the wise.
Having struck me and made me double, and having then struck that next one (riṃ),
and having proclaimed it, and having struck it again after pausing,
when this [scale] is made to descend from its own position by making it the third; 681.
Then, the fourth position of Mālavaśrī is declared;
another *ṣaḍja* or some other note is fixed as the *graha* (tonic) of this *mūrcchanā*. Having designated that [other note] as *ṣaḍja*, the others are then designated as *ṛṣabha* and so forth.
"The wise Śārṅgin has stated that one should apply all this as the *lakṣmā* (characteristic mark).
Thus ends Mālavaśrī;
having made Madhyama the *sthāyin* (tonic note), it itself causes the other [note] to tremble."
Having prolonged the fourth [note] and made the third [note] struck rapidly (drutāhata),
and having performed that again and uttered it with the placement of the *graha*,
the first *svasthāna* of Toḍī is thus declared by the best of sages. (685–686)
Having ascended as far as the fifth note from the original tonic position (*svasthāna*), one descends back down to the end of the tonic note; where this occurs, that is the second *svasthāna*.
Alternatively, the ascent and descent may extend to the sixth note, with the limit being the *graha* (the primary note). 687.
In its third own place and in the fourth up to the eighth limit,
it would be ascending and descending, as held by those who know it, just as before;
moreover, such a planet is declared "sealed" (mudrita) by those who understand the *lakṣya* in the *lakṣya*.
Thus, having established the middle *graha* of the *toḍī*, and having uttered the preceding *graha*,
he then causes the second, third, and fourth *grahas* to vibrate. 690.
Having shortened the third [syllable], having uttered and struck that [note],
and then having uttered the preceding vowel, when it is placed upon the *sthāyin*,
then that becomes the first *svasthāna* of the *Baṅgāla-rāga*. (691–692)
The ascending [scale] should end on the fifth note in its own position, on the second in the second [position], on the seventh in the third, and should extend up to the eighth in the fourth. 693.
In each preceding case, it should descend as before, but in its own position, it should proceed progressively upward.
"In the *lakṣya*, however, one belonging to all *vaṃśas* is considered its second *graha*;
thus says the Bāṅgāla [tradition].
Having made *dhaivata* the *sthāyin*, that [same] ancient [note] is the third."
Then, having again performed the forward [movement] and shaken the third [note],
having delayed it and struck the second [note] two or three times,
through the placement (nyāsa) upon the Grāha, the first [note] shall become the station of Bhairava.
In the second [measure], the ascent should end with the fifth; then in the third, it ends with the sixth or the seventh; and in the fourth, it extends up to the eighth.
In each subsequent measure, there should be a descent according to the previous pattern within its own position.
"The second note is seen as the stable tone (sthāyin) in all flutes.
Thus, Bhairava,
having made the stable ṣaḍja double, should then play half [of it].
One should play the first *graha*, then the second, and then the third.
When the second [note] arrives and is applied to the *sthāyin* note, then the first *svasthāna* of the *varāṭī* arises. (699–700)

In this case, as in the Bhairava [rāga], the three primary positions (svasthāna) are supreme; this very procedure regarding the primary positions should be understood to apply to other rāgas as well. Furthermore, its second note is observed in practice to function as the *graha* (the keynote). 701.
Thus, when the *ṛṣabha* note remains stationary, one should cause the preceding [note] to vibrate, take half of it, and then take the second and third notes below that sound; this is the *varāṭī*.

Then, having approached the planet and caused it to tremble, one should utter half of this [mantra] while the planet is fixed by means of the *nyāsa* of the *garjarī*; thus, the first station shall be established.
Generally, the third planet is seen within the range of observation in this [station].

Thus, in the Gurjarī rāga, with *ṣaḍja* as the primary note (*graha*), the second [note] and the third are each uttered once; then, having proceeded with speed to the fourth, one returns to the third and the one below it (the second). (705)

Having stated the third and fourth [notes], the third [note] below that is the placement (nyāsa) in the *graha* of Vāsanta; it occurs in its own place as the first, while the third is found as the *sthāyin* among its *vaṃśas*. 706
Thus, when the spring (vasanta) tāna is established on the doubled ṣaḍja, one should play its half as a short note;
then, having struck that once, [one should play] the third note from that grāha.
Having uttered the fourth and the third [notes] once each, then having made the following one swift, and having delayed the fifth, then having made the two below this light,
the placement (nyāsa) occurs in its own place at the first [measure] during the *graha*. 708.
"In the lineage of Dhannāsī, the second note (svaragraha) is seen; thus, having made that very [note] the stationary (sthāyin), one should play the second [note] rapidly.
Thus, in the case of Dhannāsī, one should play the second [note] rapidly, having established that very [note] as the stationary.

Having made the two following notes light, one should play the next note after them with a long duration (vilambita). Then, having played the fifth note twice with a tremolo (sphurita), and having uttered the three lower notes in succession, when it is placed upon the sustained note (sthāyin); ||| 710 ||

"Then its first [note] is to be performed in its own place (svasthāna), and the second is grasped by the people. Thus it is *deśī*. When *gāndhāra* is the *sthāyin*, having uttered the second and the third...
Having prolonged the fourth [syllable] and made it precede that [third], and having touched the second,
and having lengthened the third and uttered the second in the vowel of the planet— if the placement (nyāsa) occurs thus, then the first [syllable] is the "place" (deśa) of the name. (712–713)
"The seizure (graha) of this [lineage] is marked by those who know the marks; thus, having doubled the number called 'place' (deśa), one first touches the third.
714. Thus, having doubled the number known as the place, one first touches the third.

Having performed the ritual, touched [the object], and announced the planet, one should then speak of its throbbing twice or thrice; when the planet trembles, preceded by that [announcement], then the first location is declared to be that of the *Ḍombakriya*.
That Bhūpālī is heard in the world as having resorted to a second *graha*.
Thus ends the section on Ḍombakrī;
when the *dhaivata* has been brought to the state of the *sthāyī*, one should utter the next short note twice.
Then, having first placed that [hand] forward with its half facing east, and having held it steady, one should shake that half; then, striking it repeatedly, shaking its half forward,
and extending that half, one should proceed to the grasp (graha).
Then, having made the two preceding *grahas* half-projected, having pronounced the second, touched the *graha*, and having pronounced the one following it while shaking it,
one should repeatedly utter the third *graha* and the two rear *grahas*.
Then, having shaken the third [note] and lingered upon that which is below it (the second),
and having paused slightly and touched the second, when it is finally placed upon the *graha*,
then the first [note] is proclaimed as its own place in the *velāvalī*.
However, its third capture is seen within the scope of the lineage (vaṃśa).
Thus, Velāvalī,
having established the fifth note as the *graha*, then ascends by the fifth [note] through the *ārohi* [scale].
Having gone to and lingered upon that [note], one should lead it from there to the lower [note] (722).
Then, having prolonged the one situated below and touched it,
and having further prolonged the one beyond that, one should speak again by means of the descending [scale] (723).
Therefore, having arrived at the placement of the *grahas*, the first [position] shall be its own place;
in the *rāga* [section], it is the second in this *janman* of the *prathamamañjarī*.
Thus ends the *prathamamañjarī*.
Having ascended from the *sthāyin* [note] to the fourth note starting from the third,
having caused it to vibrate (*kampita*), and even having lingered (*vilambita*) while performing the sixth and fourth notes,
and then having returned to the fifth note from that point and descended down to the end of the *graha* [note].
Having gone half-way toward a planet and then having reached the first planet, one should then touch it;
having caused the second to tremble and the third to throb,
that initial point where the stationary [planet] settles shall be its own place.
In the *āḍīkāmodikā* [melodic form], there is a second *graha* (tonic) among the people;
thus, in the *sthāyin* (fixed note) *āḍīkāmodī*, when the *ṣaḍja* is doubled, one should strike the third [note] twice.
Then, having touched [the instrument] three or four times and uttered the first *graha*,
when the *sthāyin* trembles, the first *svasthāna* occurs through the placement (*nyāsa*).
In the *rāga* Śuddhavarāṭī, that [placement] occurs at the second *sthāyin* among people.

Thus, having established that same *sthāyin* (the tonic note) as the pure *varāṭī*, and having uttered it twice or thrice at its half-value, one should then cause the second [note] to vibrate and linger. 730

Having struck [the number] twice or four times from this, and having made the subsequent [number] light by pronouncing the [preceding] number, when it is then placed upon the long vowel following the half-measure of the *graha*, that is the first position of the pure *naṭṭā*. 731.
"In this *vaṃśa* as well, for the most part, a second *graha* is observed" (732).
Thus, having stated that in the *śuddhanaṭṭā* the *graha* is double and the second is half of that—
Then, when the third [note] is slow, one should bring the second to a rapid tempo (733). Having become steady at the half-measure (*grahārdha*) and having caused the measure (*graha*) to tremble,
one should thereafter make the next two notes rapid and make the following note light (734).
When the Nyāsa is performed, the first [note] shall be its own place (svasthāna) for Rāmakṛti;
we observe its graha in the second svara within its lineage.
Thus ends Rāmakṛti.
Having performed the third and second [syllables] upon that very same *graha*, one should quickly utter half of the *graha* while touching the previous *graha*;
then, having pronounced the half and paused, one touches the third [syllable] as before. (736)
Having made light the two preceding [notes] of the light [note], and then having touched the two following [notes] of the stationary [note],
when the second [note] is made light— that is, made swift— and the *graha* (the leading note) is placed there, then the first *svasthāna* occurs according to the Gauda style. (737–738)
In this [raga] as well, a second *graha* is generally seen in the *lakṣya* (practical examples). Thus says the Gauḍa school:
when *dhaivata* is the *sthāyin*, the third *graha* is the ancient *graha*.
Having made the fourth [note] and struck it, one should then cause the second to vibrate;
having descended through the sequence beginning with the third, one should designate the first position of the divine creation by means of the placement of the four notes.
"We see its third note, however, within the scope of the lineage.
Thus says Devakri;
having established *dhaivata* as the *graha*, and having descended from the third [note].
Then, having paused at the three *svaras*, one should place another *graha* and then another *graha* (742).
Having first performed that and struck it with the *grahanyāsa*, the first station of Bhairavī arises; for her, the third is the *graha* among people (743).

Thus, in the *bhairavī* [jāti], having placed the third note below the stationary *ṣaḍja* which is doubled, and having caused the lower note to tremble, one should then linger upon the stationary note. (744)
Having brought the preceding [note] to lightness and struck that grāha twice or thrice,
having made it light and touched half of the lower [note], one should delay at the fifth note from the grāha and then,
having made it quick, perform the third touch.
Then, having uttered that fifth [note] and slightly lengthened the lower lip,
by shaking it through the application of the *graha*, the first *sthāna* arises;
this is the third *graha* in the flute for the rāga known as Chāyānaṭṭa.
Those who know the technical definitions call this the *sālaganattā*.
Others, however, having made the fifth [note] the *sthāyin* and having established *ri*, shake *ma* and then stabilize it; then, on the fifth [note], they repeat *pa* and *madhyama* twice.
Having formed half of the *gamṛṣabha* and touched the other half, one should proceed again;
then, having made the two *irimas* long, if it is placed upon the *graha*, those who know it recognize that as the original position of *sālaganaṭṭā*. 750.
Having performed *maṃ*, having quickly uttered that *graha* and then the *para*, having spoken the *turya* with a pause, and then having touched the *parama* and the *pañcama* with a pause—
when he thus reaches the *graha* by descending from there, then [it is so].
The first [rāga] is Svasthāna; the second in the lineage of Rāmakṛti is Cindhamarāmakrīḥ; that is established on the path of the world. (752) Thus ends Cindhamarāmakrīḥ.
Having relied upon that very *graha*, having struck it twice or thrice,
and then having brought it to a state of slowness (*vilambita*), having lengthened the middle [note],
and having made *ri* and *ga* into a *ridala*, one should then slow down *ni* and *ma*.

Having uttered that [note] again and made it the *dhaivata*, and having played the *niṣāda* struck once, it becomes the first *svasthāna* of the Nāṭyarāmakṛti, according to those who know it— by means of the *graha* and *nyāsa*. (755)
Alternatively, having made the middle [note] the starting point and struck the fifth note twice or thrice in descent, one should quickly reach the *ṛṣabha* from the *dhā*,
and then play half of that [note], as well as the *ṣaḍja* and half of the *re*. 656–757.
Then, having pronounced *rimau* and having paused for a long duration (*vilambya*), it is applied (*nyasyate*) to the planet; that which is its first position is the opinion of Nāṭyarāmakṛt.
Thus ends [the section on] Nāṭyarāmakṛt.
Having performed the *graha* and struck [the bell] once, having produced the sound following the *graha*,
and having struck the bell twice after the *graha*,
if one then speaks the first and second [syllables] in sequence and places them upon the *graha*, then—
The first *svasthāna* is in the *mahlāra*; the second *graha* is in the *vaṃśa*. (760) Thus is the *mahlāra*:
having doubled the *graha* and made it swift (*druta*), then [placing] the lower [note]. (761)

Having oscillated that [first] and performed the second, then the third; when the *sphurita* and the two preceding *grahas* have been played upon the *graha*, that is the first *svasthāna* of the Kaṇāṭagauḍa *nyāsa*. 762.
"In the *vaṃśa* meter, the third *graha* (syllable) of this [line] is taken by those who know the characteristics [of the meter].
Thus ends the *Karṇāṭagauḍa*.
Having made that very same *graha*, and having stated the fourth and third [syllables], [the *Gauḍavaṃśa* follows].
Having stated the *sthāyin* and its corresponding *dala*, one should then state the *pūrva-sthāyin* and its *dala*.
From the placement of the *sthāyin*, the first *deśavālagauḍa-svasthāna* arises;
furthermore, in its lineage (*vaṃśa*), a second *graha* is observed.

Thus Deśavālagauḍa, having first stated [the scale] with *niṣāda* as the tonic, then [states] the subsequent [scale]; when one descends three notes from the second [note] to the fourth note in the [descending] *graha*, [it is so called]. 766.
The Nyāsa of Turuṣkagauḍa was then his first original location;
this Mālavagauḍa became his third *graha* in the world. (767) Thus ends the section on Turuṣkagauḍa.
If it is brought from the *niṣāda* to the state of *graha*, one should ascend up to the fourth [note];
then, having lingered there, one should proceed to the *graha* by descending.
In that case, for the Drāviḍa-Gauḍa style, the first [note] shall be its own place (*svasthāna*).
"In the world, this Sālagagauḍa is considered the second *graha* of this [style].
Thus, the Drāviḍagauḍa,
having adopted the fifth *graha*, as well as the third and the second.

Having released the third [note] and touched the end, and having released the third again and touched it while lingering on the second, when the *graha* (the leading note) vibrates, then the first [note] becomes the *svasthāna* (the resting place) of the *kaiśikī* [mūrcchanā]. 770–771.
"The third note of this [scale] is seen in its lineage, and the *graha* (tonic) is observed in the practical applications.
Thus, having doubled the second *sthāyin* (*ṣaḍja*) and made it swift, [one reaches] the second [note]. 772. [This is] the *Kaiśikī*.
Having spoken [the first note], having made the second and third notes rapid and [repeated] below the lower lip (773),
and having uttered that [first note] and made it rapid, one should then play the second;
having struck the third twice or thrice, when it is placed upon the *syāyin* (774).
Then, its own position was first declared by the wise for Lalitā;
in this [jāti] as well, the third *svara* is seen as the *graha* in the practical application (*lakṣya*). Thus ends Lalitā.
Having doubled the *graha* and likewise made the lower [note] the *sthāyin*, one should touch the second and fourth [notes] as the two *sthāyins* of the second [measure].
Then, when it is applied to the slow tempo (*vilambita*), the second *sthāyin* is placed.
Then, the wise have declared its first natural place (svasthāna) to be the second note in the flute; this [note] is characterized as its *graha* (tonic).
Thus ends Śrīrāga.
One should apply here [the second and subsequent notes] in relation to whichever *graha* (tonic) is perceived in the lineage (*vaṃśa*).
However, when the *grahas* and so forth are situated in the *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic),
as many notes as there may be in a particular *rāga*, for that many [notes should they be applied].

That by which a stable [melody] arises, therein the stable [melody] should take refuge for the sake of favoring the ignorant; thus have these few *rāgas* been described by me— O wise ones, behold others by this same path.
Thus ends the section on the bamboo flute (*vaṃśa*). It should be produced from bamboo, nine finger-breadths in length, and wrapped with bamboo leaves; it is played according to worldly custom. (781)
Thus is the characteristic of the *pāva*.
The *pāvikā* should indeed be made of bamboo, twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length, one finger-breadth in thickness, and provided with a hollow within its own length. (782)
Its thickness should be equal to the tip of the little finger according to worldly custom;
it should have one hole for blowing, but five for the accomplishment of the musical notes. Its various modes of playing bring about the possession by nāgas and yakṣas. (783)
Thus is the definition of the *pāvikā*:
a flute that measures more than two cubits, is provided with a mouth-opening, possesses four tone-holes, and produces a beautiful sound. (784)
Thus, the auspicious *madhukarī* flute may be made of bamboo, horn, or wood; it should have the shape of a *kāhalā* and measure twenty-eight finger-breadths in length. (785)
And its mouth-opening should be like the seed of a *tuvarī* bean;
leaving four finger-breadths from the mouth-opening, one should fashion seven holes like a bamboo flute, maintaining the proper distance between the openings.
And situated in the lower part of the center of their mouth-cavity,
for the sake of achieving a sweet sound, a copper tube four finger-breadths long and as thick as a barley grain should be inserted into that mouth-cavity.

Above that, a ring should be placed—either made of ivory or mother-of-pearl—with a hollow in its center; or else, one made of kusha grass or from *devanala* fiber, shaped like a mother-of-pearl shell or slightly opened jasmine bud. (789)
Then, having placed the *madhukarī* flute, which is soft due to being boiled in milk,
one should play it like a bamboo flute; one should close the lower hole with the tip of the left thumb— thus it was stated by the master Niḥśaṅka.
Thus is the description of the *madhukarī* [vessel]:
made of copper, silver, or gold, with a hollow interior, it is adorned with a face shaped like the flower of the thorn-apple (*dhattūra*). 792.
A *kāhalā* three cubits in length, sounding like the syllables "hā-hū" and used by people to proclaim the heroic titles (*biruda*) of warriors, is played;
such is the definition of the *kāhalā*. (793)
That which is formed with both hands is considered *tuṇḍakinī*;
it is also called *turuturī* in the world and is termed *tittirī*.
Experts in musical instruments know that the *yamala* is a pair of *tuṇḍakinyas*. 794
Thus is the definition of the *tuṇḍakinī*;
the *tuṇḍakinī* itself is the *cukkā*, which is four cubits in length.
(975) Thus is the definition of the *cukkā*.

A horn made from the smooth, glossy, and well-fashioned horn of a buffalo— its shape resembling the face of a female elephant and free from defects— or likewise the horn of a bull shaped like a *dhattūra* flower; 796.
Having placed a piece eight finger-breadths long at its base to increase the resonance,
one should cut two or three finger-breadths from its tip to create a whistling hole; then, by blowing with a "tuthukāra" sound, one should produce various tones.

"This indeed is the deep-toned musical instrument used during the cowherds' sports. (798) Thus ends the description of the horn; it should be from a flawless conch with its whorls removed, measuring eleven finger-breadths in length.
A beautiful pinnacle (śikhara) should be fashioned by those desiring the [deity’s] relics;
from its base to its tip, it should gradually decrease in height,
and at the opening of the pinnacle, there should be a hole measuring half a finger-breadth.

The wise man, having held such a gong (śaṅkha) with its interior measuring only one māṣa, should sound it with his hand like a crab, while filling his belly with deep breaths and awakening the resonance of these syllables: "Huṃ bhuṃ tho digi di. 801.
Thus is the definition of the *śaṅkha*;
as it pertains to those who have reached the path, the drum (*paṭaha*) is of two kinds.
First, the definition of the drum situated on the path is stated here: 802.
Its length should be two and a half cubits,
while its circumference is sixty finger-breadths; the middle portion should be wide, and the southern face should be made measuring eleven and a half finger-breadths.

On the right face, a ring made of iron ten and a half [finger-breadths] in measure should be fashioned; on the left, one made of creeper-wood. Taking the *pārikā* from a calf that died at six months of age, [one should fashion it].
Having wrapped a creeper-made bracelet around the left arm with that [creeper],
and having made it possess seven holes by means of very firm, fine cords, the jars should be tied loosely to those holes once they have been inserted therein. (806–807)
Those seven [rings], made of gold and other metals, should be four finger-breadths (aṅgula) in length;
leaving aside four finger-breadths on the left side,
one should firmly wrap a copper leaf, three finger-breadths in width, around the drum (paṭaha).
One should bind the two covered faces with the thick hide of the sacrificial animal, known as a *kambala*,
which has a hole made all around the mouth of the southern face. 809–810.
One should pull them firmly with cords cast through the apertures and passing through the other mouth;
then, for the sake of achieving firmness, one should properly bind those cords within the ring.
[811] By means of the seven cords inserted into the apertures situated within the cavity of the left mouth—
Having wound threads around the jars with strong iron bands,
one should insert [the substance] inside and, having drawn the bands tight, bring them to a state of firmness; then they are bound externally to the jars and at the end of the left-hand band.
This drum, known as the *kaccha*, which has the shoulder (*skanda*) as its presiding deity and originates from the excellent city of Yajñapura, is used for wrapping around the waist;
even when situated in the regional style (*deśī*), it is likewise [used], measuring one and a half cubits in length. 814.
The southern face is seven finger-breadths [in width], while the other is six and a half;
the inner skin of the belly of the animal is called the *uddalī*, and with it, his left mouth is fastened according to one's own preference. 815–816.
This distinction would exist in this case: both [types] are made from khadira wood;
this has been stated as threefold by others for the two [types]: superior, middling, and inferior.
The superior one should have the prescribed measurement, while the other is reduced by a twelfth part.
The middle [measure] diminished by one-sixth becomes the lowest.
Now, the initial letters of the classes, excluding *ṅ*, as well as the *ka*-class, the *ṭa*- and *ta*-classes, and also *ra* and *ha*—
Thus, there are sixteen phonemes known as *pāṭas* for both [the vowels and consonants].
Through conjunction and separation, through sequential and reverse order, and through being accompanied by vowels or not, these *pāṭas* may be of many kinds.
The sound *jheṃ* occurs at the tip, while the sound *deṃ* is predominant in the mouth;
people call this the *deśī-ḍamaru*, and it is known as the *aḍḍāvajra*.
