It measures eighteen finger-breadths, with its tip slightly curved and its middle broad.
A corner should be made at the base, encircled with garments of passion (madana).
Seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana) within the assembly upon his two thighs,
he should skillfully play the *mārgapaṭaha* drum during the arising of the musical notes.
In drama, however, this half-faced drum is played like a jar-drum; the wise know its playing to be done with either a hand-stick or the hand itself.
(824) Thus ends the description of the *paṭaha*.

Those *pāṭas* which have been described for the *paṭaha* [drum], through their various combinations, the resulting varieties of *pāṭas* produced by the hands are proclaimed as *hastapāṭas*. They are infinite and cannot be known individually by people.
To illustrate these, I shall set forth a few examples:
from Sadyojāta comes the Nāgabandha; from Vāmadeva, the Svastika;
from Aghora, the Alagna; and from the one named Tatpuruṣa, Śuddhi. (826–827)
From the five faces of the Lord of Pārvatī, there arose five [beings] known as the Samaskhalitas, beginning with Īśānavaktra;
therefore, these are considered the most principal among all the recensions (pāṭas).
In sequence, those deities are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śarva (Śiva), Ravi (the Sun), and Indu (the Moon); then the Nāgabandha and Pavana, each designated as a single lake (sara).
Following that are the disturbances arising from the difficult movement within the Nāgabandha.

Now, there are seven [types] born of the Svastika: the Svastika, the Baliko-hala, the Phulla-pūrva-vikṣepa, that which begins with Kuṇḍalī, the Saṃcāra-vilikhi, the Khaṇḍanāga-bandha, and the Pūraka. 831.

There are seven varieties; thus these seven are proclaimed for the *alagna* [type]. (832) *Alagnotsāra*, *viśrāmā*, *viṣamādyā*, *khalī*, *sarī*, *sphurī*, and *sphuraṇaka*: in the pure [type], the first would be purity (*śuddhi*). (833)
From that [cluster], there are the *svarasphuraṇa*, *koccha*, *llava*, *latā*, and *vighaṭā*;
then the *takāra* and the *māṇikyavallī*—these are recognized as the seven varieties.
(834) The first variety of the *samaskhalita* is known by the name *samaskhalita*.
Vikaṭa, Sadṛśa, Pāṭakhali, Cāḍukhalī, Anucchalla, and likewise Khutta— these are the seven varieties. Thus,
these thirty-five types of hand-strikes (hastapāṭas) and palm-strikes (talapāṭas) have been proclaimed.

Struck on the corner and agitated— these are the four types of hand-beats (hastapāṭa), namely *viṣama*, *ardhasama*, and so forth, as spoken by Nandikeśvara. Likewise, there are *utphulla*, *khalaka*, and *pāṇyantaranikuṇṭaka*.
Daṇḍahasta, Piṇḍahasta, Yugahasta, Ardhahastaka (the two), Sthūlahasta, Ardhardhapāṇi, Pārśvapāṇi, and Ardhapāṇi;
then Kartarī, Samakartarī, and Viṣamakartarī. (838–839)
The *samapāṇi*, *viṣamapāṇi*, *pāṇihastaka*, *nāgabandha*, *avaghaṭa*, *svastika*, and *samagraha*—
these are the twenty-one hand-movements (*hastapāṭas*) used for the *paṭaha* drum and other instruments. (840)
Ullola, pāṇyantara, nirghoṣa, khaṇḍakartarī,
daṇḍahasta, samanakha, bindu, yamalahastaka,
recita, bhramara, vidyudvilāsa, and also ardhakartarī. (841)
Then follows the *alagnaka* (unattached), then the *repha* (the letter 'r'), and after that the *samapāṇi* (even-handed).
These sixteen [varieties] are used in percussion instruments such as the *paṭaha*;
experts in instrumental music generally employ these in the *huḍukkā*.
There are eight types of uneven *pāṭa* (rhythmic beats); I shall now describe those known as *apāṭas*:
*talaprahāra*, *prahara*, *valita*, *guruguñjita*, *ardhasañca*, *trisañca*, *viṣama*, and *abhyasta*. (844–845)
The two *alaga-pāṭas* are known as *sañcavichurita* and *bhramara*, while the *kuñcita* and [the other] are considered both to be *citra-pāṭas*.
These eighty-eight hand-beats (*hasta-pāṭas*) have been proclaimed by Niḥśaṅka.
I shall explain the nature of the *pāṭas* arising from the mouth of Śiva;
the wise man should recognize their originating hands according to worldly convention:
by joining the little finger and the thumb, while extending the remaining fingers. (848)
The hand-play struck with a plectrum (*koṇāhata*), as taught by Śārṅgadeva:
*khuṃkhuṃdhari khuṃkhuṃdhari karagiḍa karagiḍa*. Thus ends the section on the plectrum-struck [style]. 1.849.
Striking with the tips of all the fingers and the turning of all the fingers—he who accomplishes this is here said to be "confused" (*saṃbhrānta*), as in:
*daragiḍa daragiḍa girigiḍada dāṇakiṭa maṭaṭaku*. 850.
Thus he was bewildered; there was trembling of the wrist, then the shaking of the banner-like hand, and then a tremor of the feet, which produced a state as unstable as poison. 851

*dahreṃ dahreṃ khuṃkhuṃ dahreṃ khuṃkhuṃ dahreṃ tataki tataki*—this is the *viṣama* (irregular) [meter]. 3. Due to the reversal of the characteristics previously mentioned, there occurs the *ardhasama* (half-regular), as follows: 852.
"Dada-gida gigiri-kiṭadagi thaoṃ thaoṃ gidathaoṃgida"—
this is an *ardhasama* [vṛtta], verse 4.
"The blossoming [of the face] arises from the striking of the lotus-like palm with the claws," verse 853.
When, with the thumb extended, the *śukatuṇḍa* is struck by the fingers held apart while saying "katheṃ katheṃ," then the *khalaka* instrument is played in sequence. 854.

"Dāṃgiḍa giḍadagidā" is indeed the *khalaka*. Furthermore, by striking the index finger with the thumb of the right hand, and by striking [the fingers] of the left hand in both sequential and reverse order, it is like the sound of the letter *ra*.
That which is called the *pāṇyantaranikuṭṭaka* by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow is thus produced:
*da-giḍa-dām*, *kha-ri-kka-dām*, *kha-ri-kka*, *kha-ri-kka-daṃ-dām*, *kha-ri-kha-ri-dām*, *gi-ḍa-dām*.
Thus ends the *pāṇyantaranikuṭṭaka*. 3.
Having performed one *ūrdhvaghāta* with the *patāka* hand, and then two *ūrdhvaghātas* made from the *repha* [hand], that becomes the *daṇḍahasta*;
as in "dātarikiṭa dāṃ kharikharidāṃ," this is the *daṇḍahasta*. 856. 4.
Successively, from the *repha* [sound] and the two half-hands (*ardhahasta*), the "hand of the mass" (*piṇḍahasta*) is produced;
with "tharikaṭajheṃ tharikaṭajheṃ," it is the hand of the mass (5).
If, with the two hands consisting of the *repha*, there are two separate upward strikes (857).
When it is performed for the purpose of splitting open [the enemy's body], it becomes the *yugahasta*;
*dreṃdreṃ dāṃdāṃ* is the *yugahasta*. 6.
The *ūrdhvahasta* [is formed] by striking forcefully with the palm of the right hand. 858.

When one strikes the pair of cymbal-skins with the palms of the hands after performing two upward blows while the hands are raised, with the sound "daragiḍa dāṃdāṃ," that is declared to be the *sthūlahasta* (thick-hand) stroke. 859.

*Khuṃkhuṃdakhuṃkhuṃda* refers to the *sthūlahasta* (thick-hand) gesture. 8. By striking with the two half-hands (*ardhārdhapāṇi*), the *khudāṃ khudāṃ* sound is produced; this is the *ardhārdhapāṇi* gesture. 9.
Striking with the tips of the fingernails is described as *pārśvapāṇi*. 860.
*Tharagiḍa*, *dāgiḍa*, *dagiḍa*, *dagiḍa*—this is *pārśvapāṇi*. 10.
*Ardhapāṇi* occurs from striking with the tip of a single hand.

*dagiḍa dagiḍa daragiḍa daragiḍa*—this is the half-hand gesture (ardhapāṇi). 11. From the washing of the fingers of the left hand, the *kartarī* [gesture] is considered [to be formed]. 861. *ṭiri ṭiri ṭiri kiṭathaoṃ digidāṃ tiri ṭiri kiṭajheṃjhe taki-*
*Kiṭa* is the *kartarī*;
with two *kartarīs* together there is a blow; with both hands it is the *samakartarī*:
*jhiṃnakiṭa*, *kanakiṭa*, *kiṭajheṃthaoṃ*, *digida*, *tiriṭi*, *tiriṭiki*—this is the *samakartarī*. 13.
From striking [the fingers] in sequence with both hands, the *viṣamakartarī* (uneven scissors) arises.
"Ṭiri ṭiri thaoṃ digida ṭiri ṭiri kida"—thus is the *viṣamakartarī*.
When the thumbs and fingers of both hands are joined together...
One should press the two hollows of the hands together; at that time, it becomes the *samapāṇi* (even-handed) gesture.
"Dāṃ giḍa giḍa dāṃdāṃ"—this is the *samapāṇi*.
When the two hands are engaged in reverse order with the thumbs and fingers respectively, it is [the *vyatyastapāṇi*].
That which has uneven fingers is called *viṣamapāṇi* by the beloved of Śaṅkara (864);
its sound is "dāṃ-dāṃ giḍa giḍa dāṃ-dāṃ," thus it is *viṣamapāṇi*.
However, when the fingers of the *samapāṇi* are spread apart, it is the *pāṇihastaka* (835).

"Taragiḍa daragiḍa" is the *pāṇihastaka* (hand-clasp) [17]. The *nāgabandha* (serpent-bind) is formed by striking with the hands from the opposite direction; this occurs either on each individual side or on both sides of the hollows (*puṭa*) by striking with both hands. [866]
Thus is the "Nāgabandha" (18).
Having struck with the palm, one should strike with the thumb and fingers in succession;
if each hand forms a single hollowed cup (*puṭa*), then it becomes the *avaghaṭa* (867).
*Tatagiḍa giḍa dagiṭana ginaginanagi*—thus is the *avaghaṭa* (19).
One should strike a single *puṭa*; with the hands in the *svastika* position, [the phrase] *takiṭa takiṭataki* constitutes the *svastika* (20).
By striking with both palms together in a hollowed gesture (*puṭa*), there is the *samagraha* [rhythm]. Some here say that the *tala* [rhythm] is [performed] excluding the thumbs and fingers;
"takiṭa kiṭataka" is the *samagraha*. 869, 21.
Thus there are twenty-one hand-movements.
When the practitioner’s right hand is restless with the thumb drawn back, and the left hand is panting and tossing the arm upward, they call that the *ullola* (the surging) gesture. 870.
Others here say that the right hand, with the thumb and middle finger [joined], should be placed in the center of the cavity;
others [say] one should strike with the right thumb within the cavity.
If the right hand, without the thumb, should repeatedly flash forth within the cavity—
One should press the left palm; then it becomes the *pāṇyantara* [mudrā].
Some wise ones declare that the movement of the separated fingers and the striking of the thumb with half-and-half force produces the *pāṇyantara*. 872–873.

Others say that *pāṇyantara* is characterized by the separation of the fingers starting with the thumb; from that, *hastāntara* is characterized by the fingers being further separated and so forth. 874.
*Nakheṃ nakheṃ nakheṃ kheṃkheṃkheṃ nakheṃ nakheṃ nakheṃ kheṃkheṃkheṃkheṃ dakhuṃ khuṃda khuṃda*—thus is *pāṇyantara*. 1.

With a resounding *koṇa* strike, he spoke fearlessly with the sound *nirghoṣaṃ niḥśaṅkaḥ samabhāṣata*. Then, following that sound of *nakhakhi tha oṃ tha oṃ digidā*, [he struck] with his right hand, whose fingers were spread apart.
The *khaṇḍakartarī* [mudrā] is formed by striking with the thumb and pressing with the left hand. 876.
*Dāṃ khukhudāṃ2 khukhuga thaoṃṭajheṃdeṃ jheṃdaoṃ githaoṃṭe*. Thus is the *khaṇḍakartarī* (4).
By pressing with the tips of the fingers and rubbing with the thumb, or by pressing with the left hand, the *daṇḍahasta* [mudrā] is produced;
it sounds "khukhuṇaṃ khukhuṇaṃ jheṃdrajheṃdra ṭiriṭiri," thus is the *daṇḍahasta*. 877. 5.

Where the evenness of the syllables (*pāṭa*) and the vowels (*varṇa*) is observed, except for the fingers and the nails (*aṅgulī-nakha*), that they call the *pāṭa* known as "with-nails" (*samanakha*).
*Raha raha tarakiṭa kikiṭa takidhaki ṭeṃheṃṭaheṃtraḥ*—this is the *samanakha*. 6.
By pressing the hollow with the left hand and striking it with the index finger, a drop is produced; thus it was stated by the son of Soḍhala:
"deṃdigi deṃdigi girigiḍa 2."
Thus is the *bindu* (7). If one presses the left nostril with the left hand and sounds [the breath] while squeezing it with the right hand, that is the *yamalahastaka* (880).

*Kuṃda kuṃda jheṃdra jheṃdra jheṃheṃ jheṃheṃ*— thus with joined hands (8). Raising the instrument high, vibrating the shoulder, and striking with the thumb and forefinger— they perform the *pāṭa* known as *recita* (881).
"Dendeṃ thāṃ thaoṃ deṃdeṃ nakhajheṃ3 nahanajheṃ" is the *recita* (9).
The *bhramara* hand-gesture (*hastapāṭa*) occurs from striking with all the fingers (882).
Khe-khe-ṇaṃ, khukhu-ṇaṃ, khu-ṇaṃ, jheṃ-dra-ra, ṇaha kareṃ jheṃ; thus is the *bhramara*. 10.
From the striking of the thumb and forefinger, with the hands folded half by half, it is called *vidyudvilāsa*, or else *vidyudvilasita*. (883) Taṇe3.
*Tira jha oṃ jha oṃ driḥ trāṃ*— this is *Vidyudvilāsa*.
(11) If the index, middle, and ring fingers strike while being held apart, [it is so].
Then Śrī-Śrīkaraṇanātha spoke this half-kartarī:
"dokhuṃkhuṃ3 greha gheṭa3."
When the nails are pressed together and the fingers are slightly bent, it is the *itthalagna* (13).
When the thumb is placed at the shoulder and all the fingers are extended, it is the *repha* (885).
*Hanathaoṃ jheṃjheṃ draṃ2 jheṃdra jheṃheṃdra*— thus is the *repha*.
(14) [This is produced] by striking with both hands evenly, without rest, and with fingers not too widely separated.
Nanagi2 degi thaoṃ ginaha2 jheṃ; thus, with both hands equalized (samapāṇiḥ). 15.
The *hastapāṭa* (hand-beating) is reversed by striking with both pairs of hollowed hands (*puṭa*).
Jheṃ thaoṃ4 giṇanā3.
Thus ends the sixteenth [section]: the sixteen common *hauḍukkha* hand-beats. The cause for striking with the palm is the shifting of the left shoulder.
Pressing with the left hand into the middle of the left nostril:
*deṃ thaoṃ dreṃ dhikiṭa kiṭa jheṃdhitiri2 trā*—this is the palm-strike (talaprahāra). 1.
The blow with the palm and thumb is designated as "prahara" by the wise;
the mantra for this blow is *jhedāṃ thaoṃ gidigida2 kiṭa dhaoṃ dhaoṃ*. This is the second blow.

When the drum or similar instrument has its head facing upward and is struck while holding it with the index finger and thumb, those skilled in the art know that produced sound as *apāṭa-valita*. (888) *khuṃkhudari*.
By turning [the hands] repeatedly with the sound "dāṃ thaoṃgi thaoṃgi" three times,
and by the rolling of the thumb and ring finger in the right nostril along with exhalation from the left hand, a deep *guñjita* resonance arises. 889.
*Thukara* (phlegm),
*thaoṃra* (the four directions), *giḍidā* (the eight directions), *dhiki thaoṃṭeṃ* (the ten directions)— thus is the resonance of the Guru. (4)
Trembling of the left foot, likewise movement of the hips,
exhaling, and the half-closed palm gesture—
kheṃ kheṃ dari2.
"Kheṃ kheṃṭaḥ 2"—this is the half-movement (ardhasañca).
Due to the movement of the triad, the friction of the left thumb, and the shifting of the shoulder, that which is produced is called the triple-movement (trisañca). 891.
*Kheṃda kheṃ kheṃ dakheṃda*—this is the *trisacca* (threefold measure).
That which arises from an irregularity of the hands is considered "uneven" (*viṣama*) by the wise.
Kheṃdaṃdhari 2 thaoṃ digidharikheṃ 4 kharakaṭa 2
Thus ends the *viṣama* (irregular) [meter].
Now, the *apāṭa* is designated as *abhyasta* (repeated) due to the turning of the hands; [it consists of] *khaṇagiṇa* and *khaṅgi*. 892.
2. *khaṇagiṇakhaṅgi*.
*takidhikitta* is practiced repeatedly; these are the eight hand-beats known as *apāṭas*.
They describe the *sañca* as that which arises from striking with the tips of half the fingers, as follows:
"Thukara giṇaṇaṃ" (spitting and swallowing)—
this is the truth. 1.
By means of the pure *karasañca* and the successive striking of the thumb, the *alagapāṭa* arises, which is adorned with the name *jheṃdra*. 893.
jheṃdra 2.
"Jheṅgiri, giḍidā, nagiri, giḍanam"—thus it is interspersed;
twice thus is the *alagapāṭa* (the two-fold sequence).
The palm-strike (*talaprahāra*) is differentiated by the twist (*valitabhedita*), like a bee (*bhramara*).
Daṃ, thaṃ, dreṃ, jheṃdra (four times), khuṃkhuṃdhari, dathaoṃgiṃ—thus is the *bhramara* [mudrā];
it is described as being contracted like the clapping of hands from the *saṃkara* [position]. (894)
Khuṃ-khuṃ-dhari, dharigigiḍa, datheṃ.
Khuṃ-khuṃ! Datheṃ-datheṃ!
Girigiḍida-girigiḍida! Dattha-oṃgi thaoṃgi!
Thus ends "Kuñcita" (2).
These two constitute the pair of "Citrapāṭas" for the *paṭaha* drum; now I shall describe the five "sañcas" for the *huḍukkā*.
The trembling of the shoulders, elbows, and the thumbs and wrists of both hands, as well as the trembling of the left foot, is called *sañca*;
it is the most excellent among the movements of the drummer (*pāṭahika*), consisting of the thumbs and wrists.
A drum-beater who moves [the hand] from the shoulder and the elbow is low;
a superior *hauḍukkika* moves [the hand] from the thumb, the elbow, and the shoulder.
A middling one, however, uses movements arising from the wrist and the elbow. (897)
"By the movement of the left foot, it becomes the lowest [type] of *vādana*.
(898) Thus ends the definition of the five movements (*pañcasañcala*).
There are various types of instrumental music (*vādya*) for drums (*paṭaha*) and other instruments, consisting of different arrangements of strokes (*pāṭavinyāsa*). (899)
Vollāvaṇī, Callāvaṇyuḍu, Kucumbiṇī,
Cāruśravaṇikā, Alagnapariśravaṇikā, followed by Samaprahāra, Kuḍupavāraṇā, and Karavāraṇā. 900.
Daṇḍahasta, Ghanarava, and Tāni—these are the twelve [types];
Valli and Vallipāṭa are varieties of Ghattā; Jhaḍappaṇī, Anuśravaṇikā, Hasta, Joḍaṇī, and Triguṇā follow thereafter. 901–902.
The *pañcahasta*, the *pañcapāṇi*, the *vādya*, the *pañcakartarī*, and then the *candrakalā*—these they call the thirteen musical instruments (*vādya*).
Generally, these are seen within the scope of the *huḍukka* drum and other instruments. 903.
This [performance] of both types of musical instruments shall consist of twenty-five [beats].
At the beginning, middle, and end, it should abound with the syllable *deṃ*;
the first section and the second are played separately in that same manner.
That which is called *vollāvaṇī* by those learned in the science of percussion instruments [is performed] on the *paṭaha* drum (905).
Its two sections (*khaṇḍa*) should be joined with other instrumental interludes (*vādya-antara*) (906). Here, in the case of the *huḍukkā* drum, the sound *jheṃkṛti* occurs in place of *deṃkṛti*.
In the *ḍakkā* and the *mardala*, there should be *thaoṃ*; in the *trivallī*, however, it should be *daoṃ*.
In the *karaṭā*, it is indeed *ṭe*; such is the application of the principal syllables. By this same method, the wise should infer [the rules] for other instruments as well. (907–908)
Where it is performed in the Vollāvaṇī maṇḍala, they called this [performance] Callāvaṇī;
thus it is known as Callāvaṇī.
With the left hand [held] palm-down and the right hand moved with a slight bend, there arises the *uḍuva* [mudrā] from its sounding;
thus is the *uḍuva*.
When the mouth is covered by the upper lip and struck with the hands in the form of a *svastika*, the instrument produces a sound abounding in the syllable "khuk"; they call this the *kucumbiṇī*.
Thus ends [the description of] the *kucumbiṇī*.
When filled with abundant *pāṭas* performed by both hands either successively or simultaneously, it becomes the beautiful *cāruśravaṇikā*.
That [type] is of two kinds: pure (*śuddhā*) and variegated (*citreti*), according to whether the *pāṭas* are performed successively, being either pure or variegated. 911.
Thus ends the *Cāruśravaṇikā*;
[the section on] the *Alagna* [melody], which occurs through the striking of the corner [of the hand] without contact with the *kuṇḍalī*. 912.
Thus ends the *Alagna*.
Where the hands are level with the blade and the vessel is shaped like a *avaghaṭa* in succession,
that is called a *pariśravaṇikā* by the venerable Yajñapura Sūri.
(913) Thus ends the section on the *pariśravaṇikā*.
A "simultaneous blow" (*samaprahāra*) is a strike delivered by both hands acting together; thus,
a *samaprahāra* refers to the musical instrument called *kuḍupodbhavapāṭa*, which is a shield made of leather (*kuḍupavāraṇā*).

It is said that the stick is called *vādana*, *koṇa*, or even *kuḍupa*. (914) Thus, the warding off by the *kuḍupa* has been explained; however, the warding off by the hand occurs solely through the recitation of mantras (*japa*) performed with the hands. (915)
Thus, when each individual [hand] from the pair of hands— specifically the soft right hand— is joined with such palms, one is designated as "staff-handed" (daṇḍahasta). 916
Thus, when one with staff in hand produces continuous gaps with the palm or both hands, resulting in a continuous, dense sound, that is called *ghanarava*. (917)
Thus, from the movement of the shoulder, the wrist, and the forearm with great vigor, three kinds of resonance arise for the *vallī* drum and others. 918

Thus, whether it be half or two halves of a *valli*, if there is no application of its own respective *pāṭas* (readings), or if there is an application [of others], then it would be a *vallipāṭa*. 919.
Thus, one should play the first half of the *vallipāṭa* as it was composed, beginning with the sound "jheṃ" according to the ancient tradition;
then, one should play the second half with one's own intellect using both hands. 920

If the first [part] is composed with instrumental music and then the *dhattā* is applied again, it is called *dhattā*. Another [type], arising as a subsidiary (*upāṅga*), is produced by means of a single *yoni*. 921.

*Pāṭa* refers to the mutual joining of limbs; through these combined *pāṭas*, which serve to fill out the meter and arise from various musical instruments, there is a threefold division according to the three tempos (*laya*).
Thus is the classification.
In which, at the beginning, in the middle, or otherwise, various musical instruments are played in manifold ways; they called that *jhaḍappaṇī*.
(923) Thus ends the *jhaḍappaṇī*.
If a syllable of a verse is heard again and again, one says, "It is an *anuśravaṇikā*," and then [the follower of Śaṅkara] speaks. (924) Thus ends the section on *anuśravaṇikā*.

There are two, four, eight, or sixteen segments beginning with the syllable *deṃ*; that hand [gesture] is of four types, according to the application of square, triangular, mixed, and *tāla* segments. 925.

Thus, when *pāṭas* (articulated syllables) joined with uninterrupted *tālas* are applied— whether in regular or reverse order— according to the divisions of a *hasta* (one hundred and twenty-eight beats) or half thereof, and so on, that is then called *joḍaṇī*. 926.
Thus, there are three *joḍaṇī* sections; where each one is played in a triple manner, it is called *triguṇā*, and that [performance] is of three kinds. 927
Because of the threefold nature of the beginning, middle, and end sections, that [practice] is again twofold;
one should illustrate its threefold nature through both sequential and reverse order.
Having employed the three sections, one should employ the first two.
Therefore, it is declared that "the first" refers to the first section (*khaṇḍa*) concerning the three qualities (*traiguṇya*).
(929) Thus, the three qualities [are present] in the middle; however, the three qualities become twofold.
Because of this twofold nature of the three qualities in the middle section, it is so described. (930)
Then, having applied the first two sections and then the middle one— thus [forming three sections]— or else,
after playing the final two sections, the middle section (dala) should be employed.
Then, in the final *triguṇā*, one should play the first three sections;
thereafter, one should likewise play the last two sections or the very last section.
Thus Bhavavallabha has described the eightfold *triguṇā*. 932–933.
Alternatively, having employed three petals in some *tāla* such as the square (*caturasra*) and so forth, one should then construct two petals according to the measure of one segment,
continuing until those three petals become tripled.
This [Tāla] consists of petals joined in squares, triangles, and their mixtures, respectively;
however, other wise men have declared it to be threefold when composed of sections (khaṇḍas) in one-kalā, two-kalā, and four-kalā Tālas, respectively. 935–936.
In *caccatpuṭa* there is one [unit], and two units in *ācapuṭa*; thereafter, in *miśra*, there are three units, which others call "threefold" (triguṇā).
In this [meter], there should be one unit consisting of four feet, and then another foot.

"It is measured by eight parts," so it was said by the sage Śārṅgin (Viṣṇu). Thus, [the measurement] is threefold; five cubits [are formed] by the hand-beats (hastapāṭas) designated by the term "cubit" (hasta).
Thus, with five hands and five arms, it is characterized by *pāṭa* strokes designated by terms containing the word "pāṇi.
Thus ends [the section on] *pañcapāṇi*.
By means of the rhythmic patterns (pāṭas) designated by the term *kartarī*, there arises the *pañcakartarī* (940).
Thus ends the *pañcakartarī*.
Furthermore, the morae (mātrās) increase and decrease like the digits of the moon.
The *tāla* called *candrakalā* should then be the *candrakalā*;
others say this *candrakalā* consists of thirty-two *mātrās*.
They know that there are sixteen *kalās* of two *mātrās* each, characterized by increase and decrease.
"Such is that sixty-four-fold art (kalā) which they call [the path] on the southern way.
Thus, the *candrakalās* should be composed here according to the *udgrāha* and other structural divisions, like a musical composition (*gītaprabandha*).
I shall now describe the compositions for instrumental music (*vādyaprabandha*), their definitions and divisions:
*yati*, *rotā*, *gajara*, *rigoṇī*, *kavita*, *pada*, *melāpaka*, *upaśama*, *udgrāha*, and *prakaraṇa*. (943–944)
Avatsaka, chaṇḍaṇa, tuḍuka, malapa, then malapāṅga, malapapāṭa, cheda, and then rūpaka;
antara, antarapāṭa, khoja, and then khaṇḍayati. 945.
*Khaṇḍaccheda*, *avayati*, *khaṇḍapāṭa*, and *khaṇḍaka* (946);
*khaṇḍahulla*, *sama*, *pāṭa*, *dhruvaka*, *aṅga*, and *aṅgarūpaka*;
*tāla*, *vitāla*, *khalaka*, *samudāya*, and *joḍaṇī* (947).
Udavastala, pāṭa, coṭṭavaṇī, tuṇḍaka,
aṅgapāṭa, and paisāra— these forty-three compositions based on instrumental music have been described by the eminent master Śrīkaraṇa. 948.

Likewise, "cool water," "pride in bathing," and other such "determinations of pride" (garvanirṇaya) are merely born of poetic fancy (utprekṣā), devoid of defining characteristics, and thus neglected by us;
for generally, the sound "deṅkāra" is placed at the end of musical compositions. 949–950.
Composed of two distinct syllables, it is exceedingly delicate;

consisting of identical characters, it is radiant, manifesting rhythmic meters (*tāla*) and prosodic feet (*chandas*); and this musical section (*vādyakhaṇḍa*), which is repeatedly played with many pauses, [is the *mukhacapalaka*]. (951)
When experts play that *yati* and *jakkā* on instruments such as the *maṇṭha* and *sālaga*,
and when those who know it play them as an introductory member (*aṅga*) of some musical composition (*vādya-prabandha*), they then call it *uṭavaṇa*. (952–953)
*gaḍda-gatha-oṃ gakkaya-oṃṭeṃ gaḍda-gatha-oṃ gakkatha-oṃṭeṃ gaḍda-gatha-oṃ gakkatha-oṃṭeṃ |* Some wise scholars do not accept the arrangement of *pāṭas* here.
(954) Thus ends the pause (*yati*).
Then follows a double *udgrāha*, after which there is a *khaṇḍa* in which the sound *bhu-ri-deṃ-kṛ-ti* occurs twice; this is slightly longer than the second and third sections,
being composed of pure *kūṭa-khaṇḍas* interspersed with *pāṭas*.
Then, it should be fashioned again from individual and combined [syllables] as something possessing form; that should be employed once, consisting of both consonants and vowels,
long and short, and composed of the original pure [sounds] and so forth.
Some say that *otā* ends with *chaṇḍaṇā*;
this [rhythm] occurs in a pair of single *kalās*, and the *chaṇḍaṇa* would be devoid of essence (*niḥsāra*).
Here the sound should be elevated (*uddhata*), and the tempo (*māna*) is generally slow (*vilambita*). 957–958.
Some call this dance *dīpta*, others call it *kedāra*; some refer to it as *āvahanī*, while others have sung of it differently.
It is composed with abundant *daṃkāra* syllables in the *pāṭa* style and with all types of *tālas*.
The wise call that [mantra] the *āhavanī* in which there is a manifold arrangement;
if it begins with the syllable *deṃ*, it is then called *deṃkārādi*.
For example: *taddhiṭa katthaoṃkaṭa naganathaoṃgakuthaoṃgadā*.
Fie upon you!
O you who have abandoned the practice of dharma!
Fie, fie! You have shattered the vessel of virtue!
Thus, the *udgrāha* (the introductory section) should be performed twice.

*Taḍdagade ginadeṅgak tu thaṃ haṃ deṅgak deṅganatha ganatadigi nattattekkaṭadeṅgadeṅginatakkaṭa khukhughaṃghaṃ deṅgak*. Thus, the *deṅkāra-khaṇḍa* (the section consisting of the syllable *deṅ*) is twice.

On the second occasion, however, it is stated further as follows: *gaḍpak deṃgak gaḍaḍdak deṃgak*. Then: *tadeṃgaḍadakṭeṃ thaoṃkadathaoṃgak taṭe kaṭadakaṭ dare haoṃkathore-heṭaitakkeṃ dhikathaoṃṭaiṃ thaoṃ ṭaiṃ thaoṃ ṭaiṃ*; this is the arrangement of the recitation beginning with the pure [syllables] in the third section. Thereafter, again, the ancient *deṃkāra* section once. Then: *gaḍdak dagnina-*...
Dhikādhika, takadeṅgi, kathana, hakadaka, daḍak, daragaḍa, dhirigiḍa,
dharagaḍdak; daragaradaga, dhiragaḍadaga, takadhiṃgathaoṃgaṭe, dhikathaoṃ.
Gaṭai thika thoḍiṃ khuṃ khutatak thoragaḍa2 tak thoragaḍatak thotak thotak thoragaḍa thoragaḍa tak dhikathaoṃgaṭeṃ. Thus ends the section consisting of the *varṇasaras*.
The *khaṇḍa* (section). Thenceforth, it is ancient, composed of pure [syllables] and so forth, and very brief. Up to this point, it is in the *caccatpuṭa* meter.
Gaḍdag ṭeṃdrag thohaṭeṃ hete dahaṃ tho2.
Then: *dhidhi thaoṃ thaoṃ raghaṭe ṭaiṃ thaoṃ tathaoṃ takathaoṃ dhikathaoṃṭeṃ*. This is the *niḥsāra* *chaṇḍaṇa*. Others say that in place of *ṭeṃ*, there is *ṭeṃkāra*.

Having performed the *udgrāha* once, neither too long nor too short, maintaining a deep resonance like the sound of a drum, it is practiced three times in sections, either bound by *kūṭas* or by a series of syllables (*varṇasara*). 962.
Having repeatedly established tranquility, that which one takes delight in is *chaṇḍaṇa*. This *gajara* should be performed at the beginning again and again;
its *uṭṭavaṇa* occurs in the *ekatālī* rhythm, or alternatively, in the *niḥsāraka*.
There may be a cessation elsewhere, but his *tāla* is not restricted;
all the limbs of the elephant are played upon continuously.
965 Just as—so here, so here, *dhiyoṃ*.

*Haṭe* | *Thaoṃhadaga thohaṭa* | This is the *udgrāha*, performed repeatedly in a single rhythm (*ekatālī*) with the *tha-oṃ-ṭeṃ* beat, the *daṃ-daga* beat, and the *tha-oṃ-ga-ṭeṃ geṃ dhikataka* beat. It is stated by way of the *pratigrāha*: "This indeed has been composed in a single rhythm.
*Gaḍdagata deṃgaganagdihik* | *Kathaoṃgatakadhika thaoṃgaṭeṃheṃ thodagak* | *Giḍdakthaoṃgakkathaoṃ3* | 3.
*deṃthaoṃhaṭagathaoṃ 3 deṃ*. This is the section [ending] with the *ekatalī* stroke, repeated three times. This section alone is also called the *gajara*. *gaḍdakthaoṃgakthaoṃ*.
*gakkathoharaghaṭa thare*—thus, in the *ekatālī* measure, there is repeated *upaśama*. *thohaṭeṃ*—this is the *cchaṇḍaṇa*. All of this is played without interruption; thus is the *gajara*.
Each [measure] is joined with an *anta-yoga* consisting of *upaśama* applied twice, and is composed of three sections (*khaṇḍa*) formed by pure (*śuddha*) and composite (*kūṭa*) segments.

That cow of speech (*vāg-goṇī*), whose end is the *chaṇḍanā* meter, possesses a supreme resonance; she is bound by syllables (*varṇa*)—whether arranged individually or in combination—or by the flow of phonemes (*sara*), and is filled with the thick, mingling clamor of the Proponent of Non-absolutism (*syādvāda*). 966–967.
In this [context], the *uṭṭavaṇa* (elaboration) should be performed optionally at the beginning;
it occurs in the *dīpta-nṛtta* (vigorous dance), while this [other] is considered *upaśama-lalitā* (serene and graceful).
If the *uṭṭavaṇa* is graceful (*lalita*), then it occurs in the *lalita* [dance].
From the final section, due to the suppression of the impulse toward tranquility, there is the "Blazing Dance" (Dīptanartana).
969. For example: *takkeṃ dhikkeṃ takadhika takaki thaoṃkaṭagena2 thaoṃgakkathaoṃ3*.
Thus ends the first section.
*ṭaithoṭeṃgeṃ tthaoṃdhithaoṃhadhihaṭeṃ*. Thus, the pacification (*upaśama*) is repeated twice. *tarkkarga daḍa-rada kuthikurgadaḍadhikka dakkarga daḍagdakthaoṃgattakadhika kadhikata dhika-*

*Kadhi ṭeṃgeṃnathaoṃga2 thaoṃgakkathaoṃ*—thus ends the second section. *Ṭaiṃ thaoṃ haṭageṃ thaoṃṭeṃ*; thus the pacification (*upaśama*) is repeated twice. *Theoṃgaṭaṃ daragaḍa dhiragaḍa dhitthāḥ thaoṃkaṭa takathaoṃ kaṭadhikkak. Thaoṃdhika taddhitak*. Thus ends the third section.

*katthaoṃṭakka thaoṃhakaṭage dhikaṭai thau haṭageṃ thaoṃ haṭeṃ*—thus the *upaśama* occurs twice. *tathaoṃ giḍdak diganadigana diganaka thaoṃgataddhitak thaoṃhaṭeṃ*—thus the *cchaṇḍaṇa*. This is an example in the *ekatālī* meter. Thus ends the *rigoṇī*.
A *khaṇḍa* composed of pure (*śuddha*) and other [varieties] should have its first part repeated twice and should not be too long.
Alternatively, a section (khaṇḍa) of similar [length] may occur once by means of a sequence of syllables (varṇasara).

Having thus established the *udgrāha* and the *dhruva*, or else at the final quarter of one's own *udgrāha*, or wherever there is a release (*mukti*) within the *udgrāha* itself—poets know that as *kavita*. 970–971.
Others call this by another name, *avaccheda*; here, the tempo is swift, the syllables are generally elevated, and there is much dancing; thus it is proclaimed by Niḥśaṅka. 972

For example: *gaḍdakdaginadaṃdaṃ ginathaoṃga dhikkaṭa nakādhitaka deṃhakadara gaḍadariktha riktha ridaragaḍa tharika thaoṃ gaṃḍake | dhikthaoṃṭeṃ2*—this is the *udgrāha*, repeated twice. *jheṃkaka nakhakhina2 taheṃ hake nakhakhinathaoṃ*—this is the section called the *dhruvā*.

Then, the *tyāga* (the concluding section) is performed either with the *udgrāha* consisting of the final segment beginning with "deṃhakaḍaragaḍe" etc., or with the entire *udgrāha* beginning with "gaḍgat" etc. This is the illustration for the *niḥsāru-tāla*. Thus it is said:
the *udgrāha* is short, the *dhruva* is not too long, and both are composed in the *śuddha* (pure) or other [melodic] forms.
When a *chaṇḍaṇa* occurs at the end of a verse composed in a specific meter (*varṇasarabaddha*), those who know instrumental music call that a *pada*; this generally occurs in the *dīpta-nartana*.
For example: *Taddehaṃ taddeṃ tataktaddai*—this is the *udgrāha*. *Takaṭa dhikaṭa dhidhikiṭa dhikiṭargāḍdagadhikataka dhikathaoṃgaṭeṃ*—this is the *dhruva*.

*gata kaṭadhidhi kaṭadhikkiḍadagadhidhikaṭa dhikkiraḍāḍagadhigakki-gḍāhagathaoṃṭaiṃ haṃdhikkathaoṃgaṭeṃ* | Thus ends the *cchaṇḍaṇa*. This is an example in the *varṇatāla*. Having played the *yati* in the middle of the composition (*prabandha*), it is released.
"Where it is called *pāṭa* by other wise scholars, that is the *pada*. (974) Thus,
the *pada* [is defined] in the context of the commencement of dance, when the tempo (*māna*) is fast (*druta*) and the rhythm (*tāla*) is single (*ekatālī*).
When the karaṭa, aṭīpikā, and halāvādina instruments are played in unison (sama), and the practiced musical section (vādyakhaṇḍa) is composed with a single *kūṭa* [syllable],
ending with *dhīmi*, *iti*, and *cchaṇḍaṇa*, it is known by the wise as a *melāpaka*. 975–976.
Those possessed of knowledge, in their own tradition, call this *melāpaṇī*; the repetition of these syllables, such as *ṭirikī*, is called *ṭīpi*.
For example: *thaoṃgaṭeṃ gaḍdagnaṃ thaoṃgaṭeṃ*. This should be played again and again until the completion of the composition. That is *dhīmi*. Thus ends the *chaṇḍaṇa*. Thus ends the *melāpaka*.
A section bound by pure and other rhythmic patterns (*pāṭa*), or by a sequence of syllables (*varṇasara*), which is brief, possesses a soft resonance, is endowed with delicate syllables,
and is practiced in a gentle dance, is called *upaśama*. (978)
As follows: *ṭeṃthaoṃkkage thoṭeṭe thaoṃhaṭage thātheṃ thaoṃṭe*. This is the *upaśama* (concluding section).

At the beginning of musical compositions (*vādyaprabandha*), that section which is played, constructed from pure syllables (*śuddhakūṭa*) and so forth, the great masters call that the *udgrāha* (the introductory theme). 979

Although the *udgrāha*, the *upaśama*, and so forth are stated to be members (*aṅga*) of another [section] until its completion through repetition, nevertheless there may be continuity (*prabandhatā*).
Whether there be a double repetition or no repetition at all, it remains as a member. (980–981)
"Teṃ-teṃ," "hai-taṭṭeṃ," and "takka-taṭe"—up to this point is the *udgrāha* (the introductory theme), which is completed by repetition according to the requirements of the composition.
Its status as a subordinate member (*aṅga*) occurs either twice or once; the initial performance of both the subordinate members and the *udgrāha* is the same. Thus ends the *udgrāha*.
[The subsequent part] is played forcefully, with resonant sounds, in a fixed melodic pattern (*kūṭabaddha*), in fragments, again and again.
The *praharaṇa* (striking) should be employed within the scope of the *dhruvā* and other *ābhoga* sections;
it is generally to be used in dance (*nṛtta*), though it may also be applied elsewhere according to one's desire.

For example: *kathaoṃgakka thaoṃgatthaoṃgaṭathaoṃgakka thoga thogathok kathogak thaoṃkaṭa yogakthokaṭaṃ thogak | gaḍdakkādhika thaoṃgak | ṭageṃ daṃthaoṃha | diṅ-nikukudhittho hadhikkaṃ dhiṭaiṃ* This should be repeated again and again. This is an illustration for the *ekatālī* [rhythm]. Thus ends the *praharaṇa*.

Then there should be an *udgrāha*, followed by a *khaṇḍa* constructed from pure *kūṭas* and so forth, either bound by the same syllables [as the previous] or not; having employed this pair twice, there follows a *dala* consisting of similar *kūṭas* together with the preceding *khaṇḍa*. 983–984.
And at the end, where the *chaṇḍaṇa* is played, that is the *avatsaka*;
it is to be employed in a brilliant dance, as proclaimed by Śārṅgadeva.
(985) For example: *gaḍ-dag-daṃ-daṃ gaḍ-dak-thikkaṭa takadhikkaṭa takdhiktak*. This is the *udgrāha*.

*Khaḍi khaḍi khakhanakha khidak jheṃkhakhanakha khidaktadakka dhikkaka-kagiṇanaga thaoṃgadihikiṃ thogadihikkitaka dhikathaoṃgaṭe gaḍak | takadhika thaoṃgaṭeṃ |* Thus ends the second section (*khaṇḍa*). This should be played again and again along with the *sahodgrāha*. *Jhaka jhakhikhinnakhanakhakhita hreṃ khakhanakhajheṃ khana khariba tuḍi hidihi | kathaoṃgak |* Thus is the third section, [to be played] with the preceding section.

One should play [the instrument] together: *takadhika*, *takkare*, *ghaṭathathaoṃgakka*, *thaoṃgakkaṭeṃ*. This is the *chaṇḍaṇa* [rhythm]. This is an illustration in the *raṅgavidyādhara* *tāla*. Thus ends the *avatsaka*. A section (*khaṇḍa*) constructed from *kūṭa* syllables and so forth is the *chaṇḍaṇa*, which serves as the release for the instrumental music (*vādyamokṣaka*). 986.

Thus, when the *cchaṇḍaṇa* is bound by pure *kūṭas* and so forth, or when it is practiced as a *khaṇḍa* with a sequence of syllables (*varṇasara*), it is called *tuḍukā* in the measurement of the rapid tempo (*druta*) during the radiant dance (*dīptanartana*).
In this [form], a tempo that is fast or even faster is observed among the targets (lakṣya).

For example: *ṭeṃ daṃdagitathaoṃgaṭeṃdhikataḥ raghaṭe he kathoḥ ṭegedhika taṭathaoṃgaḥ gaṇanagiḥ thaoṃgataka dhikathaoṃgaṭeṃ*. This is an illustration within the *ekatālī* [rhythm]. Where one of the sections—the *udgrāha*, *dhruvaka*, or *ābhoga*—[is repeated], [that is the *ekatalī*]. 987–988.
Others say it is to be played on the *vādya* [instrument], while others have declared it to be the *tuḍuka*;
the playing of the *udgrāha*, *dhruvaka*, *ābhoga*, and *udgrāha* follows in sequence.
(989) Thus ends the *tuḍuka*.

Wherein a section bound by pure (*śuddha*) and other [types of *mātrā*] may be extensive through the sequence of syllables (*varṇasara*), having a fast tempo (*drutalaya*) at the beginning but a slow tempo (*vilambita*) at the end,
and being beautifully composed with syllables that are sometimes brilliant (*dīpta*) and sometimes soft (*komala*). 990.
In this context, that which is called *malapa* is generally employed in the *dīptanartana* (the blazing dance). For example:

*Gaḍdak taddhitthaoṃ hathaoṃ hare ghaṭaiṃ gaṇanagataka dhikaka thauṃ haṭeṃ haiṃ thodagak |* *takka tahadhika thokathohaka tho3 haṭṭai ḍiṃ khikharakhikhikherathaṭaiṃ haiṃ thohagak |* *dihaṃ kaṭadahaṃ kaṭagaḍda gatharikaṭaṃ2* 991. Thus it is said. As for instance: *gaḍdak taddhitthaoṃ hathaoṃ hare ghaṭaiṃ gaṇanagataka dhikaka thauṃ haṭeṃ haiṃ thodagak | takka tahadhika thokathohaka tho3 haṭṭai ḍiṃ khikharakhikhikherathaṭaiṃ haiṃ thohagak | dihaṃ kaṭadahaṃ kaṭagaḍda gatharikaṭaṃ2*.
*Tharikaṭataka3 tataka dhidhika tho'thaoṃdaṭeṃ*. This is an example of the *mudrita-maṇṭha-tāla*,
wherein the *udgrāha* occurs once or twice, and the *dhruvaka* occurs once.

They say that when it is bound by the syllables *tha*, *dhi*, *tha*, *oṃ*, *ṭeṃ*, *deṃ*, and others mixed with pervasive syllables (*vyāpakākṣara*), and is continuous, that is called *malapa*; thus ends the section on *malapa*.
For the sake of instructing the young, I have previously set forth the definitions along with examples;
now, fearing prolixity, I shall state merely the definitions.
(993) [The figure] *malapāṅga* consists of a *malapa* limb, a *malapa* member, and a *malapa*.
Thus is the *malapāṅga*;
with uneven *pāṭas*, it would be the *malapapāṭa*, resembling the *malapa*.
(994) Thus ends the *malapapāṭa*.
Where musical instruments are played with swift and expressive strokes of the palms,
repeatedly interrupted, the wise call that *cheda*.
Having performed the *otā*, there is a double *udgrāha* or a single one, accompanied by pervasive syllables (*vyāpakākṣara*).
Where it is composed with *sapāṭas* at the end, arranged with *daṅkṛtis*,
and possesses a *chaṇḍaṇa* in the middle and the *laya*, that is defined as a *rūpaka*.
(996) Thus ends the section on *rūpaka*.
The *nibaddha* (fixed) is played at the juncture of song and instrumental music; this is considered the *antara* (intermediate).
Thus is the *antara*.
If, after playing the *antara*, one plays the *anibaddha* (unfixed), [that is the *antara*].
"If an *antarapāṭa* were to be performed, then it would be accepted by Niḥśaṅka.
Thus ends the *antarapāṭa*,
composed of well-joined, thick, smooth, and distinct syllables.
"Endowed with manual dexterity, *khoja* is thus described by the wise.
(999) Having performed the *khoja*, there should be a playing like that of an ascetic (*yati*), with the musical sections (*khaṇḍa*) bound together by *pāṭas*.

Thus, because it causes a turning back, the wise call it *khaṇḍayati* (the "breaker"). It is called *khaṇḍayati* because of its connection with breaking and cutting, as well as with the continuity of breaking and cutting.
Others have declared that *khaṇḍaccheda* is that which is joined with clear pauses (*cheda*) and has a pause at the end;
in this [form], there is a cessation at the conclusion through the pervasive syllables of the *tāla*. Thus ends *khaṇḍaccheda*.
"That which has its sections bound together by *pāṭas* is called *avayati* by the wise" (1002). Thus,
because the *pāṭa* is divided (*avayati*), it is first termed *khaṇḍapāṭa*.
Thus, when there is playing in sections, even within a section, it is a *khaṇḍapāṭa*; it may also be a *khaṇḍa*. When played in fragments, it is a *khaṇḍaka*. 1003. Thus ends the *khaṇḍaka*.
That which is called *khaṇḍaḍulla* is defined by a *yati* (caesura) occurring at the end of each quarter;
thus it is *khaṇḍahulla*.
A composition (*prabandha*) that is equal in its measure (*māna*) is called *sama*, being equal in both song and dance. 1004.
Thus,
when completed as a whole through its individual sections, it is designated as a "pāṭa";
such is the pāṭa.

"A *dhruvaka* occurs in various musical compositions (*bhūrivādya*) when it is repeated at intervals" (1005)— thus [is defined] the *dhruvaka*. "The *aṅga* is that which is accepted by the dense, faultless, and pervasive syllables."
Thus, the *aṅga* consists of the *dvirudgrāha*, the *dhruvābhoga*, and that which is called the *dhruva* in succession; where he speaks of this form of *aṅga*, that is the *tejonvayadīpaka*. 1006
Thus is the *aṅgarūpaka*;
the *tāla* consists of sixty-four beats (*kala*) in both the *yugma* and *dakṣiṇa* *mārgas*.
This is the *tāla*.
"Vitāla is considered to be a *tāla* whose beginning, middle, and end are modified.
(1007) Thus ends Vitāla.
With the hand, the thumb extended and the fingers spread apart, [the beat is struck] in succession.
When [the instruments] are struck with flags (*patākā*) and produce *pāṭa* strokes, it is called *khalaka*;
thus,
the ensemble known as *khalaka* arises from the playing of all the musical instruments together with their respective *pāṭas*.
Thus, the combination of the separately stated *pāṭas* through their mixing is considered *joḍaṇī*. (1009) Thus ends *joḍaṇī*.

The *uḍuva* consists of [beats] with tempo (*laya*), double tempo (*tāla*), and those devoid of tempo; the *talapāṭa*, however, arises from a composition of mixed *malapa* and *pāṭa* recitations. 1010.
Thus is the *talapāṭa*:
it is composed by one's own *taddhita* suffixes, pervasive syllables (*akṣara*), or *pāṭas*, and it rests upon a slightly slow tempo (*vilambita-laya*). 1011.
They call this *uṭṭavaṇī*, which is adorned at its beginning and end with *dekāras*.
Thus, *uṭṭavaṇī* consists of a portion of instrumental music (*vādya*) ending in a group (*varga*), occurring at the beginning and middle of the performance.

Because it is played with light hands, that which they call *tuṇḍaka* [is so named]. (1013) Thus, *tuṇḍaka* has its caesura (*yati*) by means of the *pāṭas* alone; it is the *aṅgapāṭaka*, characterized by dense and graceful *pāṭas*.
Thus, a section consisting of the performance of individual limbs with various musical instruments is called *paisāra*.
This concludes the *paisāra*.
I have described these few compositions merely for the sake of illustration;

let those who know the subject recognize other compositions as well by this same method. (1015) Furthermore, there are variations in notation, instrumental pieces, and compositions based on instruments.
"These [rules] are considered applicable, as appropriate, to all musical instruments such as the mardala and others.
(1016) Thus ends the definition of the musical composition (*vādyaprabandha*).
[The drumstick] originates from a flawless seed-tree, measures half a finger-breadth in thickness at its base (*piṇḍa*), and...
Furthermore, the left face should be twenty-one finger-breadths in length;
its measurement should be fourteen finger-breadths on the right, while its middle part is slightly broader by one finger-breadth. 1017–1018.
From the two openings [of the mouth], there are two round, thick pieces of leather; at their two edges, there are forty separate apertures, each separated by a finger’s breadth.
When these are placed upon the straps and provided with the method of stitching, [the drum is ready].
The *vignikā* is formed by standing upright and bending forward so that the belly and back touch;
it is then wrapped firmly in the middle with three bindings,
and there, a *gomūtrikā* binding should be made with two pieces of cloth.
In such a way that the two firm leather straps may be fastened to the mouth [of the vessel],
having placed them at the ends of the two loops— specifically in the left loop— one should throw the thong over the right side, pull it through, and bring it to a double fold.

One should place upon the hip a piece of silk cloth measuring eight finger-breadths in length, provided with two fringes; or alternatively, one made of another fine fabric that follows the aesthetic requirements.
They call this the *mṛdaṅga*, as well as the *mardala* and the *muraja*.
The sage declared that the three types of drums (puṣkara) are indicated by the sound of the mṛdaṅga; however,
because they are utterly unfit for practical use, he plays them without hesitation [only] after they have been thoroughly rubbed with a thick mixture of flour and oil.
One should place a ball of dough shaped like a *pūrikā* into the left mouth;
with a small amount of that which is called *bohaṇā*, one should smear the right mouth.
In this way, the sound becomes as deep as the roar of a rain-cloud.
And here, the deity is declared by Niḥśaṅka to be Nandikeśvara;
it should be made of red sandalwood, or else this [linga] is considered by others to be made of acacia wood.
It should be thirty finger-breadths in length and one finger-breadth in thickness.

Its left face measures twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas), while the right is measured at eleven and a half finger-breadths; and its various parts are proclaimed here according to their respective proportions. 1029–1030.
Elsewhere, they consider the readings to be *taṭahā* and *dadhalāḥ*;
here, however, the sixteen consonants beginning with *ka* are said to be the *paṭaha*.
Others, moreover, describe the additional letters *bha*, *ja*, and *ma* as being present here.
Among those, the seven beginning with *ta* (ta, tha, da, dha, na, pa, pha) are exclusively designated as "pure" (*śuddha*).
When these are mixed with the sixteen known as "pervasive" (*vyāpaka*)— namely *ka*, *kha*, and so on, whether joined with vowels or not— they are designated as "composite" (*kūṭa*).
Those pure [verses] mixed with *kūṭa* are considered by the wise to be called *khaṇḍa*.
(1033) A poet of noble intellect, whose form is manifest through a meter that is both abundant and heart-pleasing, composes a verse (*śloka*) with words that provide a festival for the ears. (1034)
Just so, having fashioned syllables that are captivating through their repetition in some rhythmic measure (tāla), the instrumentalist ought to compose musical compositions;
those who are wise call such an instrumentalist a "poet-composer" (kavitakāra). 1035–1036.
Thus is the definition of the mṛdaṅga.
There are four types of mṛdaṅga players: the vādika, the mukharī, and then the one called the pratimukharī; the fourth is considered the gītānuga (the follower of the song). 1037

The proponent is the one who conducts the debate; *syādvāda* is the adoption of a position, which includes the establishment of one's own thesis as well as the refutation of the opposing side. (1038) Other varieties of debate, such as *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*, along with their defining characteristics, are likewise included.
Fearing the proliferation of voluminous texts, I shall not speak of them;
rather, in this discourse, the first thing to be performed is the "striking" (trāṭana), for there can be no sound on a drum without a beat and without striking. 1039.
That which is performed as "dehaḍaḍ" and so forth is considered *trāṭana* (1040).
One should perform the "voḍavāḍa" with a deep sound and with great exertion of the hands;
thereafter, it consists of the sounds "mukta," "reha," "ḍaḍa," and so on.
The setting up of the *udhāra* (the tuning peg) is described next; one should play it after that.
Having applied the *bohaṇa* (the tuning string) to the two mouths, one should play the left face with the sound "gaḍdagnem" and the right face with "gaḍdagnām. 1041–1042.

Then, in the middle tempo (*madhyalaya*) and the second beat (*tāla*), one should produce the union of sounds for the two faces; the three petals should be raised very high in sequence, separately in the slow (*vilambita*), middle (*madhya*), and fast (*druta*) tempos. 1043.
Likewise, that which is fashioned with one, two, or three *oṃkāras* and brings about the liberation from planetary afflictions;
and that which, like a vocal recitation, is purified in the three registers (*tri-sthāna*) and played sweetly by experts with both hands—that is declared by the knowers to be *sthāpana*. (1044–1045)
Then, there should be an internal release of many *oṃkāra*s;
in squares, triangles, mixed, or fragmented sections, by means of one or another, the *ṭākaṇī* and other instruments should be played for a duration of one *tāla*, and immediately thereafter—
Between those two, one is *sara* and the other is *joḍā*; thus, a twofold division is recognized.

Having performed the bearing of the effort (*śrama*) in a rhythmic cycle (*tāla*) consisting of eight *kalās*, a musical segment (*vādyakhaṇḍa*) has been composed in accordance with the expansion of the rhythmic *kalās*.
By performing [the practice] once, one attains the state of having a single scar that is never broken;
by practicing it purely one, two, three, or four times, there arises here the method known as "removing fatigue" in the art of playing, just as in the following example. 1048–1049.

*taddhitoṭeṃ tatadhidhi thaoṃ thaoṃ ṭeṃ ṭeṃ tatatadhi dhidhi thaoṃ thaoṃ thaoṃ ṭeṃ ṭeṃ ṭeṃ | tatatata dhi dhi dhi dhi tho tho tho tho ṭe ṭe ṭe ṭe |* Thus, having performed the *śramavahanī* like a single callus (*kiṇī*) of a lizard (*saraṭa*), [one plays] *takadhikaṭa*, *takadhikaṭa*, *dhikaṭataka*, *takadhikaṭa*, *takatakadhikaṭa*, *dhikaṭakatadhikaṭa*. These are the eight sections of the musical instrument (*vādyakhaṇḍa*) for the eight beats (*kalā*). That same [sequence] is joined twice. Having made the entire preceding section like a *ṭākaṇī*, thereafter— 1050. [The text continues with further rhythmic syllables. *iti śramavahanīṃ kṛtvaikasaraṭākiṇī yathā | takadhikaṭa | takadhikaṭa | dhikaṭataka takadhikaṭa takatakadhikaṭa dhikaṭakatadhikaṭa | ityaṣṭau vādyakhaṇḍasya khaṇḍā aṣṭāsu kalāsu | saiva dvivāraṃ joḍā | ṭākaṇīvatsamastaṃ prākkhaṇḍaṃ kṛtvā tataḥ param 1050* Having performed the *śramavahanī* like a single callus of a lizard, [one plays] *takadhikaṭa*, *takadhikaṭa*, *dhikaṭataka*, *takadhikaṭa*, *takatakadhikaṭa*, *dhikaṭakatadhikaṭa*. These are the eight sections of the musical instrument for the eight beats. That same [sequence] is joined twice. Having made the entire preceding section like a *ṭākaṇī*, thereafter... [1050].
In that which is designated as an instrument (*vādya*), it is played in pieces or twice over;
therein, the single-syllable *sarajoḍātva* is illustrated as being like *ṭākiṇī*.
For example: *daṃdaṃ*, *ṭiri*, *ṭiṭṭikaḍda*, *kaḍadagajhe*. (1051)

*Tharikathari*, *ṭagaṇa-gaṇadhari*, *gaṇagaṇadhari*, *dathari gaḍadaga*, *datharigaḍadaga*, *datharigaḍadaga*, *dathari datharitargaḍdaktharikkaṭatattak*. Thus, having performed the sixteen-part instrumental music (*ṣoḍaśakhaṇḍaka-vādya*) upon the sixteen beats (*ṣoḍaśakalāsu*) of the *ṣoḍaśakala-tāla*, one should repeat each of those sixteen sections twice; this is the "single-syllable" (*ekasaravāda*).
By the syllable *ta*, the abandonment of all these is intended;
thereafter, one should perform *digidigi*, *tāṭava*, and so forth.
These syllables *vaṇā* and *digidigi* are declared by the wise as *digidige*.
That which is fragmented when the time limit is exceeded is called *tāṭasthavāda* (neutral debate).
1053 Other methods of debate may also be inferred by this same path.
Thus, victory shall belong to the one whose mode of debate is correct. 1054

Thus, the performer is one who composes musical compositions, is skilled in the training of dance, proficient in singing and instrumental playing, possesses excellent lines [of the body], and is inward-looking. 1055
Standing on the stage, with his face watched by the other musicians for the sake of the performance, he should play like the half-body of a dancer;
thus he is called *mukharī*.
That which is slightly inferior to the *mukhariṇa* is called the *pratimukharī*. (1057) Thus ends the *pratimukharī*. [Now, regarding] the syllables of the pure *sālagagītā*, whether hard or soft—

Through playing, one properly follows the even and uneven notes, as well as the low (*mandra*), middle (*madhya*), and high (*tāraka*) registers; likewise, in the *pūrvabhāga*, the *ābhoga*, and the *jakka-praharaṇa*, one proceeds in due order, whether with maturity or sweetness. (1058–1059)
Alternatively, one may perform it in its optional form, or when based on a complete song;
or when it has arisen through either direct or reverse order, or by both.
When the song is in the *niḥsāru-sālagas* style, that which follows the song is known as *gītānuga*.
"In due order, he should employ the syllables *ta*, *ra*, *tha*, and *oṃ* for the seizing and releasing [of the drum]; thus follows the Gītā.
This is the fourfold definition of the Mārdalika."
Clarity of color, excellence of lines, following the tradition,
proficiency in sweet and spirited instrumental music, dexterity of hand, attentiveness,
overcoming fatigue, and skill in facial instruments. 1062.

Affection for the *āvarjika*, continuity, and abundance [of performance], as well as knowledge of the *yatitāla* and *laya*, and following the melody—these are the qualities of a *mārdalika*; the opposite of these would be his faults. (1063–1064)
Thus are the merits and defects of the mṛdaṅga; that ensemble should be primarily composed of two, three, or four experts who hold the mṛdaṅgas, and they must follow the lead of the mukha-drum. 1065.
That which is measured by the span of the hand in length, twenty-eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in circumference,
seven aṅgulas in thickness,
and eleven aṅgulas at the opening— these two circular vessels with mouths like creepers [are to be placed] between the two faces.

With a thickness of one and a quarter finger-breadths and joined by the *uddalī* knot, there should be two [sockets] together with the two openings; one should make six apertures in those two for the purpose of inserting the bound ropes,
and three bolts on the front side.
At the rear, there should be two kalaśas joined at their ends and two argalas;
between the binding threads in the middle, there shall be a belly-band three finger-breadths wide, smooth and heart-captivating. 1069.
Having firmly bound both sides with a rope made from thirty-two strands,
and having arranged two shoulder-straps there, one should place a double-layered band between them measuring half a finger-breadth.

That [wind instrument] which has a hole in its fourth part that causes the awakening of the *nāda* (sound) is called a *huḍukkā* by the wise; having placed its shoulder-band upon one's shoulder, the playing should be performed with the right hand. 1072.
A band is prescribed for the belly; upon it, one should place the left [hand].
(1073) The seven Mother Goddesses were proclaimed by Śārṅgadeva; one should fashion the syllables of the *pāṭaha* here, excluding the syllable *deṃ*. (1074)
Regarding this, other wise men have stated that there are two additional *ma* syllables and one *e* syllable;
those who know the characteristics [of the meter] call this *avaja*, and likewise *skandhāvaja*. (1075) Thus ends the definition of *huḍukkā*.
Arising from seeds and trees, it should measure one-fourth of a finger-breadth in thickness;
it should be twenty-one fingers long, or perhaps one cubit (twenty-four fingers) in length,
and it should possess a circumference of forty fingers.
The mouth [of the bell] is fourteen finger-breadths wide, though for some it is twelve;
the rim, made of copper, wound with thread and bound with leather,
measures forty-two finger-breadths.
It possesses three strings on each of its two ends and two rings;
it is entirely pervaded by fourteen [components] and is provided with holes at every other interval, into which one should insert as many tuning pegs (*vignikā*). 1079.

When two pairs of strings are bound so as to form the shape of a fish, that is called a *karaṭā*; it should be worn at the edge of the garment, bound at the ends, over the shoulder region or at the waist during performance. (1080–1081)

The deity of this [tāla] is Carcikā, and its recitations (pāṭas) are known as Karaṭa and so forth. Śārṅgadeva has proclaimed that the playing [of the cymbals] with the *kuḍupa* measures consists of two recitations, generally considered to be "tiriki" and "tirikirī. 1082–1083.
Such is the description of the *karaṭa*:
smooth, well-baked, slightly curved, and large-bellied;
a jar with its mouth covered by leather that is played upon with the hands by those skilled in it.
The sounds and colors described for the *mardala* drum are considered to apply to the *ghaṭa* drum as well (1084).
The *ghaḍasa* is explained by means of the *huḍukka* alone; however, the *maṇḍalī* has its right side bound with a thong and its left side restrained with a cord (1085).
On the broad band [of the instrument], the left [hand] is not employed here (1086).
Those who know this say that one should play this [instrument] with many *oṃ* sounds,
using the thumb and middle finger with their tips smeared with *madana* (1087).
By rubbing the mouth with the right hand, the sound *goṃ* arises;
striking it with the fingers of the left hand, and pressing it with the left thumb—this is the definition of the *ghaḍasa* [mudrā]. 1088.
It may be a span in length, with a circumference of thirty-nine finger-breadths,
and a mouth twelve finger-breadths wide, joined with a series of coils;
it possesses seven apertures on each of its two coils.
Likewise, when the two hollows [of the hands] are joined with bracelets at the mouth [of the vessel] and firmly covered, they are bound together by straps placed through the openings; this,
as declared by the learned Śārṅgadeva, is called the *ḍhavasa* [hand position].

Placing it upon his shoulder or under his arm, he should play it with his left hand; while holding the *kuḍupa* (small cymbal) in his right hand at his right side, he is known among people as *Ḍhavasa*, due to his mastery in chanting the sound *ḍheṃ*. 1092.

Thus has the characteristic of the *ḍhava* drum been explained by Ḍhavasena himself; however, its two faces are thirteen finger-breadths [in diameter], and one should hold it with the left hand. (1093)
One who knows it should play it by striking with the corner [of the hand] held in the right hand;
the syllables *ḍheṃ* and *kāraḥ* are its melodic ornaments (*pāṭavarṇāḥ*), as proclaimed by Niśaṅka. (1094) Thus ends the description of the *ḍhakkā*.
The *kuḍukkā* is like a *huḍukkā* but without a bolt; however, its playing is with the hand using a plectrum (*koṇa*), and Kṣetrapāla is its presiding deity.
(1095) Thus ends the description of the *kuḍukkā*.

The seed-vessel made of wood is twenty-one finger-breadths in length, with two openings having a cavity of seven finger-breadths; it is uniform in shape and possesses a thickness of three finger-breadths, resembling the form of three conjoined fires. 1096.

When a nine-finger-wide cavity has been made, and two bracelets fashioned from creepers—each provided with seven apertures—are placed upon her two faces, they are fastened at the mouth by means of two morsels of food. Thus she becomes possessed of two face-adorned bracelets. (1097–1098)
In a hollowed-out gourd, well-constrained by strings placed through its cavity, there arises a great *kreṅkāra* sound from the syllables uttered by the *huḍukka*;
it is played with two plectrums smeared with *madana*, while the *jheṃkṛti* sound is abandoned. (1099–1100)
Thus is the description of the *kuḍuvā*:
eighteen finger-breadths in length, firm, straight, and symmetrical;
at its mouth, eleven finger-breadths wide, it is joined with a ring. (1101)
Similarly, for those who have two *kuṇḍalī*s within the interior of the left side of the mouth made of skin:
one of them should be the size of the mouth itself, while the other should be four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) long;
between the two *kuṇḍalī*s there should be a meshwork (*jālikā*) composed of sinew.

With a single opening on the left side and joined with the thread-reality (sūtratattva), the small niches (vignikās) should be made as before, seven on each of the two faces; and [the structure] should be one and a quarter cubits in measure, firm, and provided with serpent-nooses (nāgapāśa). 1103–1104.
Placing the girdle upon her shoulder, its sounding is known by the wise as *vādana*.
Because it produces the sound "ruṃ," it is called *ruñjā*, and its presiding deity is Bhṛṅgin (Śiva).
These syllables spoken by Mataṅga are *karaga* and *dhaṭana*: *kha-hau*.
"In this treatise on musical instruments, the *vignikā* is proclaimed to be a *karkarā*.
Thus ends the description of the *ruñjā*.
It should be one *vitasti* in length and have two openings of eight *aṅgulas* each."

When the mouth of the *yoga* is joined with the *maṇḍalī* and bound with leather, it has a slender middle like the three folds [of the abdomen] and is fastened with cords of thread; having been brought to a state of firmness in the middle, the two *rañcanīs* are used for playing. 1107–1108.
With the two balls of the drum held firmly at the ends by both hands,
this *ḍamaruka* should be held in the middle and played with the sound *ḍagh*; thus it was taught by the master Niḥśaṅka.
Other letters are said to be *ka-kha-ra-ṭa*, with the addition of *ḍa* and *ma*.
(1110) Thus ends the description of the *ḍamaruka*.
Its length should be one *vitasti*, and its middle should be slightly slender.
At the opening, the ball is eight finger-breadths [in diameter], and there are two strings, each half a finger-breadth thick.
At each opening, there are four pegs made of copper;
below each [opening], two are placed one above the other for the purpose of securing the strings.
One should place a blade of grass or a small stick upon the two strings for the enrichment of sound;
its other characteristics, such as its rhythmic syllables (*pāṭākṣara*), are like those of the *huḍukka* drum.
It should have a length of ten finger-breadths, and its playing is performed with a *kuḍupa* measure.
That [instrument] is proclaimed as the *ḍakkā* by Niḥśaṅkaśārṅgadeva (1114).
Others say its playing is done with the hand and with the *kuḍupa*; the sound *ḍaṃkāra* occurs when playing with the hand, while with the *kuḍupa* it is different (1115).

They say that its *mukhas* (syllabic feet) are *gha*, *ṭa*, *sta*, *ga*, and *ḍagi*; the *pāṭas* (variations) are said to be *na*, *ga*, *kha*, *ka*, *ra*, *ṭa*, and *va*. These are declared by others here to be the primary [feet]. And in this [meter], the wise declare the deity to be Vindhyavāsinī.
The middle [pipe] is one finger less, and the smallest is two fingers less;
such is the definition of the *ḍakka*.
The *maṇḍiḍakka* is indeed the same as the *ḍakka*, except that its length is sixteen fingers.
The two inner cavities at the two openings should be eight finger-breadths in length;
the circumference of the middle part should be sixteen finger-breadths; there should be no bolt here, nor a side-strap or shoulder-strap, but rather two pivots in the middle.
Placing the two anklets on the raised armpit and holding them with the three fingers of the left hand while pressing the edge of the circular ornament on the face with the index finger,
one should strike her right knee with the right hand. (1120)
With the ring finger,

the little finger, and the thumb joined and pressed together to form a circle, one should play it either with the index finger or the middle finger, or else with another hand, keeping the wrist raised above the wrist-band (maṇibandha). || 1121-1122 ||
They say its playing is done with the hand or with a *kuḍupa*; it is employed for the sake of power during ritual practice (*caryā*), song, and worship.
(1123) Thus ends the description of the *maṇḍiḍakkā*.
The *ḍaddulī* should be made of bell-metal, cow-horn, or the tusk of a tusked animal;
it should be five finger-breadths in length and four finger-breadths at its mouth.
It should be bound with a strap of sheep-skin and provided with its respective wheels.
He made two separate wheels, either of bell-metal, copper, or iron;
each having five holes, they were fitted with leather thongs passed through the holes, tied firmly together by a cord, and wrapped tightly around the middle with a thread.
Neither too loose nor too tight, one should place the middle finger on the central thread; having opened the middle and index fingers joined like a wheel,
and having placed the thumb upon the other wheel, one should then apply it with a slight bend.
Having prepared a single *añcanikā* drum, one should play it with the sound "dundum";
others say it is "tuṃtum. These are the rhythmic patterns (*pāṭas*) arising from the *mardala* drum, as proclaimed by Śārṅgadeva according to their respective possibilities.
Thus is the description of the *ḍakkulī*:
it should be twenty-six finger-breadths in length and thirty finger-breadths in circumference; it should have a symmetrical body, be made of *selluka* wood, and be fashioned from seed-wood. (1130)
Its opening should be ten finger-breadths wide, and it should be pierced at eleven finger-breadths;
it is said that the binding and the lifting are performed by these two [ends] when they are increased by one finger-breadth each.
The cord made of creeper should have the thickness of the index finger, and there should be two rings at the two openings.
The six-holed [instrument] is firmly secured with cords passing through the holes;
it is one finger-breadth longer than that [previous instrument], and its mouth is again provided with two openings.
One should play the left-hand part, which contains the strings, with the left hand. 1132–1133.
The right face [is formed] with the *kuḍupa* held in the right hand;
the syllable *jheṃ* is in the left mouth, and the syllable *dhiṃ* is in the right mouth.
(1134) Thus is the definition of Sellukāla.
It should be made from twenty-five palas of material, twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in length,
and eighteen finger-breadths in circumference; it should have a symmetrical form,
possess two holes in the neck along with a corded ring.
The *jhallarī* is described as having its mouth covered with leather;
it is held in the left hand and played with the right hand.
Thus ends the definition of the *jhallarī*.
A *bhāṇa* should weigh half a *pala*, and its circumference should be twelve *aṅgulas*;
furthermore, the characteristics of the *jhallarī* for it were declared by the illustrious wielder of the Śārṅga bow (Viṣṇu).
Thus ends the definition of the *bhāṇa*.
Her face measures seven finger-breadths across, and her two hands possess a length of three folds;
moreover, when her mouth is covered by a morsel of food, her waist can be grasped by a fist. Within that mouth, there are two iron rings, each with seven holes, placed separately.
Bound by strings placed in the hollows and with a firm wrapping around the middle, the *kacchā*— a cord of thread one cubit in length hanging from the shoulder—
is described as being played with both hands by Śārṅgadeva. (1140–1141)
The syllables *tad-aṃ-doṃ-de-ti* are the phonemes here, and the deity is Tripurā;
she has a face eleven finger-breadths wide and possesses a length of twenty finger-breadths. Her middle part measures half the face, and in the center, she is joined with a golden girdle.

"Combined with half that number of syllables, it is called *trikulyā* by the wise. (1143) Thus ends the definition of the *trivalī*. [Then there is: "Born from the mango tree, possessing a large body and a great sound..."
Containing a collection of bronze vessels, devoid of bracelets, its mouth bound with leather and fastened tightly all around with straps,
the drum was played with breath using a firm-colored drumstick. 1144–1145.
The *oṃkāra* sound, deep as the roar of a thundercloud, is primary here;
it is sounded in temples for the sake of auspiciousness and victory.
(1146) Thus ends the description of the drum (*dundubhi*).
A drum (bherī) made of copper should be three vitastis in length;
its mouth, twenty-four aṅgulas wide, should be provided with a rim. That [mouth], along with the rim, should be covered with leather and provided with holes. 1147–1148.
When it is firmly restrained by a rope and bound in the middle with a cord,
by striking it with the left hand from the right corner,
a powerful, deep sound arises that strikes fear into enemies. 1449.

"The letter *ta* is declared by Niḥśaṅka to be the primary sound-color (*varṇa*) in this [bherī]; thus ends the description of the bherī. It is made of bell-metal, copper, or iron, being respectively superior, middling, or inferior."

He has one face; he is large in his mouth yet small within it, shaped like half a barley grain at the bottom. His womb is filled with the weight of bronze vessels, his face is covered by a buffalo hide, and his skin is bound together with leather straps inserted through its openings.

The drum (niḥsāṇa), which strikes terror into enemies, was sounded by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow; having been cast down and placed within the circle of leather straps, it was repeatedly whirled and played with the plectrum of his leathern hand. 1153. The playing of this [drum] was accompanied by a second [instrument].
"With this sound 'dṛḍha', he pierces the hearts of the timid,
while from it the bodies of the heroes of battle become covered with horripilation"—
this is the definition of the *niḥsāṇa* drum.
"The *tambakī* is like a *niḥsāṇa*, but with slightly less [thickness] in its body and neck" (1155)—
thus is the definition of the *tambakī*.
Whether the natural woods are specified or not, they may be used optionally.
For wooden musical instruments, *khadira* and red sandalwood (*raktacandana*) are to be known as suitable woods (1156).
For all types of *pāṭa*, *pāṭaha*, and *mārdaḷa* drums, [these woods] should be used as appropriate (1157).
[The wood should be taken] from a tree that is sapless, grown on elevated ground, old, and struck by the wind (1158).
When the interior has been split open and cleared out, one should have musical instruments made from the remaining wood;
whatever sprout grows from another sprout once the previous one has been cut,
every instrument produced from that tree is highly praised.
This, however, is the extraction of the core from a bamboo, not from another tree.

There are three types of trees: those that increase bile (pittala), those that increase wind (vātalā), and those that increase phlegm (śleṣmalā); among these, the bile-increasing type grows in sapless soil.
That which grows on land with very little moisture is *vātalā* (wind-dominant), while that which grows on ground near water bodies and is saturated with moisture is *śleṣmalā* (phlegm-dominant).
The *pittalā* (bile-dominant) variety is the most excellent, whereas the *vātalā* is the lowest quality.
"Wood that is excessively resinous (śleṣmalā) is to be avoided even before cutting from a dry tree.
(1163) Thus ends the characteristics of wood. "One should avoid softness, as well as cracks and knots, in pieces of wood.
(1164) Thus end the defects of wood.

The skin of a six-month-old calf should be used for the binding of the vessel; others say it should be that of a two-year-old, but that is not seen in practical applications. The leather strap should be fashioned from the hide of an old bull.
Resembling a jasmine flower, the moon, or snow, and similar to a mango sprout— [that] cowhide which is devoid of sinews and flesh,
having been soaked for one night in cold water, is then taken out.

"That which was spoken by the illustrious wielder of the Śārṅga bow should be taken up for the purpose of beating musical instruments. (1167) Thus end the qualities of leather. [Leather] that is corrupted by fat, overcome by old age, damp, or struck by the beak of a crow— [The following is the continuation of the verse: ...is to be avoided. That which is free from these defects, thick, and of even thickness, is praised as the best. It should be used for drums, cymbals, and other instruments; it brings success in all undertakings. One should avoid that which is torn, burnt, or has a foul odor. Leather that is naturally white, soft, and smooth is auspicious. It increases strength and fame, and is beneficial for the body. One should always wear leather that is well-prepared and free from disease. Thus have been described the characteristics of leather for the sake of musical performance.
"A leatherworker does not use worn-out leather that has been damaged by fire and smoke" (1168).
Thus end the defects of leather.
[Now for its virtues: He whose [leather], bound with exceedingly noble qualities, encompasses the three worlds.
This [instrument] is called *avanaddha* by the god Śārṅgin (Viṣṇu).
Now, regarding the *ghana* instrument: in the case of a *kāṃsyaja-ghana-vādya*, the bronze should be thoroughly purified in fire. 1169–1170.
A circular cymbal made of bell-metal (kāṃsya) has a mouth measuring two and a quarter finger-breadths;
its middle is one finger-breadth in width, and it has a deep, downward-sloping hole.
Its mass should be the size of a single guñjā seed less a quarter, or the measure of a barley grain.
Its height should be one and a half finger-breadths; it should be even, smooth, and of auspicious form.
It should be fashioned in such a way that there arises a sound pleasing to the ear.
Having made the ends of the cloth covering the eyes into a cord, one should fix it in place. 1172–1173.
One should form a firm knot so that the tips do not emerge from the opening;
having thus made a pair of loops, one then encircles the left index finger with the edge [of the cloth] and performs the wrapping with the thumb. 1174.

Having stepped forward and grasped the middle of the palm with the right hand turned sideways, one should extend the remaining fingers upward; meanwhile, with the other [left] hand, one should hold a row of immovable palm-leaves hanging down from its edge. 1175–1176.
Holding the tips of the index finger and thumb sideways and striking the middle finger with their tips, the Śakti will produce a faint sound, while Śiva will produce a loud sound. 1177.
In Śiva, who is gentle, the sound is thick; in Śakti, it is the opposite.
One should hold Śakti with the left hand and Śiva with the right hand;
thus one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice (aśvamedha), but otherwise, one incurs fault.
The deity is Tumburu; Śakti is in the pair, and Śiva is in Śakti.

For the attainment of powers such as *druta* and others, its maintenance through sound (*nāda*) with the fingers raised is called "Kalpanā" (Mental Construction); its function is the holding of the *tāla*. 1180.
"All the *pāṭas* here have been proclaimed by Niḥśaṅkaśārṅgadeva. (1181) Thus ends the definition of *tāla*.
The two bronze cymbals (*kāṃsyatāla*) are similar in shape and resemble lotus petals.
In a vessel made of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*), the mouth measures thirteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and the two bases measure two finger-breadths each;
the middle parts are one finger-breadth wide and deep, while the rest of those two [bases] is like a palm-leaf (*tāla*).
The *pāṭā*, *jhanakaṭā*, and others are the primary types, though there are other varieties of *pāṭā* as well.
"Nārada is the presiding deity here," thus it was said by the son of Soḍhala (verse 1184).
This concludes the definition of the *kāṃsyatāla*.
A bell made of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*) should be half a finger-breadth in thickness.
Eight finger-breadths in height, wide at the mouth and narrow at its base, it is attached to the temple, shaped like a pin,
and joined to the foundation while supporting a staff with three prongs at its tip.

Holding that downward-facing [instrument] by its handle with the left hand— the one which has a six-finger-long and a half-finger-thick iron tongue hanging down inside— it, the wise man, should play it with many *ṭaṇat* sounds. 1187.
That [bell] is sounded by those who know it during the worship of the deities for all the gods.
Thus ends the description of the bell.
