It should consist of two hollow cups made of bell-metal, with a sharp spherical interior. 1188–1189.
Solid, made of a fine variety of jujube seeds, with strings placed through holes in their heads, these are small bells; they are called *ghargharikās* in the world, as well as *ghargharas*. (1190)
With those [small bells], the supreme performance of various *gharghara* rhythms is achieved in dancing.
(1191) Thus ends the definition of the small bell (*kṣudraghaṇṭikā*).
It should be made of bronze, one cubit in length, and half a finger-breadth thick in its mass. (1192)
The *jayaghaṇṭā* (victory-bell) should be even, smooth, round, and provided with two holes at its edge; holding it by a string placed through those holes with the left hand,
one should strike it with the right hand using a firm corner [of the palm] held on the right side.
"All recitations of this [goddess] by the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow consist largely of the syllable 'ḍeṃkāra'. (1193) Thus ends the description of the Jayaghaṇṭā.
It may be made of Khadira wood, or from solid bamboo, or else from four pieces of Kamra wood. (1194)
It is smooth, with a width of two finger-breadths and a length of twelve finger-breadths;
the central mass is as beautiful as possible, being slightly less at both ends.
That which possesses such a reed-pipe (*kamrikā*) is the musical instrument; in that [instrument], there are two reeds each.
Placing one *kamrikā* on each hand,
holding one at the base of the middle finger and the thumb, and then holding the other at the tip of those same fingers, one should play them with a relaxed mind.
The sounding of the *kamrikā* by shaking the wrist is considered [the *maṇibandha-kampa*];
therein are the *pāṭas*, primarily the *kiṭakiṭa*, as well as other varieties of *pāṭas*.
Having created an interval between the *kamras*, with the right-hand ring finger—

Others have declared that for the left hand, there should be striking with the palm and rubbing with the thumb (1199). Thus ends the description of the *kamra* [type of lute]. Furthermore, it may be shaped like a serpent, concave, made of bell-metal, or made of iron.
The oyster-shell [mirror] is considered to be three finger-breadths in width and two and a half cubits in length;
it is adorned with horizontal lines and resembles a deer's horn, being polished by means of a straight iron point applied with force. (1200–1201)
It is played as "kirikiṭṭe," according to the reading; the deities here are the Yakṣas.
Regarding the realization of the measure (mātrā) in this [rhythm], it was stated by Niḥśaṅka Sūri that what is called "kirikiṭṭaka" is beloved of Rudra in the world. 1202.
Thus ends the section on the *śuktivādya*.
A cloth-strip (*paṭṭa*) made from *śrīparṇī* wood should be four-cornered and long;
it is said by others to be thirty-two finger-breadths in length, or thirty finger-breadths.
It should be one cubit in width, with two iron rods positioned vertically above and below,
resembling triple-stranded ropes and joined by an even number of small rings inserted through them.
That which is played while being held against the chest, the throat, or between the knees,
and which is smeared with resin and rubbed by the tips of the fingers—
this is recognized here as the *karava*, *thaḍaraṭa*, *pāṭa*, and *pāṭaha* drums. (1206)
"Seven divine sages are declared here as the deities of the *śārṅgin* [drum]"; thus ends the section on the *paṭṭa* drum. Furthermore, there are many other musical instruments in the world as well.
Regarding these, Soḍhalātmaja remains indifferent due to the fear of prolixity. (1208) Thus ends the definition of the *ghana* drum. [The types of sound are:
passionate (*rakta*), dispassionate (*virakta*), sweet (*madhura*), even (*sama*), pure (*śuddha*), soft (*kala*), and thick (*ghana*).
The son of Soḍhala has described ten types of musical instruments, characterized by clear strokes, ease of playing, and renown for their qualities;
in this context, the names are literal, and they are considered to be eightfold when grouped together. 1209–1210.

It begins with the syllables and the limbs [of the body], followed by the *tālas* and preceded by the *yatis*; it includes the *layas* and so forth, along with the *nyāsa* and *apanyāsa*, as well as the *pāṇisama*. Likewise, there is the *akṣarasama*, which follows the long and short syllables (*guru-laghu*) of the song.

Furthermore, that in which the structural components (aṅga) of a song—such as its beginning (graha), its conclusion (mokṣa), and so forth—are present, is considered *tālasama*; it follows the rhythm (*tāla*) and is regarded as being equal to the rhythm.
A *yati* is the placement of a pause (*nyāsa*), and it is characterized by the symmetry of that placement.
The four types of *sama* should be understood in sequence, beginning with *yati* and so forth.
That which is equal through the *gīta-grahas* known as *pāṇis* is considered *pāṇisama*.
These are declared to be the qualities of instrumental music (*vādya*); its opposite constitutes a defect.
Thus are the qualities and defects of the instruments:

one who knows how to strike with the hand and the corner [of the instrument], who is skilled in singing and playing, who is conversant with *yatitāla* and rhythm (*laya*), who knows the *pāṭas*, and who possesses the five types of *sañcavas*. 1215.

Endowed with tenfold qualities of the hand, he speaks according to the intended meaning of the vessel; he knows the true principles of musical instruments and understands the equalization of the scales (grahas); he is an expert in concealing the flaws in singing, instrumental performance, and dancing.
He knows the points for releasing the musical instruments, understands the proper measures of song and dance, knows all the varieties of instrumental music, possesses beauty and symmetry,
is skilled in striking the instruments, and can distinguish between all types of musical instruments.
A skilled debater is one who knows how to increase or diminish the resonance of his voice;
a debater deficient in even a few qualities—or indeed in all of them—is inferior.
[The hands] should follow the desire [of the speaker], be firm, distinct, smooth, with strong nails, and light. (1219–1220)
Hands that move the fingers with ease, are free from fatigue, possess mastered exertion, and are applied with proper blows are said to have tenfold merit. (1221) Thus end the qualities of the hands.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, on Instruments (Vādya), in the *Saṃgītaratnākara* composed by Śrī Śārṅgadeva—known as Niḥśaṅka, the son of Śrī Soḍhaladeva, the lord of the royal court and the enjoyer of stainless learning.
Now begins the seventh chapter, on Dance (Nartana). He whose bodily [expression] is the universe and whose vocal [expression] is all speech...
We bow to that auspicious Śiva, who is the source of the moon, stars, and other such [manifestations], and who is characterized by the quality of goodness (sattva).
By Śārṅgadeva, who has attained the wealth of unsurpassed knowledge through the grace of Śiva, this dance— which cuts away all suffering— is performed.
Drama (*nāṭya*), dance (*nṛtya*), and choreography (*nṛtta*)—thus it is proclaimed to be threefold.
In the beginning, the Four-faced One bestowed the *Nāṭyaveda* upon Bharata;
thereafter, Bharata [taught it] together with the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases.

He performed drama (*nāṭya*), dance (*nṛtya*), and choreographed movement (*nṛtta*) before Śambhu. Then, recollecting the performance he himself had previously employed, Hara instructed Bharata— through his foremost attendant, Taṇḍu— on that very same practice.
Out of affection, Pārvatī taught Lāsya to him (Śiva) in his presence;
then, having learned Tāṇḍava from Taṇḍu, the sages spoke of it to mortals.
Pārvatī, however, instructed Uṣā, the daughter of Bāṇa, in Lāsya.
By her [the practice] was taught to the cowherd women of Dvāravatī; by them, to the women of Saurāṣṭra;
and by them, the women residing in various other lands were instructed.
Thus, having been transmitted through this succession, it became established in the world.
Having sequentially extracted from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as from the Atharva Veda,
the recitations, dramatic gestures, songs, and aesthetic sentiments, the Lotus-born One (Brahmā) composed these three [epics], which bestow dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.

It is the promoter of fame, confidence, good fortune, and cleverness; the cause of generosity, steadfastness, fortitude, and elegance. It is the means for severing the pain of suffering, grief, despondency, and exhaustion. (10–11)
This [world] is certainly superior even to the bliss of Brahman and the like;
otherwise, how could it have captivated the minds of Nārada and others? (12) Nothing whatsoever is seen in this world that is more worthy of being seen or heard than this. (13)
One should always behold those two— nāṭya and nṛtya— which, though their purpose has been accomplished, bestow desired results without affliction, especially during festival times;
for among these, *nṛtta* is performed at the great festival of the consecration of kings.
During a journey, a procession of the gods, a wedding, a meeting with a beloved,
upon entering cities or houses, and at the birth of a son— the auspicious hymn spoken by Brahmā should be employed in all such rites.
Therefore, we shall now describe the detailed exposition of the triad beginning with drama (*nāṭya*).
The word *nāṭya* is primarily applied to aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), for it is the cause of the manifestation of flavor.
It is endowed with the fourfold representation (*abhinaya*) and is understood by the wise through its secondary metaphorical function (*lakṣaṇā*).
Dancing is called *nāṭya*, and that here constitutes *abhinaya* (acting).

It consists of the *vibhāvas* and so forth composed in poetry, which, as the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) residing in the actor, generates for the members of the audience an unimpeded cognition of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). (18–19)
In the determination of rasa, I shall describe the characteristics and other qualities of the excitants (vibhāva) and so forth.

Therein, abhinaya is fourfold: the physical (āṅgika), the vocal (vācika), the artificial (āhārya), and another, the internal (sāttvika). Among these, the physical is considered that which is manifested by means of the limbs. 20–21.
That which is composed by speech, such as poetry and drama, is the vocal (vācika);
that which consists of ornaments such as necklaces, armlets, and crowns is the artificial (āhārya);
and that which is manifested by the actor through the internal states (sāttvika-bhāvas) is the natural (sāttvika). 22–23.
The manner of its performance is proclaimed to be twofold:

that pertaining to worldly life and that pertaining to drama; and these two types, moreover, are further [divided], one being that which conveys internal mental states and the other being that which imitates external objects. (24)
Thus, the ancient authorities on worldly conduct have declared two types [of movement]:
one that relies upon the *kaiśikī* style for use in drama, and the other which produces worldly beauty appropriate to that [drama] through movements such as the *āveṣṭita*. 25–26.

The wise have declared that this world proceeds by subsisting on only a portion [of the arts], and thus there exists another, the dramatic art (*nāṭyadharmī*); they speak of this as a pair of distinctions.
For it is through bodily gestures (*āṅgika*) alone that [the dramatic art] manifests the internal states (*bhāva*).

That dance is known by the term *mārga* among those who understand dancing (28). However, those who know *nṛtta* recognize *nṛtta* as consisting merely of the movement of the limbs, devoid of all dramatic representation (*abhinaya*), according to the methods described for the *aṅgika* [acting] (29).
This pair, namely *tāṇḍava* and *lāsya*, is declared to be twofold;
it is primarily performed with *vardhamāna*, *āsārita*, and other songs accompanied by their respective *dhruvā* refrains, as well as with *karaṇas* and *aṅgahāras*. 30.
The *taṇḍava* is considered to be characterized by movements that are mostly forceful and vigorous;
the *lāsya*, however, consists of delicate limbs and increases the power of the god of love (Kāma).
Others recognize three further varieties: the *viṣama*, the *vikaṭa*, and the *laghu*.
In that [type of dance], the straight circular movements and so forth may be irregular (viṣama). That which possesses deformed dress, limbs, and gestures is considered "vikaṭa" (monstrous);
that which is accompanied by few *karaṇas* such as the *añcita* and others is known as "laghu" (light). 33–34.

That which consists of the representation of the meaning of sentences and the meaning of words found within a drama, endowed with aesthetic flavor (rasa) and emotion (bhāva), was first described by Bharata as "dramatic art" (nāṭya);
therefore, it is employed specifically within dramas. 35. Since it is contained therein, [it is not found elsewhere].
Having set aside the three types of abhinaya, the *āṅgika* (physical) is described here.
Of that, *śākhā*, *aṅkura*, and *nṛtta* are considered the primary triad; therein, *śākhā* is renowned as the manifold movement of the hands. 36–37.

The performance (vartanā) that proceeds by depending upon the meaning of an already existing sentence would be a "needle" (sūcī), because it depends upon a sentence yet to come. (38) Dance (nṛtta) is said to be that which is accomplished through instrumental gestures and bodily movements.
In this context, the needle and the finger are mentioned incidentally as being useful;
however, the six limbs here are said to be the head, the hands, the chest, the sides, the hips, and the feet, though others have also declared the shoulders to be included. 39–40.

Regarding the secondary limbs (pratyaṅga), some say there are six here: the neck, the two arms, the back, the belly, the two thighs, and the two shanks; others, however, declare three more: the two wrists, the two knees, and the ornaments. 41.
The eyes, the eyebrows, the pupils, the two cheeks, the breath of the nose,
the lower lip, the teeth, the tongue, and likewise the chin—
these twelve are the secondary limbs (*upāṅga*) of the head, as well as the other parts of the body. 42.
The heels, the ankles, the toes, and the soles of the hands and feet;
the complexion of the face, the movements of the hands, and the techniques—these are the fields of the hands. Furthermore, the techniques are twofold. (43–44)
Pure [movements] preceded by leaps, *aṅgahāras* with *recakas*, pure *cārīs* established in regional styles (*deśī*), as well as the postures (*sthānakas*), the dramatic modes (*vṛttis*),
the rules of conduct (*nyāyas*) along with the *pravicāras*, and all the *maṇḍalas* as well. 45–46.

Then follow the components of *lāsya*, the lines [of the stage], the exertion, the characteristics of the performer, the merits and defects, and his adornment; likewise, the characteristics of the teacher, the tradition, its merits and defects, and the pure method of instruction. (47)
Then follows the proper rule for the *gauṇḍalī* dance, the characteristics of the *peraṇi*, and its manual;

thereafter, the definitions of the teacher (*ācārya*), the actor (*naṭa*), and the dancer (*nartaka*), as well as the herald (*vaitālika*), the bard (*cāraṇa*), the *kolāṭika*, and the members of the assembly (*sabhāsada*). 48–49.
In this chapter, we shall explain in due order the assembly hall, its arrangement, the characteristics of rasa, and the characteristics of bhāva; as well as *dhuta*,
*vidhuta*, *ādhūta*, *avadhūta*, and *kampita*.

The head should be known as being of fourteen types: *ākampita* (shaken), *udvāhita* (raised), *parivāhita* (swayed), *mañcita* (bent forward), *nihatita* (lowered), *parāvṛtta* (turned back), *utkṣipta* (lifted up), *adhomukha* (downward-facing), and likewise *lolita* (waved). 51–52.

Others have declared five further varieties: the head tilted sideways, the head raised, the shoulders bent forward, the *ārātrika* (the head held level with the chest), and the head turned toward the side.
The head is said to be "shaken" (*dhuta*) when it is slowly moved sideways in succession.

Bharata and others have prescribed the use of *eva* for one who remains standing in an empty place while looking toward the side, as well as in cases of lack of confidence, astonishment, dejection, non-desire, and negation. (54–55)

Thus, that which is shaken with rapid motion is "dhuta"; it is employed for one afflicted by cold, for one suffering from fever, for one who is terrified, and likewise for one who has just drunk wine. 56
Thus, the head is considered *vidhuta* when it is shaken once, and *ādhūta* when moved sideways or upwards;
it is used for looking at one's own limbs with pride or for glancing sideways or upwards.
And when there is the conceit "I am capable," its application is proclaimed [as *adhūta*]. Thus, that which is shaken downward once and brought down is called *avadhūta*.
The wise say that this [term] should be employed when indicating half a place by its location, as well as in conversation regarding perception and the vehicle;
thus is the *Avadhūta*. 58.
The head, shaken by rapid up-and-down movements many times, is to be employed in cases of knowledge, acceptance, anger, deliberation, and likewise in threatening;
as well as when there is a question posed with haste. (59)
Thus, if that same *kampita* is performed twice slowly, it becomes *ākampita*. This [term] is used in the eastern tradition for indication, questioning, naming, and instruction.
It is employed for summoning and for describing that which resides within one's own mind. Thus, the "trembling" [gesture] is described as the head being raised once; it is called "uplifted."
"I am capable in this task"—it is in such self-conceit that [the term] *prayujyate* (is employed).
Thus, *udvāhitam* means raised up; *parimaṇḍalitākārabhrāmitam* means whirled in a circular form; and *parivāhitam* means carried around.
Experts in discernment state that this movement of the head is used for pride arising from the weight of modesty, as well as for mimicking a beloved;
likewise, for astonishment, a smile, joy, indignation, approval, and deliberation. (63–64)
Thus, the head should be turned away, slightly bent toward the side with the neck inclined;
this is to be employed in cases of pain, anxiety, delusion, and fainting, as well as when supporting the jaw.
Thus,
with the tips of the arms raised and the neck bent down,
she is curved in playful grace, charm, pride, coquetry, and passionate agitation. (66)
That [grace] occurs in the states of coquetry (*moṭṭāyita*), affectedness (*kuṭṭamita*), pride (*māna*), and paralysis (*stambha*).

*Vilāsa* consists of movements such as walking and so forth, performed by one whose limbs are embraced [by passion]. They know *lalita* to be the delicacy of the limbs and minor members of another woman. 67.
*Vivvoka* is disregard born of pride upon obtaining a desired object.
*Kilakiñcita* is said to be weeping, laughing, and so forth, arising from joy.
*Moṭṭāyita* is the state of being absorbed in the beloved during conversations, glances, and the like. 68–69.
When joy arises from the seizing of the hair and so forth, that which consists of acting like one who is suffering is *kuṭṭamita*; pride born of affection is *māna*;
and the state of inactivity during the first union with a beloved is *stambha*. 70–71.
Thus, "nihañcita" refers to the head being turned away; it is described as being rotated when the face is withdrawn due to anger,
shame, or similar causes.
In imitation of turning away, in looking behind,
and likewise when the face is turned upward, the head is to be known as *utkṣipta* (uplifted); it is employed for the sight of lofty objects moving in the sky, such as the moon and so forth.
Thus, "uplifted" (utkṣipta) would be a literal name for bowing down out of shame or sorrow; thus [the face] is downward-turned (adhomukha).
74 Thus [ends the section on] the downward-turned face.
The head should be swaying with eyes slackened in every direction;
that is considered [the posture] for sleep, sickness, possession by a spirit, intoxication, and fainting.
(75) Thus ends the description of *lolita*.

When the head reaches a state of being tilted and raised sideways, that application is declared by experts to be *tiryaṅnatonnata* (sideways-tilted-and-raised) in the *vivvoka* and other gestures of lovely women.
Thus ends *tiryaṅnatonnata*.
That which is called "leaning on the shoulder" (skandhānata) is that head which is placed upon the shoulder;
it is employed during sleep, intoxication, fainting, and in anxious reflection.
Thus ends [the section on] leaning on the shoulder.
Having slightly embraced the shoulders, the *ārātrika* is considered to be performed while moving around;
it is observed in cases of wonder and when perceiving the intentions of others.
(78) Thus ends the section on the *ārātrika*.

The natural head is considered even in the expression of natural state; it is "even" when facing the side, and it is appropriately termed "side-facing" when looking at someone standing at the side. 79
Thus, facing the side; these are the five types of head-gestures:
*patāka*, *tripatāka*, the one called *ardhacandra*, and *kartarīmukha*.
The curved fist (arālamuṣṭi), the peak (śikhara), the wood-apple (kapittha), the scissor-mouth (khaṭakāmukha),

the parrot-beak (śukatuṇḍa), the heron’s beak (kāṅgūla), the lotus-bud (padmakośa), the tender leaf (alapallava), the needle-mouth (sūcīmukha), the serpent-head (sarpaśiras), and the fourfold deer-head (mṛgaśīrṣaka). 80–81.
The Haṃsāsya, the Haṃsapakṣa, the Bhramara, the Mukula,
the Ūrṇanābha, the Sandaṃśa, and another hand called the Tāmracūḍa—
these twenty-four hands are considered to be uncombined (asaṃyuta). 82.
Due to the requirements of dramatic performance, their combination is also accepted:
the añjali, the one called kapota, the karkaṭa, the svastika, as well as the dolā, puṣpapuṭa, utsaṅga, khaṭakā, and vardhamānaka. 83–84.
The *gajadanta*, *āvahittha*, *niṣadha*, *makara*,
and *vardhamāna*— these joined hands (*saṃyuta-hasta*) are thirteen;
these are considered by the Sage to be the thirty-seven *abhinaya-hastas*.
Then, the two hands, with palms facing upward, are called *talamukha*;
when they form a *svastika*, they are known as *viprakīrṇa*; the *arāla* and *khaṭakāmukha* gestures;
the *āviddhavaktra* and *sūcyāsya*; and the *recita* and *ardharecita*. (87)
The *nitamba*, *pallava*, *keśabandha*, *uttānavañcita*, *latākhya*, *karihasta*, and that which is called *pakṣavañcitaka*— these are the [hand gestures]. 88.
The two wings of the bow that illuminates the quarters are the two wings of Garuḍa (89).
The hands may be positioned in the upward circle (*ūrdhvamaṇḍalinau*), the side circles (*pārśvamaṇḍalinau*),
the chest circles (*uro-maṇḍalinau*), or the chest-side half-circles (*uraḥ-pārśvārdha-maṇḍalau*) (90).
The Muṣṭika, Svastika, Avantya, Nalinī, Padmakośaka, Alapadma, Ulbaṇa, Valita, and Lalita—
these thirty dance-hands (nṛttahasta) are considered to be employed exclusively in dance. 91.
According to the scriptures and the oral tradition, they say that these [terms] apply to dramatic representation (*abhinaya*) as well.
For the Sage declares that the two called *latā* pertain to both dance (*nṛtta*) and dramatic representation (*abhinaya*);
therefore, by association, the others are also indicated as pertaining to dramatic representation.
Through reasoning, tradition, and worldly convention, there arises here a specific cognition;
for just as an elephant is represented in the world by means of its trunk, so too is this accepted by Bhaṭṭa Abhinavagupta and others. 94.
And all these hands, when combined, amount to sixty-seven (95).
Their number being sixty-four is not within the scope of logic or scripture;
thus, let the wise consider their number to be sixty-four (96).
The two hands should be formed into *svastika*s with the fingers spread apart;
for when the two hands have become *svastika* and are then moved apart, they are called *viprakīrṇaka*. Therefore, there is no application of the *viprakīrṇaka* gesture for independent [hands].
In this case, for the two side-mandalas, just as with the central mandala, the two "tender sprouts" (alapa-pallava) must be employed as qualifiers for the two [deities] who are preeminent;
furthermore, the qualifier and the qualified should not reside in different locations. 98–99.
In the expression "a blue lotus," two lotuses are certainly not intended;
this reasoning has been stated by me for the sake of establishing what is well-known.
For all the Teachers, however, there are distinct definitions for each [term].
When used in gestures such as the *svastika* and others, it is not considered a qualifying attribute (of the hand).
Furthermore, in the *nikuñcaka* gesture, the hand has two peaks; however, when combined with other *nṛttahastas*, the *varada* and *abhaya* [mudrās] are added. 101–102.

Some teachers, speaking thus, have stated that [the height] is seventy *hasta*s; even if there is a slight variation in their measurements, there is no difference in their ritual applications (103). The thumb should be bent and joined at the base of the index finger.
The *patāka* (flag) mudrā has a compact form with the fingers and palm extended.
(104) This [mudrā] is used for touching, slapping, clapping the hands, and so forth;
when representing flames rising upwards, its fingers are sparse and moving. (105)

When the wings are positioned at the waist, the hand moving downward through the streams [of water] is used for the bird's flight; moving upward, it is used for striking with a lotus leaf when held aloft;
and moving upward from the region of the waist, it is employed in the gesture of lifting up. 106.
When facing forward, it is the field of the mouth; coming from one's own side, it is on one's own side. When trembling, it serves for prohibition;
when quickly rubbing while presiding over the *patāka* [hand gesture], it is supreme for cleansing. 107–108.

While gently rubbing a banner, as well as in massaging, wiping, lifting, or holding heavy objects such as stones, these two [hands] should be employed facing one another when they are appropriate for the task. 109. When they have slipped from their position, they should be brought back into mutual alignment.
With fingers moving up and down and flickering, it denotes the force of wind and waves (110).
Thus is the *patāka* [gesture];
that same gesture becomes the *tripatāka* when the ring finger is bent.
It is prescribed for touching auspicious substances such as curd and the like (111).

One should turn one's face away during an invitation; by contracting two fingers at the joint, with the pair of fingers cast outward and the palm facing downward, this gesture is used when rejecting with disregard (112).

In the act of salutation (namaskāra), this [mudrā] should be performed with the palms at the sides and placed upon the head; it is considered appropriate for raising the face when both pairs of fingers are turned upward.
When in doubt, one should hold the two fingers in a sequence of alternating depression and elevation.
When wearing a turban (*uṣṇīṣa*), one should move it with the face downward at the edge of the head;
likewise, when wearing a crown (*kirīṭa*), it should be positioned above the top of the head.
In the event of undesirable odors, speech, or sounds, one should close the nostrils, mouth, and ears.
Moving the two fingers sequentially through the subtle currents of the bird-like [subtle] channels— upward, downward, and sideways— one should likewise hold them while the hand,
with its fingers moving downward, reaches the region of the hips.
While wiping away tears, she should hold her ring finger downward;
when applying collyrium to the region of the eyes, she should hold it toward the forehead; and when removing curls from the hair, she should hold it together with the thumb.
Thus is the *tripatāka* [gesture].
When the fingers are joined on one side and the thumb remains on the other, that which shines with the form of a crescent moon is called the *ardhacandra*. 119

The *ardhendau* (half-moon) posture described above, when directed upward, is used for the "young tree" (*bālapādapa*); however, when turned away, it is used in dejection. Holding the cheek-plate (*kapolaphalaka*), it should be employed with force for emaciating the waist and for expulsion and other such acts. 120.
When the middle finger of the *tripatāka* hand is positioned on the back with its middle unjoined and the index finger is like a half-moon, then it is the *kartarīmukha* (scissors-mouth) mudrā.
When dyeing the feet with lac-dye and the like, upon falling [on the ground],

one should again place the middle finger in the position of the index finger; then, while facing downward, one should hold the index finger in that very same place, and finally, with the hand turned upward, one should engage in reading the written text.

Thus is the *kartarīmukha* [mudrā]: among the fingers beginning with the index finger (*tarjanī*), each subsequent one is further away and more elevated than the preceding; it is slightly curved, while the index finger itself is curved like a bow. 124.
Where the thumb is bent, that is called the *arāla* [mudrā]; it is prescribed for blessings and the like, and when held at the heart by men.
Next, regarding women, it is used for binding the hair and for loosening the hair.
Twice or thrice, one should perform a circular motion on one's own side from the other side. When approaching a crowd of people, there should be a beckoning with falling fingers;
however, at a wedding, it is joined in the form of a svastika held at the tips of the fingers.

In performing circumambulation of the deities, one should rotate clockwise; furthermore, while turning, both hands should be joined at the heart alone. Regarding incoherent speech such as "Who are you?", "Who am I?", or "What is our connection?", [one should remain silent].
Furthermore, when the fingers are repeatedly flicked outward while the hand remains at the forehead—
whether for wiping away sweat from the forehead or when the three folds of the brow are raised—
it is called *itārāla*.
When the tips of the fingers are placed on the palm, held without being concealed, and the thumb remains pressing against the middle finger, it is known as the *muṣṭi* (fist) mudrā;
it is used for seizing spears, swords, staffs, and the like in various forms of combat. 130.
In washing, the thumb is turned forward; in wrestling, both hands [are used].
(131) Thus is the fist (*muṣṭi*).
When the thumb is raised upward from the fist, it is employed as the *śikhara* [hand-gesture]. (132)
In the discharge of spears and javelins, in the grasping of bows, barbed arrows, and goads, and in the binding of hair-tufts, the fist must be employed; this too is to be learned from the world.
Thus ends the section on the *śikhara*.

If the index finger, with its tip touching the tip of the thumb, forms a *kapittha* (wood-apple) shape at the peak [of the hand], then it should be employed for holding a spear (*kunta*) or a thunderbolt (*vajra*),
as well as for the wheel, bow, mace, and other weapons, and for actions such as drawing an arrow. 134.
"Somewhere, the two *kapittha* tips [of the fingers] have their functions interchanged.
(135) Thus, the *kapittha* [mudrā]: the ring finger and the little finger are raised and bent. (136)
If the hand is sparse, it is the "wood-apple" (kapittha) gesture;
then, when holding the reins or a chowrie for a horse and so forth, it is the "upturned palm" (khaṭakāmukha).
Likewise, it is used in the gathering of flowers and in wearing a string of pearls or a garland. 137.
It is prescribed for drawing a reed from a thicket, for grasping a mirror face-to-face,
for grinding substances such as musk, and for cutting the stems of betel rolls and the like. 138–139.
Thus, when the index and ring fingers of the *arāla* hand are extremely curved like the beak of a parrot, it is the *khaṭakāmukha*;
that [gesture] should be used with love and anger by a woman.

In the same way, when saying "not you," "not I," or "I have no business with you," one should extend the fingers in sequence— outward, inward, and again outward— during a dismissive dismissal, such as the throwing down of dice in gambling and the like, or during an invitation. (140–141)
Thus, the *śukatuṇḍa* [mudrā] is formed when the ring finger is bent at the knuckle, the little finger is raised,
and the index, middle, and thumb fingers are positioned like the three sacrificial fires (*tretāgni*). 142.
"When the fruit is small and the morsel measured, such as in the case of a cat's paw and so forth, and even when the chin is held [by the teacher], this is prescribed for children"—
thus says Kāṅgūla (verse 143).

That hand in which the fingers, including the thumb, have their tips joined, are curved like a bow, and are slightly spread apart, is called the *padmakośa*; it should be employed for the worship of deities and for offerings (*bali*).
For scattering handfuls of flowers, the hand may have its tips scattered twice or thrice.
In fruits such as the *bilva* and *kapittha*, and in the jar-like breasts of women—
thus ends the section on the *padmakośa*.
Having performed the hand-position known as *vyāvartita*, they remain thus established.

He whose fingers run along the side of the palm is called *alapallava* (146). He is also known as *alalpadma*; some authorities state that this term refers to a position where the fingers are turned back (147).

To the two statements, "Whose [daughter] are you? and "I am not," women respond with denials such as "I am worthless" or "I am false. This concludes the minor digression. 148. Thus ends the *Alapallava*.

Where the index finger is extended upward while the hand is in the *khaṭakāmukha* position, that is the *sūcīmukha* (needle-mouth) hand; it is prescribed here for the representation of a weapon called a discus (*cakra*) as well as a potter’s tool. 149.
Moving within the circle of the chariot-wheel amidst the multitude of people, the index finger should become upward-facing, downward-facing, and likewise positioned at one's own side;
then it should gradually move from one side to its own side. 150–151.
The hand raised upward signifies a banner; when shaken, it signifies praise. When the index finger is raised alone, it signifies a threat. Placed at the nose, it signifies observing one's breath.
When joined below and on the side, it signifies union; when separated, it signifies separation.

When separation is to be expressed, it is proclaimed by Śārṅgadeva that the hand which has the *sūcīmukha* and *patāka* gestures with its middle part depressed is the *sarpaśiras* (serpent-head) hand. 153.
When giving water to the gods, this [hand] is turned upward;

when facing downward, it is used for the movement of serpents, for striking the frontal globes of elephants, for the slapping of arms by wrestlers, and is prescribed for wrestling matches and the like. 154–155.
Thus, when the serpent-head (sarpaśiras) mudrā has its thumb resting on the middle joint of the middle finger, with the little finger pointing upward, they know that hand to be *catura*. 156.
Others among the wise have taught that in the *patākā* [hand-gesture], the little finger is positioned at the base of the middle finger and slightly behind it (157).
In the *naya* [gesture], both hands are joined at the wrists and placed in the region of the face.
In the Vinaya, in deliberation, or when standing at one's side, the hand should be placed against the heart (158).

In reasoning and refutation, in play, or when entwined, the hand is joined with the fingers curled; in deceit, in rolling the dice, or when making a level surface, it should have the palm facing upward (159).
When the thumb and middle finger press against each other for softness, and these two are joined for skillful speech, they are declared to be *catura* (the clever). Thus ends the four [mudrās].
When the thumb and little finger are raised above the "serpent-head" hand,
that hand is then the "deer-head" (mṛgaśīrṣa); it should be turned face downwards for matters concerning today or the present, and for the upward casting of dice.
When situated in the *gaṇḍa* and other fields, it is for the wiping away of sweat from the *gaṇḍa* and other parts.
(162) Thus ends Mṛgaśīrṣa. The index finger, thumb, and middle finger are positioned in the three fires of the ascendant.
In the remaining cases, where the upward strokes are sparse, it is called *haṃsāsya*.
This [letter] is used for words meaning soft, insubstantial, smooth, small, loose, or light;
it conveys the senses of being rubbed (*mardita*), churned (*mathita*), cast away (*kṣipta*), foremost (*agra*), or shaken (*vidhūnita*).

"But in cases such as the gathering of flowers, it should be joined with the *aucitya* [proper decorum]," so said Haṃsavaktra (164). If the three fingers beginning with the index finger (*tarjanī*) have their bases slightly bent...
At that time, the hand of Patāka is said to be the "swan-wing" (haṃsapakṣa).
This [mudrā] is to be employed for sipping water (ācamana) and for anointing with sandalwood paste and the like;
however, when positioned on the region of the jaw, it serves for the removal of suffering and for supporting the jaw.
With their arms drawn into circles like great pillars, they were seen in direct embrace and in indirect embrace with hands joined in the *svastika* gesture (167).
Through the transitory states (*anubhāvas*) such as horripilation, this [state] occurs according to the specific rasa among the various rasas.
"Anubhāvas should be performed according to the influence of the rasa, even with the hands positioned elsewhere.
Thus ends the section on the *haṃsapakṣa* (swan-wing) gesture:
the tips of the thumb and middle finger are joined, and the index finger is considered [to be extended].
When the remaining part of the hand is positioned with the fingers extended upwards, it becomes the *bhramara* (bee) hand;
this is prescribed for grasping flowers on long stalks, as well as for ear-ornaments, palm leaves, extracting thorns, and similar tasks. (169–170)

Thus is the *bhramara* (bee) [mudrā]; when all the fingers are joined together with their tips touching the tip of the thumb and pointing upwards, it is the *mukula* (bud), used for the shape of lotus buds and the like. 171.
In the rites for the deceased, in the worship of the gods, in eating and other such acts, he repeatedly assumed his natural state;
yet when it came to giving with haste, or to kissing the mouths of beloved women in the presence of libertines, he remained transformed. (172)
The hand positioned on the breasts, armpits, or other such areas constitutes the *ācchuritaka* (the scratching gesture).
When one makes a sound while scratching the breasts or other parts with all five fingers, those who know the *Kāmasūtra* recognize that as the *ācchuritaka*.
Thus, when the five fingers are contracted like the bud of a lotus calyx, it is the *ūrṇanābha* (spider-web) mudrā;
it is used for seizing by theft, such as in the grasping of hair and similar acts. 175.
When scratching the head, those two [hands] should be placed in the region of the chin;
they should be formed into the *sakhastika* (crossed) position when [the hands] have claws as weapons, such as those of lions, tigers, and other beasts.
(176) Thus says Ūrṇanābha.
When the curved thumb and forefinger have their tips joined and the middle of the palm is slightly depressed, it is called *saṃdaṃśa* (the pincer).
This [mudrā] is of three kinds, in order: *agraja* (born from the tip), *mukhaja* (born from the mouth), and *pārśvaja* (born from the side). 177.
Facing forward, facing directly, or facing sideways—such are its characteristics (178).
The *agrasaṃdaṃśa* (fore-finger pinch) should be employed for extracting thorns, gathering delicate flowers, and the like; however, it is used out of anger when saying "fie! (179).
When removing a flower from its stalk, when applying a wick, a probe,
or eye-salve, the *mukhasaṃdaṃśa* (mouth-pincer) should be used; furthermore, the *pārśvaja-saṃdaṃśa* (side-pincer) is for the threading of pearls and likewise for piercing them.
This [gesture] was described by the venerable Śārṅgin as being used for the investigation of reality, for speaking with a companion,
for expressing anger, for slightly turning the tip of the hand with the left hand, and even for the crushing of lac-dye and similar substances. (181–182)

Thus is the *saṃdaṃśa* (tongs) gesture; if the little finger and ring finger are placed on the palm of the bee-gesture, it is then the *tāmracūḍa* (cock) hand, used for calling children or for scolding. 183

In the measurement of tempo (*tāla*) for songs and the like, as well as in matters requiring speed and confidence, one should employ the "clapping" (*choṭikā*), which consists of a snapping sound produced by the release of the fingers; this is known as *choṭikā*.
(184) When the little finger of a closed fist is extended, it assumes the state of a *tāmracūḍa* (cock).

Regarding the application (*viniyoga*) and the mention of its number as one thousand and so forth, some have said [it refers to recitations]; however, Niḥśaṅka did not accept this, because it is not observed in the case of the *lakṣas*.
Thus says Tāmracūḍa. (185)
The joining of the palms of the hands like the surface of a banner is considered the *añjali* gesture.
This should be performed by men respectively at the head, the face, or the chest when bowing to deities, gurus, and Brahmins; for women, it may be done as they wish.
When the fingers of this *kapota* (pigeon) gesture have their bases, tips, and sides joined together, those who know the hands recognize it by another name: the *kūrma* (tortoise). 188

In salutation, in conversation with a guru, and in accepting a request with humility, this [gesture] should be performed facing east with a nod of the head; it is used by women and eunuchs. (189) Thus ends the *kapota* [gesture].

When the fingers of both hands emerge from between one another and are seen both inside and outside, that is called the *karkaṭaka* (crab) mudrā. With the fingers positioned inward, it should be employed for reflection as well as yawning.
With the palms turned away and the fingers pointing upward, sideways, or forward, it is used for the wringing of limbs;
furthermore, when directed toward oneself on the large body, it resides in the region of the abdomen, while on the back, it rests upon the jaw with the fingers extended. 191–192.

With the fingers slightly contracted and turned toward one another in dejection, it is used for holding a conch; with the fingers extended outward during yawning and similar acts—this is the *karkaṭa* (crab) gesture. 193.
Thus ends the *karkaṭa*.
When one hand is at the wrist and the other hand is placed upon it, both hands situated on the left side of the body and turned upward, this is considered the *svastika* (crossed) gesture.
In this position, the hands may be held in the *ārāla* or *patāka* (flag) shapes, moving as required by the dramatic expression (*abhinaya*). 194.
The *svastika* (crossed-vault) is employed when one says "it is so" (*evamasti*) by women, as well as for the sky and the vast ocean; thus ends the description of the *svastika*. 195.
Thus, the *svastika*.
When the two banners hang down with slack shoulders and limp fingers, this is the *dolā* gesture;
it is used in illness, dejection, intoxication, fainting, and agitation, as appropriate, whether held stiffly or swaying to the side. (196–197)
Thus, the *dola* (swinging) hand-gesture,
with the tips of the fingers meeting at the outer sides, becomes the *puṣpapuṭa* (flower-bud) gesture;
it is used for taking or offering grains, flowers, fruits, and the like, as well as water.
"This [mudrā] is to be performed with a handful of flowers; thus it was taught by the son of Soḍhala.
(198) This concludes the *puṣpapuṭa*.
The two arms, placed upon each other's shoulders, are crossed in the form of a svastika.
The *utsaṅga* hand is described as having the two palms facing each other and spread out (199).
Some have stated that the *svastika* is located on the right side of the body, while others say it consists of the palms being turned downward with the fingers interlaced behind the armpits (200).

The wise know that the fingers of both hands, with their backs turned toward each other and the sides facing outward, are called *sarpaśīrṣa* (serpent-heads) when placed in the position of the palms; others say they are so called when used for an object requiring great effort, as well as for coldness and embracing. 201.
When women do not accept being soothed, or when there is shame and the like, this is the *utsaṅga* (lap) position;
the two hands, with palms facing outward (*khaṭakāmukha*), have their wrists joined in the *svastika* configuration.
Or, when facing one another, it is the *khaṭakāvardhamānaka* (203).
In the first opinion, this occurs among lovers during the grasping of the base of the [woman's] thighs and so forth;
in the other opinion, it occurs during the stringing of flowers, speaking the truth, and so forth (204).
When the two hands, like the heads of serpents, are placed between the shoulders and the elbows against one another, that is called the *gajadanta* (elephant-tusk) [mudrā].
When the elbows are bent and the two *sarpaśīrṣaka* (serpent-head) [hands] are positioned at the region of the shoulders, [it is likewise]. 205.
Others say that the mark on the elephant’s tusk consists of two [lines] facing each other;
this trunk, joined by its coming and going, is for the uprooting of mountain rocks,
and it serves to lead the bride and groom to the place of their wedding.
"In cases of seizing a pillar or excessive weight, [the application] spoken by the son of Śrī Soḍhala [is prescribed]. (208) Thus ends the section on the elephant-tusk.
When the two [instruments] are facing the chest and shaped like a parrot's beak with their tips pointing downwards, [they are used].
Having concealed [one's true state] and brought it down [to a lower level], where it is expressed with dissimulation (*avahittha*),
that occurs in cases of weakness, longing, sighing, and emaciation of the limbs.
(209) Thus ends *avahittha*.
From the wrapping of a bud with a wood-apple fruit, there arises the term *niṣadha*;
it is used for the correct grasping of the meaning of a scripture, as well as for pressing, for placing something properly, and for speaking that "this is indeed the truth. (210–211)

Some have called the first [mountain] Gajadanta, while others have called it Niṣadha; it is likewise considered to signify heroism, courage, profundity, pride, and so forth. (212) Thus ends the section on Niṣadha.
When two hands, known as *patāka*, are placed one above the other with their palms facing each other, their thumbs pointing upward, that is the *makara* hand (213).
It [is used] for crocodiles, sea-monsters, and the like, as well as for carnivorous beasts such as tigers.
In the mimetic representation of lions and the like, as well as for a surging river, this [gesture] is desired. (214) Thus ends the section on the Makara.
If the two wings of a swan are turned backward and assume the form of a *svastika*, (215) [it represents the following].

At that time, the *vardhamāna* hand should be used for opening a door-panel; likewise, the *vicyuta-svastika* is used for tearing open the chest. Others have stated that in this position, the *sarpaśīrṣa* and *haṃsapakṣa* hands are employed. 216.
Others accepted that [position] as being devoid of the *svastika*;
thus, the *vardhamāna* [hand-position] consists of the two hands facing forward with the shoulders and elbows aligned, forming the *khaṭakāmukha*.
When positioned on the chest or the region in front of the chest at a distance of eight finger-breadths from the breast,
the two hands are said to be "square" (caturasra) when used for drawing in garlands and other objects.
Thus they are square.
When the two hands have been made square and formed into the shape of swan’s wings—
one is moved upward while the other goes downward toward the chest—
then these two are called *udvṛttas* in the definition of the *tālavṛnta*.

Those two, known as the *tālavṛnta*, were declared by experts in dance to be used for the word "Victory" (*jaya*). Others, however, considered that the two called *haṃsapakṣa*, when turned away and turned around while facing east, should be employed when they are raised upward. 221–222.

Having thus become raised and remaining raised, the two "swan-wing" (haṃsapakṣa) hands form a triangle on their respective sides; when their palms are turned toward each other, they are known as *talamukha*.
The wise declare those two to be the "sweet" (*madhura*) sounds of the *mṛdaṅga* drum.
(223) Thus [are described] the *tala-mukha* hands; with palms joined like the wings of a swan, they form the *svastika-svastika* gesture. (224)

Thus, those two [breasts], which were previously spread out like swastikas, suddenly fall from their swastika position; they remain before her breasts with their tips either turned downward or upward.
Others sang of the two swan-wings turned away and scattered;
thus, having performed the *viprakīrṇa*, *patāka*, and *svastika* gestures, they executed the *vyāvṛtta* and *parivartana* movements.

Having performed the upward-facing lotus-bud gestures (*padmakośa*) with the hands turned outward and inward respectively (226), one should then, in sequence, execute the left hand with the palm facing upward and the fingers curved, while the other hand—
either in the *khaṭakāmukha* or another form— is held downward from a square position (227).
Alternatively, having formed the *ārāla* hands or having made them known as *khaṭakāmukha*, those two— being *ārāla-khaṭakāmukha*—
are employed in deliberation by merchants, ministers, and others. (228)

Others, however, say: the *arāla* [hand] is situated on the chest, facing forward, with the fingers curved like a *khaṭakāmukha*; its tip is raised, slightly extended sideways, or else the two hands are positioned on one's own sides with their palms turned outward.
Then, with the tips of the arms at the same level, there should be the *arāla* and *khaṭakāmukha* hand gestures;
thus are defined the *arāla-khaṭakāmukha* gestures when the tips of the arms,
the elbows, and the shoulders are gracefully positioned.
If, having quickly performed a withdrawal of the two *sata* hand-gestures with their banners raised, the hands are then placed below with their faces turned inward,
the experts say that these two constitute the application for *vikṣepa-valana*. 231–232.
Thus, with the faces turned inward,
the middle fingers joined with the thumbs, positioned at the corners of a square,
the two "serpent-head" hands extend their index fingers sideways in succession.
When the two hands, shaped like needle-points, are extended outward, they then form the *patāka* [hand-gesture].
First, these two should be performed with a turning and a revolving; some have stated that the specific feature here is the extension after having whirled. 233–234.

Some have stated that the definition of *sūcyāsya* consists of two hands in the form of a serpent’s head with the thumbs extended toward the middle, crossed in the *recita-svastika* position. Thus ends [the description of] the *sūcyāsya* mudrās.
The two hands with palms extended and turned upward are called *recita*;
alternatively, the *haṃsapakṣa* hands, when whirled rapidly, are declared to be *recita*.
Or rather, these two [definitions] are combined as the characteristics (*lakṣma*) of the *recita* hands. 236.
Those two were employed by Nṛsiṃha for the rending of the Daitya’s chest; thus, when released by one [hand] with a square movement, they become *ardharecita* (half-released). 237–238.

If the two *patāka* hands, having been extended sideways and then raised— one upward-facing and the other downward-facing— emerge from the region of the shoulders in succession and come to rest in the region of the hips;
When the two hands perform *recaka* and the hips are raised, it is called *nitamba*. Then, having extended the arms upward with a *vyāvartita* movement, they are rotated.
The two hands, when brought into the form of a svastika, are considered *pallava*;
some, however, describe them here as *tripatāka* when they are relaxed.
When the wrists are relaxed and the hands are raised and lowered like a lotus bud, they are called *padmakośa*. (240–241)
Others say that two sprouts (*pallava*) should be placed on his two sides or in front;
others have declared that they should be in the position of lotus-buds held in the hands, while still others say they are banners (*patākā*). Thus ends the section on the sprouts.

Those two hands which, rising from the sides, do not touch the sides as they move toward the head, and which, having emerged repeatedly from the region of the hair like buttocks, move back and forth separately, are considered *keśabandha*. 243.
Thus, for the gesture of binding the hair,
when the hands are positioned upon any one of the areas of the cheeks, shoulders, or forehead,
they form the *tripatāka* (three-fold crested) hand, slightly turned sideways and facing each other.
When the palms move slightly upward from the shoulders and elbows, having remained there for a moment and then shifting, they are to be known as *uttāna-vañcita*.
Others maintain that there is a slight downward movement of the shoulders and elbows [in this case]. 245–246.
Thus, the two *patāka* hands, deceived while turned upward, are swung and extended obliquely; these are the *latākara* gestures, as well as those for binding hair and for the hips.

Some teachers maintain that it has the form of a triple-bannered hand (tripatākā). Thus, when the two *latā* hands touch [the head] and take the shape of an elephant’s trunk on both sides, it is the *latākara*.
When one [hand] is raised and the other is swung while resting at the ear in the *khaṭakāmukha* position, or likewise in the *tripatāka* position, they know this as the *karihasta*.
Now, why is the dual number not used here, as it is in the case of the other hands? 248–249.
We say that where both hands of the same genus are expressed by a single word, there the dual number applies, as in the case of "two jars" or "two squares" (250);
whereas for two words that are distinct and of different genera, the dual number applies to those two.
Just as a jar and a cloth might take the forms of an *arāla* and a *khaṭakāmukha*, respectively, here a single vine-hand (*latākara*) is seen to have the shape of an elephant’s trunk;
yet its function (*itikartavyatā*) would be different, and therefore it is designated by the singular number. (251–252)

Nor is there here the state of being a "trunk" (karihasta) as a single entity, like "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) in each individual case; nor is it that one member, "elephant" (karī), is denoted by the word while the other is "hand" (hasta).
It is neither an *ekaśeṣa* nor a *dvandva* compound, for [in those cases] a dual number would occur. (253)
And the singular number was employed by the all-seeing Sage with reference to that which is supported [by the hands].
(254) "With the two *tripatāka* hands placed on the hips and the tips bent like wings—this is the *pakṣavañcita*.
(255) Thus ends the description of the *pakṣavañcita*.
These two, with their tips turned toward the sides, are considered the *pakṣapradyotaka* (wing-illuminators).
Others, however, say that these hands shine when they are turned upward with fingers pointing up and facing away [from the body], immediately following the previous pair. 256.
Thus, while one [hand] illuminates the shoulder and moves like a swan’s wing toward the chest, the other, moving gracefully and obliquely extended, acts as a creeper-like hand beside it. (257)
In this manner, by means of another limb, the two wings (daṇḍapakṣau) are formed in sequence;
however, others consider the stretching out of the hands to occur here simultaneously. Thus ends the description of the *daṇḍapakṣau*.
With faces turned downward, situated in the region of the hips with elbows bent,
the two *patāka* hands moving swiftly sideways and upward constitute the *garuḍapakṣaka*;
these have been described by some as *tripatāka*, but they are not considered such by the Sage.

Thus, his two hands, like the wings of a Garuḍa, having reached the forehead from the region of the chest and arrived at its sides, were spread wide in a circular whirling motion, forming an upward-pointing circle.
Others say that these two marks extend as far as the forehead;

they are known as the *cakravartinikā* among those who know the science of dance. Others, however, state that when these two are shaped like banners (*patākā*), placed at the sides facing one another, they are called *pārśvamaṇḍalinau*; yet others say they are so called when [the hands] are on their own respective sides.
Experts in dance consider that when the arms are cast and whirled, these two [positions] are known as *kakṣavartanikā* and *pārśvamaṇḍalī*.
Thus ends the section on the *pārśvamaṇḍalī* positions.

Having performed the *udveṣṭita* (unwinding) and *paveṣṭita* (twisting) movements simultaneously, the two hands move to their respective sides from the chest; then, by rotating in a circular manner (*maṇḍala*), they reach the chest again in reverse order—these are the *ura-maṇḍalina* hand gestures. 265.
Others say that when these two are located on the chest,
their rotation is called *urovartanikā* by those who know them; others, however, call these two "swan's wings" (*haṃsapakṣau*) among the three types of upward circular movements (*ūrdhvamaṇḍali*).

Thus, the two *uromaṇḍalinas* are formed when one hand is placed flat upon the chest while the other is extended along the side; when these are rotated, they form the *nālapadmī* position, with the hand resting on the chest. 268.
One hand is led to one's own side by means of the action of twisting (udveṣṭita);
at that very moment, having attained a curved state, the chest assumes a circular form.
Likewise, through the practice of the hands, both the chest and the sides become half-circular (ardhamaṇḍala). 269–270.

Having repeatedly formed one hand with the chest and side as half-circles and a curved shape through the movement of the fingers, and likewise the other hand as a fresh sprout, they are then made into the form of a *svastika* in succession. 271

If the hands have the *khaṭakāmukha* form and are in the *muṣṭika-svastika* position, they are then called *kapittha*; or else, if the fists are in the shape of a *śikhara* or in the form of a *svastika*, the two hands, being unjoined, constitute the *vyāvṛtta-svastika*. (272)

Thus, having formed the *muṣṭika* and *svastika* gestures facing away from each other, those which are then made into *padmakośas* are called *nalinī-padmakośa*; however, others have described them differently.
When two lotus buds, facing one another with their wrist-joints joined,
are separated by a rotation and turning, some say they constitute the *nalinī-padmakośa* (the lotus-bud gesture of the goddess Nalinī). 274–275.

Others have stated that the characteristic mark is when these two lotus-buds, having turned away and then turned around, reach the vicinity of the shoulders and breasts, or alternatively, reach the vicinity of the knees. 276.

Thus, the two lotus-buds of her hands performed the action of unfolding; reaching the vicinity of her shoulders from their position upon the field of her chest, those two lotuses of her arms extended outward like tender sprouts.
If, having extended the fingers toward the shoulders with the hands facing the shoulders,
the two palms are turned upward like lotuses, they are then called *ulbaṇau*.
Thus [are] the *ulbaṇau*.
When joined by the elbows in a cross (svastika) and curved like creepers, they are considered *latā*; others know them as *muṣṭikasvastika* when opened at the head.
Others, however, declare them to be *khaṭakāmukha* with their tips touching one another. 279.
When the two hands are directed upwards with the elbows bent backwards, they are considered *valita* (twisted);
when placed at the region of the head, they are known by the wise as *pallava* (sprout) and *lalita* (graceful). 280. Thus ends the description of the *valita* hands.
Others say that the *lalita* hands are those which do not break the square shape, with the hands placed motionless at the head;
yet others maintain that the *lalita* hands are those which, having slowly reached the head, have their tips joined to one another like the faces of *khaṭaka* hands. 281–282.
Thus, the wise know that the two *lalita* dance hands (*nṛttahasta*) should also be employed in succession.
(283) Thus end the thirty dance hands (*nṛttahasta*).
The *patāka* hand with the thumb touching the base of the middle finger is the *nikuñcaka*;
it is employed in slight gestures and in the recitation of the Vedas. (284) Thus ends the section on the *ayuta* hands.
The union of two *śikhara* (peaks) is considered the *dviśikhara* hand;
it is used for the purpose of lying down, for snapping the fingers, and likewise for the conciliation of women.
However, for the purpose of expressing "it does not exist," the two *śikhara*s are joined and then separated. 285

Thus, with the hands joined, if the right and left hands are separate, granting the boons and fearlessness respectively, and the *arāla* hands are placed at the sides of the hips, then they are called "granting boons and fearlessness. (286)

Thus, for the purpose of illustration, these seventy hand gestures (hastas) have been described by me; however, because the objects of dramatic representation (abhinaya) are infinite, there are other hands that are likewise infinite. 287
Following worldly conventions, these [gestures] should also be inferred in this manner.

(288) Augmented by secondary limbs such as the eyes, eyebrows, and facial coloration, the hands should be employed as minor limbs to manifest the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and emotional states (*bhāva*). (289)

In superior dramatic performances, [the glances] should move across the region of the forehead; in middling ones, they should rest upon the chest; but in inferior ones, they should be directed downwards.
This rule regarding performers of superior and other grades has been stated by others. 290–291.

In a superior performance, the hands should be held close; in a middling one, they should be positioned at mid-distance; but in an inferior representation, the hands should move at a great distance. When the emotion is directly perceived and predominantly *sāttvika*, the movement of the hands should be minimal.

When out of sight, it should be abundant; for those of middling status, it is considered to be moderate. (293) The hands should be made with very distinct marks by means of superior or middling vessels, while for the lowly, they should be made with elegance, yet different from that [standard]. (294)
When one is despondent, agitated, terrified, fainted, or overcome by lethargy;
when scorched by loathing or anxiety; when asleep, exhausted, or afflicted by paralysis;

or even when one is afflicted by disease, cold, motionless, or gathered in a state of intense heat—[in all these states, the yogi remains steadfast]. 295. In such ascetics, [the practice of yoga is perfected].
In the case of those who are intoxicated, insane, or distracted, there should be no gesturing with the hands (296).
Those hands such as the *karkaṭa* and others, which indicate an internal state of being,
are generally considered by the wise to be applicable even in cases of despondency and the like (297).
Thus ends the section on the hand. The eye is of five kinds: even, slightly bent, fully bent, trembling, and raised; we shall now describe their characteristics. 298.

They say that a chest which is established in excellence, supported by well-proportioned limbs, and remaining in its natural state is "even" (*sama*); and this is also [the basis for] the natural gesture (*svabhāvābhinaya*). Thus ends the section on the even.

Śaṅkarakiṅkara states that the chest should be depicted as sunken, flaccid, and bent in cases of pride and shame, coldness, heart-thorns, grief, fainting, fear, agitation, disease, and despondency. (300)

Thus, "bent" (*ābhugna*) refers to that which is curved; "straightened" (*nirbhugna*) refers to that which is elevated due to a sunken back; "stiff" (*stabdha*) refers to the front part [of the body];
and it also denotes pride, truthful speech, paralysis, and a look of wonder.
This [gesture] is employed in speaking with great joy and in the arrogance of pride (301); thus it is called *nirbhugna*. It becomes *prakampita* or *kampita* through continuous upward tosses.
It may occur in fear, laughter, fatigue, labored breathing, coughing, hiccups, and weeping (302).
Thus has the *prakampita* (trembling) been described; it is motionless, straight, raised upward, and elevated.
In long exhalation, yawning, and gazing upward—that [is the gaze]. Thus:
raised, turned, withdrawn, extended, then again withdrawn and extended, and then bent.
The wise have enumerated five types of *pārśva* (side): *unnata* (elevated) and so forth.
When there is a turning over of the three [parts] due to a twisting motion, it is called *vivartita* (twisted).
Thus ends the description of *vivartita*.

But by withdrawing those [limbs], there would be *apasṛta* (withdrawn) in the case of turning to the side; whereas *prasārita* (extended) occurs from the expansion on both sides in cases such as the *muda* gesture. 306
Thus, with the shoulders extended and the hips bent downward, it is "bent" (nata) in the act of approaching;
this is called *nata*.
The opposite side, however, would be elevated during the movement away [from the ground];
thus is "elevated" (unnata).
Furthermore, there are the [hand gestures] known as kampita, udvāhitā, chinna, vivṛtā, and likewise recitā.
The hip is said to be of five kinds; now describe its characteristics. (308) When it moves swiftly back and forth while the sides are trembling, it is considered *kampitā* (trembling);
this is employed for the gait of those who are hunchbacked, dwarfed, and so forth. (309)
Thus, with her waist slightly trembling, slowly rising, and lifted on both sides,
this [grace] belongs to women of full-limbed form even in their playful gait. 310
Thus, when raised and severed at the edge of the vessel facing obliquely due to the turning of the middle [of the body],
this [gesture] is used in exertion, agitation, and in such acts as looking back with averted gaze. (311)
Thus, when the hip is turned away by one side of the vessel and then rotated toward the front, it is called *vivṛtta*; it is to be employed in the movement of turning. 312.
Thus, it is called *vivṛttā* because of its turning in all directions; it becomes *recitā* during the whirling. Thus ends the description of *recitā*.

The sage’s foot is considered to be of six types: even (sama), raised (añcita), contracted (kuñcita), moving on the tip of the toe or the sole (sūcyagratalasaṃcara), struck upward (udghaṭṭita), and likewise, scraped (trāṭita), joined (ghaṭita), elevated (utsedha), rubbed (ghaṭṭita), and pressed (mardita). 314.

The foremost, the rear-guard, the foot, and another, the flank-mover by enemies—thus seven other feet are mentioned; I shall now state their definitions. A foot that stands naturally on the ground is called "even" (sama).
In the enactment of natural state (*svabhāva*), that [hand] should be steady; in *recaka* (exhalation), it is moving.
Thus it is "equal" (*sama*).
With the heel placed on the ground, the top surface raised, and the fingers extended—this is the *samapādasthita* posture.
He should be *añcita* (bent) during the striking of the feet, the whirling, and so forth. Thus, *añcita* is [defined as] having the toes contracted and the middle of the heel raised.
The *kuñcita* (contracted) position occurs in the *atikrāntaka* step and when grasping a high object.
Thus ends the *kuñcita*.
The left foot is in its natural state, while the other [the right] is placed on the ground with the tip of the big toe.
"The *sūcī* [posture] is for tying the anklets; it is that in which the heel is raised and the big toe is likewise extended.
(319) Thus is the *sūcī*.
In this posture, the heel should be lifted and the big toe extended.
With the toes bent downward, that foot is used for moving on the tips of the toes;
it is employed in urging forward, trampling, standing still, pressing, striking the ground, shifting the position of the feet, in the *recaka* movement, in whirling, and in intoxication. (320–321)
Thus is the *agratālasaṃcara* (forefoot movement);
if, while standing on the tips of the soles of the feet, the heels are repeatedly or even once struck against the ground, then it becomes the *udghaṭṭita*. 322
That foot which, having been struck with the heel, supports the ground and then strikes it with the front, is called *trāṭita*; it should be employed in states of anger and pride. 323
Thus, having been extended,
he repeatedly strikes while gradually raising his height by means of the tips of his heels and toes; this is called "raised height" (ghaṭitotsedha).
"Ghaṭṭitaḥ" refers to that which strikes the ground; it is also used for the striking with the heel or the foot.
Thus, "ghaṭṭitaḥ" is that which crushes the earth with its side or its sole; it is also called "marditaḥ."
Thus, having been trampled,
the vanguard should be employed as they move swiftly like a snake upon muddy ground.
(325) Thus ends the section on the vanguard.
Moving backward with the heel is called *pārṣṇiga*; standing at the side or moving toward the side is considered *pārśvaga*. 326.

Thus, the shoulders— described as being on the sides, high, elevated to the ears, raised, drooping, and trembling— are said to be of five kinds, their characteristics made clear by their very names. 327
The shoulders are said to be raised and elevated during the strikes with fists and spears (328).
In the embrace and the *śiśira* [graceful] movement, the shoulders are considered by the wise to be touching the ears.
They are raised in states such as joy and pride; they are drooping in sorrow, fatigue, and intoxication (329).

In a faint, they should be made to swing; in the dancing of a libertine, they are described by those skilled in dance as being used for laughter, the *huḍukka* call, and the playing of musical instruments.
Thus, the shoulders are of five kinds.
Straight, turned back, contracted by *vali*, bent, curved, triangular, and depressed-convex: thus the neck is of nine types.
Straight is its natural state; it is used in meditation, in recitation, in natural activities, and in that which arises from one's own nature. (331–332)

Thus, when the neck, having turned toward [the object], returns to its original state, it is said to have "returned" (nivṛtta); this occurs in cases such as when one is facing toward one's own place. 333
Thus she turned away, her face directed toward her side; with her neck bent and her gaze likewise turned,
she was thus "valitā" (turned).
Recitā is shaken and free from confusion; likewise, in circular churning, it is recitā.
Ākuñcitā is contracted; kuñcitā occurs when there is a weight on the head or when one's own [body] is concealed.
Thus, [the hands] are contracted (*kuñcitā*),
extended (*añcitā*), outstretched (*prasṛtā*), or restless (*lolā*) during the pulling of hair or during gazing; thus they are "extended" (*añcitā*).

The *tryasrā* (triangular) [gaze] is directed toward the sides in cases of exhaustion, looking at the sides, or when bearing a burden on the shoulders; it is bent and downward-turned in the arrangement of ornaments and when hanging from the neck. 336.
Thus, the neck is bent, raised, and lowered; this is the "adorned" (alaṃkāra) [manner] for looking upward. 337 Thus ends the "raised" (unnata) [neck].

The arm is described by the wise as being of ten kinds: upward-pointing, downward-facing, cast obliquely, extended, bent, moving in a circular path, crossed in the svastika fashion, entwined, and following along the back. (338)

Others say there are six additional arm positions: the *āviddha* (twisted), the *kuñcita* (contracted), the *namra* (bent), the *sarala* (straight), and the *āndolita* (swaying). They call the *utsārita* (extended) as well.
When the arm moves upward from the head, it is called *ūrdhvastha* (upraised) for the purpose of looking at something high. 339–340.
Thus is the one standing upright.
"Facing downward, touching the earth"— thus is the one facing downward.
It should be positioned diagonally along the side.
Thus, moving horizontally with a gait like that of a circle of arms, it has emerged from the field of the chest; this is the *apaviddha* (cast-off) [breath]. 341.
Thus is the "cast-off" (apaviddha);
now, the "stretched-out" (prasārita) is one who runs after the front of the [enemy] army.
Thus, having been extended from the region of the chest to reach the head, it returns to the chest bent; thus it is "bent" (añcita). 342 Thus [the term] "bent" (añcita) [is explained].
It is said that the *maṇḍalagati* (circular movement) is so called because of its revolving in all directions; it is employed for the brandishing of the sword and other weapons.
Thus ends the *maṇḍalagati*.
The *svastika* occurs when the two arms are joined at the elbows and positioned with their sides crossed;
it is used in the worship of the Sun, in embracing, and in salutation.
(344) Thus ends the description of the *svastika*.
The arm, resting upon the rotation located at the wrist while emerging [from the body],
becomes twisted; thus it is called *udveṣṭita* (the twisted).
"Following from behind" means he should go behind [the opponent] during the drawing of an arrow from the quiver and during the taking up of the betel-roll;
thus ends the section on "following from behind."
"Āviddha" means cast inward; thus, when [the foot] is bent inward, it is called āviddha.
"Kuñcita," however, is said to be that which is contracted.

That which is bent at the elbow like a sharp hook for the purpose of wielding a sword or similar weapons, and is prescribed by the teacher Niḥśaṅka for striking, eating, and drinking, is called *kuñcita*. (347)
Slightly curved and inclined, this [hand] is used for praising and for holding a garland (348). Thus, the *namra* (inclined) hand is straight, extended toward both sides, above, and below.
"In the case of a measurement resembling a wing, it is 'syāt'; in the case of indicating something on the ground, it is 'mānaḥ'—respectively.
Thus is the straightforward [term]; 'āndolitah' is etymologically appropriate in the sense of 'motion'."
Thus the arm is swung about; again, being pushed aside, moving here and there, it may serve for clearing away the crowd. (350)
Thus, by the movement of the arms through their application both collectively and individually,
and through the successive variety of tempos such as *druta* (fast) and so forth, thousands [of variations] arise here.
Those movements, richly laden with an abundance of beauty, are to be executed by the skillful;
if those arms, bearing many graceful gestures, are moved without transgressing the *reṣās*, they are then designated as *cārīs* by those who know the technical definitions. 351–352.

In the *khaṇḍa* following the *gajaropaśama*, there is the *padapralapa* of cows one year old; furthermore, at the end of the *dhruva* located in the *sālagas*, there occurs that which is called *praharaṇa*. 353–354.
These [ornaments] should be employed on the tip of that [tusk], elsewhere, or even on the *tuṇḍaka* and *aiśika* when they are raised; others have stated that they are not to be used anywhere else.
(355) Thus ends the section on the arms.
The back, however, is transformed by the same techniques as those prescribed for the abdomen;
therefore, it need not be described separately, and the abdomen is now discussed. The abdomen is considered to be of three types: emaciated, sunken, and full. (356)
*kṣāma* (emaciated) occurs from bending, yawning, laughing, sighing, and weeping (357).
Thus ends *kṣāma*.
*Nimna* (depressed/sunken), *khalla* (sunken), [and *kṣāma*] occur in one afflicted by hunger or one emaciated by fatigue.
Taking on the belly-like form of Vetālas, Bhṛṅgiriṭi, and others;
thus, it is indeed hollow when empty, but becomes full, gross, diseased, pot-bellied, and likewise bloated when overfed.

Thus others have declared that "pūrṇa" (full) is according to its literal meaning, while another [type], "rikta-pūrṇa" (empty-full), is taught for the disease of dyspnea (śvāsa). Thus ends the section on "rikta-pūrṇa."

The thigh is of five types: *kampita* (trembling), *valita* (contracted), *stabdha* (stiff), *udvartita* (upturned), and *nivartita* (turned back). Among these, that which repeatedly bends and rises on its sides is known as *kampita*; it is used for the gait of low-born persons. (360)
Thus, when the knee is bent inward during a woman's natural gait, it is called *kampita* (trembling);
thus is *valita* (twisted).
"One who is *stabdha* (stiff) is devoid of action; likewise, one is *stabdha* in despondency or terror.
Thus, one is *stabdha* through the inward and outward tossing of the heels and the tossing of the forepart of the foot.
It should be repeatedly turned upward during physical exercise as well as in the *tāṇḍava* dance.
(362) Thus ends the description of *udvartita*.
When the heel is drawn inward, it is called *nivartita*, used in cases of agitation or fatigue.
Thus, the fivefold types of the shank— nivartitā, āvartitā, natā, ākṣiptā, and udvāhitā, as well as parivartitā— have been proclaimed by Śārṅgadeva. 363
Others describe five other types of gait: the emerging, the turning back, the sidelong, the outward-moving, and the trembling;
these occur when the left foot is placed on the right side and the right foot on the left side. 364.
When turned repeatedly, it is called *āvartitā*; it is used in the performance of the *vidūṣaka*.
Thus, with the knees bent and the shanks inclined, it is employed in standing, sitting, moving, and other such actions.
Thus, when bent outward, it is cast in throwing and in the *tāṇḍava* dance; this is the *kṣiptā* [hand gesture]. 366.
Thus ends the *kṣiptā*.
"Raised upward" (*ūrdhvam nītā*) means "lifted up," as in the acts of leaping and so forth;
"carried away" (*udvāhitā*) refers to the shank of one moving against the current in the *tāṇḍava* dance, which is rotated.
Thus, the thigh that is turned back and extended forward is proclaimed as "emerged" (niḥsṛtā). 368 Thus ends [the section on] the emerged.
Turning back with the left knee touching the ground is for rites for the ancestors (*pitṛkārya*); with the other [knee], it is for rites for the gods (*surakarma*).
Thus ends the section on turning back.
"It is considered that in the *āsana* [posture], the leg is horizontal with its outer side touching the ground";
thus, in *nṛtta*, the leg is considered to be extended horizontally and outward, with its side spread out. 370.
Thus, when [the sound] has gone outside,
it should be made trembling due to the shaking; when there is fear, the *ghargharikā* should be made in a gurgling sound—
thus it is "trembling."
