The wrist (maṇibandha) is of five kinds: nikuñca, akuñcita, cala, bhramita, and sama. Among these, that which is made concave on the outside is called nikuñca; it is used for the gestures of giving (dāna) and granting fearlessness (abhayadāna). 371–372.
Thus, the *nikuñca* (contracted) hand— contracted, with the palm depressed inward— is to be employed by the wise for retreating;
thus ends the description of the *ākuñcita*.

They know *nikuñca* as that which is contracted through practice; it is used for the invocation of the mobile [breath]. (373) Thus ends the section on the mobile. *Bhramita* is so called because of its whirling, as in the whirling of swords, daggers, and the like.
Thus, when straight and even, it is used for holding or receiving a book; thus it is "even. 374.
Thus [it is] even.

The wise have declared that the knee is of seven types: contracted (*saṃhata*), bent (*kuñcita*), half-bent (*ardhakuñcita*), depressed (*nata*), elevated (*unnata*), opened (*vivṛta*), and even (*sama*).
When the knees are joined together, it is called *śliṣṭānyajānu*; this contracted (*saṃhata*) position is used in cases of fear, joy, and envy. (375)
Thus, with the knees joined together and the thighs and shanks touching, it is the *kuñcita* posture on the seat;
this is called *kuñcita*.
When the knee is bent halfway from the hip, it is called *ardhakuñcita* (half-bent);
this is the *ardhakuñcita*.
When the knee is bent while on the ground, it is considered *nata* (bowed), used for falling and prostration. (377)
Thus,
"bent" refers to [the body] when climbing a mountain or the like, reaching down to the region of the breasts with the knees raised; "raised" refers to the same posture.
In the case of mounting an elephant, however, "opened" (vivṛta) means that both knees are extended outward;
"even" (sama) means the knees are in their natural state, remaining as they naturally are. 378
Thus,
those who frequent various regions consider their respective ornaments to be true adornments.
(372) Thus end the nine minor limbs.
The eight aesthetic perspectives (rasadṛṣṭi) to be observed are: the lovely, the comic, the pathetic, the furious, the heroic, the terrifying, the loathsome, and the marvelous.
Furthermore, [the emotional states] are: affectionate, joyful, distressed, angry, haughty, and fearful.
The eight glances born of the permanent emotions (*sthāyibhāva*) are: the loathsome, the astonished, and so forth;
these are the "permanent glances" which occur when the permanent emotions have attained a state of non-deviation.
They are: the vacant, the dejected, the weary, the bashful, and likewise the apprehensive. (381)
The *mukulā*, the *ardhamukulā*, the *glānā*, the *jihmā*, and the *kuñcitā*;
the *vitarkitā*, the *abhitaptā*, the *viṣaṇṇā*, and that called *lalitā*;
the *ākekarā*, the *vikośā*, the *vibhrāntā*, and the other, the *viplutā*—these are the [types of glances]. (382–383)

*Trastā* (frightened) and *madirā* (intoxicated)—these twenty transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāvas*), when combined with all [the other] thirty-six, are considered the [thirty-six] glances (*dṛṣṭis*).
That [glance] which is expansive and exceedingly pure, as if drinking in the visible object, is [the *āvarjitā*]. 384.
That lovely woman, with her side-glances accompanied by the knitting of her eyebrows, increases the god of love.
Those who are experts in the arts declare that the movement of the pupil, characterized by the variety of its coming, going, and resting, is what constitutes a *kaṭākṣa* (side-glance). 385–386.
Thus the beloved woman,
her pupils slightly agitated by a strange delusion within,
gradually narrowed her eyelids with slow, moderate, and intense force.
When the act of causing amazement is to be portrayed, the *hāsyā* (laughing) gaze is praised. Thus, the *hāsyā* [gaze] has its eyelids drooping and raised, with tears and pupils sluggish with grief.
The compassionate gaze is said to be directed precisely toward the tip of the nose.
(389) Thus, the compassionate gaze has slightly opened eyelids, fixed pupils, and is intensely red.
"Harsh, terrifying with a frown, and fierce—this is declared to be the Raudrī gaze.
(389) Thus [ends] the Raudrī;
it is unwavering, wide-open, deep, and has level pupils.
The *vīrā* (heroine) is described by the wise as having radiant, slightly contracted outer corners of the eyes;
she manifests the seven varieties consisting of magnanimity, fortitude, depth, sweetness, charm, splendor, and grace. (391–392)
Thus, the gaze of heroes— with eyelids stiff and upturned, and pupils extremely restless and rolling— is terrifying as it flees from the visible object out of fear. 394.

Thus, in the *bhayānaka* (terrifying) and *bībhatsa* (disgusting) [rasas], the eyes— with their lashes meeting and rolling, their pupils tremulous, and their outer corners contracted due to agitation— should be depicted with the lids slightly closed. 394.

Thus, her eyes are loathsome yet serene, with pupils that are glossy, white, and reach both inward and outward; their lashes are slightly curved at the tips, and they expand with a wondrous glance from the corners. 395.

Thus, these eight marvelous [perceptions] occur respectively among the eight aesthetic sentiments (*rasas*), headed by the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*). (396) Thus are the eight perceptions of aesthetic sentiment; the perception of aesthetic sentiment arises through non-excessive emotional states (*bhāvas*).
The *snigdha* (affectionate) glance is said to be one that possesses eyebrows which are expansive, glossy, sweet, and clever, and whose side-glances (*kaṭākṣa*) are full of longing.
Regarding this, Kīrtidhara and others state that there should be the raising of only one eyebrow. 397–398.
Thus, the joyful gaze is described as affectionate, with full cheeks, slightly contracted pupils, flickering, blinking, smiling in appearance, and delighted. (399)

Thus, that gaze which is joyful, with the pupils slightly constricted and positioned high in the partially closed lids, accompanied by tears, moving slowly, and dejected, is considered the *dīnā* (dejected) look. 400.
Thus spoke the beloved of Hara, casting a wrathful gaze that was dejected, with fixed and upturned lids, harsh, slightly tremulous in its pupils, and curved by a frown. 401
Thus, the gaze— angry, exuding vitality, haughty, expanded, and steady—
is "haughty. 402 Thus ends [the description of] the haughty gaze.

That gaze in which the eyelids are expanded with emotion and the pupils are trembling, while intent on looking away from the center, is the "fearful" (bhayānvitā) gaze. Thus ends the description of the fearful gaze.
With indistinct vision, with blinking pupils, and with closing lids,
the gaze that becomes agitated upon seeing an object is called "disgusted" (jugupsitā). Thus ends the description of the disgusted gaze.
The gaze that is motionless, with the two eye-lids wide open and distended in form, and with the pupils dilated, is known as *vismitā* (the astonished). Thus ends the description of *vismitā*.
These eight views are applied respectively to the eight permanent emotions (sthāyibhāva), beginning with love;
thus, there are eight views of the permanent emotions:
the even gaze (samatārāpuṭā), the empty gaze (dṛśyadṛṣṭiśūnyā), and the observing gaze (vilokinī).
The gaze during reflection is held to be unwavering, greyish,
and empty; thus,
when the eyes have withdrawn from the visible object, they are slightly closed at the corners.
The outer corners of the eyes become lusterless, and likewise there is a trickling from the tips of the eyelashes;
the gaze of women becomes blurred—this is employed in the *vihṛta* [state].
When the time has come, yet there is no conversation with the beloved, this is considered *vihṛta*.
Thus, though her eyes were dull from sleep, her eyelids faded, and her gait languid, she appeared weary with fatigue— her pupils sinking slightly and the corners of her eyes somewhat contracted. 409

Thus, when the lashes are exhausted from meeting one another, the pupils have sunk low, and the upward-turned lids have fallen, such a gaze is considered "ashamed" (lajjitā) in the context of bashfulness. 410
Thus, overcome with shame, she repeatedly shifted from moving to stillness; looking toward her side, then turning her face outward, and finally casting a hidden glance, she quickly withdrew her gaze.
"When there is doubt, the gaze is said to be 'doubtful' by the teacher who is free from doubt" (411).
Thus, the "doubtful" gaze has trembling eyelashes that are slightly joined, with the pupils resting comfortably.
The *mukulā* gaze occurs upon seeing something delightful or when experiencing a pleasant touch or fragrance. Thus,
the *mukulā* is characterized by the two eyelids being half-open and the pupils slightly trembling.
Where the eyes are half-closed for the sake of the "half-bud" (ardhamukula) state, which bestows bliss— this is the "half-bud" [gaze]:
with pupils sinking, moving slowly, and relaxed as if by those who are fainting.

When the eyelashes, the tips of the brows, and the sockets are joined together and appear languid, it is prescribed as *glānā* (the languid). When the sockets are slightly contracted and the pupils are hidden during the act of looking, that which is slowly and obliquely concealed is employed as *jihmā* (the sidelong glance).
In cases of envy, when a matter is concealed, and also in dullness and laziness—
thus, if the tips of the eyelashes are slightly curved and the eyelids [are likewise]... [416] it is *jihmā* (sidelong).
When the pupil is properly contracted, it is then called *dṛkkuñcitā* (the contracted gaze);
it is used when indicating something undesirable, a harsh glare, or when there is pain in the eyes.
Thus ends the description of *kuñcitā*.
"The gaze that, though moving downward, has its pupils dilated and wide-open as if raised upward, is called *vitarkitā* when it is directed toward deliberation. (418) Thus ends the *vitarkitā*.
She whose pupils are sluggish in their movement and whose eyelids tremble with pain appears as if scorched;
she is called "Abhitapta" (the Scorched). She is to be recognized in states of despondency, as well as from physical injury and affliction.
That gaze which is thus intensely heated,
with corners drooping, the two lids wide open, blinking, with a fixed pupil, and dejected— that is the despondent (viṣādinī) gaze. 421

Thus, the *lalitā* (graceful) glance is considered to be dejected, sweet, with contracted outer corners, accompanied by a knitting of the brows and a smile, and agitated by love; it is deemed graceful, O graceful one. 422
Thus, with her eyes slightly contracted at the outer corners and half-closed,
Lalitā’s gaze repeatedly rolls its pupils along a path distinct from the other eye.
"Ākekarā" occurs when an object is difficult to see or when one's desire for it is thwarted;
thus,
*ākekarā* is that [gaze] in which the pair of eyelids are wide open, being both expanded and unblinking.
With unsteady pupils and wide-open eyes, she is described by the wise as *vikośā* (the Unsheathed).
She appears when there is pride in knowledge and discernment, and when one’s gaze is fierce with impatience.
Thus ends the description of *vikośā*.

That gaze which looks about restlessly and without confidence, with wide, flickering, and dilated pupils, is called *vibhrāntā* (wandering); it occurs in moments of confusion, haste, or agitation. 426
Thus, she whose eyelids are wide open, dilated, and gradually become fixed and drooping due to the pain of distress, is "viplutā"; she is likewise [found] in insanity and agitation. 427
Thus, in confusion, her pupils would be wide with trembling; in terror, her eyelids would be raised and agitated. (428) Thus ends the description of the terrified [gaze].

Wine is said to be of three kinds, which are appropriate for application during the stages of youth, middle age, and old age, each possessing its respective characteristics. Among these, the low stage of intoxication is considered intense when it occurs in a person of inferior character.

In the early stage of intoxication, the gaze has its outer corners dilated, the eyes become narrowed, and the pupils roll; the eyelids are slightly contracted and the movement is somewhat unsteady. 430.
In the middling stage of intoxication,
the gaze has its pupil slightly lowered; in the lowest stage of intoxication, the gaze moves downward with the pupil slightly visible, the eyes blinking and remaining half-closed.
Thus, these thirty-six glances have been described by me for the purpose of illustration;
they are infinite, as they are drawn from the context of the ritual of the *ārāpuṭa* [the ear-whispering]. 433.
"Even Viriñca is unable to describe each of those views individually;
therefore, for the sake of brevity and to awaken understanding of them, we shall speak of them starting from the eyebrows.
(434) Thus ends the section on the views (*dṛṣṭiprakaraṇa*).

The wise have declared that the eyebrow is of seven kinds: natural (*sahajā*), fallen (*patitā*), raised (*utkṣiptā*), expanded (*recitā*), contracted (*kuñcitā*), frowning (*bhrukuṭī*), and clever (*caturā*). Among these, the natural eyebrow occurs in expressions that are not crooked. (435)
Thus, the *sahajā* (inherent) [mudrā] may fall downward, or else proceed with its companion in succession;
it is employed in lifting up, in wonder, in joy, in anger, in envy, and in loathing.
"When laughter and smelling occur, both eyebrows should be raised";
thus,
"raised" (*utkṣiptā*) is considered appropriate as a literal term for each [action] in sequence, and otherwise when used together.
In women’s anger, deliberation, looking, listening, their own [affairs],
and in playful gestures or indifference, this eyebrow is raised by the wise for specific purposes.
(437) Thus ends the "Raised" eyebrow.

The *lalitotkṣiptā* alone, when employed in dance (*nṛttagocara*), is called *recitā*; it may be performed either singly or accompanied by another [gesture], characterized by gentle flexion (*nikuñcitā*) and soft modulation (*mṛdubhaṅga*). 438.
In *moṭṭāyita*, *kuṭṭamita*, *vilāsa*, and *kilakiñcita*—
thus [are the movements of] the eyebrows;
when raised from the root along with their companion [the other eyebrow], it is called *bhrukuṭī* in anger.

Thus, the *bhrukuṭī* (knitted brow) is accompanied by a slight contraction; it becomes elongated, slow, clever, beautiful, and graceful in touch, in the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), and in the playful (*lalita*). 441.
Thus,
the two hands in the *prasṛta* position may be bent, opened and closed,
turned, throbbed, covered, or spread out. (442)
The two *puṭa* [hand gestures] have been described as equal and ninefold by the son of Soḍhala;
they should be extended and spread out in the *vīra*, *harṣa*, and *vismaya* [rasas].
(443) Thus ends the section on the *prasṛta* [gestures].
The *ākuñcita* and *kuñcita* [hand gestures] are used for beautiful forms and so forth; the *kuñcita* are those with the fingers contracted,
while the *unmeṣita* are from separation and the *nimeṣita* are from joining together.

These three—unmesita (opening), nimesita (closing), and vivartita (rolling)—are the domain of *krodha* (anger). Likewise, sphurita (throbbing) and spandita (quivering) are considered the objects of *īrṣyā* (envy). 444–445.

Thus, when the eyes are excessively pulsating, extremely contracted, fixed, and closed, it indicates pain, as well as sleepiness, fainting, excessive rain, heat, smoke, wind, or affliction from collyrium. 446
Thus, when the eyes are closed,
they are said by some to be "moved" due to the impact from a blow below;
however, others say that during the act of opening wide, the two sockets become invisible.
Thus, these two natural [movements], when moved equally, are considered to be the *svabhāvābhinaya* (natural acting). 447.
Thus ends the section on the equal [movements].
I shall now describe those actions by which the distinctions of the *tārakas* arise;
they are twofold: those centered on oneself and those directed toward external objects.
These are: whirling, turning, falling, moving, and entering. (448)
The wise declare that there are nine types of *tārā-karma* (eye diseases) established within themselves: *vivartana*, *samudvṛtta*, *niṣkrāma*, and likewise *prākṛta*.
Among these, *tārā-maṇḍala-bhrānti* is considered to be the wandering [of the eye] within the lids. 450–451.
Valana is the movement of the three corners; pāta is downward motion;
calana is said to be trembling; then praveśana is to be known as entering.
Praveśa is the interior of the two lids, while vivartana is the side-glance (kaṭākṣa).
*Udgati* is the upward movement; that which is the exit from within is *niṣkrāma*. *Prākṛta*, however, is said to be the state of natural composure.
*Samudvṛtta*, *valana*, and *bhramaṇa* are used for the heroic (*vīra*) and the furious (*raudra*) sentiments. 452–453.
In the *karuṇa* (pathetic) rasa, there should be a falling; in the *bhayānaka* (terrifying), a trembling; in the *bībhatsa* (disgusting), an entrance; and in the *hāsya* (comic), a turning about.
In the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic), there should be an exit; likewise in the *vīra* (heroic), the *raudra* (furious), and the *bhayānaka* (terrifying).
"In the case of the marvelous, however, it is the natural [state] when one partakes in possession through intense emotion.
(454) Thus, there are nine *tārā*-actions centered on oneself;
now I shall describe the eight *tārā*-actions directed toward external objects. (356)

Those skilled in the characteristics of the target and its observation define these modes of looking: *sama* (even), *sāci* (oblique), *anuvṛtta* (following), *avalokita* (looking down), *vilokita* (looking around), *ullokita* (looking up), and *ālokita* (gazing); these are also called *pravilokita*. 457.

A gaze that is gentle, with the pupils positioned centrally, is called "even" (sama). Thus, the "even" gaze is described; the "sidelong" (sāci) gaze is one in which the pupils are directed toward the inner corners of the eyes.

Thus, the sage’s considered opinion was that the act of gazing (*nirvarṇanā*) is properly defined as a continuous and repeated observation, characterized by a long-lasting desire to see the object in its entirety. 459
Thus, that downward-looking vision which continues [from the previous stage] is called avalokita;
this is avalokita.
"That which is a glance toward the back is called *vilokita* (460). Thus ends *vilokita*. *Ullokita* is the looking at an object situated above.
Thus, that sudden glance which is cast upward is called *ālokitam*. 461.
Thus ends the section on *ālokitam*.

The wise have declared that *pravilokita* (the side-long glance) is the act of looking; those who know the [essence of] aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) and emotional states (*bhāva*) call these [glances] common to all such states. 462
Thus, there are eight types of cheeks: contracted, trembling, full, emaciated, blooming, and even; these six varieties have been described, and their characteristics are now stated. 463
In cases of cold fever and fear, the hands should be contracted and curled;
however, in instances of horripilation, they should be made to quiver and tremble by the wise. 464.
Thus, those two cheeks, trembling, elevated, and full, were full within the sphere of pride and vigor.
"When [the cheeks] are emaciated and sunken, these two should be employed by actors in [representing] suffering;
when the cheeks are expanded and blooming, they are proclaimed [to represent] great joy."
Thus, these two [eyes] are considered naturally full and even when there is no immersion in objects; thus they are equal. 466.
Thus they are equal.

The nose is said by the wise Śārṅgin to be of six kinds: natural (*svābhāvikī*), bent (*natā*), slow (*mandā*), drawn back (*vikṛṣṭā*), contracted (*vikūṇitā*), and with exhalation (*socchvāsā*). The natural one is so called because it is devoid of intense absorption in [any particular] states. (467–468)

Thus, the nose is considered to be naturally curved, with its nostrils repeatedly joined and separated; it is used in the representation of breathing and when the range of vision is dull or interrupted. 469
Thus, when the nose is slightly bent and its inhalations and exhalations are slow, it is called *nāsā*; it is prescribed for anxiety, longing, sorrow, and despondency. (470)
Thus, the "Slow" (mandā) gaze—with eyes drawn wide and extremely dilated—is to be employed in anger, pain, and fear, as well as in heavy breathing;
it should be used when smelling something of intense fragrance. 471
Thus, [the face] drawn out,
contracted, and shriveled occurs in laughter, envy, and disgust.
(472) Thus ends the section on the "contracted" [face].

The nose, with its breath drawn in, becomes exhaling when there is fragrance; and it becomes characterized by long exhalations during states such as despondency. Thus ends the section on "with exhalation."
Natural, moving, increased, suppressed, uplifted,
liberated, astonished, faltering, and likewise extended—
thus are the inhalation and exhalation described by Kohala in nine ways.
Equalized, wandering, dissolved, oscillating, and another that is trembling;
with the suspension of inhalation and exhalation, and the sounds *sūtkṛta* and *sītkṛta*—
thus the wind is said by experts in the signs to be of ten kinds.

"The two winds known as inhalation and exhalation, which arise from their own nature, are to be employed in healthy activities by one who is free from doubt; thus [the author] has described the two healthy [winds]. (477) Thus [ends the section on] the healthy.

These two [lips], when hot, long, and accompanied by sound, are made to quiver by the mouth; these two are considered appropriate in cases of longing, despondency, grief, and anxiety. (478) Thus ends the section on "quivering."
When it has increased and issues forth from the mouth with sound,
that breath is called *pravṛddha* (increased), and it pertains to conditions such as the disease of consumption (*kṣaya*). Thus ends the section on *pravṛddha*.
When the breath is expelled with sound and repeatedly, it is called *nirasta* (expelled);
this is prescribed for one who is afflicted by suffering, possessed of passion, or in a state of tranquility.
Thus ends the section on *nirasta*.
The breath, drawn in slowly and gently through the nose, should be made to expand toward a pleasing fragrance; this is how it should be performed by the wise when there is doubt.
(481) Thus ends the section on "Expansion."

Having been restrained for a very long time, the wind (prāṇa) is said by the wise to be "liberated" when it is released during yoga, meditation, and breath control (prāṇāyāma). Thus ends the section on the liberated state.
"One who proceeds with effort because his mind is intent on something else is *vismita*; it occurs when wonder has arisen or when there is reflection upon an object. Thus ends *vismita*.

"Due to its greatness, the wind that has escaped from suffering is said to be 'skhalita'; it occurs in the tenth stage, during illness, and when things have faltered. (484) Thus ends the section on *skhalita*.
"When one is asleep, [the breath] flows out long and with sound from the mouth"—thus it is called *prasṛta*.
Here, "equal" (*sama*) is a synonym for being in a healthy state (*svastha*); "confused" (*bhrānta*) refers to the wind (*marut*) due to its internal whirling.

Others, however, have names that correspond to their literal meaning: *sūtkṛta* and *sītkṛta* refer respectively to the imitation of sounds and to the wind that is to be rejected or accepted by the mouth;
*sama* is natural in the first instance of union with a lover, while *bhrānta* is [the state] when it is otherwise. (486–487)

The *vilīna* (dissolved) state occurs during fainting; the *āndolita* (swaying) is considered to occur when climbing a mountain; the *kampita* (trembling) occurs during sexual union; and the *stambhita* (paralyzed) state occurs from the discharge of weapons and the like.
(488) *Ucchvāsa* (inhalation) occurs from smelling flowers; *niḥśvāsa* (exhalation) occurs from remorse and the like.
*Sūtkṛta* occurs at the onset of pain and so forth; *sītkṛta*, however, occurs in cold or in passion (489).
Regarding the nail-marks of gazelle-eyed women and the merciless chewing of the lips, let the wise understand other applications of these sounds from common worldly usage (490).

Thus, according to another school of thought, the lower lip is considered to be of six types: the tenfold breath (śvasana), the turned-upward (vivartita), the trembling (kampita), the emitted (visṛṣṭa), the concealed (vinigūhita), the gazed-at (saṃdṛṣṭaka), and the opened (samudga). 491.

Others spoke to one another with their lips raised, opened wide, and extended; when these are swollen and turned aside by a contraction, they are employed in expressions of contempt, pain, envy, laughter, and the like. 492
Thus, *vivartitaḥ* is used in the sense of "distressed" (*vyathāyām*), "trembling" (*kampitaḥ*), and as an appropriate term for "fear," "cold," "muttering prayers" (*japa*), and "anger";
thus ends [the section on] *kampitaḥ*.

It is "visṛṣṭa" when it has been cast out or departed; it is described by the divine Śārṅgin as occurring in the context of women's dalliance and playful gestures (*vilāsa* and *vivvoka*), using red lac and the like.
It is "nihita" when placed within the mouth, and "vinigūhita" when concealed for the sake of an object to be accomplished through one's vital breath.
"When a lover kisses women by force during anger or jealousy," thus it is said; "the concealed bite" (vinigūhitasaṃdaṣṭaka) is defined as the lower lip being bitten with the teeth in a fit of rage.
Thus is *saṃdaṣṭaka*; *samudga*, however, is the joining of the lips when they are raised. It occurs in blowing, in compassion, in kissing, and in welcoming. (497)
Thus, *samudga* refers to being raised up;
when that [raised state] is turned upward due to being lifted from the mouth, it is *udvṛtta*, used in the senses of contempt and derision.
Thus ends *udvṛtta*.
"With slightly visible upper teeth, it is known as 'expanding' (vikāsī) in a smile" (498).
Thus, that expanding [smile] occurs together with the upper lip; thereafter, in a [fuller] smile, it becomes elongated.
Thus,
because it moves from its full extent to its limit, the lower lip is called *vilāsa-recita*. (499) Thus ends the *recita* [movement].
We shall now describe the operations on ivory for the purpose of perfecting its characteristics.

They declare that the eightfold operation on ivory consists of: cutting (kuṭṭana), splitting (khaṇḍana), carving (chinna), chipping (cukkita), grasping (grahaṇa), biting (daṣṭa), and extraction (niṣkarṣaṇa). 500.
"Rubbing" (saṃgharṣaṇa) is the grinding [of the teeth] during cold, illness, fear, or old age; thus ends "grinding.
"Breaking" (khaṇḍana), however, is considered the repeated joining and separating of the teeth.
This [rule] applies during recitation, study, conversation, and eating (502). Thus the objection is refuted:
there should be firm contact [of the lips] when weeping, in fear, and in cold.

And it is taught that during illness, during the chewing of betel, during physical exercise, and so forth, [the teeth] are "separated" (chinna). When they remain far apart in the two rows of teeth, it is "cukkita," as in yawning and similar instances. (503)
Thus, the gathering of grass with the fingers and the holding or grasping of it between the teeth when in fear (verse 504)— this is "grasping."
"Any slight contact that is even is considered *svabhāvābhinaya* (natural expression).
Thus ends the section on *sama*.
"Biting with the teeth upon the lower lip is said to be performed in anger."
Thus, when bitten, the extraction [of the fangs] must be performed; this is the "monkey's weeping" (markaṭarodana) method.
Thus ends the section on extraction.

The tongue is of six kinds: straight (*ṛjvī*), following the teeth (*ṛkvānugā*), curved (*vakrā*), raised (*unnatā*), trembling (*lolā*), and licking (*avalehinī*). Among these, the straight tongue is extended when the mouth is open; it is employed by predatory beasts in cases of fatigue and thirst. (507–508)
Thus, "sṛkkānugā" means straight, following the corners of the mouth, licked along the corners of the mouth, or pertaining to provocation and pleasant food.
This is "sṛkkānugā."
With mouth wide open, teeth prominent at the tips, and curved—such is the form in the manifestation of Nṛhari (the Man-Lion).
Thus, *vakrā* (the crooked) is so named because its meaning corresponds to its nature; it is used in the acts of yawning and gazing from within the mouth. (509–510)
Thus, when the mouth is wide open, the raised, moving, and flickering [hand] constitutes the *vetālābhinaya*;
this is called *lolā*.
"The tongue licks the teeth and lips; this is considered the 'licking' (lehinī) [mudrā] of the Sage.
Thus, by the action of the tongue, lips, and teeth, the chin is indicated; therefore, it is called *lehinī*.
What has been said regarding the purpose of pleasure is largely concluded; however, I shall now describe [the movements] according to their specific characteristics:
the chin is of eight kinds—opened wide, breathed upon, curved, pressed together, pressed together while moving, quivering, moving, and trembling. (512)
"Vyādīrṇa is known [to occur] in yawning, lassitude, and so forth, when [the eye] has moved far outwards.
(513) Thus, *vyādīrṇa* is [a state where] a single finger-breadth [of the eye] has sagged downward; it is used for gazing in wonder.
Thus, that breath which is exhaled crookedly and directed obliquely downward is prescribed for possession by a spirit;
such is the crooked [breath].

"When the mouth is closed, motionless, and held in silence, it is considered 'contracted' (saṃhata); when the lips are pressed together but moving during a woman's kiss, it is 'moving-contracted' (calasaṃhata). (515)
Thus they say that "calasaṃhata" (trembling and stiffened), "kampita" (shaking), and "sphurita" (throbbing) occur in cold-fever;
such is "sphurita."

*Calita* (moving) is used for that which is joined and disjoined, as well as for the paralysis of speech and for agitation or anger; *calita* also refers to rumination (*romantha*) and simple regurgitation (*kevalāvarta*). *Lola* (wavering) refers to movement to and fro in a horizontal direction. (516)

Thus, the wise have declared the face to be of six kinds: the restless (lolam), the distorted (vyābhugnām), the bent (bhugnam), the upraised (udvāhi), the shaken (vidhutam), and likewise the opened (vivṛtam) and the turned away (vinivṛttam). 517
A face that is somewhat elongated and crooked, yet bent, is called *vyābhugna*;
this was stated by the ancient masters regarding states such as despondency, longing, and anxiety.
(158) Thus ends the section on *vyābhugna*.
"Downward-facing" (adhomukha) means bent; "in shame" refers to the natural state of an ascetic.
Thus, "bent" (bhugnam) [is used].
"Thrown up in play" (līlāsūtkṣiptam) means held aloft; "out of pride" (garvāt) means out of disregard in one's gait. 519
Thus, when "no" is said in the sense of warding off, that which is tossed upward is called *udvāhi*; when "not so" is said, that which is shaken sideways and extended is called *vidhuta*.
Thus ends *vidhuta*.
"With parted lips" is the open [mouth] in laughter, grief, fear, and so forth (520). Thus ends "the open. "Withdrawn" or "turned away" refers to that [mouth] in anger, jealousy, and malice (521).
Thus, "withdrawn" (vinivṛtta) and so forth are the twelve subsidiary movements (upāṅga) pertaining to the head:
the raised (utkṣiptā), the fallen (patitā), the raised-and-fallen (utkṣiptapatitā), the fallen-and-raised (patitotkṣiptā), and likewise the inward-turned (antargatā).
The *pārṣṇi* (heels) are seen in eight ways in various positions during footwork: outward-turned, joined together, separated, and with the fingers joined;
likewise, when the ankles and big toes are joined, they are either turned inward or turned outward. 522.
When joined together or separated, they are fivefold in their positions and so forth;
likewise, they are sevenfold as contracted, extended, curved, twisted, fallen, with the base of the fingers contracted, and with the fingers of the hand spread out. 523–524.
These variations, beginning with the heel (pārṣṇi), are characterized by their specific names and definitions.
Furthermore, the toes of the foot are considered to be of five types: cast downward, lifted upward, contracted, extended, and joined together. (525–526)
Repeatedly cast down as she falls, tossed up in playful gestures and amorous agitation,
and raised again and again due to the weight of her modesty at being newly wed; likewise,
they are contracted when afflicted by cold, fainting, fear, or seizure.
Extended, straight, and stiff; these [positions] are used for supporting, sleeping, and twisting the limbs (528).
Experts in dance should know that these are also variations of the big toe (*aṅguṣṭha*).
When the respective big toes are joined together, they are considered "clenched" (*saṃlagna*) for the purpose of friction (529).
They know the sole (tala) to be of six kinds: with the tip fallen, with the tip raised, touching the ground, raised from the ground, with the middle contracted, and horizontal.
Thus [are described] the heels, ankles, toes, and soles, which are the secondary parts of the hands and feet.
It reveals the mental state through the coloration of the face, which is of the nature of rasa;
therefore, because it serves the purpose of rasa, the coloration of the face is designated as such.
It is naturally clear and bright, while another is reddish-dark.
In this context, the fourfold change of facial expression is considered "natural" (*svābhāvika*) because its meaning is literal;
it is prescribed by the wise for those emotional states that are not overtly manifested.
Thus, it is called "natural."
"Clear and stainless, it should be present in the comic (*hāsya*), the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), and the marvelous (*adbhuta*).
Thus is the "clear" (*prasanna*).
It should be red or reddish-brown (*aruṇa*) in the pathetic (*karuṇa*), the furious (*raudra*), the heroic (*vīra*), and likewise the marvelous (*adbhuta*).
Thus, "red" (rakta) is [a term] according to its literal meaning; "dark-blue" (śyāma) [is used] in the sentiments of the loathsome (bībhatsa) and the terrible (bhayānaka).
Thus ends the section on "dark-blue."
Like the moon [illuminating] the quarters, the limbs shine by means of the color of the face (535).
When there is a change in rasa or bhāva, the eyes become one thing and then another moment by moment;
thus, the color of the face should be made appropriate for each specific rasa (536).
Thus Bharata considered the movement of the face to be fourfold—
namely, upward-turned, downward-turned, and turned to the side— and the movement of the hand to be threefold;
however, others have declared it to be fivefold.

"The *agraka* (upward-facing) and the *adhastala* (downward-facing)—these two, along with the three previously mentioned [in verse 537]," thus says Bhaṭṭa; by including the *agraka* within the *adhastala*, he establishes that there are indeed only three [types of hands]. (538–539)

The hand may be palm upwards, face downwards, or positioned on its side; it may have the palm facing forward, or the palm facing oneself, or be turned upwards, or likewise face downwards. It may be turned away from the observer, facing toward them, or with its face turned to the side. (540)

Śārṅgadeva, who knows the truth of the definitions and characteristics [of hand gestures], has described these fifteen modes of movement: upward-moving, downward-moving, sideways-moving, forward-moving, backward-moving, and facing-coming. (541–542)

Thus, there are fifteen movements of the hand; that specific action which is performed for the purpose of gesturing with the hand when it is independent [of other factors] in its accomplishment is considered *hastakaraṇa* (hand-formation). 543

Enveloping (*āveṣṭita*), unwinding (*udveṣṭita*), turning away (*vyāvartita*), and thereafter turning around (*parivartita*): these four are approved by the wise. (544) That which is the successive enveloping of the fingers, beginning with the index finger, is [the first].
When the hand, facing the palm, also comes from the side,
it is called *āveṣṭita* (the encircling) by the wise. That which is the gradual emergence of the fingers from the outside of the palm is [known as *nirveṣṭita*].
The same [movement] from the chest to the hand is called *udveṣṭita* (unwinding).
By the process of *āveṣṭita* (winding), the action performed on the hand is explained as *parivartita* (revolved) by means of *udveṣṭita*. 546–547.
However, this pair of hand-gestures is formed with the little finger and the other fingers [joined].
(548) Thus, there are four hand-gestures:
shaking, joining and separating, throwing, and protecting and releasing.
Seizing, restraining, drawing upward, drawing downward, and drawing away;
beating, weighing, cutting, piercing, bursting, and crushing; as well as releasing, summoning, and threatening—these constitute the twenty [actions]. 549.
Those skilled in dance have described the functions of the hands as being consistent with their names.
Thus, there are twenty hand-functions: both sides, the front, the back, above, below, and the head. (550–551)
The forehead, ears, shoulders, chest, navel, waist, head, and the two thighs— these are the fourteen fields of the hands.
(552) Thus end the fields of the hands.

I bow to that Lord, the destroyer of the bodiless one (Kāma), who, though transcending all instruments of action, performs the dance of the limbs upon the stage of heaven and earth with his own movements;
for such is the nature of action—performed through the grace of hands, feet, and so forth—with its aesthetic flavor never interrupted. 553–554.
The *karaṇas* are dance-movements; like Bhīma and Bhīmasena, we shall now describe the various divisions of these *karaṇas* as proclaimed by Bharata:
*talapuṣpapuṭa*, *līna*, *vartita*, and *litoru*.
The *maṇḍalasvastika*, the *vakṣaḥsvastika*, the *ākṣiptarecita*,
the *svastika* variations such as the *ardha*, *dik*, and *pṛṣṭha*, the *svastikamañcita*, the *apaviddha*, the *samanakhonmatte*, and the *svastikarecita*. (556–557)
The *nikuṭṭa*, the *ardhanikuṭṭa*, the *kaṭīchinna*,
the *kaṭīsama*, the *bhujaṅgatrāsita*, the *alāta*, the *vikṣipta*, and the *ākṣiptaka* (558);
the *nikuñcita*, the *ghūrṇita*, the *ūrdhvajānu*, and the *ardharecita*.
Matta, ardhamatta, recaka,
nikuṭṭaka, lalita, valita, daṇḍapakṣa, pādāpaviddhaka, nūpura, bhramara, chinna, and bhujaṅgatrastarecita. (559–560)

Then follow the *bhujaṅgāñcita*, the *daṇḍarecita*, the *catura*, the *kaṭibhrānta*, the *vyaṃsita*, the *krānta*, the *vaiśākharecita*, the *vṛścika*, and the *vṛścikārdha*; these two, the *kuṭṭita* and the *recita*, should also be performed. 561.
The *latāvṛścika*, the *ākṣiptārgala*, the *talavilāsita*,
the *lalāṭatilaka*, the *pārśvanikuṭṭa*, the *cakramaṇḍala*, the *urormaṇḍala*, the *āvarta*, the *kuñcita*, and the *dolapādaka*. (562–563)
The *vivṛtta*, the *vinivṛtta*, the *pārśvakrānta*, the *niśumbhita*,
the *vidyuddhānta*, the *atikrānta*, the *vikṣipta*, and the *vivartita* (564);
the *gajakrīḍitaka*, the *gaṇḍasūcī*, and the *garudapluta*.
The palm-clapping, the side-knee, the vulture-swoop (gṛdhrāvalīnaka),
the needle, the half-needle, the needle-pierced, the deer-leap, the turned-back, the staff-foot, and then the peacock-graceful (mayūralalita). 565–566.
The swaying, the bending, the gliding, the trunk-like gesture,
the forward movement, the withdrawal, the hip-turning, the stumbling, the lion’s play, the lion’s draw-in, and the dissimulation. 567.
And those produced by entering, meeting, and sporting; 568 those in which the *viṣṇukrāntā* plants are uprooted by the impact of palms; the *lolita*;
those agitated by stumbling through intoxication; and those struck by the *viṣkambha* movement. 569
Then there are those called Śakaṭāsya and Ūrvivṛtta, followed by Vṛṣabhakrīḍita,
Nāgāpasarpita, and likewise Gaṅgāvataraṇa. Thus, I have enumerated one hundred and eight karaṇas.
Since movements, postures, and applications are infinite, the instruments (of gesture) in the *aṅgahāras* must also be infinite; yet, for the sake of practical utility,
I shall now state their definitions according to the opinion of those who know the subject matter.
Generally, at the commencement of a dance, the feet should be even and the hands in the *latākara* position;
the body should be in the *caturasra* posture. However, this specific distinction is now stated:
when the right foot steps forward with the *dvyardhika* gait, [the hands follow]. 573.
As she turned away, her right side came forward; as she turned back, her left side was constantly brought near, so that his hand,
holding a flower-vessel, rested upon the field of her breast.
That is the *talapuṣpapuṭa*; it occurs when the foot moves on its forepart (*agratala*).
(575) If this [movement] follows immediately after another movement (*karaṇa*), then that is the *karakriyā*, which follows the hand that is to be abandoned or grasped. (576)

This is employed for the offering of a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) and for the gesture of modesty (lajjā). Thus, having placed the hands with palms joined and fingers curled upward at the chest, it is the añjali mudrā.
When the shoulders are slightly bent and the neck is made to incline, that gesture is called *līna*;
it should be employed by the wise when making a request to a beloved. (578) Thus ends *līna*.

Having placed the two hands clasped together with the palms facing each other at the wrists, one should simultaneously rotate them outward and inward against the chest; where they are then cast upward over the thighs with the palms facing up, that is considered the *vartita* (revolved) mudrā.
If one were to let fall the *patāka* hand [in such a manner], it would be employed in the expression of envy (580).
When those two hands are rubbed with their palms facing downwards, they indicate anger.
Other hands, such as the *śukatuṇḍa* and so forth, are also used here according to their specific application (581).

Having thus performed the movement upon the field of the chest with both hands turned outward and inward, one should join them together through the *parivartana* (turning) movement by means of the *ākṣiptā* (thrown) step.
Having brought them there, they are placed with their beaks downward;
that position where they remain bound is called *valitoru*.
Its application is prescribed by Śārṅgin for the bashfulness of an innocent woman.

Having thus formed the hands into the *valitoru* and *caturasra* positions, and having performed the *vicyava* gesture, he then makes the two hands circular above, preceded by the action of unwinding (*udveṣṭita*). 585.
Having fashioned two *svastikas*, one should establish the site and the mandala;
that shall be the "mandala-svastika" for the observation of well-known objects.
Thus ends the section on the mandala-svastika.
Having placed the two square hands at the chest and then extended them outward,
one brings them back by means of *vyāvartita*; when they are thus bent against the chest, and the feet are in the *svastika* position, that is considered *vakṣaḥsvastika*.
And this [position] with the shoulders not bent is to be employed for shame and remorse.
Thus ends the *vakṣaḥsvastika*.
Where the two hands, having turned upward from the sides, are placed upon the field of the heart—
Having thrown one swan-wing (haṃsapakṣa) downward with rapid whirling,
and having brought the other to the chest in the same manner, one should then extend it outward; with the feet raised in the needle (sūcī) position, that is the *ākṣiptarecita* [gesture].
By this gesture, the succession of giving and receiving [is indicated].
(590) Thus is the *ākṣiptarecita* [gesture]:
the right hand should be the *karihasta*, while the left should be the *khaṭakāmukha*.
When the two feet are in the *svastika* position with the hands placed upon the chest, that is the *ardhasvastika*.
Others know the *pakṣavañcitaka*, the *pakṣapradyotaka*, and the *ardhacandra* as being located at the place of the "elephant-trunk" (*karikara*) and on the hips respectively. 591–592.
When there is a half-svastika on the two sides, a svastika at the front and behind, and the hands and feet extended toward the directions, that is called diksvastika. 593
This was employed by the ancients in the various sections of their songs;
this may be the *svastika* procedure even within other discourses on the *svastika*.
Thus ends the *dik-svastika*.
Having first performed the action of unwinding while the two arms are being cast aside,
and having executed the *apakrāntā* foot-step while the unwinding is being carried out,
one should, after shifting the other foot, perform the *sūcī-svastika*.

Where the hands and feet form a *svastika* on the back, this is called *niṣedharābhasya*; it is employed by those who know the principles of drama (*nāṭyatattvajña*) for searching for others and speaking, as well as by others during the maneuvers of combat. (596–597)
Thus, having drawn out the *pṛṣṭhasvastika* by unwinding it, while the two hands turn away, one leaps up and simultaneously forms a *svastika* with the hands and feet. 598.
That *svastika* should be employed by the wise for the two aforementioned objects (599).
Thus ends the *svastika*.
When the hand, having moved to the region of the nose through both turning away (*vyāvarta*) and turning around (*parivarta*), [is positioned there]...
When the *karihasta* (elephant-trunk hand) assumes the form of an *alapa* lotus, it is then called *añcita*;
this should be employed when looking directly at someone out of great curiosity. Thus ends the description of *añcita*.
Standing in the *caturasra* posture, having turned the right hand outward and drawing it back, one should perform the *ākṣiptā* movement; then,
with the right hand in the *śukatuṇḍa* gesture, one should cause it to fall upon the thigh.

"When that [hand] is cast aside upon the left breast in the *khaṭakāmukha* position, it is to be employed for anger and envy; thus it was stated by the son of Soḍhala. (603) Thus ends the *apaviddha*.
In this natural posture (*svābhāvika*), the feet are joined with the nails,
and the arms are like creepers with the nails together; at the very beginning of the entry, the *cārī* is performed with the feet pierced and bent, while the hand is alternately *recita*.
"Whereas *unmatta* (the intoxicated) occurs in pride arising from beauty, fortune, and so forth.
(605) Thus ends the description of *unmatta*.
The *caturasra* (square) [dance] is performed by placing the wings of the swan (*haṃsapakṣa*) in rapid rotation.
If, by means of withdrawal and rotation, the two hands are brought from below and from above the head region,
bent and drawn back, and then formed into *svastika* gestures at the chest, they should thereafter be performed as the *pakṣavañcita* hands.
The two arms, illuminating the sides, move backward; she should then come under their control.
At the end, there is the *avahitthaka* posture, which is then the *svastikarecita*;
it is employed in the dramatic representation of dance and in states such as great joy.
Having thus performed the *svastikarecita* in the position of the mandala and standing in a square formation, he should unwrap his right hand and bring it to his shoulder and head. (609)

Having formed the two smallest fingers (the little fingers) and so forth into the shape of a closed lotus bud while engaged in the movements of falling and rising, and having turned the right foot upward,
one should bring the hand here to a square, rotated position with its face turned askance.
Likewise, when the left hand and foot are [extended] while the other is bent, it is called *nikuṭṭaka*;
this is employed in speech intended for expressing self-praise.
Thus ends the description of *nikuṭṭaka*.
That very same [gesture] becomes the *ardhanikuṭṭaka* (half-strike) when performed with only one limb;
it is employed for that same purpose when uttered with words that are not fully articulated.
Thus ends the description of the *ardhanikuṭṭaka*.
Having performed the *bhramarī* with the side [of the body], one stands in the position of the mandala;
having made one hip severed, with the arms and head as the sprouts,
and likewise with the hand between the limbs— thus, three or four [positions] are formed.
"Revolutions [are performed] with the waist-broken [movement] when describing that wonder.
Thus, having performed the *ākṣiptā* and *apakrāntā* *cārīs*, both hands—
Having formed the *svastika* with the right hand placed at the navel in the *khaṭakāmukha* position,
while the other [left hand] is made into the *ardhacandra* on the hip and that side is bent, and the other side is raised, such is the movement (*vṛtti*) along with the other limbs. (615–616)
That which is prescribed as level with the waist, accompanied by the Vaiṣṇava stance,
should be employed by the stage-manager during the consecration of the *jarjara* (the central pillar).
Thus ends the section on "level with the waist."

Having performed the *bhujaṅgatrasitā* foot-stance and lifted the bent leg, one should rotate it so that the thigh, hip, and knee form a triangle; while performing this with both *vyāvṛtti* (turning away) and *parivṛtti* (turning around), one hand should be like a swing (*dolākara*) and the other likewise.

The *khaṭaka* is so named because it is meaningful to its form; it is considered to be the *bhujaṅgatrāsita*. Thus ends the *bhujaṅgatrāsita*. Then there are the *cārī* called *alātā*, the *nitamba*, and the *hasta* called *caturasraka*.
If the left [foot] is likewise placed to the right of this [right foot] with the knee raised,
and there is a shift to another limb, that is considered the *alāta* (firebrand) in the *salalita* dance.
(620) Thus ends the *alāta*.

When the hand is being turned away, that foot is cast out; the other hand is square, while the first one is then rotated. Where the hand is thrown back and the foot likewise, and another limb is similarly disposed, [that is the *parivartana*]. (621)

There may also be the "scattered" (*vikṣipta*) and "unscattered" (*akṣiptaka*) movements when determining the coming and going [of the limbs]. However, those who know the true principles of drama do not consider this to be a formal application,
because in that context where there are gestural hand-movements (*abhinayahastakāḥ*), there is the dramatic representation of the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārthābhinaya*).
These are prescribed primarily for the sake of dance alone;
therefore, they are employed during the transitions between intervals, in the movement of gaits, and likewise in the shifting of *cārīs* and *sthānakas* within combat and wrestling.
In the performance of the *tālānusaṃdhāna* (the coordination of rhythmic beats), such a technique (*karaṇa*) should be employed:

having formed the foot in the *vṛścika* (scorpion) posture, one places the hand in the *ārāla* position at the level of the head, directed toward that same side, while keeping it straight across the field of the nose.
Another [hand] is placed on the chest with the fingers slightly bent; they call this *nikuñcita*.
It is employed in situations such as the eagerness to leap up or when reflecting upon something.
Others know that in this [gesture], the *patāka* and *sūcyāsya* hands are positioned at the tips of the nose. 627–628.
Thus, when the hand is being moved from the side region— contracted upward, turned downward by rotation— one should perform the *jaṅghā-svastika*. 629.

When the foot that has moved away from that direction is the left one and performs a swinging motion, then the *karaṇa* called *ghūrṇita* (the whirling) is said to have occurred. Thus ends the *ghūrṇita*.
When the foot is bent in a movement (cārī) with the knee raised, the hand should be either *alapadma* facing that same direction, or *arāla* with the palm turned upward; likewise,
when the knees are raised to the level of the breasts, the hands should be in the *pakṣavañcita* position.
Another [mudrā] called *khaṭaka* is then described as having the knees raised against the chest;
thus is the *ūrdhvajānu*.
Standing in the *maṇḍala-sthānaka* posture, with the hands placed on the chest in the *khaṭakāmukha* gesture, [one performs this].
When the *sūcīmukha* (needle-mouth) has been withdrawn and the foot is placed near it,
the foot is then dragged; when the side is bent during the withdrawal, that is to be applied as the *ardharecita* (half-bent), used for awkward or unsteady movements.
The *ityardharecita* is performed by making a *svastika* with the two ankles and simultaneously drawing back the feet while performing the unwinding and winding of the two hands.
One should perform that *mattalli* repeatedly, which causes the intoxication of passion;
thus ends *mattalli*.
Having approached [the partner], if the feet are not extended and the left hand is *recita*, [it is called] *upeta*.
Then, when one half of the *mattalli* is placed upon the hip during the youthful stage of intoxication,
the right hand is extended; where the left hand, acting as a swing, strikes that foot which has been raised up, it is the *recakanikuṭṭaka*.
Thus is the *recaka-nikuṭṭaka*;
the right hand performs the movements of the hip and the binding of the hair,
while the other [left] hand is repeatedly formed as a *karihasta* and the foot is likewise extended in an upward strike.
If another limb is graceful, then it is *lalita* (the graceful) in a dance performed by one full of charm.
Thus is *lalita*:
when the hand known as *sūcīmukha* (needle-point) recedes from the field of the body.
The *sūcīpāda* (needle-foot) and the *apasṛta* (withdrawn) *cārī* follow, and from that comes the *dhamarī*;
thus, in both limbs in succession, there is the *lalita* (graceful), which becomes the *valita* (twisted). Thus ends the *valita*.
Where one moves with the knees raised and the hands formed into *latāhasta* gestures,
one should then place one of them above the raised knee; that which is performed again with another limb is called *daṇḍapakṣa*.

Thus, with the two hands turned away from the side of the staff, placed at the level of the navel in the *khaṭakāmukha* position, and joined by the other foot in the *sūcīpāda* position accompanied by the *apakrānta* step— this is [the *daṇḍapakṣa*].
If the other foot is likewise placed [in that same position], then it is *pādāpaviddhaka* (643).
Having thus performed *pādāpaviddhaka*, one then performs the *bhramarī-cārī* and the *nūpurapādikā* (644).
One should extend one hand in that same direction with one foot, while the second hand is in the *latāhasta* (vine-hand) position; they know this to be the *nūpura* (anklet). Thus ends the *nūpura*.
Having performed the *ākṣiptacārī* step with one foot, simultaneously twisting the hand and turning the trunk (*trika*), one should execute the *pādasvastika*.
Then, likewise, the second limb [should be moved], while the two hands are simultaneously raised prominently.
"Where that *bhramara* [hand-gesture] is to be employed, that is in the *uddhata-parikrama* (the haughty circumambulation).
(647) Thus, where the two hands are placed in sequence upon the regions of the navel-lotus and the sides of the waist, it is the *bhramara*.
When the waist is severed, that stance is called *chinna*;
it is used in the breaking of palm trees as well as in the rubbing of the limbs.
Thus ends *chinna*.
The *bhujaṅgatrastarecita* is that where the dancer performs the *bhujaṅgatrāsita* step and both hands are executed as *recita* on the left side;
thus ends the *bhujaṅgatrastarecita*.
If there is a *cārī* of the right foot and the previously mentioned right hand is *recita*, while the other hand is a *latāhasta*, then that is the *bhujaṅgāñcitaka*;
thus ends the *bhujaṅgāñcita*.
If the feet are in the *daṇḍa* position and the hands are in the *daṇḍapakṣa* position,
then that *daṇḍarecita* [movement] pertains to the joyful dance;
however, others say its application is in a dignified progression.
Thus is *daṇḍarecita*;

when the two hands are positioned at the region of the chest, the left hand is like a sprout (*alapa* or *pallava*) and the right is *catura*, while the foot is *udghaṭṭita* and *catura*, then it is so called.

If one performs the left *sūcīpāda* (needle-step), having executed it as "clever" (*catura*) or "quickly withdrawn" (*drutāpasārita*), it is employed in the *vaidūṣikī* gait to indicate astonishment. 652.
One should place [the hand] on its right side and exhale at that time, rotating the hips;
or, while performing the *bhramarī* with the hands turned outward and inward,
one should form a square at the end— then that becomes *kaṭibhrānta*.
Niḥśaṅka states that the application [of this] is for the fulfillment of the *yatis* (caesuras) within the intervals of the *tālas*, as well as in the progression of the movement;
thus ends the *kaṭibhrānta*.
One hand is extended downward with the palm turned outward,
while the other is likewise raised upward; then, having been rotated, one is placed upon the region of the chest, supine and extended, while the other is extended with the face turned downward.
That stance in which the *ālīḍha* position is employed is called *vyaṃsita*; it is to be used during the movements of great monkeys such as Añjaneya and others. (657)

Thus it is concealed by the *atikrānta* (overstepping) āryā; however, as the foot is being brought down, one should bend it, and then, by means of the *vyāvartita* (turning back), one should withdraw the hand from that position at that very moment. 658

Having drawn it back with a turn, one should form the *khaṭakāmukha* [hand] at the chest; where the second limb is thus desired to be extended, the teachers call that the *uddhata-parikrama* (the haughty gait). 659
When the hands, feet, hips, and neck have moved forward and then the standing posture is again made into the *vaiśākha* stance, that should be known by the wise as *vaiśākharecita*. 660
Thus is the Vaiśākha-recita;
when the hands are in the *karihasta* position, the feet are like the tail of a scorpion,
and the back is deeply arched, they know that as the *vṛścika*.
This is employed for the aerial travel of Airāvaṇa and others.
(661) Thus, having made the scorpion [gesture], when one places the feet on the head of the arms in succession—
When the two lotuses (hands) are slightly contracted, that is the *vṛścikakuṭṭita* [gesture];
it is employed with wonder at the beginning of a desire for a celestial vehicle (*vyomayāna*), and so forth.
Thus ends the *vṛścikakuṭṭita*.
When the feet have become scorpions (*vṛścikībhūta*) and the hands are in the *svastika* and *recita* positions and then released, that is the *ākāśayāna-vṛścikarecita*;
thus ends the *vṛścikarecita*.
Where the scorpion is at the feet and the left hand is called the creeper, that should be employed by the wise as the "creeper-and-scorpion" (*latāvṛścika*) for leaping into the sky.
(664) Thus ends the *latāvṛścika*.

Where the *cārī* (foot-step) is cast forward (*ākṣiptā*) and the hand gesture (*khaṭakāmukha*) or the *catuḥ* (four-finger pose) is likewise cast forward (*ākṣiptaḥ*), that is considered the *ākṣipta* [movement] in the gait of the *vidūṣaka*.
Thus ends the section on *ākṣipta*.
If the right foot is placed at the base of the little toe of the left foot,
with the shank held rigid and extended for one and a half tālas,
and at that same time the arm is held rigid on the left side like a sprout; (this is the *alapaṭṭikā* posture).
Then, the hand other than the left, with its fingers slightly extended, is called *argala* (the bolt) by Śārṅgadeva during the circumambulation (*parikrama*) of Aṅgada and others.
Thus ends the description of *argala*.
When one foot is placed on its side with the sole turned upward and the fingers extended, and the other limb follows in succession with the hand like a banner (patāka) joined to its tip,
that is the *talavilāsita* [gesture], used in relation to the stage director (*sūtradhāra*) and others. 669–670.
Thus, when the thumb performs this movement of the palm and draws a tilaka on the forehead of the "scorpion-foot" (vṛścikāṅghri) mudrā,
then that forehead-tilaka is considered effective for traveling to the realm of the Vidyādharas.

Thus is the *lalāṭatilaka* (forehead-mark). When the two hands are in the *svastika* position, one foot is stamped upward on the side and the other downward; where [the hands] are likewise, that is the *nikuṭṭita* [stance]. 672.
Its manifestation is in the practice of *saṃcāra*; [it is called] *pārśvanikuṭṭaka*.
(673) Thus ends *pārśvanikuṭṭaka*:
where, having performed the *uḍḍita* step, one should move like a wheel with two swings. (674)
With their limbs bent inward, they spoke thus during that circular dance performed for the worship of the gods in that exalted movement.
(675) Thus ends the section on the circular dance (*cakramaṇḍala*).
When the two hands are bound in the *asthitāvarta* [mudrā] and placed upon the chest in the *uraḥmaṇḍala* [position],
that which is the *uraḥmaṇḍala* has been spoken by the beloved of Śiva.
(676) Thus ends the *uraḥmaṇḍala*.
When the hands designated as *dolā* are unwound and then wound around [each other], that *cārī* is called *āṣagati*; it is known as *āvarta*, used for fleeing in fear or like a serpent.
(677) Thus ends *āvarta*.
Where the left side is supine and the right hand is in the *alapa-dama* position,
while the right foot is bent and moves on its forepart— that is the *kuñcita* (contracted) posture;
with it, one should represent deities who are completely overwhelmed by the weight of bliss.
When the *dolāpādā* *cārī* occurs— where the knee is bent upward and the feet swing like a swing— and the hands are likewise swinging, it is called *dolāpāda* by the best among the learned. (680)

Thus, having performed the *dolāpāda* (swing-step) by repeatedly drawing back one foot with a *cārī*, and likewise drawing back both hands, one performs the *bhramarikā* (whirling) movement with the hands through the *vyāvṛtta* (turning away) and *parivṛtta* (turning around) motions.
"If it is reversed during the recitation, that occurs in the *uddhata-parikrama* (the raised-step movement)"— thus [is defined] the *vivṛtta*.
By means of the pointed foot (*sūcyaṅghri*), a *svastika* (crossed-leg posture) is formed from the heel of the second foot.

Where one performs the *abhidhā* foot-binding movement by encircling one side through both the turning away (*vyāvṛtti*) and the turning back (*pratyāvṛtti*), while the two hands are in the *recita* position,
that is the *vinivṛtta* movement; it possesses the same applications as previously described.
Thus,
when the hands follow the feet, it is the *pārśvakrāntā* gait; or rather, the hands may be governed by the requirements of the dramatic representation (*abhineya*).
This should be employed in a movement characterized by ferocity, such as that of Bhīmasena and others. (686) Thus ends the *pārśvakrānta* [step].
In the region of the heel, the second foot—the foot that is bent—should be placed.
When the middle finger of the hand known as *khaṭaka*— with the chest raised— is placed so that its tip touches the forehead, that is the *niśambhita* gesture;
alternatively, it may be the *vṛścikahasta*, which is used to represent Maheśvara.
Thus,
having pressed down and whirled the foot around the back, one who leaps in a circular motion in every direction should whirl the head within the field; that is then called the *vidyuddhānta*.
And they call this the *prayoga* (preliminary application) for the movement of those who are exalted; having performed the *vidyuddhānta*,
one should extend the foot forward in the *atikrāntā* step.
Where the wise know the two hands to be ready for application and have transcended intoxication (691)—
thus, having performed the *atikrānta* [movement] by executing the *vidyuddhānta*, *daṇḍapāda*, and *krama* gaits;
When the two hands have moved along a single path by means of the *udveṣṭita* (twisting) and *apaveṣṭa* (untwisting) movements, one should then cast them forward, backward, and to the sides;
this is to be enacted as the *vikṣipta* gesture, accompanied by a haughty gait.

When one has thrown back the hand that was cast aside and drawn up the foot, and while performing a triple turn (*trikavivartana*), the other hand is likewise extended in the *recita* position— that they call *vivartita*. 694.

When the legs of the swing (dolāpāda) are thus turned outwards and the hand is placed at the ear in the *karihasta* position, engaged in action, then that is the *gajakrīḍika* (elephant-play) gesture, which is true to its name. 695.
Thus is the *gajakrīḍitaka* (elephant-play) posture: the foot is pointed, the side is bent, and the left hand, resting on the chest, is in the *khaṭakāmukha* position. 696. Left.
If the sprout-like lip is located in the field of the cheek, it is called *gaṇḍasūcita*.
Regarding this field, some desire it to be the *sūcīpāda* hand, others the *sūcīmukha*, others the *nṛttahasta*, and still others the *abhinayahastaka*. (697)
Then, the ornamentation of the cheek is to be performed by means of this [gesture].
(698) Thus ends the Gaṇḍasūcī;
the two hands are in the Latārecita position, with the feet in the Vṛścikāṅghri posture, well-raised.
Where there is the chest (uraḥ), that is the *garuḍapluta*, whose name corresponds to its meaning;
thus [ends] the *garuḍapluta*.
It is performed with the *daṇḍapāda* ācaryā, or else it is performed rapidly (*druta*) by means of the *atikrānta* ācaryā. 699–700.

When the foot is being lifted and brought down, if the two hands produce a sound by clapping at the front, that is *talasaṃsphoṭita*, which is thus appropriately named. (701) Thus ends *talasaṃsphoṭita*.
If one foot is on the ground while the other foot is placed upon the back,
with the fist held at the chest and the hand in the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) position at the hip,
that should be known as *pārśvajānu*; it is to be employed in both open combat (*yuddha*) and wrestling (*niyuddha*).

When the feet are extended along the sides and knees toward the back with the big toes touching the ground, and the hands are in the *latākara* posture, that is the *gṛdhrāvalīnaka* posture, used in the great combat of winged birds. 704.

Thus, having performed the *gṛdhrāvalīnaka*, the bent foot is placed on the ground without touching it; the hand called *khaṭaka* is directed toward that same side, while the other hand is placed at the chest. (705)
The *alapadma* [hand-gesture] is located at the region of the head; thereafter, one proceeds gradually through the other parts of the body.
That which is described by Śārṅgadeva as being used for wonder (*vismaya*) is the *sūcī*.
Thus ends the *sūcī*.
When one [hand] is formed like a needle and the other is described as a half-needle, this is called the *ardhasūci* (half-needle);
or, when the hand is placed on the hip with the wings bent inward, it is the *ardhacandra* (half-moon) hand. (707) Thus ends the description of the *ardhasūci*.
When one [hand] is called *khaṭaka* on the chest and another is placed at the heel of the opposite [foot], and the foot is in the *sūcī* position,
then it is *sūcīviddha*, which pertains to the sphere of anxiety and so forth.
Thus ends *sūcīviddha*.
With the *hariṇapluta* gait, the *dolākhaṭaka-hastaka* [gesture] is performed;
this is declared to be the *hariṇapluta*, with its name and application as stated.
Thus ends the *hariṇapluta*.
When the two hands are raised with the fingers pointing upward, and the feet are bound together like needles and then turned around, it is called *bhramarikā*; that is termed *parivṛtta*.
Thus ends *parivṛtta*.
When the feet, with their moving anklets, and then the hand, are placed down rapidly like a staff, it is called *daṇḍapāda*; the wise employ it in a majestic circumambulation. (711)

Thus, when the feet are in the *daṇḍa* position, the hands are *recita*, and the thighs are bent in the *vṛścikāṅghri* posture, the *bhramarī* is performed; that is then appropriately called *mayūralalita*. 712.

Thus, when one performs the *mayūralalita* (peacock-playful) movement by leaping from the foot known as the *dolāpāda* stance with the other foot and executing a *bhramarī* (swirling) motion, it then becomes the *preṅkholita* (swinging). 713.

Having thus performed the *preṅkholita*, where the *mṛgapluta* is made and the feet are placed in *svastika* in front, with the hands in *dolau* and the body bent, that becomes the *adhamāpasṛta*. 714.
Thus, as she bent down, her head was tilted toward the other foot which was drawn back;
likewise, this hand was directed toward that side and the intervening parts of her body.
Wherein that *sarpita* consists of the approaching and retreating of one who is intoxicated—thus is the *sarpita*.
If the left [hand] is a *khaṭaka* on the chest by way of being twisted, the other [hand] is likewise. (715–716)
When the hand is in the *tripatāka* position at the ear and the foot is bent and extended in that same direction, it is called *karihasta* by the wise. Thus ends [the description of] *karihasta*.

If the hand that was extended moves slowly toward another foot by rubbing the ground, while the other hand remains like a creeper, then it is the *prasarpita*, the range of movement for a sky-walker. 718
When the two hands have performed the *baddhājñi* and *apakrānta* movements, and then follow their respective specific applications, that is called *apakrānta*. (719) Thus ends *apakrānta*.
If the two hands, with their fingers pointing downward, are brought to the region of the head in the *patāka* gesture,
and then, having turned around, are drawn out over the two upper shoulders and placed facing each other with the fingers directed toward one's own body; 720.
When the two [hands] are positioned at the hips, that is the *nitamba* posture (*karaṇa*). (721) Thus ends the *nitamba*.
For the coming and going of the feet during the swing (*dolā*), the *haṃsapakṣaka* [is used].
"Having approached in this manner, when another limb falters, that is considered *skhalita* (the faltering).
Having thus performed the *skhalita*, if one quickly places the foot before the *alātā* [position] like a slap (*capeṭavat*), [that is the *capeṭaka*].

Having performed the *hasta* (hand gesture) and likewise the other limbs, one should then apply the *siṃhavikrīḍita* (lion’s play); this is to be employed in the *raudra-gati* (fierce movement), so says the eminent leader of the Śrīkaraṇa school.
Thus ends the *siṃhavikrīḍita*.
When the hands are like scorpions and the feet are like lotus buds,
and when the other two feet are likewise made into scorpions with the toes bent forward,
that is the *siṃhākarṣitaka* (the lion-drawn) gesture used in the performance of the lion.

Having thus performed the *siṃhākarṣita* and the *janitā* *cārī*, if the two hands, in the form of the *arāla* and *ālapallava* gestures, are positioned on the regions of the forehead and the chest with their fingers directed forward; 726.
Having performed them sequentially with a twisting motion, then turning away so that they are at the sides,
and then likewise with an unwinding and a revolving motion toward the region of the chest, when they are placed facing one another, that is *avahitthaka*.
It is employed in the representation of the meaning of sentences that are mostly composed of *gauṇa* (secondary) words.
Others call it *avahitthaka* because it is joined with the gesture of concealment (*avahittha-hasta*), and they say it is capable of representing anxiety, weakness, and so forth. (728–729)
Thus is *avahitthaka*:
when the two *khaṭakāmukha* hands are placed upon a slightly curved chest,
that is the *maṇḍala* stance, employed in riding an elephant.
Thus, when the *elakākrīḍitā* foot-position is established, and the hands are in the *dolaka* and *khaṭaka* gestures while the body is bent and turned, that is the *elakākrīḍita* posture.
This is considered the range of movement for beings of an inferior nature.
(731) Thus ends the *Elakākrīḍita*;
if the *cārī* is performed and the *muṣṭi* is placed at the chest, while the other hand forms the *latākara*.
"When that [moment] occurs, it should be produced in the enactment of the commencement of an action" (732); thus, having performed the *janita* step,
one turns back from the left, performing the *ākṣiptā* and *parivartita* movements (733).
Having made a hand gesture with the right side bent, one should bring it to a curved position;
where that occurs, it is the *upasṛta* (approaching) gesture, which should be employed in approaching.
Thus ends the description of the *upasṛta*.
Performing the *dolāpādā* foot-step and the *saṃghaṭṭitatalau* hand-movement, having extended the *patāka* hands, if one stands in the *vaiṣṇava* posture,
one should place the right hand on the hip and extend the left.
"In the performance of compassion, it would then be 'joined palms' (talasaṃghaṭṭita). Thus, "joined palms" refers to that [gesture] where the hand and foot are moved away and then brought back.
The wise know that movement in which the body is turned upward as *udvṛtta*.
Thus ends the description of *udvṛtta*.
Where the bent foot extends forward with its tip directed toward an upward motion, [that is another form].
Both hands are extended; that is Viṣṇukrānta, used for the stepping of Hari.
(738) Thus ends Viṣṇukrānta.
One hand should be extended at the chest, while the other is the alapallava.
When the head is swayed (*lolita*) and both sides are likewise rested,
that which is called the Vaiṣṇava posture (*sthānaka*), the wise call it *lolita*.
Thus ends the description of *lolita*.
When the feet are drawn back in the *svastika* position and then gradually rotated,
and the head and hands sway, that is the *madaskhalita* (staggering with intoxication);
the Beloved of Bhava says this should be employed when one is intoxicated by passion.
When one thus performs the *cārī* known as *madaskhalita*, which is cast with a whirling motion, and having turned and revolved,
places the hand with its palm downward upon the back of the thigh; at that time—
That *saṃbhrānta* [movement] should be employed when there is a hurried circumambulation.
Thus, having moved away with *saṃbhrānta*, one should approach from the left with the right hand in the *nṛttahastaka* position.

If the left hand is bent with the foot, it becomes the *sūcīmukha*; having made the other limb likewise, the right foot becomes the *sūcī*, and that hand becomes the *alapaṅkaja* (lotus-hand), while the left hand remains as before. 744.
Thus, wherever there was a resistance, they spoke of it again and again.
(745) Thus, when the foot is raised in *viṣkambha*, that side is bent as the hands are raised for the clap (*tālika*).
When the two hands are struck upward there, with the limbs turned back, that is *pramodaka* (746).
Thus ends *udghaṭṭita*.
The *śakaṭāsya* stance occurs when one extends the foot along with the [other] limb (747).
Where one hand is [extended] while the second is at the chest in the *khaṭakāmukha* position, that is the *śakaṭāsya* (cart-mouth); such is the play of a child. (748) Thus ends the *śakaṭāsya*.

When the two hands, with the *arāla* and *khaṭaka* gestures, are turned back and placed upon the backs of the thighs by the *ūrūdvṛtta* āryā movement, that is the *ūrūdvṛtta*; it is used in expressions of jealousy, longing, love, and anger. (749)
Thus, performing the *ūrūdvṛtta* (upward-turned thighs) and the *alātā* (fire-brand) *cārī*, one should make the hands *recita*;
having turned them away and made them *kuñcita* (contracted), one forms the *alapadma* [mudrās] at the tops of the arms.
Where these two are placed, the wise call that the *vṛṣabhakrīḍita* (the Bull’s Play).
Thus ends the *vṛṣabhakrīḍita*;
if the hands are in the *recita* position and the head is turned (*parivāhita*).
When the feet are drawn back from the *svastika* position, the wise call that application *nāgāpasarpita*; this occurs during the early stage of intoxication.
Thus ends *nāgāpasarpita*.
If, following the lifting and lowering of the feet, the two hands perform the *tripatāka* gestures while simultaneously rising and bowing,
that is the *Gaṅgāvataraṇa*; this was taught by the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow at the descent of the Gaṅgā.
Thus, the Gaṅgāvara mudrā should be performed; in its execution, generally the left hand is placed upon the chest,
while the right hand follows the specific requirements of each respective gesture.
Thus there are one hundred and eight *karaṇas*; now, in accordance with various regions, the beloved of Hara, whose fame shines in every land, describes the *karaṇas* preceded by the *utpluti*. 756.
Then there is *añcita*, *ekacaraṇāñcita*, *bhairavāñcita*, *daṇḍapraṇāmāñcita*, and *kartaryañcitaka*.
Following that are three types of *alaga*: *kūrma*, *ūrdhva*, and *antarapūrvālaga*.
The *lohaḍī*, the *kartarīlohaḍī*, and the *ekapādādilohaḍī* (758).
Following that, there is the *darpasaraṇa*, the *śayana* preceded by water,
the *nāgabandha*, the *kapālādya*, the *cūrṇana*, and the *natapṛṣṭhaka* (759).
Next is the Matsya-karaṇa, then that known as Kara-sparśana;
after that, the Eṇapluta, the Tiryak-karaṇa, and the Tiryagañcita;
then the one named Tiryak-svastika, and finally the Sūcyanta is proclaimed.
The seven *bhramarīs* are: *bahya*, *antara*, *channa*, *tiripa*, *alaga*, *cakroci*, and *ādi*; the *bhramarī* beginning with the head is the first of the directions;
then follow *samapādāñcita* and *bhrāntapādāñcita*. 761–762.
And Soḍhala’s son taught that there are thirty-six variations involving confusion of the *skandha*,
having condensed the *karaṇas* that begin with the *utpluti*.
(763) Having stood in the *añcita* posture with feet together, one should perform the *uttālautpluta*.
Thus, the *ityañcita* (bent-in-this-way) posture,
which is formed by bending on one leg, is called *ekapādāñcita*;
this is the *ekacaraṇāñcita*.
When one leg is placed on the back of the thighs and there is a leap, it is called *bhairavāñcita*; in this *bhairavāñcita*,
having leaped, one falls to the ground like a staff, as if bending forward.
"The *daṇḍapraṇāmāñcita* (prostrated bow) is described by those who know the art of dance as follows: [it is] the *añcita* (bent) posture,
where the two feet are in the *svastika* position, and it is released from the *kartarī-añcita*."

Thus, when the añcita gesture is performed by the agent, one should leap with the face downward and, having fallen forward, assume the kukkuṭāsana (cock-fighting posture); this is declared as *alaga* by the wise Śārṅgin. 766.
If the tortoise-seat (kūrmāsana) is in such a position, and if that which is in the position of the tortoise is in the position of the tortoise,
then it is called "the tortoise-position" (kūrmālagam).
Having performed the *ūrdhvālaṅga*, one falls and stands with both feet level;
thus is the *ūrdhvālaṅga*.
Having performed the *kṛtālaṅga*, one falls to the earth and remains with the chest facing upward (*uttāna*).
"The head should touch the hips from behind in the *antarālagam* [stance]" (768);
thus, in the *antarālagam*,
standing with feet even, one leaps after having turned the pelvis.
When there is a lateral fall, it is called *lohaḍī* or *luṇṭhita* by the wise (769).
Thus, whether it is *lohaḍī* or *luṇṭhita*,
that same movement performed with the feet in a *svastika* position is considered *kartarī-lohaḍī*.
