Thus, the *kartarīlohaḍī* is [performed] by leaping;
or, when performed with one leg, it is considered by the wise to be the *ekapādalohaḍī*.
Thus ends the *ekapādalohaḍī*, or the *ekapādaluṇṭhita*.
If, while standing in the Vaiṣṇava posture, one should fall to the ground on one's side, that is called the Darpasaraṇa posture; thus says the Lord of Postures. (771) Thus ends the Darpasaraṇa.

That very posture called *jalaśayyā* (the water-bed) is like lying in water when performed on a seat; that same *nāgabandha* (serpent-bind) becomes [the water-bed] when performed on a seat like the serpent-bind. 772
Thus, standing with feet together and touching the ground with the head, turning back so as to crush its skull— this is described by the wise as the *nāgabandha* (serpent-binding) posture. 773.
Thus ends the description of the *kapālacūrṇana* (the "crushing of the skull").
Having performed the *kapālacūrṇana*, the chest is then placed face upwards; that which is described as having a bent back is called *vaṅkola* by others. 774.
If, having leaped up and whirled around, one turns over on the left side like a fish, that is described as the *matsyakaraṇa* (fish-movement);
thus ends the description of the *matsyakaraṇa*.
Having performed the *alaga* movement and supported the ground with the hand, one should roll about; where this [movement] is called *karasparśana*.
Thus ends *karasparśana*.
Having leaped up and placed one of the toes in the air,
when he performs the *utkaṭāsana* (wide-spread posture) while standing upright, that is then called *eṇapluta*.
Thus ends *eṇapluta*.
If, after leaping up with one foot and landing on the ground with the other, one remains there, that is "transverse movement" (tiryakkaraṇa). Thus ends the description of transverse movement.

From the *samapāda* position, when one leaps sideways, it is called *tiryagañcita*; having performed the *tiryaksvastika*, when one leaps sideways from the *svastika* position, it is *tiryagañcita*. 779.
Thus, when one holds the *tiryak-svastika* or any other *sūcī* at the conclusion, if the *karaṇas* are then directed forward, they are called "ending in *sūcī*" (*prāñci sūcyantāni*). 780.
Standing with the right foot pointed forward, one should bend the left foot; wherever there is a counter-clockwise rotation, that is considered the *bāhyabhramarī*. 781.
Thus is the external *bhramarī*; by its reversal, the internal *bhramarī* occurs—
this is the internal *bhramarī*.
Assuming the form of Trivikrama, he stands in such a way that,
due to his counter-clockwise rotation, the wise call it *channabhramarī*.
Thus ends the description of *channabhramarī*.

"Tiripabhramarī" refers to the horizontal wandering [of the gaze] after the *aṅghrisvastika* posture (783). Thus, having remained in the Vaiṣṇava stance (*vaiṣṇavasthānaka*), when one stands with the left foot...
Then, the *alagabhramarī* causes the body to whirl crosswise;
thus ends the *alagabhramarī*.
The *cakrabhramarikā* is so called because it is whirled like a wheel upon the half-moon (*khaṇḍasūcī*).
If, immediately after the *samapādā* [stance], one causes the body to rotate obliquely like a spinning wheel, Śaṅkaravallabha then calls that the *ucitabhramarī*. 785.
When one who is skilled in the *śirobhramarī* stands on the ground with the head alone, holding the feet raised upward, and whirls around three times, that is considered the *śirobhramarī*. 786.
Thus, having whirled the head once each time as before, when one stands in the four directions in succession while holding the ground with the rotation of the hands, that is the *dig-bhramarī*. 787.

Thus, having performed the *digbhramarī* with both feet in the *añcita* position, standing on the ground with one shoulder [bent], if one turns sideways and then causes the feet to swing (*ullolayet*), then—
The master, the foremost of the illustrious performers, spoke thus regarding the *samapādāñcita*:
"Having whirled the right foot around behind the surface of its sole... (789). Thus ends the description of the *samapādāñcita*.
Having grasped the middle of the lower leg with the left foot bent, and having placed and turned the feet sideways, one should swing them; that is then called *bhrāntapādāñcita*. 790–791.

Thus, having assumed the *utkaṭāsana* posture with the feet bent and drawn in, and having performed the *añcita* movement, standing with the limbs joined together on the ground and in the air, one then [performs it] upon the earth. 792.
If, having grasped with both hands and whirled around as before,
one stands facing each direction, that is called *skandhabhrānta* (shoulder-whirling) by the wise.
Thus ends *skandhabhrānta*.

There exist many other varieties as well that depend upon the instruments (karaṇas), but they were not mentioned by the illustrious wielder of the Śārṅga bow (Kṛṣṇa), for fear of increasing the bulk of the book.
Thus end the thirty-six *utplutikaraṇas*.
I shall now describe, both by name and by definition, the *aṅgahāras*— which yield both visible and invisible fruits— that are to be employed during the *pūrvaraṅga*.
These consist of the graceful placement of the limbs in their appropriate positions.
The *aṅgahāra* is said to be accomplished by means of the *mātṛkās*;
alternatively, it is traditionally remembered as "this practice of Hara (Śiva) by means of the limbs" (*aṅgaiḥ*).
A *mātṛkā* consists of two *karaṇas*, while a *kalāpa* consists of three *karaṇas*.

"A *khaṇḍaka* is to be known as consisting of four [lines], while a *saṃghāta* is considered to consist of five"—thus others have declared the distinction in nomenclature based on the specific groupings of the *saṃghas*.
The Sage himself, however, maintained that the difference between them lies in the deficiency or excess of the *karaṇas*. 798.
"By two, or by three or four"—this is what is indicated by the word "or" (vā). 799.
Then there are the *sthirahasta*, the *paryasta*, the *sūcīviddha*, the *aparājita*, the *vaiśākharecita*, the *pārśvasvastika*, and another, the *bhramara*. 800.
The Ākṣiptaka, the Paricchanna, the Madavilasita,
then the Ālīḍha and the Acchurita, the one known as Pārśvaccheda, the Apasarpita, the Mattākrīḍa, and likewise the Vidyuddhānta— these sixteen have been declared.
The bodily movements (aṅgahāra) performed by the best of sages according to the measurement of the square [dance-ground] are:
viṣkambha, apasṛta, mattaskhalita, gatimaṇḍala, apaviddha, viṣkambha, udghaṭṭita, ākṣipta, and recita. (802–803)
Then there are the *ardhanikuṭṭa*, the *vṛścikāpasṛta*,
the *alātaka*, the *parāvṛtta*, the *parivṛtta* and others, the *arecita*, the *uddhṛttaka*, the one known as *saṃbhrānta*, and the *svastikarecita*. (804)
Sixteen [are considered] by the measure of the triangle; thus, thirty-two are recognized in both [systems].
(805) Due to the infinity of the arrangement of the multitude of instruments (*karaṇa*), they are infinite;
nevertheless, those thirty-two have been stated according to their primary application. (806)
"The leader of the *karaṇas* has stated that each individual *karaṇa* of all the *aṅgahāras* should be performed with a portion in the form of a *guru*:
having made the *līna* [karaṇa] with the nails together, and the *vyaṃsita* here in the *vicyuti*. (807)
Having performed the *ujjhitālīḍha* with both hands, one should then proceed to the *pratyālīḍha*;
then follow the *nikuṭṭaka*, *ūrūdvṛtta*, *svastika*, *ākṣiptaka*, *nitamba*, *karihasta*, and *kaṭīchinna* in succession. (808–809)
With these ten instruments, one becomes steady-handed and dear to Śiva.
(810) Regarding all *aṅgahāras*, some experts in drama say that the *pratyālīḍha* stance should be employed at the beginning and at the end. (811)
Thus, with a steady hand,
he performed the *talapuṣpapuṭa*, the previously cast-off *vartita*, the *nikuṭṭaka*, the *ūrūdvṛtta*, the *ākṣipta*, and the *romaṇḍala* [gestures]. 812.
The *paryastaka* (overturned) is described by the wise as being performed through these ten *karaṇas* in sequence: *nitamba*, *karihasta*, and *kaṭīchinna*.
Thus ends the *paryastaka*.
The half-needle, the scattered, the whirlpool, the trampled,
the raised thigh, the thrown back, that known as the chest-circle,
the elephant-trunk, and the hip-cut— these are the nine *karaṇas*. 814.
The *aṅgahāra* named *sūcīviddha* was proclaimed by Bharata and others;
thus ends *sūcīviddha*.
[It consists of] *daṇḍapāda*, *dvyaṃsita*, and that which is called *prasarpitaka*.
Then, with the *nikuṭṭa*, *ardhanikuṭṭa*, and *ākṣipta* [movements] of the hair-circle (*romaṇḍala*),
followed by *karihasta* and *kaṭīchinna*— thus endowed with these nine *karaṇas*, the *aparājita* [stance] has been described by the master Niḥśaṅka. (816–817)
Thus [ends] Aparājita;
then the Vaiśākha-rechita with two limbs, then the nūpura, then the bhujaṅga, trāsita, unmatta, maṇḍala, and svastika. 818.
With the eleven *karaṇas*— namely *nikuṭṭaka*, *ūruvṛtta*, *ākṣipta*, *ūrūmaṇḍala*, *karihasta*, and *kaṭīchinna*— in their respective order,
there is an *aṅgahāra* known by the name *vaiśākharecita*. (819–820)
Thus is the Vaiśākharecita;
then the Diksvastika with one leg, followed by the Ardhanikuṭṭaka; again the Diksvastika, and then the Ardhanikuṭṭaka with the other leg. (821)
The *apaviddha*, *ūrūdvṛtta*, *ākṣipta*, *nitambaka*, *karihasta*, and *kaṭīchinna*—thus there are eight *karaṇas*.
Through practice, this becomes the *pārśvasvastika*; however, it may consist of ten [elements] starting from the first two. (822)
Thus is the *pārśvasvastika*; then follow the *nūpurākṣiptaka*, the *chinnasūcī*, the *nitambaka*, the *karihasta*, and the *uraḥmaṇḍalaka* as a *karaṇa*.
The *kaṭīchinna* (waist-broken) is said to consist of eight *bhramara* movements. Having thus performed the *bhramara*, one then performs the *nūpura-vikṣipta-ālāta* and the *ākṣiptaka*.
And with these eight *karaṇas*, the *ākṣiptaka* known as *uro-maṇḍala-saṃjña* is performed;
others have declared that its application consists of two types: *vikṣiptālātaka* and *ākṣipta*.
Thus ends the *ākṣiptaka*.
Having performed the *samanakha* (nail-to-nail) cut, one then executes the *saṃbhrānta* on the left;
this is followed by the *bhramara*, the *vāmapārśvārdhasūci*, and the *aṅghrikrānta*.
Above the *bhujaṃgatrāsita*, the *karihasta* is then performed. 827.
"Severed at the waist, it is cut apart by the nine instruments"—
thus it is "cut apart";
and there are also the *mada-skhalita*, *mattalli*, and *lasa-sphoṭita* [rhythms].

Beyond that, they say there are seven [movements] in the *vilāsita* (sportive) gait due to intoxication: the *bahuśaścitragumpha*, the *nikuṭṭaka*, the *ūrūdvṛtta*, the *karaṇa* called *karihasta*, and the *kaṭīchinna*. (829–830)
"By repeating the three instruments three times, there are thirteen repetitions;
some desire four, five, or more repetitions for each of the three.
Thus ends my own composition.
With the two shoulders turned away (*dvyaṃsita*), accompanied by the *sanikuṭṭa* movement, there should be the *nūpura* gesture on the left foot;
then, on the other side, the *alātakākṣipta*, followed by the *uraḥmaṇḍalaka*, and then the *karihasta* and *kaṭīchinna*—by means of these *karaṇas* in succession. (832)
When performed with the eight [steps], this *aṅgahāra* is approved by the sages as *ālīḍha*.
Thus ends *ālīḍha*.
Then follow *nūpura*, *bhramara*, *vyaṃsita*, and *lātaka*. 833–834.
The *nitamba*, the one called *sūci*, then the *karihasta*,
and the *kaṭīchinna*— the wise know these eight *karaṇas* in the *ācchurita* [movement].
(835) Thus ends the *ācchurita*.

First, there is the *vṛścika* (scorpion) and so forth; then, with the knees raised, one performs the *ākṣiptasvastika*, followed by the rotation of the torso (*trika*), the movement known as *uraḥmaṇḍala*, the *nitamba*, and the *karihastaka*. 836.
"The *kaṭīchinna* movement is considered the eighth [variant] in the *pārśvaccheda*.
Thus ends the *pārśvaccheda*.
In the *apakrānta*, there is merely the action of the two hands of one who has been deceived (*vyaṃsita*).
The *karihasta*, the *ardhasūcī*, the one called *vikṣipta*, the *kaṭīyuta*,
the *chinnamūru*, the *udvṛtta*, the *ākṣipta*, the *karihastaka*,
and the *kaṭīchinna*— these are the seven *karaṇas* in the *apasarpaṇa*.
Two and a half [times], twice, the severed-hip, the elephant-trunk, and nine—
thus is the *apasarpita* (withdrawn) [step];
then the *bhramara*, the *nūpura*, and that called *bhujaṅgatrāsita*.
Having performed [the movement] with the right side alone, one should execute the vaiśākharecita;
then follow the ākṣipta, chinnakaraṇa, bhramara,
vyaṃsita, as well as the uromaṇḍala, nitamba, and karihastaka.
When the hips are severed by these twelve movements in succession,
and by eleven through practice, the calculation for the *bhramara* [movement] is completed; this *aṅgahāra*, beloved of Hara, is known as *mattākrīḍā*.
Thus is the *mattākrīḍa*;
with the left side it becomes the *ardhasūci*, while on the right it is the *vidyuddhānta*. Furthermore, by reversing the limbs, these two become the *chinna*. 844.
Then, having passed [the left side], one should perform the *latāvṛścika* (the creeper-scorpion) on the left;
likewise, the *kaṭīchinna* (waist-cut) six times through the practice of both [sides].
Furthermore, the wise have declared that there are eight movements in the *vidyudbhrānta* (lightning-twirl). 845.
Thus, having performed the *nikuṭṭaka* movement with the "wandering lightning" (*vidyudbhrānta*), one performs the *ardhanikuṭṭaka*;
from the *bhujaṃgatrāsita*, one proceeds to the *bhujaṃgatrastarecita*. 846.
Having performed the *ākṣipta* and *romaṇḍala*, and having gradually formed the *latākara* [hand-gesture],
the seventh, the *kaṭīchinna*, occurs when one has moved away from the *viṣkambha*.
Thus ends the *viṣkambhāpasṛta*.

The *mattalli*, *gaṇḍasūcī*, *līna*, *mattāpaviddhaka*, and *talasaṃsphoṭita* should be performed as part of that [sequence], followed by *karihasta* and *kaṭīchinna*; these are the *karaṇas* in their proper order. 848.
The seven types of steps (*saptāṅgahāra*) are said to be included within that which is designated as *mattaskhalita* (the stumbling of the intoxicated). Thus ends *mattaskhalita*.
Following the *maṇḍalasvastika*, there is that designated as *niveśonmatta* (the placement of the insane).
The one called *udghaṭṭita*, *mattalli*, and after that *ākṣipta*;
then *uraḥmaṇḍalaka* and *chinna*—these eight *karaṇas* occur in the *gatimaṇḍala*, as stated by Niḥśaṅka. (850–851)

Thus, having performed the *gatimaṇḍala*, one first executes the *apaviddha* and then the *sūcīviddha* with the hands; then, having simultaneously performed the *udveṣṭita* with the *baddhā* gait, one should rotate the triple-joint (*trika*). 852.
Then there is the *ūrūdvṛtta* movement, followed by the *uraḥmaṇḍalaka*;
the fifth is the *kaṭīchinna*, and if that is performed as an *apaviddha*, then it becomes the *apaviddha*. (853) Thus ends the *apaviddha*.
The *karaṇa* called *nikuṭṭaka* consists of the leg being bent and extended;
from that comes the *ūrūdvṛtta*, then the *ardhanikuṭṭaka* *karaṇa*,
then the *bhujaṃgatrāsita*, and then the *bhramara* upon the winding of the hand.

The *karihasta* with the hand cut at the waist (*kaṭīchinna*) shall be the ninth in the *viṣkambha* [section]. (855) Thus ends the *viṣkambha*. Next, in the *udghaṭṭita* [movement], there is that called *nikuṭṭa*, followed by the *uraḥmaṇḍalaka*.
The *nitamba*, the *karihasta*, and the *kaṭīchinna* as the fifth—
thus is the *udghaṭṭita*;
from the *svastika* and so forth, the *recita* is that which is known by the name *pṛṣṭhasvastika*.
The *diksvastika*, *kaṭīchinna*, and the one named *sama-ghūrṇita*;
the *bhramara*, *vṛścika* and so forth, and the *recita* preceded by the side; the *nikuṭṭaka* preceded by the chest, and then the *maṇḍala* and *saṃnata*. (857–858)
The *siṃhākarṣitaka*, the one called *nāgāpasarpita*,
and then the *vakṣaḥsvastika*— some wise authorities maintain that these are [the names]; and the *daṇḍapakṣa* gesture is called the *lalāṭatilaka*.
Then there is *vilāsita*, *talādya*, and *niśumbhita* (860);
after that which is called *vidyuddhānta*, there follows *gajakrīḍitaka*,
as well as those known as *nitamba*, *viṣṇukrāntā*, *ūrūdvṛtta*, and *ākṣiptaka* (861).

The ancient authorities maintain that there are twenty-five *karaṇas* [of the hands]: the *uromaṇḍala*, the *nitamba*, the *karihasta*, and optionally the *kaṭīchinna*, as employed in the *ākṣipta* and *recita* movements. (862)
By repeating [the movements] on both buttocks and the circle of hair, there are twenty-seven [varieties].
(863) Those who consider the *vakṣaḥsvastika* and the *kaṭīchinna* to be included here, even when the repetition is performed, would have only twenty-five [varieties] according to their view. (864)

Thus, the *ākṣiptarecita* [is described]; from the *svastika* comes the *recita*, and from that, the *ardharecitaka*; then the *vakṣaḥsvastika*, the one known as *unmatta*, and the *ākṣiptarecita*. (865)
The *ardhamattallikaraṇa*, the *recakanikuṭṭaka*,
the *bhujaṃgatrasta* preceded by the *recita*, and then the *nūpura*;
having performed the *vaiśākharecita*, one should execute the *bhujaṃgāñcita*.
The *daṇḍarecitaka*, the *cakramaṇḍala*, and that beginning with the scorpion (*vṛścika*);
the *recita* above the scorpion, the *vivṛtta-vinivṛttaka*, the *vivartita*, the *garuḍaplutaka*, and the *lalita*—these constitute [the sequence]. (867–868)
The Peacock and so forth, the Serpent-like, the known as the Stumbling, the Creeping, then the Clashing of the Soles, and thereafter the Bull’s Play;
the Leaping— these are declared to be the thirty-six *karaṇas*.
Having divided that [space] into four parts with unequal portions in the four directions (870), one should apply it by means of a circular rotation; at the end,
one should perform the *ura-maṇḍalaka* (chest-circle) where the waist is severed— that is the *recita* (871).
Thus, after the *recita* has been performed, there should be the *vivṛtta*, the *nikuṭṭa*, and the *ardhanikuṭṭaka*; following the *ardharecitaka*, there should be the *recakanikuṭṭaka*. (872)
Then there are the movements called Lalita, Vaiśākharecita, and Catura;
following Daṇḍarecitaka, there is Vṛścikakuṭṭita, then Nikuṭṭāka preceded by the side [movement], and finally Saṃbhrānta and Udghaṭṭita. 873.
Above the circle of the chest, [the arms] are called "elephant trunk" (karihasta) and cut off at the waist; this constitutes the seventeen [counts] in the *ardhanikuṭṭaka*.
Thus ends the *ardhanikuṭṭaka*.
First there is *latāvṛścika*, then *nikuñcita*; after that, *mattalli*, the *karana* called *nitamba*, and *karihastaka*.
The sixth is known by the wise as *kaṭīchinna*, which occurs when one has moved away from the *vṛścikāpasaṃsṛta* posture. 875.
In this place, some have described the *bhramara* of the hip. Thus ends the section on the scorpion-step (*vṛścikāpasṛta*).
Now follow the *svastika*, the *vyaṃsita*, and the two known as *dvirālāta* and *ūrdhvajānu*.
Then there are the *nikuñcita*, *ardhasūcī*, *vikṣipta*, and *udvṛtta*;
likewise, *ākṣipta*, *karihasta*, *kaṭīchinna*, and *alātaka*.
These constitute eleven *karaṇas*, with one additional [movement] when the action is doubled. 877–878.
Thus is the *alātaka*:
the *alātaka* with a cart-mouth (*śakaṭāsya*) produced by the right limb, as well as the *bhramara*, accompanied by the clenched hand placed on the cheek. 879.

The *karihasta*, *kaṭīchinna*, and the other *karaṇas* are performed in succession; thus, six have been described for the *parāvṛtta* by the illustrious son of Soḍhala. The experts have called the bending and raising of the limbs *nikuṭṭaka*.
Thus, having turned back and performed the *nitamba* movement, one should perform the *svastika*,
the *vikṣiptākṣiptaka*, and that known as the *latāvṛścika*. 882.
Then one should perform the *unmatta*, *karihasta*, *bhujaṅgatrāsita*,
*ākṣiptaka*, and *nitamba*; these nine, ending with the *nitamba*, should then be executed in a circular sequence known as the *bhramaraka*.

Having directed the face toward the edge of the horizon and turned away from the two opposite directions, one who stands facing the first direction should perform the *karihasta* and *kaṭīchinnaka* gestures;
where this occurs, the teachers call it *parivṛttakarecita*.
This method of reversal, excluding the final two *karaṇas*,
is proclaimed by the learned Śārṅgadeva, who was well-versed in the doctrines of Bhaṭṭa Abhinavagupta and others, for all the *aṅgahāras*. (886–887)
Thus ends the *parivṛttakarecita*;
following the *nūpurakaraṇa*, one should perform the *bhujaṅgāñcita*, the two *gṛdhrāvalīnakas*, and the two *vikṣiptas* separately for each limb. 888.

The *udvṛtta*, *madhya*, *sūcī*, *nitamba*, *vṛścika*, *latāpūrva*, and *kaṭīchinna*—these are the nine *karaṇas*. Furthermore, there are two additional ones: the *dvirvikṣipta-udvṛtta* and the *udvṛttaka*. (889)
Thus [ends] the *udvṛttaka*;
then the *vikṣipta*, the *añcita*, the *gaṇḍasūcī*, and finally the *sarvāntima*;
then the *ardhasūcī* and the *daṇḍapāda* performed with the left side of the body. 890.
Next are the *catura*, the *bhramara*, and those named *nūpurākṣipta*,
*ardhasvastika*, *nitamba*, *karihastaka*,
*urormaṇḍala*, and *kaṭīchinna*, in that order. (891)
The wise have described the *saṃbhrānta* [movement] by means of fifteen constituent parts (892). Thus, after the *vaiśākharecita*, this pair of *vṛścika* movements is performed twice.
If, after the one called *nikuṭṭaka*, the hands are raised in succession to form a creeper (*latā*) and the fourth [hand] is severed at the waist, then it should be known as *svastikarecita*;
it consists of two additional movements beyond the practice of the first two.
Thus, with the *svastika* gesture performed, accompanied by mṛdaṅgas, gomukhas, bhambhās, bherīs, paṭahas, ḍiṇḍimas,
paṇavas, darduras, and other instruments following the rhythm and tempo (*tāla-laya*).

The *aṅgahāras* should be employed by those who desire the highest welfare during the *vardhamāna*, *āsārita*, *pāṇikā*, *gītakā*, and other such elements of the *pūrvaraṅga*, as well as during the *utthāpana* and other parts performed by the wise.
The application of the *karaṇas* is said to be within the *aṅgahāras*;
they say that even when the *karaṇas* are performed separately, there is great fruit.
Thus ends the definition of the thirty-two *aṅgahāras*.
Now we shall describe the four *recakas* proclaimed by Bharata;
they occur at the feet, the hands, the waist, and the neck.
Their movement is constant, both internally and externally, between the heels and the tips of the big toes.
That which is accompanied by bending and raising [of the body] is called *pādarecaka* (foot-extension). 900.
Rapidly circling around with both hands like the wings of a swan, performed in alternation, is what constitutes *kararecaka* (hand-extension). 901.
The *kaṭirecaka* (waist-extension) is said to consist of the circular rotation of the waist in all directions by means of a transverse whirling of the fingers and the extended thumb;
the *kaṇṭharecaka* (throat-extension) is described as the shaking and turning of the neck.
These also produce a combined fruit from the various components of the *aṅgahāra*.
Thus ends the definition of *recaka*.
When the movements of the feet, shanks, thighs, and hips are performed in a balanced manner, it is called *vicitra* (varied).

The term *cārī* is derived from the root *car* with the suffix *ṅīṣ* (forming *carī*), or from the root *car* with the suffix *iñ* (forming *cari*), or it may be *hasta* when referring to a gesture (*abhinaya*). Regarding movement (*gati*), the *caraṇa* (foot) is that which is desired;
the *cārī* appropriate for the accomplishment of that [movement] should be performed, and another [subsequent one] should be made suitable for that. 904–905.
Thus, due to their mutual restriction, that very [movement] is called *vyāyāma* (exertion), as well as its divisions: *cārī* (step), *karaṇa* (posture), *khaṇḍa* (segment), and *maṇḍala* (circle).
Among these, that which is accomplished by a single foot is celebrated simply as *cārī*.
The *karaṇa* consists of two feet; it is distinct from the *nṛttakaraṇa*.
A *khaṇḍa* is formed by three *karaṇas*, and a *maṇḍala* by three *khaṇḍakas* or four, respectively, in the *tāla* known as *tryasra* (triangle) and *caturasraka* (square). 907–908.
This [gait] is twofold: terrestrial and aerial. Here, the terrestrial ones are sixteen:
*samapādā*, *sthitāvartā*, *śakaṭāsyā*, *vicyavā*, *adhyardhikā*, *cāṣagati*, *elakākrīḍitā*, and likewise—
Samosarita, mattallī, mattallyutsanditā, āḍḍitā (910),
syanditā, apasyanditā, baddhā, and that called janitā, as well as ūrūdvṛttā— these sixteen we now declare to be the ākāśikīs. 911.
Atikrāntā, apakrāntā, pārśvakrāntā, mṛgaplutā,
ūrdhvajānu, alātā, sūcī, nūpurapādikā,
dolāpādā, daṇḍapādā, vidyuddhāntā, and bhramarī. 912.
The *bhujaṅga*, *trāsitā*, *ākṣiptā*, *viddhā*, and *udvṛttā* are thus proclaimed;
these thirty-two āryās are approved by Bharata.
However, there are others well-known in regional styles (*deśī*), which we shall now describe. 913–914.
The *rathacakrā*, the *parāvṛttatalā*, the *nūpuraviddhikā* (915),
the *tiryaṅmukhā*, the *marālā*, the *karihastā*, the *kulīrikā*,
the *viśliṣṭā*, the *kātārā*, the *pārṣṇirecitā*, and also the *ūrutāḍitā*. (916)
The ūruveṇī, the talodvṛttā, the hariṇatrāsikā, the parārdhamaṇḍalikā, the tiryakkuñcitā, and the madālasā;
then the saṃcāritotkuñcitā and the stambhakrīḍanikā. 917.
The *cārī* known as *laṅghitajaṅghā*, as well as *sphuritā*, *apakuñcitā*,
*saṃghaṭṭitā*, *khuttā*, *svastikā*, *taladarśinī*,
*purāṭī*, *ardhapurāṭī*, *sarikā*, *sphurikā*, and then [the others]. 918–919.
The *nikuṭṭaka*, the *latākṣepa*, the *apyuḍuskhalitikā*, the *samaskhalitikā*, and the *bhaumya*— these thirty-five are thus declared.
The *vidyuddhāntā*, the *puraḥkṣepa*, the *vikṣepa*, and the *hariṇaplutā*.
The *apakṣepā*, the *ḍamarī*, the one struck by the foot of the staff (*daṇḍapādāṅghritāḍitā*),

the leaping of the shanks (*jaṅghālaṅghanikā*), the fire-brand (*alātā*), the whirling of the shanks (*jaṅghāvarta*), the encircling (*veṣṭana*), the uncoiling (*udveṣṭana*), the upward throw (*utkṣepa*), the upward throw of the back (*pṛṣṭhotkṣepa*), and the needle (*sūcikā*). 921–922.
In the verse beginning "viddhā prāvṛttamullola," nineteen [syllables] are said to be sky-going (vyomagā), while both [halves] together are declared to be fifty-four;
these are considered to be eighty-six according to the teacher who followed the Mārgadeśī school.

We shall now describe in order the characteristics of those *cārīs*. When one stands with the feet placed close together and with the nails aligned, in the *sthāna* known as *samapāda*, it is then called *samapādā*.
"Because it possesses the mere fitness for movement, this *cārī* is considered to exist even in a stationary position.
(926) Thus ends the *samapādā*.
If one moves to the side of the other foot and proceeds on the surface of the ground...
When one knee is placed within [the opposite thigh] so that the foot attains the *svastika* position, and the other side is drawn together by separating [the feet], it is then called *sthitāvarta*.
Thus ends the description of *sthitāvarta*.

When one holds the upper body steady while the feet move on their toes, and having extended the chest, it is raised upward, that is the Śakaṭāsya (Cart-Face) posture; indeed, the face should be cast forward by those who have resorted to this *cārī* movement. 928–929.
Thus, when one has stepped out from the *śakaṭāsya* stance and, with feet together, strikes the earth with the tips of the soles of both feet, it is then called the *vicyavā*. 930.
Thus, in the *vicyavā* [gait],
the left foot is placed at the heel-region of the right leg, while the right [foot] steps back and remains in its own side in a triangular position. 931
If the right [foot] is likewise at a distance of one and a half *tālas*,
and that [left foot] forms a triangle upon the left heel, then it is the *adhyardhikā*;
thus ends the description of the *adhyardhikā*.
Having stepped forward a *tāla* and moved back a *dvitāla*,
with both feet together on the right foot, preceded by a slight leap,
they should approach and then retreat, and retreat and then approach.
"Where, in the *satrāsagati* and other such movements, this very *cāṣagati* is considered to occur;
thus, the *cāṣagati* is that in which, after leaping slightly, both feet move on their toes."
The *ailakākrīḍitā* is considered to occur when [the feet] fall in alternation;
thus, in the *ailakākrīḍitā*,
while one foot is on the inside, the other foot moves on its forepart.
When the two shanks are crossed like a svastika and one foot moves on its toes while the other two feet whirl about,
with both withdrawing and advancing,
that is the *samosaritamattallī*, which occurs during the middle stage of intoxication.

Thus, when the two feet— whose entire soles are pressed against the ground, joined in the *jaṅghā-svastika* posture, and shaped as semi-triangles— either rotate or glide forward, it is called *samosarita-mattallī*. (938)
Alternatively, it is said: "When [the hand] is withdrawn, that is the *mattallī* in the youthful stage of intoxication.
Thus, the *mattallī* is formed by the portion of the little finger and the portion of the thumb, respectively.
Where one slowly performs the coming and going of the feet in imitation of exhaling (*recaka*), that *cārī* is called *utsanditā* by the wise;
some, however, describe it here as the *recita* dance-hand gesture (*nṛttahasta*).

When the feet are raised by both the forepart and the back of the even feet, and one foot moves upon the surface while the other is rubbed against it in succession, they know that to be the *aḍḍita* gait. 942.
When the left thigh is bent and seated while the right leg is extended five *tālas* away horizontally, that posture is considered *syanditā*. 943.
Thus, that very same *syanditā* (flowing) is considered *apasyanditā* (non-flowing) due to the reversal of the movement of the feet; this is *apasyanditā*. 944.
Thus ends *apasyanditā*.
When the two thighs are bent and joined with the *jaṅghā-svastika*,

or having broken the *svastika* at the tips of the soles of the feet and performed circular rotations (*maṇḍala-bhrama*), it is considered "bound" (*baddhā*) when each has moved to its respective side. (945)
Thus is the *baddhā* posture formed,
in which one foot moves on its forepart,
while the fist is at the chest and the other hand is positioned as is most graceful. 946.

"The action of the foot (*aṅghrikriyā*) shall be the primary element, while the other [elements] constitute the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Thus, when the heel of the foot is brought forward, it is designated as *agratalasaṃcara*.
If the other leg is turned toward the back of the foot, or if there is a reversal;
or if one leg is bent while the other knee is depressed and the thigh is rotated outward, then that *cārī* is employed in situations such as shame or jealousy. (948–949)
Thus, these [steps] known as ūrūdvṛtta are established in wrestling, in the movements of the limbs, and in dance;
they are proclaimed by the Nāṭyaveda, which has the beginningless Veda as its root. 950
Thus are the sixteen earth-bound movements (bhaumacārīs).
Now, the aerial ones (ākāśikyas):
having raised one foot in the region of the ankle of the other foot, with the [raised] foot bent forward...

Having extended and then retracted [the foot] somewhat according to its natural state, as is common in the world, one should then cause it to fall forward at an interval of four *tālas* or more; he declared that *cārī* to be "unhesitating" (*niḥśaṅka*) when it has thus transcended the previous position. 951–952.
Having performed the *atikrāntā* step and the *baddhā* movement, if one lifts the foot and casts the bent leg to the side, then one should designate that as the *apakrāntā* step. 953
Having thus withdrawn and drawn [the foot] upward along her own side with the foot bent, if she then strikes the ground with the heel, it is called *pārśvakrāntā* (the side-step). 954
This is well known in the world as *pārśvadaṇḍapāda*.
Others have said that in this [stance], one should lift the foot up to the edge of the other thigh and then place it on the ground with the heel raised. 955–956.
Thus, when one has performed the *pārśvakrāntā* by lifting the bent foot, leaping up, and bringing it down to the ground,
one should then throw the other leg and calf back toward the rear.
Then it is to be known as the *mṛgaplutā* (leaping deer), performed by the Vidūṣaka. Thus,
the *mṛgaplutā* occurs when the foot is bent and lifted so that the knee reaches the level of the breast.
Having placed [the foot] and made it rigid, the other leg should then be with the knee raised;
this is *ūrdhvajānu*.
If the sole of one foot is directed toward the thigh of the other foot which has its leg extended backward, [it is *pṛṣṭhaprasāritāṅghri*].
Having placed the heel on one's own side with the foot resting on the ground, it is then called *alātā* (959).
Thus ends the *alātā*;
having lifted the bent foot and extended its shank (960).

That [stance] in which one lets the foot fall on the ground, bent forward at the initial application, reaching as far as the knees or the thighs, is called *sūcī*. Thus ends the description of *sūcī*.
Having drawn back one bent foot, one should touch the hip with its heel;
then, if one causes that leg, with its calf bent, to fall to the ground on its forepart, that is called the *nūpurapādikā* carriage. 962
Thus, when one raises the bent foot of the *nūpurapādikā* stance and swings it to both sides, placing the heel against one's own side, it is then called *dolāpādā*. 963
Thus, if one places the swinging foot with its anklet upon the heel of the other,
while the knee is directed toward the region of one's own body with speed; 964.
When the *cārī* is extended forward, it is then called *daṇḍapādā*. Thus, the *daṇḍapādā* [is performed] by turning back, touching the head, and whirling in all directions.
Where the foot is extended and there is a flash of lightning,
that is the *vidyuddhāntā*. Having performed the *atikrāntāgata* step and the turning of the hips in a triangle,
the body is rotated by means of the circling of the sole of the other foot.
Where that *bhramarī* movement was proclaimed by Śārṅgadeva [as verse 967],
thus ends the *bhramarī*:
having raised the foot from the region of the root of the other thigh, it is bent.
When the heel is turned toward the hip and the knee is brought to one's own side,
with the sole of the foot facing upward due to the twisting of the hips and knees, that is the *bhujaṅgatrasitā* (the "terrified serpent") posture, which indicates fear of a snake. 968–969.
Thus, terrified by the serpent,
she should draw back her bent foot, which was previously raised within the interval of three claps; then, having crossed the shank over to the other side, she should let it fall.
When they know this [stance] as *ākṣiptā* on the ground by means of the heel;
thus, in the *ākṣiptā*,
having formed a *svastika* with the separated calves, one [leg] is bent.
When one foot is extended, bent, and placed beside its own side, and then it is brought down with the heel into the space between the heels, that is called *āviddhā*. (972) Thus ends *āviddhā*.
With the heel remaining steady in the region of the thighs while the foot is cast aside, having leaped up and performed a *bhramaraka*, she should cause [the opponent] to fall;
likewise, lifting the other foot, she becomes one whose entire form is turned upward.
Thus, these noble movements,
characterized by elevated and graceful bodily actions, should be employed by the wise in combat, wrestling, dance, drama, and gait. 975
Whichever [limb], whether the hand or the foot, is the primary one at a given time and place, the other should follow it; however, when there is equality [of importance], they occur simultaneously.
Where the foot is, there the hand follows; where the hand is, there the *trika* (the three parts from the navel up) follows.
The wise say that the limbs and minor limbs (*aṅga-upāṅga*) are the followers of the movements (*caraṇa*).
Thus, when the movements are primary, there is an application of the limbs;
but when the hand gestures (*hastaka*) are primary, the hands attend to the limbs.
Just as the foot, having moved according to its gait, rests upon the earth, so too the hand, having performed its movement, comes to rest upon the hip;
in the art of dance, the half-moon hand-position likewise rests upon the hip.
The *pakṣavañcitaka* or the *pakṣapradyotaka* in dance—thus is the definition of the thirty-two *cārīs*.
If, having taken a square position, the two [feet] move forward while remaining joined; 980.
When the feet are [placed] in front or behind [the knees], it is then called *rathacakrā*.
Thus, in the *rathacakrā*,
the foot is extended outward with its sole turned upward.
That in which the soles are turned upward was described by Śārṅgadeva (982).
Thus, having stood with the soles turned upward in the *svastika-bandha* posture, [the feet are positioned] with the heels and likewise the foreparts [of the feet].
Where the two feet are recited [in such a way], it is called *nūpuraviddhikā*.
Thus, when the *nūpuraviddhā* is situated in the *vardhamāna* position, with [the feet] on the left and right sides; 983.
Then, with the feet drawn forward rapidly by the *sarata* [movement], they are called *tiryaṅmukhā*;
in the *nandyāvarta* posture, the feet are extended with the heels and the tips of the toes.
That [stance] in which the two [feet] are extended forward is called *marālā*. Thus,
having stood in the *saṃhata* position, one rubs the ground with both sides [of the feet].
Where both feet are positioned as in the *karihastā* posture, that *cārī* is proclaimed as *karihastā*.
Thus ends the *karihastā*.
Then, having moved the two feet obliquely while remaining in the *nandyāvarta* position, one performs the *kulīrikā*.

Thus, when the feet are in the *kulīrikā* posture with the heels pierced [by the hands], and they move apart and approach, or alternatively, move away from each other, it is called by the wise the "Separated" (*viśliṣṭā*) stance. 987
Thus, with her feet positioned in the *nandyāvarta* stance, she has moved backward; thus she is called "the Timid One" (*kātarā*).
If, standing in a position where the heel has moved to the side,
the heel is drawn back (recita), then that *cārī* is called *pārṣṇirecitā* by those who are experts;
thus ends the description of *pārṣṇirecitā*.
If, while standing on one foot in that position, one strikes the thigh with the foot remaining on the ground, it is then called *cāryūrutāḍitā* (989). Thus ends *ūrutāḍitā*.
When the two feet, positioned in the *svastika* posture upon the thighs, rub against the ground on both sides, the wise call that the *ūruveṇī*.
(990) Thus ends the description of the *ūruveṇī*.
When one moves forward rapidly with the back of the fingers leading, and the forepart of the feet is raised,
that *cārī* is considered by the wise to be *talodvṛttā*.
Thus ends *talodvṛttā*.

When, having bent the feet and crossed them in the *svastika* position, one leaps up and falls with the soles of the feet turned toward the sides, that is the *hariṇatrāsikā*. Thus ends the *hariṇatrāsikā*.
When the two feet, having been dragged along the ground and led outside, turn back slowly and successively, the wise call that the *ardhamaṇḍalikā*.
Thus ends the *ardhamaṇḍalikā*.
The Lord of the Śrī-Karaṇa says that when one repeatedly casts the foot obliquely after contracting it, that is the *tiryak-kuñcitā* (oblique-contracted) *cārī*.
Thus ends [the description of] *tiryak-kuñcitā*.
Where one places the feet here and there in an unsteady manner like a person intoxicated, the wise call that *cārī* "Madālasā" (Sluggish with Intoxication).
Thus ends Madālasā.
When one foot is contracted and repeatedly lifted up to be joined with the other, while the latter moves sideways,
that is then called *tiryaksaṃcāritā* (sideways movement).
Thus ends *tiryaksaṃcāritā*.
Having lifted both feet and bent them, one should place them one by one in front; that in which this occurs is called *utkuñcitā* cārī by the son of Soḍhala. (997) Thus ends *utkuñcitā*.
If one extends a single foot horizontally and repeatedly brings the other side against its sole, that is called *stambhakrīḍanikā*. Thus ends *stambhakrīḍanikā*.
When one foot, standing on a spot called *khaṇḍasūcī*, is drawn up with speed and leaped over by the other foot,
that is called *laṅghitajaṅghikā*.
Thus ends *laṅghitajaṅghikā*.
When the sides of the feet of two dancers touching the ground move forward with speed, it is called *sphuritā*; when they subsequently move backward with bent feet, it is called *apakuñcitā*. 1000.
When one stands in the *apakuñcita* posture in the position called *viṣamasūcī*, and while leaping and falling to the ground, strikes the feet together there, that is called the *saṃghaṭṭitā*. 1001.
Thus, when the earth is struck by the tip of the foot, it is called *khuttā*; that which is pressed down is termed *khuttā*.
When the feet are made into the form of a *svastika*, it is called *svastikā*. (1002) Thus, *svastikā* occurs when the two feet, having been placed together, are drawn apart sideways.
Touching the ground with the outer sides [of the feet], she gazes at the surface;
thus is the *taladarśinī*.
The *nikuṭṭana* consists of striking [the ground] with both feet raised together, while the *purāṭikā* [is performed] as follows.
Thus, when one foot is raised and the other is stamped down, and while that foot is raised the other foot is likewise stamped down, it is called *ardhapurāṭikā*. 1004.
Where one foot moves forward while the other half remains stationary, that is considered a *sarikā*. (1005) Thus ends the *sarikā*.
When one moves forward with both feet together, it is called *sphurikā*;
the posture of *sphurikā* involves the toes being curled, while *nikuṭṭikā* is performed with the tips of the feet. 1006.
Thus, having performed the *nikuṭṭikā* (stamping) behind, if one then extends the foot forward and stamps the ground with it, that is declared to be the *latākṣepa* (the vine-throw). 1007
Thus is the *latākṣepa*; when the foot slips, there is the *tiryagaḍḍaskhalitikā*. (1008) Thus ends the *aḍḍaskhalitikā*.
When both feet stumble simultaneously— forward, backward, or sideways—
that is called the *cārī* known as *samaskhalitikā*.
(1009) Thus ends the *samaskhalitikā*.
That [gati] in which one quickly lifts the foot from the front, whirls it rapidly above the forehead, and places it on the ground, they know as *vidyuddhāntā*.
(1010) Thus ends *vidyuddhāntā*.
Having lifted the bent foot and extended it forward with speed, one should place it upon the ground where that forward projection occurs; this is the *puraḥkṣepā* (forward projection). 1011.
Thus ends the *puraḥkṣepā*.
If one repeatedly extends the foot in the space before and then contracts it in the front portion of the sky, that *cārī* is called *vikṣepā* by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow (Viṣṇu).
Thus ends the description of *vikṣepā*.
Because she leaps repeatedly from her bent foot and lands [on the other], it is called *hariṇaplutā* (the deer-leap).
In this [movement], one foot touches the back of the thigh with its outer side, while the other foot [is raised]. 1013. Thus ends the description of *hariṇaplutā*.
When she moves toward the vicinity of the hips with a downward toss [of the foot], it is called *apakṣepā* (1014).
Thus ends *apakṣepā*;
it is characterized by the rotation of the bent foot from right to left or left to right.
Thus, when one performs the *ḍamarī* by rotating the *svastika* and throws the feet obliquely and upward, that *cārī* is celebrated as *daṇḍapādā* by Niḥśaṅka. 1015
Thus, having extended the feet of the staff-step and performed a leap, one should strike the gait alternately;
when both soles of the feet [strike], it is then called the *aṅghritāḍitā* movement. 1016.
If, while being struck slightly by the foot, one leaps into the air with that same foot while the other leg is bent, then that is considered the *jaṅghālaṅghanikā* (thigh-leaping) *cārī*. 1017
Thus is the *jaṅghālaṅghanikā*;
when the firebrand is on the back foot, the other foot quickly leaps over it—
this is the *alātā*.
If one places the sole of the foot that is being rotated inward upon the back of the knee of the foot that is being rotated outward,
then there shall be the *jaṅghāvarta* (thigh-turn).
Thus ends the description of the *jaṅghāvarta*.
If one who is encircling should encircle another with one foot,
then experts in dance call that very movement *veṣṭana* (the encircling).
Thus ends the section on *veṣṭana*.
Having wrapped [the leg] in the *udveṣṭāna* position, with the foot extended behind;
thus is the *udveṣṭāna*.
Likewise for a bent foot, [it is performed] in front or behind.
The raising [of the foot] up to the knee is called *utkṣepa* by the wise (1022). Thus is *utkṣepa*; if that same movement occurs specifically behind the back, they know it as *pṛṣṭhotkṣepa*.
Thus is the *pṛṣṭhotkṣepa* (the backward throw).
When one places the foot on the side of the thigh and extends it, making its tip sharp, Śrīkaṇṭhavallabha calls that the *sūcī*. 1023.
Thus, when the feet are in the *svastika* position and one foot is slightly swayed forward and bent at the knee, that is known by the wise as the *viddhā* (pierced) posture. 1024.
When the body is thus pierced,
bent, and turned, and the foot is raised, that should be known as *prāvṛta*, the very life of the god of love. 1025
Thus, when covered [by the garment],
there may be a "swelling" (*ullola*) at the feet through the successive tossing upward; this is called *ullola*.

Position (*sthāna*), stability (*sthiti*), and movement (*gati*) constitute *cārī*. Since one moves after having stood still, and stands after having moved, these movements are inseparable from position;
therefore, immediately following those [movements], position is described. (1027)
A specific, steady arrangement of the limbs is called a *sthāna* (posture).
Among men, there are six postures: the Vaiṣṇava, the Samapāda, the Vaiśākha, the Maṇḍala, as well as the Ālīḍha and the Pratyālīḍha. (1028–1029)
Now we shall describe the three postures (*sthāna*) of women according to the sage’s doctrine: those called *āyata*, *avahittha*, and *aśvakrānta*, as well as another quartet [of gestures].
Furthermore, I shall explain what was indicated by the sage when he said, "And also... (1030).
Going and coming, turning, twisting, and reversing (1031).
Next, twenty-three regional standing postures (*deśī-sthānaka*) are described:
the *svastika*, the one called *vardhamāna*, the *nandyāvarta*, and the *saṃhata* (1032).

The *samapāda* (even-footed), the *ekapāda* (single-footed), the *pṛṣṭhottānatala* (back-upturned-soled), the *caturasra* (square), the *pāṣṇividdha* (heel-pierced), the *pārṣṇipārśvagata* (side-heel-positioned),
the *ekapārśvagata* (one-side-positioned), and that which is called *ekajānunatā* (single-knee-bent). 1033.
The postures called Parāvṛtta, Sūcī, Samādi, and Viṣamādi;
then Khaṇḍasūcī, followed by Brāhma, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Gāruḍa, Kūrmāsana, Nāgabandha, and Vṛṣabhāsana. (1034–1035)

The *svastha* (natural), *madālasa* (intoxicated-slack), *krānta* (striding), *viṣkambhita* (obstructed), *utkaṭa* (exalted), *srastālasa* (drooping-slack), *jānugata* (knee-bent), and *vimuktajānu* (released-knee)—
these nine, Bharata declared, are the standing postures (*sthānaka*) for one who is seated. 1036.
The even, the contracted, the extended, the turned, the raised, and the bent— these are the six sleeping postures (sthāna).
Thus, there are six postures for men, while for women there are seven others as well.
Twenty-three [postures] have been described, along with nine sitting postures and six sleeping postures; the leader of the *karaṇas*, Niḥśaṅka, states that all these combined amount to fifty-one.
Now I shall state the characteristics of all these [postures] according to the opinion of those who know them:
one foot is placed flat on the ground, while the other is positioned on the side, forming a triangle;
with a space of two and a half *tālas* between them, the shank should be slightly bent. (1040–1041)
That which possesses excellence should be known as Vaiṣṇava, having Viṣṇu as its deity (1042).
The Sage has declared that it should be employed by superior and middling men in conversation with one who abides in Prakṛti and is not joined by any other purpose (1043).
Others say it was by a dancer wearing the dress of Viṣṇu;
still others claim it was by the stage-manager (*sūtradhāra*) or another who established the dramatic performance.
That foot which stands on its side with the toes directed toward the flank—this is the *pakṣasthita* position.
That same [space], if it faces slightly toward the front, is triangular.
When the hand is extended, the wise call the space between the tips of the thumb and the middle finger a *tāla*. 1045–1046.

Where the hips are level with the knees, the elbows are level with the shoulders and head, and the chest is well-elevated while the limbs are relaxed—that is *sauṣṭhava* (graceful poise). (1047) *Sanna* means resting in its own place; *niṣaṇṇa* means remaining motionless. (1048)
The limb should be steady, not too high, motionless, and not hunched (1049). Such is the limb in *sauṣṭhava*; it should be performed by those of superior and middling [capacity].
This is the Vaiṣṇava posture, the life-breath of the square [form] (1050).
The Vaiṣṇava stance is that wherein the hands are at the waist and navel, the chest is raised separately, and it is said to be square; thus is the Vaiṣṇava [stance]. 1051.
Thus ends the Vaiṣṇava.
Where the feet are equal, with their soles well-formed and placed at the distance of one *tāla* apart, that is the *samapāda* [stance], which has the four-faced Brahmā as its presiding deity;
it is used for accepting blessings bestowed by Brahmins or for gazing.

"Among the middle-class birds, when there is curiosity regarding a bride and groom, [the movement] is desired among those situated in the palanquins of ascetics and observers of vows, and those in chariots"—
thus it is described as *samapāda*.
If the two [feet] are seated above the ground at a distance of three and a half *tālas*, with the thighs in the air and the feet on the ground at that same interval, then,
when they are situated in the corners of a triangle, that position is called *vaiśākha*.

That [constellation] has Viśākhā as its presiding deity; it occurs during the observation of the thick-winged bird (the peacock) and at the beginning of the horses' impulsion, the taking up of speed, and their driving.
Thus ends Vaiśākha. (1056)
When the two feet are placed on the ground with the toes pointing toward the sides, the heels separated by one *tāla*,
and the thighs resting in the air level with the hips and knees at a distance of two and a half *tālas* from each other, that is the *maṇḍala* posture, presided over by Indra.
The Sage has taught this regarding the employment of weapons such as the bow and the vajra, the riding of elephants, and the visualization of Garuḍa and other beings;
others declare that in the mandala, the two feet should be separated by a distance of four tālas.
Thus, in this maṇḍala,
the left leg is first bent at the knee in the sky,
while the right foot is extended five tālas in front. 1060.
One should know that when both [feet] form two triangles, it is the *ālīḍha* posture, having Rudra as its presiding deity;

speech produced by envy and anger should be performed with this [posture], as should the subsequent actions such as wrestling, contending, and clapping, which are characterized by the heroic (*vīra*) and fierce (*raudra*) sentiments. (1061)
"Having thus aimed his weapons, he should resort to the *pratyālīḍha* stance.
(1062) Thus, the *ālīḍha* is described; the *pratyālīḍha* is said to be the inversion of the limbs of the *ālīḍha*.
One should release the weapon aimed while in the *ālīḍha* stance;
the one beloved by Śambhu declares Rudra to be the presiding deity there.
(1063) Thus ends the *pratyālīḍha*.
Of these, the first four are seen in both dramatic performance (*nāṭya*) and dance (*nṛtta*);
however, according to experts, the application of the last two is desired as being the exclusive domain of drama.
Others, moreover, maintain that there are six postures (*sthānaka*) even within the fivefold dance.

Thus are the six positions of the person: the right foot is placed between the *ghāma* and the *tāla*, forming a triangle; the face is serene; and the chest is elevated yet not overly protruding. 1066.
When the right hand rests on the hip and buttocks while the other is like a creeper, that is called the *āyata* (extended) posture; Kamalā is the presiding deity here.
This posture should be employed when one desires to stand still or when performing movements involving wounds.

When addressing a friend, a lover, or others; at the beginning of entering the stage; when scattering handfuls of flowers; in cases of indignation, prohibition, or the maintenance of pride—[these are the occasions for such speech]. 1068.
In the preliminary ritual (*pūrvaraṅga*), the invocation (*āvāhana*) and dismissal (*visarjana*) performed with pride, gravity, and silence should be carried out by women alone; so some have said.
Alternatively, men or women may perform them; however, at the entrance, the standing posture (*sthānaka*) belongs to the woman.
Others say that when [the actors] have entered, the stage positions should be performed according to the requirements of the drama;

immediately following the *āyati*, the entry onto the stage and other such actions should be carried out, and among those, the movements of the hands and feet should be understood as appropriate to the occasion. 1072.
This view has been expressed by Bhaṭṭa Abhinavagupta:
"That very *āyata-avahittha* (the 'extended' pose) would become [the *viparyasta-avahittha*] through the inversion of the feet. (1073)
Cintā (thought) and vitarka (reflection) occur in contentment and in conversation arising from one's nature;
in astonishment; in gazing at one's own limbs born of pride in great good fortune; and in the observation of grace, sportiveness, beauty, and the path of the beloved. (1074–1075)
"This task is difficult; this position indicates concealment.
(1076) Thus ends *avahittha*.
When one foot is standing evenly, the other heel is slightly raised.
When, at the start of mounting a horse, one stands with the foot like a needle on one's own side or at a distance equal to the full length of the arm, it is called *aśvakrānta*;
this occurs when one stumbles, when garments are slipping off, or when one seeks to conceal what should be hidden. (1077–1078)

This posture should be employed when gathering clusters of flowers, when leaning against the branches of a tree, in natural conversation, and in graceful amorous gestures; and the goddess Bhāratī is the presiding deity here. (1079)
Thus, when a dancer who is about to move has raised one foot and remains poised, that state— due to the cessation of both movement and stillness— is "the gone-and-not-yet-gone" (gatāgata). 1080
Thus, when the body has moved forward and back and is slightly turned, one foot is directed toward the cardinal points,
while the other has its little toe touching the ground and its big toe resting upon the earth.
Then, when there is a longing glance, it is called *valita* (the turned).
Thus ends *valita*.
One foot is flat on the ground, while the other is bent with its toes touching the half-sole.
When the two hands are raised at the front and bent like crabs, that is called *moṭita*;
its application is proclaimed to be in all the states of love (*kāmāvasthā*). (1082) Thus ends *moṭita*.
When that same [position] is turned back by rotating the limbs toward the rear,
it is called *vinivartita* (1083).
In the *svastika*, when both feet are bent at the knees in the position of a swan (*haṃsaka*), it is likewise [known as] *vinivartita*.
When the little fingers are mutually interlocked, the wise call that the *svastika* (1084).
Thus ends the *svastika*.
In the *vardhamāna*, however, the two feet are placed crosswise with the heels joined (1085).
If the distance between his feet increases accordingly by six finger-breadths or even a span (vitasti), then that is declared to be the *nandyāvarta* [mandala]. 1086.

Thus is the *nandyāvarta* posture; when the two feet are naturally placed together with the thumbs joined and the ankles pressed against each other, that is the posture used for offering a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). 1087.
Thus, Śārṅgadeva has prescribed that stance where the body is naturally compact and the two feet are straight, separated by a span (vitasti); this is known as *samapāda*. 1088.
Thus, when one foot is placed with its outer side joined to the outer side above the knee of the other leg, it is called *ekapāda* (the single-footed stance). 1089.
When one foot has its toes and heel touching the ground while the other foot is behind it and the remaining foot is level in front, that is designated by the wise as *pṛṣṭhottānatala*. 1090.
Thus, with the backsoles turned upward,
if the distance between the two feet of the *nandyāvarta* posture is eighteen finger-breadths, that square position is declared by the wise. 1091.
Thus, the square [stance] is described;
when the heels are joined with the big toes, it is prescribed as the *pārṣṇividdha*,
thus it is called *pārṣṇividdha*.
"When the heel has gone to the side, the heel is situated within the other side"—
thus is the *pārṣṇipārśvagata* [stance].
When the other foot is positioned slightly in front of the foot that is the subject of the description, [it is called *samapāda*].
If one foot is on the outer side while the other is positioned horizontally on the same side,
that is the *ekapārśvagata* (one-sided) stance.
This occurs when one foot is even and the other is at a distance of four *aṅgulas*.
When the knees are bent sideways, that is the *ekajānunata* (one-knee-bent) posture.
(1094) Thus ends the description of *ekajānunata*.
When the feet are turned around, the heels, big toes, and little toes should be level.
When the feet, having turned back so that they are joined to the ground by the heels, calves, and thighs, are extended sideways, it is then called *samasūci*. 1095.
Thus,
when the two *sūcī* feet are extended separately, one in front and the other behind, that position is called *viṣamasūci* by those who know it. 1096.
Some have described those two feet as being with the heels touching the ground and the knees and ankles raised;
this is called *viṣamasūci*.
One foot is bent, while the other has its thigh and heel touching the ground.
When [the foot] is extended obliquely, it is then called *khaṇḍasūci*.
(1098) Thus ends *khaṇḍasūci*.
If one foot is straight and the other is bent backward, [it is called *ardhasūci*].
When raised to the level of the knee-joint, that is called the *brāhma* [stance].
(1099) Having thus established one foot evenly in the *brāhma* position, if the other foot is slightly bent—

When the foot is extended forward and placed obliquely, that is the Vaiṣṇava posture (1100). Thus ends the description of the Vaiṣṇava. When the left foot is brought together and the other [right] knee is level with the top of the [left] knee—
Where the raised foot is in a contracted form, that is called Śaiva (1101).
Thus ends the Śaiva [stance]:
the left leg is bent forward, while the other is behind with the knee [touching the ground].
"When both feet have reached the ground, that is declared to be the Gāruḍa posture.
(1102) Thus ends the Gāruḍa.
The right foot has its knee, outer side, and ankle touching the earth.

"Where the left [side] becomes equal, they know that to be the tortoise posture (kūrmāsana). Thus ends the description of the tortoise posture. When, having sat down, one places the right [foot] upon the back of the left thigh—
Then the foremost of practitioners taught the *nāgabandha* for the shanks.
Thus ends the *nāgabandha*:
if the two knees are placed on the ground, whether separated or joined.
The Vṛṣabhāsana (Bull-seat) posture is thus described as being established with grace: in this posture,
the feet are extended and slightly bent, and the chest is somewhat raised.
When both hands are placed upon the hips, that is called the *svastha* posture (1106). Thus, in the *svastha*,
one leg is extended while the other rests upon the seat.

Where the head is turned to the side and the eyes are languid with intoxication, that is known as *madālasa* (intoxication-languid); it occurs in states of intoxication, calamity, despondency, longing, or separation.
(1107) Thus ends *madālasa*.

With both hands placed on the chin, the head resting upon the shoulders, and the eyes slightly tearful—this is considered the *krāntamada* (intoxicated with pride) pose; it occurs when one has conquered or subdued [an enemy], or when one is exhausted by grief. 1108
When the arms are extended from the thighs and the feet are extended and bent,
while the eyes are closed, that is called *viṣkambha*. (1109)
In yoga and meditation, this occurs by its very nature in the *bhaṭāsana*. Thus it is described as being level with the seat, touching the ground, with both feet even.
When that intensity arises in yoga, meditation, twilight prayers, recitation, and so forth—when the hands are relaxed and released, and the body is languid; 1111. Thus, [it is] intense.
Then, the eyes, assuming a sluggish form, become drooping and languid; this occurs in states of loss, exhaustion, intoxication, disease, fainting, and fear.
(1112) Thus ends the description of the "drooping and languid" gaze.
The posture known as jānugata is considered to be that in which both knees rest upon the ground.

This [posture] is employed during fire offerings (homa), worship of the deities, begging from the destitute, observing wild animals, frightening away base beings, and for appeasing those who are angry. (1113–1114)
Thus,
when one knee of the *utkaṭa* posture itself is placed upon the surface of the earth, it is called *muktajānu*, which is used for propitiating proud women.

Falling on the ground with knees released is prescribed for making offerings, for consoling virtuous people, and for the acts of the righteous; it is also remembered for expressions of grief, weeping, and the like.
Thus it is liberated,
sleeping with face upturned, with arms relaxed and released, and even—
thus it is even.
"With the limbs contracted and the knees drawn up, it is called *ākuñcita*;
its application in the representation of suffering from cold has been declared by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Thus ends *ākuñcita*.
"Placing one arm down, with the knees extended,
sleeping in an outstretched position— this is prescribed for one who sleeps comfortably.
Thus ends the *prasārita* (outstretched) posture.

"Vivartita (the turned-over) is when one sleeps with the face downward due to wounds from weapons and the like. Thus ends the description of *vivartita*. *Supta* (the reclining) is when one sleeps with the head resting on the shoulder and the elbows placed upon the ground.
"That which was described as 'uplifted' refers to the Lord’s playful posture; thus, 'uplifted' means with the shanks slightly extended, while 'reclining' means with both hands relaxed. (1120)

"That bent posture (nata-sthānaka) is prescribed for states of exhaustion, fatigue, indolence, and so forth. Thus ends the section on the "bent" [posture]. Activity arising from speech, mind, and body is that which is conducive to the goals of human life.
The dramatic style (vṛtti) is to be known as fourfold: Bhāratī, Sāttvatī, Ārabhaṭī, and Kaiśikī. Their origin is now described:
Bhāratī was born from the Ṛgveda, and Sāttvatī from the Yajurveda.
The Ārabhaṭī style originates from the Atharvaveda, while the Kaiśikī style originates from the Sāmaveda. The mode of speech (vāgvṛtti) employed by Bharata and his followers,
which primarily consists of Sanskrit dialogue, is considered the Bhāratī style due to its predominance.
That which reveals the quality of goodness (*sattva*) is said to be endowed with *sattva*; the mind originates from that, and joy, heroism, and generosity are the characteristics of the *sāttvatas*.
A drama in which that [quality] predominates is *sāttvatī*, characterized by an abundance of the heroic, the furious, and the marvelous sentiments.
The *ārabhaṭī* style is inferior due to its lack of erotic, pathetic, and compassionate sentiments;

it arises from a violent basis and occurs when soldiers who are intensely enthusiastic produce [a performance] based on their own physical prowess, as well as in the case of the violent (*raudra*) and other such elevated rasas.
Abounding in illusions and sorcery, increasing diverse modes of combat,
fashioned with the delicacy of speech, limbs, and ornaments, enriched by shimmering song and dance, and overflowing with the sentiment of erotic love.
Free from hesitation, he speaks in the Kaiśikī style, which has beauty as its sole lifeblood;
through that beauty and delicacy, this [style] may even be employed in the Furious (raudra) and other sentiments.
Furthermore, there are the prologue (āmukha), the comic interlude (prahasana), the vīthī, and the prologue-introduction (prarocanā).
The four "divisions" (aṃśas) which are considered by the sage Bharata to belong to the *āmukha* are:
*udghātyaka*, *avalagita*, *kathodghāta*, *pravartaka*, and *prayogātiśaya*; these are its five varieties. (1130–1131)
The varieties [of the Sāttvatī style] are known as *utthāpaka* (the rousing), *parivartaka* (the exchange),

the fourth is called *saṃlāpaka* (the conversation), as well as *saṃghātyaka* (the combination), *saṃkṣiptaka* (the abbreviated), *avapāta* (the descent), and likewise *vastūtthāpana* (the presentation of the subject matter). 1132.

In *Ārabhaṭī*, there is *saṃpheṭa*; thus, there is a set of four divisions. In *Kaiśikī*, it is held that there is *narma*, and likewise another, *narmasphuñja*, as well as *narmasphoṭa* and *narmagarbha*; thus, there is a set of four divisions. (1133–1134)

The three varieties of jesting— which distract the mind of others, involve censuring others, and likewise indicate anger or envy— along with their definitions and examples, are these that fall within the scope of the drama (*nāṭaka*).
Those whose minds are distracted by fear do not perform poetry, song, or dance without hesitation; likewise, that which is devoid of *vṛtti* does not shine.
Therefore, one should understand these *vṛttis* as they were spoken by Bharata.

Thus, having described the characteristics of movement, that which is appropriate for effecting the successive displacement and striking down of the weapons of oneself and the enemy in battle— the maneuvering of the body— is called *nyāya*. 1138
The Bhārata, Sāttvata, Vārṣagaṇya, and that known as Kaiśika—
these are its four divisions corresponding respectively to the four modes of conduct (vṛtti).
Now, for the purpose of establishing their definitions, I shall describe their specific characteristics.
Those movements which are preeminent and diverse are the *parikramas*; these same movements become *pravicāras* when they fall within the scope of discharging weapons.
Holding a shield with the left hand and a sword with the right hand—
Having seized them and moved away, they then raised their hands and cast [the opponent] down; then,
having performed the whirling of a shield on both sides,
they whirled the weapon around the head of the sword-wielder.
Wrapping the hand between the head and the cheek from the wrist, one should perform a circular motion even above the head;
this procedure is performed once upon the hip, and it is the "falling of the weapon" (śastrapāta) in the Bhārata.
In the Sāttvata rite as well, it should be exactly the same; however, the confusion regarding the weapon must be avoided. The one skilled in this matter should strike the weapon upon the feet;
such is the deliberation prescribed here for the Vārṣagaṇya rite, just as in the Sāttvata.
In this case, there should also be an additional whirling of the shield behind one's back;
likewise, while holding the weapon in hand, there should be a winding motion over the shoulder or the chest.
Furthermore, the delivery of the blow here is considered to be directed toward the region of the chest.
In the Kaiśika style, as in the Bhārata, there should be the striking of the head with weapons;
one endowed with grace should employ weapons such as spears and lances, as well as bows, thunderbolts, and the like, according to these rules.
Movements performed without grace do not look beautiful;
one should execute a strike by means of mere appearance, but not as a reality.
Or else, one should display it like a strike through illusions or sorcery. (1150)

These principles (nyāyas) should be employed by means of the *cārīs* during the discharge of weapons. Thus ends the definition of the principles; the specific collection of *cārīs* known as the *prāṅmaṇḍala* has been explained.
Now the wise one, the foremost of the illustrious masters of *karaṇa*, describes its varieties:
the *bhramarāskandita*, the *āvarta*, the *śakaṭāsya*, the *āḍḍita*, the *samosarita*, the *madhyardha*, and then the *melakākrīḍita*. (1152–1153)
Piṣṭakuṭṭa, cāṣagata, and the ten known as the bhaumas;
then atikrānta, daṇḍapāda, krānta, lalitasaṃcara, sūcīviddha, vāmaviddha, vicitra, and vihṛta. 1144.
They say there are ten types born of the sky: *alāta* and *lalita*, among others.
Due to the predominance of those performed on the ground and those performed in the air, these *maṇḍalas* also receive the designations "terrestrial" (*bhauma*) and "celestial" (*ākāśika*).
The application of these [steps] should be understood in the discharge of weapons;
the predominance of those born of the sky (celestial beings) is to be recognized in the course of battle.
Now, I shall describe the footwork known as *cārī* here, with the intent of discussing *cārīs*.
A deficiency or excess in the steps does not vitiate the *maṇḍala*.
(1158) The right foot is raised, the left is glided forward, and then the right again;
likewise, the left foot may be moved like the mouth of a cart, or it may be glided backward. (1159)
When the right foot is whirling (bhramara) and the left is gliding (syandita),
while the other [foot] is like the mouth of a cart (śakaṭāsya) or has the gait of a blue jay (cāṣagati), and the left foot at the end is whirling— this is called the *bhramara* by the wise. (1160)
Thus,
when the right leg is in the *bhramara* posture,
the left is bent, and then the right leg, having assumed the form of a cart-mouth (*śakaṭāsya*), reaches the state of being turned upward upon the thigh. (1161)

When the left [leg] becomes extended by one and a half units, while the right [leg] is again in the *syandita* position, and the left [leg] is in the *śakaṭāsya* position, the ground is clearly struck by that; this is considered by the wise to be the *āskandita* gait. 1162
Thus, first there is the *āskandita*, then the *dakṣiṇa-janita* and the *vāma-sthitāvarta*; after that, there is the *śakaṭāsya*, and finally the one called *elakākrīḍita*. 1163.
Then, having performed the *ūrūdvṛtta* and *āḍḍita* steps and resorted to the *janita* posture,
the right foot should successively perform the *samosarita*, *mattalli*,
*śakaṭāsya*, and *ūrūdvṛtta* movements; thereafter, the other [left] foot should do the same.
When the right foot performs the *cāṣagati* twice and is then moved forward (*syandita*),
while the left foot is in the *śakaṭāsya* position and the other foot follows with the *bhramara*, and the left foot then performs the *cāṣagati*, they have called that the *āvarta*. 1165–1166.

Thus, having been produced as an eddy, it sequentially assumes the previously mentioned seven varieties such as the stationary eddy and so forth; furthermore, another [wind] blows from the south in the form of a plow-mouthed [eddying current]. (1167)
Then, the foot [should be placed] with its mouth like a cart (śakaṭāsya) until the completion of the circle;
that which is performed in this sequence should be known by the wise as the one named Śakaṭāsya.
Thus ends the section on Śakaṭāsya.
Then there are the *udghaṭṭita*, the *baddha*, the *samosaritapūrvaka*,
the *mattalli*, the *ardhamattalli*, the *apakrānta*, and the *dakṣiṇa* (1169);
as well as the *udvṛtta*, the *udyuddhānta*, the *bhramara*, and the *syandita*.
The left [foot] is like a cart (śakaṭāsya), while the other is doubled; then follows the cāṣagati.
Next, the left foot is raised (aḍḍita) and increased by one and a half [matras], followed in sequence by another cāṣagati, then the samosarita, the mattalli, and likewise the bhramara.
When the left [leg] becomes extended and the right performs the slapping of the ground,
they call that the *aḍḍita* circle (maṇḍala).
Thus ends the *aḍḍita*.

Standing with feet together in the *sthāna* posture, one should extend both hands; having placed them close together and raised them upward, one should rotate them as if winding and unwinding, and then throw them down. Then, one should cause the feet to revolve on the right side of the hips.
One should extend the left foot forward in succession or immediately;
having thus circled in this manner, wherever the rotation of the mandala occurs in the four directions, that is declared to be known by the name *samosarita*.

Thus, in sequence, the right foot is brought together, generated, and then moved; thereafter, the fourfold division described as *aḍḍita* (the half-step) and so forth for the left foot, beginning with the *adhyardhika* (one-and-a-half step), is explained. 1176.
The right [movement] should have the shape of a cart; where there is a circular movement at the end in the four directions, that is the *adhyardhamaṇḍala* in wrestling.
Thus ends the section on the *adhyardha*.

Then, with feet joined by the *sūcīviddha* technique and employing the *cāryā*, *velakākrīḍita*, and *bhramara* gaits as before, one performs the *sūcīviddha* dance with feet in the *sūcīviddha* position.
1178. Then, with the *bhramara* gaits completed as previously described, using feet in the *sūcīviddha* position; then—
By means of the four directions established at the end through the whirling of a mandala that has been projected, it is to be known as the "Play of the Assembly" (melakākrīḍita).
Thus ends the "Play of the Elephant" (elakākrīḍita).
The right foot should be in the *sūcī* position, and from there, the left foot should be in the *apakrāntaka* position;
then, the right and left feet are repeatedly placed in the *bhujaṃgatrāsita* positions in succession, ending with a circular movement (*maṇḍalabhrānti*). This is called *piṣṭakuṭṭa*.

Thus, performing the *piṣṭakuṭṭa* with all the feet in the gait of a blue jay (*cāṣagati*), and finally executing a circular turn (*maṇḍalabhrama*) ending in the *cāṣagati*, this constitutes the *niyuddha* (wrestling) category. 1182.

Thus, the *cāṣagata* (crow's gait) is produced; then the right foot is placed in the *śakaṭāsya* (cart-mouth) position, followed by the left in *alāta*, the right in *pārśvakrānta*, and then the other. 1183.
That very *sūcī* (needle) movement, when turned upward, becomes the *bhramara* (bee);
when on the left side, it is the *alātaka* (firebrand), or the *āghrī*; these are based on the *chinnā* (severed) *karaṇa*.
Where the left limb is extended (*recita*), that is the external *bhramaraka*.
Then, having stepped across with the left foot while the right leg remained behind, he who is dear to Śaṅkara spoke regarding that which had been traversed: "The mandala has been crossed.
Thus [it is] "crossed" (atikrānta).
The right foot should be in the *janita* position, then the *daṇḍapāda*;
the left [foot] should be in the *sūcī* or *bhramara* positions, while the right is then raised (*udvṛtta*).
The left foot is in the *alāta* position, while the right is in the *pārśvakrānta*.
When that left foot, terrified by a serpent, has moved beyond its limit (1187),
and then the right foot is in the *daṇḍapāda* position while the other is in *sūcī* and *bhramara*, the wise have called that formation the *daṇḍapāda-maṇḍala*. (1188)

Thus, with the right foot in the *daṇḍapāda* position and the left foot withdrawn in the *sūcī* posture, then the right foot moves to the side (*pārśvakrānta*) and likewise the left; this constitutes the circular movement (*maṇḍalabhrama*) all around. 1189.
When the left [foot] is in the *sūcī* position and the right has stepped forward, that is called *krānta*,
which is the domain of natural gait;
thus ends the description of *krānta*.
The *ūrdhvajānu* (raised knee), the *sūcī* (needle), and the right foot [in sequence];
then the left foot is *apakrānta* (stepped aside) and the right is *pārśvakrānta* (stepped across).
Then, in sequence, the left foot becomes *sūcī* and the right foot becomes *bhramaraka* (the bee). 1191.
Then the left foot performs *pārśvakrānta*, and the right foot again performs *atikrānta*.
Next, the left foot performs *sūcyapakrāntaka*, followed by another *pārśvakrānta*. Then the left foot performs *atikrānta*; thus there is a pair of feet [performing these movements]. 1192–1193.

If it is said to be *chinnakaraṇa*, and it rests upon the left foot placed [therein], one should know that as *bāhyabhramaraka*; then, one should know that as *lalitasaṃcara*. (1194) Thus ends *lalitasaṃcara*.
Then the right foot becomes *sūcī* and *bhramara*;
then the left foot performs *pārśvakrānta*, and the right foot performs *apakrānta*.
Then the left foot performs *sūcī* and *apakrānta*, while the right foot performs *pārśvakrānta*.
Where that maṇḍala is described by the ancients as *sūcīviddha*:
thus is *sūcīviddha*.
The right foot is extended forward, and then the left, and then the right. (1196–1197)
Then the *daṇḍapāda* [stance] may be like a needle (*sūcī*), and the left one is the *bhramaraka*;
the right one is the *pārśvakrānta*, while the other (the left) is the *ākṣipta*. Immediately thereafter, the right foot becomes the *daṇḍapāda* with the thighs rotated upward (*ūrūdvṛtta*).
The left [foot] shall be in the *sūcī*, *bhramara*, and *alāta* positions in succession;
the right foot shall be in *pārśvakrānta*, and the left shall reach the state of *atikrānta*.
Where this occurs, that mandala is called *vāmaviddha*, as proclaimed by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Thus, when the left foot is pierced [by the other], the right foot becomes the *janita*; then, with the thighs turned upward, it is the *vicyava*.
Following that, there are the varieties known as *samasthita*, *āvarta*, and *dvyāvarta*. 1201.
The left foot should be in the *syandita* position, while the right is in *pārśvakrānta*;
the left should be *bhujaṃgatrāsita*, and the right should be *atikrānta*. Furthermore, the left should be *udvṛtta*, and the right *alāta*.

Or, having performed the *pārśvakrānta* or *sūcī* with the left [foot], one throws the right [foot] forward; when the left foot is then brought into the *apakrānta* position, that is called *vicitra*.
Thus ends the *vicitra*.
The right foot, having become *vicyava*, should immediately become *syandita*.
Then the right foot is *pārśvakrānta* and the left is *syandita*;
the right *alāta* is *udvṛtta* and the right [foot] is *sūcī*.
The left foot, having performed the *pārśvakrānta* (side-step), and the right foot,
