having been cast forward and whirled to the left and right, attain the state of *daṇḍapāda* (staff-foot);
then the left foot gradually becomes *sūcī*, and the right becomes *bhaumara*.
When the left [foot] is extended while terrified by a serpent, it is called *vihṛta*. (1207) Thus ends *vihṛta*.
Then, in sequence, one performs *sūcī* and *bhramarī* on the left foot and the right foot respectively. (1208)
Having performed six or seven times the *alātā* movement on the left side, which is terrifying to serpents, and having sequentially performed these movements,
one should swiftly whirl about in the four directions with a circular form.
When the *bhramarikā* movement has departed from the right foot and proceeded in turn to the left foot, and it is performed there with graceful steps of the feet,
the wise call that the *alāta-maṇḍala*.

Thus, the right foot becomes the "firebrand" (alāta) and the speech (the left foot) moves away; then, having reached the state of crossing over to the right side, it becomes "terrified by a serpent" (bhujaṅgatrāsita). 1212.
First, the left foot is stepped across; then the right is drawn back.
Having brought the left to the state of being stepped across, the thighs are rotated in succession to form the *alātaka* (firebrand) movement.
Then the right foot performs the *pārśvakrānta* (side-step), and the left becomes the *sūcī* (needle).
When the left foot has stepped out and crossed over so that one moves gracefully, that is said to be the *lalita* mandala; thus ends the *lalita*. 1214.
Thus, there are ten ākāśika-maṇḍalas:
cāli, cālivaḍa, laḍhi, sūka, uroṅgaṇa, dhasaka, aṅgahāra, oyāra, vihasī, and manaḥ. 1215.
Those who know the *deśī* style recognize these ten as the limbs of *lāsya*:
it should be soft, graceful, sweet, and joined with rhythm and dance;
neither too fast nor too slow, and likewise abundant in triangularity (*tryasratā*). 1216–1217.
The simultaneous movement of the feet, thighs, waist, and arms is *cāli*; when it is characterized by speed and directed forward, it becomes *cālivaḍa*.
That which is delicate, oblique, and imbued with the essence of grace is [the *vilāsa*].
The simultaneous movement of the hips and arms is considered *laḍit*.

(1219) When the playful ear-ornaments (*līlāvataṃsa*) are shimmering, the slow or rapid movement of the head in accordance with the rhythm (*laya*), accompanied by many amorous gestures (*hāva*), is called *sūka*. (1220)

Experts say that a graceful, slow or rapid lateral movement of the breasts and the tops of the arms is called *uroṅgaṇa*; when the gaze is directed very gracefully toward the area below the breasts in accordance with the rhythm (*laya*), it is known as *dhasaka*. 1221–1222.
The two [hands] should be bent in succession, endowed with sixty-four graces;
this is the *dhanurvaṅga-hāra*, as stated by Niḥśaṅka. The movement of the head slightly obliquely downward is considered the *oyāraka*.

That which is full of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) is a smile (*smita*), while that which is a laugh (*vihasī*) is entirely different from the practiced [smile], possessing exceedingly subtle and fresh gestures.
When it arises from song and the like, its stable state (*sthāyi*) is considered to be the mind absorbed in that [melody].

Thus, when there is a combination of the limbs such as the head, eyes, and hands, these ten components of *lāsya* constitute the bodily posture that captivates the mind and the eyes; this is proclaimed as *rekhā*. (1226)
Thus ends the description of the lines [for the mandala]:
Vighneśa, the goddess Bhāratī, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara; then the stage, their respective deities, and the musical instruments such as cymbals and drums, in due order. 1227.
The dancing girls [should worship] the preceptor, the pair of pillars,
and the staff with fragrant ointments such as musk and sandalwood,
as well as with white, sweet-smelling flowers, incense, and lamps.
Having worshipped with various food offerings, garments, betel leaves, and oblations, the wise man should commence his labor at an auspicious moment;
he should place [the beam] upon two pillars, having made it equal in height to his heart.
Having put on a bright garment and donned a firm bodice for support, the girl, leaning upon a staff held in her hand, should practice the turning of her limbs.
1231. Leaning upon the staff, the girl should practice the turning of her limbs.

With a well-disposed mind, the virtuous woman should learn turning, positioning, drawing lines, rhythmic timing, the various tempos (*layas*), all the previously mentioned limbs (*aṅgas*) and so forth, as well as all the components of the *lāsya* dance, and following the melody and the instrumental accompaniment.
Thus is the rule for the actor; the vessel [of performance] is the support for the dance, and in dance, the vessel is generally the female dancer (*nartakī*).
The vessel is celebrated as being threefold: the innocent (*mugdha*), the intermediate (*madhya*), and the bold (*pragalbha*). 1234
The characteristics of the "infatuated" (mugdha) and other stages have been declared; now, the three types of youth are described in order:
That first stage of youth is considered to be when the fullness of the lips, breasts, cheeks, hips, and thighs has just begun to appear, and one is full of enthusiasm for sexual union. (1235–1236)
With full thighs and hips, and full, firm, high, and dense breasts—
this is called by the wise the second youth, the very life of the God of Love,
intoxicating, endowed with beauty, and perfected in the art of sexual pleasure. 1237.
They know the third stage of youth to be one whose nature is trained in passion;
there is also a fourth stage of youth, in which the mind becomes dull in its enthusiasm,
and the lips, the fullness of the breasts, the cheeks, and the hips become withered.
Therefore, it is said that a vessel [of beauty] is most audacious during youth;
once it faces old age and its luster is impaired, it is no longer respected by the wise.
A child, due to the lack of mental development, is not a vessel that delights those who know. (1240)
Thus are the characteristics of a worthy recipient: excellence of form, perfection of beauty, a lovely and broad face, large eyes, lips like the bimba fruit, and beautiful teeth. (1241)
The state of having a beautiful neck and arms like lotus stalks, arms that are graceful,
supple, and full, a slender waist with elevated and ample hips, thighs like the trunks of elephants,
the absence of excessive height, shortness, or fatness, and the absence of visible veins; 1142, 1243.
Loveliness, radiance, sweetness, fortitude, generosity, boldness, fairness of complexion, or darkness—these are considered by the connoisseurs to be the qualities of a performer.
That performer who, through gentle movements of the limbs and graceful rhythmic pauses, [expresses these qualities]... 1244.
As if vomiting forth syllables from the drums,
the sounds of the singing and instrumental music were brought to the state of visual perception by his limbs;
and his body bore the appearance of flowers through its fullness of aesthetic flavor (rasa).

"He dances; he describes it as most excellent"—this is the foremost of the *karaṇas*. Thus are the qualities of the actor (*pātra*); the defect of these, whether taken individually or collectively, is their opposite.
One should examine the merits and defects of the performer for the sake of the success of the dance (1247).
The *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* states that in dance, the performer is the sole essential factor (1248). Success is achieved through the form of the dance alone, and not by any other means.
"Dancing that possesses a beautiful foundation is true dancing; any other is mere mockery.
(1249) Thus end the defects of the performer.
[The ideal performer] is one whose mass of hair is well-settled, glossy, and broad.
The knot at the back of her hair is loosened, adorned with shimmering flower-earrings; her braid is straight and long, beautified by strings of pearls;
and her forehead is marked with musk, sandalwood paste, and other unguents amidst her tresses.
A tilaka-mark was fashioned upon her forehead; her eyes were adorned with a thin application of collyrium; shimmering circles of luster shone upon her ears like palm-leaf ornaments;
and her row of teeth illuminated the stage of her mouth with a web of radiance.
Her cheeks were marked with decorative patterns of musk; a necklace of large pearls hung from her neck as an ornament for her breasts;
and her forearms were adorned with golden bracelets set with excellent jewels.
The fingers bear rings of rubies, blue diamonds, and other gems;
the body is greyed with sandalwood paste or else dyed with saffron;
[he wears] garments such as silk from the Milk-Ocean (kṣīroda) and a thin bodice.

Whether the movement is accompanied by a bodice or otherwise, according to the respective regions, this or some other ornament should be provided for the two characters—the dark and the fair—as is appropriate; so says Śivavallabha. (1256–1257)

Thus, one who adorns the vessels, who is handsome, who knows the principles of dance, who is skilled in the seizing and releasing [of movements], who understands the various *grahas*, and who is an expert in playing musical instruments— 1258.

Possessing knowledge transmitted through tradition, knowing the truth of the sweetness of resonance, and discerning the relative strength or weakness of the musical notes (*sthāya*), he is skilled in tempo (*laya*) and rhythm (*tāla*),
a composer of instrumental compositions, and an expert in wind instruments.
An innovator of novel artistic styles, skilled in training his disciples,
and the establisher of the proper arrangement of dance, song, and instrumental music—
he has entered both the heart of the actor and his own.
The preceptor (upādhyāya) should be one who inspires passion and is knowledgeable in the rules governing the defects of dance;
such is the definition of a preceptor.
In this context, there is one excellent *mukharī* as well as a *pratimukharī*.
Two *aḍāva* players who strike the shoulders, two with *karaṭa* drums;
thirty-two excellent players of *mardala* drums, two players of *tāla*, eight preferred players of bronze *kāṃsya-tāla*, and two players of the *kāhalikā*. 1263–1264.
The two flautists are connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor (rasika), producing clear, intensely passionate, and abundant sounds;
these four hands of theirs possess sweet resonance. There are two principal singers together with eight other singers.
There should be eight principal singers and two assistant singers for each of them; one actor among them should be endowed with virtues and shine through the traditional style.
All of these should be handsome and adorned with various ornaments.

Those who are skilled in the art of singing and so forth, their minds blossoming with great joy—this is called the "excellent" (uttama) tradition in the world; half of that is called "middling" (madhyama), and less than that is declared "inferior" (kaniṣṭha). 1268

Thus, the definition of the *saṃpradāya* (tradition) consists of these four qualities in the *kuṭila* (curved) style: continuity (*anuvṛtti*), resonance (*mukharitva*), filling the deficiency (*talayoḥ nyūnapūraṇam*), and following the tempo (*tālānuvṛtti*). 1269.
"The defect of the tradition would be the reversal of these qualities" (1270)—
thus, while the wise experts in music stand as both performers (*nāyaka*) and spectators (*prekṣaka*), [they consider] the merits and defects of the tradition.
Having entered the stage, those masters of tradition stand with their minds composed; having brought the sounds of the instruments into harmony,
they should play the *melāpaka*, and then the *prabandha* known as *gajara*.
Then, while the curtain is withdrawn, he should stand holding a handful of flowers in a vessel, occupying a position endowed with graceful poise (sauṣṭhava).
Then, when the commencement has begun and the curtain has been removed...
The vessel, captivating the minds of the assembly, shall enter the stage (1274).

While the musical composition is being played by the performers, and during the introductory rites of pacification and so forth, one should cast a handful of flowers into the center of the pedestal of the limbs while the limbs are in a state of repose (1275).
Since the Lord of the Gods himself has taken his place in the midst of the stage,
therefore, filled with great joy, the actor— endowed with mental focus— should dance here accompanied by instrumental music and silence, using only his limbs while they appear as if asleep. (1276)

With the musical compositions (prabandhas) known as Padamotā, Kavita, Malapāvatsaka, Rigoṇī, and Tuḍuka— whether performed according to a fixed sequence or with a sequence created at will— they are played on all sides. || 1277 ||
One should perform the dance with symmetrical limbs, asymmetrical limbs, or both;
then, having designated the performer as the subject according to one's own desire while pure compositions are being sung, one should perform the threefold dance-station (*sthāna*). 1278–1279.
"There is nothing after the elephant except for the vessel [of the head] which enters the supreme support (the mouth) through tranquility; thus say those who know it.
This is the manual that has been declared, proclaimed among the people.
They say that *vādana* (playing) occurs with equal hands before the entry;
they describe the entry as being performed with well-rounded *pāṭas* such as *samahasta*, with excellence of the back [of the hand], and while standing on the *samapāda* stance. 1281–1282.
Some say there is the performance of singing and instrumental music alone; others maintain that singing and so forth may also be performed individually.
This is the pure method (śuddhapaddhati).
She dances with instrumental compositions that are complex yet devoid of *melāpaka* and other such elements, as well as with songs based on the *sālagasūḍa* form, including *dhruva* and other types,
and with the graceful limbs of the *lāsya* dance alone. 1284.

She herself sings and plays the musical instrument, and she herself plays the *trivalī*. Some consider that the *gauṇḍalī* style involves playing [the instrument] upon that vessel; however, others do not regard this as playing at all, for bearing the *trivalī* on the shoulder produces vulgarity in a woman. (1285–1286)
If she does not sing and is bodiless, she would be like a mute Gauṇḍalī;
the circle (maṇḍala) born in the Karṇāṭa country is said by those who know it to be [associated with] Gauḍalī. And they declare her dance to be Gauṇḍalī, based on its defining characteristics.
Those who know it call the procedure used therein the Gauṇḍalī-vidhi (the Gauṇḍalī method). That is said to be the Deśī-paddhati (the regional method); we shall now state its characteristics.
In that [method], there should be traditionalists who are joined with the Karṇāṭa maṇḍalas. 1288–1289.
As before, the equality of the musical instruments is prescribed;
they should play the *melāpaka* with a single rhythm (*ekatālī*), being composed, once the *jagara* has been played upon any rhythm whatsoever. 1290.
When there is a cessation of that which has begun with the *niḥsāraṇa* and *ekatālī* [rhythms], the actor enters the stage and,
standing in the center of the arena, should scatter a handful of flowers while revealing his right,
left, and front limbs as he dances.
Then, with the *gajaropaśama* alone, there is the dancing of all the limbs;
thereafter, one resorts to the *aḍḍatāla*, the *nisāru*, and the *ekatālī*; and after that, with the *ri-goṇī* which is free from the restriction of *tāla*.
One should perform dances in succession with the *avatsaka* and *kavitā* meters (1294),
and then dance again in various ways through the nature of the *ṛgoṇī* and *uṭṭavaṇa* (1295). Then, when the instrumental music has ceased and the flautists have provided the resting place...
Then, together with those joined [musicians], the Gauṇḍalī sings;
having uttered the *sthāyin*, she should perform the fourfold *rāgālapti*.
Or another principal female singer (*gāyanī*) may perform various types of *ālapti*.
Having sung the entire *dhruvaka* section joined with another *tāla* following the *maṇṭhaka* and *pratimaṇṭhaka*,
while the *jakkā* drum is being played continuously along with the smooth portion known as the *dhruva*.
Having performed a dance accompanied by singers and instrumentalists that is enchanting to the mind’s very essence, and then, once the singing and instrumental music have become quiet,
one should repeatedly move through various *sthāyas* (musical modes) and arrive at the *dhruvapada* (refrain).

Some [he taught] by means of the rhythm (*tāla*) of song, others by means of the syllables of the rhythmic song; these were neither too long nor too low, but were refined by sweetness and maturity, endowed with passion, and possessed of rhythm—or rather, having first established that rhythm for them. (1301)
In the *dhruva* section, one should place the ends [of the instruments] upon the *sutāla*;
in the *kalāsa*, the players should strike the instruments with equal force.
In the *kalāsas*, the performer should remain absorbed as if fixed in a painting.
When the procedure has been performed in this manner, the performer should again engage in dance as before while the *dhruvā* section is being sung (1304). Then,
he should dance to the accompaniment of the instruments being played by the musicians (1305).
When that [performance] is joined with the *gauṇḍalī* and *yojanā*, and when the *tyāga* (release) is present,
one should perform a dance characterized by various types of mature *cārīs* and *cālakas*.
In this context, the use of weapons and instrumental music is also desired during the *ābhoga* (the concluding section).
Then, having performed [the dance] with rhythmic equality (*vādyasāmya*), one should practice renunciation and rest (verse 1307).
Having thus performed the dance with the *dhruva* measure, and likewise with the *maṇṭhaka* and others,
this specific distinction regarding their sequence in dancing is now declared (verse 1308).

In the Maṇṭha and other forms, there may be dancing performed solely with the *dhruva* section; however, in the Maṇṭha, it is considered that the performance begins with the Maṇṭha rhythm (*tāla*), and thereafter the Maṇṭha dance proceeds step by step using only a single rhythm. 1309.
Dancing in the *pratimaṇṭha* and other forms is prescribed to be performed with its own specific *tāla*.
In these *sālagas* songs, the dance is based on a quick tempo (*druta-laya*),
whereas in the *tāṇḍava*, scholars always state that the tempo is slow (*vilambita*).

Having danced with rhythmic gestures (*rūpaka*) ending in the *ekatālī* measure, and likewise with those belonging to the *sālagasūḍa*, where the withdrawal (*tyāga*) is performed, that is the procedure for the *gauṇḍalī*.
Thus ends the procedure for the *gauṇḍalī*.
His limbs were smeared with white ashes and the like; he wore a shaven head with a single tuft of hair remaining;
his shanks were adorned with a shimmering network of small bells; he was graceful in body, skilled in the five limbs [of percussion], and expert in the nuances of rhythmic timing (*tāla*).
He who dances, captivating the assembly and the mind, is the *peraṇī* (1314).
The *gharghara*, the *viṣama*, the *bhāvāśraya*, the *kavicāraka*,
and *gīta*— these five limbs (*pañcāṅga*) are taught by the beloved of Hara (1315).
Among those, in the case of the *ghargharikā* instrument, the *vahanirgharghara* is considered first;
then the *paṭivāṭa*, the *cāpaḍapa*, the *siripiṭyalagādima*,
the *vāṭa*, the one called *sirihirā*, and thereafter the one named *khaluhula*.
Thus, these six varieties of *gharghara* are recognized by those who know them.
(1317) When the tips of both feet touch the ground alternately while the heels strike the earth, it is called *paṭivāṭaka*.
(1318) It may be performed with both heels or with a single heel.
One should become a treeless mountain by stamping the earth with the soles of the feet;
with the sole of the foot pressed against the ground, there should be frequent forward movement of the foot, as well as backward movement, and the *siripiṭī* [should be performed]. 1319.
The gentle, alternating movement of both feet in the air is here proclaimed as *alagavāṭa*;
when one foot is on the ground, the other foot should be thrust forward. 1320–1321.
That which is called the "Sirihiro" by the wise is the trembling of his shank;
when two feet remain naturally on the ground,
the learned say that the trembling of the shanks is then termed Sirihiro.
The striking of the ground with the heel of the left foot while its tip touches the earth,
and the whirling of the other [foot] whose tip likewise touches the ground from right to left and left to right—
this is indeed called *khaluhula* by those skilled in dance. 1323–1324.
In this manner, other *gharghara* movements accompanied by grace should also be inferred;
all those varieties of *gharghara* must be performed in accordance with the rhythmic beats (*tāla*).
And here, the movement known as *viṣama* (the uneven) should be preceded by a leap (*utpluta*).
The imitation of extraordinary events is considered by the wise to be based on *bhāva* (emotional state).
Herein, there should be the poet’s creative imagination (*kavicāra*) consisting of the description of the hero of the highest type;
and here there should be the *sālaga* song, as described in the rules for the *gauṇḍalī* style.

Thus is the characteristic of the *peraṇi*; and here, following the ritual of the *gauṇḍalī*, those traditionalists standing on the stage should produce a deep sound from their musical instruments, uttering "dhidhi-dhi-dhi. 1328.
Then,

when three quarters of the *ṛgaṇyuṭṭavaṇa* measure have been played at a slow tempo, the *aṭṭaboḍaka*— adorned with distorted speech, dress, and ornaments— should enter the stage twice to the *niḥsāru* rhythm.
While he dances, consisting solely of the essence of laughter, the *peraṇī* enters;

once the *rigoṇī* has subsided, he should enter and perform the dance. When the ensemble of musical instruments has become quiet, then, together with the keepers of the rhythm (*tāladhara*), [he proceeds].
While the musical instrument known as the *gāruḍika-tāla* was being played with great skill,
or likewise while the sound of the *mardala* and other drums was being produced by the musicians in accordance with the *sarasvatī-kaṇṭhābharaṇa* rhythm;
The performer should produce various gurgling sounds with his lips and feet;
then, through a composition constructed with deceptive structures or consisting of a series of syllables, he should perform a difficult dance to the accompaniment of instrumental rhythm (*nisāru*).
Then, while the *sālagasūḍa* is being danced there, one should display the lines (*rekhā*), the heart-pleasing formations (*sthāpanā*), the rhythmic movements (*vahanī*), and the singing and dancing;
as well as the difficult maneuvers (*viṣama*) and the performance of the *ābhoga* following the musical instruments.
"Likewise, the poetic modes (*kavicārāḥ*) based on the emotions (*bhāvāśrayāḥ*) [are described] in the *Peraṇīpaddhati*.
(1336) Thus ends the *Peraṇīpaddhati*.
The teacher who is to be known through the characteristics of the definitions in the triple symphony (*tauryatraya*) has been proclaimed.

"He shall be eloquent, handsome in appearance and dress, skilled in composing hymns of praise for the gods, knowledgeable in the art of wit and humor in assemblies, and an expert in playing musical instruments," so says the Teacher.

"One who is proficient in the fourfold dramatic representation and knows the distinctions between *bhāṇa* and other forms is called a *naṭa* by the wise; a *nartaka* is one who has exerted effort in the *mārga* dance. (1338–1339)
Thus, a dancer who is proficient in all varieties of languages, who provides amusement to people, and who is skillful in speaking ill of others, is known by the wise as a *vaitālika*. 1340.
Thus, one who is a bard (*vaitālika*),

skilled in playing the *kiṅkiṇī* (small bell), and who has performed with wild dancers, is considered a *cāraṇa* who knows the vital points (*marmajña*) in all melodies and is proficient in them. 1341.
Thus was the *cāraṇa*—
a mature bearer of heavy burdens, skilled in the *bhramarikā* and other such feats, adept at moving along ropes, and proficient in the dance of the sword.
One who is skilled in the sudden onset of the perils of weapons is considered a *kohlāṭika*.
Thus ends the section on the *kohlāṭika*.
Those who are impartial, vigilant, eloquent, and knowers of justice [are the mediators].
They possessed both broken and unbroken supernormal powers; their necks were bowed in discipline;
they were free from pride, knew the aesthetic sentiments and emotions, and were experts in the three types of musical performance.
They were capable of refuting false doctrines, were clever, and severed the bonds of envy.
"May the members of the assembly have hearts flowing with the essence of the nectar of poetry.
Thus [ends the section on] the members of the assembly;
they should be full of aesthetic sentiment (*śṛṅgārin*), abundant, honorable, and capable of discerning worthy recipients of honor.
He was illustrious, a perceiver of even the slightest virtue, and devoted to curiosity;
eloquent, free from envy, skilled in the composition of humor, wise, profound in character, and proficient in all the arts.
Endowed with the knowledge of all the scriptures, eager for fame,
pleasant of speech, knowing the minds of others, intelligent, possessed of retentive memory,
an expert in the three types of musical instruments, and skilled in the distribution of rewards.

Equipped with all necessary implements, knowing the distinctions between local and traditional paths, discerning the difference between what is deficient and what is excessive, wise, possessing a balanced and steadfast mind, having his retinue under his own control, and full of devotion, the practitioner is saturated with aesthetic flavor (rasa). 1348–1349.

A speaker of truth, of noble birth, with a serene countenance, steadfast in affection, grateful, an ocean of compassion, most righteous, fearful of sin, a friend to the learned— such is the presiding officer of the assembly. (1350)
Thus are the characteristics of the assembly hall: it should be a diverse dance hall, adorned with heaps of flowers, provided with various canopies, and embellished with jeweled pillars. 1351

Seated upon a beautiful lion-throne in that assembly hall is the Lord of the Assembly; to his left are the ladies of the inner apartments, while the principal ministers are to his right. Behind the principal ministers stands the treasury and the chief minister of the royal secretariat.

In his presence, however, he should seat among the learned those who are experts in worldly and Vedic lore, connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor, poets skilled in all literary styles, as well as venerable astrologers and physicians.
On the right side, however, there should be a circular area for the ministers;
in that very place are the seating arrangements for the chief military officers and others. Around it are the pleasure-seekers, the courtesans, and the women of the inner apartments.
Both in front of the king and behind the monarch were women bearing beautiful chowries, endowed with beauty and youth,
who captivated the minds of the people with the jingling sound of their own bracelets.
In the front, on the left side, should be the singers, composers, storytellers, and bards; here they should be learned and sweet-spoken, skilled in praise, and otherwise clever in all matters. (1358)
Thereafter, the assembly hall should be presided over by skillful cane-bearers seated all around as an entourage; meanwhile,
bodyguards with weapons in hand should stand on every side.
Having thus arranged the assembly, the leader observes the musical performance.
(1361) Thus ends the arrangement of the assembly.
Those who know declare that this triple symphony (tauryatrika) should have rasa as its primary element.
Now, by means of its general and specific characteristics, I shall describe rasa:

it is produced by the determinants (vibhāvas), the consequents (anubhāvas), and the transitory states (vyabhicāribhāvas) residing in the actor, even without the presence of an actual self, another, an enemy, or a friend as a substratum. (1362–1363)
Grasping exclusively the form of the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), such as love or laughter, which is devoid of distinctions or combinations of states, places, times, and so forth,
it therefore attains supreme repose due to its uninterrupted nature. (1364)
Distinct from other cognitions such as intuition, experience, and memory,
and unlike the consciousness of Brahman due to its association with various forms of aesthetic delight (rasa) and so forth,
this consciousness— consisting of bliss, self-perceived, and termed "tasting" (āsvādana)— is [the nature of rasa]. 1365.

Alternatively, rasa may be the stable emotion (sthāyin) itself as it becomes the object [of aesthetic experience], just as [a base substance] is transformed by condiments such as curd and the like, by medicinal herbs such as turmeric and the like,
or by substances such as molasses that possess sweet and other flavors. || 1266–1367 ||

Just as another taste called *ṣāḍava* is produced by the application of specific methods of cooking, so too is *rasa* produced through the employment of the *vibhāvas* and other factors. [The eight rasas are:
the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), the comic (*hāsya*), the pathetic (*karuṇa*), the furious (*raudra*), the heroic (*vīra*), and the terrifying (*bhayānaka*).

The aesthetic sentiments (rasas) are considered to be ninefold: the loathsome, the marvelous, and the peaceful. Some have objected that there are only eight sentiments in dramatic performances, because the peaceful sentiment is achieved through tranquility, and that is impossible for an actor. 1369–1370.

That is not to be questioned, because the actor does not taste any flavor at all, whereas the members of the audience do taste the flavors; the actor is considered merely the vessel. Those [members of the audience] possess pure hearts and experience the *śānta* (quiescent) flavor as it is manifested by its own determinants (*vibhāva*).
It is logical that those who are virtuous experience these with one-pointed minds:
love, mirth, sorrow, anger, energy, fear, disgust, wonder, and then dispassion—these nine are the stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*). 1372–1373.

Some have declared disgust to be the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of the Quietistic (*śānta*), while others say it is energy (*utsāha*); still others [say it is] tranquility (*śama*), and yet others recognize all [of these].
(1374) This is said with reference to the permanent emotions when the occasion for the transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*) arises.
Since the sage first spoke even of inauspiciousness and indeed of despondency, he surely intended these to be the stable (sthāyin) and transitory (vyabhicārin) emotions of this [hero];
for the connection between the preceding and following parts follows as a consequence for that which stands in the middle.
This [state] may be stable regarding its objects if it arises from the knowledge of reality;
however, when caused by the loss of the desired or the acquisition of the undesired, it is inconstant. [Its concomitants are:
despondency, exhaustion, apprehension, ferocity, dejection, envy, self-restraint, and fatigue. (1377)

Thought, fortitude, memory, shame, delusion, indolence, and restlessness; joy, impatience, despondency, epilepsy, as well as dullness; deliberation, sleep, longing, dissimulation, and likewise intelligence. (1378–1379)
Awakening, illness, insanity, pride, agitation, death,
terror, and sleep— these thirty-three are the transitory states (vyabhicāribhāvas).
Stiffness, perspiration, horripilation, change of voice, and trembling;
Change of color, tears, and fainting— these eight are the *sāttvika* emotions (1381).
When the *vibhāvas* and other factors become inappropriate due to their context and undergo a transformation,
they produce semblances (*ābhāsa*) of the *śṛṅgāra* and other rasas, which serve as causes for the *hāsya* (comic) rasa (1382).
Those who know the truth have declared that the fruit [of the Raudra rasa] is the slaughter of kinsmen, and its determinants (vibhāva) are the same as those of Karuṇa;
therefore, they say that Raudra is the cause of Karuṇa. Furthermore, they explain that Raudra is the cause of Bhayānaka only when it possesses a specific motive.

The wise have declared that the arising of the *karuṇa* (pathetic) sentiment is desired from the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) known as *vipralambha* (separation), and that the *vīra* (heroic) is the cause for the *bhayānaka* (terrifying) and *adbhuta* (marvelous). Furthermore,
the laughter of the *vidūṣaka* (jester) serves as the cause of laughter for the hero.

Due to the similarity [of causes], from the determinants such as blood and fainting, and from the transitory states, when the *bībhatsa* (the loathsome) arises, the *bhayānaka* (the terrifying) may arise for those who are timid;
thus, these aesthetic flavors (*rasas*) become mutually productive and produced.
Dark, white, grey, red, fair, black, blue, yellow, and then white— these are the colors of the [tastes] in order.
Viṣṇu, Manmatha, Kīnāśa, Rudra, Indra, and the one named Kāla [are their presiding deities].

Mahākāla, Brahmā, Buddha, and the deities of the [other] flavors are said by some to be the presiding deities of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), while others say it is the god of love (makaradhvaja). Now, I shall describe in due order the specific characteristics of the sentiments and so forth. 1388–1389.

Through his own performance, the actor brings about—as if it were a direct perception—the permanent emotion of love (*rati*) by means of the transitory moods (*vibhāvas*), such as the beautiful woman and others, which have been woven by the poet into his poem; thus, he leads that emotion to the state of being relished as aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) by the audience. (1390)

The Śṛṅgāra [rasa] has been described by the wise Śārṅgin as that which is depicted by an actor through manifested *anubhāvas* such as lovely glances, and which is led to a state of intense absorption by *vyabhicāribhāvas* such as joy, anxiety, and the like. (1391–1392)

Its two states are proclaimed as union (*saṃbhoga*) and separation (*vipralambha*); their respective characteristics are the conjunction with a beloved and the absence thereof. [This occurs] between a man and a woman, both excellent and youthful, for whom the arising of perfect bliss is possible. (1393)

In this [context], *sthāyin* (the stable emotion) is the play (*krīḍā*) consisting of *rati* (passion), which is sustained by the memory [of the beloved] and extends from the beginning until the attainment of the fruit; it arises through the realization of the identity of the two consciousnesses.
In the world, the causes for the manifestation of the stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*) and the others are the means for their perception.
Those things which, presented by the best of poets, produce aesthetic flavors (rasas) as if they were directly perceived, are called *vibhāvas* because of their power to manifest those flavors.
In the case of a beautiful woman overcome by intense passion, these include people such as female messengers and friends. (1395–1396)
Even ornaments such as crowns and bracelets appropriate for that [state],
the season such as spring, objects such as sandalwood paste, songs and the like, and even the place such as beautiful palaces and forests— [all these serve to enhance the experience]. (1397)
The imitation of a beloved, the sight of pairs of swans, variegated patterns, and so forth—
whether heard or seen— as well as water-sports and similar activities, are renowned as the excitants (*vibhāva*) for the aesthetic flavor known as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*). (1398–1399)

Those effects of the emotions (*bhāva*) which are enacted by skilled actors are the *anubhāvas*, because they are the causes for the experience of those very [original] causes; for they lead toward and bring about the manifestation of those emotions. 1400.
Indeed, they cause one to arrive at and understand them.
Therefore, even by the term "acting" (abhinaya), these artificial [expressions] are denoted by actors:
a lovely glance called a sidelong look, the movement of the pupils which bestows happiness, clever eyebrows with beautiful range, and sweet words. 1401–1402.
The multitude of *sāttvika* emotions, such as horripilation, changes in facial color, and so forth, constitute these *anubhāvas* which nourish the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*).
Here, the transitory mental states (*vyabhicāribhāvas*) are those other than indolence, ferocity, and disgust.
The triad beginning with laziness (ālasya), which has its own specific internal states as its sole domain, is to be avoided [in this context].
This is considered the *parikara* (accessory) pertaining to the erotic sentiment of union (*saṃbhoga-śṛṅgāra*).
In the erotic sentiment of separation (*vipralambha*), the glances and other gestures directed toward the beloved are not accepted as *anubhāvas* (consequent effects). 1404–1405.

Anxiety, envy, fatigue, longing, despondency, exhaustion, and death; likewise, madness, disease, epilepsy, agitation, and dullness; as well as wretchedness, sleep, dreaming, waking, thought, and so forth—these are the states. 1406.
The separation [of the lovers] should be enacted through his [the lover's] own gestures (anubhāvas);
one should not display here the most painful states such as madness, nor should one directly show his death, but rather indicate it. 1407–1408.
One should, however, show the happy state arising immediately after that,
or indicate the state in which death is imminent, but one must not speak of this [present] state.
(1409) Now, why is the sentiment of separation (*vipralambha*) considered to be essentially sorrowful?
Do not say so; for the pursuit of pleasure is observed even in the state of separation (vipralambha).
Indeed, the apprehension arising from separation is certainly difficult to abandon during union (saṃbhoga), because their mutual diversity makes the nature of rasa easily accessible in both.
Like sugar, this [pleasure] would not be long-savored in its manifold forms (1412).
Furthermore, there is no sleep even during union for two who desire one another; why then is this awakening restricted solely to the state of separation? (1413)
This is not the destruction of sleep, for how can there be awakening without it?
(1414) Sleep caused by the fatigue of passion exists even during sexual union; if that were the case, it should not be mentioned, as it is contrary to the excellence of passion. (1415)

If it is argued that there is no distinction between *karuṇa* (compassion) and *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) because the transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāvas*) such as anxiety are common to both, that is incorrect;
for grief is considered the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) in *karuṇa*, whereas love is held to be the stable emotion in *vipralambha*. 1416–1417.

Therefore, the distinction between those two [types of love] arises from the difference in the permanent emotion (sthāyibheda), occurring in a superior person but not in a base one, because of the impossibility of excitants such as garlands and the like [in the latter].
If there is an absence of *rati*, how can the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) arise as "love-in-separation" (*vipralambha*)?

Therefore, the clearly manifest *karuṇa* (pathetic) rasa there arises from the separation from a desired object. (1419) If it is argued that because of the absence of garlands and such, sexual union is also impossible for one in a low state, that is not so; for that [state] arises from the mere presence of a woman as its determinant cause (*vibhāva*), not from being a base person.

Likewise, how can there be *rati* (pleasurable passion) in separation when there is an absence of garlands and such? (1420) Separation (*viraha*), characterized by the mental transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*) of anxiety and so forth arising from the slackening of the bond of hope, is distinct from *karuṇa* (pathos), because it is produced by the loss of hope for the beloved. (1421)
And in the *Kāmasūtra*, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is shown to have ten stages:
longing, then reflection, recollection, and the praising of virtues; then agitation, lamentation, madness, and the onset of disease.
Stupefaction and death—these are proclaimed as the ten stages [of love]. 1423.
The enjoyer is the Pradhāna (the primary principle), while the beloved is the object of enjoyment and thus subordinate;
therefore, her attachment to another man causes the destruction of his erotic passion.
Because the enjoyer is not dependent on another, the lover does not break [the experience];
erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is considered to be threefold by means of speech, costume, and bodily gestures.
The attire that manifests [characters] such as Rāma is intended as "costume" (*nepathya*) for the actor.
Thus is *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment): it consists of the transformation of dress, ornaments, gait, and speech,
as well as the imitation of these qualities found in others and a lack of shame.

Disinterest in sense objects, speaking with a detached gaze, and touching the armpits or other parts of one who is intended to be made to laugh—these and others are the excitants (*vibhāvas*); the consequents (*anubhāvas*), however, are those of the eyes. (1427–1428)
Trembling of the cheeks and lips, dilation of the eyes, their slight closing, partial contraction, pressing against the sides,
perspiration, and changes in the color of the face— these are its transitory mental states (vyabhicāribhāvas). 1429.
Dreaming, dissimulation, laziness, sleep, drowsiness, and others—
these are established as appropriate within the various sub-types of the smile (smita) and so forth;
and since the stable emotion (sthāyibhāva) is laughter, this is proclaimed as the Comic (hāsya).
It is held that this [rasa] has two varieties: residing in oneself (ātma-stha) and residing in another (para-saṃstha).

That which resides in oneself arises for the spectator merely through the perception of the determinants (vibhāva), while that which resides in another arises upon seeing someone else laughing and so forth, accompanied by the determinants. 1432.
That which is the rasa of humor (hāsya) is proclaimed by those who know it to be "situated in another" (parastha).
It may belong to the superior, the middling, or even the inferior;
thus it is said to exist in three states, and it has six other varieties as well.

The wise have declared that a smile (*smita*) and a laugh (*hasita*) belong to a superior person; a loud laugh (*vihasita*) and a derisive laugh (*upahasita*) belong to a middling man; while a scornful laugh (*apahasita*) and an excessive laugh (*atihasita*) are proclaimed for an inferior person. (1435)
A smile characterized by slightly blooming cheeks and gentle side-glances,
in which the teeth are not visible, is called a slow or languid smile (manthara-smita).
However, if it is observed through a face, eyes, and cheeks that are fully blossomed, [it is a different kind].
When the teeth are slightly visible, that is considered *hasita* (a smile).

The wise know *vihasita* (a laugh) to be one that is accompanied by sound, sweet, occurring at the appropriate time, characterized by a reddening of the face, and with the eyes and cheeks slightly contracted. 1437–1438.
With shoulders and head bent, looking with a squinting gaze,
the nose expanded, and laughing— the smile known by the name "derisive" (upahasita) is thus defined.
[Verse 1439] Born out of place, accompanied by tears in the eyes, and with the shoulders and head trembling—
Śārṅgadeva has described the comic (hāsya) as being of two types: the "laughed-at" (apahasita) and the "excessive laugh" (atihasita).
1440 The "excessive laugh" (atihasita) is considered to be when the ears are large, the sound is harsh, the eyes are flooded with a stream of tears, and the sides are gripped by the hands. 1441
In the three pairs beginning with the smile, the former [expressions] arise from within oneself, while the latter ones reside in another because they are born from what was previously transferred.
Laughter and fury are also threefold, through speech, costume, and bodily gestures. (1442)
This, however, is merely an illustration, as these [afflictions] can occur in all [beings]. (1443) Thus it is said:
"The separation from beloved kin, the loss of wealth, slaughter, and imprisonment. (1444)
The causes of calamity, such as the death of a son or others, as well as exile from one's country and so forth— whether heard of or witnessed—
are recognized as the excitants (*vibhāvas*) for superior men who rely on others. (1445)
But for men of middling and inferior capacity, those [emotions] have the self alone as their object.
(1446) Tearful weeping, dryness of the mouth, lamentation, wailing, paralysis, pallor, drooping of the limbs, and likewise fainting; (1447)

In this state, sighing and gasping, falling from the body, striking one's chest, and so forth are the *anubhāvas* (consequent effects); furthermore, there are exhaustion, fatigue, fear, delusion, despondency, self-reproach, anxiety, longing, and wretchedness. (1448)
Inertness, disease, insanity, indolence, epilepsy, death, as well as paralysis,

trembling, tears, discoloration, loss of voice, and so forth— where these are the transitory emotions (saṃcārin) and sorrow is the stable emotion (sthāyin), that is considered the pathetic sentiment (karuṇa). 1449–1450.
The classification of these emotional intensities (*anubhāvas*) here is according to their suitability for superior and other types of characters.
(1451) Lamentation (*vilāpa*) is weeping preceded by a praise of the virtues of the object of grief;
it is that weeping which consists of reproaching fate, oneself, or others.
This is what is called "lamentation" by those skilled in terminology:
that which arises from the destruction of dharma, from the loss of wealth, and from the death of kinsmen.
Among these, the first type—arising from the destruction of dharma—is found only among the most excellent.
Weeping is of three kinds, caused by joy, distress, or envy.

That which arises from joy accompanied by the recollection of suffering, characterized by blooming cheeks, horripilation, and tears at the outer corners of the eyes, is considered "joy-born" weeping. (1454–1455)
Lamentation with a loud voice, accompanied by the movement of the eyebrows,
a stream of flowing tears, and unsteady movements of the limbs, is considered the expression of distress (ārta).
It also includes the heaving of the head with sighs and the quivering of the lips and cheeks.

The side-glances and frowns of women arise from jealousy. Among superior and middling women, tears do not flow due to fortitude even when their own misfortune occurs; however, they may flow when it concerns another. But for base women, those tears flow in both circumstances.
Thus, Karuṇa [describes] the slayers by nature— Rākṣasas, Daityas, and others who act unjustly—
as well as battle, anger, false speech, and the violation of another's wife and so forth. (1459)

Censuring another's country, caste, family conduct, or learning; making promises regarding the killing of others, seizing their wives, or traveling abroad; harsh speech; the destruction of houses and so forth; the seizure of kingdoms; and likewise envy. 1460.
Where the excitants (*vibhāvas*) described by the poets consist of the desire to kill and so forth—
such as the knitting of eyebrows, redness of the eyes, throbbing of the cheeks,
biting of the lips with the teeth, and the clenching of fists during combat with another— [that is the Furious Sentiment]. (1461–1462)
Striking with the palms of the hands, cutting, crushing, splitting, and tearing;
seizing weapons, falling, striking, and the flow of blood—these are the external manifestations (anubhāvas), while their function consists of acts such as striking and the like. (1463)
That [inner state] should not be expressed directly; rather, it should be indicated by actors through [the following]:
enthusiasm, correct understanding, indignation, agitation, intensity, and restlessness, as well as perspiration, trembling, horripilation, faltering voice, and so forth. 1464–1465.
Perspiration is to be represented either directly or by means such as the taking up of a fan;
however, enthusiasm (*utsāha*) is merely a transitory state (*saṃcārī-bhāva*) here, and therefore there is no confusion with the heroic sentiment (*vīra-rasa*).
[Objection: But surely, it is held that a state becomes a permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) only through its invariable presence.

[Objection: Since that [pleasure] is transitory, how could this enthusiasm (utsāha) exist even in the heroic rasa? [Reply: Do not say so; for while flashes of lightning are momentary and flickering, the stable emotions (sthāyins) are constant. Therefore, this [enthusiasm] exists in two forms within these two rasas.

[Objection: But surely even the stable emotion (sthāyin), being a mental state (bhāva), must by its very nature be momentary. [Reply: True; however, it attains stability through the form of a latent impression (saṃskāra).
Other emotions, whose impressions are obscured by that [stable one], are instead characterized by its persistence.
In this world, those subject to the laws of manifestation and concealment are constrained;
anger toward the guru, the beloved, the enemy, and the servant is fourfold.
Toward the guru, anger remains unmanifest in its impulse, restrained by discipline. (1471–1472)
With a few tears falling from the corners of her eyes, her face contorted by a frown and her lips quivering,
such is the anger born of love in gazelle-eyed women toward their beloved; whereas the anger of others bites the lip,
crushes the hands, and features a wide, gaping frown.
When looking at one's own arm, anger toward an enemy becomes unrestrained;
when looking with distorted eyes, wide-open stares, and abundant threats, anger toward a servant is feigned and devoid of cruelty due to the exigencies of business.

That determination of the true nature of things which the virtuous must apply regarding specific matters such as dharma and other goals— arising from freedom from wonder, freedom from delusion, and freedom from despondency— as well as prudence, discipline, fame, and the capacity for valor; 1476.

Majesty, sovereign power, the possession of an invincible and formidable army, the power of counsel consisting of wealth, noble lineage, and wise ministers— these and other such determinants (vibhāvas) exist in the actor when combined with the poetic work.

Expertise in the application of means such as conciliation according to their respective contexts, steadiness, fortitude, heroism, appropriate generosity, and speech characterized by profound sentiment— these and other qualities [constitute the nature of a leader]. 1479.
All the manifestations of pride (*garva*) are indeed *anubhāvas*; furthermore, there is *smṛti* (remembrance).

Cruelty (*augrya*), agitation (*āvega*), horripilation (*romāñca*), indignation (*amarṣa*), fortitude (*dhṛti*), and intelligence (*mati*)—such states as these are the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*) that may be present therein. 1480–1481.
Enthusiasm is its permanent emotion (sthāyibhāva); the wise have declared him to be the Heroic (vīra).
This [heroism] arises only in persons of the highest character.
Having correctly understood this, the application of the sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya) is proclaimed as "Naya" (statecraft).
Alliance, war, marching, halting, seeking refuge,
and duplicity— these are declared in the treatises on statecraft to be the six measures of policy.
Śiva, the beloved of Śaṅkara, has taught that self-control is the mastery of the senses.
*Pratāpa* is renown arising from prowess that scorches one's enemies;

*kīrti* is fame that bestows joy upon friends and neutral persons; and the four means (*upāya*) are conciliation (*sāma*), bribery (*dāna*), sowing dissension (*bheda*), and force (*daṇḍa*). 1485–1486.
Steadfastness (*sthairya*) is the state of an unshakable mind; fortitude (*dhairya*) is the possession of profundity;
and heroism (*śaurya*) is the engagement in battle without the manifestation of fear.
(1487) One may be a *vīra* (hero) in a suitable battle, but in an unsuitable one, one would be *raudra* (fierce). (1488)
The heroic sentiment is threefold: the hero of generosity (*dānavīra*), the hero of righteousness (*dharmavīra*), and the hero of battle (*yuddhavīra*).

Among these, acts such as giving are the determinants (*vibhāva*) in the case of the antagonist (*pratināyaka*), whereas they serve as the consequents (*anubhāva*) in the case of the protagonist (*nāyaka*); such is the opinion of the learned. (1489)
Thus, for the hero,
the sight and hearing of terrifying forms such as rākṣasas, piśācas, and bears, as well as the entering of empty houses and forests, [are obstacles]. (1490)

The hearing of distorted sounds that cause fear and agitation in others, and the contemplation of the killing or imprisonment of one's kinsmen— these and similar factors are the excitants (*vibhāvas*); furthermore, there are those pertaining to the eyes, hands, and feet.
From time to time there occur paralysis and trembling, as well as a mass of horripilation;
dryness of the lips and palate, a quivering heart, discoloration of the face, hoarseness of voice, drooping of the limbs, and a look of embarrassment.
These effects of the sight [of the enemy] arise from the state of being terrified;
furthermore, there are the eight [states] beginning with paralysis (stambha), as well as dejection, agitation, fickleness, apprehension, delusion, fear, epilepsy, death, and so forth.
That rasa in which transitory fear is the dominant permanent emotion (sthāyibhāva) is the Frightful (bhayānaka).
Fear is said to be of two kinds: real and artificial.
Real fear occurs in women and in men of base nature.
That which is exhibited by a man of middling or superior character is called "artificial" (kṛtrima).
For those two, being naturally free from fear, display a lack of genuine fear toward their master and teacher only for the sake of manifesting humility. 1497–1498.
To awaken the mind to its lowly nature, that effect [of fear] should be produced through gentle gestures.
(1499) The *vitrāsita* (terrified), the *kṛtrima* (artificial), and the *bhayānaka* (terrible)—thus the *bhayānaka* is threefold. Among these, the first is true to its name. (1500)

The artificial (kṛtrima) [fear], produced by the best [of poets], is unreal with respect to teachers and others; it is intended for the purpose of intimidation, such as to terrify children and the like.
Thus ends the Furious (bhayānaka).
By its very nature, due to the defects of the elements, or because it is essentially extremely repulsive,
forbidden, disgusting due to over-satiety, mixed with impurities, and—
by yielding undesirable results— it repeatedly causes agitation. (1502)

There may be the vibhāvas (determinants) and then the anubhāvas (consequents): trembling, shaking of the limbs, contraction of the nose, lips, and jaws, spitting, as well as irregular stepping and covering of the nose and eyes. 1503–1504.
Furthermore, where transitory states such as delusion, agitation, epilepsy, death, and disease are present, that is the *bībhatsa* (the loathsome).
It is considered to be of three kinds: pure, impure, and extremely pure, according to its underlying stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), which is disgust (*jugupsā*). (1505–1506)
The first two arise from the pure and impure vibhāvas such as blood and excrement;
that which arises from pure dharmas is extremely pure and pertains to the sphere of saṃsāra.
(1507) Thus ends the description of the *bībhatsa* (the loathsome).

The attainment of rare and desired objects, the sight of sky-farers, and the vision of celestial chariots, illusions, and sorcery; as well as unprecedented and magnificent palaces, groves, and other such wonders. 1508.
Sight, hearing, speech, and excellence in the arts and so forth—
where these serve as the excitants (vibhāvas), while the consequents (anubhāvas) consist of the widening of the eyes, gazing without blinking, and the rising of horripilation; 1509–1510.

The uttering of cries of "Excellent! and "Hail!", as well as tears from joy, faltering speech, perspiration, and trembling—all these are the transitory mental states (saṃcāribhāvas) belonging to the sphere of joy, characterized by the apprehension of touch. 1511.
Stiffness, perspiration, horripilation, fainting, faltering speech,
agitation, confusion, and numbness— where these occur along with wonder as the stable emotion (sthāyibhāva), the illustrious son of Soḍhala calls that the "Wonderful" (adbhuta) rasa. 1512–1513.
*Māyā* is the transformation of form and so forth manifested through falsehood (1514). The display of an impossible being by means of various medicines,
manual dexterity, or mantras is proclaimed as *indrajāla* (1515).

Shaking the limbs from joy is considered "rolling about" (*ulluṇṭhana*); the eyes slightly contracted, contact with the shoulders and cheeks, and the knitting of the eyebrows—these are the attendant emotions (*anubhāvas*) based on the perception of touch. 1516
The marvelous (*adbhuta*) rasa is declared to be of two kinds: that born of bliss (*ānanda-ja*) and the divine (*divya*).
The former arises from the fulfillment of a desire, while the latter originates from a divine object.
(1517) Thus ends the section on the marvelous.

Fear of saṃsāra, perceiving the defects in sense objects, association with yogis, and hearing the teachings of the sages; 1518 discourses on the subject of the inner self, ascetics, and the hermitages of ascetics.
The waters resound with the gurgling of many waterfalls; there are sacred fords and those who frequent them; rivers with holy waters and sandy banks marked by wild grain;
and the sacred sites of Śiva and Viṣṇu, as well as solitary forests.
There, the devotees—intoxicated by the essence of devotion to Śaṅkara and Hari—are esteemed as the *vibhāvas* (excitants) arising from the power of Viṣṇu-bhakti;
their external consciousness is characterized by slow movement, and their eyes are flooded with tears of bliss. 1521.
A physical form with horripilation as its bodice, contemplation on the meaning of the scriptures of liberation, instruction in the knowledge of Brahman, and dialogue concerning the ultimate reality;
the eyes fixed upon the tip of the nose and the display of the gesture of wisdom (jñānamudrā). 1522–1523.

These and others are the *anubhāvas* (consequent emotions), while these following are the *vyabhicāribhāvas* (transitory mental states): intoxication arising from drinking the essence of supreme bliss (*paramānanda-rasa*),
joy, fortitude, composure, awakening, memory, and discernment.

This *śānta* rasa is the permanent emotion (*sthāyin*) arising from the awakening to reality; it is devoid of the distinctions of love and the other [emotions], and is free from the disturbances of sense objects. It is called *śānta* because its manifestation consists solely of the singular essence of supreme bliss. (1525–1526)

Tranquility (*śama*) is the natural turning away from sense objects; it may serve as the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), or it may arise intermittently as a transitory emotion (*saṃcārībhāva*) during the course of a performance.
Regarding the natural modes of representation (*svabhāvābhinaya*), those which were previously described as *āṅgika* (pertaining to the body) [are now to be considered]. 1527.
Since their objects have become tranquil, they are peaceful; for the nature of the self is peace.
Since it remains in its own bliss after abandoning the orientation toward objects, that natural state of the self is therefore called "peaceful."
Thus, some consider the peaceful (śānta) rasa to consist of three: devotion (bhakti), affection (sneha), and longing (laulya);
they know that faith (śraddhā), moistening (ārdratā), and desire (abhilāṣa) are the permanent moods (sthāyibhāva) within them. 1530
Indeed, devotion (*bhakti*) and affection (*sneha*) directed toward human objects are inferior forms of love (*rati*);
because these two are transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*) in men and women, they are actually [instances of] the permanent emotions (*sthāyibhāva*).
Greed for improper objects is fickleness (*laulya*), which is a cause for laughter (*hāsya*).
Therefore, the Sage determined that there are exactly nine rasas.

The permanent emotions (sthāyibhāvas), such as love (rati) and the rest, arise predominantly from excitants (vibhāva); when these same emotions arise from only a few excitants, they become transitory emotions (vyabhicārin).
At that time, they also occur appropriately within other rasas:

for instance, laughter is seen in the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) rasa, and love in the *śānta* (quiescent); anger in the *vīra* (heroic), fear in the *karuṇa* (pathetic), and disgust in the *bhayānaka* (terrifying). 1533–1534.
"Excitement and wonder are transitory states (*vyabhicārin*) in all rasas;
tranquility (*śama*) exists in all rasas, yet it is not a transitory state when it constitutes steadiness. Thus ends the definition of the nine rasas.
Now, the definitions of the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas), beginning with despondency (nirveda), are as follows:
reproach, insult, disease, anger, beating, poverty, separation from the beloved, and the sight of another's prosperity. (1536)
In the case of inferior persons, these would be the determinants (*vibhāva*); however, in the case of superior persons, they consist of humiliation and the realization of the truth (*tattvabodha*).
As for the consequents (*anubhāva*), there is weeping, sighing, gasping, a dejected facial expression, and deep reflection. (1537)
"Such as these, that state of world-weariness (*nirveda*) is intended by the wise.
Thus ends the section on *nirveda*.
Sickness, vomiting, purging, fasting, religious observances, and austerity [are its causes].

Mental anguish, excessive drinking, over-exertion, sexual indulgence, deprivation of sleep, traveling on foot, hunger, thirst, and the like are the determinants (vibhāvas). Furthermore, the drooping of the lips, eyes, and cheeks are the ensuants (anubhāvas). 1539–1540.

Slowness in lifting and lowering the feet, emaciation of the limbs, discoloration and looseness of the body, trembling, lack of enthusiasm, and so forth— where such states and consequent expressions occur, that is designated as *glāni* (lassitude). 1541
Thus, despondency arises when people are apprehended for improper acts such as theft or offenses against the king; if other accomplices are present, it may also arise from oneself. (1542)
When one cannot see [the object] due to another [obstruction], there is frequent glancing toward the sides,
dryness of the throat, lips, and mouth, licking of the tongue, trembling, discoloration of the face, and heaviness and agitation of the tongue. (1543)
When the group of consequent emotions (anubhāva), such as looking up at the face and so forth,
occurs through gentle gestures toward lowly, superior, or middling men,
it produces fear even in noble women due to their timidity.
Fear arising from what is pleasant or unpleasant is said by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow (Viṣṇu) to belong to the erotic sentiment;
however, that which originates from theft, royal offense, and the like belongs to the terrible sentiment.
Fear is described as being twofold: residing in another or arising within oneself.

Among men who are timid by nature, that suspicion of guilt in others arising from such things as tremulous glances is "situated in another. This [suspicion] is "self-originated," thinking: "Others will perceive my offense. (1547–1548)
The suspicion regarding another's knowledge that arises from one's own suspicion is seen as coexisting with the suspicion regarding the poison in the food;
thus is suspicion [defined]. 1549.

Offenses against the king, the proclamation of false faults, and deceitful concealment are its determinants (*vibhāvas*); furthermore, imprisonment, execution, beating, and threats are its consequents (*anubhāvas*). That which consists of these is "cruelty," characterized by mercilessness. (15.50)
Thus,
from the excitants (vibhāva) of harshness, anxiety, mental distress, and misfortune, and from the ensuants (anubhāva) of turning away the head and heaviness of the limbs; 1551.
One should cultivate the state of wretchedness by renouncing one's body and possessions;
thus ends the section on wretchedness.
Enmity consists of various offenses against the sovereign power and prosperity of another.
The observation of good fortune, intelligence, learning, and so forth, is the excitant (vibhāvaka).
The ensuants (anubhāvas), however, are the expression of faults such as indignation, the concealment of virtues,
the representation of virtues as faults, and looking downward with averted eyes.
Where contemptuous frowns and the like are known as this *asūyā* (envy);
thus is envy [defined].
Now, where the drinking of intoxicants is the *vibhāva* and there are five *anubhāvas*:

Sleeping, laughing, singing, weeping, and harsh speech—these occur in a superior man; sleeping, laughing, and singing occur in a middling man; while weeping and harsh speech occur in an inferior man. (1555–1556)
That intoxication is threefold: mild, moderate, and low.
Here, the mild is slight; however, the low becomes intensified through association with the low.
The mild is said to belong to all, while the moderate belongs to both the middling and the base.
Among men, those of inferior character possess the lowest form of intoxication (mada).
One should represent this youthful intoxication through indistinct and disjointed speech, the bristling of the body's hair, and a delicate, faltering gait. (1558–1559)
In the middle stage of intoxication (madhyama-mada), the arms droop, become agitated, and are cast about; the eyes stumble and roll; the gait is crooked;
and the physical manifestations include a faltering step, loss of memory, hiccuping, vomiting, and the secretion of phlegm. (1560)
A heavy tongue and spitting are the symptoms of the lowest degree of intoxication (1561).
Having consumed the drink on the stage, one should perform gestures that increase the state of intoxication;
however, having drunk it upon entering the stage, a wise man should act for the sake of displaying his sobriety.
One should simultaneously display many means of joy, sorrow, and fear.
(1562) Thus ends the description of *mada* (intoxication/arrogance).
Through determinants such as travel, physical exertion, and service, and through consequents... (1563)
Fatigue is that which arises from massaging the limbs, contracting the mouth, twisting the body,
sighing, yawning, and the slow movement of the feet. (1564) Thus ends the section on fatigue.
In this [state], the manifestations (vibhāvas) are poverty, loss of sovereignty, the deprivation of desired objects, and moreover, downward-turned inhalation and exhalation;
as well as anguish, remembrance, meditation, emaciation, and the lack of bodily adornment. (1565)
Lack of fortitude (*adhṛti*) shall be its *anubhāvas*; that is proclaimed as *cintā* (reflection).
A *vitarka* (deliberation) arises either in its initial moment or in its subsequent moment. Thus ends *cintā*.
Discrimination, mastery of the scriptures, devotion to the guru, and asceticism—these exist as both objects and instruments;
for the attainment of desired goals superior to what is sought occurs through their status as objects. (1567–1568)

In this [rasa], the excitants (vibhāvas) are considered to function as instruments of play for one who has attained the enjoyment of fortune, yet for whom there is neither the enjoyment of what is unattained nor the memory of what is past; furthermore, even when [objects] are worn out or lost, there is no despondency, but rather an absence of lamentation. (1569)
"Where there are two effects, the wise call that *dhṛti* (fortitude).
Thus, *dhṛti* [is characterized by] composure during the final watch of the night, as well as the cessation of sleep.
Meditation and repeated practice similar to what was heard and seen—
where these are the determinants (vibhāvas), the consequents (anubhāvas) are trembling, the raising of the head, and an unusual look. 1571–1572.
Memory (*smṛti*) is that which bestows pleasure and pain;
it is called memory when there is the recollection of things long forgotten.
(Verse 1573) Thus ends [the section on] memory. Transgression against the guru is contempt; it is remorse felt after having committed an act of abandonment.
The fulfillment of the promised purpose arises through these internal states (vibhāvas):
bowing the face, speaking cryptically, deep reflection, touching the ring-finger of her garment, and repeatedly clipping one's nails. (1574–1575)
"Writing on the ground," and so forth, manifest the state of shame;
it is observed through shame, remorse, and grief when a deed has been committed. (1576) Thus ends the section on Shame (*vrīḍā*).
Due to divine afflictions, there is bodily suffering, separation from loved ones, and so forth;
even a blow to a vital spot in an improper place, as well as fear arising from terrible thieves and the like.
For one who lacks the means to counteract these, there is the constant recollection of past enmities and similar anxieties. (1577)
When there are such *vibhāvas* as falling down and the reeling of the body,
the instability of the heart, and the lack of movement in the sense organs—
wise men call these and others like them *anubhāvas* of delusion (*moha*). 1578–1579.

When one perceives a cause of fear but does not perceive its remedy, the mental state that is indecisive regarding what ought to be done is called delusion (*moha*). Thus ends the section on delusion.
Excessive satiation, innate nature, the pains of pregnancy, fatigue, and so forth are its *vibhāvas*.
Its *anubhāvas*, however, are sleep, lassitude, and a distaste for all activities except for eating; that state is called *ālasya* (laziness). 1581.
Thus, where the determinants (*vibhāvas*) are indolence, impatience, hostility, envy, passion, hatred, and avarice, the consequents (*anubhāvas*) are threats and the like. (1582)
Harshness of speech, striking, beating, killing, and binding—
this is considered *cāpala* (restlessness), which is the performance of improper acts without reflection.
Thus ends the section on *cāpala*.
The grace of gods, lords, teachers, or masters; union with loved ones; the fulfillment of desires; the acquisition of wealth for unattainable wishes;
and the birth of sons and other such things—wherever these causes arise, that is the *vibhāva*. (1584–1585)
The clarity of the eyes and face, affectionate speech, the arising of horripilation, tears, perspiration, and so forth are the *anubhāvas*; one should designate that as *harṣa* (joy).
Thus ends *harṣa*.

When men who are superior in learning, wealth, strength, and sovereignty are insulted in the midst of an assembly, indignation arises, characterized by a desire for retaliation; this occurs only among those men who are enterprising, and it is the motivating force behind their action. (1587)
Perspiration, downward gaze, trembling of the head, a mind devoid of focus, seeking a remedy, and mental agitation are its manifestations. (1588) Thus ends indignation (*amarṣa*).
The failure to achieve one's objective despite the presence of a means is caused by adverse fate (durdaiva).
The king’s hostility and being apprehended for theft and other crimes are its manifesting causes.
Despondency regarding the search for allies and the contemplation of means [are also included]. 1589–1590.

In the superior and middling [types of fear], the manifestations (anubhāvas) are based on energy; in the inferior type, they are running, brooding, parched mouth, looking about, sleep, sighing, and licking the corners of the mouth. 1591. These are the manifestations.
"That state in which there is despondency is considered by those who know the nature of states to be *viṣāda* (despair).
Thus ends *viṣāda*.
[It is experienced] by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, piśācas, and brahmarākṣasas.
Possession by fierce spirits such as Bhūtas and others, as well as the recollection of that [possession], the long-term retention of impurity, frequenting empty houses,
the imbalance of the bodily constituents (dhātus), and so forth— by means of such indicative (vibhāva) and consequential (anubhāvaka) factors. (1593–1594)

One should recognize epilepsy (apasmāra) by such symptoms as throbbing, trembling, labored breathing, running, falling to the ground, licking with the tongue, perspiration, stiffness, frothy at the mouth, and loss of consciousness. 1595–1596.

Thus, epilepsy consists of a lack of discrimination regarding what is to be done, and dullness; its determinants (vibhāvas) are the sight or hearing of the beloved or the unpleasant, as well as pain. 1597.
Furthermore, the indicators of this [delusion] during the non-articulation of a counter-argument are the failure to discern what is desired or undesired, unblinking eyes, and so forth;
it is the opinion of the learned that such [a person] may have been previously or subsequently deluded. (1598)
Thus, where there is dullness,
there may be contradiction, doubt, or deliberation, once both sides have stated their proofs and refutations. (1599)

These are the determinants (vibhāvas) and the consequents (anubhāvas): shaking the head, knitting the brows, and clever hand gestures; these they call vitarka (deliberation). That stable emotion (sthāyibhāva) accompanied by vitarka is joined with avahittha (concealment). 1600–1601.
Thus, *vitarka* (reflection) is considered to be *supta* (sleep), which arises from the *vibhāva* (determinant cause) of sleep and consists of the state of sleep;
its *anubhāvas* (consequent effects) are the stillness of the limbs and the closing of the eyes.

Dreaming, prattling, inhalation and exhalation, and withdrawal from the external senses—thus sleep has arisen; it is inflamed by the separation from the beloved due to the recollection of that dear one. 1602–1603.
"Restlessness is characterized by sleep, lassitude, heaviness of the limbs, and anxiety; thus it has been described by those skilled in the nature of emotions.
(1604) This concludes the section on restlessness (*autsukya*).
The mental state (bhāva) called *avahittha* is said to have the purpose of concealing one's internal experience.
It is to be manifested through fear, shame, impudence, crookedness, and gravity; furthermore, these—along with disregard arising from pride—are its indicative manifestations (*anubhāvas*). 1605–1606.
The interruption of conversation concerning beloved ones and the like, feigned composure,
speaking otherwise than one truly feels, and likewise looking away or acting differently—
this is *avahittha* (concealment). 1607.

There may be a prior flash of intuition (*pratibhāna*); one should cultivate that mind through cognitions arising from positive and negative concomitance, through reflections on the scriptures, and through various forms of reasoning and refutation (*ūhāpoha*). (1608) Then, one should experience it.
With hands such as the *saṃdaṃśa* (tongs) and others, and by lifting his eyebrows, he instructed his disciples on the subjects of various scriptures;
thus, the two means of valid cognition known as *tarka* consist of *ūha* (inclusion) and *apoha* (exclusion) regarding injunctions and prohibitions. (1609–1610)
Thus, consciousness arises through the termination of sleep at the end of a dream, through the digestion of food,
through sounds, touches, and so forth, or through dreams, or through those things remembered while awake. (1611)
Then, awakening is manifested through yawning, rubbing the eyes, rising from bed, cracking the fingers, and twisting the limbs;
it is experienced through the tossing of the arms and labored breaths. (1612)
"Or rather, it is right knowledge derived from the world, or the cognition of their respective manifestations and influences.
Thus, there is cognition arising from the provocation of each one individually, of two together, or of all three.

The state of wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha) is designated as "disease. Furthermore, fever (jvara) is to be represented through [gestures such as] stiffness, drooping of the limbs, tossing of the body, contraction of the face, crying out, trembling, and groaning. 1615.
That [suffering] born of desire also exists; it is twofold because it proceeds from cold and heat (1616).
It is manifested by the movement of the jaw, trembling of all the limbs, and dryness of the mouth, as well as by lamentation, horripilation, the contraction of the face, and so forth (1617).
Then, the cold fever is to be represented by [gestures of] thirst for water and burning heat,
by the tossing of hands, limbs, and body, by the longing for a bed upon the ground,
by the desire for cooling ointments, and by piteous lamentations. 1618

Thus, for the noble, illness arises from separation from a beloved during a period of estrangement; for the base, it arises from the loss of wealth; and for all, it arises from a derangement of the humors (saṃnipāta). 1619
Likewise, insanity arises from physical injury; one should recognize it by these symptoms:
laughter, weeping, and reciting [texts] without cause, as well as dancing, singing, lying down, sitting, rising, and running about. (1620)
Incoherent prattle, the throwing up of dust and ashes,
and the adorning oneself with skulls, rags, and discarded flower-garlands—
this is called insanity (*unmāda*), which, although included among the [other] diseases, is mentioned separately. (1621–1622)
For this [unmada] produces the greatest variety in cases such as deception;
apasmāra (epilepsy) is likewise [varied] in the loathsome and the terrible.
Thus ends unmāda.
Arrogance arises repeatedly and predominantly among the base on account of lineage, beauty, strength, sovereignty, learning, wealth, and youth; however,
among the excellent, it is like a flash of lightning, and among women, it is most prevalent.

By looking with the neck upturned, by contempt, by envy, by failing to give an answer, by not speaking, by indignation, by harshness, by distraction, by the movement of the eyes of a woman, and by insulting or transgressing against the guru; 1626.
The foremost of experts on dramatic techniques states that its representation should be performed as follows:

"The displacement of vocal, physical, internal (sāttvika), and external (āhārya) actions, arising from joy, passion, intoxication, and pride, constitutes the *vibhrama* (bewilderment) of women. (1627–1628)
Thus, pride arises immediately after grief for those who are undisciplined; however, this powerful agitation is restrained by the steadfast through their fortitude. (1629)

And since this [rasa] possesses various distinct and manifold consequents (anubhāvas) corresponding to each determinants (vibhāva), it is eightfold according to the distinction of its causes, which are the forms of the determinants:
portents, wind, rain, fire, and the uprooting of elephants. (1630)
