Hearing what is pleasant or unpleasant, and enmity or calamity—these are the causes [of agitation].
(1631) Agitation arises from lightning and the falling of meteors, from thunderclaps and earthquakes, from eclipses of the sun and moon, and from the sighting of comets. (1632)
The resulting *anubhāvas* (consequent expressions) of this [fainting] are said here to be pallor, drooping of the limbs, and states of despondency and astonishment born of portents.
In the case of fainting caused by wind (*vātaja*), however, there is covering with a cloth and rubbing of the eyes.
Furthermore, the symptoms arising from rain are a hurried arrival,
a sensation of pressure throughout all the limbs, seeking shelter in houses and the like, and running quickly.
In the case of fire, there is a burning sensation in the limbs and the eyes being clouded by smoke.
The gait may be characterized by excessive striding or by retreating;
when elephants wander without limit, there occurs a running away from the path, and therein, due to haste, there is trembling from fear. (1636–1637)
Upon seeing [the beloved], there is astonishment; thereafter, upon hearing pleasant news, there is the giving of garments and ornaments, rising from one's seat, and embracing.
Furthermore, upon hearing unpleasant news during conversation, there are tears and horripilation. These are the signs. 1638.
Lamentation, falling to the ground, moving about, rolling over,
brooding, and so forth— these occur when one suffers from the calamity of an enemy.
Sudden flight, and the taking up of weapons, shields, armor, and the like [are the responses to such danger].
Mounting elephants and horses, and their separate management— these are the external manifestations (*anubhāvas*) when agitation (*āvega*) consists of confusion.
(1641) Thus ends agitation.
Death is said to be of two kinds: that born of disease and that born of injury.
That which arises from disorders of the humors, such as eruptive boils (gaṇḍa), fever, and the like, is "born of disease.
Here, wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha) are recognized as the humors when they are vitiated.
That which arises from weapons, poisons, water, wild beasts, horses, elephants, fire, falling from heights, and so forth, is known as *abhighātajam* (trauma-induced).
It is characterized by limbs that are motionless and extended, and by the closing of the eyes. (1643–1644)
The manifestation of disease born from [internal] causes is characterized by hiccups, upward breath, vomiting, being surrounded by people, indistinct speech, and so forth;
whereas that born from weapons consists of falling suddenly to the ground and trembling. (1645)
In the case of poison arising from the drinking of snake venom, the [physical] manifestations such as throbbing and so forth should be employed;
furthermore, these eight symptoms of the stages of poisoning occur in succession:
blackness, trembling, burning sensations, hiccups, and phlegm as the fifth. 1646–1647.
The dissolution of the aggregates, insentience, and death are recognized as the manifestations arising from a subsequent blow,
like those produced by a weapon;
this is because diseases and the like are irreversible once death has been determined.
In this context, mental activity prior to the final breath is considered death (1649);
thus, death is [described],
while trembling of the limbs is called *camatkāra* (astonishment) and sudden [trembling] is called *trāsa* (terror).
From his appearance—marked by a terrible roar and a fearsome sight—the [resulting] emotional states (*anubhāvas*) are:
contraction and trembling of the limbs, paralysis, a faltering voice, horripilation, and drooping of the body. (1650–1651)

The closing of the eyes and what is called "dissolution" (pralaya) arise from the deliberation on past and future events; fear resulting from such deliberation is distinct from terror (trāsa). Thus ends the section on terror.
The first cessation of the sense organs from their respective objects, overeating, one's own nature, anxiety, laziness, intoxication, fatigue,
and the distinctiveness resulting from the exertion of explaining [the scriptures] and so forth are the causes [of sleep]. (1653)
The manifestations of sleep are yawning, heaviness of the face,
shaking of the body, rolling of the eyes, stretching of the limbs,
sighing and gasping, drooping of the limbs, and closing of the eyes. (1654–1655)
Thus, sleep has been described by me as producing the stable aesthetic flavor (sthāyī rasa) because it brings about thirty-three varieties; however, there are thousands of others.

In some cases, there is an inclusion of longing within sexual passion (rati); in feigned indifference (avahittha), there is that of hypocrisy (dambha); and in languor (glāni), there is that of hunger and thirst.
In despondency (udvega), there is that of world-weariness (nirveda); in other cases as well, it should be inferred in this manner.
Thus end the thirty-three transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*).
Now, the definition of the involuntary states (*sāttvikabhāva*):
when consciousness is transformed by the aforementioned emotions such as love (*rati*) and so forth, [the involuntary states arise].
She superimposes herself upon the vital breath (prāṇa), and that vital breath expands the body;
then these transformations, such as stiffness and the like, arise within the body.
This being so, through their own excitants (vibhāvaka) such as the relished erotic sentiment (rati) and others, [the aesthetic experience unfolds].
Manifested by those residing within the body and accompanied by physical symptoms such as paralysis,
these internal states shine forth within the vital breath (*prāṇa*) when consciousness is superimposed upon it;
these are the *sāttvika* emotions, so called because they are manifested through the *sattva* aspect of the vital breath.

Either the *sattva* mentioned by the Sāṃkhyas is called "goodness" (*sādhutva*), or "goodness" here is understood as the state of having a pure vital breath and body; the states that arise from that *sattva* are considered by the wise to be "sāttvika. (1662)
Sometimes this vital breath (prāṇa) moves independently; at other times, when it relies primarily upon the four elements beginning with earth, it moves within doubt.
When it presides over the earth, it then contemplates the state of a pillar.
From the breath situated in water, tears arise; from that situated in fire, discoloration;
from that abiding in space, perspiration; and from that, dissolution (pralaya) is born.
This [breath] is independent and, in due order, possesses the distinctions of being mild, moderate, or intense.
One should cultivate horripilation, trembling, and a change in the voice (1666).
These external signs, such as paralysis and the rest, are easily attained by men who identify with the body, but they are difficult for the virtuous who are free from such identification (1667).

Stupefaction (stambha) may arise from joy, passion, fear, suffering, despondency, wonder, anger, or distraction; its attendant manifestations (anubhāvas) are numbness and emptiness, characterized by a lack of consciousness, rigidity of the limbs, motionlessness, and the absence of trembling. (1668)
Thus, paralysis,
mental anguish, disease, joy, shame, anger, fear, fatigue,
pain, physical injury, heat, delusion, and exertion are the excitants (vibhāvaka). 1669.
The wise have declared that *sveda* (perspiration) is that [dramatic representation] wherein there is the taking up of a fan, sweating, and wiping the forehead with the back of the hand;
thus ends the section on perspiration.
Through embracing, stroking, cold, joy, fear, and anger,
these manifest gestures express horripilation; likewise,
during the touching and scratching of the limbs, the body repeatedly becomes bristling with thrill.
Thus [is] horripilation; the determinants (vibhāvas) are fierceness, disease, old age, anger, fear, joy, intoxication, and so forth;
and the vocal qualities (anubhāvas) are a broken voice and a faltering sound. 1673
At that time, the emotional state (bhāva) is said to be a change in the voice;
a deviation from the proper pitch is called *visvara*, while a broken or interrupted flow is termed *bhinna*.
Furthermore, instability and the fluctuation between high and low tones constitute *gadgada* (stammering). 1674
Thus is the variation of voice (*svarabheda*).

In the *āliṅgana-ucchuritaka* [gesture], joy, anger, fear, old age, cold, and disease are the determinants (*vibhāva*), while these [aforementioned vocal qualities] are the consequents (*anubhāvaka*) therein. 1675.
"Trembling, throbbing, shaking, and shivering—they describe that as *vepathu*.
Trembling and the others are varieties of shaking; each subsequent one is more intense than the preceding.
Thus ends the section on *vepathu*.
Pallor may arise from disease, delusion, fear, anger, cold, heat, or fatigue (1677).
Its representation is achieved through the application of pressure on the pulse,
or by the application of vermilion and other substances to bring about a change of color on the face (1678).
Thus, from discoloration, from the application of collyrium due to joy or impatience, from smoke, from fear, from grief, from yawning,
from unblinking gazing, from cold, and from disease, the state of tears arises.
And one should experience that [pleasure] through the flowing of tears and the wiping of the eyes.
(1679) Thus, [it arises] from tears, intoxication, fainting, and injury, as well as from sleep, delusion, fatigue, and so forth.
That [state] becomes *pralaya* (fainting) by means of acting out the collapse of the body;
thus, the three types of mental states— *sthāyins* (permanent) and *vyabhicārins* (transitory)— have been described.
All *sāttvika* [emotions] may occur within all *rasas*, and all *rasas* may possess *sāttvika* qualities. (1681) In a drama, there should always be one *sthāyibhāva* as the primary *rasa*;
other *rasas* follow it and are therefore classified as *vyabhicāribhāvas*. (1682)
Those conflicting sentiments should be arranged within them with distinct bases;

in drama, the composition of the sentiments should be variegated like a garland of flowers, while the permanent sentiment (sthāyī rasa), according to the connoisseurs of rasa, is considered to be like the thread [that holds it all together]. 1683
This entire essence has been extracted from the ocean of the Nāṭyaveda by the illustrious scholar Śāraṅgadeva; let it be enjoyed by the wise until they are satisfied.
If there is any merit whatsoever in this work of mine, let it be accepted for its own sake.
O wise ones, I do not request even the slightest merit from others, for in you it is as vast as a mountain.
Whether this work composed by me be flawed or flawless, what does that matter?
My mind is intent upon pleasing you; for whom indeed do the virtuous not surpass [all else] with their excellence?
What object in the three worlds is capable of withstanding your scrutiny?
Nevertheless, O virtuous ones, out of affection for me, please hold my work in high esteem;
or rather, I have merely followed the ancient path of the sages.
The virtuous naturally feel affection for one who treads the path of the righteous.
What need have I for the power of my own wisdom in seeking to please the holy?
Even the monkeys, those lords of beasts, brought joy to Rāma.

"My engagement with this treatise is not out of pride in my learning; rather, O learned one, it is intended as provisions for my journey to dwell within the minds of the wise. Thus ends the seventh chapter, on Dancing, in the *Saṃgītaratnākara* composed by Śrī Śārṅgadeva—known as Niḥśaṅka, the son of Śrī Soḍhaladeva, the lord of the royal treasury and the delight of faultless knowledge. 7.1690.
This *Saṅgītaratnākara*, together with the *Kalānidhi*, has reached its conclusion. Appendix 1:
The [melodic types] arising from the Ṣaḍja-grāma, namely Ṣaḍjakaiśika and Madhyamā.
The *ṣaḍjagrāma* consists of the pure (*śuddha*) and the supported (*sādhārita*) [notes]; in the *madhyamagrāma*, however, there are the *pañcama*, the *madhyama-ṣāḍava*, and the *śuddhakaiśika*.
Thus, including the seven pure notes, there are five distinct [varieties], along with the *kaiśikamadhyama*.
Bhinna-ṣaḍja in the [raga] named Ṣaḍja, Tāna and Kaiśika in Madhyama,
and Bhinna-pañcama— these constitute Gauḍakaiśikamadhyama (10).
Gauḍapañcamaka is in Ṣaḍja, and Gauḍakaiśika is in Madhyama.
Thus, there are three Gauḍas in Ṣaḍja; Ṭakka, Veśara, and Ṣāḍava [are also there].
In Madhyama, however, there are Sauvīrī, Boṭṭa, and Mālavakaiśika;
then there is Mālava ending in Pañcama, and the two-fold Grāmarāga Ṭakkakaiśika.
There are eight Hindola-jātis; among them, seven are common (*sādhāraṇa*).
Of these, Rūpasādhāra, Śaka, and Bhammāṇapañcama belong to the scale of Ṣaḍja.
Narta, Gāndhārapañcama, and Ṣāḍjakaiśika belong to the scale of Madhyama. 13.
The *kakubha* has two villages; these are considered to be the thirty village-rāgas (*grāmarāga*s):
the eight *uparāga*s, *tilaka*, *śaka*, *iṣṭakka*, *saindhava*, *kokilā*, *pañcama*, *revagupta*, and *pañcamaṣāḍava*.
Bhāvanāpañcama, Nāgagāndhāra, and Nāgapañcama;
Śrīrāga, Naṭṭau, Baṅgāla, Bhāsa, Madhyamaṣāḍava, Raktahaṃsa, Kohlahāsa, Prasava, and Bhairavadhvani. 15–16.
Megharāga, Somarāga, Kāmoda, Abhrapañcama, those known as Kandarpa and Deśākhyau, Kakubhānta, Kaiśika, Naṭṭa, and Nārāyaṇa— these twenty rāgas have been proclaimed. 17.
Sauvīra, Kakubha, Aṣṭaka, Pañcama, and Bhinnapañcama (18); Ṭakkakaiśika, Hindola, Boṭṭa, Bhālavakaiśika,
Gāndhārapañcama, Bhinnaṣaḍja, Vesara, and Ṣāḍava (19).
Mālava with Pañcama as its final note, and the *tāna* Pañcama-ṣāḍava—these fifteen, proclaimed by Yāṣṭika, are the progenitors of the *bhāṣās*.
There are four *bhāṣās* in Sauvīra: Sauvīrī, Vegavatī, and Madhyamā.
Sādhāritā and Gāndhārī belong to the Kakubha [Jāti]; Bhinnapañcamī, Kāmbojī, Madhyamagrāmā, Ragantī, Madhurī, and Śakamiśrā—these six are the Vibhāṣās of the Bhogavardhanī [Jāti]. 21–22.
Ābhīrikā, Madhukarī, likewise Ekāntarabhāṣikā, Śālavāhanikā, Ṭakke, Travaṇā, Travaṇodbhavā (23),
Vairañjī, Madhyamagrāmadehā, and Mālavavesarī.
Chevātī, Saindhavī, Kolāhalā, marked by Pañcama;
Saurāṣṭrī, Pañcamī, Vegarañjī, Gāndhārapañcamī; Mālavī, Tānavalitā, Lalitā, and Ravicandrikā. 24–25.
Tānā, vāherikā, dohyā, and vesarī—these are the twenty-one bhāṣās. Then, in the fifth [chapter], there are four vibhāṣās: devāravardhanī, āndhrī, gurjarī, and bhāvanī. (26)
Kaiśikī, Travaṇī, Tānodbhavā, Ābhīrī, Gurjarī (27), Saindhavī, Dākṣiṇātyā, Āndhrī, Māṅgalī, and Bhāvanī— these are the ten;
then there are the two dialects (vibhāṣe), namely Bhaṃmāṇī and Andhālikā (28).
When the fifth [note] is split, there are four languages (bhāṣās) adorned with dhaivata:
Śuddhā, Bhinnā, Vārāṭī, and Viśālā; then there are Kauśalī, Vibhāṣā, Mālavā, Abhinavā, Lelitā, Ṭakka, and Kaiśikī. 29.
There are two types of Drāviḍī; one is the Vibhāṣā, and there are nine in the Preṅkhaka.
The languages (bhāṣās) would be Vesarī, Cūtamañjarī, Ṣaḍjamadhyamā, Madhurī, Bhinnapaurālī, Gauḍī, and Mālavavesarī.
Chevāṭī and Piñjarī are one; Boṭṭe and Bhāṣā are Māṅgalī (31).
Vāṅgālī, Māṅgalī, Harṣapurī, Mālavavesarī (32), Khañjinī, Gurjarī, Gauḍī, Paurālī, and Ardhaveśarī.
Śuddhā, Mālavārūpā, Saindhavī, and Ābhīrikā—
these thirteen dialects (bhāṣās) are to be known by the learned in the Mālavakaiśika; furthermore,
there are two regional dialects (vibhāṣe), namely Kāmbojī and likewise Devāravardhanī.
In the Gāndhāra-pañcama [jāti], there are the Bhāṣās: Gāndhārī, Bhinna-ṣaḍjakā, Gāndhāravallī, Kacchellī, Svaravallī, Niṣādinī, Travaṇā, Madhyamā, Śuddhā, Dākṣiṇātyā, and Pulindikā. (35)

Tumburā, Ṣaḍjabhāṣā, Kālindī, Lalitā, Śrīkaṇṭhikā, Bāṅgālī, Gāndhārī, and Saindhavī— these seventeen are to be known as the primary dialects (bhāṣās), while four others are the sub-dialects (vibhāṣikās). 36.
Paurālī, Mālavā, Kālindī, and Devāravardhanī (37); in the Vesara and Ṣāḍava [tunes], there are two Bhāṣās: Bāhyā and Bāhyaṣāḍavā (38); in the Vibhāṣā, Pārvatī; and in the Śrīkaṭha, Mālavapañcama.
There are three *bhāṣās*: Vedavatī, Bhāvinī, and Vibhāvinī (39).
These various *bhāṣās* arise from those [melodic structures]; some learned ones know the *bhāṣā* called Śakā in the Pañcama-Ṣāḍava and in the Revagupta (40).
The *Vibhāṣāpallavī*, the *Bhāsavalitā*, and the *Kiraṇāvalī*— which is also called the *Śaṅkādyāvalitā*— these three are the intermediate dialects (antarabhāṣikā).
These four are known as the *Bṛhadveśyā* dialects, which have no [specific] progenitor mentioned.
Thus, ninety-six languages (bhāṣās) and twenty dialects (vibhāṣās) are recorded;
there are also four intermediate languages (antarabhāṣās), according to the opinion of Śārṅgadeva. (42) The primary language is called Svara, while the others are known as Deśī and Uparāgaja. (43)
Matanga has declared four types [of musical scales]: the primary (mukhyā), which does not depend on others;
that known by the names *svara* and *deśa*; the one called *svaraja*; and the *deśaja*, in that order.
Furthermore, those arising from the influence of others (*anyoparāgajā*) have been described by Yāṣṭika as distinct from these.

The Mālava-veśarī is of three kinds: the *saṃkīrṇadeśajā-mūlā* (root-born of mixed regions), the *chāyāmātrā*, and the *itināmā*. The pure [Mālava-veśarī] and the *ābhīrī* are also included, making six principal types; the remaining varieties are well-known and have clearly defined characteristics.
However, there is a similarity of name among some [works], even though they differ in their characteristics (lakṣma).
Now, the son of Ṣoḍhaḷa undertakes the determination of the *rāga-aṅgas*, *bhāṣā-aṅgas*, *kriyā-aṅgas*, and *upāṅgas*, relying upon the opinion of certain authorities. 46–47.
Because they produce delight (*rañjanāt*), even *bhāṣārāga*, *rāgāṅga*, and so forth are accepted as *rāgas*;
thus the fourfold group beginning with *rāgāṅga* is declared to be *deśī*.
While those well-known as *grāmarāga* and so on are some that are also called *deśī*. (48)
Now, a brief enumeration is made of those [styles] previously established:
Śaṅkarābharaṇa, Ghaṇṭārava, Āhaṃsa, Dīpaka, Rīti, Pūrṇāṭikā, Lāṭī, and Pallavī—thus they have been declared. (49–50)

The eight limbs of passion (*rāgāṅga*) are Gāmbhīrī, Vauhāṭī, Khaśikotpalī, Gollī, Nādāntarī, Nīlotpalī, Chāyā, and Taraṅgiṇī; together with Gāndhāragatikā and Arañjā, these are considered to be eleven. 51.
Then there are Bhāṣāṅga, Bhāvakrī, Svabhāvakrī, Śivakriya, Marukakrī, Trinetrakrī, Kumudakrī,
Danukriya, Ojakrī, Indrakriya, Nāgakṛti, and Dhanyakṛti. (52–53)
The wise have declared that there are twelve *vipāyakrī* musical compositions (*kriyāṅga*), and three *upāṅgas*: the *pūrṇāṭa*, the *devāla*, and the *gurujikā*.
These thirty-four *rāgas* are proclaimed as those established in antiquity.
Now, the enumeration of the well-known [rāgas] is set forth:
Madhyamādi, Mālavaśrī, Troṭī, Vaṅgāla, Bhairava, Varāṭī, Gurjarī, Gauḍa, Kolāhala, and Vasantaka. (55)

The thirteen components of *rāga* are known by the names of various regions: Dhānyāsī, Deśī, Deśākhyā, Ḍombavanyāsāvarī, Velāvalī, Prathamamañjarī, Āḍikā, Modikā, Nāgadhvani, and Śuddhavarāṭikā. (56–57)
The lost Karṇāṭa and Vaṅgāla have declared nine subsidiary languages (bhāṣāṅga).
Then, the three subsidiary modes of action (kriyāṅga) are: the Rāyakṛti, the Gauḍakṛti, and the Devakrī; thus, twenty-seven subsidiary elements (upāṅga) are enumerated.
Kauntalī, Drāviḍī, Saindhavī, Sthānavarāṭikā,
Hatasvaravarāṭī, and Pratāpavarāṭikā— these are the six *varāṭīs*. Their *chāyā* (shadow-variation) occurs in *toḍikas* such as the *Turuṣka* and others.
Mahārāṣṭrī, Saurāṣṭrī, Dakṣiṇā, and Drāviḍī—these four have been mentioned. Then there are the Gurjarīs: Bhuñchikā, Stambhatīrthikā, Chāyāpratāpa, Upapada, Belā, Balī, and Bhairavī.
